· The Doctrine of Essence › Concrete existence
Hegel citations:
The truth of being is to be, not an immediate something, but essence that has come forth into immediacy.
— The Science of Logic, Concrete existence (tr. di Giovanni)
For concrete existence is the immediacy that has come forth from the sublating of the mediation that results from the connection of ground and condition, and which, in coming forth, sublates this very coming forth.
— The Science of Logic, Concrete existence (tr. di Giovanni)

Head: The Thing and Its Properties
Path: 一. Logic › 2. Doctrine of Essence › ii. Appearance › α. Existence › a. The Thing and Its Properties
Gloss: The existing thing considered as a unit with many properties.
Hegelian gloss: The existent as a thing with many properties, the unity of reflection-into-self and reflection-into-other.
Nouns: the thing and its properties; thing, object, article, item, body, entity, substance, bearer, owner, possessor of properties, substrate, subject of predication; bundle, bundle of qualities, cluster, set of properties; also. substantiality, hypostasis, person, being, a being, an existence, creature, flesh and blood, matter &c H0239, corporeity†, essential nature, groundwork, materiality, substantialness, vital part. matter, brute matter, stuff, element, principle, parenchyma [Biol.], substratum, hyle†, corpus, pabulum, frame. something, materials &c H0760. the propertied thing, the bearer of properties, the one and its many properties.
Verbs: have, possess, bear, carry, exhibit, display, show.
Adjective: thingly, thinglike, objectual, concrete, bodily, material, propertied. substantive, substantial, hypostatic, personal, tangible &c H0239. corporeal, corporal, physical, somatic, somatoscopic†, sensible, tangible, ponderable, palpable.
Adverbs: as a thing, in itself, as such. substantially, essentially.
Foreign: German: Ding, Auch [the "also" of properties], Vorhandenheit [presence-at-hand] [Heidegger], Sache, etwas; Latin: res; Greek: pragma, chrēma, ti, ousia, on, onta; Sanskrit: dravya [substance] and guṇa [quality]; Arabic: shayʾ, maʿnā; French: chose, quelque chose, subsistant, disponible, présence-subsistance, disponibilité, sous la main, à portée de la main; Italian: cosa, qualcosa; Spanish: algo, estar-ahí-delante, estar a la mano.
Phrases: nothing but a collection of simple ideas, that are united by the imagination, and have a particular name assigned them [Hume, Treatise 1.1.6]; a thing among things; the thing itself.
Hegel definition: The thing is the concretely existing something, an immediacy that has arisen through the reflection of mediation into itself. It is distinct from its concrete existence as something is from its being, yet immediately one with it. This distinction is that of the thing in itself and external existence. The thing's relation to others lies in its properties; these become self-subsisting matters, of which the thing is composed, and as a mere collection of them it dissolves.
Hegel texts:
The Science of Logic
· The Doctrine of Essence › Concrete existence › The thing and its properties
Hegel citations:
[T]he concretely existent something is different from the something that exists immediately. The former is essentially an immediacy that has arisen through the reflection of mediation into itself. The concretely existent something is thus a thing.
— The Science of Logic, Concrete existence › The thing and its properties (tr. di Giovanni)
Concrete existence as such contains this very distinction in the moment of its mediation: the distinction of thing-in-itself and external concrete existence.
— The Science of Logic, Concrete existence › The thing and its properties (tr. di Giovanni)

Head: Thing-in-Itself and Existence
Path: 一. Logic › 2. Doctrine of Essence › ii. Appearance › α. Existence › a. The Thing and Its Properties › i. Thing-in-Itself and Existence
Gloss: The thing as it is in itself, apart from its relations, and the thing as it exists among other things.
Hegelian gloss: The thing-in-itself as the empty abstraction of the thing without its relations, set over against its existence.
Nouns: thing-in-itself and existence; thing-in-itself, noumenon, noumena, the intelligible, the unknowable, the inscrutable, x, unknown substrate; existence, outward existence, relational being; the noumenal and the phenomenal. the thing in itself, the unknowable thing, the abstract thing, external existence.
Verbs: be in itself, withhold itself, elude knowledge, lie behind appearance; exist, appear, relate. stand apart.
Adjective: noumenal, intelligible, unknowable, inscrutable, inaccessible, transcendent, in itself; phenomenal, existent, relational, uncomeatable†. unfathomable, incognizable†, inexplicable, inapprehensible†, insolvable†. in-itself, abstract.
Adverbs: in itself, intrinsically; for us. apart from relations.
Foreign: German: Ding an sich, an sich, für uns; Latin: mundus intelligibilis, esse in se and esse ad aliud, in se; Arabic: ʿayn [essence, entity]; Sanskrit: svalakṣaṇa [the particular in itself]; Korean: muljache [thing in itself].
Phrases: we can have no cognition of an object, as a thing in itself, but only as an object of sensible intuition, that is, as phenomenon [Kant, Critique of Pure Reason Bxxvi, tr. Meiklejohn]; the thing-in-itself is a caput mortuum [Hegel]; behind the scenes.
Hegel definition: The thing in itself is the concrete existent as the essential immediate that results from sublated mediation, the unmoved, indeterminate unity that is the substrate of external existence. It is supposed to have no determinate manifold in it, and gets one only from an external reflection, as colour from the eye and smell from the nose. But that external existence is the other side of the same concrete existence, and the thing in itself, abstracted from all relation, shows itself to be empty.
Hegel texts:
The Science of Logic
· The Doctrine of Essence › Concrete existence › The thing and its properties › The thing in itself and concrete existence
Hegel citations:
The thing in itself, as the simple reflectedness of the concrete existence within itself, is not the ground of unessential existence; it is the unmoved, indeterminate unity, for it has precisely the determination of being the sublated mediation, and is therefore the substrate of that existence.
— The Science of Logic, The thing and its properties › The thing in itself and concrete existence (tr. di Giovanni)
(The thing-in-itself has color only when exposed to the eye, smell when exposed to the nose, and so on.)
— The Science of Logic, The thing and its properties › The thing in itself and concrete existence (tr. di Giovanni)

Head: Property of the Thing
Path: 一. Logic › 2. Doctrine of Essence › ii. Appearance › α. Existence › a. The Thing and Its Properties › ii. Property of the Thing
Gloss: A feature by which a thing acts on, and is known by, other things.
Hegelian gloss: The thing's determinateness as its relation to other things: a property is the way a thing has effects on others and shows itself in them.
Nouns: property of the thing; property, attribute, quality, characteristic, feature, trait, mark, note, capacity, power, disposition, dispositional property, tendency, propensity, virtue [archaic sense: active power], potency. faculty. diagnostic, lineament. particularity, peculiarity. aptitude, susceptibility. potentiality, force, energy &c H0131. predicable.
Verbs: have, possess, exhibit, display, manifest, affect, act on, influence. act through.
Adjective: proper, characteristic, distinctive, peculiar, inherent, dispositional, active, effective, attributive. discriminative, distinguishing, dioristic†.
Adverbs: characteristically, properly, by virtue of. by its properties.
Foreign: German: Eigenschaft, Eigentum, eigen; Latin: proprium [property proper to a kind], proprietas, proprius; Greek: idion, idiotēs, to idion, idios; Arabic: khāṣṣa [proprium]; Sanskrit: dharma [property]; French: propriété, propre.
Phrases: by their fruits ye shall know them [Bible]; true to type; a mark of.
Hegel definition: A property is the thing's negativity of reflection, by which it relates to something else as to itself. Unlike quality, with which a something is immediately one, the property is a way of reciprocal relating that the thing maintains through alteration. A thing has the property of effecting this or that in another and of expressing itself in a characteristic way, under the condition of a suitable other, but the property is its own, its self-identical substrate. In its properties the thing in itself is present as ground.
Hegel texts:
The Science of Logic
· The Doctrine of Essence › Concrete existence › The thing and its properties › Property
Hegel citations:
A thing has the property to effect this or that in an other, and in this connection to express itself in some characteristic way. It demonstrates this property only under the condition that another thing has a corresponding constitution, but at the same time the property is characteristically the thing’s own and its self-identical substrate
— The Science of Logic, The thing and its properties › Property (tr. di Giovanni)
The thing thereby passes over into an externality, but the property maintains itself in this transition.
— The Science of Logic, The thing and its properties › Property (tr. di Giovanni)

Head: Reciprocal Action of Things
Path: 一. Logic › 2. Doctrine of Essence › ii. Appearance › α. Existence › a. The Thing and Its Properties › iii. Reciprocal Action of Things
Gloss: The mutual influence of things on one another through their properties.
Hegelian gloss: Things related through their properties, so that their distinction lies in the properties, and the properties become self-subsistent.
Nouns: reciprocal action of things; interaction, mutual influence, reciprocal action, interplay, interchange, intercourse, commerce, give and take, crosstalk, feedback, causal nexus, network, web, mesh, interdependence &c H0151; contact, impact, communication, influx; indra's net. reciprocalness†, reciprocity, mutuality, correlation, interdependence, interrelation, connection, link, association, barter. reciprocation, alternation. interaction of things, reciprocal influence.
Verbs: interact, interplay, act upon one another, affect each other, influence one another, react, reciprocate, interrelate, communicate. counterchange†, commute. alternate, interchange &c H0151, exchange. reciprocate &c H0151, return the compliment. act and react.
Adjective: interactive, interacting, reciprocal, mutual, interdependent, interrelated, correlative, networked. commutual†, reciprocative, closely related, international, complemental, complementary. interchanged, commutative, interchangeable, intercurrent†, endosmosmic†.
Adverbs: mutually, reciprocally, each upon the other, back and forth. vice versa, each other, one another, by turns &c H0151. through their properties.
Foreign: Latin: nexus, influxus physicus, mutatis mutandis; Sanskrit: indrajāla; Chinese: ganying [mutual resonance].
Phrases: all things are connected; the butterfly effect; each to each; rub off on.
Hegel definition: The reciprocal action of things follows because things that have properties are many, distinct through themselves, and stand in essential relation by means of those properties. The property is the very relation between them, apart from which the thing is nothing. A thing differs from others only through its property; without it nothing remains but an external gathering of abstract being. So the things vanish as self-subsisting extremes into the continuity that is the property, and thinghood passes over into property.
Hegel texts:

Hegel citations:

— The Science of Logic, The thing and its properties › The reciprocal action of things (tr. di Giovanni)
The determinateness, in virtue of which a thing is this thing only, lies solely in its properties.
— The Science of Logic, The thing and its properties › The reciprocal action of things (tr. di Giovanni)

Head: The Constitution of the Thing out of Matters
Path: 一. Logic › 2. Doctrine of Essence › ii. Appearance › α. Existence › b. The Constitution of the Thing out of Matters
Gloss: The thing seen as a bundle of independent stuffs, such as heat, color or weight, each a separate "matter."

Nouns: constitution of the thing out of matters; composition, makeup, constitution, structure, fabric, texture, ingredients, components, constituents, elements, materials, stuffs, matters; caloric, phlogiston, imponderables, imponderable fluids, electric fluid, magnetic fluid, luminiferous ether; compound, composite, aggregate; porosity, pores, interpenetration. component part, integral part, integrant part†, element, ingredient, leaven, part and parcel, contents, appurtenance, feature, member &c H0130, personnel. crasis†, combination &c H0298, inclusion, admission, comprehension, reception, embodiment, formation. alloy, amalgam. stuff, stock. total, sum, complexus†, intrication†. the free matters, caloric matter, the porosity of matters, the thing as an also.

Adjective: composite, compound, complex, constituent, component, elemental, material, porous, permeable. pervious, honeycombed, foraminous†, cribriform†, infundibular†, tubulous†, tubulated†, tubate†. constituted, composed. complicated, leaky.
Adverbs: in composition, by composition, materially. out of matters.
Foreign: German: Materien.

Hegel definition: The constitution of the thing out of matters comes about when properties, being what is essential in things and their true self-subsistence, pass over into self-subsisting stuffs, as chemistry speaks of colouring or odorous matter. The thing then consists of matters that are continuous across different things. Thinghood is reduced to an unessential moment, yet it preserves itself as the negative unity that makes this thing out of these matters, as a merely quantitative combination of them.
Hegel texts:

· The Doctrine of Essence › Concrete existence › The constitution of the thing out of matters
Hegel citations:

— The Science of Logic, Concrete existence › The constitution of the thing out of matters (tr. di Giovanni)
Equally current is the saying that things consist of various matters or stuffs.
— The Science of Logic, Concrete existence › The constitution of the thing out of matters (tr. di Giovanni)

Hegel definition: The dissolution of the thing follows from its being a merely quantitative combination of free matters, absolutely alterable. Head: Appearance Proper
Path: 一. Logic › 2. Doctrine of Essence › ii. Appearance › β. Appearance Proper
Gloss: The shifting surface of things, ordered by laws.
Hegelian gloss: Existence as appearance: a world of things having their subsistence in an other, yet with a stable content, the law.

Adjective: phenomenal, apparent, empirical, observable, lawful, regular, patterned. salient, striking, demonstrative, prominent, in the foreground, notable, pronounced. seeming, ostensible, on view. visible, perceptible, perceivable, discernible, in view, in full view, in sight, exposed to view, en vidence, unclouded, unobscured†.

Foreign: French: coup d'oeil, mise en sc ne.

Hegel definition: Appearance proper is concrete existence posited as what it is: essence in its concrete existence, whose immediacy is reflected and has negativity within it. To call something appearance is not to set it below some truer immediate thing, for appearance is the higher truth, concrete existence as essential. The reflection that makes it appearance is its own and not an external comparison. It unfolds as the law of appearance, the opposition of an apparent world and a world in itself, and the dissolution of that opposition into essential relation.

The Science of Logic
· The Doctrine of Essence › Appearance › Appearance
Hegel citations:

— The Science of Logic, Appearance › Appearance (tr. di Giovanni)

Hegel definition: The law of appearance is the positive side of the mediation of what appears. Each concrete existent subsists only through another's non-subsistence, and in this passing and shining something persists: law, the self-identical positedness in which each side is only so far as the other is. It stands over against the immediacy of what exists, yet appearance and law have one and the same content: law is the reflection of appearance into self-identity.

Head: The Absolute
Path: 一. Logic › 2. Doctrine of Essence › iii. Actuality › α. The Absolute
Gloss: The all-inclusive reality in which every limited thing is contained; the unconditioned whole.
Hegelian gloss: The absolute identity of form and content, in which all determinations have vanished, positive only as their abyss.
Nouns: the absolute; the unconditioned, the infinite, the all, the whole, the totality, the One, Godhead, deity, the divine; substance, God or nature; ground of being, ultimate reality, totality of being. all, sum total, tout ensemble, Alpha and Omega, be all and end all. Divinity. the one and all.

Hegel definition: The absolute is the simple, solid identity into which every determinateness of being, essence and reflection has dissolved, so that determining it seems to be pure negation and the absolute a void of all predicates, yet equally their position. The task of saying what it is cannot be met by external reflection that picks up determinations here and there; it can only be the absolute's own exposition, a displaying of what it is, through its attribute and its mode.
Hegel texts:

· The Doctrine of Essence › Actuality › The absolute
Hegel citations:
The simple solid identity of the absolute is indeterminate
— The Science of Logic, Actuality › The absolute (tr. di Giovanni)
The task is indeed to demonstrate what the absolute is. But this demonstration cannot be either a determining or an external reflection by virtue of which determinations of the absolute would result, but is rather the exposition of the absolute, more precisely the absolute’s own exposition, and only a displaying of what it is.
— The Science of Logic, Actuality › The absolute (tr. di Giovanni)

Head: Exposition of the Absolute
Path: 一. Logic › 2. Doctrine of Essence › iii. Actuality › α. The Absolute › a. Exposition of the Absolute
Gloss: The setting out of the all-inclusive whole, showing that every limited thing vanishes into it.
Hegelian gloss: The exposition that shows each finite determination to vanish into the absolute, a negative exposition, Spinoza's method.
Nouns: exposition of the absolute; exposition, explication, unfolding, display, setting forth, presentation, revelation, disclosure; negative theology, apophasis, apophatic theology; vanishing of the finite, abolition of the finite, annihilation of the finite; acosmism; emanation, outpouring. unveiling, revealment. manifestation, demonstration. setting-forth, exhibition, interpretation, the self-exposition of the absolute. monism.
Verbs: expound, explicate, unfold, set forth, display, lay out, reveal, disclose; vanish into, be swallowed up in, be absorbed into. illustrate, exemplify. lift the veil, unveil. make manifest, exhibit. set out.
Adjective: expository, explicative, apophatic, negative, acosmic, acosmistic, emanative, disquisitionary†. explanatory, explicatory. exhibitive, interpretive.
Adverbs: in exposition, by way of negation. by exposition.
Foreign: German: Auslegung; Latin: via negativa; Arabic: fanāʾ [passing away in God]; Sanskrit: neti neti.
Phrases: neti neti [Skt.] [Brihadaranyaka Upanishad]; all is one; the night in which all cows are black.
Hegel definition: The exposition of the absolute is the display by which the absolute, the unity of inner and outer, shows itself. It is absolute form and absolute content together, an identity each of whose moments is itself the whole, so that determinateness has become a wholly transparent shine. Essence, existence, whole, parts and force have gone to ground in it. Since its form is simple self-identity the absolute does not determine itself, and the exposition appears as a negating of what reflection brings to it.

Thus the identity of the absolute is for this reason absolute identity, because each of its parts is itself the whole or each determinateness is the totality
— The Science of Logic, The absolute › The exposition of the absolute (tr. di Giovanni)

Head: The Absolute Attribute
Path: 一. Logic › 2. Doctrine of Essence › iii. Actuality › α. The Absolute › b. The Absolute Attribute
Gloss: A single basic aspect under which the all-inclusive whole is understood, such as thought or physical extension.
Hegelian gloss: The absolute as it is for reflection, the whole absolute under one determination, as Spinoza's thought and extension.
Nouns: the absolute attribute; attribute, essential aspect, fundamental aspect, perspective on the whole; thought and extension; dual-aspect theory, double-aspect monism, parallelism; face of God, aspect of the One. the absolute in a determination, relative absolute.

Adjective: attributive, aspectual, dual-aspect, parallel, fundamental, essential. determinate.
Adverbs: under the aspect of, qua, in respect of. under an attribute.
Foreign: Latin: attributum, cogitatio et extensio [Spinoza], sub specie; Arabic: asmāʾ wa-ṣifāt [names and attributes].
Phrases: Deus sive natura [Lat.] [Spinoza]; one substance, two attributes; sub specie aeternitatis; under one aspect.
Hegel definition: The absolute attribute is the relative absolute, the absolute in a determination of form. Since the form is the absolute's own, the attribute contains the whole content of the absolute, a totality that earlier appeared as a world or as one side of the essential relation, now its single true subsistence. But the determination that makes it an attribute is posited as unessential, a mere reflective shine; so the attribute is the absolute only in the determination of identity.
Hegel texts:
The Science of Logic
· The Doctrine of Essence › Actuality › The absolute › The absolute attribute
Hegel citations:
The attribute is just the relative absolute, a combination which only signifies the absolute in a form determination.
— The Science of Logic, The absolute › The absolute attribute (tr. di Giovanni)
But because form is at the same time as the form of the absolute, the attribute is the whole content of the absolute
— The Science of Logic, The absolute › The absolute attribute (tr. di Giovanni)

Head: The Mode of the Absolute
Path: 一. Logic › 2. Doctrine of Essence › iii. Actuality › α. The Absolute › c. The Mode of the Absolute
Gloss: A particular, outward manner in which the all-inclusive whole shows itself; a passing form or mode.
Hegelian gloss: The absolute's own externality, its loss of itself in mutability, yet the mode is the absolute's own self-showing.
Nouns: the mode of the absolute; mode, modification, affection, manner, way, form, guise, shape, fashion, state, phase, aspect, instance, manifestation, expression; finite thing as mode. modality, schesis†, form &c H0277. tone, turn, style, character. wise, modus operandi. shape &c H0277, look. the externality of the absolute.

Adjective: modal, modified, manifest, finite, particular, dependent, derivative, transient, paronymous†. formal.

Foreign: Latin: modus, affectio, natura naturata; Arabic: shaʾn [mode, state]; Sanskrit: vivarta [apparent transformation], pariṇāma [modification].
Phrases: natura naturans et natura naturata [Lat.] [Spinoza]; after a fashion.
Hegel definition: The mode of the absolute is the externality of the absolute, its going out of itself into the changeability and contingency of being. Yet it is not merely this: it is externality posited as externality, a mere way and manner, shine as shine, and so the reflection of form into itself. Only in the mode, therefore, is the absolute posited as absolute identity, as self-referring negativity, and the exposition, which passed from identity to attribute and mode, proves to be the absolute's own movement.

Hegel citations:
But the mode, the externality of the absolute, is not just this. It is rather externality posited as externality, a mere way and manner, hence the reflective shine as reflective shine, or the reflection of form into itself
— The Science of Logic, The absolute › The mode of the absolute (tr. di Giovanni)
In actual fact, therefore, the absolute is first posited as absolute identity only in the mode
— The Science of Logic, The absolute › The mode of the absolute (tr. di Giovanni)

Head: Modal Actuality
Path: 一. Logic › 2. Doctrine of Essence › iii. Actuality › β. Modal Actuality
Gloss: Actuality considered in terms of possibility, chance and necessity.
Hegelian gloss: Actuality as the unity of the actual and the possible, unfolding through contingency to necessity.
Nouns: modal actuality; modality, modalities, modes of being, the modal categories, possibility, actuality and necessity, contingency; modal logic; alethic modality; the possible, the actual, the necessary. liability. possibility actuality and necessity, formal actuality.
Verbs: be possible, be actual, be necessary; could be, must be, may be. happen to be.
Adjective: modal, alethic, possible, actual, necessary, contingent. conditional, provisional. extrinsic, adventitious. incidental. casual, fortuitous, accidental, random.

Phrases: what can be, may be; what must be, will be; as it may be.
Hegel definition: Modal actuality is actuality proper, the absolute as the manifestation that has no content save to manifest itself, absolute form. It stands higher than being, which is not yet actual, and higher than concrete existence, which is not yet the posited unity of reflection and immediacy. Its moments are the modal ones: actuality, possibility and necessity, developed first formally, as contingency, then really, as relative necessity, and finally as absolute necessity.

Hegel definition: Contingency belongs to formal actuality, actuality that is only immediate and unreflected. What is actual is possible, and possibility is actuality reflected into itself, the empty form of self-identity: everything is possible that does not contradict itself, yet every manifold content also contains opposition and so is equally impossible. An actuality that is only possible, that is but could just as well not be, is contingent; it both has a ground and has none.

Hegel citations:

And so it is nothing more than a being, or concrete existence in general. But because by essence it is not mere concrete existence but is the form-unity of the in-itselfness or inwardness and externality, it immediately contains in-itselfness or possibility. What is actual is possible.
— The Science of Logic, Actuality › Contingency (tr. di Giovanni)
In this formal sense of possibility, everything is possible that does not contract itself; the realm of possibility is therefore limitless manifoldness.
— The Science of Logic, Actuality › Contingency (tr. di Giovanni)

Head: Relative Necessity (Real Actuality, Possibility, and Necessity)
Path: 一. Logic › 2. Doctrine of Essence › iii. Actuality › β. Modal Actuality › b. Relative Necessity (Real Actuality, Possibility, and Necessity)
Gloss: What must happen given a definite set of real conditions, but only relative to those conditions.
Hegelian gloss: Real possibility is the totality of conditions present; when they are all there the fact must follow, but only relative to them.

Verbs: necessitate, require, entail, compel, constrain, oblige, dictate; follow necessarily, must follow, be bound to happen. compel &c H0712. follow, be conditioned, result.
Adjective: relatively necessary, conditionally necessary, hypothetically necessary, determined, conditioned, circumstantial, inevitable given, constrained, compelled; really possible, feasible, viable, practicable. possible, in posse, conceivable. contingent &c H0667. impossible. relative, conditional.

Hegel definition: Relative necessity arises in real actuality, the existing world of many properties that preserves itself in its manifold and can act, announcing itself by what it produces. Its possibility is real possibility, the fact's full content of conditions and circumstances, and when all of these are present the fact must be actual. Yet this necessity is relative, for it starts from something presupposed and contingent, and so still has contingency within it.

— The Science of Logic, Actuality › Relative necessity (tr. di Giovanni)

Its conversion of actuality and possibility into each other is a rejoining of form with itself: it is because it is, and passes into the absolute relation.

The determinateness of necessity consists in its having its negation, contingency, within it.
— The Science of Logic, Actuality › Absolute necessity (tr. di Giovanni)

Head: Absolute Relation
Path: 一. Logic › 2. Doctrine of Essence › iii. Actuality › γ. Absolute Relation
Gloss: Actuality as the necessary relation of things to one another.

Nouns: absolute relation; necessary relation, necessary connection, necessary nexus; relation of substance, cause, and reciprocity; ontological dependence; relationality as such. relation, bearing, reference, connection, correlation &c H0151. the absolute relationship, substance causality and reciprocity, the relation of necessity.

Hegel definition: The absolute relation is necessity as being that is simply reflection: a distinguishing whose moments are each the whole of necessity, so that their subsisting is one and their difference only the shine of the movement in which the absolute expounds itself. In its immediate concept it is the relation of substance and accidents; as real it is causality; and returning upon itself it is reciprocity, whose truth is the concept.

Gloss: Cause and effect taken in their bare form: the cause is a cause only in producing its effect and is spent in it, so that neither has meaning without the other.

Hegel definition: Formal causality is the relation of cause and effect taken first by itself. Head: The Determinate Relation of Causality

Gloss: Causality among limited things with a definite content: the same content appears once as cause and once as effect, as rain and wetness, and each cause is itself an effect, giving an endless chain.

Hegel definition: The determinate relation of causality is causality with a content, and therefore real and finite. Phrases: the devil is in the details; every particular is a species; of a kind; le style est l'homme meme [Fr.].
Hegel definition: The particular concept is determinateness as it belongs to the concept: not a limit toward something beyond, but the universal's own moment, in which it is only with itself. The particular contains the universality that is its substance, and the genus is unaltered in its species, which differ from each other and not from it. The species of the universal are only the universal itself and the particular, so that the universal is both itself and its opposite.
Hegel texts:
The Science of Logic
· The Doctrine of the Concept › The concept › The particular concept
Hegel citations:
The particular contains the universality that constitutes its substance; the genus is unaltered in its species; these do not differ from the universal but only from each other.
— The Science of Logic, The concept › The particular concept (tr. di Giovanni)
The particular is the universal itself, but it is its difference or reference to an other
— The Science of Logic, The concept › The particular concept (tr. di Giovanni)

Head: The Singular Concept
Path: 一. Logic › 3. Doctrine of the Concept › i. Subjectivity › α. The Concept as Such › c. The Singular Concept
Gloss: A general idea realized in a single instance, as this particular dog.
Hegelian gloss: The concept returned into itself from its difference: the determinate universal, the subject.
Nouns: the singular concept; singular, singularity, individual, individuality, the individual, this one, this-here, haecceity, thisness, ipseity, uniqueness, instance, specimen, exemplar, token, case, example; the concrete individual, concrete universal; person, self, subject. speciality, particularity, peculiarity, personality, idiosyncrasy, specificness†, singularity &c H0073. case in point. the this, the single instance.
Verbs: individualize, individuate, singularize, single out, identify, pick out, instantiate, exemplify, embody, personify.
Adjective: singular, individual, single, unique, particular, concrete, specific, personal, idiosyncratic, one-off, one of a kind. special, proper, peculiar. one, sole.
Adverbs: individually, singly, uniquely, one by one, each, severally, in particular. respectively. per se.
Foreign: German: Einzelheit; Latin: individuum, haecceitas, sui generis, in concreto; Greek: atomon, tode ti; Sanskrit: vyakti [individual].
Phrases: individuum est ineffabile [Lat.]; sui generis [Lat.]; this rose, this one, here; this one here; the individual case.
Hegel definition: Singularity is the concept reflected out of its determinateness into itself, the determinate determinate, in which it restores itself as self-equal in absolute negativity. Universality and particularity are in it what they are in and for themselves. Abstraction, which climbs from the singular to ever higher genera, goes astray: its highest universal is an empty surface, while the singularity it scorns is the depth in which the concept grasps itself and is posited as concept.
Hegel texts:
The Science of Logic
· The Doctrine of the Concept › The concept › The singular
Hegel citations:
At first, therefore, singularity appears as the reflection of the concept out of its determinateness into itself.
— The Science of Logic, The concept › The singular (tr. di Giovanni)
Its higher and highest universal to which it rises is only a surface that becomes progressively more void of content; the singularity which it scorns is the depth in which the concept grasps itself and where it is posited as concept.
— The Science of Logic, The concept › The singular (tr. di Giovanni)

Head: Judgment
Path: 一. Logic › 3. Doctrine of the Concept › i. Subjectivity › β. Judgment
Gloss: A statement joining a subject to a predicate, saying that an individual is of a certain kind; the dividing of a concept into its parts.
Hegelian gloss: The concept's own self-division into its moments, an original division (Ur-teil): the singular is the universal.
Nouns: judgment, proposition, statement, assertion, predication, declaration, affirmation, enunciation, pronouncement, verdict, finding, ruling, decision, determination, opinion, sentence; subject and predicate, copula; division of the concept, self-division.
Verbs: judge, adjudge, adjudicate, assess, appraise, evaluate, estimate, pronounce, rule, decide, determine, declare, assert, affirm, predicate, state, hold, deem, consider, reckon; divide, sunder. pass judgment. conclude. appreciate, value, rate. subdivide.
Adjective: judicial, judgmental, judicatory, judicative, judicious, evaluative, predicative, propositional, assertoric, declarative, apophantic. reigning.
Adverbs: in judgment, judicially, in my judgment, to my mind, in my estimation. by judgment.
Foreign: German: Diremption, Ur-teilung, Aussage, aussagen, Satz, Rede; Latin: iudicium, subiectum et praedicatum, me judice, praedicatio, praedicare, propositio, praemissa, oratio, oratio enuntiativa, sententia, elocutio, enuntiatio, sermo; Greek: krisis, apophansis, lekton, katēgoria, katēgorō, protasis, logos, phasis, apophasis, logos apophantikos, thesis, axiōma; Arabic: ḥukm [judgment], qaḍiyya [proposition]; Korean: pandan [judgment]; French: dictum, dit, énoncé, énonçable, exprimable, prédication, prédiquer, attribuer, phrase; Italian: attribuzione, attribuire.
Phrases: judge not, that ye be not judged [Bible]; every judgment is an Ur-teil, an original division [Hölderlin]; to pass judgment.
Hegel definition: Judgement is the determinateness of the concept posited in the concept itself, the concept's own dividing and setting its determinations against each other. It is the other function of the concept beside conceiving, its first realization. It contains two self-standing sides, subject and predicate, which are determined only through the judgement itself, and their connection is the unity of the concept. Its development into a series of forms is the progressive determination of the concept.
Hegel texts:
The Science of Logic
· The Doctrine of the Concept › Judgment
Hegel citations:
Judgment is the determinateness of the concept posited in the concept itself.
— The Science of Logic, Judgment (tr. di Giovanni)
Judging is therefore another function than conceiving; or rather, it is the other function of the concept, for it is the determining of the concept through itself.
— The Science of Logic, Judgment (tr. di Giovanni)

Head: Judgment of Existence (Qualitative Judgment)
Path: 一. Logic › 3. Doctrine of the Concept › i. Subjectivity › β. Judgment › a. Judgment of Existence (Qualitative Judgment)
Gloss: A judgment that ascribes a simple, directly perceived quality to a single thing.
Hegelian gloss: Judgment in which the predicate is an immediate quality of the immediate singular.
Nouns: judgment of existence; qualitative judgment, judgment of inherence, judgment of quality, simple judgment, immediate judgment, perceptual judgment, observation statement, report of perception, attribution, ascription, characterization. imputation. the judgment of determinate being.
Verbs: ascribe, attribute, assign, predicate, characterize, describe, report, observe, note. inhere.
Adjective: qualitative, descriptive, perceptual, observational, attributive, immediate, simple. inherent.
Adverbs: descriptively, observationally, at first sight. immediately, qualitatively.
Phrases: the grass is green; as it strikes the eye.
Hegel definition: The judgement of existence, or qualitative judgement, is judgement in its immediacy, before any reflection or movement of its terms. Judgement should be truth, the agreement of concept and reality, but at first it is not so. It is also the judgement of inherence: the subject, as immediate, is the first and essential term, and the predicate is something without subsistence of its own that has its foundation in the subject. It runs from positive through negative to infinite judgement.
Hegel texts:
The Science of Logic
· The Doctrine of the Concept › Judgment › The judgment of existence
Hegel citations:
The judgment is thus truth, for it is the agreement of the concept and reality. But it is not at first constituted in this way
— The Science of Logic, Judgment › The judgment of existence (tr. di Giovanni)
The judgment of existence is also the judgment of inherence because, though immediacy is its determination, it is the subject that in the distinction between subject and predicate is the immediate and hence the first and the essential term in the judgment, and the predicate consequently takes on the form of something that does not subsist on its own but has its foundation in the subject.
— The Science of Logic, Judgment › The judgment of existence (tr. di Giovanni)

Head: Positive Judgment
Path: 一. Logic › 3. Doctrine of the Concept › i. Subjectivity › β. Judgment › a. Judgment of Existence (Qualitative Judgment) › i. Positive Judgment
Gloss: A judgment that affirms a quality of a thing, as "the rose is red."
Hegelian gloss: The singular is a universal: the rose is red; the subject is not wholly its predicate, so the judgment is untrue.
Nouns: positive judgment; affirmation, affirmative judgment, assertion, positive statement, yes, aye, yea, avowal, averment, declaration, sempiternity†, athanasia†. affirmance, statement, allegation, predication, word, confirmation, assentment†. assent, admission, acknowledgment. positive proposition, the simple assertion.
Verbs: affirm, assert, aver, avow, declare, state, maintain, posit, predicate, say yes, attest, certify. make an assertion, have one's say, say, protest, profess. confirm, ratify, corroborate &c H0776. acknowledge, own, admit, allow, concede &c H0689. avouch, asseverate.
Adjective: positive, affirmative, assertive, assertoric, declaratory, categorical. asserting. unqualified, absolute.
Adverbs: affirmatively, positively, yes, aye, yea, indeed, certainly. ay. yeah. okay, OK, alright, all right, yep, yup, sure, of course, absolutely, totally, definitely, right, exactly, true.
Foreign: Latin: iudicium affirmativum; Greek: kataphasis; Sanskrit: vidhi [affirmative injunction].
Phrases: the rose is red; let your yea be yea [Bible]; to say yes to; avec plaisir [Fr.]; chi tace accousente [It.]; the public mind is the creation of the Master-Writers [Disraeli]; you bet your sweet ass it is; what are we waiting for? whenever you're ready; anytime you're ready.
Hegel definition: The positive judgement connects an immediate singular subject with an abstract universal predicate by a copula that means only immediate being, without mediation or negation. Its first expression is the proposition that the singular is universal. What it says is correct, but it is not true: the singular is not merely universal, nor is the universal this single quality, so that it contradicts itself and has its truth in the negative judgement.
Hegel texts:
The Science of Logic
· The Doctrine of the Concept › Judgment › The judgment of existence › The positive judgment
Hegel citations:
The first pure expression of the positive judgment is, therefore, the proposition: the singular is universal.
— The Science of Logic, The judgment of existence › The positive judgment (tr. di Giovanni)
It is because of this connection, which still does not contain any mediation or negation, that this judgment is called “positive.”
— The Science of Logic, The judgment of existence › The positive judgment (tr. di Giovanni)

Head: Negative Judgment
Path: 一. Logic › 3. Doctrine of the Concept › i. Subjectivity › β. Judgment › a. Judgment of Existence (Qualitative Judgment) › ii. Negative Judgment
Gloss: A judgment that denies a quality of a thing, as "the rose is not red."
Hegelian gloss: The singular is not this abstract universal but a particular: the rose is not blue, but of some other colour.
Nouns: negative judgment; negation, denial, negative statement, contradiction, gainsaying, disavowal, disclaimer, refusal, no, nay, declinature†. abnegation, abjuration, contravention, recusation [Law], protest, recusancy &c H0667, flat contradiction, emphatic contradiction, emphatic denial. negative proposition. garbage, scraps.
Verbs: deny, negate, gainsay, contradict, refute, rebut, disavow, disclaim, repudiate, reject, say no, demur. contravene, controvert, give denial to, shake the head. disown, disaffirm, recant &c H0679, revoke &c H0797. dissent, disagree, say no &c H0662, refuse assent. confute, disprove. refuse. repudiate &c H0679, rebut &c H0670, refuse &c H0689.
Adjective: negative, negatory, denying, contradictory, apophatic, privative. denied, recusant &c H0667, at issue upon.
Adverbs: negatively, no, nay, not, not at all, by no means, nowise. non. nah, nope, no way, not really, never.
Foreign: Latin: iudicium negativum, dementi; Greek: apophasis; Sanskrit: niṣedha [negation, prohibition]; German: Verneinung [negation that admits the repressed] [Freud]; French: dénégation [disavowal].
Phrases: the rose is not red; omnis determinatio est negatio [Lat.]; to say no to; a white horse is not a horse, bai ma fei ma [Chin.] [Gongsun Long].
Hegel definition: The negative judgement is the truth of the positive. Since in the positive judgement the content contradicts itself, it has to be said that the singular is not universal. The negation does not remove all relation of predicate to subject: it denies the abstract determinateness and keeps a universal sphere, so that to say the rose is not red still implies that it has a colour. The singular is thus determined as particular, and the judgement moves on to the infinite judgement.
Hegel texts:
The Science of Logic
· The Doctrine of the Concept › Judgment › The judgment of existence › The negative judgment
Hegel citations:
It is because of this purely logical content that the positive judgment is not true but has its truth in the negative judgment.
— The Science of Logic, The judgment of existence › The negative judgment (tr. di Giovanni)
The positive judgment first attains its truth in the negative judgment
— The Science of Logic, The judgment of existence › The negative judgment (tr. di Giovanni)

Head: Infinite Judgment
Path: 一. Logic › 3. Doctrine of the Concept › i. Subjectivity › β. Judgment › a. Judgment of Existence (Qualitative Judgment) › iii. Infinite Judgment
Gloss: A judgment in which subject and predicate have nothing to do with each other, as "the mind is not an elephant"; or one that denies a whole kind of a thing, as crime denies right.
Hegelian gloss: The positive infinite judgment, the singular is singular, and the negative, in which subject and predicate do not fit at all: crime.
Nouns: infinite judgment; nonsense judgment, absurd predication, category mistake, category error, incongruity; negatively infinite judgment, positively infinite judgment; total negation, radical negation; crime as negation of right, negation of the genus; meaninglessness, senselessness, absurdity; spirit is a bone &c H0559. the nonsensical judgment, the identical judgment, total incompatibility, crime as infinite judgment.
Verbs: misapply, misattribute, confound categories, talk nonsense; negate wholly, deny utterly. disjoin wholly, sever.
Adjective: infinite, absurd, incongruous, nonsensical, senseless, meaningless, category-mistaken, wildly inapplicable; radical, total, sweeping, macaronic†. unmeaning. preposterous. negative. incommensurable, tautologous.
Adverbs: absurdly, nonsensically. infinitely, wholly, without relation.
Foreign: Latin: iudicium infinitum, non sequitur, reductio ad absurdum, toto caelo.
Phrases: the mind is not an elephant; a lion is not a table; colourless green ideas sleep furiously [Chomsky]; neither here nor there.
Hegel definition: The infinite judgement negates not only a particular predicate but its whole universal sphere, so that the very form of judgement is cancelled. Its negative examples, that spirit is not red, that the understanding is not a table, are correct but nonsensical; a real instance is crime, which negates not a particular right but right as such. Its positive side is the negation of negation, singularity reflected into itself: the singular is singular.
Hegel texts:
The Science of Logic
· The Doctrine of the Concept › Judgment › The judgment of existence › The infinite judgment
Hegel citations:
But the infinite judgment which is supposed to be its truth is, according to its negative expression, the negative infinite, a judgment in which even the form of judgment is sublated.
— The Science of Logic, The judgment of existence › The infinite judgment (tr. di Giovanni)
But crime is the infinite judgment that negates, not only the particular right, but the universal sphere, the right as right.
— The Science of Logic, The judgment of existence › The infinite judgment (tr. di Giovanni)

Head: Judgment of Reflection
Path: 一. Logic › 3. Doctrine of the Concept › i. Subjectivity › β. Judgment › b. Judgment of Reflection
Gloss: A judgment that ascribes a relational or practical property, such as "useful" or "dangerous."
Hegelian gloss: The predicate is an essential universality of relation, by which the subject is related to other things.
Nouns: judgment of reflection; relational judgment, judgment of quantity, practical judgment, judgment of use, judgment of value-for, evaluation, appraisal, assessment; predicate of relation, relational predicate, dispositional predicate; useful, harmful, dangerous, healing, edible. valuation. appraisement, estimation. the reflective judgment, the judgment of relation, the quantitative judgment, the judgment of subsumption.
Verbs: assess, evaluate, appraise, estimate, rate, gauge, weigh. value. appreciate. relate, subsume, ascribe.
Adjective: relational, reflective, evaluative, practical, dispositional, functional. subsumptive. grievous.
Adverbs: in relation, relatively, for practical purposes. reflectively.
Phrases: one man's meat is another man's poison; good for what ails you; for what it's worth.
Hegel definition: The judgement of reflection is that in which the subject is a singular as such and the predicate no longer an abstract quality but a universality gathered through the relation of different terms, as in saying that humans are mortal or that something is useful. Such predicates express an essentiality which is relational. The movement falls on the side of the subject, which is extended from this one through some to all.
Hegel texts:
The Science of Logic
· The Doctrine of the Concept › Judgment › The judgment of reflection
Hegel citations:
[T]he universal is no longer an abstract universality, or a singular property, but is posited as a universal that has collected itself together into a unity through the connection of different terms
— The Science of Logic, Judgment › The judgment of reflection (tr. di Giovanni)
They express an essentiality which is however a relational determination, or a comprehensive universality.
— The Science of Logic, Judgment › The judgment of reflection (tr. di Giovanni)

Head: Singular Judgment
Path: 一. Logic › 3. Doctrine of the Concept › i. Subjectivity › β. Judgment › b. Judgment of Reflection › i. Singular Judgment
Gloss: A judgment of this kind about one thing: "this plant is healing."
Hegelian gloss: This singular is essentially universal: this plant is curative.
Nouns: singular judgment; singular proposition, judgment about an individual, individual statement; this-statement; case, instance. the this-judgment, the individual judgment, the judgment about a single thing, this, the singular subject.
Verbs: single out, point to, name, designate, instance. individuate, indicate.
Adjective: singular, individual, particular, one-off, demonstrative. indicative. single.
Adverbs: in this case, in this instance, singly.
Phrases: this plant is medicinal; this one and no other.
Hegel definition: The singular judgement is the immediate judgement of reflection, in which the singular is universal, or this is an essential universal. But a this is not an essential universal, so the judgement must be taken negatively. Since the predicate is the implicit being of the subject, the negation falls not on the predicate but on the subject, which needs further determination: not merely a this. So the singular judgement has its truth in the particular judgement.
Hegel texts:
The Science of Logic
· The Doctrine of the Concept › Judgment › The judgment of reflection › The singular judgment
Hegel citations:
But a “this” is not an essential universal.
— The Science of Logic, The judgment of reflection › The singular judgment (tr. di Giovanni)
On the contrary, it is the subject that is alterable and needs determination. The negative judgment is therefore to be understood as saying: “‘not a this’ is a universal of reflection”; such an in-itself has a more universal concrete existence than it would have in a “this.” Accordingly, the singular judgment has its proximate truth in the particular judgment.
— The Science of Logic, The judgment of reflection › The singular judgment (tr. di Giovanni)

Head: Particular Judgment
Path: 一. Logic › 3. Doctrine of the Concept › i. Subjectivity › β. Judgment › b. Judgment of Reflection › ii. Particular Judgment
Gloss: A judgment of this kind about some things: "some plants are healing."
Hegelian gloss: Some singulars are universal; positive and negative at once, pointing toward totality.
Nouns: particular judgment; particular proposition, partial statement, some-statement, existential statement, qualified generalization, hedge; some, several, certain, a few; partial quantification. plurality, a number, a certain number. the some-judgment, partial judgment, particular quantification.
Verbs: qualify, hedge, limit, restrict. modify. particularize.
Adjective: particular, partial, qualified, hedged, restricted, limited, some. qualifying, conditional. any.
Adverbs: sometimes, in some cases, partly, in part, to some extent. partially, to a certain extent.
Phrases: some swans are white; some but not all.
Hegel definition: The particular judgement takes as subject not this one but some: the singular extended by external reflection. Its form is that some singulars are a universal of reflection. It looks positive but is just as much negative, since some is both comprehensive and short of universality, so that "some humans are happy" at once implies that some are not. Positive and negative here no longer fall apart, but the judgement remains indeterminate.
Hegel texts:
The Science of Logic
· The Doctrine of the Concept › Judgment › The judgment of reflection › The particular judgment
Hegel citations:
The non-singularity of the subject that must be posited in the first judgment of reflection instead of the subject’s singularity is particularity.
— The Science of Logic, The judgment of reflection › The particular judgment (tr. di Giovanni)
The positive and the negative judgment no longer fall outside one another, but the particular immediately contains both at the same time, precisely because it is a judgment of reflection.
— The Science of Logic, The judgment of reflection › The particular judgment (tr. di Giovanni)

Head: Universal Judgment
Path: 一. Logic › 3. Doctrine of the Concept › i. Subjectivity › β. Judgment › b. Judgment of Reflection › iii. Universal Judgment
Gloss: A judgment of this kind about all things of a class: "all humans are mortal."
Hegelian gloss: All singulars, the empirical allness, which becomes the genus, so the subject is a universal in itself.
Nouns: universal judgment; universal proposition, all-statement, universal generalization, generalization, sweeping statement, blanket statement, general rule, law, universal quantifier, ∀; allness, totality. generality, universality, catholicity. all, the whole. the judgment of allness, the all-judgment, universal quantification, every.
Verbs: generalize, universalize, extend to all, apply across the board. quantify.
Adjective: universal, general, total, sweeping, blanket, comprehensive, all-encompassing, exceptionless. generic, collective, broad, encyclopedical†, widespread &c H0042. catholic, common, ecumenical. all-inclusive.
Adverbs: universally, in all cases, always, without exception, across the board, one and all. generally, in general, generally speaking, speaking generally. whatever, whatsoever, to a man. invariably.
Foreign: German: Allheit.
Phrases: all men are mortal; omnis homo mortalis [Lat.].
Hegel definition: The universal judgement makes its subject all: the external universality of reflection, the all of all the singulars, in which each singular remains unchanged. This universality is only a commonality of self-standing singulars, an association made by comparison, which is what representation first takes universality to be, as what fits many. Its truth lies beyond mere allness, in the objective universality of the genus, and with it the judgement of necessity.
Hegel texts:
The Science of Logic
· The Doctrine of the Concept › Judgment › The judgment of reflection › The universal judgment
Hegel citations:
The universality of the subject of the universal judgment is the external universality of reflection, “allness”; the “all” is the all of all the singulars in which the singular remains unchanged.
— The Science of Logic, The judgment of reflection › The universal judgment (tr. di Giovanni)
This universality is therefore only a commonality of self-subsisting singulars, an association of such singulars as comes about only by way of comparison.
— The Science of Logic, The judgment of reflection › The universal judgment (tr. di Giovanni)

Head: Judgment of Necessity
Path: 一. Logic › 3. Doctrine of the Concept › i. Subjectivity › β. Judgment › c. Judgment of Necessity
Gloss: A judgment that states the essential nature of its subject.
Hegelian gloss: The judgment in which the universal is the subject's substantial nature, its genus.
Nouns: judgment of necessity; necessary judgment, essential predication, judgment of substance, judgment of kind, judgment of essence, de re necessity; definition, classification, categorization. the essential judgment, the judgment of the genus, the objective universal, categorical hypothetical and disjunctive judgments.
Verbs: classify, categorize, subsume, define, place, rank. necessitate, determine essentially.
Adjective: necessary, essential, substantial, generic, classificatory, taxonomic, categorical.
Adverbs: necessarily, essentially, by nature.
Foreign: Latin: per se, de re.
Phrases: gold is a metal; in the nature of things.
Hegel definition: The judgement of necessity is that in which universality exists in and for itself, the objective universality which in the sphere of essence corresponds to substance, but which here has its differences immanent within it. It is posited with a determinateness essential to it and with a particularity diverse from it, so that the universal is determined as genus and species. It unfolds as the categorical, the hypothetical and the disjunctive judgement.
Hegel texts:
The Science of Logic
· The Doctrine of the Concept › Judgment › The judgment of necessity
Hegel citations:
The determination to which universality has advanced is, as we have seen, the universality that exists in and for itself or the objective universality that in the sphere of essence corresponds to substantiality.
— The Science of Logic, Judgment › The judgment of necessity (tr. di Giovanni)
In this way the universality is determined as genus and species.
— The Science of Logic, Judgment › The judgment of necessity (tr. di Giovanni)

Head: Categorical Judgment
Path: 一. Logic › 3. Doctrine of the Concept › i. Subjectivity › β. Judgment › c. Judgment of Necessity › i. Categorical Judgment
Gloss: A judgment that places a thing in its kind: "gold is a metal."
Hegelian gloss: The genus or species predicated of the subject as its substantial nature: gold is a metal.
Nouns: categorical judgment; categorical proposition, unconditional statement, judgment of genus, generic statement, subsumption, classification, typing; categorical assertion. kind, genus, species. the judgment of the genus, the substantial judgment, classification under a kind, the unconditional assertion.
Verbs: categorize, classify, subsume, class, type, rank, sort, pigeonhole, assign. place under a kind.
Adjective: categorical, generic, taxonomic, classificatory, unconditional, unqualified, flat, absolute. affirmative, positive. substantial.
Adverbs: categorically, unconditionally, flatly, absolutely, without qualification.
Foreign: Arabic: ḥamliyya [categorical proposition].
Phrases: the rose is a plant; flat out.
Hegel definition: The categorical judgement is the first, immediate judgement of necessity: its predicate is the universality in which the subject has its immanent nature, as in saying that the rose is a plant or that this ring is gold. What is necessary is the substantial identity of subject and predicate, so that it differs wholly from predicating an accidental property. Yet the subject's singularity still belongs to the immediacy of external existence.
Hegel texts:
The Science of Logic
· The Doctrine of the Concept › Judgment › The judgment of necessity › The categorical judgment
Hegel citations:
Now the categorical judgment has for predicate such a universality as in it the subject possesses its immanent nature.
— The Science of Logic, The judgment of necessity › The categorical judgment (tr. di Giovanni)
But what is necessary in it is the substantial identity of subject and predicate
— The Science of Logic, The judgment of necessity › The categorical judgment (tr. di Giovanni)

Head: Hypothetical Judgment
Path: 一. Logic › 3. Doctrine of the Concept › i. Subjectivity › β. Judgment › c. Judgment of Necessity › ii. Hypothetical Judgment
Gloss: A judgment of conditional form: "if A, then B."
Hegelian gloss: The connection of two contents as necessary, though their being is not posited: if A is, then B is.
Nouns: hypothetical judgment; conditional, conditional proposition, conditional statement, hypothetical, if-then statement, implication, material conditional, antecedent and consequent; supposition, hypothesis, assumption. postulation, condition, presupposition, postulate, theory, proposition. condition and conditioned.
Verbs: suppose, assume, hypothesize, posit, conditionalize, imply, entail. theorize, presume, presuppose. involve.
Adjective: hypothetical, conditional, suppositional, contingent, implicative, if-then. assumed, suppositive†, conjectural, theoretical, supposable, presumptive, postulatory†. given, provisional.
Adverbs: if, if so, in that case, supposing, assuming, provided that, then. provided, unless, conditionally. if so be, on the supposition, in the event of. hypothetically.
Foreign: Latin: ergo, ex hypothesi, illatio, inferentia, consequentia; Greek: protasis and apodosis, sympeplegmenon, symperasma, synēmmenon, akolouthia, antakolouthia; Arabic: sharṭiyya muttaṣila [conjunctive conditional]; Sanskrit: vyāpti [invariable concomitance]; German: nachsichziehen, zurfolgehaben, Folge(-rung), Schluß, Konsequenz, Implikation, Implikatur.
Phrases: if A, then B; if wishes were horses, beggars would ride; what if.
Hegel definition: The hypothetical judgement says that if A is, then B is, so that the being of A is just as much the being of another. It posits the necessary connection of immediate things, which the categorical judgement had not yet posited. It asserts neither that A is nor that B is: only their connectedness is posited as existing. In it the being of finite things is expressed as it truly is, as being their own and also not their own.
Hegel texts:
The Science of Logic
· The Doctrine of the Concept › Judgment › The judgment of necessity › The hypothetical judgment
Hegel citations:
What is posited in this judgment is the necessary connectedness of immediate determinacies, a connectedness which in the categorical judgment is not yet posited.
— The Science of Logic, The judgment of necessity › The hypothetical judgment (tr. di Giovanni)
[T]he hypothetical judgment does not say either that A is, or that B is, but only that if the one is, then the other is; only the connectedness of the extremes is posited as existing, not the extremes themselves.
— The Science of Logic, The judgment of necessity › The hypothetical judgment (tr. di Giovanni)

Head: Disjunctive Judgment
Path: 一. Logic › 3. Doctrine of the Concept › i. Subjectivity › β. Judgment › c. Judgment of Necessity › iii. Disjunctive Judgment
Gloss: A judgment of alternatives: "A is either B or C."
Hegelian gloss: The genus as the totality of its species, each excluding the others: A is either B or C.
Nouns: disjunctive judgment; disjunction, alternative, either-or, dilemma, choice, option, exclusive disjunction, inclusive disjunction; division, complete division, exhaustive alternatives, partition. distribution. alternation.
Verbs: disjoin, separate, divide, alternate, choose, opt. disconnect, dissociate. part, partition &c H0687.
Adjective: disjunctive, alternative, exclusive, exhaustive, either-or, binary. disjoined, disparate. discontinuous, discrete.
Adverbs: either ... or, or else, alternatively, otherwise. disjunctively. instead.
Foreign: German: Entweder-Oder; Latin: vel and aut, aut ... aut, aut-aut; Arabic: sharṭiyya munfaṣila [disjunctive conditional].
Phrases: Either/Or, Enten-Eller [Danish] [Kierkegaard]; tertium non datur [Lat.]; one or the other.
Hegel definition: The disjunctive judgement says that A is either B or C. Its subject is the genus in simple form and its predicate the same universality as the totality of its differentiated species, so that both sides have one content and extent. The species together constitute the genus, "as well as" expressing the identity of the particular with the universal, and they exclude one another by "either-or". In it the necessity of the concept is posited.
Hegel texts:
The Science of Logic
· The Doctrine of the Concept › Judgment › The judgment of necessity › The disjunctive judgment
Hegel citations:
It thus contains, first, the concrete universality or the genus in simple form, as the subject; second, the same universality but as the totality of its differentiated determinations.
— The Science of Logic, The judgment of necessity › The disjunctive judgment (tr. di Giovanni)
This is the necessity of the concept in which, first, the self-identity of the two extremes is of the same extent, content, and universality.
— The Science of Logic, The judgment of necessity › The disjunctive judgment (tr. di Giovanni)

Head: Judgment of the Concept
Path: 一. Logic › 3. Doctrine of the Concept › i. Subjectivity › β. Judgment › d. Judgment of the Concept
Gloss: A judgment that measures a thing against what it ought to be: good, bad, true, beautiful.
Hegelian gloss: The judgment of the concept, in which the subject is measured against its concept, its ought.
Nouns: judgment of the concept; value judgment, evaluation, appraisal, assessment, verdict, normative judgment, critical judgment, taste, criticism, critique, rating, grading, review; good, bad, true, false, right, wrong, beautiful, ugly; ideal measure, standard, norm, criterion. valuation, appraisement. discrimination, distinction, appreciation of difference, estimation &c H0069. model, pattern, paradigm. the judgment of value, evaluative judgment. scaling, leveling.
Verbs: evaluate, appraise, assess, rate, grade, rank, judge, criticize, critique, review, approve, disapprove, commend, condemn. measure, value. estimate, appreciate. measure against the ought.
Adjective: evaluative, normative, critical, axiological, appraisive, judgmental, ideal. correct. appraising.
Adverbs: by any standard, on the merits, in the final analysis, judged by its own concept. evaluatively, normatively.
Phrases: by their fruits ye shall know them [Bible]; weighed in the balances and found wanting [Bible]; as it should be; up to standard.
Hegel definition: The judgement of the concept is that in which the predicate, such as good, bad, true or right, measures the fact against its concept as an ought it presupposes. It has been called the judgement of modality and taken to concern only the copula's value for thought, but it is objective and the truth of the earlier judgements, since it rests on the concept itself and not on external reflection. It is assertoric, then problematic, then apodictic.
Hegel texts:
The Science of Logic
· The Doctrine of the Concept › Judgment › The judgment of the concept
Hegel citations:
The judgment of the concept has been called the judgment of modality, and has been regarded as containing the form of the connection of subject and predicate as this obtains in an external understanding, and as concerned with the value of the copula only in connection with thought.
— The Science of Logic, Judgment › The judgment of the concept (tr. di Giovanni)
But the judgment of the concept is instead objective and, as contrasted with the others, it is the truth, for it rests on the concept precisely in its determinateness as concept, not in some external reflection or with reference to some subjective, that is, accidental, thought.
— The Science of Logic, Judgment › The judgment of the concept (tr. di Giovanni)

Head: Assertoric Judgment
Path: 一. Logic › 3. Doctrine of the Concept › i. Subjectivity › β. Judgment › d. Judgment of the Concept › i. Assertoric Judgment
Gloss: A judgment of value stated as a bare claim: "this house is good."
Hegelian gloss: The singular is judged good or true by bare assurance, which stands against the equal assurance of its opposite.
Nouns: assertoric judgment; bare assertion, mere assertion, dogmatic claim, say-so, fiat, decree, pronouncement, verdict without reasons, bald statement, unsupported claim, opinion, gut feeling, intuition, taste. asseveration, assurance, protestation, profession. persuasion, conviction. the simple claim, affirmation.
Verbs: assert, declare, pronounce, proclaim, aver, say so, lay down the law, opine. make an assertion, have one's say, say, affirm, predicate, state, protest, profess. insist upon, assert roundly, assert positively, dogmatize. put forth, advance, allege, propound, maintain, contend. avow, avouch, asseverate. claim.
Adjective: assertoric, assertive, dogmatic, unsupported, ungrounded, bald, flat, bare, unargued. asserting, declaratory, affirmative, positive, emphatic, decided, confident, predicatory†, pronunciative†, unretracted†. naked.
Adverbs: dogmatically, flatly, baldly, by fiat, on one's say-so. assertorically.
Foreign: Latin: ipse dixit.
Phrases: ipse dixit [Lat.]; because I said so; de gustibus non est disputandum [Lat.]; take my word for it; because I say so.
Hegel definition: The assertoric judgement is the judgement of the concept in its immediacy: its subject is a concrete singular and its predicate expresses the relation of that singular's actual constitution to its concept, as in "this house is bad" or "this action is good". The singular ought to be something and may or may not conform. Since the connection is only asserted, its warrant is a subjective assurance, and its being good or bad hangs on an external third.
Hegel texts:
The Science of Logic
· The Doctrine of the Concept › Judgment › The judgment of the concept › The assertoric judgment
Hegel citations:
The subject is a concrete singular in general, and the predicate expresses this same singular as the connection of its actuality, its determinateness or constitution, to its concept.
— The Science of Logic, The judgment of the concept › The assertoric judgment (tr. di Giovanni)
For this reason the judgment is so far only assertoric; its credential is only a subjective assurance. That something is good or bad, right, suitable or not, hangs on an external third.
— The Science of Logic, The judgment of the concept › The assertoric judgment (tr. di Giovanni)

Head: Problematic Judgment
Path: 一. Logic › 3. Doctrine of the Concept › i. Subjectivity › β. Judgment › d. Judgment of the Concept › ii. Problematic Judgment
Gloss: A judgment of value stated as uncertain: "this house may be good."
Hegelian gloss: The subject judged according to whether it corresponds to its concept, so the judgment is only possibly true.
Nouns: problematic judgment; possible judgment, tentative judgment, conjecture, surmise, guess, speculation, supposition, hypothesis, maybe, perhaps; uncertainty, doubt, hedging, qualification, conjecturality†. guesswork, suspicion, estimate. incertitude, doubtfulness, dubiety. assumption. probability, likelihood, credibleness†, likeliness, verisimilitude, plausibility, color, semblance, show of, presumption, presumptive evidence, circumstantial evidence, credibility. reasonable chance, fair chance, good chance, favorable chance, reasonable prospect, fair prospect, good prospect, favorable prospect, prospect, wellgrounded hope, chance &c H0142. improbability, unlikelihood, unfavorable chance, bad chance, ghost of a chance, little chance, small chance, poor chance, scarcely any chance, no chance, bare possibility, long odds, incredibility &c H0532. the uncertain judgment, the doubtful verdict, the may-be, possibility. guessing.
Verbs: conjecture, surmise, guess, speculate, suppose, suspect, wonder, hazard, venture, hedge, presurmise†, wis†. divine, presume. be probable, give color to, lend color to, point to, imply &c H0776, bid fair &c H1164, stand fair for, stand a good chance, run a good chance. think likely, dare say, flatter oneself, expect &c H0646, count upon &c H0667. be improbable, have a small chance. question.
Adjective: problematic, problematical, tentative, conjectural, speculative, uncertain, doubtful, dubious, open, moot, possible, hypothetical. supposable, presumptive, putative. undecided, undetermined, open to discussion, in question &c H0667. probable, likely, hopeful, to be expected, in a fair way. plausible, specious, ostensible, colorable, well-founded, reasonable, credible, easy of belief, presumable, apparent. improbable, unlikely, contrary to all reasonable expectation, wild [Coll.], far out [Coll.], out of sight [Coll.], outtasight [Coll.], heavy [Coll.]. rare &c H0232, unheard of, inconceivable, unimaginable, inimaginable†, incredible &c H0532, more than doubtful, strange, bizarre &c H0073. debatable, baffling.
Adverbs: perhaps, maybe, possibly, perchance, conceivably, for all one knows, it may be, it might be. by possibility, peradventure, may be, haply, mayhap. probably, belike†, in all probability, in all likelihood, very likely, most likely, like enough, odds on, odds in favor, ten to one, apparently, seemingly, according to every reasonable expectation, to all appearance. problematically.
Foreign: Latin: primâ facie; French: vraisemblance; Italian: ben trovato; Arabic: ẓann [conjecture, opinion].
Phrases: it may be good, it may not be; who knows?; as may be; it remains to be seen; Heaven knows; who can tell? who shall decide when doctors disagree? ambiguas in vulgum spargere voces [Lat.].
Hegel definition: The problematic judgement is the assertoric taken negatively as well as positively. Whether the predicate ought to be joined to the subject appears open, and the problematic element lies in the immediacy of the subject, which is thereby determined as contingent: one cannot say that the house is good, but that it is so according to the way it is made. The subject is thus distinguished into its universal nature, what it ought to be, and its particular constitution.
Hegel texts:
The Science of Logic
· The Doctrine of the Concept › Judgment › The judgment of the concept › The problematic judgment
Hegel citations:
The problematic judgment is the assertoric judgment in so far as the latter must be taken positively as well as negatively.
— The Science of Logic, The judgment of the concept › The problematic judgment (tr. di Giovanni)
Consequently the subject is itself differentiated into its universality or objective nature, that is, its ought, and the particularized constitution of immediate existence.
— The Science of Logic, The judgment of the concept › The problematic judgment (tr. di Giovanni)

Head: Apodictic Judgment
Path: 一. Logic › 3. Doctrine of the Concept › i. Subjectivity › β. Judgment › d. Judgment of the Concept › iii. Apodictic Judgment
Gloss: A judgment of value stated with its reason, and so as necessary: "this house, being built thus, is good."
Hegelian gloss: The subject's constitution named as the ground of its agreement with its concept: the house, so constituted, is good.
Nouns: apodictic judgment; apodicticity, demonstrative certainty, necessary truth, grounded judgment, reasoned verdict, justified evaluation; demonstration, proof; certain knowledge. rigorous proof, conclusiveness, apodeixis†, apodixis†, probation, comprobation†. the necessary judgment of value, the judgment with its ground, the grounded verdict.
Verbs: demonstrate, prove, establish, ground, justify, warrant, show conclusively. substantiate, verify &c H0776.
Adjective: apodictic, apodeictic, demonstrative, demonstrable, necessary, certain, conclusive, incontrovertible, grounded, reasoned, justified, warranted. demonstrating, probative, unanswerable, apodeictical†, irresistible, irrefutable, irrefragable. unimpeachable, undeniable, unquestionable, indisputable, incontestable, indubitable, irrefutable &c H0670. sure, assured, solid, well-founded.
Adverbs: apodictically, demonstrably, necessarily, conclusively, beyond doubt, QED. certainly, for certain, no doubt, doubtless, of course, to a certainty. of necessity, needs must. consequently.
Foreign: Latin: quod erat demonstrandum; Greek: apodeixis; Arabic: burhān [demonstration], yaqīn.
Phrases: quod erat demonstrandum [Lat.]; the house, being so built, is good; it goes without saying; by its very nature; cela va sans dire [Fr.]; there is no question, no question, not a shadow of doubt, there is not a shadow of doubt; the die is cast.
Hegel definition: The apodictic judgement states that the subject, as so and so constituted, is good or right. Its subject contains what it ought to be and also its constitution, which holds the ground why the predicate belongs to it or not. This judgement is truly objective, the truth of judgement in general: subject and predicate correspond and have the same concept. The fact is divided into ought and being and joins them, and this filled copula passes into the syllogism.
Hegel texts:
The Science of Logic
· The Doctrine of the Concept › Judgment › The judgment of the concept › The apodictic judgment
Hegel citations:
This judgment is now truly objective; or it is the truth of the judgment in general.
— The Science of Logic, The judgment of the concept › The apodictic judgment (tr. di Giovanni)
The truth of the latter, however, is that it is internally fractured into its ought and its being; this is the absolute judgment on all actuality.
— The Science of Logic, The judgment of the concept › The apodictic judgment (tr. di Giovanni)

Head: Syllogism
Path: 一. Logic › 3. Doctrine of the Concept › i. Subjectivity › γ. Syllogism
Gloss: An argument that joins two terms through a third, the middle term; inference.
Hegelian gloss: The unity of concept and judgment: the extremes joined through a mediating middle; everything rational is a syllogism.
Nouns: syllogism; inference, deduction, reasoning, ratiocination, argument, argumentation, demonstration, derivation, conclusion, consequence, entailment, illation; premises, major premise, minor premise, middle term, extremes, conclusion; mediation; enthymeme, epicheireme, sorites, polysyllogism, prosyllogism. dilemma, perilepsis†, a priori reasoning, reductio ad absurdum, horns of a dilemma, comprehensive argument, empirema†, epagoge†. result, corollary, porism†. case, plaidoyer†, opening, lemma, proposition, terms, postulate, data, starting point, principle, inference &c H0669.
Verbs: syllogize, infer, deduce, reason, ratiocinate, argue, conclude, derive, draw a conclusion, follow, mediate, connect. gather, collect, draw an inference, make a deduction, weet†, ween†. chop logic. come to a conclusion.
Adjective: syllogistic, inferential, deductive, illative, ratiocinative, argumentative, demonstrative, logical, valid, sound, mediated. rationalistic, dialectic, discursive, discursory†, discoursive†. by implication, steganographic†.
Adverbs: syllogistically, deductively, by inference, therefore, thus, hence, consequently, it follows that. whence, seeing that, since, for that reason, inasmuch as, whereas. thence.
Foreign: German: Vermittlung, Schluß, Begriff; Latin: syllogismus, ratiocinium, terminus medius, ergo, argumentum ad hominem, nomen; Greek: syllogismos, horos; Arabic: qiyās [syllogism, analogy]; Sanskrit: anumāna [inference], pañcāvayava [five-membered syllogism]; Korean: churon [syllogism], samdannonbeop [three-step syllogism]; French: terme.
Phrases: everything rational is a syllogism [Hegel]; all men are mortal, Socrates is a man, therefore Socrates is mortal; barbara, celarent, darii, ferio [Lat.]; to put two and two together.
Hegel definition: The syllogism is the restoration of the concept within judgement, and so the unity and truth of both. In it the determinations of the concept stand as extremes, as in judgement, and at the same time their determinate unity is posited in a middle. It is therefore the completely posited concept and the rational: not only is the syllogism rational, but everything rational is a syllogism. It is no mere subjective form set apart from the reason that deals with content.
Hegel texts:
The Science of Logic
· The Doctrine of the Concept › The syllogism
Hegel citations:
