The syllogism is the result of the restoration of the concept in the judgment, and consequently the unity and the truth of the two.
— The Science of Logic, The syllogism (tr. di Giovanni)
Therefore, it is not just that the syllogism is rational but that everything rational is a syllogism.
— The Science of Logic, The syllogism (tr. di Giovanni)

Head: Syllogism of Existence (Qualitative Syllogism)
Path: 一. Logic › 3. Doctrine of the Concept › i. Subjectivity › γ. Syllogism › a. Syllogism of Existence (Qualitative Syllogism)
Gloss: Inference in which the connecting term is a single, directly perceived quality.
Hegelian gloss: Inference through an immediate determinateness, contingent and external: S–P–U.
Nouns: syllogism of existence; qualitative syllogism, formal syllogism, syllogism of the understanding, categorical syllogism of the schools; middle term as single quality; contingent middle; figures of the syllogism. the immediate syllogism, the syllogism of determinate being.
Verbs: syllogize formally, infer by quality. infer, conclude, mediate through a quality.
Adjective: formal, qualitative, contingent, external, abstract. immediate.
Adverbs: formally, by quality. immediately, qualitatively.
Foreign: Latin: figurae; Greek: schēmata.
Phrases: barbara celarent darii ferioque prioris [Lat.]; from the particular to the general; by the book.
Hegel definition: The syllogism of existence is the syllogism in its immediate form, whose terms are the abstract determinations of the concept not yet developed through mediation. Singularity and universality are its extremes and particularity stands between them as middle, uniting them immediately. It is the strictly formal syllogism, and formalism consists in stopping there. Its dialectical movement consists in positing the moments of mediation, through its figures.
Hegel texts:
The Science of Logic
· The Doctrine of the Concept › The syllogism › The syllogism of existence
Hegel citations:
The syllogism in its immediate form has for its moments the determinations of the concept as immediate.
— The Science of Logic, The syllogism › The syllogism of existence (tr. di Giovanni)
Now the dialectical movement of the syllogism of existence consists in positing the moments of the mediation that alone constitutes the syllogism.
— The Science of Logic, The syllogism › The syllogism of existence (tr. di Giovanni)

Head: First Figure
Path: 一. Logic › 3. Doctrine of the Concept › i. Subjectivity › γ. Syllogism › a. Syllogism of Existence (Qualitative Syllogism) › i. First Figure
Gloss: The form of inference that joins an individual to a general idea through a specific one: Socrates is a man, men are mortal, so Socrates is mortal.
Hegelian gloss: Singular joined to universal through the particular: S–P–U, the scheme of the understanding's reasoning.
Nouns: first figure; S–P–U, singular–particular–universal; perfect syllogism. S-P-U, the particular as middle, the perfect figure, the major and minor premise.
Verbs: subsume, apply, bring under. mediate, conclude.
Adjective: perfect, primary, paradigmatic, standard. first-figure, subsumptive.
Adverbs: in the first figure. through the particular.
Foreign: Latin: Barbara, Celarent, Darii, Ferio [mnemonic moods], figura prima; Greek: prōton schēma, teleios syllogismos.
Phrases: all men are mortal; Socrates is a man; therefore Socrates is mortal; all men are mortal, Socrates is a man.
Hegel definition: The first figure, singular, particular, universal, is the general schema of the determinate syllogism: the singular is connected with the universal not immediately but through particularity, and the universal descends to the singular through it. Its meaning is that the singular, otherwise only inward, emerges through particularity into existence. But the connection is still subjective, and its premises, themselves unmediated, demand proof, which leads to the further figures.
Hegel texts:
The Science of Logic
· The Doctrine of the Concept › The syllogism › The syllogism of existence › First figure of the syllogism
Hegel citations:
Singularity connects with universality through particularity; the singular is not universal immediately but by means of particularity
— The Science of Logic, The syllogism of existence › First figure of the syllogism (tr. di Giovanni)
The general meaning of this syllogism is that the singular, which as such is infinite self-reference and consequently would be only an inwardness, emerges through the medium of particularity into existence, into a universality wherein it no longer belongs just to itself but stands in external conjunction
— The Science of Logic, The syllogism of existence › First figure of the syllogism (tr. di Giovanni)

Head: Second Figure
Path: 一. Logic › 3. Doctrine of the Concept › i. Subjectivity › γ. Syllogism › a. Syllogism of Existence (Qualitative Syllogism) › ii. Second Figure
Gloss: The form of inference whose connecting term is an individual instance.
Hegelian gloss: The universal joined to the particular through the singular: P–S–U.
Nouns: second figure; P–S–U, particular–singular–universal; individual as middle term. U-S-P, the singular as middle, the mean as individual, the particular conclusion.
Verbs: infer through the individual. mediate, conclude, infer through the singular.
Adjective: secondary, negative-concluding. second-figure, singular, mediating.
Adverbs: in the second figure. through the individual.
Foreign: Latin: Cesare, Camestres, Festino, Baroco, figura secunda.
Phrases: no fish is a mammal; every whale is a mammal; therefore no whale is a fish; by example.
Hegel definition: The second figure, particular, singular, universal, expresses the truth of the first: that something is joined to a universal quality not in and for itself but by means of a contingency, in a singular, which is therefore the true middle. Since a conclusion is mediated, it contains negation. One premise is already mediated by the first syllogism, so that the two presuppose each other, and the terms exchange places.
Hegel texts:
The Science of Logic
· The Doctrine of the Concept › The syllogism › The syllogism of existence › The second figure
Hegel citations:
The truth of the first qualitative syllogism is that something is not in and for itself united to a qualitative determinateness which is a universal, but is united to it by means of a contingency or in a singularity.
— The Science of Logic, The syllogism of existence › The second figure (tr. di Giovanni)
[T]he second syllogism thus presupposes the first just as, conversely, the first presupposes the second.
— The Science of Logic, The syllogism of existence › The second figure (tr. di Giovanni)

Head: Third Figure
Path: 一. Logic › 3. Doctrine of the Concept › i. Subjectivity › γ. Syllogism › a. Syllogism of Existence (Qualitative Syllogism) › iii. Third Figure
Gloss: The form of inference whose connecting term is a general idea.
Hegelian gloss: Singular and particular joined through the universal: S–U–P, the transition to the mathematical figure.
Nouns: third figure; S–U–P, singular–universal–particular; universal as middle term. P-U-S, the universal as middle, the mean as universal, the figure of the abstract universal.
Verbs: infer through the universal. mediate, conclude.
Adjective: tertiary, particular-concluding. third-figure, universal, mediating.
Adverbs: in the third figure. through the universal.
Foreign: Latin: Darapti, Disamis, Datisi, Felapton, Bocardo, Ferison, figura tertia.
Phrases: all men are mortal; all men are rational; therefore some rational beings are mortal; as a rule.
Hegel definition: The third figure, singular, universal, particular, has no immediate premise left, both having been mediated by the other two figures, so that it presupposes them as each presupposes the others. Its middle is the abstract, indeterminate universal, in which the extremes are contained only according to their universality and not their essential determinateness. It is the truth of the formal syllogism and shows its formalism.
Hegel texts:
The Science of Logic
· The Doctrine of the Concept › The syllogism › The syllogism of existence › The third figure
Hegel citations:
This third syllogism no longer has any single immediate premise; the connection S-U has been mediated by the first syllogism; the connection P-U by the second.
— The Science of Logic, The syllogism of existence › The third figure (tr. di Giovanni)
Considered in itself, the syllogism S-U-P is the truth of the formal syllogism; it expresses the fact that its mediating middle is the abstract universal and that the extremes are not contained in it according to their essential determinateness but only according to their universality
— The Science of Logic, The syllogism of existence › The third figure (tr. di Giovanni)

Head: Fourth (Mathematical) Figure
Path: 一. Logic › 3. Doctrine of the Concept › i. Subjectivity › γ. Syllogism › a. Syllogism of Existence (Qualitative Syllogism) › iv. Fourth (Mathematical) Figure
Gloss: The form of inference in which all terms are interchangeable quantities: things equal to the same thing are equal to each other.
Hegelian gloss: U–U–U: the abstract, relationless syllogism in which the terms are equal and the mediation is equality, as in mathematics.
Nouns: fourth figure, mathematical syllogism; U–U–U, universal–universal–universal; Galenic figure; equality, equation, transitivity, axiom of equality; quantitative inference, calculation. the quantitative syllogism, equality as middle, U-U-U.
Verbs: equate, calculate, substitute, transpose, abalienate†. equalize.
Adjective: mathematical, quantitative, equational, transitive, Galenic. equal, interchangeable.
Adverbs: by equation, by substitution, transitively. mathematically, by equality.
Foreign: German: mathematischer Schluss; Latin: Bramantip, Camenes, Dimaris, Fesapo, Fresison.
Phrases: things equal to the same thing are equal to each other [Euclid]; Q.E.D.
Hegel definition: The fourth, or mathematical, figure is the syllogism that results when all quality is abstracted from the terms: if two things are equal to a third, they are equal to each other. Here there is no longer any relation of inherence or subsumption, and each term can stand as middle. Its evidence rests on this poverty of thought. Its positive result is that mediation must rest on reflection, that is, on a concreteness of the terms.
Hegel texts:
The Science of Logic
· The Doctrine of the Concept › The syllogism › The syllogism of existence › The fourth figure
Hegel citations:
The fourth figure: U-U-U, or the mathematical syllogism 1. The mathematical syllogism goes like this: if two things or two determinations are equal to a third, then they are equal to each other.
— The Science of Logic, The syllogism of existence › The fourth figure (tr. di Giovanni)
The self-evidence of this syllogism rests, therefore, solely on the indigence and abstractness of its mode of thought.
— The Science of Logic, The syllogism of existence › The fourth figure (tr. di Giovanni)

Head: Syllogism of Reflection
Path: 一. Logic › 3. Doctrine of the Concept › i. Subjectivity › γ. Syllogism › b. Syllogism of Reflection
Gloss: Inference whose connecting term is a collection of cases.
Hegelian gloss: Inference whose middle is the subject's reflected totality: all, then many, then one like another.
Nouns: syllogism of reflection; empirical inference, inference from collections, reasoning from cases; middle term as totality of instances; aggregation of cases. the reflective inference, inference through a collection, the syllogisms of allness induction and analogy, the empirical syllogism.
Verbs: collect, aggregate, survey, gather instances. bring together, colligate†, gather. infer from cases, reflect.
Adjective: reflective, empirical, collective, aggregative.
Adverbs: empirically, by reflection, from the cases. reflectively, from cases.
Phrases: from many, one; one and all; as far as anyone knows.
Hegel definition: The syllogism of reflection arises when the abstractness of the terms is sublated, each determinateness being posited as concrete, with the others shining in it. Its middle is no isolated particularity but the totality of determinations, the posited unity of the extremes, though only as a reflection that embraces them, not yet the identity of the concept. It runs as the syllogism of allness, of induction and of analogy.
Hegel texts:
The Science of Logic
· The Doctrine of the Concept › The syllogism › The syllogism of reflection
Hegel citations:
The course of the qualitative syllogism has sublated the abstractness of its terms
— The Science of Logic, The syllogism › The syllogism of reflection (tr. di Giovanni)
This term is now posited as the totality of the determinations; thus it is the posited unity of the extremes; but this unity is at first that of a reflection embracing the extremes within itself
— The Science of Logic, The syllogism › The syllogism of reflection (tr. di Giovanni)

Head: Syllogism of Allness
Path: 一. Logic › 3. Doctrine of the Concept › i. Subjectivity › γ. Syllogism › b. Syllogism of Reflection › i. Syllogism of Allness
Gloss: Inference from what holds of all members of a class to what holds of one.
Hegelian gloss: All men are mortal; Gaius is a man; the major premiss presupposes the conclusion.
Nouns: syllogism of allness; universal instantiation; deduction from all, application of a general rule to a case; question-begging generalization, circular deduction. the syllogism of totality, the inference from all, universal inference, the all as middle. petitio principii.
Verbs: apply, instantiate, deduce from the general, bring under the rule. infer from all, apply to each, subsume.
Adjective: deductive, universal, general, instantiating, circular. generic, collective. all-inclusive, distributive.
Adverbs: by universal instantiation. universally, from all to one.
Foreign: Latin: dictum de omni, dictum de omni et nullo, a fortiori.
Phrases: what holds of all holds of each; dictum de omni et nullo [Lat.]; all the more; begging the question.
Hegel definition: The syllogism of allness is the syllogism of the understanding in its perfection, but no more. Its middle contains all singulars, so that only a predicate belonging concretely to the subject can be attached to it. Yet allness gathers the singular into universality only externally. Its major premise already presupposes the conclusion, since one can assert of all only if the singular case is already included, and so it points to induction.
Hegel texts:
The Science of Logic
· The Doctrine of the Concept › The syllogism › The syllogism of reflection › The syllogism of allness
Hegel citations:
The syllogism of allness is the syllogism of the understanding in its perfection, but more than that it is not yet.
— The Science of Logic, The syllogism of reflection › The syllogism of allness (tr. di Giovanni)
[I]n other words, allness is not yet the universality of the concept, but the external universality of reflection.
— The Science of Logic, The syllogism of reflection › The syllogism of allness (tr. di Giovanni)

Head: Syllogism of Induction
Path: 一. Logic › 3. Doctrine of the Concept › i. Subjectivity › γ. Syllogism › b. Syllogism of Reflection › ii. Syllogism of Induction
Gloss: Inference from many observed cases to a general rule.
Hegelian gloss: The middle is the complete series of singulars, an incomplete and unending task.
Nouns: syllogism of induction; induction, generalization, empirical generalization, enumerative induction, inference from instances, inductive reasoning, bottom-up reasoning, extrapolation, data-driven inference. dialectics. inductive inference, enumeration of cases, the syllogism of experience. epagoge.
Verbs: induce, generalize, extrapolate, infer from instances, reason from particulars. infer from cases.
Adjective: inductive, empirical, enumerative, generalizing, data-driven, bottom-up.
Adverbs: inductively, by induction, from the evidence.
Foreign: Latin: inductio, inductio per enumerationem simplicem, a posteriori; Greek: epagōgē; Arabic: istiqrāʾ [induction].
Phrases: one swallow does not make a summer; all swans are white, until one is black; so far as experience goes.
Hegel definition: Induction is the syllogism of reflection whose middle term is singularity completed, all the singulars, gathered into a genus and joined to a universal property on the ground that it is found in each of them. It is not the syllogism of mere perception but of experience. Yet it remains essentially subjective, since the collecting of singulars into the genus is an external reflection and the singulars persist in their immediacy.
Hegel texts:
The Science of Logic
· The Doctrine of the Concept › The syllogism › The syllogism of reflection › The syllogism of induction
Hegel citations:
Induction, therefore, is not the syllogism of mere perception or of contingent existence, like the second figure corresponding to it, but the syllogism of experience – of the subjective gathering together of singulars in the genus, and of the conjoining of the genus with a universal determinateness on the ground that the latter is found in all singulars.
— The Science of Logic, The syllogism of reflection › The syllogism of induction (tr. di Giovanni)
On the contrary, induction is essentially still a subjective syllogism.
— The Science of Logic, The syllogism of reflection › The syllogism of induction (tr. di Giovanni)

Head: Syllogism of Analogy
Path: 一. Logic › 3. Doctrine of the Concept › i. Subjectivity › γ. Syllogism › b. Syllogism of Reflection › iii. Syllogism of Analogy
Gloss: Inference from likeness between cases: what holds of one thing holds of another similar to it.
Hegelian gloss: The middle is a singular taken in its essential universality, so that like things are inferred to be alike.
Nouns: syllogism of analogy; analogy, argument from analogy, analogical reasoning, likeness, resemblance, similitude, parallel, comparison, correspondence, homology, isomorphism, model, metaphor. similarity, semblance, approximation, parallelism, analogicalness†, homoiousia†, parity. simile, type &c H0906, image &c H0834, close resemblance. association, association of ideas. correlation &c H0151, affinity. conformity &c H0073, agreement &c H0097. figure, trope. analogical inference, reasoning from likeness. paralogism.
Verbs: analogize, compare, liken, parallel, extrapolate by likeness, model on, reason by analogy. be similar, resemble, bear resemblance, approximate. infer by analogy.
Adjective: analogical, analogous, comparable, similar, parallel, homologous, isomorphic, metaphorical. such as, so, homoiousian†. resembling, like, alike, twin, equiparant†.
Adverbs: analogically, by analogy, by parity of reasoning, likewise, similarly.
Foreign: Latin: analogia entis, mutatis mutandis, proportio; Greek: analogia; French: of a piece; Arabic: qiyās [analogical reasoning, as in jurisprudence]; Sanskrit: upamāna [comparison as a means of knowledge].
Phrases: as above, so below; like causes, like effects; like father, like son.
Hegel definition: The syllogism of analogy has as its middle a singular taken in its universal nature: another singular sharing that nature is concluded to share the predicate, as when the earth has inhabitants, the moon is an earth, and so the moon has inhabitants. It is superficial in proportion as the shared universal is a mere quality or mark and identity is taken for similarity. Its form, not any empirical content put into the premises, is what counts.
Hegel texts:
The Science of Logic
· The Doctrine of the Concept › The syllogism › The syllogism of reflection › The syllogism of analogy
Hegel citations:
But its middle term is no longer some single quality or other but a universality which is the immanent reflection of a concreted term and is therefore its nature
— The Science of Logic, The syllogism of reflection › The syllogism of analogy (tr. di Giovanni)
Analogy is all the more superficial, the more the universal in which the two extremes are united, and in accordance with which the one extreme becomes the predicate of the other, is a mere quality or, since quality is a matter of subjectivity, is some distinctive mark or other and the identity of the extremes is therein taken as just a similarity.
— The Science of Logic, The syllogism of reflection › The syllogism of analogy (tr. di Giovanni)

Head: Syllogism of Necessity
Path: 一. Logic › 3. Doctrine of the Concept › i. Subjectivity › γ. Syllogism › c. Syllogism of Necessity
Gloss: Inference whose connecting term is the essential nature of things.
Hegelian gloss: Inference whose middle is the universal as essential nature, the genus, so the mediation is substantial.
Nouns: syllogism of necessity; necessary inference, essential inference, reasoning from essence, demonstration proper, strict deduction. inference through the essential nature, the objective universal as middle, categorical hypothetical and disjunctive syllogisms.
Verbs: demonstrate, deduce necessarily, derive. necessitate, infer necessarily, conclude.
Adjective: necessary, essential, demonstrative, strict, rigorous. apodictic.
Adverbs: necessarily, of necessity, strictly.
Phrases: it cannot be otherwise; by definition.
Hegel definition: The syllogism of necessity has for its middle the genus, the universal nature of the fact: a simple universality that nevertheless contains the whole determinateness of the extremes. Its middle is no adventitious immediate content but the immanent reflection of the extremes' own determinateness, so that the terms are moments of one necessary existence. It is realized, through the categorical, hypothetical and disjunctive forms, when the extremes are posited as the same totality as the middle.
Hegel texts:
The Science of Logic
· The Doctrine of the Concept › The syllogism › The syllogism of necessity
Hegel citations:
This syllogism is for this reason the syllogism of necessity, because its middle term is not any adventitious immediate content but is the immanent reflection of the determinateness of the extremes.
— The Science of Logic, The syllogism › The syllogism of necessity (tr. di Giovanni)
The realization of this syllogism is a matter of determining it in such a way that the extremes are equally posited as this totality which initially the middle term is, and the necessity of the connection, which is at first only the substantial content, shall be a connection of the posited form.
— The Science of Logic, The syllogism › The syllogism of necessity (tr. di Giovanni)

Head: Categorical Syllogism
Path: 一. Logic › 3. Doctrine of the Concept › i. Subjectivity › γ. Syllogism › c. Syllogism of Necessity › i. Categorical Syllogism
Gloss: Inference whose connecting term is a kind or genus.
Hegelian gloss: The middle is the genus, the substantial nature of the extremes.
Nouns: categorical syllogism; inference through the genus, generic inference, classificatory reasoning, taxonomy-based inference. the categorical inference, the syllogism of the kind, the substantial middle.
Verbs: classify, subsume under a genus, infer by kind. subsume, infer categorically, conclude.
Adjective: categorical, generic, taxonomic. substantial.
Adverbs: categorically, by kind. through the genus.
Phrases: all metals conduct; gold is a metal; gold conducts; as a matter of kind; true to type.
Hegel definition: The categorical syllogism has one or both premises categorical and takes objective universality as its middle term. In its full import it is the first syllogism of necessity, in which a subject is joined with a predicate through its substance, the essential nature of the singular and not just any property. The contingency of connecting a subject with just any quality through just any middle falls away, and with it the endless demand for proof.
Hegel texts:
The Science of Logic
· The Doctrine of the Concept › The syllogism › The syllogism of necessity › The categorical syllogism
Hegel citations:
Taken in its full import, the categorical syllogism is the first syllogism of necessity, one in which a subject is conjoined with a predicate through its substance.
— The Science of Logic, The syllogism of necessity › The categorical syllogism (tr. di Giovanni)
But since the middle term is the essential nature of the singular and not just one or other of its determinacies or properties, and likewise the extreme of universality is not any abstract universal, nor just any singular quality either, but is rather the universal determinateness of the genus, its specific difference, we no longer have the contingency of a subject being conjoined with just any quality through just any middle term.
— The Science of Logic, The syllogism of necessity › The categorical syllogism (tr. di Giovanni)

Head: Hypothetical Syllogism
Path: 一. Logic › 3. Doctrine of the Concept › i. Subjectivity › γ. Syllogism › c. Syllogism of Necessity › ii. Hypothetical Syllogism
Gloss: Inference whose connecting term is a condition: if A then B; A; therefore B.
Hegelian gloss: The middle is the being of the condition, which is the being of the conditioned.
Nouns: hypothetical syllogism; conditional inference, affirming the antecedent, denying the consequent, chain argument. the hypothetical inference, the if-then syllogism, the antecedent, the consequent.
Verbs: infer conditionally, affirm the antecedent, deny the consequent. condition.
Adjective: hypothetical, conditional, inferential. consequential.
Adverbs: if so, then; given that, it follows. hypothetically, conditionally.
Foreign: Latin: modus ponens, modus tollens; Arabic: istithnāʾī [exceptive syllogism].
Phrases: if it rains, the ground is wet; it rains; the ground is wet; if so, then so.
Hegel definition: The hypothetical syllogism adds to the hypothetical judgement, "if A is, so is B", the immediacy of being: but A is, therefore B is. A is then no mere immediacy but essentially the middle term, an immediate being that is also contingent and sublates itself. The two sides are not independent beings but beings held in necessity, such as condition and conditioned, and what is posited is their necessary connection as an accomplished mediating unity.
Hegel texts:
The Science of Logic
· The Doctrine of the Concept › The syllogism › The syllogism of necessity › The hypothetical syllogism
Hegel citations:
The hypothetical judgment contains only the necessary connection without the immediacy of the connected terms. “If A is, so is B”; or, the being of A is also just as much the being of an other, of the B; with this, it is not as yet said either that A is, or that B is.
— The Science of Logic, The syllogism of necessity › The hypothetical syllogism (tr. di Giovanni)
The conclusion contains the connection of subject and predicate, not as the abstract copula, but as the accomplished mediating unity.
— The Science of Logic, The syllogism of necessity › The hypothetical syllogism (tr. di Giovanni)

Head: Disjunctive Syllogism
Path: 一. Logic › 3. Doctrine of the Concept › i. Subjectivity › γ. Syllogism › c. Syllogism of Necessity › iii. Disjunctive Syllogism
Gloss: Inference through a complete set of alternatives: A is B, C or D; it is neither B nor C; therefore D.
Hegelian gloss: The middle is the genus as the totality of its exclusive species, the mediating and the mediated in one: the syllogism completed.
Nouns: disjunctive syllogism; process of elimination, elimination, exclusion of alternatives, argument by elimination, exhaustive division; dilemma, trilemma. the disjunctive inference, inference by elimination, exhaustive alternatives, the either-or as middle. exhaustion.
Verbs: eliminate, exclude, rule out, narrow down, whittle down. disjoin, conclude.
Adjective: disjunctive, eliminative, exhaustive, exclusionary.
Adverbs: by elimination, by exclusion, either ... or. disjunctively.
Foreign: Latin: modus tollendo ponens.
Phrases: when you have eliminated the impossible, whatever remains, however improbable, must be the truth [Arthur Conan Doyle]; if not this, then that.
Hegel definition: The disjunctive syllogism has as middle a universality full of form, the genus sorted out into its species, which includes the particular and excludes the species from one another: A is either B or C or D; but A is B; therefore it is neither C nor D. Mediator and mediated are the same A, so that it is the truth of the hypothetical syllogism and no longer a syllogism at all. With it the formalism and subjectivity of inference sublate themselves.
Hegel texts:
The Science of Logic
· The Doctrine of the Concept › The syllogism › The syllogism of necessity › The disjunctive syllogism
Hegel citations:
What is posited in the disjunctive syllogism is thus the truth of the hypothetical syllogism, the unity of the mediator and the mediated, and for that reason the disjunctive syllogism is equally no longer a syllogism at all.
— The Science of Logic, The syllogism of necessity › The disjunctive syllogism (tr. di Giovanni)
In this way the formalism of the syllogistic inference, and consequently the subjectivity of the syllogism and of the concept in general, has sublated itself.
— The Science of Logic, The syllogism of necessity › The disjunctive syllogism (tr. di Giovanni)

Head: Objectivity
Path: 一. Logic › 3. Doctrine of the Concept › ii. Objectivity
Gloss: Thought realized as a world of self-standing objects; the kinds of order (mechanical, chemical and purposive) that belong to objects themselves.
Hegelian gloss: The concept realized as immediacy: a totality of self-subsistent objects, the concept sunk in externality.
Nouns: objectivity; object, world of objects, objective world; externality, outwardness, thinghood, thing-world, the objective; realization of the concept; immediacy regained. the realized concept, objecthood.
Verbs: objectify, objectivize, externalize, realize, embody, reify.
Adjective: objective, external, outward, real, realized, thingly.
Adverbs: objectively, externally, in reality, out there. in the object.
Foreign: German: Objekt, Gegenstand; Latin: objectum, obiici, obiectum, esse obiective; Sanskrit: viṣaya [object]; French: objet, être objectif; Greek: antikeimenon.
Phrases: the world is everything that is the case [Wittgenstein]; the facts of the matter.
Hegel definition: Objectivity is the concept that has sublated the mediation in its self-determination and raised it to immediate self-reference: being in and for itself, pervaded throughout by the concept. Hegel compares the transition into it with the ontological proof. It is not mere sensuous existence but is free of accidentality. It runs through mechanism, where objects stand indifferent to one another; chemism, where they are specifically related; and teleology, where the concept is posited as purpose.
Hegel texts:
The Science of Logic
· The Doctrine of the Concept › Objectivity
Hegel citations:
At the present standpoint of our treatise, objectivity has the meaning first of all of the being in and for itself of the concept that has sublated the mediation posited in its self-determination, raising it to immediate self-reference.
— The Science of Logic, Objectivity (tr. di Giovanni)
Third, this essential unity of the objects is thereby posited as distinct from their self-subsistence. It is the subjective concept, but posited as referring in and for itself to the objectivity, as purpose. This is teleology.
— The Science of Logic, Objectivity (tr. di Giovanni)

Head: Mechanism
Path: 一. Logic › 3. Doctrine of the Concept › ii. Objectivity › α. Mechanism
Gloss: The relation of things that are external to one another and act only by outside force, like the parts of a machine.
Hegelian gloss: The object whose determinations are external to it, so that its combinations are indifferent to it.
Nouns: mechanism; mechanics, machine, apparatus, contraption, device, engine, clockwork, works, gearing, gear train; mechanistic world, world-machine, clockwork universe; externality, indifference, aggregation, juxtaposition, mere assemblage; push and pull, pressure and impact; automatism, automaton; determinism, mechanical determinism, mechanism versus vitalism. instrument. mechanical relation, external relation, machinery. robot. mechanicalness.
Verbs: mechanize, automate, push, pull, drive, propel, transmit, assemble. impel. act externally, aggregate.
Adjective: mechanical, mechanistic, machinelike, clockwork, automatic, automated, rote, robotic, external, indifferent, inert, deterministic.
Adverbs: mechanically, automatically, like clockwork, by rote, by force. externally.
Foreign: Latin: machina mundi; Sanskrit: yantra [machine, device]; German: Gestell [enframing] [Heidegger].
Phrases: l'homme machine [Fr.] [La Mettrie]; the world is a great machine; the ghost in the machine [Ryle]; cogs in a machine.
Hegel definition: Mechanism is objectivity in its immediacy: the differentiated moments are complete, self-standing objects which, even in connection, relate as each on its own and remain external in every combination. Whatever connects them is alien to their nature, mere composition, mixture or aggregate. There is spiritual mechanism too: a mechanical memory, habit or mode of acting lacks the pervading presence of spirit in what it grasps or does.
Hegel texts:
The Science of Logic
· The Doctrine of the Concept › Mechanism
Hegel citations:
This is what constitutes the character of mechanism, namely, that whatever the connection that obtains between the things combined, the connection remains one that is alien to them, that does not affect their nature, and even when a reflective semblance of unity is associated with it, the connection remains nothing more than composition, mixture, aggregate, etc.
— The Science of Logic, Mechanism (tr. di Giovanni)
A mechanical mode of representation, a mechanical memory, a habit, a mechanical mode of acting, mean that the pervasive presence that is proper to spirit is lacking in what spirit grasps or does.
— The Science of Logic, Mechanism (tr. di Giovanni)

Head: The Mechanical Object
Path: 一. Logic › 3. Doctrine of the Concept › ii. Objectivity › α. Mechanism › a. The Mechanical Object
Gloss: A thing complete in itself and related to others only from outside.
Hegelian gloss: An object complete in itself, indifferent to its determinateness and combined with others only as an aggregate.
Nouns: the mechanical object; inert object, passive object, body, lump, mass, aggregate, heap, assemblage, unit, part, piece, cog, component, billiard ball; indifference, inertness, passivity, externality. inertia. solid body, block. bulk. the mechanical thing, the indifferent object, the self-enclosed object, monad, atom.
Verbs: lie inert, remain passive, be pushed, be acted on. stand indifferent, remain external.
Adjective: inert, passive, indifferent, external, self-enclosed, aggregate, impenetrable. inactive. mechanical, aggregated.
Adverbs: inertly, passively, from without. externally, indifferently.
Foreign: Latin: vis inertiae.
Phrases: a cog in the machine; a mere thing; dead weight.
Hegel definition: The mechanical object is the syllogism whose mediation has settled into immediate identity, a universality that pervades particularity and in it is immediate singularity. It has neither matter and form nor properties and accidents, since those relations belong to a past the concept has ended. Without determinate opposition within, it holds an indifferent manifold, so that there are several objects, each an aggregate in itself; yet it does not consist of atoms.
Hegel texts:
The Science of Logic
· The Doctrine of the Concept › Mechanism › The mechanical object
Hegel citations:
It is therefore in and for itself a universal – universality, not in the sense of a commonality of properties, but a universality that pervades particularity and in it is immediate singularity.
— The Science of Logic, Mechanism › The mechanical object (tr. di Giovanni)
Because this indeterminate determinateness is essential to the object, the object is in itself a plurality, and must therefore be regarded as a composite, an aggregate.
— The Science of Logic, Mechanism › The mechanical object (tr. di Giovanni)

Head: The Mechanical Process
Path: 一. Logic › 3. Doctrine of the Concept › ii. Objectivity › α. Mechanism › b. The Mechanical Process
Gloss: The pushing and pulling of mechanical things upon one another.
Hegelian gloss: Objects acting upon one another through the identity of their nature, which they show only as indifferent to it.
Nouns: the mechanical process; mechanical action, impact, collision, push, pressure, thrust, impulse, transmission, communication of motion, force transfer, chain reaction. impulsion, impetus, momentum, shove, propulsion &c H0238. percussion, concussion, shock. mechanical interaction, push and pull, impact and pressure, communication and resistance.
Verbs: push, press, thrust, impel, propel, strike, hit, collide, transmit, communicate, pass on. set going, drive. knock. be in motion, move. impel &c H0242, propel &c H0238. pull, act upon, react.
Adjective: mechanical, impulsive, collisional, transmissive, impellent†. interactive.
Adverbs: by impact, by contact, by transmission. mechanically, by push and pull.
Phrases: action and reaction; push comes to shove; knock-on effect.
Hegel definition: The mechanical process is the interaction of objects. Taken merely as self-enclosed totalities they could not act on one another, and would resemble monads, whose conception Hegel judges deficient: a self-reference that merely mirrors is passivity toward the other, and a pre-established harmony only presupposes the influence it should explain. The determinateness of each object thus has its ground in another, which sets the process going.
Hegel texts:
The Science of Logic
· The Doctrine of the Concept › Mechanism › The mechanical process
Hegel citations:
If objects are regarded only as self-enclosed totalities, they cannot act on one another.
— The Science of Logic, Mechanism › The mechanical process (tr. di Giovanni)
To project the reciprocal influence of substances into a predetermined harmony means nothing more than to make it a presupposition, in effect to remove it from the scope of the concept.
— The Science of Logic, Mechanism › The mechanical process (tr. di Giovanni)

Head: The Formal Mechanical Process
Path: 一. Logic › 3. Doctrine of the Concept › ii. Objectivity › α. Mechanism › b. The Mechanical Process › i. The Formal Mechanical Process
Gloss: Mechanical interaction as the mere passing on of motion or condition.
Hegelian gloss: The communication of determinations between objects, as motion passed on, a mere sharing.
Nouns: the formal mechanical process; communication, transmission, propagation, imparting, passing on, contagion, infection, spread, diffusion, dissemination, osmosis; mere sharing. distribution. communication of motion, the passing-on, formal communication. transference.
Verbs: communicate, transmit, impart, pass on, propagate, spread, diffuse, disseminate, infect. distribute.
Adjective: communicative, transmissible, contagious, infectious, diffusive, communicatory†. formal, communicated, transmitted.
Adverbs: by transmission, by contagion, by osmosis. by communication, formally.
Phrases: a rolling stone gathers no moss; pass it on; to set going.
Hegel definition: The formal mechanical process is the positing of the objects' identical connection by giving the determinateness it generates the form of universality: this is communication, which passes on without turning into the opposite. In spirit a determinateness spreads unaltered from one person to another, like a scent in unresisting air; laws, morals and rational conceptions pervade individuals unawares, as motion or heat spreads among bodies.
Hegel texts:
The Science of Logic
· The Doctrine of the Concept › Mechanism › The mechanical process › The formal mechanical process
Hegel citations:
This positing consists simply in giving to the determinateness which is generated the form of universality – and this is communication, which occurs without transition into the opposite.
— The Science of Logic, The mechanical process › The formal mechanical process (tr. di Giovanni)
Laws, morals, rational conceptions in general, are in the region of the spirit communicable entities of this kind; they pervade individuals unconsciously imposing themselves on them.
— The Science of Logic, The mechanical process › The formal mechanical process (tr. di Giovanni)

Head: The Real Mechanical Process
Path: 一. Logic › 3. Doctrine of the Concept › ii. Objectivity › α. Mechanism › b. The Mechanical Process › ii. The Real Mechanical Process
Gloss: Mechanical interaction in which one thing overpowers another.
Hegelian gloss: Communication that becomes the power of one object over another, the negativity of the object's self-subsistence.
Nouns: the real mechanical process; domination, subjugation, overpowering, overmastering, power, violence, force, might, coercion, compulsion, mastery, superiority, ascendancy, preponderance, the stronger and the weaker; fate as mechanical power. upper hand, whip hand, conquest, victory, expugnation†. energy &c H0131, ascendency†, sway. pressure, predominance, dominance, predominancy†. resistance, fate.
Verbs: overpower, overwhelm, subdue, subjugate, dominate, master, crush, conquer, prevail, override, steamroll, bulldoze. vanquish, overcome, overmaster, overmatch. have the upper hand, preponderate, overrule. resist.
Adjective: overpowering, overwhelming, dominant, superior, preponderant, crushing, coercive, irresistible. resistless, invincible. predominant. resistant, violent.
Adverbs: by force, by main force, perforce. forcibly. overpoweringly. overwhelmingly.
Foreign: German: Gewalt, Schicksal; Latin: vi et armis.
Phrases: might is right; the strong do what they can and the weak suffer what they must [Thucydides]; might makes right; to get the upper hand; tel maure tel valet [Fr.].
Hegel definition: The real mechanical process takes up the result of the formal one: the objects and the process now stand in a more determinate relation, differing definitely from one another. The opposition is distributed among objects as self-standing singularity and dependent universality, the weaker yielding to the stronger only so far as it accepts it and forms one sphere with it. Communication is followed by resistance, and the weaker is overcome by violence.
Hegel texts:
The Science of Logic
· The Doctrine of the Concept › Mechanism › The mechanical process › The real mechanical process
Hegel citations:
They are not merely diverse, but are determinedly differentiated as against one another.
— The Science of Logic, The mechanical process › The real mechanical process (tr. di Giovanni)
The weaker can be seized and invaded by the stronger only in so far as it accepts the stronger and constitutes one sphere with it.
— The Science of Logic, The mechanical process › The real mechanical process (tr. di Giovanni)

Head: The Product of the Mechanical Process
Path: 一. Logic › 3. Doctrine of the Concept › ii. Objectivity › α. Mechanism › b. The Mechanical Process › iii. The Product of the Mechanical Process
Gloss: The state of rest reached when mechanical interaction has run its course.
Hegelian gloss: The fate of the mechanical process: rest, a product in which the object has the determination externally posited.
Nouns: the product of the mechanical process; rest, repose, equilibrium, standstill, stasis, inertia, quiescence, stillness, settlement, settling; result, outcome, residue, product. stagnation, fixity, immobility, indisturbance†. effect, consequence, resultant, upshot, issue. inertness, quiescence &c H0238. remainder, residuum, ditchwater†, bilgewater†, offscourings†, outscourings†, draff†. the neutral result, the aggregate.
Verbs: come to rest, settle, subside, stop, halt, stand still, wind down, run down. be quiescent, lie still. remain, stay, stop &c H0009. cease, pause.
Adjective: at rest, still, static, quiescent, settled, stationary, inert, motionless, spent. resting, equilibrated.
Adverbs: at rest, at a standstill, at last. in equilibrium.
Phrases: the dust settles; to come to a standstill.
Hegel definition: The product of the mechanical process is, formally, the object as a determinate thing, the process dying out in rest. But the determinateness also withdraws into itself, so that the object becomes an objective singular and the semblance of a self-standing singularity set against universal substance is sublated. This reflected oneness is an individual self-standing unity, the centre; and the universality that particularizes itself from within, a rational fate, is law.
Hegel texts:
The Science of Logic
· The Doctrine of the Concept › Mechanism › The mechanical process › The product of the mechanical process
Hegel citations:
This resulting immanent reflection, the objective oneness of the objects, is now a oneness which is an individual self-subsistence – the center.
— The Science of Logic, The mechanical process › The product of the mechanical process (tr. di Giovanni)
Secondly, the reflection of negativity is the universality which is not a fate standing over against determinateness, but a rational fate, immanently determined – a universality that particularizes itself from within, the difference that remains at rest and fixed in the unstable particularity of the objects and their process; it is the law.
— The Science of Logic, The mechanical process › The product of the mechanical process (tr. di Giovanni)

Head: Absolute Mechanism
Path: 一. Logic › 3. Doctrine of the Concept › ii. Objectivity › α. Mechanism › c. Absolute Mechanism
Gloss: A mechanical system organized around a centre, as a solar system.

Hegel definition: Absolute, or free, mechanism is the totality in which centre, relative centres and dependent objects each serve as the middle term of one of three syllogisms. Hegel finds the same threefold structure in government, individual citizens and their needs. Merely external order passes into immanent determination, that is, law.

Head: The Centre
Path: 一. Logic › 3. Doctrine of the Concept › ii. Objectivity › α. Mechanism › c. Absolute Mechanism › i. The Centre

Phrases: the centre cannot hold [Yeats]; all roads lead to Rome; the centre of gravity; the hub of the universe.
Hegel definition: The centre is the empty manifold of objects gathered into objective singularity, the self-determining middle point that is their objective universality, their pervading immanent essence. In nature it is the central body, genus of the single bodies, toward which they strive and in union with which they rest, though this unity remains an ought. In spiritual things the centre takes higher forms, but the unity of the concept with its reality must there too be fundamental.
Hegel texts:
The Science of Logic
· The Doctrine of the Concept › Mechanism › Absolute mechanism › The center
Hegel citations:
In the material world it is the central body which is the genus or rather the individualized universality of the single objects and their mechanical process.
— The Science of Logic, Absolute mechanism › The center (tr. di Giovanni)
In things spiritual the center, and the union with it, assume higher forms; but the unity of the concept and the reality of that unity, which is here in a first instance mechanical centrality, must there too constitute the fundamental determination.
— The Science of Logic, Absolute mechanism › The center (tr. di Giovanni)

Head: Law
Path: 一. Logic › 3. Doctrine of the Concept › ii. Objectivity › α. Mechanism › c. Absolute Mechanism › ii. Law
Gloss: The principle that holds a mechanical system in order.
Hegelian gloss: The objective universal become the immanent principle of the system: law, the soul of the object.
Nouns: law; law of the system, governing principle, organizing principle, regulative principle, rule, order, regulation, norm, constitution, code; immanent law, internal order; regularity &c H0126. principle, order of things, normal state, natural state. canon, formula. statute, canon &c H0775, ordinance. ordering principle, free necessity. lawfulness. thirdness [Peirce].
Verbs: govern, order, rule, regulate, organize, determine, direct. methodize, systematize, coordinate, settle, fix. guide.
Adjective: lawful, regular, orderly, governing, regulative, constitutive, normative, immanent. conformable to rule, regular &c H0232, well regulated. uniform. methodical, systematic. lawlike, ordering.
Adverbs: by law, lawfully, in order, according to rule. methodically, systematically, by clockwork.
Foreign: Greek: nomos; Arabic: sunna; Sanskrit: dharma, ṛta; Chinese: li, fa.
Phrases: order is heaven's first law [Pope]; the law of the land; laid down in law.
Hegel definition: Law is the determinateness of the self-moving principle in which centrality, now opposed to an externality posited as not existing in and for itself, differentiates itself while remaining self-identical. It is the real ideality, the soul of the objective totality. Dead mechanism, which ends in rest, shows at best a uniformity that is a rule but not a law; only free mechanism has law, which as the source of its own differences is free necessity.
Hegel texts:
The Science of Logic
· The Doctrine of the Concept › Mechanism › Absolute mechanism › The law
Hegel citations:
This real ideality is the soul of the hitherto developed objective totality
— The Science of Logic, Absolute mechanism › The law (tr. di Giovanni)
This uniformity is indeed a rule, but not law. Only free mechanism has a law, the determination proper to pure individuality or to the concept existing for itself.
— The Science of Logic, Absolute mechanism › The law (tr. di Giovanni)

Head: Transition of Mechanism
Path: 一. Logic › 3. Doctrine of the Concept › ii. Objectivity › α. Mechanism › c. Absolute Mechanism › iii. Transition of Mechanism
Gloss: The passage of mechanism beyond purely external relations.
Hegelian gloss: Mechanism whose self-determination is law, and which passes beyond indifferent externality into chemism.
Nouns: transition of mechanism; passage beyond externality, inner tendency, orientation, self-relation of the object; breakdown of indifference. the passage out of mechanism, the sublation of externality, the transition to chemism, the law become immanent.
Verbs: pass beyond, outgrow, transcend, become inward. pass over, go beyond, sublate.
Adjective: transitional, tending, oriented. passing, self-sublating.
Adverbs: beyond the mechanical, toward affinity. in transition, beyond externality.
Phrases: more than a machine; beyond mere mechanism; to break the mould.
Hegel definition: In the transition of mechanism the law, soul of the objective totality, is still immersed in its body: free necessity that has not yet stepped over against its object. The objects have their self-standing only in the central unity and its laws, so that their dependence becomes a striving toward the object determinately opposed to them, and the centre itself falls apart into opposition. Centrality is now the reciprocally negative, tense relation of objects: free mechanism determines itself as chemism.
Hegel texts:
The Science of Logic
· The Doctrine of the Concept › Mechanism › Absolute mechanism › Transition of mechanism
Hegel citations:
This soul is however still immersed in its body.
— The Science of Logic, Absolute mechanism › Transition of mechanism (tr. di Giovanni)
Centrality, therefore, is now the reciprocally negative and tense connection of these objectivities. Thus free mechanism determines itself to chemism.
— The Science of Logic, Absolute mechanism › Transition of mechanism (tr. di Giovanni)

Path: 一. Logic › 3. Doctrine of the Concept › ii. Objectivity › β. Chemism
Gloss: The relation of things defined by their attraction to one another, which combine and change in combining, like chemical substances.
Hegelian gloss: Objects whose determinateness is their relation to their other, which they strive to complete.

Hegel definition: Chemism is the moment of judgement in objectivity, of difference become objective, and of process. Unlike mechanism it begins from objects whose determinateness and relation to others belong to their very nature. The name is not confined to chemistry proper: meteorological processes fall under it, as do the sex relation among living things and, as their formal basis, the spiritual relations of love and friendship.

Head: The Chemical Object
Path: 一. Logic › 3. Doctrine of the Concept › ii. Objectivity › β. Chemism › a. The Chemical Object
Gloss: A thing whose nature lies in its affinity for another.
Hegelian gloss: An object which is, in its own being, the contradiction of its one-sidedness with its whole nature, and strives to sublate it.

Verbs: crave, lack, need, tend toward, strive for, seek out. tend, strive toward, attract, seek its other.
Adjective: reactive, polar, incomplete, one-sided, acid, alkaline, basic, needy. chemical, affine, tensed, biased, non-indifferent, disquiparant†.
Adverbs: in tension, toward the other. by affinity, toward its other.
Phrases: one half seeking its other half [Plato]; drawn to its other; made for each other.
Hegel definition: The chemical object differs from the mechanical in that its determinateness, and with it its relation to another and the manner of that relation, belong to its nature. Implicitly the whole concept, yet existing one-sidedly, it cannot be understood from itself, since the being of one such object is the being of another. It is thus a contradiction between its immediate existence and its concept, which gives it the necessity and drive to sublate its one-sidedness in a real whole.
Hegel texts:
The Science of Logic
· The Doctrine of the Concept › Chemism › The chemical object
Hegel citations:
Accordingly, a chemical object is not comprehensible from itself, and the being of one object is the being of another.
— The Science of Logic, Chemism › The chemical object (tr. di Giovanni)
Since in this way the object is implicitly the whole concept, it has within it the necessity and the impulse to sublate its opposed, one-sided subsistence, and to bring itself in existence to the real whole which it is according to its concept.
— The Science of Logic, Chemism › The chemical object (tr. di Giovanni)

Head: The Chemical Process
Path: 一. Logic › 3. Doctrine of the Concept › ii. Objectivity › β. Chemism › b. The Chemical Process

Verbs: react, combine, unite, bond, fuse, merge, neutralize, synthesize, catalyse, dissolve, precipitate. amalgamate, blend. liquefy, resolve.
Adjective: reactive, combinatory, synthetic, neutralizing, catalytic, solvent. analytical, resolvent. chemical, combinative.
Adverbs: in combination, in solution, by reaction. chemically, by neutralization.
Foreign: Latin: menstruum, solve et coagula [dissolve and coagulate]; Greek: hieros gamos [sacred marriage].
Phrases: solve et coagula [Lat.]; to cancel each other out; neutral ground.
Hegel definition: The chemical process starts from objects in tension with one another, their affinity, each striving to sublate its own one-sidedness and so the other's, to produce a reality adequate to the concept. They meet in a medium of communication, water among bodies, and in spirit the sign and language. Their opposed independence is sublated and tension blunted in a tranquil neutrality, where the process dies out until something external rekindles it.
Hegel texts:
The Science of Logic
· The Doctrine of the Concept › Chemism › The process
Hegel citations:
In the realm of bodies, water fulfills the function of this medium; in that of spirit, inasmuch as there is in it an analog of such a relation, the sign in general, and language more specifically, can be regarded as fulfilling it.
— The Science of Logic, Chemism › The process (tr. di Giovanni)
Their prior self-subsistent determinateness is thus sublated in the union that conforms to the concept, which is one and the same in both; their opposition and tension are thereby blunted, with the result that in this reciprocal complementation the striving attains its tranquil neutrality.
— The Science of Logic, Chemism › The process (tr. di Giovanni)

Head: Transition of Chemism
Path: 一. Logic › 3. Doctrine of the Concept › ii. Objectivity › β. Chemism › c. Transition of Chemism
Gloss: The passage beyond the neutral product of combination.
Hegelian gloss: The neutral product separated again into differents; chemism thereby frees the concept and passes into purpose.
Nouns: transition of chemism; exhaustion of reaction, spent reaction, end of tension, neutrality; passage to purpose, emergence of purposiveness. the passage out of chemism, the sublation of the neutral product, the transition to teleology, the freed concept, the emergence of purpose. decomposition.
Verbs: exhaust, spend, neutralize, settle, pass beyond. pass over, go beyond, sublate, free itself.
Adjective: spent, neutral, exhausted, inert. transitional, passing, self-sublating.
Adverbs: at the end, past the reaction. in transition, beyond neutrality.
Foreign: German: Zweckmäßigkeit.
Phrases: the fire burns out; to break apart again; to take a new turn.
Hegel definition: In the transition of chemism it appears as the first negation of indifferent objectivity, still burdened with the immediate independence and externality of its object. It forms a totality of three syllogisms, running from neutrality through disruption to the concept that posits its own presupposition, but because of that immediacy they fall apart. As they sublate the externality, the concept is freed to exist for itself, and so becomes purpose.
Hegel texts:
The Science of Logic
· The Doctrine of the Concept › Chemism › Transition of chemism
Hegel citations:
Chemism is itself the first negation of the indifferent objectivity and of the externality of determinateness; it is still burdened, therefore, by the immediate self-subsistence of the object and with externality.
— The Science of Logic, Chemism › Transition of chemism (tr. di Giovanni)
Yet, on account of the immediacy and externality by which the chemical objectivity is still determined, these three syllogisms fall apart.
— The Science of Logic, Chemism › Transition of chemism (tr. di Giovanni)

Head: Teleology
Path: 一. Logic › 3. Doctrine of the Concept › ii. Objectivity › γ. Teleology
Gloss: The relation of means to end; purpose and its fulfilment.
Hegelian gloss: The concept existing for itself, the end, which realizes itself in the object through means.

Adjective: teleological, purposive, purposeful, goal-directed, goal-oriented, intentional, designed, final, instrumental, functional, utilitarian. intended, bound for.
Adverbs: purposely, on purpose, by design, intentionally, in order to, so as to, for the sake of, to the end that, with a view to. with a view, in order that, for the purpose of. designedly. teleologically, purposively.

Hegel definition: Teleology treats purpose, the concept in free concrete existence, set against mechanism and chemism, both of which belong to natural necessity. One of Kant’s greatest services to philosophy was in drawing the distinction between relative or external purposiveness and internal purposiveness; in the latter he opened up the concept of life, the idea
— The Science of Logic, Teleology (tr. di Giovanni)

Hegel definition: The subjective purpose is the concept as an essential striving and impulse to posit itself externally. Hegel definition: The realized purpose is reached when the purpose's activity through its means ceases to be external, sublating itself as such, so that the object merges with it in the unity of the concept. In that the purpose does not act on the object directly but interposes another object, letting mechanical and chemical processes work upon one another under its dominance, lies what Hegel calls the cunning of reason; direct action upon the object may by contrast be regarded as violence.

But that the purpose posits itself in a mediate connection with the object, and between itself and this object inserts another object, may be regarded as the cunning of reason.

Their process in this connection is none other than the mechanical or chemical one; the previous relations come up again in this objective externality, but under the dominance of purpose.
— The Science of Logic, Teleology › The realized purpose (tr. di Giovanni)

Hegel definition: The idea is the adequate concept, the objectively true or the true as such: whatever has truth has it by virtue of its idea. Hegel keeps Kant's reclaiming of the word for the concept of reason, the unconditioned, but rejects the view that an idea, because nothing in the senses is congruent with it, lacks actuality or truth. It is the unity of concept and objectivity, appearing first as life, then as cognition, then as the absolute idea.

Hegel definition: The idea of the true is the theoretical idea, in which the subjective idea is first the impulse to sublate its subjectivity by filling itself with the content of a presupposed world, and to find its identity with itself in the object. The concept is certain of itself, while the world counts as inessential. Truth here means truth for the subjective concept, in knowledge; this cognition attains only a neutral synthesis of what stays separate.
Hegel texts:
The Science of Logic
· The Doctrine of the Concept › The idea of cognition › The idea of the true
Hegel citations:
At first the subjective idea is impulse.
— The Science of Logic, The idea of cognition › The idea of the true (tr. di Giovanni)
Consequently this impulse is the impulse of truth in so far as the truth is in cognition, and therefore of truth in its strict sense as theoretical idea.
— The Science of Logic, The idea of cognition › The idea of the true (tr. di Giovanni)

Head: Analytic Cognition
Path: 一. Logic › 3. Doctrine of the Concept › iii. Idea › β. The Idea of Cognition › a. The Idea of the True › i. Analytic Cognition
Gloss: Knowing that breaks a given thing down into its elements; analysis.
Hegelian gloss: Cognition that resolves the given concrete into abstract determinations and the form of universality.
Nouns: analytic cognition; analysis, resolution, decomposition, dissection, breakdown, reduction, abstraction, isolation of elements, anatomizing, parsing, unpacking; reductionism. sifting, dissolution, disintegration, Baconian method†. analytic method.
Verbs: analyse, decompose, dissect, anatomize, break down, resolve, parse, unpack, reduce, isolate, take apart. scrutinize, sift, winnow, thresh out. decompound, resolve into its elements, unravel, disentangle, take to pieces.
Adjective: analytic, analytical, dissecting, resolutive, reductive, abstractive. resolvent, separative.
Adverbs: analytically, element by element, piece by piece.
Foreign: Greek: analusis, aphairesis [abstraction by subtraction] [Aristotle]; French: abstrait; German: Abstraktion, Entbildung; Latin: abstractio, ablatio, absolutio, abnegatio, separata, abstracta.
Phrases: we murder to dissect [Wordsworth]; to break it down; to take apart.
Hegel definition: Analytic cognition is the first premise of the syllogism of cognition, the immediate communication of the concept, in which mediation does not yet belong to it. Its principle is abstract identity, excluding transition into an other. Starting from a presupposed concrete subject matter, it brings out conceptual determinations immediately contained there. To say that analysis only explicates what is already in the object is one-sided.
Hegel texts:
The Science of Logic
· The Doctrine of the Concept › The idea of cognition › The idea of the true › Analytic cognition
Hegel citations:
The specific difference of analytic cognition is already established by the fact that, since it is the first premise of the whole syllogism, mediation does not as yet belong to it; analytic cognition is rather the immediate communication of the concept, a communication that does not as yet contain otherness and in which activity divests itself of its negativity.
— The Science of Logic, The idea of the true › Analytic cognition (tr. di Giovanni)
Accordingly, analytic cognition has in general this identity for its principle, and the transition into an other, the linking of different terms is excluded from it and from its activity.
— The Science of Logic, The idea of the true › Analytic cognition (tr. di Giovanni)

Head: Synthetic Cognition
Path: 一. Logic › 3. Doctrine of the Concept › iii. Idea › β. The Idea of Cognition › a. The Idea of the True › ii. Synthetic Cognition
Gloss: Knowing that connects the elements of a thing into a coherent whole; synthesis.
Hegelian gloss: Cognition which grasps what is in its necessity, moving through definition, division and theorem.
Nouns: synthetic cognition; synthesis, combination, composition, construction, integration, unification, connection, systematization, building up, putting together. union, incorporation, amalgamation, embodiment, fusion. process of reasoning, chain of reasoning, deduction. constitution, combination &c H0298, comprehension. link, bond of union, copula. production, formation, organization. synthetic method.
Verbs: synthesize, combine, compose, construct, integrate, unify, connect, systematize, put together, build up. constitute, form, make up. join, unite, conjoin, associate. incorporate, amalgamate, embody, blend, fuse, consolidate, coalesce.
Adjective: synthetic, synthetical, integrative, constructive, compositional, systematic, connective. combinative.
Adverbs: synthetically, systematically, all together.
Foreign: Greek: synthesis; French: piece together.
Phrases: putting two and two together; to put it all together; to join the dots.
Hegel definition: Synthetic cognition aims to comprehend what is, grasping the manifold determinations in their unity, and so seeks necessity; it is the second premise, connecting the diverse as such. Its identity is still inner, its determinations external to one another, and the singular content is something it finds. Though it transforms the objective world into concepts, it gives it only the form, and proves necessity as that of its own cognition, not from the concept.
Hegel texts:
The Science of Logic
· The Doctrine of the Concept › The idea of cognition › The idea of the true › Synthetic cognition
Hegel citations:
Synthetic cognition aims at the comprehension of what is, that is, at grasping the manifoldness of determinations in their unity.
— The Science of Logic, The idea of the true › Synthetic cognition (tr. di Giovanni)
Consequently, although this cognition transforms the objective world into concepts, what it gives to it in accordance with conceptual determinations is only the form
— The Science of Logic, The idea of the true › Synthetic cognition (tr. di Giovanni)

Head: Definition
Path: 一. Logic › 3. Doctrine of the Concept › iii. Idea › β. The Idea of Cognition › a. The Idea of the True › ii. Synthetic Cognition › 1. Definition
Gloss: A statement of what a thing is, giving its kind and its distinguishing mark.
Hegelian gloss: The given object brought into the form of the concept: genus and specific difference.

Foreign: Latin: definitio, genus proximum et differentia specifica, ex definitione, connotatio, consignificatio, nota; Greek: horismos, horos; Arabic: ḥadd [definition]; Sanskrit: lakṣaṇa [defining mark]; German: Merkmal [characteristic mark] [Kant, Frege], Konnotation; French: marque distinctive, marque, note; Spanish: marca.
Phrases: omnis definitio in iure periculosa est [Lat.]; definitio fit per genus proximum et differentiam specificam [Lat.]; genus and difference.
Hegel definition: Definition reduces the subject matter to its concept, abstracting from the externalities of its concrete existence, and apprehends it as a determinate universal, simplifying the wealth that description collects for representation. Its content is given and contingent, and there is no principle for deciding which features belong to the concept and which to external reality, though for products of purposive activity the purpose readily supplies the definition.
Hegel texts:
The Science of Logic
· The Doctrine of the Concept › The idea of cognition › The idea of the true › Synthetic cognition › Definition
Hegel citations:
Description is for representation; it collects this extra content that belongs to reality. But definition reduces this wealth of manifold determinations of the intuited existence to its simplest moments
— The Science of Logic, Synthetic cognition › Definition (tr. di Giovanni)
There is in fact no principle, therefore, for determining which aspects of the subject matter are to be regarded as belonging to its conceptual determination and which only to its external reality.
— The Science of Logic, Synthetic cognition › Definition (tr. di Giovanni)

Head: Division
Path: 一. Logic › 3. Doctrine of the Concept › iii. Idea › β. The Idea of Cognition › a. The Idea of the True › ii. Synthetic Cognition › 2. Division
Gloss: The sorting of a kind into its subkinds; classification.

Hegel definition: Division is the step after definition, moving toward the particular. It would need an immanent principle beginning from the universal, which synthetic cognition lacks, so that it takes its determinations from what is given, ordering empirical particulars and finding grounds of division by comparison. Its laws are therefore empty formal rules: it is indifferent to the exhaustion of a concept whether a dozen further species of parrot are discovered.
Hegel texts:
The Science of Logic
· The Doctrine of the Concept › The idea of cognition › The idea of the true › Synthetic cognition › Division
Hegel citations:
Because of the lack of a principle of self-determination, the only possible laws for this business of division consist in formal, empty rules that lead nowhere.
— The Science of Logic, Synthetic cognition › Division (tr. di Giovanni)
Actually, what is meant is that the determinateness of the concept should be exhausted; but there is nothing in an empirical manifold of species, internally void of determination, that contributes to this exhaustion whether few or many of them have been discovered
— The Science of Logic, Synthetic cognition › Division (tr. di Giovanni)

Head: Theorem
Path: 一. Logic › 3. Doctrine of the Concept › iii. Idea › β. The Idea of Cognition › a. The Idea of the True › ii. Synthetic Cognition › 3. Theorem

Phrases: quod erat demonstrandum [Lat.]; there is no royal road to geometry [attrib. Euclid]; Q.E.D.; it can be shown that.
Hegel definition: The theorem is the properly synthetic element of synthetic cognition, presenting the subject matter in its reality, in the conditions and forms of real existence, where the relations of its determinations are necessary. Because it joins diverse determinations whose unity is not yet posited, it needs proof. A first difficulty is to distinguish what belongs in the definition from what belongs in theorems, for which no principle lies ready, as Euclid's axiom of parallels shows.
Hegel texts:
The Science of Logic
· The Doctrine of the Concept › The idea of cognition › The idea of the true › Synthetic cognition › The theorem
Hegel citations:
Now according to the definition just given, the theorem is the properly synthetic element of a subject matter, because the relations of its determinacies are necessary, that is, are grounded in the inner identity of the concept.
— The Science of Logic, Synthetic cognition › The theorem (tr. di Giovanni)
The synthesis contained in the theorem no longer has, therefore, the form of the concept to justify it; it is a joining together of such as are diverse; consequently, the unity not yet thereby posited still remains to be demonstrated; here proof thus becomes necessary to this cognition itself.
— The Science of Logic, Synthetic cognition › The theorem (tr. di Giovanni)

Hegel definition: The idea of the good is the practical idea, the concept as determinate subject, certain of its own actuality and of the nullity of the given world, and impelled to realize itself in it. Hegel texts:

Hegel citations:
This determinateness which is in the concept, is equal to the concept, and entails a demand for singular external actuality, is the good.
— The Science of Logic, The idea of cognition › The idea of the good (tr. di Giovanni)
This idea is superior to the idea of cognition just considered, for it has not only the value of the universal but also of the absolutely actual.
— The Science of Logic, The idea of cognition › The idea of the good (tr. di Giovanni)

Head: The Absolute Idea
Path: 一. Logic › 3. Doctrine of the Concept › iii. Idea › γ. The Absolute Idea
Gloss: Thought that grasps itself as the whole of its own development; the method of reason, complete.
Hegelian gloss: The idea that knows itself, the concept of the idea as its own object: pure form, which is the method.
Nouns: the absolute idea; method, dialectical method, speculative method; the whole, totality, system, completion, consummation, self-knowledge of reason, thought thinking itself; the logical idea, the Logos; truth in and for itself; personality, pure personality. fulfillment, culmination. arrangement. all, sum total. the absolute method, the self-knowing idea, the idea thinking itself, the unity of the theoretical and practical idea, the speculative idea.
Verbs: complete, consummate, close, round off, comprehend the whole, know itself. accomplish, perfect. grasp itself, comprehend itself, think itself.
Adjective: absolute, total, complete, consummate, self-knowing, self-comprehending, methodical, systematic. entire, whole &c H0130.
Adverbs: absolutely, in and for itself, completely, as a whole. methodically.
Foreign: German: Methode, an und für sich; Greek: noēsis noēseōs; Arabic: al-ʿaql al-kullī [universal intellect]; Sanskrit: brahman, cit [pure consciousness]; Chinese: dao; Korean: jeoldae inyeom [absolute idea].
Phrases: the absolute idea alone is being, imperishable life, self-knowing truth, and is all truth [Hegel]; the truth is the whole [Hegel]; the alpha and omega.
Hegel definition: The absolute idea is the identity of the theoretical and the practical idea: the rational concept that in its reality rejoins only itself, free subjective concept with personality that is at the same time universality and cognition, with its other as its object. It alone is being, imperishable life and self-knowing truth. It is the sole content of philosophy, which shares that content with art and religion but apprehends it in the highest way, through the concept.
Hegel texts:
The Science of Logic
· The Doctrine of the Concept › The absolute idea
Hegel citations:
All the rest is error, confusion, opinion, striving, arbitrariness, and transitoriness; the absolute idea alone is being, imperishable life, self-knowing truth, and is all truth.
— The Science of Logic, The absolute idea (tr. di Giovanni)
Philosophy has the same content and the same purpose as art and religion, but it is the highest
— The Science of Logic, The absolute idea (tr. di Giovanni)

Hegel definition: The beginning of the method is an immediate in the element of thought, simple and universal: not an immediate of sense or representation, but something assumed and found. It has no other determinateness than that, and this is precisely what makes it deficient. Because the method is objective and immanent, the lack belongs to the beginning itself, which must therefore have the impulse to carry itself further: the universal is implicitly the concrete totality, not yet posited.

Hegel citations:
The beginning, therefore, has for the method no other determinateness than that of being the simple and universal; this is precisely the determinateness that makes it deficient.
— The Science of Logic, The absolute idea (tr. di Giovanni)
Where the method, however, is the objective and immanent form, the immediate character of the beginning must be a lack inherent in the beginning itself, which must be endowed with the impulse to carry itself further.
— The Science of Logic, The absolute idea (tr. di Giovanni)

Path: 一. Logic › 3. Doctrine of the Concept › iii. Idea › γ. The Absolute Idea › b. Advance
Gloss: The middle step of method: the unfolding of what was contained in the start.

Nouns: advance, progress, progression, procession, development, unfolding, explication, evolution, movement, course, march, onward movement, forward movement, headway, step, stage, phase; determinate negation; differentiation, diremption, judgment; immanent development. progressiveness, advancement. evolvement, unfoldment, eversion.

Hegel definition: The advance is the universal determining itself and becoming for itself, a singular and a subject, since only in its consummation is it the absolute. The concrete totality that begins already holds the beginning of development in it: as concrete it differentiates itself, and the method finds the determination of the universal within it. Through the negative of the negative it returns to immediacy, so that the form of the method may be counted as threefold or fourfold.
Hegel texts:
The Science of Logic
· The Doctrine of the Concept › The absolute idea
Hegel citations:
The advance is not, therefore, a kind of superfluity; this is what it would be if that which is at the beginning were already the absolute; the advance consists rather in this, that the universal determines itself and is the universal for itself, that is, equally a singular and a subject.
— The Science of Logic, The absolute idea (tr. di Giovanni)
This negativity is as self-sublating contradiction the restoration of the first immediacy, of simple universality; for the other of the other, the negative of the negative, is immediately the positive, the identical, the universal.
— The Science of Logic, The absolute idea (tr. di Giovanni)

Hegel definition: The end is the result in which the method returns to its beginning, restoring the first immediacy through sublated determinateness, as a system of totality. Each result is a new beginning, so that cognition rolls on from content to content, growing richer and more concrete. Hegel texts:

· The Doctrine of the Concept › The absolute idea
Hegel citations:

Hegel definition: Elasticity is cohesion displaying itself in motion, the totality of cohesion. A body gives way to another's violence while keeping its own character: its parts, mutually external, do violence and give way to one another, and being no less self-subsistent they sublate the negation suffered and reinstate themselves. Yielding and self-preservation outwardly are bound up with this inner activity.

— Encyclopedia §297 (tr. Miller)

Head: Physics of Total Individuality
Path: 二. Nature › 2. Physics › iii. Physics of Total Individuality
Gloss: The physics of bodies that give themselves a definite shape and set of properties.
Hegelian gloss: Bodies as total individuals, matter that forms itself from within: shape, specification and the chemical process.
Nouns: physics of total individuality; self-determining body, individual body, formed matter, figure, shape &c H0277, properties &c H0281. conformation, configuration, formation. the physics of the total individual, the self-shaping body, individual totality, shape properties and chemical process, the physical individual.
