Adjective: individual, formed, shaped, self-determining. total, self-shaping.
Adverbs: individually, in its own right. as total individual.
Phrases: each after its kind; to take shape.
Hegel definition: The physics of total individuality treats bodies as individuals whose centre is no longer a point matter merely seeks but a subjectivity immanent in it, with form-determinations developed from within outwards. Such individuality is for itself yet conditioned, involving relation to another, and as it develops these are sublated until it becomes in principle life.
Hegel texts:
The Philosophy of Nature
· §§308–336
Hegel citations:
Material individuality, being thus identical with itself in its development, is infinitely for itself, but is at the same time conditioned: it is the subjective totality, but at first only in immediate fashion.
— Encyclopedia §308 (tr. Miller)
Therefore, though infinitely for itself, it involves relationship to another
— Encyclopedia §308 (tr. Miller)

Hegel definition: The properties of bodies arise as the process of shaping passes into physical specification. Gloss: The behaviour of a body toward light.
Hegelian gloss: The body's relation to light as its own physical identity, which is transparency, refraction and colour.
Nouns: relation to light; optics, optical properties, behaviour toward light, opacity, translucency, reflectivity, refractivity, absorption, colour. transparency, refraction, reflection, lustre.
Verbs: reflect, refract, absorb, transmit, scatter, filter. darken.
Adjective: optical, opaque, translucent, transparent, reflective, refractive, absorbent. pellucid, lucid, diaphanous, limpid, clear, crystalline, clear as crystal, vitreous.
Adverbs: optically. in the light.
Foreign: Arabic: ʿilm al-manāẓir [optics].
Phrases: light and its affections; in a good light; to see through.
Hegel definition: The body's relation to light is the first determination of shaped corporeality. Shape's self-identical selfhood, its abstract manifestation of itself as simple individuality, is light; but shape is not itself luminous, so this property is a relation to light: transparency in the pure crystal, then refraction, then the darkening of the body from which colour arises.
Hegel texts:
The Philosophy of Nature
· §§317–320
Hegel citations:
The first determination of shaped corporeality is its self-identical selfhood (Selbstischkeit), the abstract self-manifestation of itself as an indeterminate, simple individuality—Light.
— Encyclopedia §317 (tr. Miller)
But shape as such is not luminous, for this property is (previous §) a relationship to light.
— Encyclopedia §317 (tr. Miller)

Head: Refraction
Path: 二. Nature › 2. Physics › iii. Physics of Total Individuality › β. Properties of Bodies (Specification of the Individual Body) › a. Relation to Light › ii. Refraction
Gloss: The bending of light as it passes from one transparent medium into another.
Hegelian gloss: Light passing between two media of different density, whose relation is seen in the displacement of the image.
Nouns: refraction; bending of light, deflection, diffraction, dispersion, double refraction, birefringence, refractive index, lens, prism, spectacles, magnifying glass, distortion, apparent bending, deflexion†, deflexure†, megascope†, tienoscope†. deviation. reflection, refractivity. diffraction grating, beam splitter, half-wave plate, quarter-wave plate. meniscus. flexure, flexion, bending, inflection, curvity†, curvation†, incurvature†, incurvity†, incurvation†, flection†, conflexure†, concameration†, recurvity†, recurvation†. dioptrics, catoptrics†. glasses, specs. refrangibility.
Verbs: refract, bend, deflect, diffract, disperse, distort, angle, incurvate†, concamerate†, intervert†. inflect.
Adjective: refractive, refracting, refringent, dioptric, birefringent, prismatic. refracted. sloping.
Adverbs: obliquely, at an angle, aslant. by refraction.
Foreign: Latin: refractio.
Phrases: the bent oar in the water; bent out of shape; a broken stick in water.
Hegel definition: Refraction concerns the first determinateness of the transparent medium, specific gravity, which shows itself only in comparison with a medium of different density. An image seen through water into air is displaced, as if the volume of air containing the water were contracted by the water's density. The stick that appears broken is a merely sensuous description; the physical meaning is far harder.
Hegel texts:
The Philosophy of Nature
· §§318–319
Hegel citations:
The volume of water with the image in it is thus seen in the transparent air as if the same volume of air in which the volume of water is placed had the greater specific gravity, that of water, i.e. as if the volume of air were contracted into a correspondingly smaller space—so-called refraction.
— Encyclopedia §318 (tr. Miller)
The expression refraction of light is primarily a sensuous description, correct in so far as, e.g., a stick held in water, as is well known, appears to be broken
— Encyclopedia §318, Remark (tr. Miller)

Foreign: Latin: experimentum crucis; French: arc-en-ciel; Sanskrit: indradhanus [Indra's bow].

Hegel definition: Prismatic colour is produced when the prism acts as a means of external obscuration, dimming the light both by its edges and by its shape, whose thickness varies, so that transparency is lessened unevenly. Following Goethe, Hegel says that in the prism the bright overrides the dark or the reverse, each acting independently while displaced.
Hegel texts:
The Philosophy of Nature
· §320
Hegel citations:
The most celebrated means for producing external obscuration is the prism, whose dimming action stems from two factors: first, from its outer boundary as such, its edges, and secondly, from its prismatic shape, from the variable transverse diameter between the whole spread of one side and the opposite edge.
— Encyclopedia §320, Remark (tr. Miller)
He says that in the prism, the bright overrides the dark or vice versa: so that the bright, though modified by the dark, still acts independently qua bright, though dimmed, and (in the case of the prism), disregarding the common displacement, remains in its own place at the very time of its displacement.
— Encyclopedia §320, Remark (tr. Miller)

Head: Entoptic Color
Path: 二. Nature › 2. Physics › iii. Physics of Total Individuality › β. Properties of Bodies (Specification of the Individual Body) › a. Relation to Light › iii. Color › 2. Vision › a. Entoptic Color
Gloss: Color produced inside a transparent body by its internal structure.
Hegelian gloss: Colour produced within a transparent body by its own inner structure and tension.
Nouns: entoptic colour; colour within a transparent body, interference colours, polarization colours, stress patterns, photoelasticity; inner coloration. internal colour, polarization colour, the colours of double refraction, entoptic figures, Seebeck, Goethe's entoptic colours. birefringence.
Verbs: show colour within. polarize, show within.
Adjective: entoptic, internal, interference. polarized, birefringent.
Adverbs: within, inly†. within the body, internally, withinside†.
Phrases: colour in the heart of glass; colours within; a play of light.
Hegel definition: Entoptic colours arise within a transparent body whose darkening principle is brittleness: brittle glass, though perfectly transparent, is their condition. Brittleness is here an immaterial punctiform determinateness, active only as a force, which becomes outwardly existent as opacity when a transparent crystal is reduced to powder, and so is the inner beginning of darkening.
Hegel texts:
The Philosophy of Nature
· §320
Hegel citations:
(It is a familiar fact that brittle glass, though perfectly transparent, is the condition for the entoptic colours.)
— Encyclopedia §320 (tr. Miller)
The interesting fact about the entoptic colours is that the darkening principle which here is brittleness, is an immaterial punctiform determinateness (i.e. active only as a force), which exists outwardly and produces opacity when a transparent crystal is reduced to powder
— Encyclopedia §320, Remark (tr. Miller)

Head: Epoptic Color
Path: 二. Nature › 2. Physics › iii. Physics of Total Individuality › β. Properties of Bodies (Specification of the Individual Body) › a. Relation to Light › iii. Color › 2. Vision › b. Epoptic Color
Gloss: Color produced at the surface of a thin film or plate, as on a soap bubble.
Hegelian gloss: Colour formed on the surface of thin plates and films, by their mutual pressure.
Nouns: epoptic colour; thin-film colour, iridescence, interference colours, Newton's rings, soap-bubble colours, oil-slick sheen, nacre, mother-of-pearl, opalescence. semitransparency, translucency, film. spectrum, rainbow, iris. surface colour, interference colour, the colours of the soap bubble.
Verbs: iridesce, shimmer, play.
Adjective: epoptic, iridescent, nacreous, opalescent, pearly, shimmering, shot. opaline†, prismatic, gorge de pigeon, chatoyant†, irisated†, pavonine†. translucent.
Adverbs: iridescently. on the surface.
Phrases: the colours of a soap bubble; like a soap bubble; oil on water.
Hegel definition: Epoptic colours, allied to the entoptic, have a mechanical origin: when a lens is pressed on a glass plate the point of contact is first black and then spreads into rings of different colours. Here merely mechanical pressure produces the colour, and pressure is nothing but an alteration of cohesion in the nearest parts.
Hegel texts:
The Philosophy of Nature
· §320
Hegel citations:
Allied to this phenomenon are the epoptic colours, which have a mechanical origin: when a lens is pressed on a glass plate (see above, pp. 206), the point of contact is at first black, but as the pressure is increased, the point spreads out into a number of rings of different colours, green, red, yellow.
— Encyclopedia §320, Addition (tr. Miller)
Here, it is merely the mechanical pressure which produces the colours; and this pressure is nothing but an alteration of cohesion in the nearest parts
— Encyclopedia §320, Addition (tr. Miller)

Head: Paroptic Color

Hegel definition: Paroptic colours appear when the interruption of cohesion goes further than in the epoptic: lamellae and fine cracks are produced in glass, and especially in calcite, where the colour often becomes iridescent. Hegel texts:

· §320
Hegel citations:

— Encyclopedia §320, Addition (tr. Miller)
Here a darkening results from the transparent body's being pressed to the point of an actual breakdown in its togetherness.
— Encyclopedia §320, Addition (tr. Miller)

Hegel definition: The plant's inner structure is quite simple, consisting of cells, spiral vessels and tubes. Its general texture is cellular tissue, which separates into woody fibres or spiral vessels on one side and the vessels that carry the plant's circulation on the other. This separation is itself an immediate production, generally a mere multiplication.
Hegel texts:
The Philosophy of Nature
· §346
Hegel citations:
Consequently, the inner physiological construction of the plant is also quite simple.
— Encyclopedia §346, Addition (tr. Miller)
This separation of the plant in its inner structure, the production of spiral vessels, etc., this, too, is an immediate production, generally a mere multiplication.
— Encyclopedia §346, Addition (tr. Miller)

Head: Parenchyma
Path: 二. Nature › 3. Organics › ii. Plant Nature › α. The Plant's Process of Formation › a. Formation as Such › ii. Cellular Tissue and Vessels › 1. Parenchyma

Phrases: omnis cellula e cellula [Lat.] [Virchow].
Hegel definition: The general texture of the plant is cellular tissue, made up, as in the animal organism, of small cells, a universal product of animal and vegetable life. In the botanical account Hegel quotes, its regular, loose, spongy form with broad cells is the parenchyma, found especially in bark and pith, unlike the tight, fibrous bast with its narrow cells.
Hegel texts:
The Philosophy of Nature
· §346
Hegel citations:
The general texture of the plant is formed by cellular tissue which, as in the animal organism, consists of small cells; it is the universal animal and vegetable product—the fibrous constituent (Moment).
— Encyclopedia §346, Addition (tr. Miller)

Head: Bast and Spiral Vessels

The Philosophy of Nature
· §346

— Encyclopedia §346, Addition (tr. Miller)
[T]he second, more intimate diremption is the plant's own separation of itself into woody fibres or active spiral vessels and into other vessels which Prof. Schultz has called 'vital vessels'
— Encyclopedia §346, Addition (tr. Miller)

Path: 二. Nature › 3. Organics › ii. Plant Nature › α. The Plant's Process of Formation › a. Formation as Such › iii. Saps

Hegel definition: The saps carry the plant's inner formation. Where the spiral vessels first absorb moisture just as it is, the second function is to elaborate the sap into organic form, which the plant, having no stomach, does immediately. Hegel texts:
The Philosophy of Nature
· §346

— Encyclopedia §346, Addition (tr. Miller)

The Philosophy of Nature
· §346

— Encyclopedia §346, Addition (tr. Miller)

— Encyclopedia §346, Addition (tr. Miller)

— Encyclopedia §346, Addition (tr. Miller)

Head: The Plant's Process of Assimilation

Phrases: the plant drinks the sun; to draw nourishment; to drink in.
Hegel definition: The plant's assimilation is its self-specifying process outward, directly bound up with formation: the seed germinates only when stimulated from outside, and root and leaf are turned toward earth and water, light and air. Hegel texts:
The Philosophy of Nature
· §347
Hegel citations:

The Philosophy of Nature
· §347
Hegel citations:

— Encyclopedia §347, Addition (tr. Miller)

The Philosophy of Nature
· §347
Hegel citations:
The specifying of air within the plant in the air-process is manifested by the plant giving out the air again as a specific gas, for, in appropriating the elemental matter, it differentiates it.
— Encyclopedia §347, Addition (tr. Miller)

— Encyclopedia §347, Addition (tr. Miller)

Hegel definition: The practical process begins with a division within the organism, the feeling of externality as negation of the subject, which is also its self-certainty against that negation: a feeling of lack and the urge to remove it. Head: Breathing, Cutaneous Process, and Thirst
Path: 二. Nature › 3. Organics › iii. Animal Nature › β. The Animal's Process of Assimilation › b. Practical Process › ii. Breathing, Cutaneous Process, and Thirst

Hegel definition: The mammals are the perfect animals: they have breasts, four articulated limbs and every organ developed. Because they suckle their young from themselves, they come to feel the unity of one individual with another, the genus, which exists in the offspring, though in nature this unity falls back into single individuals. They are classed truly not by marks we pick out but by the animal's own weapons, its teeth, feet and claws, by which it sets itself against its non-organic nature and shows itself a subject for itself. So there are four classes: animals with hands (man and the monkey), animals with claws (beasts of prey, rodents, bats, sloths), animals with fins (the Cetacea) and animals with hoofs (swine, elephants, cattle, horses), which can be tamed to work for man. Further subdivision is left to the contingency of nature, above all to climate.
Hegel texts:
The Philosophy of Nature
· §370 and Addition: The classes of mammals by their weapons, after Lamarck
· §368 Addition: The classification of animals in general
· §362 Addition: The skin and its formations
Hegel citations:
Mammals have breasts, four articulated extremities, and all their organs are developed. Because they have breasts, they suckle and feed their young from themselves. These animals thus attain to the feeling of the unity of the one individual with the other, to the feeling of the genus, which achieves an existence in the progeny in which the two individuals are precisely the genus, even though, in Nature, this unity of the individual with the genus falls back again into singularity.
— Encyclopedia §370, Addition (tr. Petry)
Of all animals, monkeys are the most docile (bildsamsten) and have most affection for their young; the satisfied sexual instinct persists for them in objective form, for they have passed over into an other, and in caring for the needs of their young, they have the higher, disinterested intuition of this unity.
— Encyclopedia §370, Addition (tr. Petry)
In mammals, the skin continues its growth into wool, hair, bristles, spines (in the hedgehog), and even into scales and armour (in the armadillo). Man, on the other hand, has a skin which is smooth, pure, and much more animalized and which also sheds anything of an osseous nature.
— Encyclopedia §370, Addition (tr. Petry)
Further essential classifications have been based on the behaviour of animals as individuals to other animals: that is, on their teeth, feet, claws, and beaks. It was a correct instinct which led to the choice of these parts, for it is by them that animals themselves distinguish themselves from other animals: if the difference is to be a true one, it must not be simply a sign which we have picked out, but a difference of the animal itself. By opposing itself as an individual to its non-organic nature through its weapons, the animal demonstrates that it is a subject for itself.
— Encyclopedia §370, Addition (tr. Petry)
On this basis, the classes of mammals are very accurately distinguished: αα. into animals whose feet are hands, man and the monkey (the monkey is a satire on man, a satire which it must amuse him to see if he does not take himself too seriously but is willing to laugh at himself); ββ. into animals whose extremities are claws, dogs, wild beasts like the lion, the king of beasts; γγ. into rodents, in which the teeth are specially shaped; δδ. into cheiroptera, which have a membrane stretched between the toes, as occurs even in some rodents (these animals come nearer to dogs and monkeys); εε. into sloths, in which some of the toes are missing altogether and have become claws; ζζ. into animals with fin-like limbs, the Cetacea; ηη. into hoofed animals, like swine, elephants (which have a trunk), horned cattle, horses, etc. The strength of these animals resides in the upper part of the body, most of them can be tamed to work; and the formation of the extremities shows a special relationship to the animals' non-organic nature.
— Encyclopedia §370, Addition (tr. Petry)
If the animals under ββ, γγ, δδ, εε are grouped together as animals with claws, then we have four classes: 1. Animals with hands, 2. with claws, 3. with hooves, which work for man, 4. with fins.
— Encyclopedia §370, Addition (tr. Petry)
[Lamarck, quoted:] The unguiculate mammals have four limbs, flat or pointed claws at the tips of their toes which latter do not envelop the claws. The limbs are, in general, fitted for seizing, or at least hanging on to, objects. These animals include those which are most highly organized. The hoofed mammals (Ungulata) have four limbs, the toes of which are completely surrounded at their extremities by a rounded, horny substance called a hoof (sabot). Their feet can be used only for walking or running on the ground; they cannot be used for climbing trees, or for seizing an object or prey, or for attacking and rending other animals. They are completely herbivorous. The mammals without hooves have only two extremities, and these are very short and flat, and shaped like fins. Their toes, covered by skin, have neither claws nor hooves (corne); they are the least highly organized of all the mammals. They have neither a pelvis, nor hind legs; they swallow their food without masticating it; lastly, they usually live in water but come up to the surface to breathe air.
— Encyclopedia §370, Addition (tr. Petry)
As regards the further subdivisions, these must be left to the chance and contingency proper to Nature, that is, to be determined by external factors. Climate, however, still constitutes the great determining factor. In southern latitudes, the animal kingdom is particularized more according to differences of climate and country than it is in northern latitudes: thus the Asiatic and African elephants are essentially distinct from each other, while in America there are none; lions and tigers, etc., are similarly distinguished.
— Encyclopedia §370, Addition (tr. Petry)

Head: Waking and Sleeping
Path: 三. Spirit › 1. Subjective Spirit › i. Soul (Anthropology) › α. Natural Soul › b. Natural Changes › iii. Waking and Sleeping
Gloss: The alternation of the soul between conscious activity and rest.
Hegelian gloss: The soul's dividing itself from its natural immediacy: waking, its being-for-self, against sleep, its retreat into undivided substance.
Nouns: waking and sleeping; waking.

Hegel definition: Waking and sleeping are the alternation in which the individual soul distinguishes its being for itself from its mere being. Waking is the soul's own judgement, setting itself against its self-absorbed natural life as one natural state against another. Unlike the passing differences of the ages of life and the fixed difference of the sexes, this opposition is an enduring alternation that produces itself in one and the same individual, and its empty repetition points on to sensation.

Hegel definition: Sensation is the form in which mind stirs dully in its unconscious and unintellectual individuality. The waking soul finds within itself, as its own, the determinacies of the content of its sleeping nature; each is simply found, not produced, and yet is taken up into the soul's universality and made ideal. Everything in sensation is immediate, undeveloped in content and not yet set over against a subject as an object, and so it is limited and transient. Everything that emerges in consciousness and reason first appears in it.
Hegel texts:
The Philosophy of Mind
· §§399–402
Hegel citations:
Sensation is the form in which the mind weaves its sombre web in its unconscious and unintellectual individuality, where every determinacy is still immediate, posited in an undeveloped way both in its content and as an objective counterpart to the subject, belonging as it does to the subject's own most particular, natural peculiarity.
— Encyclopedia §400 (tr. Wallace and Miller, rev. Inwood)
Everything is in sensation, and, if you like, everything that emerges in the conscious mind and in reason has its source and origin in sensation; for source and origin just mean the first, most immediate manner in which something appears.
— Encyclopedia §400, Remark (tr. Wallace and Miller, rev. Inwood)

Head: The Senses
Path: 三. Spirit › 1. Subjective Spirit › i. Soul (Anthropology) › α. Natural Soul › c. Sensation › i. The Senses
Gloss: The faculties by which the soul receives sensation.
Hegelian gloss: The system of the bodily senses, through which the soul is determined from outside: the ideal, the real difference, and earthly totality.
Nouns: the senses; five senses, sense organs, faculties, sensorium, sight, hearing, smell, taste, touch; sixth sense. sensory faculties, the totality of the senses.
Verbs: see, hear, smell, taste, touch, feel, perceive. handle. sense, receive.
Adjective: sensory, sensuous, sensual, perceptual, sense-based. sensible, sensitive, aesthetic, perceptive, conscious &c H0646. sentient, sensorial.
Adverbs: through the senses, by the senses. sensorily.
Foreign: Latin: sensus; Greek: aisthēseis; Sanskrit: indriya [sense faculties].
Phrases: come to one's senses; the five senses; a sixth sense.
Hegel definition: The senses form the simple system of the specific bodily functions through which the sentient soul is determined from outside. Each is not tied to some single item but is a universal possibility of being determined, a whole circle of sensations. The five reduce to three classes answering to the moments of the concept: sight and hearing, the senses of physical ideality; smell and taste, the senses of real difference; and feeling, the sense of earthly totality. Around the centre of the sentient individual they arrange the distinctions of natural corporeality more simply.
Hegel texts:
The Philosophy of Mind
· §401
Hegel citations:
The senses form the simple system of specific corporeal functions
— Encyclopedia §401, Remark (tr. Wallace and Miller, rev. Inwood)
But the quintet of senses reduces quite naturally to three classes of senses. The first is formed by the senses of physical ideality, the second by those of real difference; in the third class falls the sense of earthly totality.
— Encyclopedia §401, Addition (tr. Wallace and Miller, rev. Inwood)

Head: Sight and Hearing
Path: 三. Spirit › 1. Subjective Spirit › i. Soul (Anthropology) › α. Natural Soul › c. Sensation › i. The Senses › 1. Sight and Hearing
Gloss: The senses that perceive at a distance.
Hegelian gloss: The senses of ideality, sight of physical light and hearing of the body's inner tremor.
Nouns: sight and hearing; the ideal senses, the theoretical senses, the distance senses, the eye and the ear, vision and audition. spy, sentinel &c H0662. hearing. covercle†.
Adjective: audiovisual, ideal.
Adverbs: by eye and ear, at a distance.
Foreign: Sanskrit: dṛṣṭi and śruti [seeing and hearing, also revelation].
Phrases: all eyes and ears; looking before and after [Hamlet]; thy rapt soul sitting in thine eyes [Milton]; full many a flower is born to blush unseen [Gray].
Hegel definition: Sight and hearing are the senses of physical ideality, the first class of senses. Because they sense the abstractly universal and ideal, their totality cannot be concrete but is divided between two moments: for sight the ideal takes the form of simply relating to itself, for hearing the form of producing itself through the negation of the material. Sight is related to space become physical, which is light, and hearing to time become physical, which is sound. Neither requires the direct contact with the object that taste does.
Hegel texts:
The Philosophy of Mind
· §401
Hegel citations:
Hence the first class embraces two senses—seeing and hearing. For seeing, the ideal takes the form of simply relating to itself, for hearing it takes the form of producing itself by the negation of the material.
— Encyclopedia §401, Addition (tr. Wallace and Miller, rev. Inwood)
Just as sight is related to space become physical, to light, so hearing is related to time become physical, to sound.
— Encyclopedia §401, Addition (tr. Wallace and Miller, rev. Inwood)

Hegel definition: Sight is the sense of the physical ideal that we call light, which is, as it were, space become physical, weightless and without inwardness, whose essence is to manifest its other. It is concerned only with this ideal element and with its darkening, that is, with colour. It lets things subsist calmly and relates itself only to their ideal side, so that its relation to them is theoretical and not yet practical, and for this it may be called the noblest sense. It is also very imperfect, since it gives a body only as surface and not at once as a spatial whole.
Hegel texts:
The Philosophy of Mind
· §401
Hegel citations:
Sight is the sense of the physical ideal that we call light.
— Encyclopedia §401, Addition (tr. Wallace and Miller, rev. Inwood)
In seeing we have, as it were, a merely theoretical, not yet a practical, relationship to things; for in seeing we let things subsist calmly as beings and relate ourselves only to their ideal side.
— Encyclopedia §401, Addition (tr. Wallace and Miller, rev. Inwood)
On the other hand, sight is a very imperfect sense because by it a body does not come to us immediately as a spatial totality, as body, always only as surface, only according to the two dimensions of width and height
— Encyclopedia §401, Addition (tr. Wallace and Miller, rev. Inwood)

Head: Hearing
Path: 三. Spirit › 1. Subjective Spirit › i. Soul (Anthropology) › α. Natural Soul › c. Sensation › i. The Senses › 1. Sight and Hearing › b. Hearing
Gloss: The sense of sound, which perceives the inner trembling of bodies.
Hegelian gloss: Gehör, the sense of the body's inward ideality: it perceives the tremor in which the body gives up its material subsistence as sound.
Nouns: hearing. deafness, hardness of hearing, surdity†, inaudibility, inaudibleness†, audition, ear, earlobe, lobe, lughole [Brit. Slang], lugs [Slang], earhole, eardrum, tympanum, cochlea, ear canal, inner ear, auricle, pinna.

Hegel definition: Hearing is the sense of the pure inwardness of the corporeal, as against sight, the sense of an ideality without inwardness. It is related to time become physical, to sound. Sound is the temporal positedness of a body: a vibration or mechanical tremor in which the body, without changing its place as a whole, moves only its parts, sets its inner spatiality down in time, lets its pure inwardness come forth and at once restores itself.
Hegel texts:

· §401
Hegel citations:
In contrast to sight, which is the sense of ideality devoid of inwardness, hearing is the sense of the pure inwardness of the corporeal. Just as sight is related to space become physical, to light, so hearing is related to time become physical, to sound.
— Encyclopedia §401, Addition (tr. Wallace and Miller, rev. Inwood)
For sound is the temporal positedness of corporeality, the movement, the vibration of a body within itself, a trembling, a mechanical tremor in which the body, without having to alter its relative place as a whole body, moves only its parts, posits its inner spatiality temporally, thus sublates its indifferent asunderness and by this sublation lets its pure inwardness emerge, but immediately restores itself from the superficial alteration it has undergone from the mechanical tremor.
— Encyclopedia §401, Addition (tr. Wallace and Miller, rev. Inwood)

Head: Smell and Taste
Path: 三. Spirit › 1. Subjective Spirit › i. Soul (Anthropology) › α. Natural Soul › c. Sensation › i. The Senses › 2. Smell and Taste
Gloss: The senses that perceive through chemical contact and dissolution.
Hegelian gloss: The senses of real difference, smell and taste, which perceive the body's dissolving into air and water.
Nouns: smell and taste; the chemical senses, nose and palate.
Adjective: chemical.
Adverbs: by nose and tongue.
Foreign: Sanskrit: gandha and rasa.
Hegel definition: Smell and taste are the senses of real difference, the second class. They enter into relation with real corporeality, not yet as it persists on its own and resists, but only as it is dissolving and entering into process, the process by which bodies consume themselves by their own nature. They differ in that smell receives a body in the abstract, simple and indeterminate process of dissipation or evaporation, whereas taste is related to its real, concrete process and the chemical qualities that emerge in it.
Hegel texts:
The Philosophy of Mind
· §401
Hegel citations:
The senses of the second class enter into relation with real corporeality. But they do not yet have to do with it in so far as it is for itself, offers resistance, but only in so far as it is in the course of dissolution, enters into its process.
— Encyclopedia §401, Addition (tr. Wallace and Miller, rev. Inwood)
Now although both smell and taste stand in relation to self-dissolving corporeality, yet these two senses are distinguished from each other by the fact that smell receives a body in the abstract, simple, indeterminate process of dissipation or evaporation; whereas taste is related to the real, concrete process of the body and to the chemical determinacies emerging in this process: the sweet, the bitter, the alkaline, the acidic, and the salty.
— Encyclopedia §401, Addition (tr. Wallace and Miller, rev. Inwood)

The first is the sense of the abstract process, the second the sense of the concrete process.

— Encyclopedia §401, Addition (tr. Wallace and Miller, rev. Inwood)

[W]hereas taste is related to the real, concrete process of the body and to the chemical determinacies emerging in this process: the sweet, the bitter, the alkaline, the acidic, and the salty.

With taste, a direct contact with the object is necessary
— Encyclopedia §401, Addition (tr. Wallace and Miller, rev. Inwood)

Hegel definition: Feeling, also called touch where it resides chiefly in the fingers, is the sole sense of the third class, that of earthly totality, and the most concrete of all the senses. It relates not to the abstractly ideal or to separated qualities of bodies but to their solid reality. Only for it is there strictly another that subsists for itself, an individual standing against an individual senser. So weight, cohesion, hardness and softness, roughness and smoothness, heat and shape in three dimensions all fall to it.
Hegel texts:
The Philosophy of Mind
· §401
Hegel citations:
Feeling is the most concrete of all the senses.
— Encyclopedia §401, Addition (tr. Wallace and Miller, rev. Inwood)
Only for feeling, therefore, is there strictly an Other subsisting for itself, an individual entity for itself
— Encyclopedia §401, Addition (tr. Wallace and Miller, rev. Inwood)
Finally, shape in its three dimensions falls in the province of feeling; for the mechanical determinacy in general pertains entirely to feeling.
— Encyclopedia §401, Addition (tr. Wallace and Miller, rev. Inwood)

The Philosophy of Mind
· §402

Because they are immediate and just found, sensations are individual and transient determinations, alterations in the substantiality of the soul, posited in the soul's being-for-self, which is identical to its substantiality.
— Encyclopedia §402 (tr. Wallace and Miller, rev. Inwood)
Mere sensation, as we have just remarked, has to do only with what is individual and contingent, with what is immediately given and present; and this content appears to the sentient soul as its own concrete actuality.

Hegel definition: Embodiment is the way the determinations that originate within the soul and mind become sensed: to be as if found, they must be posited as distinct from the subject and as identical with it, and this happens only by their externalizing themselves in the body. Hegel texts:
The Philosophy of Mind
· §401
Hegel citations:
The other is the sphere of determinacies originating in the mind and belonging to it, which, in order to be sensed, in order to be as if found, become embodied.
— Encyclopedia §401 (tr. Wallace and Miller, rev. Inwood)
We should have to comprehend the connection by which anger and courage are felt in the breast, in the blood, in the irritable system, just as contemplation and mental preoccupation are sensed or felt in the head, the centre of the sensitive system.
— Encyclopedia §401, Remark (tr. Wallace and Miller, rev. Inwood)
Only by the embodiment of inner determinations does the subject get to the stage of sensing them
— Encyclopedia §401, Addition (tr. Wallace and Miller, rev. Inwood)

Hegel definition: The feeling soul in its immediacy is a monadic individual that is not yet itself, not a subject reflected into itself, and therefore passive. Its selfhood belongs to a subject different from it, which may even be another individual, its genius, which moves it without resistance. This is a magical relationship, immediate and unmediated by objective connections. It first appears as a formal subjectivity, in dreaming, in the child in the womb and in the relation to one's genius, and then as a real division of soul life in magnetic somnambulism and related states.

— Encyclopedia §405 (tr. Wallace and Miller, rev. Inwood)

Hegel definition: Formal subjectivity is the first form of the soul's magical relationship, in which the soul feels the totality of its individual life without claiming what belongs to objective consciousness, being itself a moment of objective life. It is therefore no illness but to be expected in a healthy human being. Its simplicity is undivided, so that there is as yet no relation between two self-subsisting persons and no opposition of subjective to objective consciousness. Its three states are natural dreaming, the life of the child in the womb, and the individual's relation to its genius.

Hegel definition: The magnetic states appear when the two sides of soul life, the unmediated relation of the feeling soul to its individual world and the mediated relation to an objectively connected world, come apart and break loose from each other. This divergence is an illness, in which the soul side, grown independent of mental consciousness, usurps its function. It shows itself in sleepwalking, catalepsy and other conditions, and especially in animal magnetism, whether it arises of itself in an individual or is produced in one individual by another.

The Philosophy of Mind

Hegel citations:

Among the illnesses in which this universal can appear are sleepwalking, catalepsy, the onset of puberty in young women, the state of pregnancy, also St Vitus's dance, and the moment of approaching death as well, if death brings about the relevant splitting of life into a weakening healthy, mediated consciousness and a soulful awareness approaching ever closer to complete ascendancy; but especially we must examine here the state which has been called animal magnetism, both when it develops by itself in an individual and when it is produced in a particular manner in the individual by another individual.
— Encyclopedia §406, Addition (tr. Wallace and Miller, rev. Inwood)

Head: Divining
Path: 三. Spirit › 1. Subjective Spirit › i. Soul (Anthropology) › β. The Feeling Soul › a. The Feeling Soul in Its Immediacy › ii. Magnetic Somnambulism › 1. Appearance of Magnetic States › a. Divining
Gloss: The supposed power of sensing hidden metals and water.
Hegelian gloss: The soul's immediate sympathy with metals and water, a sentience of the elemental earth.
Nouns: divining; divining, dowsing, water witching, rhabdomancy, divining rod, dowsing rod, hazel twig, pendulum; dowser, diviner, water witch, lamp of Aladdin†. metal-divining, water-divining.
Verbs: dowse, divine, witch. detect, sense.
Adjective: divining, rhabdomantic. divinatory.
Adverbs: by the rod. by divination.
Foreign: Latin: virgula divina.
Phrases: water-witching; to divine for water; a nose for it.
Hegel definition: Divining is the first appearance of immediate awareness in the magnetic states: people who, fully awake and without the mediation of sight, detect metal or water lying underground, and some who sense salt as well. They may use a forked hazel twig as a divining rod, but its movement has no ground in the wood; it is determined solely by the individual's sensation.
Hegel texts:
The Philosophy of Mind
· §406
Hegel citations:
By this we understand people who in a fully waking state, without the mediation of the sense of sight, detect metal or water lying under the ground.
— Encyclopedia §406, Addition (tr. Wallace and Miller, rev. Inwood)
It goes without saying that this movement of the wood does not somehow have its ground in the wood itself but is determined solely by the sensation of the individual
— Encyclopedia §406, Addition (tr. Wallace and Miller, rev. Inwood)

Head: Catalepsy and Sleepwalking
Path: 三. Spirit › 1. Subjective Spirit › i. Soul (Anthropology) › β. The Feeling Soul › a. The Feeling Soul in Its Immediacy › ii. Magnetic Somnambulism › 1. Appearance of Magnetic States › b. Catalepsy and Sleepwalking
Gloss: States of rigidity, and of walking or acting while asleep.
Hegelian gloss: The body made rigid or set walking while the waking self is absent: the soul's life of feeling acting without understanding.
Nouns: catalepsy and sleepwalking; catalepsy, catatonia, rigidity, trance, stupor, waxy flexibility; somnambulism, sleepwalking, noctambulism, night-walking; Lady Macbeth's sleepwalking. torpor, torpidity, lethargy, coma, suspended animation, stupefaction, paralysis, obstupefaction†. somnambulist, sleep walker, night walker, noctambulist. somnambulist.
Verbs: sleepwalk, freeze, stiffen, go rigid. walk in one's sleep.
Adjective: cataleptic, catatonic, rigid, somnambulant, somnambulistic, noctambulous.
Adverbs: in one's sleep, rigidly.
Phrases: out, damned spot! [Macbeth]; frozen stiff; walking in one's sleep.
Hegel definition: Catalepsy and sleepwalking are states of immediate feeling awareness in which an object is sensed without its specific sense, which is replaced by the common sense active chiefly in the pit of the stomach or by touch. In catalepsy the organs are paralysed. Sleepwalking is a kind of cataleptic state in which dreaming expresses itself not only in speech but in walking and other actions, guided by an often accurate, though by no means infallible, feeling of surrounding things. The eye is fixed, and with it the distance that consciousness requires.
Hegel texts:
The Philosophy of Mind
· §406
Hegel citations:
Such feeling is displayed both in catalepsy in general, a state in which the organs are paralysed, and especially in sleep-walking, a kind of cataleptic state in which dreaming expresses itself not merely in speech but also in walking about and gives rise to other actions, underlying which there is an often accurate feeling of the relationships of surrounding objects.
— Encyclopedia §406, Addition (tr. Wallace and Miller, rev. Inwood)
However, the sense of feeling by no means always guides sleep-walkers correctly; their complex actions are a contingent matter.
— Encyclopedia §406, Addition (tr. Wallace and Miller, rev. Inwood)

Head: Clairvoyance
Path: 三. Spirit › 1. Subjective Spirit › i. Soul (Anthropology) › β. The Feeling Soul › a. The Feeling Soul in Its Immediacy › ii. Magnetic Somnambulism › 1. Appearance of Magnetic States › c. Clairvoyance
Gloss: The supposed perception of what is beyond the reach of the senses; second sight.
Hegelian gloss: The seeing of the soul without the mediation of the senses, an immediate knowing confined to the sentient soul's own world.
Nouns: clairvoyance; second sight, clear seeing, extrasensory perception, ESP, telepathy, precognition, prescience, prevision, divination, foreknowledge, insight, the third eye; seer, clairvoyant, sibyl, prophet, oracle, augur, haruspex, soothsayer, prenotion†, antepast†, prelibation†, prophasis†. presentiment. medium, mesmerist. clear-seeing, lucidity. cryptaesthesia.
Verbs: foresee, foretell, divine, prophesy, see beyond. predict. see clearly.
Adjective: clairvoyant, prescient, prophetic, second-sighted, telepathic, extrasensory, visionary, fey. lucid.
Adverbs: by second sight, prophetically, clairvoyantly.
Foreign: Arabic: kashf [unveiling], firāsa [intuitive discernment]; Sanskrit: divya-cakṣus [divine eye], abhijñā [supernormal knowledge]; Chinese: tianyan [heavenly eye]; Korean: cheollian [thousand-league eye, clairvoyance].
Phrases: the gift of second sight; to see through walls.
Hegel definition: Clairvoyance is the immediate awareness in which, without any specific sense or any part of the body taking its place, an indeterminate sensation gives rise to a vision of something not sensibly near but distant in space or time. The soul in it is aware of its own world without having yet set that world outside itself as an object. Its phenomena all relate to the individual world of the feeling soul, and because its content is not set out in an intelligible connection, it is at the mercy of every contingency of feeling and imagining.
Hegel texts:
The Philosophy of Mind
· §406
Hegel citations:
Without the involvement of any specific sense and without the common sense becoming active in an individual part of the body, an indeterminate sensation gives rise to an intimation or clairvoyance, a vision of something not sensibly near but distant in space or in time, of something future or past.
— Encyclopedia §406, Addition (tr. Wallace and Miller, rev. Inwood)
The five phenomena discussed above are the principal moments of clairvoyant awareness. They all have in common the determination of always relating to the individual world of the feeling soul.
— Encyclopedia §406, Addition (tr. Wallace and Miller, rev. Inwood)
But such clairvoyance, because, in its hazy obscurity, the content is not set out in an intelligible interconnection, is at the mercy of all its own contingency of feeling, of imagining, etc., not to mention that ideas of others (see below) intrude into its vision. It is thus impossible to make out whether clairvoyants see correctly more than they get wrong
— Encyclopedia §406, Remark (tr. Wallace and Miller, rev. Inwood)

Head: Content of Magnetic States
Path: 三. Spirit › 1. Subjective Spirit › i. Soul (Anthropology) › β. The Feeling Soul › a. The Feeling Soul in Its Immediacy › ii. Magnetic Somnambulism › 2. Content of Magnetic States
Gloss: What the soul perceives in trance states.
Hegelian gloss: The content of the trance states, which is the soul's own feeling world, not an objective knowledge.
Nouns: content of magnetic states; trance content, visions, revelations, communications, the contents of trance. the matter of trance, what is seen in trance, the content of clairvoyance, presentiments, intuited content.
Verbs: perceive, receive, reveal. behold, intuit, foresee.
Adjective: revealed, visionary, revelatory. perceived, intuited.
Adverbs: in trance. in the magnetic state.
Foreign: Arabic: mukāshafāt [unveilings].
Phrases: what the trance reveals; visions and voices.
Hegel definition: The content of the trance states is the individual's own actuality, the whole circle of interests and relationships which has coalesced with that individuality and which healthy consciousness knows as an intelligibly connected external world. In somnambulism the individual is a monad inwardly aware of this actuality, intuiting it immediately without the series of mediations that waking consciousness must pass through. Only what is individually determined enters in; scientific discoveries and universal truths need the ground of thought developed to free consciousness.
Hegel texts:
The Philosophy of Mind
· §406
Hegel citations:
The individual is thus a monad which is inwardly aware of its actuality, the self-intuition of the genius.
— Encyclopedia §406, Remark (tr. Wallace and Miller, rev. Inwood)
The first conclusion to be drawn from the account we have given bears on the content: in somnambulism only the sphere of the individually determined world, of particular interests and restricted relationships, enter into consciousness.
— Encyclopedia §406, Remark (tr. Wallace and Miller, rev. Inwood)

Head: Recollecting
Path: 三. Spirit › 1. Subjective Spirit › i. Soul (Anthropology) › β. The Feeling Soul › a. The Feeling Soul in Its Immediacy › ii. Magnetic Somnambulism › 2. Content of Magnetic States › a. Recollecting
Gloss: The recovery of what was forgotten.
Hegelian gloss: The recovery, in the trance, of what was lost to waking memory.
Nouns: recollecting; recovered memory, hypermnesia, total recall, recollection of the forgotten, forgotten languages, recall under hypnosis. recovery of the forgotten, retrieval, reminiscence. anamnesis.
Verbs: recall, recollect, recover, remember, bring back. bethink oneself, call up, retrace, think back, look back upon. remember &c H0663. retrieve.
Adjective: anamnestic, hypermnesic, recovered. recollective, recalled. cured, healed.
Adverbs: from the depths of memory. from oblivion, in recollection.
Foreign: Greek: anamnēsis; Arabic: dhikr [remembrance]; Sanskrit: smṛti [recollection].
Phrases: lost and found; it all came back; on the tip of one's tongue.
Hegel definition: Recollecting is the first content of clairvoyant awareness: the soul becomes aware of a content it had long forgotten and can no longer bring into consciousness when awake. In illness or in the magnetic state people speak a language learned in early youth and since lost, or recite fluently something read long before and never learned by rote. The soul enclosed in its inwardness thus only makes present to itself again what already belongs to it.
Hegel texts:
The Philosophy of Mind
· §406
Hegel citations:
First, there are states in which the soul is aware of a content it had long since forgotten and which, in waking, it is no longer able to bring into consciousness.
— Encyclopedia §406, Addition (tr. Wallace and Miller, rev. Inwood)
An equally indisputable case is where people in such a state recite with perfect facility something they had read a considerable time before, which they have never learned by rote and which has vanished from their waking consciousness.
— Encyclopedia §406, Addition (tr. Wallace and Miller, rev. Inwood)

Head: Envisioning
Path: 三. Spirit › 1. Subjective Spirit › i. Soul (Anthropology) › β. The Feeling Soul › a. The Feeling Soul in Its Immediacy › ii. Magnetic Somnambulism › 2. Content of Magnetic States › b. Envisioning
Gloss: The seeing of things not present.
Hegelian gloss: The seeing in trance of what lies beyond the waking senses, a knowing still bound to feeling.
Nouns: envisioning; vision, envisioning, beholding, visualization, seeing without eyes, inner seeing, apparition. specter, boggart†, lemures†. illusion, virtual image. visualizing, seeing the absent, second sight, prevision. phantasm.
Verbs: envision, envisage, behold, see, visualize. conjure up a vision, picture, figure to oneself. descry. see the absent.
Adjective: visionary, envisioned, visualized.
Adverbs: in vision. in the mind's eye.
Foreign: German: vorstellen; Arabic: ruʾyā; Sanskrit: darśana [seeing, vision].
Phrases: where there is no vision, the people perish [Bible]; to see things; a vision of.
Hegel definition: Envisioning is the clairvoyant soul's unmediated awareness of events still external to the feeling subject. Ordinary consciousness knows what is distant in space only by removing the distance through mediation, but space belongs to external nature and not to the soul, which transforms the external by its ideality; so the subject sunk to merely feeling soul is no longer bound to space. It likewise rises above time past, though a fully determinate and intelligent knowledge of the future is impossible.
Hegel texts:
The Philosophy of Mind
· §406
Hegel citations:
But what can seem even more wonderful than the awareness, just considered, of a content already deposited in the interior of the soul, is the unmediated awareness of events which are still external to the feeling subject.
— Encyclopedia §406, Addition (tr. Wallace and Miller, rev. Inwood)
Space pertains not to the soul but to external nature; and this externality, in being apprehended by the soul, ceases to be spatial, since, transformed by the soul's ideality, it remains external neither to itself nor to us.
— Encyclopedia §406, Addition (tr. Wallace and Miller, rev. Inwood)

Head: Inner Vision
Path: 三. Spirit › 1. Subjective Spirit › i. Soul (Anthropology) › β. The Feeling Soul › a. The Feeling Soul in Its Immediacy › ii. Magnetic Somnambulism › 2. Content of Magnetic States › b. Envisioning › i. Inner Vision
Gloss: The seeing of what is within one's own body.
Hegelian gloss: The somnambulist's seeing of the interior of their own body.
Nouns: inner vision; inner sight, seeing within, self-diagnosis, autoscopy, introspective vision, inward eye. inward seeing, self-inspection, vision of one's own body, internal sight. introspection.
Verbs: look within, see inwardly, introspect. see within, look inward, inspect oneself.
Adjective: inward, introspective, autoscopic. internal.
Adverbs: inwardly, within. into oneself.
Foreign: Arabic: baṣīra [inner sight, insight].
Phrases: that inward eye which is the bliss of solitude [Wordsworth]; the mind's eye; to look within.
Hegel definition: Inner vision is the clairvoyant soul's awareness of its own interior, its state of soul and of body, returning from relation to something external back to itself. It can reach considerable clarity, but accurate accounts of the bodily state come only from those with medical knowledge in waking life, since the concentrated intuition is hard to put into intellectual form. In this serene inner vision, where the substantial side of the soul comes forth, noble natures find their better self and base ones give themselves up to baseness.
Hegel texts:
The Philosophy of Mind
· §406
Hegel citations:
[I]n the third case the soul, in clairvoyant awareness of its own interior, of its state of soul and physical body, returns from this relation to something external back to itself.
— Encyclopedia §406, Addition (tr. Wallace and Miller, rev. Inwood)
This side of clairvoyance has a very wide range and can also attain to a considerable clarity and determinacy.
— Encyclopedia §406, Addition (tr. Wallace and Miller, rev. Inwood)

Head: External Vision
Path: 三. Spirit › 1. Subjective Spirit › i. Soul (Anthropology) › β. The Feeling Soul › a. The Feeling Soul in Its Immediacy › ii. Magnetic Somnambulism › 2. Content of Magnetic States › b. Envisioning › ii. External Vision
Gloss: The seeing of what is outside oneself at a distance.
Hegelian gloss: The trance-seeing of what is distant in space or time.
Nouns: external vision; remote viewing, seeing at a distance, far sight, distant vision, telegnosis. far-sight, telesthesia. telaesthesia.
Verbs: see afar, view remotely. see at a distance, descry.
Adjective: distant, remote, telegnostic. far-seeing.
Adverbs: at a distance, afar. from afar.
Phrases: seeing beyond the horizon; across the miles.
Hegel definition: External vision is the clairvoyant awareness of an external circumstance removed from the senses by distance in space or in time. The soul is immersed in the vision of a single outward event, as when someone sees an absent relative far away. Such seeing is possible because the soul is not subject to the externality of space, but it is no higher knowledge: it may be more obscure or clearer, may mix what is correct with error, and belonged more to times of a more soulful life than to the modern independence of the intellect.
Hegel texts:
The Philosophy of Mind
· §406
Hegel citations:
Instances of this kind of clairvoyance occurred more frequently in earlier times, in times of a more soulful life, than in the modern period in which the independence of the intellectual consciousness has developed much further.
— Encyclopedia §406, Addition (tr. Wallace and Miller, rev. Inwood)
In the intimation of the spatially distant the consciousness can, by the way, be at one time more obscure, at another more lucid.
— Encyclopedia §406, Addition (tr. Wallace and Miller, rev. Inwood)

Head: Immediate Sympathy
Path: 三. Spirit › 1. Subjective Spirit › i. Soul (Anthropology) › β. The Feeling Soul › a. The Feeling Soul in Its Immediacy › ii. Magnetic Somnambulism › 2. Content of Magnetic States › b. Envisioning › iii. Immediate Sympathy
Gloss: The direct sharing of feelings between persons.
Hegelian gloss: The feeling life of one soul shared directly with another, without the mediation of signs.
Nouns: immediate sympathy; sympathy, fellow feeling, rapport, empathy, emotional contagion, telepathy, thought transference, communion, affinity, attunement, resonance. direct sympathy, fellow-feeling, community of feeling, shared sensation, co-sensation.
Verbs: sympathize, empathize, resonate, attune, feel with, commune, tune in. share feelings, be in rapport.
Adjective: sympathetic, empathic, empathetic, telepathic, attuned, resonant, simpatico. immediate, direct, shared.
Adverbs: sympathetically, in rapport, in tune, on the same wavelength. directly.
Foreign: German: Einfühlung, Mitgefühl; Greek: sympatheia; French: en rapport; Italian: simpatico [Spanish simpático]; Sanskrit: sahṛdaya [like-hearted]; Chinese: ganying; Korean: nunchi [tact, sensing others' moods].
Phrases: two hearts that beat as one; to feel for.
Hegel definition: Immediate sympathy is the highest degree of the rapport between subjects, in which the clairvoyant knows, sees and feels not merely about another but in another. Without attending to the other individual, the subject immediately shares that person's sensations of everything that happens to them, and has the sensations of the other's individuality as their own. The two spheres of life have become one, a substantial identity of which the soul, as truly immaterial, is capable.
Hegel texts:
The Philosophy of Mind
· §406
Hegel citations:
Finally, when this rapport attains the highest degree of intimacy and strength, there occurs, fifthly, the phenomenon in which the clairvoyant subject knows, sees, and feels, not merely about, but in another subject and, without directly attending to the other individual, immediately shares his sensations of everything that happens to him, has within himself the sensations of the other's individuality as his own.
— Encyclopedia §406, Addition (tr. Wallace and Miller, rev. Inwood)
That the somnambulistic individual senses in himself tastes and smells which are present in the individual with whom he is in rapport, that he is aware of his other current intuitions and inner ideas, but as if they were his own, shows the substantial identity with another, which the soul (which even in its concreteness is genuinely immaterial) is capable of.
— Encyclopedia §406, Remark (tr. Wallace and Miller, rev. Inwood)

Head: Inducing
Path: 三. Spirit › 1. Subjective Spirit › i. Soul (Anthropology) › β. The Feeling Soul › a. The Feeling Soul in Its Immediacy › ii. Magnetic Somnambulism › 2. Content of Magnetic States › c. Inducing
Gloss: The bringing about of a trance state in another.
Hegelian gloss: The producing of the trance in another, through the magnetizer's power over a weaker soul.
Nouns: inducing; induction, mesmerization, hypnotic induction, suggestion, passes, laying on of hands, entrancement, spellbinding. bringing on, producing the trance, hypnotization, putting to sleep.
Verbs: induce, mesmerize, hypnotize, entrance, spellbind, bewitch, put under. charm, enchant, magnetize, fascinate &c H0678. captivate, fascinate, enrapture. bring on, produce, put to sleep.
Adjective: hypnotic, mesmeric, spellbinding, entrancing. induced, inductive.
Adverbs: under suggestion. by induction, artificially.
Foreign: Arabic: ʿazīma [incantation].
Phrases: look into my eyes; to put under; you are getting sleepy.
Hegel definition: Inducing is the intentional evoking of the magnetic state, animal magnetism proper. Just as the spontaneous state ends in dependence on an alien power, so an external power can seize a person at the rupture, implicit in them, between feeling life and thinking consciousness, and bring that rupture into existence. The power is chiefly another subject, though certain substances can exercise it, and only those already disposed to the state enter it easily. Its proximate effect is sleep, the separation of the sentient soul from intellectual consciousness.
Hegel texts:
The Philosophy of Mind
· §406
Hegel citations:
Now just as the spontaneously arising magnetic state ends up as dependence on an alien power, so, conversely, an external power can also form the starting-point and—by catching hold of me at the separation, present in itself within me, between my feeling life and my thinking consciousness—bring this rupture within me into existence, and so the magnetic state can be produced artificially.
— Encyclopedia §406, Addition (tr. Wallace and Miller, rev. Inwood)
What must necessarily take place here is only the sentient soul's becoming independent, its separation from the mediated, intellectual consciousness.
— Encyclopedia §406, Addition (tr. Wallace and Miller, rev. Inwood)

Head: The Diseased State
Path: 三. Spirit › 1. Subjective Spirit › i. Soul (Anthropology) › β. The Feeling Soul › a. The Feeling Soul in Its Immediacy › ii. Magnetic Somnambulism › 2. Content of Magnetic States › c. Inducing › i. The Diseased State
Gloss: The sickly condition in which trance states arise.
Hegelian gloss: The disease state of the soul which is the condition of magnetic phenomena, the separation of feeling from waking unity.
Nouns: the diseased state; morbid condition, nervous disorder, hysteria, neurasthenia, susceptibility, suggestibility, vapours, nerves, frailty, debility, malaise. morbid state, sickly condition, pathological state, illness, nervous weakness. morbidity.
Verbs: languish, ail, be indisposed, be susceptible. droop, sicken, pine. weaken, be predisposed.
Adjective: morbid, sickly, hysterical, neurasthenic, nervous, suggestible, susceptible, delicate. unsound, unhealthy, infirm. diseased, pathological.
Adverbs: morbidly, nervously. in sickness.
Phrases: the vapours; out of sorts; not in one's right mind.
Hegel definition: The diseased state of the soul is the separation of its soul side from mental consciousness. As bodily illness consists in one organ or system fixing itself against the harmony of the whole, so the soul falls ill when its soul side, independent of the mind's power, usurps the mind's function, and the mind sinks into that form and gives up its mediated relation to the actual world. The soul side then takes on the semblance of being what the mind truly is. This illness is more or less bound up with bodily illness.
Hegel texts:
The Philosophy of Mind
· §406
Hegel citations:
[S]o too in the soul-life illness results if the merely soulful side of the organism, becoming independent of the power of mental consciousness, usurps the latter's function and the mind, in losing control of the soulful component belonging to it, no longer remains in command of itself but itself sinks to the form of the soulful and in this way surrenders the objective relationship to the actual world essential to the sound mind
— Encyclopedia §406, Addition (tr. Wallace and Miller, rev. Inwood)
But the illness of soul arising from that separation is not merely to be compared with bodily illness, but is more or less bound up with it
— Encyclopedia §406, Addition (tr. Wallace and Miller, rev. Inwood)

Head: Methods and Means
Path: 三. Spirit › 1. Subjective Spirit › i. Soul (Anthropology) › β. The Feeling Soul › a. The Feeling Soul in Its Immediacy › ii. Magnetic Somnambulism › 2. Content of Magnetic States › c. Inducing › ii. Methods and Means
Gloss: The procedures used to induce a trance state.
Hegelian gloss: The touchings and passes by which the trance is induced.
Nouns: methods and means; passes, magnetic passes, manipulation, laying on of hands, baquet, magnetized water, rituals, techniques of induction, hypnotic technique, fixation of the gaze. procedures, techniques, stroking, the magnetic rod. imposition of hands.
Verbs: manipulate, stroke, pass, fix the gaze. make passes, lay on hands, apply.
Adjective: manipulative, technical, ritual. procedural, methodical, manual, instrumental.
Adverbs: by passes, by manipulation. by stroking, methodically.
Phrases: tricks of the trade; mesmeric passes.
Hegel definition: The methods of magnetizing vary. The magnetizer usually works by contact, and must have an uncompromising will to communicate this power and to join the two spheres of animal life into one. Most often the operation is by stroking, with or without actual touch, from the head toward the pit of the stomach and the extremities, but laying on the hand, a pressure, even a glance and the invitation to sleep may suffice. Vessels with iron rods and other material means are also used.
Hegel texts:
The Philosophy of Mind
· §406
Hegel citations:
As regards, secondly, the mode and manner of magnetising, this varies. Usually the magnetizer works by contact.
— Encyclopedia §406, Addition (tr. Wallace and Miller, rev. Inwood)
More exactly, the magnetizer operates mainly by stroking, though this need not involve actual contact
— Encyclopedia §406, Addition (tr. Wallace and Miller, rev. Inwood)

Head: Effects
Path: 三. Spirit › 1. Subjective Spirit › i. Soul (Anthropology) › β. The Feeling Soul › a. The Feeling Soul in Its Immediacy › ii. Magnetic Somnambulism › 2. Content of Magnetic States › c. Inducing › iii. Effects
Gloss: The results of inducing a trance state.
Hegelian gloss: The consequences of magnetizing, a dependency of the patient's feeling on the magnetizer.
Nouns: effects; outcomes, results, aftereffects, consequences, influence, crisis, convulsion, catharsis, relief. outcome, magnetic sleep, insensibility. rapport, suggestibility.
Verbs: affect, influence, relieve, convulse, purge. result, produce, bring about, ensue.
Adjective: effective, cathartic, convulsive, relieving. resultant, consequent, effected, induced.
Adverbs: in effect, as a result.
Phrases: the cure is worse than the disease; under someone's spell; at someone's beck and call.
Hegel definition: The effects of magnetizing begin with the sinking of the magnetized person into the shrouded, undifferentiated natural life of sleep, though sleep is not strictly necessary. Bodily activity passes from the outward organs to the inner. The soul, immersed in its inwardness, intuits its individual world not outside but within itself, and sleep may pass over into clairvoyance. What results is a state of passivity in which the patient falls into the power of the magnetizer and remains in it afterwards.
Hegel texts:
The Philosophy of Mind
· §406
Hegel citations:
The proximate universal effect of magnetizing is the sinking of the magnetic person into the state of his shrouded, undifferentiated natural life, i.e., into sleep.
— Encyclopedia §406, Addition (tr. Wallace and Miller, rev. Inwood)
The diseased subject accordingly falls into, and after the state continues in, the power of another, the magnetizer
— Encyclopedia §406, Remark (tr. Wallace and Miller, rev. Inwood)

Head: The Magnetizer
Path: 三. Spirit › 1. Subjective Spirit › i. Soul (Anthropology) › β. The Feeling Soul › a. The Feeling Soul in Its Immediacy › ii. Magnetic Somnambulism › 2. Content of Magnetic States › c. Inducing › iv. The Magnetizer
Gloss: The person who induces the trance state; the mesmerist.
Hegelian gloss: The magnetizer, who stands as the genius of the patient, whose feeling becomes the patient's.
Nouns: the magnetizer; mesmerist, hypnotist, hypnotizer, magnetizer, operator, Svengali, spellbinder, charmer, enchanter, healer, faith healer, shaman, medicine man; Mesmer. medium. mesmerizer, the magnetic physician, Puységur. therapist.
Verbs: mesmerize, hypnotize, entrance, charm, control. magnetize.
Adjective: mesmeric, hypnotic, controlling, dominating, magnetic, charismatic. magnetizing.
Adverbs: under the spell of. mesmerically, by passes.
Phrases: a Svengali; to have a hold over.
Hegel definition: The magnetizer is the subject whose power brings another into the magnetic state and who becomes that person's current subjective soul, their genius, able even to fill them with content. In the magical relationship that results, one subject acts on an individual inferior in freedom and independence of will. The patient, a formal self without actuality of its own, has the sensations and ideas of the magnetizer, seeing, tasting and hearing in that other, so that there is only one subjectivity of consciousness between them.
Hegel texts:
The Philosophy of Mind
· §406
Hegel citations:
In this magical relationship, the main point is that a subject acts on an individual subordinate to him in freedom and independence of will.
— Encyclopedia §406, Addition (tr. Wallace and Miller, rev. Inwood)
In this substantial identity there is only one subjectivity of consciousness, and the individuality of the patient is indeed a being-for-self, but it is an empty being-for-self, not present to itself, not actual
— Encyclopedia §406, Remark (tr. Wallace and Miller, rev. Inwood)

Head: Healing
Path: 三. Spirit › 1. Subjective Spirit › i. Soul (Anthropology) › β. The Feeling Soul › a. The Feeling Soul in Its Immediacy › ii. Magnetic Somnambulism › 2. Content of Magnetic States › c. Inducing › v. Healing

Hegel definition: The first and most superficial practical feeling is that of the pleasant and the unpleasant. The closure of the natural mind within itself acquires a determinate content, which becomes a fixed idea because the mind, not yet in full control of itself, is absorbed in it. Head: Vanity, Pride, Narcissism
Head (German): Die Leidenschaft der Eitelkeit und des Hochmuts
Path: 三. Spirit › 1. Subjective Spirit › i. Soul (Anthropology) › β. The Feeling Soul › b. Self-Feeling › ii. Derangement › 2. Madness Proper › a. Vanity, Pride, Narcissism
Gloss: The vanity and pride that shut the soul up within itself; self-absorption.
Hegelian gloss: Vanity and pride, which Hegel names as the chief cause of the soul's cocooning itself within itself: the eremitic consciousness shut in a narrow circle of its own interests.
Nouns: vanity, pride, narcissism; self-absorption, self-cocooning, egotism, egoism, amour-propre, self-conceit, vainglory, hubris, the eremitic consciousness, the narrow circle of one's own interests. conceit.
Adjective: vain, proud, narcissistic, self-absorbed, conceited, vainglorious, egotistic, self-enclosed.
Foreign: Greek: hybris; French: amour-propre.
Hegel definition: Vanity and pride are what Hegel names as the chief cause of the soul's spinning itself into itself. The state arises mostly when someone shuts themself up in their subjectivity out of dissatisfaction with actuality. The mind thus settled in its inwardness easily loses its understanding of actuality and finds its way only among its subjective representations; and if any vitality remains, this solitary consciousness easily creates some content of its own, treats the purely subjective as objective and fixes it there.
Hegel texts:
The Philosophy of Mind
· §408
Hegel citations:
This state of soul mostly comes about when someone shuts himself up in his subjectivity out of dissatisfaction with actuality. The passion of vanity and pride is the chief cause of this self-cocooning of the soul within itself.
— Encyclopedia §408, Addition (tr. Wallace and Miller, rev. Inwood)
For if there is still any vitality present in it, this eremitic consciousness easily takes the step of creating some content or other from its own resources and regarding this purely subjective item as something objective and fixing it in place.
— Encyclopedia §408, Addition (tr. Wallace and Miller, rev. Inwood)

Head: Fixations
Path: 三. Spirit › 1. Subjective Spirit › i. Soul (Anthropology) › β. The Feeling Soul › b. Self-Feeling › ii. Derangement › 2. Madness Proper › c. Fixations
Gloss: Madness fixed on one idea, which comes either from a particular passion or from something contingent.
Hegelian gloss: Madness with an individualized content, where the fixed idea is drawn either from a particular passion (to be God or king) or from something contingent (to be a barleycorn or a dog).
Nouns: fixations; fixed ideas, idées fixes, individualized delusions, delusional content. fixed idea, monomania, obsession, fixation.
Hegel definition: Fixations are the forms of madness with an individualized content, which, unlike the indeterminate disgust that kills all vitality, are coupled with lively interest and even passion. The content depends partly on the particular passion from which the madness sprang, as with those who take themselves to be God or a king, and partly on something contingent, as with those who suppose themselves a barleycorn or a dog. In either case the sufferer has no determinate awareness of the contradiction between the fixed idea and what is objective.
Hegel texts:
The Philosophy of Mind
· §408
Hegel citations:
In contrast to the indeterminate form of deranged soul-state just described, killing off all vitality, stands an endless throng, coupled with lively interests and even with passion, of madnesses having an individualized content. This content depends in part on the particular passion from which the madness sprang; but it can also be determined contingently by something else.
— Encyclopedia §408, Addition (tr. Wallace and Miller, rev. Inwood)
But in both cases the madman as such has no determinate consciousness of the contradiction obtaining between his fixed idea and objectivity. Only we are aware of this contradiction; such a madman himself is not tormented by the feeling of his inner disruption.
— Encyclopedia §408, Addition (tr. Wallace and Miller, rev. Inwood)

Head: Mania or Insanity
Path: 三. Spirit › 1. Subjective Spirit › i. Soul (Anthropology) › β. The Feeling Soul › b. Self-Feeling › ii. Derangement › 3. Mania or Insanity
Gloss: Violent derangement of the mind; frenzy.
Hegelian gloss: The third form of derangement: the subject knows itself torn into two contradictory modes of consciousness, feels the contradiction between its subjective presentation and the objective world, and yet cannot give it up, but insists on making it actual or on annihilating what is actual.

Adjective: manic, maniacal, rabid, wild, violent. rambling, doting, wandering, stark staring mad, stark raving mad, wild-eyed, delusional, hallucinatory. insane, mad, crazy, crazed, non compos mentis, bereft of reason, unhinged. beside oneself, out of one's wits, bouleverse†. vehement, fierce. hyper, wired, bouncing off the walls, apeshit [Vulg.], batshit [Vulg.].

Hegel definition: Mania or insanity is the third main form of derangement, and only in it is the deranged subject aware of being torn apart into two contradictory modes of consciousness. The sufferer vividly feels the contradiction between their merely subjective representation and what is objective, yet cannot give the representation up and insists on making it actual or on destroying what is actual. It need not spring from an empty illusion: great misfortune, the collapse of one's individual world or an upheaval of the state of the world can bring it about.

· §408
Hegel citations:
Only when the third main form of the deranged state is present, mania or insanity, do we have the phenomenon that the deranged subject himself is aware of being torn apart into two mutually contradictory modes of consciousness, that the mental patient himself has a vivid feeling of the contradiction between his merely subjective representation and objectivity, and yet cannot give up this representation but insists on making it an actuality or annihilating what is actual.
— Encyclopedia §408, Addition (tr. Wallace and Miller, rev. Inwood)
It is implied in the concept of mania just indicated that it need not spring from an empty illusion, but can be brought about particularly by a stroke of great misfortune, by a derangement of someone's individual world, or by the violent upheaval and coming out-of-joint of the universal state of the world
— Encyclopedia §408, Addition (tr. Wallace and Miller, rev. Inwood)

Head: Frenzy
Path: 三. Spirit › 1. Subjective Spirit › i. Soul (Anthropology) › β. The Feeling Soul › b. Self-Feeling › ii. Derangement › 3. Mania or Insanity › a. Frenzy
Gloss: Raving madness; a rage of reason against unreason and of unreason against reason.
Hegelian gloss: The raving of the deranged, a rage of reason against unreason and of unreason against reason, the self in open war with its own contradiction.
Nouns: frenzy; the rage of reason against unreason, raving. raving madness, delirium, hysteria, phrensy†, distraction, hysterics, paroxysm, raver†.
Verbs: rave, storm.
Adjective: frenzied, frantic, frenetic, raving, delirious, lightheaded, incoherent.
Hegel definition: Frenzy is what the insane person's feeling of inner disruption can become. It may remain a quiet pain, but it can also rise to a rage of reason against unreason and of unreason against reason. The unhappy feeling is easily joined by suspicion and malice and by fury at the obstacle offered by surrounding actuality and by those who limit the sufferer's will; and so too the wilfulness of a spoilt person turns to insanity when the rational will sets up a dam that it cannot overleap or break through.
Hegel texts:
The Philosophy of Mind
· §408
Hegel citations:
But in the insane the feeling of their inner disruption may be a tranquil pain, but equally it can also advance to a rage of reason against unreason and of unreason against reason
— Encyclopedia §408, Addition (tr. Wallace and Miller, rev. Inwood)
[J]ust as, conversely, in spoilt people, individuals who are accustomed to getting their own way in everything, their rambling obstinacy easily turns to insanity when the rational will that wills the universal erects against them a dam, which their rearing subjectivity is unable to jump over or to break through.
— Encyclopedia §408, Addition (tr. Wallace and Miller, rev. Inwood)

Hegel definition: Fancifulness belongs to insanity as the hypochondriac mood tormented by fancies and whims that easily accompanies the unhappy feeling of disruption, together with a suspicious, false, jealous, mischievous and malicious disposition. Hegel definition: Fury is the form in which the malice of the insane becomes a positive mania for injuring others, even a suddenly awakened desire to kill, which with irresistible force drives those in its grip, despite an abhorrence of murder that may be present in them, to kill even people they otherwise love tenderly. Hegel definition: The phenomenology of spirit is the science of the experience of consciousness. Consciousness knows an object and carries its own standard within itself, so that examining knowledge is its comparing itself with itself; when knowing and object fail to correspond, both alter, and a new object arises. Driven by its necessity through a series of shapes, consciousness comprehends the whole system of consciousness, until it sets aside the semblance of being burdened with something alien, appearance becomes equal to essence, and it reaches absolute knowing.

Head: Sense-Certainty (Sensuous Consciousness)

Gloss: Awareness that takes its object as a bare "this, here, now," known directly through the senses; it claims the richest knowledge but can say the least.

Hegel definition: Sensuous certainty is the immediate knowing of what immediately is, in which consciousness receives the object without altering it or conceptualizing it. It appears as the richest and truest knowledge, but in fact yields the most abstract and poorest truth: it says of its object only that it is, as a pure this, to a pure I. Experience shows that neither the object nor the I is immediate. What is true of the this, the now and the here is the universal, and language, which says only the universal, cannot say what is merely meant.
