In addition, it appears as the most veritable, for it has not omitted anything from its object, but rather, has its object in its complete entirety before itself. However, this certainty in fact yields the most abstract and the very poorest truth.
— The Phenomenology of Spirit ¶91 (tr. Pinkard)
The universal is thus in fact the truth of sensuous-certainty.
— The Phenomenology of Spirit ¶96 (tr. Pinkard)
However, as we see, language is the more truthful. In language, we immediately refute what we mean to say
— The Phenomenology of Spirit ¶97 (tr. Pinkard)

Head: Otherness
Path: 三. Spirit › 1. Subjective Spirit › ii. Phenomenology of Spirit (Consciousness) › α. Consciousness as Such › a. Sense-Certainty (Sensuous Consciousness) › i. Otherness
Gloss: The object of sense taken as something other than the mind.
Hegelian gloss: The object of sense as simply other to consciousness.
Nouns: otherness; the object as other, externality, foreignness, objectivity, opposition, standing-against, the not-I; alterity &c H0019. otherhood, difference from the mind.
Verbs: stand opposite, confront, face, oppose. front. counteract. be other, stand over against, differ.
Adjective: other, external, foreign, alien, objective, opposite. exterior, outward. extraneous. unrelated, independent, unconnected, disconnected, strange, irrelative†. different, opposed.
Adverbs: over against, outside. otherwise, as other.
Foreign: German: Gegen-stand.
Phrases: the world out there; other than oneself.
Hegel definition: Otherness is the one determination under which sensory consciousness has its object besides bare being: that of an independent other confronting me, something reflected into itself, an individual facing me as an individual. Whether the object is inner or outer makes no difference. It is not yet determined as external within itself, spread out in space and time, which belongs to intuition, but only according to its relation to consciousness, as something external to it.
Hegel texts:
The Philosophy of Mind
· §418
Hegel citations:
Here the object is initially to be taken only in accordance with the relationship which it has to consciousness, namely something external to consciousness, and is not yet to be determined as external within itself, or as being outside itself.
— Encyclopedia §418, Remark (tr. Wallace and Miller, rev. Inwood)
[B]ut rather by the fact that at the standpoint of sensory consciousness the object, whether it be an interior or an outer object, has no other thought-determination than firstly, that of being in general, and secondly, of being an independent Other confronting me, something reflected into itself, an individual confronting me as an individual, an immediate individual.
— Encyclopedia §418, Addition (tr. Wallace and Miller, rev. Inwood)

Head: Sensuousness
Path: 三. Spirit › 1. Subjective Spirit › ii. Phenomenology of Spirit (Consciousness) › α. Consciousness as Such › a. Sense-Certainty (Sensuous Consciousness) › ii. Sensuousness
Gloss: The object as given through the senses.
Hegelian gloss: The object as given through the senses, in its here and now.
Nouns: sensuousness; sensibility, the sensuous, the sensible, sense experience, sensory manifold, sensory given, the aesthetic in the Kantian sense; materiality of experience. sensuality, sensibleness, sensory givenness, sense-content, sensible presence.
Verbs: sense, perceive, apprehend through the senses. be given, appear to sense.
Adjective: sensuous, sensible, sensory, perceptible, aesthetic, empirical. sensitive, perceptive. sentient, sensorial. given.
Adverbs: sensuously, through the senses.
Phrases: nihil est in intellectu quod non prius fuerit in sensu [Lat.]; before one's very eyes; to the touch.
Hegel definition: Sensuousness is the object as it first offers itself to immediate certainty, in its seemingly infinite wealth in space and time, taken just as it is and with nothing left out. For this certainty the thing is, and only because it is; its simple immediacy constitutes its truth, and consciousness is for its part only a pure this that knows the singular. On a closer look much more is in play: what was taken to be immediate is only an example of pure being, split into a this as I and a this as object, each mediated through the other.
Hegel texts:
The Phenomenology of Spirit
· ¶¶90–94
Hegel citations:
Rather, the item is, and it is only because it is. For sensuous-certainty this is what is essential, and this pure being, or this simple immediacy constitutes its truth.
— The Phenomenology of Spirit ¶91 (tr. Pinkard)
However, if we take a look at it there is a good deal more in play in this pure being which constitutes the essence of this certainty and which declares it to be its truth. An actual sensuous-certainty is not only this pure immediacy but also an example of it.
— The Phenomenology of Spirit ¶92 (tr. Pinkard)
I have certainty through an other, namely, the item, and this likewise is within certainty through an other, namely, through the I.
— The Phenomenology of Spirit ¶92 (tr. Pinkard)

Head: Sensuous Space
Path: 三. Spirit › 1. Subjective Spirit › ii. Phenomenology of Spirit (Consciousness) › α. Consciousness as Such › a. Sense-Certainty (Sensuous Consciousness) › ii. Sensuousness › 1. Sensuous Space
Gloss: Space as met with by the senses.
Hegelian gloss: Space as given to sense, the here which is many heres.
Nouns: sensuous space; perceived space, visual field, lived space, here and there, near and far, orientation, location, surroundings. sensible space, felt space, the sensuous here, extension, side-by-sideness. spatiality.
Verbs: locate, orient, situate. place, localize. extend, spread, lie beside.
Adjective: spatial, oriented, near, far, perceived. extended, local.
Adverbs: here, there, nearby, far off. hereabouts, thereabouts, whereabouts, in place. where, everywhere. in space, side by side.
Phrases: here is a tree; within reach.
Hegel definition: The here is the spatial form of the sensuous this. A here, for instance a tree, vanishes as soon as one turns around and is replaced by a house, while the here itself endures, indifferent to what fills it, as a mediated simplicity, a universality. Even the here that is pointed out is not a simple point but an in front and a behind, an above and a below, a right and a left, each passing into another. What endures is a negative this, a simple gathering of many heres, a universal here.
Hegel texts:
The Phenomenology of Spirit
· ¶¶98–108
Hegel citations:
For example, here is the tree. I turn around, this truth vanishes, and it has inverted itself into its contrary: Here there is not a tree but rather a house.
— The Phenomenology of Spirit ¶98 (tr. Pinkard)
The This shows itself again to be a mediated simplicity, or as being universality.
— The Phenomenology of Spirit ¶98 (tr. Pinkard)
The Here that has been pointed out and to which I cling is likewise a this here, which is in fact not this here but is rather an in-front-of and behind, or an above and below, or a right and a left.
— The Phenomenology of Spirit ¶108 (tr. Pinkard)

Head: Sensuous Time
Path: 三. Spirit › 1. Subjective Spirit › ii. Phenomenology of Spirit (Consciousness) › α. Consciousness as Such › a. Sense-Certainty (Sensuous Consciousness) › ii. Sensuousness › 2. Sensuous Time
Gloss: Time as met with by the senses.
Hegelian gloss: Time as given to sense, the now which is many nows.
Nouns: sensuous time; perceived time, lived time, the specious present, now and then, before and after, flow of experience. sensible time, felt time, the sensuous now, succession, lived duration. momentariness.
Verbs: last, pass, succeed, endure. abide, continue. elapse.
Adjective: temporal, durational, lived, successive. present, momentary.
Adverbs: now, then, before, after. in time, successively. occasionally.
Foreign: French: durée [Bergson].
Phrases: now is night; just now.
Hegel definition: The now is the temporal form of the sensuous this. The now that is night, once written down, has by midday turned stale; the now maintains itself, but as a negative that is neither night nor day, and so as a universal. When it is pointed out, it has already ceased to be: it is only as what has been. Pointing it out is therefore a movement which returns to it as reflected into itself, a now that contains many nows, as a day contains hours, and it is experienced as a result and a universal.
Hegel texts:
The Phenomenology of Spirit
· ¶¶95–107
Hegel citations:
This self-maintaining Now is thus not an immediate Now but a mediated Now
— The Phenomenology of Spirit ¶96 (tr. Pinkard)
The Now is pointed out, this Now. Now: It has already ceased to be as it was pointed out; the Now that is is an other than that pointed out, and we see that the Now is just this Now as it no longer is.
— The Phenomenology of Spirit ¶106 (tr. Pinkard)
Pointing out is thus itself the movement that declares what the Now in truth is, namely, a result, or a plurality of Nows taken together; and pointing out is the experience that the Now is a universal.
— The Phenomenology of Spirit ¶107 (tr. Pinkard)

Head: Sensuous Manifoldness
Path: 三. Spirit › 1. Subjective Spirit › ii. Phenomenology of Spirit (Consciousness) › α. Consciousness as Such › a. Sense-Certainty (Sensuous Consciousness) › ii. Sensuousness › 3. Sensuous Manifoldness
Gloss: The variety of things given to the senses.
Hegelian gloss: The variety of what is given to sense, a manifold without unity.
Nouns: sensuous manifoldness; manifold of sense, sensory manifold, variety of sensation, multiplicity of impressions, the blooming, buzzing confusion [William James]. the sensuous manifold, multiplicity, plurality, variety, diversity, multifariousness.
Verbs: manifold, multiply, vary. diversify, abound.
Adjective: manifold, multiple, various, diverse, multifarious. many, several, sundry, divers. multiform, multifold, diversified, varied. different, heterogeneous, distinguishable.
Adverbs: variously, in profusion. manifoldly, in variety.
Foreign: German: das Mannigfaltige.
Phrases: one great blooming, buzzing confusion [William James]; a feast for the senses; all sorts.
Hegel definition: Sensuous manifoldness is the boundless variety in which sensuous certainty seems to have its object: an infinite wealth found by going out into space and time or by dividing a piece of that plenitude. Certainty itself does not unfold it, since the item has for it no meaning of a rich relation of conditions or a manifold composition; it only is. Yet countless differences crop up, and the chief among them is that between the I and the object, two thises that fall apart out of pure being.
Hegel texts:
The Phenomenology of Spirit
· ¶¶91–92
Hegel citations:
The concrete content of sensuous-certainty permits itself to appear immediately as the richest cognition, indeed, as a knowing of an infinite wealth for which no limit is to be found, whether we venture out into the reaches of space and time as the place where that wealth extends itself, or when we take a piece out of this plenitude, divide it, and thereby delve into it.
— The Phenomenology of Spirit ¶91 (tr. Pinkard)
In that certainty, neither I nor the item have the meaning of a multifaceted mediation, nor does I have the meaning of a multifaceted representing or thinking, nor does the item have the meaning of a multifaceted composition.
— The Phenomenology of Spirit ¶91 (tr. Pinkard)
Among all the countless differences thereby popping up, we find in every case the chief difference, namely, that in that certainty both of the already noted “this’s,” namely, a this as an I and a this as an object, precipitates all at once out of pure being.
— The Phenomenology of Spirit ¶92 (tr. Pinkard)

Head: The Sensed Thing
Path: 三. Spirit › 1. Subjective Spirit › ii. Phenomenology of Spirit (Consciousness) › α. Consciousness as Such › a. Sense-Certainty (Sensuous Consciousness) › iii. The Sensed Thing
Gloss: The thing as sensed.
Hegelian gloss: The sensed thing, which proves to be a universal, a this that is many.
Nouns: the sensed thing; sensible object, perceived thing, sense object, phenomenon, thing as given. the sensible thing, the thing of sense, the object of sense, the sensum, the perceptible. sense-datum.
Verbs: sense, perceive, encounter. feel.
Adjective: sensed, perceived, given, sensible, tangible. perceptible. detected.
Adverbs: in sensation. sensibly, to the senses.
Phrases: the thing before me; this very thing.
Hegel definition: The sensed thing is the object of sensory consciousness, which is aware of it only as a being, a something, an existing thing, an individual. It appears to be the richest in content but is the poorest in thoughts, its wealth consisting of determinations of feeling which the I separates from itself and first determines as being. The manifold content of sensations is gathered into a unit outside me, known immediately and individually, which comes into consciousness and vanishes again.
Hegel texts:
The Philosophy of Mind
· §418
Hegel citations:
Sensory consciousness is therefore aware of the object only as a being, a something, an existing thing, an individual, and so on. It appears as the richest in content, but it is the poorest in thoughts.
— Encyclopedia §418, Remark (tr. Wallace and Miller, rev. Inwood)
The reflection of the soul into itself, I, separates this material from itself, and gives it initially the determination of being.
— Encyclopedia §418, Remark (tr. Wallace and Miller, rev. Inwood)

Head: Externality
Path: 三. Spirit › 1. Subjective Spirit › ii. Phenomenology of Spirit (Consciousness) › α. Consciousness as Such › a. Sense-Certainty (Sensuous Consciousness) › iii. The Sensed Thing › 1. Externality
Gloss: The object as standing outside the mind.
Hegelian gloss: The object as external to consciousness and to itself.
Nouns: externality; outsideness, outwardness, exteriority, the external world, mind-independence, otherness, objectivity. surface, superficies. externalness, apartness.
Verbs: lie outside, stand outside. externalize.
Adjective: external, exterior, outside, outward, mind-independent, objective. outer.
Adverbs: externally, out there, without.
Phrases: the external world; beyond oneself.
Hegel definition: Externality is the character of the sensory object in so far as it is something other than consciousness: a unit outside me. For sensory consciousness as such this is not yet the object's being external to itself, dispersed in space and time, which is the form in which intuition grasps it. The object is simply given, so that I know neither why it is, nor why it is constituted as it is, nor whether it is anything true.
Hegel texts:
The Philosophy of Mind
· §418
Hegel citations:
[I]n general a unit that is, both in its existence and in its constitution, a given for me, something, therefore, of which I know neither why it is nor why it has this determinate nature, nor whether it is something true.
— Encyclopedia §418, Addition (tr. Wallace and Miller, rev. Inwood)
But the form peculiar to the sensory, being-external-to-its-own-self, dispersion into space and time, is (as we shall see in §448) the determination of the object apprehended by intuition
— Encyclopedia §418, Addition (tr. Wallace and Miller, rev. Inwood)

Head: Content of the Thing
Path: 三. Spirit › 1. Subjective Spirit › ii. Phenomenology of Spirit (Consciousness) › α. Consciousness as Such › a. Sense-Certainty (Sensuous Consciousness) › iii. The Sensed Thing › 2. Content of the Thing
Gloss: What the sensed thing is taken to contain.
Hegelian gloss: The content that sense ascribes to its thing.
Nouns: content of the thing; what the thing contains, sensory content, qualities, features, filling, substance. the contents of the thing, the matters, the properties, the inner of the thing, constituents.
Verbs: contain, hold, comprise. include, comprehend, embrace, embody. include &c H0154, involve.
Adjective: contentful, substantial, filled. contained, internal, constituent, inherent.
Adverbs: in content. within, internally.
Phrases: what is in it; what it is made of.
Hegel definition: The content of the thing is the particular sensory filling, smell, taste, colour and the rest, which as such belongs to sensation. It is the material of consciousness, the substantial and qualitative element that the soul is and finds within itself. What marks sensory consciousness is not that this content comes through the senses but that the object receives no thought determination beyond being and independence, into which the manifold content is concentrated as one unit.
Hegel texts:
The Philosophy of Mind
· §418
Hegel citations:
That wealth of filling is constituted by determinations of feeling; they are the material of consciousness (§414), the substantial and qualitative element, that the soul, in the anthropological sphere, is and finds within itself
— Encyclopedia §418, Remark (tr. Wallace and Miller, rev. Inwood)
The particular content of the sensory, for example, smell, taste, colour, etc., belongs, as we saw in §401, to sensation.
— Encyclopedia §418, Addition (tr. Wallace and Miller, rev. Inwood)

Head: Concrete Alteration
Path: 三. Spirit › 1. Subjective Spirit › ii. Phenomenology of Spirit (Consciousness) › α. Consciousness as Such › a. Sense-Certainty (Sensuous Consciousness) › iii. The Sensed Thing › 3. Concrete Alteration
Gloss: Change as met with in the sensed thing.
Hegelian gloss: Change in the sensed thing, which undoes the certainty of the this.
Nouns: concrete alteration; change, alteration, flux, sensed change, transformation, vicissitude, the now passing. mutation, permutation, variation, modification, modulation, inflexion, mood, qualification, innovation, metastasis, deviation, evolution, revolution, diversion, break. transfiguration, metamorphosis, transmutation. changeableness, mutability, inconstancy, versatility, mobility, instability, unstable equilibrium, vacillation &c H0405, fluctuation, alternation &c H0238. lapse. sensible change. imbalance.
Verbs: change, alter, pass, vary, shift. wax and wane, modulate, turn, veer, intervert†. fluctuate, waver, vacillate. become, turn into, evolve into, develop into, pass into. modify.
Adjective: changing, altering, fluid, variable, mutable. changeable, changeful, changing &c H0007, checkered, ever changing, protean, proteiform†, versatile. altered, changed. adapted.
Adverbs: in flux, from moment to moment. changeably, by alteration.
Phrases: now it is no longer now; here today, gone tomorrow; things change.
Hegel definition: Concrete alteration is the coming and going of the sensory object in consciousness. Known immediately and singly, the object enters my consciousness by chance and disappears from it again, as something given whose existence and constitution I cannot account for. Sensory consciousness is therefore a wholly inadequate form for any content that is universal in and for itself, since it gives what is necessary and eternal a finite, singular, self-external shape.
Hegel texts:
The Philosophy of Mind
· §418
Hegel citations:
[A] unit that, at this standpoint, is known by me in an immediate, individualized manner, contingently now enters my consciousness and then disappears from it again
— Encyclopedia §418, Addition (tr. Wallace and Miller, rev. Inwood)
It is clear from this brief account of the nature of immediate or sensory consciousness that it is a thoroughly inadequate form for the in and for itself universal content of right, of the ethical and of religion, a form that spoils such content
— Encyclopedia §418, Addition (tr. Wallace and Miller, rev. Inwood)

Head: Perception (the Thing and Deception)
Path: 三. Spirit › 1. Subjective Spirit › ii. Phenomenology of Spirit (Consciousness) › α. Consciousness as Such › b. Perception (the Thing and Deception)
Gloss: Awareness that takes its object as a thing with many properties, and struggles to hold its unity and its many features together, at the risk of error.
Hegelian gloss: Consciousness that takes the object as a thing with many properties, and, failing to hold them together, deceives itself.
Nouns: perception; the thing and deception; perceiving, apprehension, discernment, observation, noticing, the thing with many properties, the one and the also; illusion, deception, error, misperception, misapprehension. impression. fallacy, misconception, misunderstanding, misstanding†, mumpsimus†. misinterpretation, misconstruction, misacceptation†, eisegesis†. attention, heed. taking-as-true, the thing with properties. mistaking. affordance [Gibson].
Verbs: perceive, apprehend, discern, notice, observe, take as true, take for; mistake, misperceive, be deceived. make out, recognize. err, be mistaken, be deceived &c H0710, deceive oneself, misapprehend, misconceive, misthink†, misconjecture†. descry, distinguish. remark, take notice. misunderstand.
Adjective: perceptual, perceptive, perceptible, observant, discerning; deceptive, illusory, mistaken. delusive, delusory. illusive, specious. perceived.
Adverbs: perceptibly, to all appearances, apparently. perceptually, in perception.
Foreign: German: das Ding und die Täuschung, affordanz, Empfindung, Apperzeption; Latin: perceptio, comprehensio, aperceptio; Sanskrit: savikalpa [conceptual perception]; Korean: jigak [perception]; French: disponibilité [of a resource], exploitabilité [of a situation], aperception; Greek: katalēpsis.
Phrases: salt is white, and also tart, and also cubical [Hegel]; things are not always what they seem; to see things as they are; an optical illusion; errare est humanum [Lat.]; mentis gratissimus error [Lat.] [Horace]; on the dubious waves of error tost [Cowper]; you lie — under a mistake [Shelley].
Hegel definition: Perception takes what exists for it as a universal, and its object is the thing with many properties. The thing is at once an Also, a passive medium in which indifferent properties permeate one another, and a One that excludes. Taking the object to be true and self-equal, consciousness knows that it can be deceived and puts every contradiction down to its own apprehending, then tries to correct itself. It learns that its perceiving is a turning back into itself out of the true, and that the dissolution of this perceiving is its result and truth.
Hegel texts:
The Phenomenology of Spirit
· ¶¶111–131
Hegel citations:
On the other hand, perception takes what, to perception, is the existent as universal.
— The Phenomenology of Spirit ¶111 (tr. Pinkard)
This simple medium is not only an Also, an indifferent unity; it is also a One, an excluding unity.
— The Phenomenology of Spirit ¶114 (tr. Pinkard)
It has learned from experience about perceiving, namely, that its result and its truth are its dissolution, or that perceiving is the reflective turn into itself from out of the true.
— The Phenomenology of Spirit ¶118 (tr. Pinkard)

Head: Experiences
Path: 三. Spirit › 1. Subjective Spirit › ii. Phenomenology of Spirit (Consciousness) › α. Consciousness as Such › b. Perception (the Thing and Deception) › i. Experiences
Gloss: The particular observations of perception.
Hegelian gloss: The particular observations of perception, its many findings.
Nouns: experiences; observations, perceptions, impressions, findings, data, empirical evidence, cases, instances. empirical findings, particular cases. empiria.
Verbs: experience, observe, find, undergo, encounter. meet with, pass through, go through. perceive, note.
Adjective: experiential, empirical, observational. observed, perceived, particular. discovered.
Adverbs: empirically, by experience. in particular cases.
Foreign: Sanskrit: anubhava [experience]; Chinese: mozhe shitou guohe [crossing the river by feeling for the stones]; German: Erlebnis [lived experience] [Dilthey]; French: vivre, faire l’experience, faire l’épreuve, le vécu; Greek: biōnai, zōē, bios; Spanish: vivir, experimentar, vivencia.
Phrases: experience is the teacher of all things, experientia docet [Lat.]; in my experience; to learn the hard way.
Hegel definition: Experiences are what the single sensory observations from which perception starts become when they are considered in their connection, reflected upon, and turned into something necessary and universal according to definite categories. Perception does not stop at seeing and hearing but relates what is sensed to a universal that is not immediately observable. Yet its demonstrations rest on presuppositions that themselves need demonstrating, so that experience runs on to infinity; philosophy must rise to proof of the necessity of things.
Hegel texts:
The Philosophy of Mind
· §420
Hegel citations:
The sensory certainties of individual apperceptions or observations form the starting-point; these are supposed to be elevated to truth, by being considered in their relation, reflected upon, generally by becoming, in accordance with determinate categories, at the same time something necessary and universal, experiences.
— Encyclopedia §420, Remark (tr. Wallace and Miller, rev. Inwood)
Everything must be experienced. But if we are supposed to be talking about philosophy, then we must rise above the demonstration that remains tied to presuppositions, above empiricism's demonstration, to the proof of the absolute necessity of things.
— Encyclopedia §420, Addition (tr. Wallace and Miller, rev. Inwood)

Head: Connection
Path: 三. Spirit › 1. Subjective Spirit › ii. Phenomenology of Spirit (Consciousness) › α. Consciousness as Such › b. Perception (the Thing and Deception) › ii. Connection
Gloss: The joining of properties into one thing.
Hegelian gloss: Perception's effort to connect the properties into one thing, an also and a one.
Nouns: connection; combination, unification, unity of properties, synthesis, binding, the also and the one, bundle, bundle theory. junction &c H0269, union, incorporation, amalgamation, coalescence, fusion. conjunction, linkage, the also, the medium, the one of the thing, togetherness of properties. concatenation.
Verbs: connect, combine, unify, bind, bundle, hold together. join, unite, conjoin, associate, put together. link.
Adjective: connected, combined, unified, bundled, coherent. joined, conjoined, linked.
Adverbs: together, as one, in combination. simultaneously. in connection, conjointly.
Phrases: the thing is one and also many; to put two and two together; to join the dots.
Hegel definition: Connection is what perception establishes: it takes the object not as merely immediate but as mediated, reflected into itself and universal, a combination of sensory determinations with extended thought determinations of concrete relations and connections. It seeks to know each individual as an internally coherent whole and the mediations between individual things, showing that when certain circumstances are present certain consequences follow. Consciousness is thereby no longer abstract certainty but a determinate awareness.
Hegel texts:
The Philosophy of Mind
· §420
Hegel citations:
The object is thus a combination of sensory determinations and extended thought-determinations of concrete relationships and connections.
— Encyclopedia §420 (tr. Wallace and Miller, rev. Inwood)
While therefore merely sensory consciousness only shows things, i.e., merely exhibits them in their immediacy, perception by contrast apprehends the interconnection of things, demonstrates that when such and such circumstances are present such and such follows from them, and thus begins to demonstrate things as true.
— Encyclopedia §420, Addition (tr. Wallace and Miller, rev. Inwood)

Head: Demonstration, Objects, and Their Properties
Path: 三. Spirit › 1. Subjective Spirit › ii. Phenomenology of Spirit (Consciousness) › α. Consciousness as Such › b. Perception (the Thing and Deception) › iii. Demonstration, Objects, and Their Properties
Gloss: The showing of objects and their properties to awareness.
Hegelian gloss: Perception's showing of objects and properties to consciousness, by which it finds its contradictions.
Nouns: demonstration, objects, and their properties; showing, display, exhibition, presentation, object and properties, thing and qualities; ostension. manifestation, exposition. appearance, phenomenon, sight, spectacle, view. pointing out, the object, the thing and its properties, the many properties.
Verbs: show, demonstrate, display, exhibit, present. make manifest, bring into view, represent, set forth. prove, establish, evince, manifest &c H0776, substantiate, verify &c H0776. point out, indicate.
Adjective: demonstrative, ostensive, exhibited, displayed. shown, propertied.
Adverbs: demonstrably, before one's eyes. demonstratively, by showing.
Phrases: see for yourself; to show one's hand; to prove the point.
Hegel definition: Demonstration, objects and their properties belong to perception, which begins to show things as true by exhibiting how they hang together. Because the individual remains the underlying being over against the universal to which it is only related, the connection is a mixture and a many-sided contradiction: between the single things of sense that are to ground universal experience and the universal that is to be their essence, and between the independent individual and its many properties, which are free of it and of one another.
Hegel texts:
The Philosophy of Mind
· §§420–421
Hegel citations:
This demonstration is, however, still a defective, not a final demonstration. For that by which something is here supposed to be demonstrated is itself a presupposition, consequently in need of demonstration
— Encyclopedia §420, Addition (tr. Wallace and Miller, rev. Inwood)
This connection of the individual and universal is a mixture, since the individual remains the being that lies at the foundation and remains firm in the face of the universal, to which it is nevertheless related.
— Encyclopedia §421 (tr. Wallace and Miller, rev. Inwood)

Head: Force and the Understanding
Path: 三. Spirit › 1. Subjective Spirit › ii. Phenomenology of Spirit (Consciousness) › α. Consciousness as Such › c. Force and the Understanding
Gloss: Awareness that explains things by forces and laws lying behind their appearance; scientific understanding.
Hegelian gloss: The understanding, which takes the thing as appearance and finds its truth in force and law behind it.
Nouns: force and the understanding; understanding, intellect, explanatory reason, scientific understanding, theoretical explanation, hidden forces, the inner of things, the supersensible. mind, reason, rationality. intelligence, comprehension, intellect &c H0646. scientific explanation, explanation by forces and laws, the explaining consciousness.
Verbs: understand, explain, account for, theorize, infer, posit forces, look behind. attribute to, ascribe to, refer to, trace to. infer the inner.
Adjective: explanatory, theoretical, scientific, intellectual, rational, analytical. mental. nomological.
Adverbs: theoretically, in explanation, behind the scenes. by explanation, scientifically.
Foreign: German: Verstand; Latin: intellectus; Greek: dianoia; Arabic: ʿaql [intellect]; Sanskrit: buddhi [intellect].
Phrases: to understand is to see the hidden force; the powers that be.
Hegel definition: The understanding takes as its object the unconditioned universal, which has returned into itself from the one-sided concepts of perception. Behind the appearance that is the play of forces it looks into the inner of things, a supersensible world that it fills with the calm realm of law, and then with the inversion of that world. In explaining, it posits differences that are no differences and sublates them again. What it experiences in the inner is in truth only itself, and so it passes over into self-consciousness.
Hegel texts:
The Phenomenology of Spirit
· ¶¶132–165
Hegel citations:
This unconditioned universal, which is henceforth the true object of consciousness, is still an object of consciousness; consciousness has not yet grasped its concept as concept.
— The Phenomenology of Spirit ¶132 (tr. Pinkard)
We see that the understanding in truth experiences in the inner of appearance nothing but appearance itself, but not appearance in the way it is as the play of forces; rather, it experiences the play of forces within their absolutely universal moments and their movement; in fact, the understanding experiences only itself.
— The Phenomenology of Spirit ¶165 (tr. Pinkard)

Head: Necessity
Path: 三. Spirit › 1. Subjective Spirit › ii. Phenomenology of Spirit (Consciousness) › α. Consciousness as Such › c. Force and the Understanding › i. Necessity
Gloss: The understanding's grasp of what must be.
Hegelian gloss: The necessity which the understanding finds in its laws.
Nouns: necessity; lawful necessity, explanatory necessity, causal necessity, nomic necessity, must, the must-be of law. inner necessity, compulsion of the concept, inevitability, lawfulness, the necessary connection.
Verbs: necessitate, compel, require. force, constrain, oblige. destine, predestine, preordain. follow necessarily.
Adjective: necessary, lawful, nomic, compelled, inevitable. apodictic.
Adverbs: necessarily, by law, of necessity. of course, needs must, perforce &c H0712, willy nilly. consequently.
Foreign: Latin: nolens volens; French: vérités de raison [Leibniz].
Phrases: it had to happen; as a matter of course; it stands to reason.
Hegel definition: Necessity is what the intellect reaches when it takes the object as appearance with an interior that is for itself. That interior is a simple inner difference which stays equal to itself in the change of appearances, the realm of laws, and the essence of law is an inseparable, necessary inner connection of distinct determinations, as of crime with punishment. Speculative reason alone comprehends this unity, but the intellect already discovers it among phenomena and, finding in laws its own nature, becomes an object to itself.
Hegel texts:
The Philosophy of Mind
· §422
Hegel citations:
This simple difference is the realm of the laws of appearance
— Encyclopedia §422 (tr. Wallace and Miller, rev. Inwood)
For the essence of law, whether this relates to external nature or the ethical world order, consists in an inseparable unity, in a necessary interior connection, of distinct determinations.
— Encyclopedia §422, Addition (tr. Wallace and Miller, rev. Inwood)

Head: Laws
Path: 三. Spirit › 1. Subjective Spirit › ii. Phenomenology of Spirit (Consciousness) › α. Consciousness as Such › c. Force and the Understanding › ii. Laws
Gloss: The stable regularities the understanding finds behind appearances.
Hegelian gloss: The calm realm of laws which the understanding sets beyond the flux of appearance.
Nouns: laws; laws of nature, natural laws, regularities, uniformities, equations, formulae, principles, constants, the realm of laws. the stable image of appearance. nomology, regularity.
Verbs: formulate, derive, discover, explain by law. govern, regulate, hold.
Adjective: lawful, law-governed, regular, nomological. lawlike, constant, nomic.
Adverbs: according to law, lawfully. by law, regularly.
Phrases: nature is the realm of laws; the laws of nature; by the book.
Hegel definition: Law is the simple difference which appearance comes to be when related to the inner: the stable picture of unstable appearance. The supersensible world is thus a motionless realm of laws, beyond the perceived world and yet present in it. It is the understanding's first truth but not appearance brought to fulfilment, for each law has its determinateness, so that laws are indefinitely many. Gathered into one, as universal attraction, they say no more than the mere concept of law, namely that all actuality is in itself lawful.
Hegel texts:
The Phenomenology of Spirit
· ¶¶148–156
Hegel citations:
It is expressed in law as the stable picture of unstable appearance. The supersensible world is thus a motionless realm of laws.
— The Phenomenology of Spirit ¶149 (tr. Pinkard)
This realm of laws is, to be sure, the truth of the understanding, which has its content in the difference that lies within the law. However, it is at the same time only the understanding’s first truth and does not completely bring appearance to its fulfillment.
— The Phenomenology of Spirit ¶150 (tr. Pinkard)
The unification of all laws into universal attraction expresses no further content than that of the mere concept of law itself, which is posited as existing therein.
— The Phenomenology of Spirit ¶150 (tr. Pinkard)

Head: Force and the Play of Forces
Path: 三. Spirit › 1. Subjective Spirit › ii. Phenomenology of Spirit (Consciousness) › α. Consciousness as Such › c. Force and the Understanding › ii. Laws › 1. Force and the Play of Forces
Gloss: Force taken as both cause and expression, and the interplay of forces that set one another in motion.
Hegelian gloss: Force which expresses itself and is driven back into itself, the play of forces.
Nouns: force and the play of forces; play of forces, interplay of forces, soliciting and solicited force, the exchange of forces, dynamic interplay, give and take, push and pull, interaction; force as expression and as withdrawn. force and its expression, the soliciting and the solicited, the vanishing of force, action and reaction.
Verbs: interplay, interact, solicit, provoke, respond, exchange. express, exert, vanish.
Adjective: dynamic, interactive, reciprocal, interplaying. forceful, interacting, solicited.
Adverbs: in play, in interplay, back and forth. dynamically.
Foreign: German: Spiel der Kräfte.
Phrases: the play of forces.
Hegel definition: Force is the movement in which self-sufficient matters spread out into their being, which is its expression, and are driven back again into a unity, which is force proper. These are not two separate things: the force driven back must express itself, and in expressing it remains within itself. First only a concept of the understanding, force becomes actual by doubling into two forces that solicit and are solicited, each of which is only through the other. So the realization of force is at once the loss of its reality: what proves to be its essence is a universal, the inner of things.
Hegel texts:
The Phenomenology of Spirit
· ¶¶136–143
Hegel citations:
This movement is, however, what is called force. One moment of this, namely, the force as the propagation of the self-sufficient matters in their being, is their expression. However, the force as the disappearance of the self-sufficient matters is the force driven out of its expression back into itself, or the genuine force.
— The Phenomenology of Spirit ¶136 (tr. Pinkard)
Rather, their essence is purely and simply this: Each is only through the other; what each is through the other is immediately no longer to be while it is the other.
— The Phenomenology of Spirit ¶141 (tr. Pinkard)
The realization of force is therefore at the same time the loss of reality
— The Phenomenology of Spirit ¶141 (tr. Pinkard)

Head: The Supersensible World
Path: 三. Spirit › 1. Subjective Spirit › ii. Phenomenology of Spirit (Consciousness) › α. Consciousness as Such › c. Force and the Understanding › ii. Laws › 2. The Supersensible World
Gloss: The realm of laws lying behind the world of appearance.
Hegelian gloss: The supersensible world, the beyond of appearance, which is first empty and then the realm of laws.
Nouns: the supersensible world; the beyond of appearance, the inner world, the realm of laws, the intelligible world, the noumenal world, the calm kingdom of laws, the world behind the world. the suprasensible realm, the beyond, the inner of things, the tranquil kingdom of laws.
Verbs: lie beyond, transcend, underlie. lie behind, transcend sense.
Adjective: supersensible, supersensuous, transcendent, noumenal, intelligible, invisible, otherworldly, indiscoverable†, unspied†, wrapt in clouds†. suprasensible, inner.
Adverbs: beyond the senses, behind appearances. behind appearance.
Foreign: German: ein ruhiges Reich von Gesetzen, Hinterwelt [Nietzsche]; Latin: mundus intelligibilis; Arabic: ʿālam al-ghayb [world of the unseen], malakūt [the invisible kingdom]; Sanskrit: paraloka [other world].
Phrases: the calm kingdom of laws [Hegel]; backworldsmen, Hinterweltler [Ger.] [Nietzsche]; the world beyond; behind the veil.
Hegel definition: The supersensible world is the enduring beyond which, over against the vanishing world of the senses, is disclosed to the understanding as the true world. At first it is empty, only the nothingness of appearance and the simple universal, and consciousness does not find itself in it. But it comes forth out of appearance, which is its mediation, essence and fulfilment: the supersensible is the sensuous and perceived posited as they are in truth, as appearance. It is therefore appearance as appearance, and in it appearance's flux is held as the motionless difference of law.
Hegel texts:
The Phenomenology of Spirit
· ¶¶144–149
Hegel citations:
In this inner true, as the absolutely universal which is purified of the opposition of universal and singular and which has come to be for the understanding, is disclosed for the first time and henceforth a supersensible world as the true world over and above the sensuous world (as the appearing world).
— The Phenomenology of Spirit ¶144 (tr. Pinkard)
The inner is still a pure other-worldly beyond for consciousness, for consciousness does not encounter itself within it.
— The Phenomenology of Spirit ¶146 (tr. Pinkard)
The supersensible is the sensuous and the perceived posited as they are in truth. However, the truth of the sensuous and the perceived is to be appearance. The supersensible is therefore appearance as appearance.
— The Phenomenology of Spirit ¶147 (tr. Pinkard)

Head: The Inverted World
Path: 三. Spirit › 1. Subjective Spirit › ii. Phenomenology of Spirit (Consciousness) › α. Consciousness as Such › c. Force and the Understanding › ii. Laws › 3. The Inverted World
Gloss: The topsy-turvy world: the world behind appearance turns out to be the reverse of the apparent one, where what is sweet here is sour there and punishment is really honour. Each side is the other's opposite.
Hegelian gloss: The inverted world, in which the supersensible is the inversion of appearance, and the inner proves to be the self.
Nouns: the inverted world; topsy-turvy world, world turned upside down, the upside-down world, inversion, reversal, mirror world, looking-glass world, antipodes, carnival, saturnalia, the world of opposites, Opposite Land, Bizarro world; the punishment that is honour, the sweet that is sour. opposition, polarity, inversion &c H0228, counterpart. eversion, subversion, reversion, contrariety &c H0102. the world upside down, the second supersensible world.
Verbs: invert, reverse, turn upside down, turn inside out, flip, overturn, stand on its head. turn the tables, turn topsy-turvy. subvert, turn topsy turvy, transpose, put the cart before the horse, retrovert†, culbuter†.
Adjective: inverted, reversed, upside-down, topsy-turvy, inside-out, back-to-front, contrary, mirror-image, antipodal. wrong side out, wrong side up. opposite, inverse. converse, antithetical, antipodean. turned.
Adverbs: upside down, topsy-turvy, inside out, the other way round, arsy-versy, back to front. inversely.
Foreign: Latin: mundus inversus, vice versa; French: sens dessus dessous, à rebours [against the grain].
Phrases: the world turned upside down; fair is foul, and foul is fair [Macbeth]; the last shall be first, and the first last [Bible]; Through the Looking-Glass [Lewis Carroll].
Hegel definition: The inverted world is the second supersensible world, in which the calm realm of laws, the immediate likeness of the perceived world, turns into its opposite. What is like itself repels itself and what is unlike posits itself as like, so that what is sweet in the first law is sour here, and the north pole is the south. This is not a second place set beside the first. It must be thought as inner difference: the supersensible world contains the other within itself and is the inversion of itself, its own opposite in one unity, which is infinity.
Hegel texts:
The Phenomenology of Spirit
· ¶¶157–160
Hegel citations:
This second supersensible world is in this way the inverted world, namely, while one aspect is already present in the first supersensible world, this is the inverted version of this first supersensible world.
— The Phenomenology of Spirit ¶157 (tr. Pinkard)
According to the laws, therefore, of this inverted world, like poles in the first world are each the unlike of itself, and the unlike in the first is just as unlike to itself, or it comes to be equal to itself. In determinate moments this will turn out to be such that what in the law of the first is sweet is, in this inverted in-itself, sour; what is black in the former is white in the latter.
— The Phenomenology of Spirit ¶158 (tr. Pinkard)
It is for itself the inverted world, which is to say, it is the inversion of itself, and it is itself and its opposed world within one unity.
— The Phenomenology of Spirit ¶160 (tr. Pinkard)

Head: Subjectivity (Transition to Self-Consciousness)
Path: 三. Spirit › 1. Subjective Spirit › ii. Phenomenology of Spirit (Consciousness) › α. Consciousness as Such › c. Force and the Understanding › iii. Subjectivity (Transition to Self-Consciousness)
Gloss: Awareness discovering that what it found behind appearance is its own activity; awareness turning back on itself.
Hegelian gloss: Consciousness discovering that in the inner it has itself before it, and so becoming self-consciousness.
Nouns: subjectivity; self-discovery, the turn to the subject, reflexive turn, recognition that the inner is oneself, infinity, the concept of life, curtain drawn back; behind the curtain there is nothing to see unless we go behind it ourselves [Hegel]. reflection into self, the turn to the self, the inner as one's own, the curtain drawn away, the understanding finding itself.
Verbs: turn inward, discover oneself, recognize oneself, see through. turn back, reflect into itself, find itself, discover.
Adjective: reflexive, self-discovering, inward-turning, subjective. self-returning.
Adverbs: inwardly, reflexively, back upon oneself. back upon itself.
Phrases: behind the so-called curtain there is nothing to be seen unless we go behind it ourselves [Hegel]; to find oneself; it's all in the mind.
Hegel definition: In infinity, the absolute restlessness in which every determinacy is the opposite of itself, consciousness at last has as its object a difference that is immediately sublated: it distinguishes what is not distinct, and so is self-consciousness. The explanation in which the understanding enjoys only itself already describes this. The curtain that seemed to hide the inner is lifted, and the inner gazes into the inner. Self-consciousness is shown to be the truth of the shapes of consciousness, though at first only for us.
Hegel texts:
The Phenomenology of Spirit
· ¶¶161–165
Hegel citations:
Consciousness of an other, of an object as such, is indeed itself necessarily self-consciousness, being-reflected into itself, consciousness of its own self, in its otherness.
— The Phenomenology of Spirit ¶164 (tr. Pinkard)
It turns out that behind the so-called curtain, which is supposed to hide what is inner, there is nothing to be seen if we ourselves do not go behind it, and one can see something behind the curtain only if there is something behind the curtain to be seen.
— The Phenomenology of Spirit ¶165 (tr. Pinkard)
Not only is consciousness of things only possible for a self-consciousness; rather, it is this self-consciousness alone which is the truth of those shapes.
— The Phenomenology of Spirit ¶164 (tr. Pinkard)

Head: Self-Motion
Path: 三. Spirit › 1. Subjective Spirit › ii. Phenomenology of Spirit (Consciousness) › α. Consciousness as Such › c. Force and the Understanding › iii. Subjectivity (Transition to Self-Consciousness) › 1. Self-Motion
Gloss: Motion that has its source in itself.
Hegelian gloss: Motion that is the self's own, the movement of what returns into itself.
Nouns: self-motion; self-movement, spontaneity, self-activity, self-starting, automotion, initiative, inner principle of motion. autokinesis.
Verbs: move oneself, self-start, initiate, stir. move itself, self-move, stir of itself.
Adjective: self-moving, self-propelled, spontaneous, self-activating, autonomous, autokinetic. self-moved, automotive.
Adverbs: spontaneously, of its own accord. of itself, of its own motion.
Foreign: Latin: sua sponte; Greek: autokinēsis.
Phrases: the soul is self-moving motion [Plato].
Hegel definition: Self-motion here belongs to the law grasped as inner difference and to the living thing that displays it. Each determination of a law lies immediately in the other, so that the difference is one which is no difference. In the living creature consciousness beholds the very process of positing and sublating distinct determinations: life is an interior that does not stay abstract but passes wholly into its expression and takes it back, a movement in which each moment is both end and means.
Hegel texts:
The Philosophy of Mind
· §423
Hegel citations:
But in this way the inner distinction is what it is in truth, the distinction within itself, or the distinction which is no distinction.
— Encyclopedia §423 (tr. Wallace and Miller, rev. Inwood)
In the living creature, by contrast, consciousness beholds the very process of positing and sublating the distinct determinations, perceives that the difference is no difference, i.e., no absolutely fixed difference.
— Encyclopedia §423, Addition (tr. Wallace and Miller, rev. Inwood)

Head: Animation
Path: 三. Spirit › 1. Subjective Spirit › ii. Phenomenology of Spirit (Consciousness) › α. Consciousness as Such › c. Force and the Understanding › iii. Subjectivity (Transition to Self-Consciousness) › 2. Animation
Gloss: The living quality of what moves itself.
Hegelian gloss: The quality of life as self-moving unity.
Nouns: animation; aliveness, liveliness, vivacity, vitality, life, quickness, spirit, verve, élan, brio; animatedness, allegresse†. briskness, energy. vital spark, vital flame. ensoulment, quickening, the vital principle.
Verbs: animate, enliven, vivify, quicken, invigorate, inspirit. infuse life into, give new life to, exsuscitate†. rouse, arouse.
Adjective: animate, animated, lively, living, vital, vivacious, spirited, quick. alive, breathing. active.
Adverbs: animatedly, vivaciously. with life.
Phrases: the breath of life; full of life; alive and kicking.
Hegel definition: Animation is life as consciousness meets it in the living creature: an interior that does not remain abstract but enters entirely into its expression, something mediated by the negation of what is external which turns that mediation back into immediacy. It is an external, sensory existence that is at the same time simply internal, a material being whose parts have lost their separateness, so that each individual is a member of the whole. Life must be conceived as an end in itself.
Hegel texts:
The Philosophy of Mind
· §423
Hegel citations:
For life is that interior which does not remain an abstract interior but enters wholly into its expression
— Encyclopedia §423, Addition (tr. Wallace and Miller, rev. Inwood)
[I]n short, life must be conceived as an end in itself, as an end which has its means within itself, as a totality in which each distinct moment is alike end and means.
— Encyclopedia §423, Addition (tr. Wallace and Miller, rev. Inwood)

Head: Consciousness of Life
Path: 三. Spirit › 1. Subjective Spirit › ii. Phenomenology of Spirit (Consciousness) › α. Consciousness as Such › c. Force and the Understanding › iii. Subjectivity (Transition to Self-Consciousness) › 3. Consciousness of Life
Gloss: Awareness of life in an object.
Hegelian gloss: Consciousness that has life as its object, which is the threshold of self-consciousness.
Nouns: consciousness of life; awareness of life, sense of the living, feeling of vitality, life-feeling, recognition of the living other. the consciousness of the living, life as object, the living thing before consciousness, the genus. vitalism, biophilia.
Verbs: recognize life, sense the living. behold life, be aware of the living.
Adjective: life-aware, vitalist, biophilic. life-conscious, vital, living, organic.
Adverbs: with a sense of life. as living, in the living object.
Foreign: German: Lebensgefühl.
Phrases: reverence for life, Ehrfurcht vor dem Leben [Ger.] [Albert Schweitzer]; the spark of life; a living thing.
Hegel definition: Consciousness of life is the threshold of self-consciousness. While it knows only laws, the intellect finds in its object a counterpart of the I but one still dead and unlike the I's activity. In beholding the living unity of what is distinct, where the differences are posited and sublated in the object itself, self-consciousness is kindled: the awareness of the simple ideal being that is its own object and is differentiated within itself, the I as the truth of what is natural.
Hegel texts:
The Philosophy of Mind
· §423
Hegel citations:
It is, therefore, in the consciousness of this dialectical, this living unity of what is distinct that self-consciousness is kindled
— Encyclopedia §423, Addition (tr. Wallace and Miller, rev. Inwood)
The I in its judgement has an object which is not distinct from it
— Encyclopedia §423 (tr. Wallace and Miller, rev. Inwood)

Head: Self-Consciousness
Path: 三. Spirit › 1. Subjective Spirit › ii. Phenomenology of Spirit (Consciousness) › β. Self-Consciousness
Gloss: Awareness that has itself as its object; the self knowing itself.
Hegelian gloss: The truth of consciousness: the I that is its own object, I = I, whose first form is desire.
Nouns: self-consciousness; self-awareness, self-knowledge, reflexivity, self-reflection, self-recognition, self-relation, the I that is a we, apperception. the I, I am I, selfhood, the native realm of truth.
Verbs: know oneself, be self-aware, reflect upon oneself, recognize oneself. be aware of oneself, reflect, apperceive.
Adjective: self-conscious, self-aware, self-knowing, reflexive, reflective, introspective. meditative, contemplative. apperceptive.
Adverbs: self-consciously, reflexively.
Foreign: German: Selbstbewußtsein; Sanskrit: ātma-jñāna [self-knowledge], sva-saṃvedana [self-awareness]; Korean: jagi uisik [self-consciousness]; French: aperception [Leibniz].
Phrases: know thyself, gnōthi seauton [Gr.]; I that is We, and We that is I [Hegel].
Hegel definition: Self-consciousness is the certainty that is equal to its truth: consciousness is its own object, and the otherness it distinguishes is for it no difference at all. With it we enter the native realm of truth. Yet it is not the motionless tautology of "I am I", for it is a return out of otherness, preserving the sensuous world as appearance whose essence is its own unity with itself. This unity must become essential to it, so it is desire; it finds satisfaction only in another self-consciousness, and so the concept of spirit appears.
Hegel texts:
The Phenomenology of Spirit
· ¶¶166–230
Hegel citations:
Thus, with self-consciousness we have now entered into the native realm of truth.
— The Phenomenology of Spirit ¶167 (tr. Pinkard)
However, self-consciousness is in fact the reflection out of the being of the sensuous and perceived world and is essentially the return from out of otherness.
— The Phenomenology of Spirit ¶167 (tr. Pinkard)
A self-consciousness is for a self-consciousness. Only thereby is there in fact self-consciousness
— The Phenomenology of Spirit ¶177 (tr. Pinkard)

Head: Immediate Self-Consciousness (Desire)
Path: 三. Spirit › 1. Subjective Spirit › ii. Phenomenology of Spirit (Consciousness) › β. Self-Consciousness › a. Immediate Self-Consciousness (Desire)
Gloss: Self-awareness in its first form, as appetite: the self proving its independence by consuming its objects.
Hegelian gloss: Self-consciousness as desire, which certain of itself negates its object and so proves the object's nothingness.
Nouns: immediate self-consciousness; desire, appetite, cupidity, craving, longing, yearning, wanting, hunger, thirst, lust, greed, avidity, concupiscence. appetition†, appetence†, appetency†. covetousness, ravenousness. hankering, coveting, aspiration, eagerness. wish, fancy, fantasy, need, exigency. carnality, tragalism†, sapphism†. greediness, rapacity, Alsatia†. appetitive self-consciousness, the desiring self, immediate self-certainty. the munchies [Slang], jones [U.S. Slang], itch, yen, FOMO [Slang], the hots [Slang]. conation.
Verbs: desire, want, crave, covet, hunger for, thirst for, lust after, long for, yearn for, hanker after. be hungry, have a good appetite, play a good knife and fork, hunger after, thirst after, crave after, itch after, run mad after, raven for, die for, burn to. consume, negate, appropriate. jones for [U.S. Slang], have the hots for [Slang], be dying for, would kill for, be gagging for [Brit. Slang], have a yen for.
Adjective: desirous, desiring, appetitive, craving, avid, covetous, greedy, hungry, lustful, concupiscent. ravening, thirsty, athirst, famished, esurient†. wishful. eager, keen, dying for, devoured by desire. immediate. horny [Slang], peckish [Brit.], gagging [Brit. Slang], itching.
Adverbs: desirously, avidly, hungrily. immediately, appetitively.
Foreign: German: Begierde; Latin: conatus; Greek: orexis, epithymia; Arabic: shahwa [appetite, desire]; Sanskrit: tṛṣṇā [thirst, craving], kāma [desire]; French: appétition [Leibniz].
Phrases: self-consciousness is desire in general [Hegel]; desire is the very essence of man [Spinoza]; hungry for; to have one's heart set on.
Hegel definition: Immediate self-consciousness is desire. The simple I is at first its own pure object and can be certain of itself only by sublating the other, which presents itself as self-sufficient life. Certain that this other is nothing, it makes this nullity its truth and destroys the object. But its satisfaction is conditioned by the object, which must be there to be sublated, so that desire reproduces both the object and itself. It can reach satisfaction only if the object negates itself, and so only in another self-consciousness.
Hegel texts:
The Phenomenology of Spirit
· ¶¶166–177
Hegel citations:
Self-consciousness is therefore only certain of itself through the sublating of this other, which, to itself, exhibits itself as self-sufficient life. Self-consciousness is desire.
— The Phenomenology of Spirit ¶174 (tr. Pinkard)
Self-consciousness attains its satisfaction only in another self-consciousness.
— The Phenomenology of Spirit ¶175 (tr. Pinkard)

Head: Drive and Activity
Path: 三. Spirit › 1. Subjective Spirit › ii. Phenomenology of Spirit (Consciousness) › β. Self-Consciousness › a. Immediate Self-Consciousness (Desire) › i. Drive and Activity
Gloss: The urge to act, and the action that satisfies it.
Hegelian gloss: The drive to sublate the object, and the activity that satisfies it.
Nouns: drive and activity; drive; activity. satisfaction.
Foreign: German: Trieb; Sanskrit: pravṛtti [activity, impulse].
Phrases: the urge to act; an urge to act.
Hegel definition: Drive and activity make up the process of desire. Self-consciousness, immediate and single, is the contradiction between its certainty of itself and an external object, and a being that bears a contradiction and feels it necessarily has the urge to sublate it. It is aware of itself implicitly in the object, which answers to the urge, and by its activity negates both one-sided moments, so that the subject is made objective and the object subjective.
Hegel texts:
The Philosophy of Mind
· §§426–427
Hegel citations:
Self-consciousness, therefore, is aware of itself implicitly in the object, which in this relation is conformable to the urge.
— Encyclopedia §427 (tr. Wallace and Miller, rev. Inwood)
In this process the given object is posited subjectively, just as subjectivity divests itself of its one-sidedness and becomes objective to itself.
— Encyclopedia §427 (tr. Wallace and Miller, rev. Inwood)

Head: Drive
Path: 三. Spirit › 1. Subjective Spirit › ii. Phenomenology of Spirit (Consciousness) › β. Self-Consciousness › a. Immediate Self-Consciousness (Desire) › i. Drive and Activity › 1. Drive
Gloss: The urge that springs from the self's lack and turns it toward the object.
Hegelian gloss: Trieb, self-consciousness's drive to sublate the contradiction between its certainty of itself and the object that stands over against it.
Nouns: drive. urge, impulse, instinct, motivation, need, appetite, impetus, conation, striving. conatus.
Verbs: drive, urge, impel, strive. push. impel &c H0242, goad, spur.
Adjective: driven, impulsive, motivated, appetitive. conative.
Adverbs: impulsively, by impulse.
Phrases: to be driven by.
Hegel definition: Drive, or urge, is the form of desire as self-consciousness first bears it: undetermined by thought and directed on an external object in which it seeks satisfaction. Where something identical with itself carries a contradiction within it and feels both its identity and the contradiction, the urge to remove it necessarily arises. The lifeless has no urge, since it cannot endure contradiction and perishes of it, while soul and mind must have urge.
Hegel texts:
The Philosophy of Mind
· §426
Hegel citations:
Where something identical with itself bears within itself a contradiction and is filled with the feeling of its implicit identity with itself as well as with the opposite feeling of its inner contradiction, then there necessarily emerges the urge to sublate this contradiction.
— Encyclopedia §426, Addition (tr. Wallace and Miller, rev. Inwood)
The non-living entity has no urge because it is incapable of enduring contradiction; it perishes when the Other of itself forces its way into it. By contrast, the ensouled creature and the mind necessarily have urge, since neither the soul nor the mind can be, without having contradiction within themselves and either feeling it or being aware of it.
— Encyclopedia §426, Addition (tr. Wallace and Miller, rev. Inwood)

Head: Activity
Path: 三. Spirit › 1. Subjective Spirit › ii. Phenomenology of Spirit (Consciousness) › β. Self-Consciousness › a. Immediate Self-Consciousness (Desire) › i. Drive and Activity › 2. Activity
Gloss: The deed by which the self acts on the object to satisfy its drive.
Hegelian gloss: Tätigkeit, the activity that negates the object's independence and so gives the drive its satisfaction.
Nouns: activity. action, deed, doing, agency. performance, exercise, operation, praxis, execution, interworking†. proceeding, step, move. revolutionary practice, sensuous human activity.
Verbs: act, do, pursue.
Adjective: active.
Adverbs: actively.
Foreign: German: Praxis, revolutionäre Praxis, sinnlich menschliche Tätigkeit.
Hegel definition: Activity is the process in which self-consciousness negates the two one-sided moments, its own subjectivity and the independence of the object, and thereby brings their identity to be for it. The object, selfless in itself, can offer no resistance: the dialectic of self-sublation which is its nature exists here as this activity of the I. Self-consciousness is not just being but absolute activity, and takes possession of an object whose independence is only pretence.
Hegel texts:
The Philosophy of Mind
· §427
Hegel citations:
To this activity the object, which in itself and for self-consciousness is the selfless, can offer no resistance; the dialectic of self-sublation, which is the object's nature, exists here as this activity of the I.
— Encyclopedia §427 (tr. Wallace and Miller, rev. Inwood)
Self-consciousness is in a position to sublate this contradiction since it is not just being, but absolute activity; and it sublates the contradiction by taking possession of the object whose independence is, so to speak, only a pretence, satisfies itself by consuming it and, since it is an end in itself, maintains itself in this process.
— Encyclopedia §427, Addition (tr. Wallace and Miller, rev. Inwood)

Head: Desire and Destruction
Path: 三. Spirit › 1. Subjective Spirit › ii. Phenomenology of Spirit (Consciousness) › β. Self-Consciousness › a. Immediate Self-Consciousness (Desire) › ii. Desire and Destruction
Gloss: Desire that destroys its object.
Hegelian gloss: Desire that destroys its object, and so must always reproduce it as other.
Nouns: desire and destruction; destruction.
Foreign: German: Begierde.
Phrases: to eat one's fill.
Hegel definition: Desire destroys the object it meets. Certain of the nullity of the other, self-consciousness sets down that nullity as its truth, annihilates the self-sufficient object and thereby gives itself a certainty of itself that has become objective. Yet the destroying cannot finish its work: for there to be a sublating there must be something other, so that through its negative relation to the object self-consciousness does not get rid of it but engenders it again, and the desire along with it.
Hegel texts:
The Phenomenology of Spirit
· ¶¶174–175
Hegel citations:
Certain of the nullity of this other, it posits for itself this nullity as its truth, it destroys the self-sufficient object, and it as a result gives itself the certainty of itself as true certainty, as the sort of certainty which, to itself, has come to be in an objective manner.
— The Phenomenology of Spirit ¶174 (tr. Pinkard)
Self-consciousness is thus unable through its negative relation to the object to sublate it, and for that reason it again, instead re-engenders the object as well as the desire.
— The Phenomenology of Spirit ¶175 (tr. Pinkard)

Head: Desire
Path: 三. Spirit › 1. Subjective Spirit › ii. Phenomenology of Spirit (Consciousness) › β. Self-Consciousness › a. Immediate Self-Consciousness (Desire) › ii. Desire and Destruction › 1. Desire
Gloss: Self-consciousness turned toward an object it wants, certain that the object is nothing in itself.
Hegelian gloss: Begierde, self-consciousness as desire, certain of the nothingness of the other and setting out to prove it.
Nouns: desire. appetite, craving. Begierde, longing, wanting, hunger, the desiring self.
Verbs: desire, crave.
Adjective: desirous, appetitive. insatiate, unquenchable, omnivorous.
Adverbs: desirously.
Phrases: das Selbstbewußtsein ist Begierde überhaupt [Ger.] [Hegel, Phenomenology]; seeking a horse in an empty market, qiu ma tang si [Chin.] [Zhuangzi].
Hegel definition: Desire is self-consciousness in its first form, as the negative relation to an independent object. It is certain of itself only through sublating that other, which shows itself as self-sufficient life. In satisfying itself it learns that the object is independent and that both its desire and the certainty gained from it are conditioned by that object. There is therefore something other than self-consciousness that is the essence of desire.
Hegel texts:
The Phenomenology of Spirit
· ¶¶174–175
Hegel citations:
There is in fact an other than self-consciousness, the essence of desire
— The Phenomenology of Spirit ¶175 (tr. Pinkard)
Desire and the certainty of itself achieved in its satisfaction are conditioned by the object, for the certainty is through the sublating of this other.
— The Phenomenology of Spirit ¶175 (tr. Pinkard)

Head: Destruction
Path: 三. Spirit › 1. Subjective Spirit › ii. Phenomenology of Spirit (Consciousness) › β. Self-Consciousness › a. Immediate Self-Consciousness (Desire) › ii. Desire and Destruction › 2. Destruction
Gloss: Desire's annihilation of its object, which proves the object nothing but must begin again.
Hegelian gloss: Vernichtung, desire's negation of the independent object, through which it is certain of itself, yet which reproduces both the object and the desire.

Hegel definition: Destruction is what desire does to its object. Its relation to the selfless object is only negative, so that the object is simply consumed: it does not fashion the object, which would preserve its matter and give the subject's form a lasting hold, but annihilates its independence, since self-consciousness cannot yet endure an independent other. Desire is thus destructive in its satisfaction and self-centred in its content, and because satisfaction is single and passing, desire produces itself again.
Hegel texts:

· §428
Hegel citations:
So desire in its satisfaction is in general destructive, as it is in its content self-centred, and since the satisfaction has only happened in the individual case, and this is transitory, the desire reproduces itself again in the satisfaction.
— Encyclopedia §428 (tr. Wallace and Miller, rev. Inwood)
The relationship of desire to the object is still completely one of self-centred destruction, not one of fashioning.
— Encyclopedia §428, Addition (tr. Wallace and Miller, rev. Inwood)

Head: Satisfaction and Identification
Path: 三. Spirit › 1. Subjective Spirit › ii. Phenomenology of Spirit (Consciousness) › β. Self-Consciousness › a. Immediate Self-Consciousness (Desire) › iii. Satisfaction and Identification
Gloss: The satisfaction of desire, in which the self finds itself again.
Hegelian gloss: The self finding its own self-identity in the satisfaction of its desire, and with it the need of another self.
Nouns: satisfaction and identification; satisfaction.
Hegel definition: Satisfaction and identification complete the process of desire. Its product is that the I closes with itself and is satisfied for itself, though outwardly still single and prey to the endless alternation of desire and satisfaction. Inwardly, in negating immediacy, the result has the character of universality and of the identity of self-consciousness with its object: it posits otherness within itself and changes the selfless object into a free one, another I.
Hegel texts:
The Philosophy of Mind
· §§428–429
Hegel citations:
The product of this process is that I joins together with itself, and is thereby satisfied for itself, actualized.
— Encyclopedia §428 (tr. Wallace and Miller, rev. Inwood)
But the self-feeling which the I gets in the satisfaction does not, on the inner side or in itself, remain in abstract being-for-self or in its individuality; as the negation of immediacy and of individuality the result involves the determination of universality and of the identity of self-consciousness with its object.
— Encyclopedia §429 (tr. Wallace and Miller, rev. Inwood)

Head: Satisfaction
Path: 三. Spirit › 1. Subjective Spirit › ii. Phenomenology of Spirit (Consciousness) › β. Self-Consciousness › a. Immediate Self-Consciousness (Desire) › iii. Satisfaction and Identification › 1. Satisfaction

Hegel definition: Satisfaction is the reflection of self-consciousness into itself, the certainty that has become truth, which desire reaches by sublating its object. But in this very satisfaction self-consciousness learns that the object is self-sufficient, since its certainty depends on there being something to sublate. It must be absolutely for itself, and can be so only by sublating the object; true satisfaction therefore requires an object that carries out the negation in itself, which only another self-consciousness does.

However, in this satisfaction it learns from experience about the self-sufficiency of its object.
— The Phenomenology of Spirit ¶175 (tr. Pinkard)

— The Phenomenology of Spirit ¶175 (tr. Pinkard)

Head: Identification
Head (German): Das Zusammenschließen des Ich mit sich selbst
Path: 三. Spirit › 1. Subjective Spirit › ii. Phenomenology of Spirit (Consciousness) › β. Self-Consciousness › a. Immediate Self-Consciousness (Desire) › iii. Satisfaction and Identification › 2. Identification
Gloss: The self finding itself again in its satisfied desire, and so needing another self.
Hegelian gloss: The product of the process: the I closes together with itself and is for itself; its satisfaction shows that it needs another self-consciousness.
Nouns: identification. return to self, self-certainty through the object. self-identification, self-feeling. the I closing with itself, self-identity.
Verbs: find oneself again. identify.
Adjective: identified.
Phrases: desire reborn from satisfaction; at peace with oneself.
Hegel definition: Identification is the result in which self-consciousness, having negated its own immediacy and the external object, raises itself above the self-centredness of destructive desire. It divides itself into a consciousness of a free object, in which the I knows itself as I but which is still outside it. It has filled the other with the I, turned it from something selfless into another self, and so brought itself face to face with itself as a distinct I.
Hegel texts:
The Philosophy of Mind
· §429
Hegel citations:
The judgement or diremption of this self-consciousness is the consciousness of a free object, in which I has awareness of itself as I, but which is also still outside it.
— Encyclopedia §429 (tr. Wallace and Miller, rev. Inwood)
On the inner side, by contrast, or in accordance with the concept, self-consciousness has, by sublation of its subjectivity and of the external object, negated its own immediacy, the standpoint of desire, has posited itself with the determination of otherness towards its own self, has filled the Other with the /, has changed it from something selfless into a free, into a selfish object, into another I.
— Encyclopedia §429, Addition (tr. Wallace and Miller, rev. Inwood)

Hegel definition: Recognitive self-consciousness is self-consciousness that is in and for itself only in being so for another: it exists only as recognized. A one-sided doing would be useless because what is supposed to happen can only be brought about through both of them bringing it about.

They recognize themselves as mutually recognizing each other.

Nouns: coercion and subjection; coercion, subjection.
Foreign: Spanish: encomienda, repartimiento [colonial forced labour]; French: assujettissement [subjection, subjectification] [Foucault].
Phrases: have it your own way; it can't be helped; amen; da locum melioribus [Lat.]; tempori parendum [Lat.].
Hegel definition: Coercion and subjection are how the combat for recognition ends. Since life is as essential as freedom, one combatant prefers life, keeps himself as a single self-consciousness and gives up the claim to recognition, while the other holds to relating to himself and is recognized by the first as subjected. Force is the basis in this appearance but not the basis of right: it is the outward beginning of states, not their substantial principle, and a necessary passage to universal self-consciousness.
Hegel texts:
The Philosophy of Mind
· §§432–433
Hegel citations:
Because life is as essential as freedom, the combat ends initially as one-sided negation with an asymmetry: one of the combatants prefers life, maintains himself as individual self-consciousness, but surrenders his chance of recognition, while the other holds fast to his relation to himself and is recognized by the first in his subjugation: the relationship of mastery and bondage.
— Encyclopedia §433 (tr. Wallace and Miller, rev. Inwood)
Force, which is the basis in this appearance, is not on that account the basis of right
— Encyclopedia §433, Remark (tr. Wallace and Miller, rev. Inwood)

Hegel definition: Coercion belongs to the life-and-death struggle and the force that ends it. Each self-consciousness puts the other's life in danger and exposes its own, bent on compelling the other to recognize it. Such combat in its extreme form occurs only in the state of nature, not in civil society and the state, where recognition is already present; and although a state may arise by force, it does not rest on force, which only brings into existence what is justified in itself.

· §432
Hegel citations:
The combat of recognition is thus a life and death struggle; each of the two self-consciousnesses puts the other's life in danger, and exposes itself to it—but only in danger, for each is equally bent on maintaining his life, since it is the embodiment of his freedom.
— Encyclopedia §432 (tr. Wallace and Miller, rev. Inwood)

Hegel definition: Subjection is the surrender in which the one who prefers life gives up recognition and becomes the bondsman. The bondsman's self-will yields to the master's will and receives the master's purpose for its content, while the master takes up only care for the bondsman's natural life. It is first free only as the universal essence, withdrawn from the manifold of objective being. Hegel definition: Stoicism is the freedom of self-consciousness as it first appeared in the history of spirit. Its principle is that consciousness is the thinking essence, and that something is essential, true or good for it only in so far as it behaves in it as a thinking being. Hegel definition: Reason is the certainty of consciousness that it is all reality. Self-consciousness, which had saved its freedom at the cost of the world, now turns its negative relation to otherness into a positive one: certain that all actuality is nothing but itself, it behaves toward the world as idealism and for the first time takes an interest in its continuing existence. This certainty is at first only an assertion that has forgotten the path leading to it, and reason must make it true by finding itself in what is.

— The Phenomenology of Spirit ¶233 (tr. Pinkard)

— The Phenomenology of Spirit ¶232 (tr. Pinkard)

Hegel definition: The certainty and truth of reason is reason as it first comes on the scene, asserting that I am I in the sense that the I is all reality and presence and nothing else counts as other. It has behind it, and forgotten, the path on which otherness vanished: that what is in itself is only in so far as it is for consciousness. As yet the reality is only a pure universal, the simple category, the unity of self-consciousness and being. An idealism that lets this unity fall apart again into consciousness and an in-itself facing it is one-sided and bad.

Hegel definition: Reason's certainty of being all reality is idealism as consciousness first expresses it: I am I, an object with the consciousness that nothing other has being. Self-consciousness, whose singular individuality has proved to be in itself the absolute essence, now discovers the world as its own and takes an interest in its continuing existence. It must be this reality not only for itself but in itself, by proving it. At first the certainty has forgotten the path that justifies it, and its reality is only a pure abstraction, the simple category.

The Phenomenology of Spirit
· ¶¶231–239
Hegel citations:
This middle expresses this unity to consciousness and thereby expresses itself to itself, the certainty of being all truth.
— The Phenomenology of Spirit ¶231 (tr. Pinkard)
It is a singular object; it is all reality and presence. However, not only is self-consciousness for itself all reality; it is also in itself all reality, as a result of its becoming this reality, or, instead by proving itself to be this reality.
— The Phenomenology of Spirit ¶233 (tr. Pinkard)
It therefore conducts itself as idealism in relation to actuality.
— The Phenomenology of Spirit ¶232 (tr. Pinkard)

Hegel definition: Certainty is reason as self-consciousness first has it: the certainty that its determinations are objective, determinations of the essence of things just as much as its own thoughts. Reason is truth in and for itself, the simple identity of the subjectivity of the concept with its objectivity and universality, so that the object once merely given to consciousness now permeates the I, and the I overarches the object.

— The Berlin Phenomenology §439 (tr. Petry)
Since spirit is implicitly reason, it is reason relating itself to reason, the certainty of reason consisting of its relating itself to what is rational.
— The Berlin Phenomenology §439 (tr. Petry)

Hegel citations:
