— The Berlin Phenomenology §439 (tr. Petry)

Hegel definition: Observing reason is consciousness that again takes up meaning something and perceiving, but now with the certainty that it is itself the other. It makes its own observations and sets out to know the truth, seeking to find in what is a thing a concept, and so to have in thinghood only the consciousness of itself. It therefore takes a universal interest in the world, certain that the present is rational. It turns first to nature, then to self-consciousness, and then to the relation of self-consciousness to its immediate actuality.
Hegel texts:
The Phenomenology of Spirit
· ¶¶240–346
Hegel citations:
Reason sets out to know the truth, and what was a thing for meaning-something and perceiving is now to be found as a concept, which is to say, reason is to have in thinghood only the consciousness of itself.
— The Phenomenology of Spirit ¶240 (tr. Pinkard)
It seeks its other, while knowing that it possesses nothing else in that other but itself; it seeks only its own infinity.
— The Phenomenology of Spirit ¶240 (tr. Pinkard)

Hegel definition: The observation of nature is reason's search for itself among natural things. It is not mere tasting, smelling and seeing, for what it observes must at least have the meaning of a universal. It begins by describing, passes to marks, genera and laws, and in organic life looks for the law relating inner and outer. Hegel texts:
The Phenomenology of Spirit
· ¶¶244–297
Hegel citations:
The meaning of what is perceived should at least be that of a universal, not a sensuous this.
— The Phenomenology of Spirit ¶244 (tr. Pinkard)
However, charming remarks are no knowing of necessity. Interesting connections are just that: interesting. However, the interest is still nothing but suppositional fancy about reason.
— The Phenomenology of Spirit ¶297 (tr. Pinkard)

Head: Logical and Psychological Laws
Path: 三. Spirit › 1. Subjective Spirit › ii. Phenomenology of Spirit (Consciousness) › γ. Reason › a. The Certainty and Truth of Reason › ii. Observing Reason › 2. Logical and Psychological Laws
Gloss: The search for laws of thinking and of the mind, as in formal logic and psychology.
Hegelian gloss: The search for laws of thought and psychological laws, which reason finds empty of real content.
Nouns: logical and psychological laws; observation of self-consciousness in its purity and its relation to external actuality; formal logic, laws of thought, psychology, faculty psychology, associationism, empirical psychology, psychological laws, character types, influence of circumstances, environment and individual. logical laws, the faculties, the individual and its circumstances, environment. psychologism.

Adjective: psychological, logical, introspective, behavioural, environmental. formal, empirical.
Adverbs: psychologically, logically. by law.
Phrases: the proper study of mankind is man [Pope]; the laws of thought; the workings of the mind.
Hegel definition: Logical and psychological laws are what observation finds when it turns from nature back to self-consciousness. First it finds the laws of thought, taken as formal and lacking reality, though as laws of pure thinking they are inseparably essentialities of both form and things. Then it turns to psychology, seeking a law relating individuality to the actuality acting on it. Since individuals can let that influence have its way or turn it on its head, the supposed psychological necessity is an empty phrase.
Hegel texts:
The Phenomenology of Spirit
· ¶¶298–308
Hegel citations:
While observation now turns back around into itself, and it directs itself to the actual concept as the free concept, it finds first of all the laws of thought.
— The Phenomenology of Spirit ¶299 (tr. Pinkard)
Psychological necessity thereby becomes such an empty phrase that it includes the absolute possibility that what is supposed to have had this influence could very well also not have had any influence whatsoever.
— The Phenomenology of Spirit ¶307 (tr. Pinkard)
This free concept, whose universality has that developed singularity just as absolutely within itself, is found by observation only in the concept existing as the concept itself, or in self-consciousness.
— The Phenomenology of Spirit ¶298 (tr. Pinkard)

Head: Physiognomy and Phrenology
Path: 三. Spirit › 1. Subjective Spirit › ii. Phenomenology of Spirit (Consciousness) › γ. Reason › a. The Certainty and Truth of Reason › ii. Observing Reason › 3. Physiognomy and Phrenology
Gloss: The attempt to read the mind from the body.
Hegelian gloss: Reason seeking the mind in its immediate bodily actuality, in face and skull.
Nouns: physiognomy and phrenology; observation of self-consciousness in its immediate actuality; reading mind from body, psychophysiology, body-mind correlation, outer expression of inner character, somatotype, biological determinism. the observation of the body as expression, the outer as expression of the inner, physiognomy and phrenology, the body as sign, the organ. somatic reading.
Verbs: read off, infer from the body, correlate. read, infer, interpret, observe the body.
Adjective: psychophysical, somatic, physiognomic, phrenological, deterministic. bodily, external, expressive.
Adverbs: from outward signs. from the body, outwardly, by signs.
Phrases: the body as the mirror of the soul; to judge by appearances; skin deep.
Hegel definition: Physiognomy and phrenology are observation's attempts to find the law relating self-consciousness to its immediate actuality, how the inner is expressed in the outer. The whole individuality is now the object: the original, inborn body and the traits that arise through acting. Physiognomy takes the outer as a sign and expression of the inner; phrenology takes it as a motionless thing, the skull. Observation thereby makes the actuality of spirit into a thing, ending in the judgement that the being of spirit is a bone.
Hegel texts:
The Phenomenology of Spirit
· ¶¶309–346
Hegel citations:
However, while the individual is at the same time only what he has done, so is his body also the expression of himself which is brought forth by him.
— The Phenomenology of Spirit ¶310 (tr. Pinkard)
What is up for examination here are the relationships between both aspects. More specifically, what is up for examination is how this relation is to be determined and how we are to understand the expression of the inner in the outer.
— The Phenomenology of Spirit ¶311 (tr. Pinkard)

Head: Physiognomic Observation
Path: 三. Spirit › 1. Subjective Spirit › ii. Phenomenology of Spirit (Consciousness) › γ. Reason › a. The Certainty and Truth of Reason › ii. Observing Reason › 3. Physiognomy and Phrenology › a. Physiognomic Observation
Gloss: The reading of character from the face.
Hegelian gloss: The interpretation of the face as the sign of the inner, which can only ever be an opinion.
Nouns: physiognomic observation; physiognomy, physiognomics, face-reading, Lavater's physiognomy, reading of features, character from countenance, metoposcopy [forehead-reading]. contour, countenance, visage, cast of countenance, profile. symptomatology [Med.], semiology, semiotics, semeiology†, oneirology acception†. the science of Lavater, features, expression, the hand, handwriting.

Adjective: physiognomic, physiognomical, facial, characterological. expressive.
Adverbs: by the face, at face value. physiognomically, from the face.
Foreign: Arabic: firāsa [physiognomic discernment], qiyāfa [reading of traces and features].
Phrases: you can't judge a book by its cover; there's no art to find the mind's construction in the face [Macbeth]; don't judge a book by its cover; the face is the mirror of the soul.
Hegel definition: Physiognomic observation takes the individual's body, with the traits that activity has formed in it, as the expression of the inner. The body is at once an original being, which the individual has not made, and a sign in which the individual makes known what they are by putting their original nature into practice. The inner is no longer empty but a determinate original character whose form is activity, and what physiognomy examines is how this inner is related to its outer and how that expression is to be understood.
Hegel texts:
The Phenomenology of Spirit
· ¶¶309–322
Hegel citations:
This being, the body of the determinate individuality, is its primordiality, its own “what-it-has-not-done.”
— The Phenomenology of Spirit ¶310 (tr. Pinkard)
The body is the unity of uncultured and cultured being and is the actuality permeated by the being-for-itself of the individual.
— The Phenomenology of Spirit ¶311 (tr. Pinkard)

Head: Phrenological Observation
Path: 三. Spirit › 1. Subjective Spirit › ii. Phenomenology of Spirit (Consciousness) › γ. Reason › a. The Certainty and Truth of Reason › ii. Observing Reason › 3. Physiognomy and Phrenology › b. Phrenological Observation
Gloss: The reading of character from the shape of the skull.
Hegelian gloss: The reading of mind from the shape of the skull, the lowest form of observing reason.
Nouns: phrenological observation; phrenology, craniology, cranioscopy, Gall's doctrine, organology, bumps on the head, skull-reading, faculties located in the brain; pseudoscience, quackery. psychology, mental philosophy, philosophy of the mind. the skull, bumps, the doctrine of Gall, the organ of murder.

Adverbs: phrenologically. from the skull.

Hegel definition: Phrenological observation takes as the outer of self-consciousness no speaking sign, like gesture or the face, but an entirely motionless actuality which, separated from self-conscious movement, presents itself as a mere thing: the skull. Observation turns from changeable expression back to hard and fast being, treating externality as the immediate actuality of spirit in the form of a dead thing, so as either to make spirit into a thing or to give dead being the significance of spirit.
Hegel texts:
The Phenomenology of Spirit
· ¶¶323–346
Hegel citations:
However, in the determination still up for examination, the outer is finally an entire motionless actuality which is not in its own self a speaking sign but which, separated from self-conscious movement, presents itself for itself and is as a mere thing.
— The Phenomenology of Spirit ¶323 (tr. Pinkard)
For this reason, observation finally turns away from this changeable language and goes back to hard and fast being.
— The Phenomenology of Spirit ¶343 (tr. Pinkard)

Head: The Being of Spirit Is a Bone
Head (German): Das Sein des Geistes ist ein Knochen
Path: 三. Spirit › 1. Subjective Spirit › ii. Phenomenology of Spirit (Consciousness) › γ. Reason › a. The Certainty and Truth of Reason › ii. Observing Reason › 3. Physiognomy and Phrenology › c. The Being of Spirit Is a Bone
Gloss: The claim that mind is a bone, the crude conclusion of reading mind from the body: a statement whose terms seem wholly incompatible, yet which hides a truth about mind and thing.
Hegelian gloss: The infinite judgment that spirit is a bone, in which the highest and lowest are crudely identified.
Nouns: the being of spirit is a bone, spirit is a bone; infinite judgment &c H0162; reduction of mind to matter, reductive materialism, crude materialism, eliminativism, biologism, neuro-reductionism; category mistake, absurdity; the organ of generation and the organ of urination [Hegel's image]. the skull-bone, the dead thing, reification, the crude identity, the absurd proposition, the high and the low conjoined.
Verbs: reduce, equate mind with matter, conflate, materialize. reify, identify, equate, reduce to a thing.
Adjective: reductive, reductionist, materialist, crude, absurd, paradoxical. reified, thing-like, osseous, incommensurable.
Adverbs: reductively, crudely. as a thing, absurdly.
Foreign: German: Verdinglichung, Versachlichung.
Phrases: the being of spirit is a bone [Hegel]; you are nothing but a pack of neurons [Francis Crick]; the highest and the lowest.
Hegel definition: The proposition that the being of spirit is a bone is where observing reason ends: the certainty of reason seeking itself as an objective actuality says that spirit is, that it is a thing. Its true meaning is the infinite judgement that the self is a thing, a judgement which cancels itself, since the thing is thereby shown to be the unity of the I and being. Held fast as an enduring proposition by representational thought, which fixes self and thing apart, it is reason grasped irrationally.
Hegel texts:
The Phenomenology of Spirit
· ¶¶343–346
Hegel citations:
Of spirit it is simply to be said, “it is.” However much it is otherwise said of spirit that it is, it has a being, it is a thing, a singular actuality, still it is not thereby meant that it is something we can see, or take in our hands, or push around and so forth, but that is what is said of it, and what in truth the foregoing has been saying may be expressed in this way: The being of spirit is a bone.
— The Phenomenology of Spirit ¶343 (tr. Pinkard)
This proposition is the infinite judgment that the self is a thing – a judgment which sublates itself.
— The Phenomenology of Spirit ¶344 (tr. Pinkard)

Head: Self-Actualization of Reason
Head (German): Verwirklichung des vernünftigen Selbstbewusstseins durch sich selbst
Path: 三. Spirit › 1. Subjective Spirit › ii. Phenomenology of Spirit (Consciousness) › γ. Reason › a. The Certainty and Truth of Reason › iii. Self-Actualization of Reason
Gloss: Reason seeking itself in the world through action rather than observation.
Hegelian gloss: Reason realizing itself through its own action, finding its other in the world it acts upon.
Nouns: self-actualization of reason; the actualization of rational self-consciousness through its own activity; self-realization, self-actualization, practical reason, active reason, striving, enterprise, the world as a field of action, the practical life. the self-making of self-consciousness, the happy people, the ethical realm sought.
Verbs: realize oneself, act, strive, undertake, make one's mark. actualize, realize, bring forth, seek oneself.
Adjective: practical, active, self-actualizing, enterprising. self-realizing.
Adverbs: practically, actively, by one's own efforts. by one's own doing, in action.
Phrases: to make one's way in the world; to make one's mark; to put into practice.
Hegel definition: The self-actualization of reason is the movement in which rational self-consciousness, having found the thing to be itself and itself a thing, no longer observes but seeks to bring about by its own activity its unity with itself in another self-consciousness. Certain that the self-sufficient object facing it is nothing alien, it must raise this certainty to truth. It does so first as pleasure, then as the law of the heart, and then as virtue struggling with the way of the world.
Hegel texts:
The Phenomenology of Spirit
· ¶¶347–393
Hegel citations:
To self-consciousness, this certainty must now be elevated to truth.
— The Phenomenology of Spirit ¶347 (tr. Pinkard)
Self-consciousness is spirit that has the certainty of having its unity with itself in the doubling of its self-consciousness and in the self-sufficiency of both self-consciousnesses.
— The Phenomenology of Spirit ¶347 (tr. Pinkard)

Head: Pleasure and Necessity
Path: 三. Spirit › 1. Subjective Spirit › ii. Phenomenology of Spirit (Consciousness) › γ. Reason › a. The Certainty and Truth of Reason › iii. Self-Actualization of Reason › 1. Pleasure and Necessity
Gloss: The pursuit of personal pleasure, which ends by running into an impersonal fate.
Hegelian gloss: Self-consciousness that plunges into life to take pleasure and is crushed by abstract necessity.

Sybarite, voluptuary, man of pleasure, epicurean, sensualist, tragalist†. predestination, foredoom. the pleasure-seeker, the plucking of life, blind necessity, the dead actuality. sybaritism.

Foreign: Latin: carpe diem, suavitas, voluptas, delectatio, fruitio; Sanskrit: kāma; French: plaisir, jouissance; German: Wohlgefallen, Vergnügen; Greek: hēdonē, chara, chairein, terpsis, euphrosynē; Italian: piacere, diletto, gusto, godimento; Spanish: goce, gozo, placer.
Phrases: he takes hold of life much as a ripe fruit is plucked [Hegel]; gather ye rosebuds while ye may [Herrick]; Verweile doch, du bist so schön [Ger.] [Goethe]; eat, drink and be merry; to live for pleasure.
Hegel definition: Pleasure and necessity is the first shape of self-actualizing reason. Self-consciousness, leaving law, custom and theory behind as grey shadows, sets out to find itself as a singular being in another and to enjoy itself there. In the pleasure attained it becomes objective to itself but is also cancelled, for what it meets as its own essence is empty, inexorable necessity, whose only work is the nothingness of individuality. Plunging from dead theory into life, it has plunged into its own lifelessness.
Hegel texts:
The Phenomenology of Spirit
· ¶¶360–366
Hegel citations:
This first purpose is to become conscious of itself as a singular essence within that other self-consciousness, or to make this other into itself.
— The Phenomenology of Spirit ¶360 (tr. Pinkard)
Instead of having plunged from dead theory into life, the only singular individuality, which at first has only the pure concept of reason for its content, has thus instead plunged into the consciousness of its own lifelessness, and, to itself, has come to be only as empty and alien necessity, as dead actuality.
— The Phenomenology of Spirit ¶363 (tr. Pinkard)

Head: The Law of the Heart and the Frenzy of Self-Conceit
Head (German): Das Gesetz des Herzens und der Wahnsinn des Eigendünkels
Path: 三. Spirit › 1. Subjective Spirit › ii. Phenomenology of Spirit (Consciousness) › γ. Reason › a. The Certainty and Truth of Reason › iii. Self-Actualization of Reason › 2. The Law of the Heart and the Frenzy of Self-Conceit
Gloss: The demand that the world conform to one's own heart, which ends in fury at a world that will not.
Hegelian gloss: The heart that wants its law to be the world's, and that rages against the world as a perversion of its law.
Nouns: the law of the heart and the frenzy of self-conceit. the law of the heart.
Foreign: German: Schwärmerei [enthusiasm, fanaticism], Eigendünkel.
Hegel definition: The law of the heart and the frenzy of self-conceit is the shape in which self-consciousness knows that it has the universal, the law, immediately within itself, and wills to realize it for the welfare of all. Once realized, the law ceases to be the law of its heart and becomes an alien order, and other hearts reject it as merely another's. The concern for humanity then turns into a mad self-conceit that denounces the universal order as a perversion made by others, though the inversion lies in the heart itself.
Hegel texts:
The Phenomenology of Spirit
· ¶¶367–380
Hegel citations:
It immediately knows that it has the universal, or the law, within itself, which on account of this determination, that it is immediately in the being-for-itself of consciousness, is called the law of the heart.
— The Phenomenology of Spirit ¶367 (tr. Pinkard)
The heart-throb for the welfare of mankind therefore passes over into the bluster of a mad self-conceit.
— The Phenomenology of Spirit ¶377 (tr. Pinkard)
It is thus not a contingent and alien individuality but rather just this very heart, which, according to all of its aspects, is in itself the inverted and inverting.
— The Phenomenology of Spirit ¶377 (tr. Pinkard)

Head: The Law of the Heart
Path: 三. Spirit › 1. Subjective Spirit › ii. Phenomenology of Spirit (Consciousness) › γ. Reason › a. The Certainty and Truth of Reason › iii. Self-Actualization of Reason › 2. The Law of the Heart and the Frenzy of Self-Conceit › a. The Law of the Heart
Gloss: The individual's demand that the world obey the law of their own heart, for the welfare of mankind.
Hegelian gloss: Das Gesetz des Herzens: the heart that holds its law immediately within itself and sets out to realize it against a world that oppresses it.
Nouns: the law of the heart. sentimental idealism, idealism of the heart, utopianism, moral fervour. the heart's law, the throb of the heart for the welfare of mankind, sentimental reformism.
Verbs: demand, impose.
Adjective: utopian, heartfelt.
Adverbs: from the heart.
Phrases: the heart has its laws; to follow one's heart; the heart wants what it wants.
Hegel definition: The law of the heart is the universal that a self-consciousness finds immediately in its own being-for-itself and holds to be necessary and valid for all, richer than the mere singular pursuit of pleasure. When the individual carries it out, the law passes into being: it becomes a universal order and a power indifferent to that heart. The individual no longer finds in it what was its own, and is entangled in an order not only alien but hostile, which its very deed has acknowledged as real.
Hegel texts:
The Phenomenology of Spirit
· ¶¶367–372
Hegel citations:
Through its actualization, the law of the heart just ceases to be a law of the heart, for it thereby receives the form of being and is now the universal power for which this heart is a matter of indifference
— The Phenomenology of Spirit ¶372 (tr. Pinkard)

Head: The Frenzy of Self-Conceit
Path: 三. Spirit › 1. Subjective Spirit › ii. Phenomenology of Spirit (Consciousness) › γ. Reason › a. The Certainty and Truth of Reason › iii. Self-Actualization of Reason › 2. The Law of the Heart and the Frenzy of Self-Conceit › b. The Frenzy of Self-Conceit
Gloss: The rage of the heart that finds its law perverted in the world and blames the world's order for its own madness.
Hegelian gloss: Der Wahnsinn des Eigendünkels: the heart, seeing its law turned into a universal order alien to it, declares that order a perversion devised by fanatical priests and despots.
Nouns: the frenzy of self-conceit. self-righteousness, self-conceit, conceit, sanctimony, rage against the world, misanthropy, paranoia, crusading zeal, Karl Moor [Schiller]. vanity, conceitedness, self-sufficiency, self-love, self-approbation, self-gratulation†. the madness of self-conceit, derangement.
Verbs: rail against the world, fulminate, crusade, rage, denounce, blame others, rave. execrate, thunder against, beshrew†. loathe.
Adjective: self-righteous, sanctimonious, conceited, zealous, fanatical, misanthropic, enraged, paranoid, self-conceited, frenzied, deranged. vain, overweening, vainglorious, puffed up. intolerant, infatuated, dogmatic.
Adverbs: self-righteously, furiously, in a frenzy, conceitedly.
Phrases: the time is out of joint [Hamlet]; das Herzklopfen für das Wohl der Menschheit geht in das Toben des verrückten Eigendünkels über [Ger.] [Hegel, Phenomenology]; defeat is not as dangerous as the fear of admitting it, ne tak opasno porazhenie, kak opasna boyazn' priznat' svoyo porazhenie [Rus.] [Lenin].
Hegel definition: The frenzy of self-conceit is what the concern for the welfare of mankind becomes when the realized law of the heart turns against the one who authored it. Others do not find their own hearts' law in it and resist it. To save itself from destruction, consciousness casts out of itself the inversion that it is, and rages against the universal order as a fabrication of fanatical priests and gluttonous despots. In truth it is the singular heart, wanting to be immediately universal, that is mad and inverted.
Hegel texts:
The Phenomenology of Spirit
· ¶¶373–380
Hegel citations:
Hence, others do not find the law of their hearts in this content; rather, they find instead that it is the law of another’s heart which has been accomplished.
— The Phenomenology of Spirit ¶373 (tr. Pinkard)
But it is the heart, or the singularity of consciousness immediately willing to be universal, which drives one mad and which is inverted
— The Phenomenology of Spirit ¶377 (tr. Pinkard)

Head: Virtue and the Way of the World
Path: 三. Spirit › 1. Subjective Spirit › ii. Phenomenology of Spirit (Consciousness) › γ. Reason › a. The Certainty and Truth of Reason › iii. Self-Actualization of Reason › 3. Virtue and the Way of the World

Hegel definition: Virtue and the way of the world is the shape in which consciousness takes the law to be essential and individuality to be what must be sacrificed, both in itself, by discipline, and in the way of the world, which makes individuality the essence and subordinates the good to itself. Virtue wants to bring the good into existence by giving up individuality, but individuality is the very activity that makes the in-itself actual. The activity of individuality proves an end in itself.

· ¶¶381–393

For the consciousness of virtue, the law is the essential, and individuality is to be sublated, and therefore to be sublated in its consciousness as well as in the way of the world.
— The Phenomenology of Spirit ¶381 (tr. Pinkard)
Therefore, what is going-on with individuality is an end in itself, and the use of powers, along with the game of giving them outward expression is what gives life to what otherwise would be the dead in-itself.
— The Phenomenology of Spirit ¶393 (tr. Pinkard)

Head (German): Die Individualität, welche sich an und für sich reell ist
Path: 三. Spirit › 1. Subjective Spirit › ii. Phenomenology of Spirit (Consciousness) › γ. Reason › a. The Certainty and Truth of Reason › iv. Individuality Real In and For Itself
Gloss: Individuality confident that its own activity is what is real.
Hegelian gloss: Individuality that knows its action to be the real, the interpenetration of self and being.
Nouns: individuality real in and for itself; confident individuality, self-expressive individuality, authenticity, self-expression, creativity, enterprise, talent, vocation, original nature. self-realizing individuality, the real individual, the individual and its work, the interpenetration of individuality and universality.
Verbs: express oneself, create, act, produce, be oneself. originate, create &c H0147. realize oneself, bring to light.
Adjective: self-expressive, authentic, creative, original, individual, confident. inventive. inimitable &c H0098, unique. personal, peculiar. real, self-realizing, self-confident, active.
Adverbs: authentically, creatively, after one's own fashion. in and for itself, actively, confidently.
Phrases: du sollst der werden, der du bist [Ger.] [Nietzsche, The Gay Science §270]; γένοι᾽ οἷος ἐσσὶ μαθών [Gk.] [Pindar, Pythian 2.72: become such as you are, having learned what that is]; one's own person; to be oneself.
Hegel definition: Individuality that is real in and for itself is self-consciousness that has grasped its own concept, being certain that in itself it is all reality, and whose purpose is now the self-moving permeation of the universal, its gifts and abilities, with individuality. It no longer sets a purpose against an existing actuality that it must overcome: doing is its own truth and actuality, and the expression of individuality is its end. It appears as the spiritual animal kingdom, then as reason giving laws, and testing them.
Hegel texts:
The Phenomenology of Spirit
· ¶¶394–437
Hegel citations:
Self-consciousness has now grasped the concept of itself, which was initially only our concept of it, namely, that in its certainty of itself, it is all reality
— The Phenomenology of Spirit ¶394 (tr. Pinkard)
The doing is in its own self its own truth and actuality, and the exhibition or expression of individuality is, to itself, its purpose in and for itself.
— The Phenomenology of Spirit ¶394 (tr. Pinkard)

Head: The Spiritual Animal Kingdom and Deceit, or the Matter in Hand Itself
Head (German): Das geistige Tierreich und der Betrug
Path: 三. Spirit › 1. Subjective Spirit › ii. Phenomenology of Spirit (Consciousness) › γ. Reason › a. The Certainty and Truth of Reason › iv. Individuality Real In and For Itself › 1. The Spiritual Animal Kingdom and Deceit, or the Matter in Hand Itself
Gloss: The individual absorbed in their work, the self-deceptions that surround it, and everyone's shared concern with the cause itself; honest and dishonest engagement.
Hegelian gloss: Individuals each busy with their own work, the matter in hand, and the deceit of claiming it as a universal concern.
Nouns: the spiritual animal kingdom and deceit; the matter in hand itself.
Adverbs: busily.
Foreign: German: die Sache selbst, das Werk, das geistige Tierreich; Latin: opus; Greek: ergon; French: mauvaise foi [Sartre].
Hegel definition: The spiritual animal kingdom and deception, or the matter in hand itself, is the shape in which individuals, each with an original determinate nature, express themselves in their works and take this to be absolute reality. The work proves transient, exposed to the interests of others, and consciousness holds instead to the matter in hand, the unity of actuality and individuality. Each then claims to care for the matter itself while caring for its own activity, deceiving others and being deceived, until the matter becomes the work of each and all.
Hegel texts:
The Phenomenology of Spirit
· ¶¶397–418
Hegel citations:
First of all, this individuality which is real in itself is again singular and determinate.
— The Phenomenology of Spirit ¶397 (tr. Pinkard)
The crux of the matter is opposed to these moments only inasmuch as they are supposed to be valid in isolation, but it is essentially their unity as the permeation of actuality and individuality.
— The Phenomenology of Spirit ¶409 (tr. Pinkard)
Actualization is instead a matter of putting into the universal element an exhibition of what is one’s own in the universal element, through which what is one’s own both becomes and indeed ought to become the fact of the matter at issue for everyone.
— The Phenomenology of Spirit ¶416 (tr. Pinkard)

Head: The Spiritual Animal Kingdom
Path: 三. Spirit › 1. Subjective Spirit › ii. Phenomenology of Spirit (Consciousness) › γ. Reason › a. The Certainty and Truth of Reason › iv. Individuality Real In and For Itself › 1. The Spiritual Animal Kingdom and Deceit, or the Matter in Hand Itself › a. The Spiritual Animal Kingdom
Gloss: Individuals each absorbed in their own work and nature, like animal species in their own element.
Hegelian gloss: Das geistige Tierreich: individuality that takes itself as real in and for itself, whose original determinate nature is its element, expressed in its work.
Nouns: the spiritual animal kingdom. the republic of letters, intellectual marketplace, academic world, the art world, careerism, self-promotion, human zoo, the work. production, handiwork, performance, creation, firstfruits†, premices premises†.
Verbs: work, produce, publish, exhibit, promote oneself, busy oneself, show off.
Adjective: self-interested, careerist, self-promoting, busy, absorbed.
Phrases: everyone's busy with their own thing; mind your own business.
Hegel definition: The spiritual animal kingdom is individuality real in itself as it first appears, singular and determinate, with an original nature that it need only bring to expression. In its work the individual places itself outside itself into the element of universality, where the work exists for others, who find in it an alien actuality and intervene in it with their own interests. The work is thus transitory, and shows the reality of individuality as disappearing rather than achieved; in it consciousness learns what it is in truth.
Hegel texts:
The Phenomenology of Spirit
· ¶¶397–408
Hegel citations:
The work is the reality which consciousness gives itself; it is that in which the individual is for the individual what he is in itself
— The Phenomenology of Spirit ¶404 (tr. Pinkard)
The work is thus something utterly transitory which is erased by the counterplay of other powers and interests and which instead exhibits the reality of individuality itself as disappearing rather than as achieved.
— The Phenomenology of Spirit ¶404 (tr. Pinkard)

Head: Deceit
Path: 三. Spirit › 1. Subjective Spirit › ii. Phenomenology of Spirit (Consciousness) › γ. Reason › a. The Certainty and Truth of Reason › iv. Individuality Real In and For Itself › 1. The Spiritual Animal Kingdom and Deceit, or the Matter in Hand Itself › b. Deceit
Gloss: The game in which each pretends to serve the common cause while serving themselves, and so deceives and is deceived.
Hegelian gloss: Der Betrug: each claims the matter in hand as a universal concern while the others find they are dealing with someone's private affair; all deceive one another and themselves.
Nouns: deceit. vanity, self-deception, honesty and dishonesty, bad faith, intellectual vanity, posturing, virtue-signalling, mutual deception.
Verbs: pretend, deceive, deceive oneself, posture, take credit, meddle, place to one's account†, fly a kite†.
Adjective: vain, disingenuous, self-deceived, hypocritical, self-deceiving, interfering. false, deceitful, mendacious, dishonest, faithless, hollow-hearted, evasive.
Adverbs: in bad faith, disingenuously.
Hegel definition: Deceit arises among individualities who each claim to be concerned with the matter in hand itself. One acts, and others suppose that it is the matter that interests this one and offer their help or announce that they have done it already; then they find that what was meant was only that individual's own activity, and feel cheated. Yet their eagerness was itself a wish to display their own doing, so that they meant to deceive in the same way. Action brings what is one's own into the light, where it becomes everyone's concern.
Hegel texts:
The Phenomenology of Spirit
· ¶¶415–418
Hegel citations:
What interests him about the crux of the matter is what it has to do with his own goings-on, and by becoming fully aware that was what he meant by the crux of the matter, they find that they have been hoodwinked.
— The Phenomenology of Spirit ¶416 (tr. Pinkard)
However, their haste to offer their assistance in fact itself consisted in nothing but their own desire to see and to show off not the crux of the matter but only their own activities, i.e., they wanted to deceive the others in exactly the same manner in which they complain about having been deceived themselves.
— The Phenomenology of Spirit ¶416 (tr. Pinkard)

Head: The Matter in Hand Itself
Path: 三. Spirit › 1. Subjective Spirit › ii. Phenomenology of Spirit (Consciousness) › γ. Reason › a. The Certainty and Truth of Reason › iv. Individuality Real In and For Itself › 1. The Spiritual Animal Kingdom and Deceit, or the Matter in Hand Itself › c. The Matter in Hand Itself
Gloss: The thing that matters for its own sake, the shared cause in which every individual's work becomes everyone's concern.
Hegelian gloss: Die Sache selbst: the true work, the unity of doing and being, of individuality and objectivity, which becomes the concern of all and passes over into ethical substance.
Nouns: the matter in hand itself. the cause itself, the thing that matters, the common concern, the matter in hand, the thing itself, the cause, honest consciousness.
Adjective: honest, sincere, committed. truthful, true, veracious, candid, frank, straightforward. artless, unaffected, naive.
Adverbs: for the sake of the cause, for the thing itself, for the cause.
Phrases: honesty is the best policy; it's the thing itself that matters.
Hegel definition: The matter in hand itself, die Sache selbst, is the unity in which actuality and individuality permeate one another: the doing of this individual and pure doing as such, purpose and its passage into actuality. Its moments are sublated as valid on their own and count only as universal moments, and in it consciousness's certainty of itself becomes an objective essence. It is an object born of self-consciousness as its own, without ceasing to be free-standing and genuine, which distinguishes it from an ordinary thing.
Hegel texts:
The Phenomenology of Spirit
· ¶¶409–417
Hegel citations:
The crux of the matter thereby expresses the spiritual essentiality in which all these moments are sublated as valid for themselves, and therefore valid only as universal moments, and in which the certainty that consciousness has of itself is, to consciousness, an objective essence, a crux of the matter.
— The Phenomenology of Spirit ¶409 (tr. Pinkard)
It is an object born out of self-consciousness as its own object, without thereby ceasing to be a free-standing, genuine object.
— The Phenomenology of Spirit ¶409 (tr. Pinkard)

Head: Reason as Lawgiver
Path: 三. Spirit › 1. Subjective Spirit › ii. Phenomenology of Spirit (Consciousness) › γ. Reason › a. The Certainty and Truth of Reason › iv. Individuality Real In and For Itself › 2. Reason as Lawgiver
Gloss: Reason laying down moral laws as self-evident, such as "everyone ought to speak the truth."
Hegelian gloss: Healthy reason that gives laws immediately, such as that everyone ought to speak the truth, which prove contingent.
Nouns: reason as lawgiver; moral legislation, lawgiving, self-evident moral laws, healthy reason, common sense morality, moral intuitionism, moral commandments, maxims, precepts, dicta. law-giving reason, legislative reason, the moral lawgiver, immediate commandments, self-evident laws, maxim, precept, sound reason.

Phrases: everyone ought to speak the truth [Hegel's example]; love thy neighbour as thyself [Bible]; one ought always to tell the truth.
Hegel definition: Reason as lawgiver is the consciousness for which the matter in hand has become ethical substance, valid in and for itself, and which supposes that it knows immediately what is right and good and can state it in commands, such as that one should love one's neighbour as oneself. On examination such laws have no universal content: whether intelligent beneficence can happen or does good is contingent. They remain at the ought without actuality; they are not laws but only commands.
Hegel texts:
The Phenomenology of Spirit
· ¶¶419–428
Hegel citations:
This fact is thus the ethical substance, and the consciousness of it is ethical consciousness.
— The Phenomenology of Spirit ¶419 (tr. Pinkard)
This law thereby has no more universal content than did the first law which was considered, and it does not express something that is in and for itself, which, as an absolute ethical law, it is supposed to do; or, such laws stay fixed at the ought but have no actuality. They are not laws; they are only commands.
— The Phenomenology of Spirit ¶424 (tr. Pinkard)

Head: Reason as Testing Laws
Path: 三. Spirit › 1. Subjective Spirit › ii. Phenomenology of Spirit (Consciousness) › γ. Reason › a. The Certainty and Truth of Reason › iv. Individuality Real In and For Itself › 3. Reason as Testing Laws
Gloss: Reason testing proposed laws only for their consistency.
Hegelian gloss: Reason that tests laws only by their formal consistency, a measure that can sanction any content.
Nouns: reason as testing laws; universalizability test, categorical imperative test, consistency check, formalism, moral formalism, tautological test, the test of noncontradiction; Kantian ethics. test &c H0667. law-testing reason, the test of consistency, the criterion of non-contradiction, the formal test, universalizability, tautology, examination of laws.
Verbs: test, examine, check, scrutinize, universalize, generalize. study, consider, probe, sound, fathom. examine closely, inspect, review. try.
Adjective: formal, formalistic, critical, universalizable, consistent, noncontradictory. testing, tautological.
Adverbs: formally, by test. for consistency.
Phrases: act only according to that maxim whereby you can at the same time will that it should become a universal law [Kant]; what if everyone did that?; consistent with itself.
Hegel definition: Reason as testing laws no longer gives laws but compares a given content only with itself, to see whether it is a tautology and free of contradiction. Such a formal standard takes in a content as readily as its opposite, so that property and community of goods can each pass or fail. To test what is right is already to have started down an unethical path: the ethical disposition holds unwaveringly to what is right because it is right, and so reason passes into spirit.
Hegel texts:
The Phenomenology of Spirit
· ¶¶429–437
Hegel citations:
Just because the criterion is a tautology and is indifferent with regard to the content, it incorporates one content into itself with the same ease that it does its opposite.
— The Phenomenology of Spirit ¶429 (tr. Pinkard)
It is not therefore because I find something’s not being self-contradictory that it is right; rather, it is right because it is the right.
— The Phenomenology of Spirit ¶436 (tr. Pinkard)
For myself, if I wanted, I could have just as easily made none of them into law, and, when I start putting myself in the position of testing them, I have already started down an unethical path.
— The Phenomenology of Spirit ¶436 (tr. Pinkard)

Head: Spirit as a World
Path: 三. Spirit › 1. Subjective Spirit › ii. Phenomenology of Spirit (Consciousness) › γ. Reason › b. Spirit as a World
Gloss: Mind as a shared world of customs, institutions and history, rather than as an individual.

Hegel definition: Spirit is reason whose certainty of being all reality has been raised to truth, conscious of itself as its world and of the world as itself. It is ethical actuality, the self of actual consciousness confronting itself as an objective world no longer alien to it. It is the unshakable ground and the purpose of the doing of each and all, and also the universal work that arises through that doing. Its shapes are those of a world: true ethical spirit, self-alienated culture, and spirit certain of itself in morality.
Hegel texts:
The Phenomenology of Spirit
· ¶¶438–671
Hegel citations:
Spirit is the self of the actual consciousness which spirit confronts, or rather which confronts itself as an objective actual world, a world which has, for the self, just as much lost all significance as something alien, just as the self has lost all sense of being a dependent or independent being-for-itself separated from that world.
— The Phenomenology of Spirit ¶438 (tr. Pinkard)
Spirit is the substance and the universal self-equal, lasting essence – it is the unshakable and undissolved ground and point of origin for the doing of each and all
— The Phenomenology of Spirit ¶438 (tr. Pinkard)
Precisely therein that it is “being” dissolved in the self, the substance is not the dead essence, but rather is actual and alive.
— The Phenomenology of Spirit ¶438 (tr. Pinkard)

Head: True Spirit: The Ethical Order
Path: 三. Spirit › 1. Subjective Spirit › ii. Phenomenology of Spirit (Consciousness) › γ. Reason › b. Spirit as a World › i. True Spirit: The Ethical Order
Gloss: The shared customs of a people, lived unreflectively as natural duty, as in the ancient Greek city.
Hegelian gloss: The immediate ethical life of a people, the beautiful ethical world of the Greek polis.
Nouns: true spirit; the ethical order, ethical substance, customary morality, unreflective harmony, the beautiful ethical life of the Greeks, the polis. ethical life, customary life, the Greek polis, immediate ethical life, custom, mores, natural duty.
Verbs: live by custom, belong, abide, observe, honour the ancestors. follow custom, fulfil one's duty.
Adjective: ethical, customary, traditional, harmonious, unreflective, immediate, ancestral. immemorial, prescriptive, inveterate, rooted. substantial, Greek.

Foreign: German: die Sittlichkeit, Sitte [custom]; Latin: mos maiorum [the ways of the ancestors]; Greek: ethos, nomos [law, custom], ēthos; Arabic: ʿurf [custom]; Sanskrit: dharma [duty, order]; Chinese: li [ritual propriety]; Korean: illyun [ethical life].
Phrases: moribus antiquis res stat Romana virisque [Lat.] [Ennius]; nomos basileus [Gr.] [custom is king] [Pindar]; the good old ways.
Hegel definition: True spirit, ethical life, is spirit in its immediacy, in which the simple ethical substance divides into a differentiated essence, a human and a divine law. Self-consciousness, facing it, assigns itself to one of these powers, knowing it and ignoring the other, and so is a deceived knowing. In acting it experiences the contradiction of the two powers, their mutual destruction and its own downfall. Through this movement the substance becomes actual self-consciousness, and just therein ethical life perishes.
Hegel texts:
The Phenomenology of Spirit
· ¶¶444–483
Hegel citations:
The substance thus fissures into a differentiated ethical essence, into a human and a divine law.
— The Phenomenology of Spirit ¶444 (tr. Pinkard)
In its deed, it thus experiences the contradiction of those powers into which substance estranged itself, and it experiences their mutual destruction and the contradiction in its knowing of the ethical life of its actions – the contradiction of what ethical life is in and for itself – and it meets its own downfall.
— The Phenomenology of Spirit ¶444 (tr. Pinkard)
However, through this movement, ethical substance has in fact become actual self-consciousness, or this self has come to be in-and-for-itself-existing, but it was just therein that ethical life perished.
— The Phenomenology of Spirit ¶444 (tr. Pinkard)

Hegel definition: The ethical world is ethical substance in its ordered subsistence, absolute spirit realized in a plurality of conscious beings. It exists in two ways, each containing the whole: as the polity, the people and its citizens, under the human law known and publicly valid, and as the family, the immediate, natural ethical community under the divine law. Each has levels and differences within it, and their examination shows how the two engage one another, connect and pass into each other.

· ¶¶446–463

In this determination, the ethical substance is thus the actual substance, absolute spirit realized in the plurality of determinately existing consciousnesses.
— The Phenomenology of Spirit ¶446 (tr. Pinkard)
The examination of these differences shows the way in which they engage themselves and the self-consciousness of the two universal essences of the ethical world, as well as showing their connection and their transition into each other.
— The Phenomenology of Spirit ¶453 (tr. Pinkard)

As the actual substance, it is a people, and as actual consciousness, it is the citizens of the nation.

Hegel definition: The human law is ethical spirit as it is conscious of itself in the form of actuality. As universal it is the familiar, known law and the prevailing customs; as singular it is the actual certainty of itself in the individual, and as simple individuality it is the government. Its truth is a validity openly in force in the light of day, an existence which takes for immediate certainty the form of something set free to stand on its own.
Hegel texts:
The Phenomenology of Spirit
· ¶¶447–448
Hegel citations:
This spirit can be called the human law because it is essentially in the form of actuality conscious of itself. In the form of universality, it is the familiarly known law and extant mores which are both present.
— The Phenomenology of Spirit ¶447 (tr. Pinkard)
Its truth is the validity in force which is publicly open to the light of day.
— The Phenomenology of Spirit ¶447 (tr. Pinkard)

Gloss: The law of the family and of the dead, unwritten and sacred.

Hegel definition: The divine law is ethical substance in the form of immediacy, the universal possibility of ethical life as it is in the family, the natural ethical community that stands against the public spirit of the people. Its relations are ethical only as spirit, and its distinctive aim is the singular individual as such, taken as a universal being, which is the one who has died. The last duty to the dead is its consummation, and it has its power in the individual who is beyond actuality.
Hegel texts:

· ¶¶449–452
Hegel citations:
This last duty thus constitutes the consummate divine law, or it constitutes the positive ethical action vis-à-vis the singular individual.
— The Phenomenology of Spirit ¶452 (tr. Pinkard)
The positive purpose distinctive of the family is the individual as such a singular individual.
— The Phenomenology of Spirit ¶450 (tr. Pinkard)

Head: The Right of the Individual (Burial of the Dead)

Hegel definition: The right of the individual is realized in burial, the duty of the family toward its dead member. Death is a natural event, not something a consciousness does, and the dead are left passive to unreasoning life and the forces of matter. The family adds to nature's movement the movement of consciousness: it takes the deed of destruction upon itself, keeps dishonouring acts away, weds its kin to the womb of the earth, and so makes the dead a member of a community again.
Hegel texts:
The Phenomenology of Spirit
· ¶¶451–452
Hegel citations:
The duty of the family member is thus to augment this aspect so that his final being, this universal being, will also not belong solely to nature and remain something non-rational.
— The Phenomenology of Spirit ¶451 (tr. Pinkard)
The family keeps the dead away from those dishonoring acts of unconscious desire and abstract creatures, and in place of them, it puts their own acts; it weds their kin to the womb of the earth, to the elemental, imperishable individuality.
— The Phenomenology of Spirit ¶451 (tr. Pinkard)

Head: The Movement of the Two Laws
Path: 三. Spirit › 1. Subjective Spirit › ii. Phenomenology of Spirit (Consciousness) › γ. Reason › b. Spirit as a World › i. True Spirit: The Ethical Order › 1. The Ethical World › b. The Movement of the Two Laws

Hegelian gloss: The movement in which the two laws pass into each other and come into conflict.
Nouns: the movement of the two laws; interplay of the laws, tension, conflict of duties, clash of loyalties, collision, dilemma, the city against the family, the public against the private. encounter. shock. the passage of each law into the other, transition, the family passing into the community.
Verbs: conflict, clash, collide, oppose, struggle, pull apart. counteract, interfere with, conflict with, contravene. disagree, jar, pull different ways. move, pass over, interplay.

Adverbs: at odds, at cross purposes, between two loyalties. in movement, in conflict, into one another.
Phrases: caught between two duties; between two fires; caught in the middle.
Hegel definition: The movement of the two laws unfolds the differences within each, through which they engage one another and pass into each other. The polity has its liveliness in government, which lets the whole spread into self-sufficient parts and gathers them again, and has the proof of its power in the divine law and the netherworld. The divine law, within the family, moves through the relations of husband and wife, parents and children, and brother and sister, from which the individual passes over into the human law.
Hegel texts:
The Phenomenology of Spirit
· ¶¶453–459
Hegel citations:
Now, there are differences and levels in the one law as well as in the other.
— The Phenomenology of Spirit ¶453 (tr. Pinkard)
The polity therefore has the truth and substantiation of its power in the essence of the divine law and in the realm of the netherworld.
— The Phenomenology of Spirit ¶454 (tr. Pinkard)
Likewise, the divine law prevailing in the family has for its part differences within itself, and the relations among those differences constitute the living movement of its actuality.
— The Phenomenology of Spirit ¶455 (tr. Pinkard)

Head: Government and War
Path: 三. Spirit › 1. Subjective Spirit › ii. Phenomenology of Spirit (Consciousness) › γ. Reason › b. Spirit as a World › i. True Spirit: The Ethical Order › 1. The Ethical World › b. The Movement of the Two Laws › i. Government and War
Gloss: The rule of the state, and war as its means of holding the community together.

Hegel definition: Government is actual spirit reflected into itself, the simple self of the whole ethical substance, in which the polity has its living individuality. It lets the whole spread out into its members and the self-sufficient systems of property, right, acquisition and consumption, and it gathers these into a negative unity. So that they do not harden in isolation and let the spirit of the whole fade, government must from time to time shake them by war, making individuals feel the power of their master, death.
Hegel texts:
The Phenomenology of Spirit
· ¶¶454–455
Hegel citations:
The government is actual spirit reflected into itself, the simple self of the whole ethical substance.
— The Phenomenology of Spirit ¶454 (tr. Pinkard)
In order not to let them become rooted and rigidly fixed within this activity of isolating themselves, which would otherwise let the whole come undone and the spirit within it fade away, the government must from time to time shake them to their core by means of war. As a result, it infringes on their established order, violates their right to self-sufficiency, and throws them into disarray.
— The Phenomenology of Spirit ¶454 (tr. Pinkard)

Head: Husband and Wife
Path: 三. Spirit › 1. Subjective Spirit › ii. Phenomenology of Spirit (Consciousness) › γ. Reason › b. Spirit as a World › i. True Spirit: The Ethical Order › 1. The Ethical World › b. The Movement of the Two Laws › ii. Husband and Wife
Gloss: The bond of husband and wife, in which each knows itself in the other through natural feeling.
Hegelian gloss: Mann und Frau: the immediate self-recognition of one consciousness in another, mixed with natural feeling, which has its actuality not in itself but in the child.
Nouns: husband and wife. marriage, matrimony, wedlock, conjugal bond, conjugality, spouse, husband, wife, consort, partner, helpmeet, the conjugal relation.
Verbs: marry, wed, espouse, cleave unto, take to wife.
Adjective: conjugal, marital, matrimonial, spousal, wedded, nuptial.
Adverbs: in wedlock, as man and wife.
Foreign: German: Ehe; Latin: conubium.
Phrases: and they twain shall be one flesh [Bible]; till death us do part.
Hegel definition: Husband and wife stand in the relation within the family in which one consciousness first knows itself immediately in another and knows the recognition to be mutual. Since this self-knowledge is natural and not yet ethical, it is only a representation and image of spirit. It has its actuality not in itself but in the child, an other whose coming to be is the relation and in which it vanishes, so that their piety toward each other remains mixed with a natural tie and with feeling.
Hegel texts:
The Phenomenology of Spirit
· ¶455
Hegel citations:
However, among the three relationships of man and wife, parents and children, and siblings as brothers and sisters, it is the relationship of man and wife which is initially the immediate self-cognizance of one consciousness in another and the cognizance of reciprocal recognition. Because it is natural self-cognizance and not ethical self-cognizance, it is only the representation and picture of spirit, not actual spirit itself.
— The Phenomenology of Spirit ¶455 (tr. Pinkard)
However, the representation, or the picture, has its actuality in an other than itself; this relationship therefore does not have its actuality in its own self but in the child – in an other whose coming into being is that relationship and in which the relationship disappears.
— The Phenomenology of Spirit ¶455 (tr. Pinkard)

Head: Parents and Children
Path: 三. Spirit › 1. Subjective Spirit › ii. Phenomenology of Spirit (Consciousness) › γ. Reason › b. Spirit as a World › i. True Spirit: The Ethical Order › 1. The Ethical World › b. The Movement of the Two Laws › iii. Parents and Children
Gloss: The piety of parents toward children and of children toward parents, each seeing in the other its own passing.
Hegelian gloss: Eltern und Kinder: the parents' piety, moved by seeing their own actuality in another that grows as they fade, and the children's, who owe their being to a source that vanishes.
Nouns: parents and children. parenthood, filiation, piety, filial piety, parental love, the generations, father and mother, son and daughter, offspring, upbringing, heirs, the household gods, Penates, ancestors.
Verbs: beget, bear, raise, rear, bring up, honour one's father and mother, inherit.

Adverbs: from generation to generation, filially.
Foreign: Latin: pietas; Chinese: xiao [filial piety].
Phrases: honour thy father and thy mother [Bible]; the child is father of the man [Wordsworth].
Hegel definition: Parents and children are bound by a piety on each side that is affected by passing over into another. Parents are moved by the awareness that they have their actuality in the child and see it come to an independence of its own which they cannot take back. Children are moved by coming to be through an other who is vanishing, and by reaching their own independence and self-consciousness only through separation from their origin, a separation in which that origin recedes.
Hegel texts:
The Phenomenology of Spirit
· ¶455
Hegel citations:
The piety of parents towards their children is affected by the emotion brought on by their awareness that they have their actuality in an other and that they see their children come to their own being-for-itself without the parents being able to get it back. The child’s being for itself remains an alien actuality, an actuality all its own.
— The Phenomenology of Spirit ¶455 (tr. Pinkard)
But conversely the devotion of children towards their parents is affected by the emotion of their coming-to-be, or having their own in-itself in an other who is vanishing, and in achieving being-for-itself and their own self-consciousness only through separation from their origin – a separation within which the origin recedes.
— The Phenomenology of Spirit ¶455 (tr. Pinkard)

Head: Brother and Sister
Path: 三. Spirit › 1. Subjective Spirit › ii. Phenomenology of Spirit (Consciousness) › γ. Reason › b. Spirit as a World › i. True Spirit: The Ethical Order › 1. The Ethical World › b. The Movement of the Two Laws › iv. Brother and Sister
Gloss: The relation of brother and sister, the purest bond within the family.
Hegelian gloss: The ethical relation of brother and sister, free of desire, the highest bond of the family.
Nouns: brother and sister; siblinghood, siblings, the bond of brother and sister, the purest ethical relation, Antigone and Polynices. family. fellowship, solidarity, confraternity. the sibling bond, the pure ethical relation, desireless recognition, Antigone and Polyneices.

Adverbs: as kin. as brother and sister, without desire, purely.
Foreign: Latin: fratres et sorores; Greek: adelphoi.
Phrases: blood is thicker than water.
Hegel definition: Brother and sister stand in the unmixed relationship within the family. They are of the same blood, which in them has come to rest and equilibrium; they neither desire each other nor owe their independence to each other, but are free individualities to one another, so that each can be recognized without the admixture of natural relation. This relation is also the limit at which the self-enclosed family dissolves: the brother passes out into the conscious ethical life of the polity, while the sister remains guardian of the divine law, and the two divide ethical substance between them.
Hegel texts:
The Phenomenology of Spirit
· ¶¶457–459
Hegel citations:
This relationship is at the same time the limit at which the self-enclosed family dissolves and moves outside of itself.
— The Phenomenology of Spirit ¶457 (tr. Pinkard)
In this way, both the sexes overcome their natural essence, and they emerge in their ethical significance as diversities who divide between them the two differences that ethical substance gives itself.
— The Phenomenology of Spirit ¶458 (tr. Pinkard)

Head: Brother
Path: 三. Spirit › 1. Subjective Spirit › ii. Phenomenology of Spirit (Consciousness) › γ. Reason › b. Spirit as a World › i. True Spirit: The Ethical Order › 1. The Ethical World › b. The Movement of the Two Laws › iv. Brother and Sister › 1. Brother

He leaves the immediate, elemental and therefore properly negative ethical life of the family to win and bring forth the actual ethical life that is conscious of itself. He passes from the divine law, in whose sphere he had lived, into the human law, finding his self-conscious essence in the polity.

The Phenomenology of Spirit
· ¶¶458–459
Hegel citations:
The spirit of the family sends the man out into the polity, and he finds his self-conscious essence in that polity.
— The Phenomenology of Spirit ¶459 (tr. Pinkard)
He makes a transition from the divine law, in whose sphere he had lived, to the human law.
— The Phenomenology of Spirit ¶458 (tr. Pinkard)

Head: Sister
Path: 三. Spirit › 1. Subjective Spirit › ii. Phenomenology of Spirit (Consciousness) › γ. Reason › b. Spirit as a World › i. True Spirit: The Ethical Order › 1. The Ethical World › b. The Movement of the Two Laws › iv. Brother and Sister › 2. Sister
Gloss: The sister, who has the highest intuition of ethical being and keeps the divine law of the family.

Hegel definition: The sister has the highest intimation of ethical essence, though it does not rise to consciousness, since the law of the family remains inner feeling. In her brother she meets a being of the same blood, equal to herself, toward whom there is no desire, so that her recognition in him is pure and unmixed with any natural relation. The loss of a brother is therefore irreplaceable to her, and her duty to him is the highest.
Hegel texts:
The Phenomenology of Spirit
· ¶456
Hegel citations:
The feminine, as the sister, hence has the highest intimation of ethical essence.
— The Phenomenology of Spirit ¶456 (tr. Pinkard)
But to the sister, the brother is the motionless essence itself, equal to her, and her recognition in him is pure and unmixed with any natural relation.
— The Phenomenology of Spirit ¶456 (tr. Pinkard)
The loss of a brother is thus irreplaceable to the sister, and her duty towards him is the highest.
— The Phenomenology of Spirit ¶456 (tr. Pinkard)

Head: The Interfusion of the Two Laws
Path: 三. Spirit › 1. Subjective Spirit › ii. Phenomenology of Spirit (Consciousness) › γ. Reason › b. Spirit as a World › i. True Spirit: The Ethical Order › 1. The Ethical World › b. The Movement of the Two Laws › v. The Interfusion of the Two Laws
Gloss: The mutual penetration of the two laws.
Hegelian gloss: The interpenetration of human and divine law.
Nouns: the interfusion of the two laws; interpenetration of the laws, mutual dependence of city and family, interfusion, intertwining, mingling, reciprocity of the public and the private. interpenetration, mutual penetration, intermingling, mutual confirmation, the union of man and woman, the middle term.

Adverbs: inextricably, hand in hand. mutually, reciprocally, through one another.
Phrases: each law lives through the other; the twain shall meet; woven together.
Hegel definition: The interfusion of the two laws is the content of the ethical world in which each is realized in the other's element. The ethical essences are substance as universal and as singular consciousness, with the people and the family as their actuality and man and woman as their natural self and activating individuality. Here the purposes of earlier shapes of reason are achieved. Justice, as human law, brings what strays from the balance back into the universal, and, as the spirit of one who has suffered wrong, avenges from the netherworld.
Hegel texts:
The Phenomenology of Spirit
· ¶¶460–461
Hegel citations:
The universal ethical essences are thus the substance as universal consciousness and as singular consciousness. They have the people and the family for their universal actuality, and they have man and wife for their natural self and their activating individuality.
— The Phenomenology of Spirit ¶460 (tr. Pinkard)
As such, justice is the government of the people, which is, to itself, the current individuality of the universal essence and the self-conscious will of all.
— The Phenomenology of Spirit ¶461 (tr. Pinkard)

Head: The Ethical World as Self-Complete Totality
Head (German): Die sittliche Welt als in sich vollendetes Ganzes
Path: 三. Spirit › 1. Subjective Spirit › ii. Phenomenology of Spirit (Consciousness) › γ. Reason › b. Spirit as a World › i. True Spirit: The Ethical Order › 1. The Ethical World › c. The Ethical World as Self-Complete Totality
Gloss: The ethical world as a complete and balanced whole.
Hegelian gloss: The ethical world as a balanced totality, at rest before action disturbs it.
Nouns: the ethical world as self-complete totality; harmonious totality, closed world, self-sufficient community, the beautiful whole, ethical harmony, equilibrium, golden age, arcadia, the lost Greek harmony, Agapemone†, Alfardaws†, Assama†. the ethical totality, the undisturbed whole, the stable equilibrium, the stainless world, the tranquil balance, harmony of the two laws.
Verbs: complete, harmonize, balance, cohere. rest in itself.
Adjective: complete, harmonious, self-sufficient, closed, balanced, whole, idyllic, Arcadian. stainless, tranquil.

Foreign: German: Griechensehnsucht [longing for Greece].

Hegel definition: The ethical world as a self-complete totality is a peaceful equilibrium of all its parts, each a local spirit that seeks no satisfaction beyond itself because it is in balance with the whole. The balance is living: inequality arises and is brought back to equality by justice, the government of the people and the avenging spirit of the family. Undivided and unpolluted, the ethical realm moves by one of its powers peacefully becoming the other, and the union of man and woman is the middle that joins them.
Hegel texts:
The Phenomenology of Spirit
· ¶¶461–463
Hegel citations:
The whole is a peaceful equilibrium of all the parts, and each part is a local spirit that does not seek its satisfaction beyond itself.
— The Phenomenology of Spirit ¶461 (tr. Pinkard)
The ethical realm is in this way an undefiled world in its stable existence, a world unpolluted by any division. Likewise, its movement consists in one of its powers peacefully coming to be the other so that each preserves and brings forth the other.
— The Phenomenology of Spirit ¶462 (tr. Pinkard)

Head: Ethical Action
Path: 三. Spirit › 1. Subjective Spirit › ii. Phenomenology of Spirit (Consciousness) › γ. Reason › b. Spirit as a World › i. True Spirit: The Ethical Order › 2. Ethical Action
Gloss: Action within the ethical world, which breaks its balance and brings guilt and fate, as in tragedy.
Hegelian gloss: The deed that breaks the balance, the guilt of acting on one law against the other, and the destiny that follows.
Nouns: ethical action; human and divine knowledge, guilt and destiny; tragic action, destiny; guilt; Oedipus. Antigone and Creon.
Foreign: German: Schuld und Schicksal, Tat, Verbrechen; Greek: hamartia [fatal error], hubris, atē [ruin, blindness], nemesis, moira [fate]; Arabic: qadar [destiny], maktūb [it is written]; Sanskrit: karma; Chinese: ming [fate].
Hegel definition: Ethical action is the deed that sets the unmoved into motion. Ethical consciousness knows what it has to do and has decided for one law, divine or human, and is therefore character. Acting links the unconscious to the conscious and turns the harmony of the two laws into their opposition, bringing a violated power out against the agent. In the deed the agent meets guilt, and at last destiny, in which the shape of ethical substance perishes.
Hegel texts:
The Phenomenology of Spirit
· ¶¶464–476
Hegel citations:
However, ethical consciousness knows what it has to do, and it has decided whether it is to belong to divine or to human law.
— The Phenomenology of Spirit ¶464 (tr. Pinkard)
Because it has decided in favor of one of them, ethical consciousness is essentially character.
— The Phenomenology of Spirit ¶465 (tr. Pinkard)
The deed consists in setting the unmoved into motion, which thereby brings forth what had been sealed off as mere possibility, and it links the unconscious to the conscious and the non-existent to being.
— The Phenomenology of Spirit ¶468 (tr. Pinkard)

Head: Human Knowledge
Path: 三. Spirit › 1. Subjective Spirit › ii. Phenomenology of Spirit (Consciousness) › γ. Reason › b. Spirit as a World › i. True Spirit: The Ethical Order › 2. Ethical Action › a. Human Knowledge
Gloss: The knowledge that belongs to the human law: what the community openly knows and decrees.
Hegelian gloss: Das menschliche Wissen: the self-conscious knowledge of the human law, manifest in the light of day, which in acting knows only one side of the ethical substance.
Nouns: human knowledge. Creon. the law of the state, public law, statecraft, the knowledge of the community, civic reason, reason of state.
Verbs: know the law, decree, enforce.
Adjective: civic, political, public, manifest.
Adverbs: by the law of the land.
Hegel definition: Human knowledge here is the knowing of the consciousness that belongs to the human law. Since ethical consciousness has decided for one power, it sees right only on its own side. The commands of government have a universal and public meaning that lies open in the light of day, and to the consciousness holding to them the other law appears as the obstinacy and disobedience of an inward being-for-itself, and as sacrilege where it contradicts them.
Hegel texts:
The Phenomenology of Spirit
· ¶¶465–467
Hegel citations:
While it sees right only on its own side and sees only wrong on the other, the consciousness that belongs to divine law beholds on the other side human, contingent violence; and that consciousness which belongs to human law beholds on the other side the obstinacy and disobedience of inward being-for-itself.
— The Phenomenology of Spirit ¶465 (tr. Pinkard)
For the commands of government have a universal, public sense lying open to the light of day, but the will of the other law is the sense of the netherworld, sealed up in innerness, a sense which in its existence appears as the will of singular individuality and, when it stands in contradiction to the first, is sacrilege.
— The Phenomenology of Spirit ¶465 (tr. Pinkard)

Head: Divine Knowledge
Path: 三. Spirit › 1. Subjective Spirit › ii. Phenomenology of Spirit (Consciousness) › γ. Reason › b. Spirit as a World › i. True Spirit: The Ethical Order › 2. Ethical Action › b. Divine Knowledge
Gloss: The knowledge that belongs to the divine law: the unwritten, eternal law of the family and the dead.
Hegelian gloss: Das göttliche Wissen: the knowledge of the divine law, unwritten and eternal, of which no one knows whence it came; kept by woman and the family.
Nouns: divine knowledge. Antigone. the unwritten law, the law of the gods, the law of the nether world, the knowledge of the family.
Verbs: obey the gods, keep the unwritten law.
Adjective: unwritten, eternal, hidden.
Adverbs: by the law of heaven.
Phrases: nicht etwa jetzt und gestern, sondern immerdar lebt es, und keiner weiß, von wannen es erschien [Ger.] [Sophocles, quoted by Hegel, Phenomenology].
Hegel definition: Divine knowledge is the knowing of the consciousness that belongs to the divine law, which sees in the law of the state merely human, contingent violence, while its own law has the meaning of the netherworld, sealed up in inwardness. With ethical knowing there arises the opposition of the known and the not known, as in substance there was one of the conscious and the unconscious, so that the absolute right of ethical self-consciousness comes into conflict with the divine right of essence.
Hegel texts:
The Phenomenology of Spirit
· ¶¶465–467
Hegel citations:
While it sees right only on its own side and sees only wrong on the other, the consciousness that belongs to divine law beholds on the other side human, contingent violence
— The Phenomenology of Spirit ¶465 (tr. Pinkard)
There thereby arises in consciousness the opposition between the known and the not known, just as in substance, there was an opposition between the conscious and the unconscious, and the absolute right of ethical self-consciousness comes into conflict with the divine right of essence.
— The Phenomenology of Spirit ¶466 (tr. Pinkard)

Head: Guilt
Path: 三. Spirit › 1. Subjective Spirit › ii. Phenomenology of Spirit (Consciousness) › γ. Reason › b. Spirit as a World › i. True Spirit: The Ethical Order › 2. Ethical Action › c. Guilt
Gloss: The guilt of the deed, which acts on one law and so violates the other.
Hegelian gloss: Die Schuld: the deed is itself guilt, for in acting on one side of the ethical substance it injures the other; only non-action is innocent.
Nouns: guilt. tragic guilt, culpability, responsibility, the deed, the crime. guiltiness, criminality, sinfulness &c H0732. the ethical deed, transgression.
Verbs: act, transgress, offend, incur guilt. sin, err, fall, lapse.
Adjective: guilty, culpable, one-sided. at fault, reprehensible, blameworthy.
Adverbs: guiltily, by the deed.
Phrases: weil wir leiden, anerkennen wir, daß wir gefehlt [Ger.] [Hegel, Phenomenology ¶470, rendering Antigone 926]; unschuldig ist daher nur das Nichttun [Ger.] [Hegel, Phenomenology].
Hegel definition: Guilt arises because the ethical essence is the unity of both laws while the deed carries out only one. In fulfilling one law, action calls up the other as a violated and hostile essence demanding revenge. Only one side of the decision lies in the light; actuality keeps hidden the other, which comes forth after the deed has been done. The agent can deny neither the crime nor the guilt, for the deed joins the conscious to the unconscious and one's own to what is alien.
Hegel texts:
The Phenomenology of Spirit
· ¶¶468–471
Hegel citations:
The essence is the unity of both, but the deed has only carried out the terms of one law in opposition to the other.
— The Phenomenology of Spirit ¶468 (tr. Pinkard)
The agent can neither deny the crime nor deny his guilt.
— The Phenomenology of Spirit ¶468 (tr. Pinkard)

Head: Destiny
Path: 三. Spirit › 1. Subjective Spirit › ii. Phenomenology of Spirit (Consciousness) › γ. Reason › b. Spirit as a World › i. True Spirit: The Ethical Order › 2. Ethical Action › d. Destiny
Gloss: The fate that overtakes the deed, in which both laws and both characters go down together.
Hegelian gloss: Das Schicksal: the movement in which both powers and both self-conscious characters perish, and their equal right appears in their common downfall.
Nouns: destiny. fate, doom, retribution. fatality, foredoom, predestination, preordination, inevitableness. denouement, pathos, downfall.
Verbs: suffer, atone, expiate, be doomed. atone for, propitiate, make amends, redeem, absolve. perish.
Adjective: tragic, fated, doomed, fateful, retributive, ill-starred.
Adverbs: tragically, fatally, inexorably, fatefully.
Phrases: whom the gods would destroy they first make mad; call no man happy until he is dead [Solon]; fate takes a hand; to pay the price.
Hegel definition: Destiny is the downfall of ethical substance in which both powers are overtaken. The conflict appears as that of the two brothers who have an equal right to the state and destroy each other, after which government honours the one and denies burial to the other. The cause of the collapse lies in the immediacy of ethical life, through which nature enters its action: a people determined by nature is a restricted individuality, its living substance is lost, and its individuals are shattered into many separate points.
Hegel texts:
The Phenomenology of Spirit
· ¶¶472–476
Hegel citations:
For that reason, these two brothers are at odds with each other, and their equal right to the power of the state shatters both of them
— The Phenomenology of Spirit ¶472 (tr. Pinkard)
Its actuality only reveals the contradiction and the germ of corruption which ethical spirit’s beautiful unanimity and motionless equilibrium have in this motionlessness and beauty itself
— The Phenomenology of Spirit ¶475 (tr. Pinkard)

Head: Legal Status
Path: 三. Spirit › 1. Subjective Spirit › ii. Phenomenology of Spirit (Consciousness) › γ. Reason › b. Spirit as a World › i. True Spirit: The Ethical Order › 3. Legal Status
Gloss: The condition of persons recognized only as holders of rights, each equal and isolated, as under the Roman empire.
Hegelian gloss: The condition of right in which the ethical substance has broken into atomic persons, equal and empty.
Nouns: legal status; legal personhood, person, juristic person, rights-bearer, citizen, formal equality, abstract right, the Roman world, universal citizenship, isolated individuals, atomized society, the emperor, the lord of the world; fading of ethical substance. the condition of right, legal personality, the legal person, abstract personhood, Roman law, atomism of persons.
Verbs: entitle, enfranchise, invest with rights, register, own. recognize, equalize, isolate, atomize.
Adjective: legal, juridical, formal, abstract, personal, atomized, Roman. atomistic, equal, isolated.
Adverbs: legally, in law. as persons, formally.
Foreign: Latin: persona, civis, ius civile, de jure; French: se tenir, position, standing; German: stehen.
Phrases: civis Romanus sum [Lat.] [I am a Roman citizen]; equal before the law.
Hegel definition: Legal status is the condition into which the living unity of the ethical world passes: a spiritless polity, splintered into the atoms of absolutely many individuals, in which all count equally as persons. The hidden divine law has come out into actuality, and the single one, formerly counting only as the blood of the family, now counts as an independent being. Being recognized is now substantial, but it is an abstract universality, since its content is this aloof self and not a self dissolved in the substance.
Hegel texts:
The Phenomenology of Spirit
· ¶¶477–483
Hegel citations:
Henceforth this counts as the essence existing in and for itself.
— The Phenomenology of Spirit ¶477 (tr. Pinkard)
This, its being recognized, is its substantiality. However, this is abstract universality because its content is this aloof self, not the self which has been dissolved in the substance.
— The Phenomenology of Spirit ¶477 (tr. Pinkard)

Hegel definition: Self-alienated spirit, culture, is the world in which substance is spirit as the unity of self and essence, but each means to the other an alienation. Consciousness faces an objective actuality that exists freely on its own, which actual self-consciousness enters by relinquishing itself, and over against this actual world stands pure consciousness and a beyond. It unfolds as the world of culture and the realm of faith and pure insight, then as Enlightenment, and ends in absolute freedom.
Hegel texts:
The Phenomenology of Spirit
· ¶¶484–595
Hegel citations:
It is in this manner that substance is spirit, or the self-conscious unity of the self and essence. However, for each other, what each of them means is also alienation from the other.
— The Phenomenology of Spirit ¶484 (tr. Pinkard)
On the one hand, through its self-relinquishing, actual self-consciousness makes a transition into the actual world, which then passes over again back into actual self-consciousness.
— The Phenomenology of Spirit ¶484 (tr. Pinkard)

Head: The World of Self-Alienated Spirit
Head (German): Die Welt des sich entfremdeten Geistes

Gloss: The world in which mind has become foreign to itself.
Hegelian gloss: The world of self-alienated spirit, a world which spirit has made and which confronts it as alien.
Nouns: the world of self-alienated spirit; the divided world, the double world, this world and the beyond, the actual world and the world of faith, here below and up above, the secular and the sacred. the alienated world, the self-estranged world, the here and the beyond, estrangement, foreignness.
