Hegel definition: The world of self-alienated spirit is the real world in which the individual has validity and actuality only through cultural formation, by relinquishing natural being. Its powers are state power and wealth, judged as good and bad, with a noble and a base consciousness relating to them; its mediation runs through service, counsel and language. Each moment inverts itself into its opposite, so that this world ends in disrupted consciousness and its vanity, and over against it there stand faith and pure insight.
Hegel texts:
The Phenomenology of Spirit
· ¶¶488–537
Hegel citations:
It is cultural formation through which the individual here has validity and actuality.
— The Phenomenology of Spirit ¶488 (tr. Pinkard)

— The Phenomenology of Spirit ¶520 (tr. Pinkard)

Nouns: culture and its realm of actuality; the cultural world, society, the social order, institutions, power and wealth, the realm of refinement, polite society. civilized life, civilization. the realm of culture, the actual world of culture, the social world, cultivated society, state-power and wealth, the world of estrangement.

Hegel definition: Culture and its realm of actuality is the formation by which the individual becomes what it is in itself and gains actuality and power in the measure that it is cultivated. Here actuality is won only by what empties itself and becomes universal, and every fixed distinction of power and wealth, good and bad, noble and base, is found to turn into its contrary.

What is determined as good is bad, and what is determined as bad is good.

— The Phenomenology of Spirit ¶488 (tr. Pinkard)

Head: Absolute Freedom and Terror

Gloss: Freedom that refuses all limits and institutions and so turns to destruction, as in the Terror of the French Revolution.

Hegel definition: Terror is what absolute freedom does when only negative doing remains to it. Earlier shapes held religion only from the side of a consciousness aware of the absolute essence. Here spirit knows itself as spirit, but at first in representation, so that its actual world still falls outside it, and its consummation lies in each becoming the same as the other. Religions differ by the shape in which spirit knows itself: natural, as art, and revealed.
Hegel texts:
The Phenomenology of Spirit
· ¶¶672–787
Hegel citations:
However, the absolute essence in and for itself, the self-consciousness of spirit, has not appeared in those forms.
— The Phenomenology of Spirit ¶672 (tr. Pinkard)
It is according to the determinateness of this shape in which spirit knows itself that one religion differentiates itself from another
— The Phenomenology of Spirit ¶684 (tr. Pinkard)

Adverbs: in nature, as nature. in natural form, immediately.
Phrases: God in the forms of nature; the gods of nature.
Hegel definition: Natural religion is the first shape in which spirit knows itself, in the form of immediate being. As self-conscious essence it is at first only its concept, the night from which its shapes are born, and it intuits itself in the manner that corresponds to immediate consciousness. It passes from the shapeless light, through the religion of plants and animals, to the artisan, who brings forth spirit as an object by an instinctive kind of work.
Hegel texts:
The Phenomenology of Spirit
· ¶¶684–698
Hegel citations:
In the first, immediate estrangement of self-knowing absolute spirit, its shape has the determination that corresponds to immediate consciousness, or to sensuous-certainty.
— The Phenomenology of Spirit ¶686 (tr. Pinkard)
This secret has its revelation within itself, for existence has its necessity in this concept because this concept is spirit knowing itself and thus has within its essence the moment of being consciousness and of representing itself objectively.
— The Phenomenology of Spirit ¶685 (tr. Pinkard)

Hegel definition: God as light, the luminous essence, is spirit intuiting itself in the form of being filled with spirit, the shape of shapelessness corresponding to sense certainty. It is the all-containing light of sunrise, which suffuses everything and preserves itself in a formless substance, with darkness as its simple other. Its creations are effusions of light and streams of consuming fire, and its sublime essence wanders without constancy, dissolving its own beauty.
Hegel texts:
The Phenomenology of Spirit
· ¶¶685–688
Hegel citations:
In virtue of this determination, this shape is the pure, all-containing, luminous essence of the sunrise, which suffuses everything and which preserves itself in its formless substantiality.
— The Phenomenology of Spirit ¶686 (tr. Pinkard)
Its otherness is the equally simple negative, darkness
— The Phenomenology of Spirit ¶686 (tr. Pinkard)

Head: Plant and Animal

Hegel definition: Plant and animal religion is the religion of spiritual perception, in which the shapeless essence falls apart into countless weaker and stronger spirits. The innocent religion of flowers, a representation of the self without a self, passes into the seriousness of warring life and the guilt of animal religion: scattered peoples take determinate animal shapes as their essence and fight one another to the death. In this hatred pure negativity wears itself out.
Hegel texts:
The Phenomenology of Spirit
· ¶¶689–690
Hegel citations:
The innocence of the flower religion, which is only a representation of the self void of any self, passes over into the seriousness of warring life, into the guilt of animal religion
— The Phenomenology of Spirit ¶689 (tr. Pinkard)
However, in this hatred, the determinateness of purely negative being-for-itself gradually wears itself out
— The Phenomenology of Spirit ¶690 (tr. Pinkard)

Hegel definition: The artificer is spirit appearing as an artisan who brings itself forth as an object by instinctive work, as bees build cells, without yet grasping the thought of itself. The first works are of the abstract understanding, the crystals of pyramids and obelisks, straight lines and plane surfaces that do not have their meaning in themselves and receive spirit only from outside. The work advances by mingling natural and thinking forms until the artisan becomes a spiritual worker.
Hegel texts:
The Phenomenology of Spirit
· ¶¶691–698

Spirit therefore here appears as the artisan, and his doing, whereby he brings forth himself as object, although not yet having taken hold of the thought of himself, is an instinctive kind of working, much like bees building their cells.
— The Phenomenology of Spirit ¶691 (tr. Pinkard)
The crystals of the pyramids and of the obelisks, simple combinations of straight lines with even surfaces and equal relations of parts in which the incommensurability of roundness is abolished, are the works of this artisan of rigorous form.
— The Phenomenology of Spirit ¶692 (tr. Pinkard)

Head: Art-Religion
Path: 三. Spirit › 1. Subjective Spirit › ii. Phenomenology of Spirit (Consciousness) › γ. Reason › c. Religion as Spirit's Self-Consciousness › ii. Art-Religion

Hegel definition: Art-religion is the religion in which the artisan has become a spiritual worker and brings forth its shape in the form of self-consciousness. It is the religion of an ethical people who know their state as the work of their own self. It moves from the abstract work of art, statue, hymn and cult, through the living work, to the spiritual work in language, epic, tragedy and comedy, where the self becomes the absolute essence and art-religion is completed.
Hegel texts:
The Phenomenology of Spirit
· ¶¶699–747
Hegel citations:
Spirit has elevated its shape, in which it is for its consciousness, into the form of consciousness itself, and it brings forth such a shape to itself.
— The Phenomenology of Spirit ¶699 (tr. Pinkard)
The people who approach their god in the cult of the art-religion are an ethical people, who know their state and its actions as the will and accomplishment of their own self.
— The Phenomenology of Spirit ¶720 (tr. Pinkard)

Head: The Abstract Work of Art
Path: 三. Spirit › 1. Subjective Spirit › ii. Phenomenology of Spirit (Consciousness) › γ. Reason › c. Religion as Spirit's Self-Consciousness › ii. Art-Religion › 1. The Abstract Work of Art
Gloss: The work of art as a made object set apart from its makers.
Hegelian gloss: The abstract work of art, the statue and temple, hymn and oracle, and the cult.
Nouns: the abstract work of art; the cult image, the statue of the god, the temple, the hymn, the oracle; sacred object, sacred art. the abstract artwork, the thing-like work, the made object, the individual work, the image of the god, the cult.

Hegel definition: The abstract work of art is the first work of art, immediate, abstract and singular. It must move from this objective mode toward self-consciousness, while self-consciousness in the cult seeks to overcome its difference from its own spirit. It appears as the statue of the god, which is a thing without self-consciousness; as the hymn, in which the god exists in language; and as the cult, in which the two sides give up their one-sidedness and become one.
Hegel texts:
The Phenomenology of Spirit
· ¶¶705–719

The first work of art exists as immediate, abstract, and singular.
— The Phenomenology of Spirit ¶705 (tr. Pinkard)
For its own part, it has to move itself from this immediate and objective mode into the contrary mode of self-consciousness, just as, on the other hand, self-consciousness, which is for itself in the cult, aims at sublating the difference which it initially gives itself contrary to its own spirit, and it thereby engenders a work of art enlivening itself in its own self.
— The Phenomenology of Spirit ¶705 (tr. Pinkard)

These ancient gods, in which the luminous essence mates with the darkness and particularizes itself initially as heaven, earth, the ocean, the sun, the blind typhonic fire of the earth, etc., are replaced with shapes which in themselves only have the dark reminiscent echo of those earlier Titans and which are no longer natural beings but rather the clear ethical spirits of self-conscious peoples.
— The Phenomenology of Spirit ¶707 (tr. Pinkard)

Hegel definition: Cult is the movement in which the god who stirred in the element of self-consciousness and the god motionless as a thing give up their separate determinations and become one, so that the self becomes conscious of the divine essence coming down to it. It begins with the pure sacrifice of a possession, in which the owner renounces property and personality; the essence has already sacrificed itself in becoming animal and fruit, and in the shared meal the self has consciousness of its unity with it.

The Phenomenology of Spirit
· ¶¶714–719
Hegel citations:
The movement of both sides constitutes the cult.

— The Phenomenology of Spirit ¶718 (tr. Pinkard)
This consumption is the negative power that sublates the essence as well as singular individuality, and this consumption is at the same time the positive actuality in which the objective existence of the essence is transformed into self-conscious existence, and the self has consciousness of its unity with the essence.
— The Phenomenology of Spirit ¶718 (tr. Pinkard)

The Phenomenology of Spirit
· ¶¶720–726

What is still lacking in them is any equilibrium. In bacchanalian enthusiasm, the self is external to itself, but in beautiful embodiment, it is the spiritual essence.
— The Phenomenology of Spirit ¶726 (tr. Pinkard)
The completed element within which inwardness is external just as externality is likewise inward is, again, language
— The Phenomenology of Spirit ¶726 (tr. Pinkard)

Head: The Spiritual Work of Art
Path: 三. Spirit › 1. Subjective Spirit › ii. Phenomenology of Spirit (Consciousness) › γ. Reason › c. Religion as Spirit's Self-Consciousness › ii. Art-Religion › 3. The Spiritual Work of Art
Gloss: The work of art in the medium of language.
Hegelian gloss: The spiritual work of art in language: epic, tragedy and comedy.

Hegel definition: The spiritual work of art is the work whose element and dwelling is language, where the particular spirits of peoples gather into one pantheon for a common undertaking. It unfolds as epic, in which the world is represented through the bard; tragedy, in which the hero speaks in person and the actor is essential to the mask; and comedy, in which the self lets the mask fall and shows itself as the fate of the gods.
Hegel texts:

· ¶¶727–747

The spirits of [different] peoples, which become conscious of the shape of their essence in a particular animal, merge into one spirit; in that way, the particular beautiful spirits of a people combine themselves into one pantheon whose element and abode is language.
— The Phenomenology of Spirit ¶727 (tr. Pinkard)
The self, coming on the scene here with the sense that it is actual, plays with the mask which it once put on in order to be its persona.
— The Phenomenology of Spirit ¶744 (tr. Pinkard)

Hegel definition: Epic is the first language of the spiritual work of art, with a universal content in the sense of the completeness of a world, though not yet that of thought. — The Phenomenology of Spirit ¶729 (tr. Pinkard)

Hegel definition: Tragedy is the higher language that draws together the scattered moments of the divine world and the world of action. Path: 三. Spirit › 1. Subjective Spirit › ii. Phenomenology of Spirit (Consciousness) › γ. Reason › c. Religion as Spirit's Self-Consciousness › iii. Manifest Religion

Hegel definition: Manifest or revealed religion is the religion in which spirit has passed from the form of substance into that of subject. Its content is that the divine essence essentially and immediately has the shape of self-consciousness, and is known as spirit. Hegel definition: Spirit in itself, represented in the element of pure thinking, is the simple eternal self-equal essence, which is absolute spirit. Were it to remain a simple essence it would be spirit only in empty words, for spirit is to be actual. As abstraction it is negativity in itself, absolute difference from itself, pure becoming other. Representation tells this necessity of the concept as an event: the eternal essence creates an other and in that otherness immediately returns to itself.
Hegel texts:
The Phenomenology of Spirit
· ¶¶769–773
Hegel citations:
Hence, the simple eternal essence would be spirit only according to empty words if it were to remain in representational thought and in the expression of simple eternal essence.
— The Phenomenology of Spirit ¶769 (tr. Pinkard)
However, in this otherness, it has equally immediately reverted into itself again, for the difference is the difference in itself, i.e., the difference is immediately distinguished only from itself, and it is thus the unity reverted into itself.
— The Phenomenology of Spirit ¶769 (tr. Pinkard)

It therefore creates a world. This creating is representational thought’s word for the concept itself according to its absolute movement

Spirit in the determination of being for an other, is the motionless stable existence of those moments which were formerly enclosed in pure thinking, and it is therefore the dissolution of their simple universality and their splitting up into their own particularity.

Head: Spirit in Its Community (Death of the Mediator, Resurrection in the Community)
Path: 三. Spirit › 1. Subjective Spirit › ii. Phenomenology of Spirit (Consciousness) › γ. Reason › c. Religion as Spirit's Self-Consciousness › iii. Manifest Religion › 3. Spirit in Its Community (Death of the Mediator, Resurrection in the Community)

Hegel definition: Spirit in its community is reached through the death of the mediator. The divine essence relinquishes itself, goes to its death and is reconciled with itself, so that this death is its resurrection as spirit. What representation holds as something that happened to a particular being is shifted into self-consciousness, whose particularity dies in its universality. The painful feeling that God himself is dead is the loss of substance as object and the certainty that substance becomes subject, universal self-consciousness.
Hegel texts:
The Phenomenology of Spirit
· ¶¶779–787
Hegel citations:
As a result, the essence has in that sensuous presence come to be itself. The immediate existence of actuality has thus ceased to be alien, or external, to that essence, as it is what is sublated, or what is universal. Thus, this death is its resurrection as spirit.
— The Phenomenology of Spirit ¶779 (tr. Pinkard)
This self-consciousness thus does not therefore actually die off in the way that the particular is represented to have actually died; rather, its particularity dies off in its universality
— The Phenomenology of Spirit ¶785 (tr. Pinkard)
This knowing is therefore spiritgiving, as a result of which substance becomes subject, its abstraction and lifelessness have died, and it has become actual, simple, and universal self-consciousness.
— The Phenomenology of Spirit ¶785 (tr. Pinkard)

Hegel definition: Absolute knowing is spirit knowing itself in the shape of spirit, comprehending knowing, in which what religion held as content in the form of representation receives the form of the self. Truth is here not only the same as certainty but has the shape of self-certainty. The form of objectivity that remained is overcome, since consciousness has related to its object according to all its determinations and found in each a determination of the self. Hegel texts:
The Phenomenology of Spirit
· ¶¶788–808
Hegel citations:
It is spirit knowing itself in the shape of spirit, or it is comprehending conceptual knowing.
— The Phenomenology of Spirit ¶798 (tr. Pinkard)
Spirit, appearing to consciousness in this element, or, what amounts to the same thing here, what is therein engendered by it, is science.
— The Phenomenology of Spirit ¶798 (tr. Pinkard)

Head: The Shapes of Consciousness Recollected
Path: 三. Spirit › 1. Subjective Spirit › ii. Phenomenology of Spirit (Consciousness) › γ. Reason › d. Absolute Knowing › i. The Shapes of Consciousness Recollected
Gloss: The forms of awareness gathered in memory as stages of a single journey.

Nouns: the shapes of consciousness recollected; recollection, retrospect, review, the gallery of images, the gallery of pictures, memory of the journey, the path retraced. retrospection, memory &c H0663. reminiscence. the recollected shapes, the gathered moments, the stations of the way, the series of shapes, the gallery of forms, the stages, résumé, recapitulation. Hegel definition: The shapes of consciousness are recollected so as to show how consciousness knows its object as itself. The object is in part immediate being, answering to immediate consciousness; in part relation and determinateness, answering to perception; and in part essence or universal, answering to understanding. Absolute knowing does not at first appear as pure comprehension of the whole: it gathers the earlier shapes, in which the totality of the object's moments and of consciousness's conduct can be shown only as distributed.
Hegel texts:
The Phenomenology of Spirit
· ¶¶789–797
Hegel citations:
The object is therefore in part immediate being, or a thing per se, something which corresponds to immediate consciousness. Hegelian gloss: The intuition recollected and made the mind's own: recollection, imagination and memory.
Nouns: representation; mental representation, idea, conception, notion, image, picture, presentation, imagery, picture-thinking, figurative thought. apprehension, impression, perception, sentiment, reflection, observation, consideration, abstract idea, archetype, formative notion, guiding conception, organizing conception, image in the mind, regulative principle. similitude, semblance. illustration, delineation, portraiture. excogitation†, a fine frenzy, cloudland†, dreamland, flight of fancy, fumes of fancy, thick coming fancies [Macbeth], creation of the brain, coinage of the brain. figure. likeness, effigy. conceit, thought. ideation, envisagement.

Foreign: German: vorstellen, übersinnliches Erkenntnisbild, Vorstellung der Vernunft, Begriff, Repräsentierung, Vertretung; Latin: repraesentatio, intentio; Greek: phantasia, eidolon, noēma; Arabic: taṣawwur [conception, representation], maʿnā; Sanskrit: vikalpa [mental construction]; Korean: pyosang [representation]; French: idée reçue [received idea] [Flaubert], intention; Italian: intenzione.
Phrases: the map is not the territory [Korzybski]; to picture to oneself; to form an idea of.
Hegel definition: Representation is the recollected intuition, the mean between intelligence's immediately finding itself determined and its freedom in thinking. It is intelligence's own possession, still one-sidedly subjective and conditioned by immediacy, and its path is to make the immediate inward and then to divest that inwardness of its subjectivity. Its stages, recollection, imagination and memory, are not independent faculties but an organic development of intelligence.
Hegel texts:
The Philosophy of Mind
· §§451–464
Hegel citations:
Representation is the recollected intuition and, as such, is the mean between intelligence's immediate finding-itself-determined and intelligence in its freedom, thinking.
— Encyclopedia §451 (tr. Wallace and Miller, rev. Inwood)
But the genuinely philosophical conception of these forms just consists in comprehending the rational connection obtaining between them, in recognizing the organic development of intelligence occurring in them.
— Encyclopedia §451, Addition (tr. Wallace and Miller, rev. Inwood)

Head: Recollection
Path: 三. Spirit › 1. Subjective Spirit › iii. Mind (Psychology) › α. Theoretical Mind › b. Representation › i. Recollection
Gloss: The inward keeping of an experience as an image.
Hegelian gloss: The intuition made inward as an image, preserved without the presence of the object.
Nouns: recollection; remembrance, recall, reminiscence, retention, internalization, storing up. recognition, rememoration†, recurrence, flashback, retrospect, retrospection. memory, retentiveness, tenacity, tablets of the memory, readiness. inwardizing, interiorization, inner keeping.
Verbs: recollect, remember, recall, retain, inwardize, internalize, store. recognize, call up, retrace, look back, bring to mind. mind, retain the memory of, retain the remembrance of, keep in view. remember &c H0663. have in the memory, hold in the memory, bear in the memory, keep in the memory, retain in the memory. lay up, treasure up.
Adjective: recollective, reminiscent, retentive, inward. retained, internalized.
Adverbs: in recollection, by heart. by rote, without book, memoriter†. inwardly.
Foreign: Latin: recordatio, veteris vestigia flammae; Greek: anamnēsis; Arabic: dhikr; German: Treppenwitz [the retort thought of on the stairs]; French: esprit de l'escalier.
Phrases: Erinnerung as Er-innerung [Ger.] [making inward]; to call to mind; memory lane.
Hegel definition: Recollection is the first and most abstract stage of representation. Intelligence places the content of intuition in its own inner space and time, making it an image; the image is preserved unconsciously; and at last it is related to a present intuition of the same content and recognized as one's own. By being summoned up often it grows vivid enough to need no outer intuition, and so children pass from intuiting to recollecting.
Hegel texts:
The Philosophy of Mind
· §§452–454
Hegel citations:
The images of the past lying hidden in the dark depths of our interior become our actual possession in the following way. They present themselves to the intelligence in the luminous, plastic shape of an occurrent intuition of the same content, and with the help of this present intuition we recognize them as intuitions we have already had.
— Encyclopedia §454, Addition (tr. Wallace and Miller, rev. Inwood)
In this way children pass from intuition to recollection.
— Encyclopedia §454, Addition (tr. Wallace and Miller, rev. Inwood)

Head: Image
Path: 三. Spirit › 1. Subjective Spirit › iii. Mind (Psychology) › α. Theoretical Mind › b. Representation › i. Recollection › 1. Image
Gloss: An experience kept in the mind, detached from its original place and time.
Hegelian gloss: The intuition freed from its immediacy and placed in the mind's own space and time.
Nouns: image; mental image, picture, impression, likeness, afterimage, memory image, mental picture, icon. similitude, semblance, representation, resemblance. idea. copy, counterpart, effigy. image &c H0834. trace, engram, phantasm, memory-image.
Verbs: image, picture, form an image, visualize. envision, figure to oneself. retain, abstract.
Adjective: imaged, pictured, imagistic, iconic, eidetic. pictorial, abstracted, detached. portrayed, depicted.
Adverbs: imagistically, in image. pictorially.
Foreign: German: vorstellen; Latin: imago, species, figura, effigies, forma, pictura, simulacrum; Greek: eidōlon, phantasma, eidolon; Arabic: khayāl [image, phantom]; French: tableau, visage; Hebrew: demut.
Phrases: a picture is worth a thousand words; in one's mind's eye; a picture in one's head.
Hegel definition: The image is the content of intuition placed in the inwardness of intelligence, in its own space and time, freed from its immediacy and abstract individuality and taken into the universality of the I. It lacks the full determinacy of the intuition, is wilful or contingent, and cut off from its original place and time. What is represented gains lasting existence only at the cost of the clarity and freshness of what is intuited.
Hegel texts:
The Philosophy of Mind
· §452
Hegel citations:
The image no longer has the complete determinacy that the intuition has, and is wilful or contingent, in general isolated from the external place, the time, and the immediate context in which the intuition stood.
— Encyclopedia §452 (tr. Wallace and Miller, rev. Inwood)
However, what is represented gains this immortality only at the cost of the clarity and freshness of the immediate individuality, the all round determinacy, of what is intuited; the intuition is obscured and blurred, when it becomes an image.
— Encyclopedia §452, Addition (tr. Wallace and Miller, rev. Inwood)

Head: The Night-Like Pit
Path: 三. Spirit › 1. Subjective Spirit › iii. Mind (Psychology) › α. Theoretical Mind › b. Representation › i. Recollection › 2. The Night-Like Pit
Gloss: The unconscious store of images held within the mind.
Hegelian gloss: The night-like pit in which a world of images is kept without being conscious.
Nouns: the night-like pit; the unconscious, the abyss of memory, the dark mine of images, the subconscious, latent memory, store-consciousness, the depths, the well of the past, the night of the mind; the treasury of images. the nightlike abyss, the dark shaft, the unconscious store, the unconscious pit, the mine of images, storehouse, repository, reservoir, latency, oblivion, reservatory†.
Verbs: store, sink, lie latent, slumber, lie dormant. bury, preserve unconsciously.
Adjective: nocturnal, latent, unconscious, subconscious, dormant, abyssal, dark. lurking, secret &c H0662, occult, abeyant. smoldering, unexerted†. buried.
Adverbs: latently, below consciousness, in the depths. unconsciously, in the dark.
Foreign: Sanskrit: ālaya-vijñāna [storehouse consciousness].
Phrases: the night-like pit in which a world of infinitely many images and representations is preserved [Hegel]; very deep is the well of the past [Thomas Mann]; the back of one's mind; buried deep.
Hegel definition: The night-like pit is intelligence as the unconscious store in which a world of infinitely many images and representations is preserved without being in consciousness. To conceive it is to grasp the concept as concrete, as a seed holds in virtual possibility the whole development of the tree, so that no special fibres or places are needed to keep them. The images are ours only formally, not yet at our command.
Hegel texts:
The Philosophy of Mind
· §453
Hegel citations:
To conceive intelligence as this nocturnal pit in which is stored a world of infinitely many images and representations, yet without being in consciousness, is on the one hand the universal requirement to conceive the concept as concrete, as we conceive e.g. the seed as affirmatively containing, in virtual possibility, all the determinacies that come into existence only in the development of the tree.
— Encyclopedia §453, Remark (tr. Wallace and Miller, rev. Inwood)
No one knows what an infinite host of images of the past slumbers in him; now and then they do indeed awake by chance, but one cannot, as we say, call them to mind.
— Encyclopedia §453, Addition (tr. Wallace and Miller, rev. Inwood)

Head: Recollection Proper
Path: 三. Spirit › 1. Subjective Spirit › iii. Mind (Psychology) › α. Theoretical Mind › b. Representation › i. Recollection › 3. Recollection Proper
Gloss: The calling up of a stored image in the presence of a new experience; recognition.
Hegelian gloss: The image called up by a present intuition, recognized as one's own.
Nouns: recollection proper; recognition, re-cognition, matching image to intuition, memory confirmed, familiarity, recall on cue. identification, diagnosis, apperception, assimilation, classification, memory &c H0663, interpretation &c H0662, cognizance &c H0646. cognizance, acquaintance, apprehension. reminiscence, recollection, rememoration†, recurrence, flashback, retrospect, retrospection. anamnesis, subsumption under an image.

Adverbs: on recognition, familiarly. at sight, again.
Foreign: French: déjà vu.
Phrases: I know that face; that rings a bell; it comes back to me.
Hegel definition: Recollection proper is the relation of an abstractly stored image to a present intuition with the same content: the intuition is subsumed under the representation, and intelligence recognizes both as already its own. By repeated summoning the image gains such vitality that no external intuition is needed, so that intelligence can externalize its own property. The more cultivated a person is, the more their intuitions are also recollections.
Hegel texts:
The Philosophy of Mind
· §454
Hegel citations:
Such an abstractly stored image needs, for its reality, a real intuition; authentic recollection, as it is called, is the relation of the image to an intuition, in fact the subsumption of the immediate individual intuition under what is universal in form, under the representation which is the same content.
— Encyclopedia §454 (tr. Wallace and Miller, rev. Inwood)
The more cultivated a man is, the more he lives not in immediate intuition, but, in all his intuitions, at the same time in recollections; so that he sees little that is altogether new
— Encyclopedia §454, Addition (tr. Wallace and Miller, rev. Inwood)

Hegel definition: Imagination is the second stage of representation, where intelligence works freely on the images it possesses and the opposition arises between the represented and the intuited content. It first reproduces images from its inwardness, then associates them and raises them to universal representations, and finally, as phantasy, gives its universals a pictorial reality in symbol and sign, so forming the transition to memory.
Hegel texts:
The Philosophy of Mind
· §§455–460
Hegel citations:
But, secondly, imagination does not merely summon up again the images present in it but relates them to each other and in this way raises them to universal representations.
— Encyclopedia §455, Addition (tr. Wallace and Miller, rev. Inwood)
The third stage in this sphere is the stage at which intelligence identifies its universal representations with the particularity of the image and so gives them a pictorial reality.
— Encyclopedia §455, Addition (tr. Wallace and Miller, rev. Inwood)

Head: Reproductive Imagination
Path: 三. Spirit › 1. Subjective Spirit › iii. Mind (Psychology) › α. Theoretical Mind › b. Representation › ii. Imagination › 1. Reproductive Imagination
Gloss: Imagination that brings stored images back into view.
Hegelian gloss: The imagination that calls images forth from the pit by its own will.
Nouns: reproductive imagination; recall of images, reproduction, evocation, calling up, summoning, re-presenting, memory imagery. repetition, duplication, reduplication. duplicate, reflex, reflection, echo. revival of images, re-presentation, reviviscence, revivessence†.
Verbs: reproduce, recall, evoke, summon, call up, conjure. recollect, bring to mind. invoke. copy, mirror, reflect, repeat. revive, bring back.
Adjective: reproductive, evocative, recalled. revived.
Adverbs: evocatively, at will. by recall, from memory.
Phrases: to conjure up the past; to call up.
Hegel definition: Reproductive imagination is intelligence calling images forth from the inwardness of the I, which from now on is the power over them. It reproduces images voluntarily and without the help of a present intuition, which distinguishes it from mere recollection. In the process the immediate spatial and temporal concretion of the intuition is dissolved, and a universal representation becomes the associating link among the images.
Hegel texts:
The Philosophy of Mind
· §455
Hegel citations:
When it is at work in this possession intelligence is the reproductive imagination, the emergence of images from the I's own inwardness; the I is from now on the power over them.
— Encyclopedia §455 (tr. Wallace and Miller, rev. Inwood)
But the reproduction of images on the part of imagination occurs voluntarily and without the help of an immediate intuition.
— Encyclopedia §455, Addition (tr. Wallace and Miller, rev. Inwood)

Head: Associative Imagination
Path: 三. Spirit › 1. Subjective Spirit › iii. Mind (Psychology) › α. Theoretical Mind › b. Representation › ii. Imagination › 2. Associative Imagination
Gloss: Imagination that links images by their likenesses and connections; association of ideas.
Hegelian gloss: Imagination that connects images according to their common features and forms general representations.
Nouns: associative imagination; association of ideas, associationism, train of thought, chain of association, linking, connection, combination, free association, stream of consciousness, laws of association, contiguity and resemblance. bond of union. analogy, association. association of thought, succession of thought, flow of thought, current of thought, succession of ideas, flow of ideas, train of ideas, current of ideas. correlation, interrelation. associating imagination, train of images, linkage, contiguity, resemblance.
Verbs: associate, link, connect, combine, relate, call to mind. bring into relation with, link &c H0269. join, conjoin. call up, suggest.
Adjective: associative, connective, combinatorial, discursive, free-associating. associational, linked, suggestive.
Adverbs: associatively, by association.
Phrases: one thing leads to another; one thing reminds one of another; a train of thought.
Hegel definition: Associative imagination relates images to one another, subsuming individual representations under a universal that forms their connection and giving them a subjective bond in place of an objective one. What enables images to relate is what they have in common, so that universal representations arise by the spontaneous activity of intelligence, not by many similar images piling up on one another while a mere spectator looks on.
Hegel texts:
The Philosophy of Mind
· §456
Hegel citations:
Hence even the association of representations is to be conceived as subsumption of the individual representations under a universal representation, which forms the connection between them.
— Encyclopedia §456 (tr. Wallace and Miller, rev. Inwood)
In the production of universal representations, the intelligence thus operates spontaneously, it is, therefore, an inept mistake to assume that universal representations arose, without any help from the mind, by the superimposition of many similar images
— Encyclopedia §456, Addition (tr. Wallace and Miller, rev. Inwood)

Head: Phantasy
Path: 三. Spirit › 1. Subjective Spirit › iii. Mind (Psychology) › α. Theoretical Mind › b. Representation › ii. Imagination › 3. Phantasy
Gloss: Imagination that gives images a meaning of its own; creative fancy.

Foreign: German: Eingebung [inspiration], vorstellen; Italian: fantasia, ben trovato [aptly invented, if not true], capriccio [fanciful invention]; Sanskrit: pratibhā [poetic genius]; Spanish: lo real maravilloso [the marvellous real] [Carpentier].

Hegel definition: Phantasy is intelligence freely combining and subsuming its store of images under a content of its own, impressing that content upon them. Hegel citations:
Fantasy is the midpoint in which the universal and being, one's own and being-found, the inner and outer, are completely welded into one.
— Encyclopedia §457, Remark (tr. Wallace and Miller, rev. Inwood)
As the activity of this unification, fantasy is reason, but only formal reason, in so far as the content of fantasy as such is a matter of indifference; whereas reason as such also determines the content to truth.
— Encyclopedia §457, Remark (tr. Wallace and Miller, rev. Inwood)

Hegel definition: Symbolizing phantasy is the activity of intelligence that, still guided by the given content of images, chooses to express its universals only through sensory material whose own meaning corresponds to them, as the eagle displays the strength of Jupiter. · §457
Hegel citations:
This activity of intelligence, which is in this way still conditioned, only relatively free, we call symbolizing fantasy.
— Encyclopedia §457, Addition (tr. Wallace and Miller, rev. Inwood)
Thus, for example, the strength of Jupiter is displayed by the eagle because this is regarded as being strong.-Allegory expresses the subjective element more by an ensemble of individual details.
— Encyclopedia §457, Addition (tr. Wallace and Miller, rev. Inwood)

Hegel definition: Sign-making phantasy is intelligence using an intuition to represent something wholly different from what the intuition shows for itself: the sensory matter is given an alien meaning as its soul, as with a flag, a tombstone or the pyramid. The sign is some immediate intuition, which represents a wholly different content from the content that it has for itself;-the pyramid into which an alien soul is transferred and preserved.

— Encyclopedia §457, Addition (tr. Wallace and Miller, rev. Inwood)

Head: Language (Speech and Writing)
Path: 三. Spirit › 1. Subjective Spirit › iii. Mind (Psychology) › α. Theoretical Mind › b. Representation › ii. Imagination › 3. Phantasy › c. Language (Speech and Writing)

Hegel definition: Language is the system in which the sign finds its most adequate form: a reality in time that vanishes as it is, sound articulated into speech, which gives sensations, intuitions and representations a second, higher existence. Spoken language is original and writing a further development of it; alphabetic writing, signs of signs that keep genuine names, Hegel judges the more intelligent form, above hieroglyphic script.

Hegel definition: Practical feeling is practical mind at first, which has its self-determination in an immediate way and finds itself an individuality determined in its inner nature. It has the content of reason, but as individual, and therefore natural, contingent and subjective, so that it may be rational or bad. To retreat to feeling against thought-out right and duty is suspect, since what feeling adds is only particular subjectivity, vanity and wilfulness.

Head: Subjective
Path: 三. Spirit › 1. Subjective Spirit › iii. Mind (Psychology) › β. Practical Mind › a. Practical Feeling › i. Subjective
Gloss: Feeling as the will's inner sense of agreement or disagreement with itself.
Hegelian gloss: The ought of the practical feeling, its judgment of what is pleasant or unpleasant to it.
Nouns: subjective practical feeling; inner feeling, private sentiment, personal pleasure and pain, agreeable or disagreeable, liking and disliking, mood. subjective feeling, inner sense, self-agreement, contentment, discontent, the ought in feeling. aversion.
Verbs: like, dislike, enjoy, mind, resent. delight in, rejoice in, relish. disrelish, object to, mislike misrelish†, disvalue†, improbate†. agree, disagree, accord, be content, be discontent.
Adjective: subjective, personal, private, agreeable, disagreeable. pleasing, pleasant, pleasurable, gratifying, acceptable, welcome, beatic†, laetificant†, leef†. content, inward. enjoyable.
Adverbs: subjectively, to one's liking. agreeably, contentedly, inwardly.
Phrases: de gustibus non est disputandum [Lat.]; against the grain.
Hegel definition: In practical feeling as subjective there is an ought: the will's own self-determination is set against an individuality that counts only so far as it is adequate to it. The feeling will compares how it is determined from outside with what its own nature determines it to be, and demands that the affection agree. Both sides being immediate, the judgement of pleasant and unpleasant that results is utterly subjective and superficial.
Hegel texts:
The Philosophy of Mind
· §§471–472
Hegel citations:
Practical feeling involves the ought, its self-determination as being in itself, related to an individuality that is in being and which is allowed to count only in its adequacy to that self-determination.
— Encyclopedia §472 (tr. Wallace and Miller, rev. Inwood)
The feeling will is, therefore, the comparing of its immediate determinedness coming from outside, with the determinedness posited in it by its own nature.
— Encyclopedia §472, Addition (tr. Wallace and Miller, rev. Inwood)

Path: 三. Spirit › 1. Subjective Spirit › iii. Mind (Psychology) › β. Practical Mind › a. Practical Feeling › ii. Intuitive

Hegel definition: Intuitive practical feelings are those whose content comes from intuition or representation, and so are more determinate than the pleasant and unpleasant: delight, joy, hope, fear, anguish and pain. In each the self feels the harmony or discord between itself and some event, thing or person, the content entering from outside. A sensible person of great character may find, or suffer, something without giving way to the feeling.

— Encyclopedia §472, Addition (tr. Wallace and Miller, rev. Inwood)

Head: Thought
Path: 三. Spirit › 1. Subjective Spirit › iii. Mind (Psychology) › β. Practical Mind › a. Practical Feeling › iii. Thought
Gloss: Feeling that carries a thought-content, such as shame, remorse or hope.
Hegelian gloss: Feelings whose content comes from thought: shame, remorse, the feelings of right and religion.
Nouns: thought in practical feeling; reflective feeling, considered sentiment, rational emotion, the feeling-content made thought, justified feeling, moral judgment. shame, remorse, repentance, contrition, hope, fear, pride, feeling with a thought-content, moral feeling. compunction.
Verbs: reflect on, justify, rationalize, consider. repent, rue, blush, be ashamed.
Adjective: reflective, considered, rational, justified. ashamed, remorseful, repentant, contrite, hopeful, fearful.
Adverbs: on reflection, upon consideration. with shame, remorsefully, hopefully.
Phrases: the heart has its reasons [Pascal]; hang one's head; pangs of conscience.
Hegel definition: Feelings whose content derives from thinking are those in which the substance of right, morality, ethical life and religion is taken up into the feeling will, such as shame and remorse. They are distinguished and justified by that content. But the content is not inseparably bound to feeling: remorse may be felt even over a good deed, and one can weigh an action against duty calmly in representation.
Hegel texts:
The Philosophy of Mind
· §§471–472
Hegel citations:
Remorse is the feeling of the discordance between my activity and my duty, or even only my advantage, in each case, therefore, between my activity and something determined-in-and-for-itself.
— Encyclopedia §472, Addition (tr. Wallace and Miller, rev. Inwood)
That this content is not inseparably conjoined with the feeling can be seen in an empirical way from the fact that remorse can be sensed even over a good deed.
— Encyclopedia §472, Addition (tr. Wallace and Miller, rev. Inwood)

Hegel definition: Interest is the moment of subjective individuality and its activity contained in what has been brought about, when the content of the urge is distinguished as what matters. · §102
Hegel citations:

But in its form it is an act of a subjective will which can place its infinity in every act of transgression and whose justice, therefore, is in all cases contingent, while to the other party too it appears as only particular. — The Philosophy of Right §102 (tr. Knox, rev. Houlgate)
[R]evenge remains defective inasmuch as it is the act of a subjective will and therefore does not correspond with the content.
— The Philosophy of Right §102, Addition (tr. Knox, rev. Houlgate)

Hegel definition: Morality is the standpoint of the will that is infinite not only in itself but for itself: the will reflected into itself, which makes the person a subject. Hegel definition: Bad conscience is the first form of evil: the subject knows the true universal, yet wills a particular content against it, and highlights the positive side of the deed to regard it as a duty or a good intention. Acting with this knowledge is acting with a bad conscience, not yet hypocrisy.
Hegel texts:
The Philosophy of Right
· §140
Hegel citations:

This aspect he knows how to highlight, and he may then proceed to regard it as a duty or a fine intention. By so interpreting it, he is able to pass off his action as good in the eyes both of himself and others, despite the fact that, owing to his reflection into himself and his consciousness of the universal aspect of the will, the essentially negative content of the action stands within him in contrast to this universal.
— The Philosophy of Right §140 (tr. Knox, rev. Houlgate)
[T]hese determinations characterize acting with a bad conscience, not yet hypocrisy as such.
— The Philosophy of Right §140, Remark (tr. Knox, rev. Houlgate)

Head: Hypocrisy

Hegel definition: Hypocrisy is the form of evil that asserts to others that an evil action is good. Head: Probabilism
Path: 三. Spirit › 2. Objective Spirit › ii. Morality › γ. The Good and Conscience › e. Evil and Its Forms › iii. Probabilism
Gloss: Holding that any action is justified if some authority can be found to approve it.
Hegelian gloss: Probabilism, the doctrine that a deed is permissible if any good reason or authority can be found for it.
Nouns: probabilism; casuistry, Jesuitry, special pleading, a probable opinion, moral loophole, rationalization, sophistry, hair-splitting, legalism; the authority of one doctor, tutiorism, laxism. equivocation, evasion, chicanery. moral laxity, the authority of a doctor, Jesuitism.
Verbs: rationalize, quibble, find a loophole, split hairs, cite authority. pervert, equivocate, evade, gloss over, varnish, cavil, subtilize†. find a reason, cite an authority, excuse, casuistize.
Adjective: casuistic, Jesuitical, sophistical, specious, lax. deceptive, plausible, evasive. probabilistic, casuistical.
Adverbs: casuistically, on some authority or other. on some authority, on probable grounds.
Phrases: there's always someone who says it's fine; there's always a reason; to find a loophole.
Hegel definition: Probabilism is the doctrine that an action is permissible, and may be done with an easy conscience, if any good reason for it can be found, even only the authority of one theologian against many others. It makes the subject's choice among reasons and authorities the deciding factor, so that the good becomes a matter of opinion.
Hegel texts:
The Philosophy of Right
· §140
Hegel citations:
In this perversion of evil into good we must first of all include the shape known as probabilism. Its guiding principle is that an action is permissible, and may be done with an easy conscience, if the agent can come up with any good reason for it, be it only the authority of one theologian, and even if other theologians are known by the agent to dissent ever so widely from that authority.
— The Philosophy of Right §140, Remark (tr. Knox, rev. Houlgate)

Head: Good Intention Justifying the Means
Path: 三. Spirit › 2. Objective Spirit › ii. Morality › γ. The Good and Conscience › e. Evil and Its Forms › iv. Good Intention Justifying the Means
Gloss: Excusing an evil deed by a good purpose.

Hegel definition: The good intention justifying the means is the maxim that the end justifies the means. Taken generally it is trivial, since a just end justifies the means and an unjust end does not. In use it means that a good intention may make right an action that is in itself a crime.
Hegel texts:

· §140
Hegel citations:

— The Philosophy of Right §140, Remark (tr. Knox, rev. Houlgate)

Head: Conviction
Path: 三. Spirit › 2. Objective Spirit › ii. Morality › γ. The Good and Conscience › e. Evil and Its Forms › v. Conviction
Gloss: Taking one's own belief as the measure of right.
Hegelian gloss: The conviction that holds whatever I believe right to be right, abolishing all objective truth.
Nouns: conviction; subjective conviction as sole standard, moral subjectivism, sincerity as warrant, fanaticism of conviction, ethics of conviction; self-righteousness. subjective conviction, sincerity, personal belief, private persuasion, good faith, subjective certainty.
Verbs: be convinced, act on conviction, justify by sincerity. hold, believe, persuade oneself, follow one's conviction.
Adjective: convinced, self-righteous, fanatical, subjectivist, sincere. persuaded, subjective, self-certain.
Adverbs: sincerely, out of conviction. from conviction, in good faith.
Foreign: German: Gesinnungsethik [Max Weber]; French: parti pris; Sanskrit: dṛṣṭi [a fixed view] [Nāgārjuna].
Phrases: the sincerity of the conviction excuses nothing; true to one's convictions; to the best of my belief.
Hegel definition: Conviction is the principle that whatever the subject holds to be right is right, so that its own conviction decides the ethical character of an action. Since the good willed is still without content, this makes the subject solely responsible for subsuming an action under the good, and abolishes all objective right and duty.
Hegel texts:
The Philosophy of Right
· §140
Hegel citations:
Since the good we will to do is here still without content, the principle of conviction only adds the further specification that the subsumption of an action under the category of good is the responsibility of the subject.
— The Philosophy of Right §140, Remark (tr. Knox, rev. Houlgate)

Path: 三. Spirit › 2. Objective Spirit › ii. Morality › γ. The Good and Conscience › e. Evil and Its Forms › vi. Irony

Foreign: Latin: ironia; Greek: eirōneia; Sanskrit: vakrokti [oblique speech]; Korean: baneo [irony].
Phrases: die endlich höchste Form, in der diese Subjektivität sich vollkommen erfaßt und ausspricht, ist die Gestalt, die man … Ironie genannt hat [Ger.] [Hegel, Philosophy of Right §140 Remark]; Socratic irony; nothing is sacred.
Hegel definition: Irony is the supreme form of this subjectivity: it knows itself as the master of every ethical content, which it may accept or set aside at will. It acknowledges law and duty, yet holds itself above them as the one who decides. The name comes from Plato, but Socrates used irony against conceit, not against the Idea.
Hegel texts:
The Philosophy of Right
· §140
Hegel citations:
Finally, the supreme form in which this subjectivity is completely comprehended and expressed is the phenomenon which has been called by a name borrowed from Plato—‘irony’.
— The Philosophy of Right §140, Remark (tr. Knox, rev. Houlgate)
You actually accept a law, it says, and honestly respect it as absolute [an und für sich seiend]. So do I, but I go further than you, because I am beyond this law and can make it to suit myself.
— The Philosophy of Right §140, Remark (tr. Knox, rev. Houlgate)

Hegel definition: Ethical life is the Idea of freedom as the living good: the good known and willed in self-consciousness and actualized by its action, while self-consciousness has its foundation and motivating end in the ethical world. It is the concept of freedom become an existing world, articulated in the family, civil society and the state.
Hegel texts:
The Philosophy of Right
· §§142–360
Hegel citations:
Ethical life is the Idea of freedom in that, on the one hand, it is the living good—the good endowed in self-consciousness with knowing and willing and actualized by self-conscious action—while, on the other hand, self-consciousness has in the ethical realm its foundation in and for itself and its motivating end.
— The Philosophy of Right §142 (tr. Knox, rev. Houlgate)
