Hegel definition: The first stage of world history. Its principle is substantiality: moral distinctions are laid down as laws that govern the subjective will from outside, with no place yet for conscience or inward assent. State and religion coincide in theocracy, so that the secular kingdom is also divine and the individual obeys a will that is not recognized as his own.
Hegel texts:
The Philosophy of History
· The Oriental World
Hegel citations:
The Oriental World has as its inherent and distinctive principle the Substantial, [the Prescriptive,] in Morality. We have the first example of a subjugation of the mere arbitrary will, which is merged in this substantiality. Moral distinctions and requirements are expressed as Laws, but so that the subjective will is governed by these Laws as by an external force.
— The Philosophy of History, The Oriental World (tr. Sibree)
What we call God has not yet in the East been realized in consciousness, for our idea of God involves an elevation of the soul to the supersensual. While we obey, because what we are required to do is confirmed by an internal sanction, there the Law is regarded as inherently and absolutely valid without a sense of the want of this subjective confirmation. In the law men recognize not their own will, but one entirely foreign.
— The Philosophy of History, The Oriental World (tr. Sibree)

Head: China and Mongolia (Theocratic Despotism)
Path: 三. Spirit › 2. Objective Spirit › iii. Ethical Life › γ. The State › c. World History › i. Oriental World › 1. China and Mongolia (Theocratic Despotism)
Gloss: The ancient empires of China and Mongolia, ruled by a single head as father and priest.
Hegelian gloss: China, the patriarchal theocratic despotism of the substance, a state without inwardness.
Nouns: China and Mongolia; theocratic despotism, the Middle Kingdom, the Celestial Empire, the Son of Heaven, the Mandate of Heaven, patriarchal state, the mandarinate, Confucianism, ancestor worship, the Mongol khanate, Lamaism; khan, Genghis Khan. the Chinese empire, the emperor, patriarchal despotism, the mandarins, the Mongols, Tibet, the Dalai Lama, theocratic rule. Cathay.
Verbs: rule, prostrate, kowtow, govern patriarchally. govern paternally, revere, obey, administer.
Adjective: Chinese, Mongolian, patriarchal, imperial, Confucian, despotic, mandarin. theocratic, paternal.
Adverbs: by the Mandate of Heaven. patriarchally, under the emperor, paternally.
Foreign: Chinese: Zhongguo, Tianchao, Tianzi, Tianming.
Phrases: the empire long divided must unite, long united must divide [Romance of the Three Kingdoms].
Hegel definition: The oldest empire, where history begins, built on the family relation extended to the state. The Emperor governs paternally as father of a people held to be in a condition of nonage; all are equal, but without freedom, so that despotism is the necessary form of government. Morality is fixed by law from above, and what belongs to inward subjectivity is wanting.
Hegel texts:
The Philosophy of History
· The Oriental World › China
Hegel citations:
Since equality prevails in China, but without any freedom, despotism is necessarily the mode of government.
— The Philosophy of History, The Oriental World › China (tr. Sibree)
Its distinguishing feature is, that everything which belongs to Spirit,—unconstrained morality, in practice and theory, Heart, inward Religion, Science and Art properly so called,—is alien to it.
— The Philosophy of History, The Oriental World › China (tr. Sibree)

Head: India (Theocratic Aristocracy)
Path: 三. Spirit › 2. Objective Spirit › iii. Ethical Life › γ. The State › c. World History › i. Oriental World › 2. India (Theocratic Aristocracy)
Gloss: The ancient civilization of India, divided into castes fixed by birth, with the priestly Brahmins at their head.
Hegelian gloss: India, the dreaming spirit of caste, theocratic aristocracy.
Nouns: India; theocratic aristocracy, caste system, Brahmins, the Vedas, Brahman, dream-like spirit, the land of desire. Hindustan, the Indian world, the land of the Ganges, the Kshatriyas, the castes, the land of dreams, the dreaming spirit. varna, Brahmanism.
Verbs: dream, stratify, contemplate. divide into castes, fantasize, ordain.
Adjective: Indian, Brahminical, caste-based, Vedic, contemplative, dreamy. Hindu, Brahmanical, caste-bound, priestly.
Adverbs: in India. by caste, by birth, in dream.
Foreign: Persian: Hindustān; Sanskrit: varṇa, jāti, brāhmaṇa, kṣatriya, vaiśya, śūdra, Bhārata.
Phrases: the land of desire [Hegel on India]; the land of the Vedas.
Hegel definition: The region of phantasy and sensibility, which advances beyond Chinese uniformity by letting differences appear, only to fix them as natural castes. Its idealism is one of imagination without distinct conception, as of Spirit in a dream. Because the distinctions are attributed to Nature, their religious unity yields a theocratic aristocracy, in which the Brahmins count as gods bodily present.
Hegel texts:
The Philosophy of History
· The Oriental World › India
Hegel citations:
For we have not the dreaming of an actual Individual, possessing distinct personality, and simply unfettering the latter from limitation, but we have the dreaming of the unlimited absolute Spirit.
— The Philosophy of History, The Oriental World › India (tr. Sibree)
For the claims of caste are, as already remarked, not merely secular, but essentially religious, and the Brahmins in their exalted dignity are the very gods bodily present.
— The Philosophy of History, The Oriental World › India (tr. Sibree)

Head: Persia (Theocratic Monarchy)
Path: 三. Spirit › 2. Objective Spirit › iii. Ethical Life › γ. The State › c. World History › i. Oriental World › 3. Persia (Theocratic Monarchy)
Gloss: The ancient empire of Persia, ruled by a monarch under a single principle of light.
Hegelian gloss: Persia, the light religion, theocratic monarchy, the first historical people.
Nouns: Persia; theocratic monarchy, the Persian Empire, Achaemenid Empire, the King of Kings, satrapy, the religion of light, Zoroastrianism. the Persian realm, Iran, the Great King, the Achaemenids, Cyrus, Darius, Xerxes, the first historical people, the empire of light. shahanshah.
Verbs: rule, conquer, unite. illumine, tolerate.
Adjective: Persian, Achaemenid, imperial, Zoroastrian. Iranian, monarchical.
Adverbs: in Persia. under the Great King, in the Persian realm.
Foreign: Persian: shāhanshāh, Īrān, Fārs.
Phrases: the beginning of history proper [Hegel on Persia]; the laws of the Medes and Persians.
Hegel definition: The empire with which continuous history begins, its people being the first that is historical, subject to development and revolution and in the end to passing away. Its principle is light, a pure unity that governs individuals while leaving them free to develop their own character, so that many peoples of distinct customs are held together without losing their individuality.
Hegel texts:
The Philosophy of History
· The Oriental World › Persia
Hegel citations:
With the Persian Empire we first enter on continuous History. The Persians are the first Historical People; Persia was the first Empire that passed away.
— The Philosophy of History, The Oriental World › Persia (tr. Sibree)
We see in the Persian World a pure exalted Unity, as the essence which leaves the special existences that inhere in it, free;—as the Light, which only manifests what bodies are in themselves; — a Unity which governs individuals only to excite them to become powerful for themselves—to develop and assert their individuality.
— The Philosophy of History, The Oriental World › Persia (tr. Sibree)

Head: The Zend People
Path: 三. Spirit › 2. Objective Spirit › iii. Ethical Life › γ. The State › c. World History › i. Oriental World › 3. Persia (Theocratic Monarchy) › a. The Zend People
Gloss: The people of the Zoroastrian scriptures.
Hegelian gloss: The people of the Zend books, whose religion of light is the first worship of a pure, universal principle.
Nouns: the Zend people; the Avestan people, ancient Iranians, Zoroastrians, Parsis, Magi, the Avesta, Zend-Avesta, Zarathustra, Ahura Mazda, the good mind, Gymnosophist†. the Zend race, the ancient Parsees, the Bactrians, Zoroaster, the people of light, the Zend books, Ormuzd-worship.
Verbs: worship light, keep the fire. purify, cultivate, serve the good.
Adjective: Zend, Avestan, Zoroastrian, Magian, Iranian. Bactrian, Parsi, pure.
Adverbs: by the light. in purity, in the light, according to the Zend.
Foreign: Persian: Pārsī; Avestan: Vohu Manah.
Phrases: good thoughts, good words, good deeds, humata, hūkhta, hvarshta [Avestan]; the good thought.
Hegel definition: The people named after the language of the Zend books, the canonical writings of the religion of Zoroaster. In that religion the one universal being is worshipped in the form of light, which is no particular natural thing but sensuous universality itself, and which signifies the good and the true. It stands opposed to darkness as Ormuzd to Ahriman.
Hegel texts:
The Philosophy of History
· The Oriental World › Persia › The Zend People
Hegel citations:
But Light is not a Lama, a Brahmin, a Mountain, a brute,—this or that particular existence,—but sensuous Universality itself; simple manifestation.
— The Philosophy of History, Persia › The Zend People (tr. Sibree)
Among the Persians, Ormuzd and Ahriman present the antithesis in question. Ormuzd is the Lord of the kingdom of Light—of Good; Ahriman that of Darkness—of Evil.
— The Philosophy of History, Persia › The Zend People (tr. Sibree)

Head: Assyrians, Babylonians, Medes, and Persians
Path: 三. Spirit › 2. Objective Spirit › iii. Ethical Life › γ. The State › c. World History › i. Oriental World › 3. Persia (Theocratic Monarchy) › b. Assyrians, Babylonians, Medes, and Persians
Gloss: The peoples of the ancient Near Eastern empires.
Hegelian gloss: The Assyrians, Babylonians, Medes and Persians, the peoples that the Persian empire gathered into one.
Nouns: Assyrians, Babylonians, Medes, and Persians; Mesopotamian empires. the Near Eastern empires.
Verbs: conquer, build, rule. succeed, overthrow.
Adjective: imperial.
Adverbs: in succession, in the Near East.
Hegel definition: The peoples in whom the other elements of the Persian empire appear beside the higher spiritual element of the Zend race. Assyria and Babylonia contribute external wealth, luxury and commerce, and great cities raised for settled trade and for protection against roving peoples; the Medes, a warlike mountain people, pass on the Zend religion; and the Persians at last embrace all Anterior Asia in their rule.
Hegel texts:
The Philosophy of History
· The Oriental World › Persia › The Assyrians, Babylonians, Medes, and Persians
Hegel citations:
As the Zend Race was the higher spiritual element of the Persian Empire, so in Assyria and Babylonia we have the element of external wealth, luxury and commerce.
— The Philosophy of History, Persia › The Assyrians, Babylonians, Medes, and Persians (tr. Sibree)

Head: Assyrians
Path: 三. Spirit › 2. Objective Spirit › iii. Ethical Life › γ. The State › c. World History › i. Oriental World › 3. Persia (Theocratic Monarchy) › b. Assyrians, Babylonians, Medes, and Persians › i. Assyrians
Gloss: The people of Assyria, with its capital Nineveh, the first great empire of the Tigris.
Hegelian gloss: Die Assyrer, whose empire with Nineveh is among the peoples the Persian empire gathered into one.
Nouns: the Assyrians. Nineveh, Assyria. Ashur, Sennacherib, Ashurbanipal, Sardanapalus, the Assyrian empire, winged bulls.
Adjective: Assyrian.
Phrases: the Assyrian came down like the wolf on the fold [Byron].
Hegel definition: The people of Assyria proper, in northern Mesopotamia, whose empire consisted in effect of a single city such as Nineveh. Founded according to tradition by Ninus, who brought Babylonia, Media and Bactriana under his sway, it ended when the satraps rose against Sardanapalus, after which it broke up into Assyrian, Median and Babylonian realms.
Hegel texts:
The Philosophy of History
· The Oriental World › Persia › The Assyrians, Babylonians, Medes, and Persians
Hegel citations:
In those times one City constituted the whole Empire,—Nineveh for example
— The Philosophy of History, Persia › The Assyrians, Babylonians, Medes, and Persians (tr. Sibree)
These cities arose in consequence of a twofold necessity,—on the one hand that of giving up the nomade life and pursuing agriculture, handicrafts and trade in a fixed abode; and on the other hand of gaining protection against the roving mountain peoples, and the predatory Arabs.
— The Philosophy of History, Persia › The Assyrians, Babylonians, Medes, and Persians (tr. Sibree)

Head: Babylonians
Path: 三. Spirit › 2. Objective Spirit › iii. Ethical Life › γ. The State › c. World History › i. Oriental World › 3. Persia (Theocratic Monarchy) › b. Assyrians, Babylonians, Medes, and Persians › ii. Babylonians
Gloss: The people of Babylon, city of trade, temple towers and the study of the stars.
Hegelian gloss: Die Babylonier, with their city on the Euphrates, its temple of Bel and the Chaldean study of the stars, gathered into the Persian empire.
Nouns: the Babylonians. Babylon, the ziggurat, Ishtar, Marduk, Hammurabi, Nebuchadnezzar, Babylonia, the Chaldeans. the tower of Babel, the hanging gardens, the Babylonian captivity, astrology.
Adjective: Babylonian, Mesopotamian, Chaldean.
Adverbs: by the rivers of Babylon.
Phrases: by the rivers of Babylon [Bible]; the writing on the wall; by the waters of Babylon.
Hegel definition: The people of the great city on the Euphrates, set in a fertile plain suited to agriculture, crossed by canals and served by river trade, with the temple of Bel on one bank and royal palaces on the other. Their accumulated wealth and commerce, an organized government with its wise men and Chaldeans, and a manner of life denounced by the prophets mark them out.
Hegel texts:
The Philosophy of History
· The Oriental World › Persia › The Assyrians, Babylonians, Medes, and Persians
Hegel citations:
Babylon lay to the south, on the Euphrates, in a plain of great fertility and well adapted for agriculture.
— The Philosophy of History, Persia › The Assyrians, Babylonians, Medes, and Persians (tr. Sibree)
The Prophets generally say much of the great commerce of Babylon; but they also draw a terrible picture of the prevailing depravity of manners.
— The Philosophy of History, Persia › The Assyrians, Babylonians, Medes, and Persians (tr. Sibree)

Head: Medes
Path: 三. Spirit › 2. Objective Spirit › iii. Ethical Life › γ. The State › c. World History › i. Oriental World › 3. Persia (Theocratic Monarchy) › b. Assyrians, Babylonians, Medes, and Persians › iii. Medes
Gloss: The Medes, a warlike mountain people of Iran, whose priestly caste were the Magi.
Hegelian gloss: Die Meder, the warlike people whose Magi kept the Zend religion, from whom rule passed to the Persians.
Nouns: the Medes. Media, Ecbatana, the Magi. Deioces, Cyaxares, Astyages.
Adjective: Median.
Hegel definition: A mountain people living south of the Caspian, fierce and warlike, who freed themselves from Assyrian supremacy and gathered their tribes under a king at Ecbatana. The Magi, one of their tribes, preserved and spread the Zend religion, though with great modifications, so that the Medes carried it on to other peoples before sovereignty passed to the Persians.
Hegel texts:
The Philosophy of History
· The Oriental World › Persia › The Assyrians, Babylonians, Medes, and Persians
Hegel citations:
Among these Medes the Magi are also noticed as one of the six tribes that formed the Median people, whose chief characteristics were fierceness, barbarism, and warlike courage.
— The Philosophy of History, Persia › The Assyrians, Babylonians, Medes, and Persians (tr. Sibree)
But all the data point to the fact that among the Magi we may look for a comparatively close connection with the Zend religion; but that, although the Magi preserved and extended it, it experienced great modifications in transmission to the various peoples who adopted it.
— The Philosophy of History, Persia › The Assyrians, Babylonians, Medes, and Persians (tr. Sibree)

Head: Persians
Path: 三. Spirit › 2. Objective Spirit › iii. Ethical Life › γ. The State › c. World History › i. Oriental World › 3. Persia (Theocratic Monarchy) › b. Assyrians, Babylonians, Medes, and Persians › iv. Persians
Gloss: The Persians, the mountain people under Cyrus who united the Near East into one empire.
Hegelian gloss: Die Perser, the free mountain people under Cyrus that united Medes, Babylonians and Assyrians into one empire under a principle of light.
Nouns: the Persians. Cyrus, the Achaemenids, the Medes and Persians, the law of the Medes and Persians. the Great King. Darius, Xerxes, Persepolis, Pasargadae.
Adjective: Persian.
Phrases: the law of the Medes and Persians, which altereth not [Bible].
Hegel definition: The people properly so called in whom the empire reaches its culmination. Closely bound to the Medes, so that the two names melt into one and the passage of sovereignty between them makes no essential difference, they set out under Cyrus, extended their rule over all Anterior Asia and so came into contact with the Greeks. Cyrus died having united that region under one sovereignty.
Hegel texts:
The Philosophy of History
· The Oriental World › Persia › The Assyrians, Babylonians, Medes, and Persians
Hegel citations:
The real culmination of the Persian Empire is to be looked for in connection with the Persian people properly so called, which, embracing in its rule all Anterior Asia, came into contact with the Greeks.
— The Philosophy of History, Persia › The Assyrians, Babylonians, Medes, and Persians (tr. Sibree)
Cyrus thus died in his mission, which was the union of Anterior Asia into one sovereignty without an ulterior object.
— The Philosophy of History, Persia › The Assyrians, Babylonians, Medes, and Persians (tr. Sibree)

Head: The Persian Empire and Its Parts
Head (German): Das persische Reich und seine Bestandteile
Path: 三. Spirit › 2. Objective Spirit › iii. Ethical Life › γ. The State › c. World History › i. Oriental World › 3. Persia (Theocratic Monarchy) › c. The Persian Empire and Its Parts
Gloss: The provinces and peoples under Persian rule.
Hegelian gloss: The Persian empire, which let its peoples keep their own natures: Syria with its trade, Judaea with its one God, Egypt with its riddle.
Nouns: the Persian Empire and its parts; satrapies, provinces. the subject peoples, Persia proper, the empire of many nations. satrap.
Verbs: rule, subject, tolerate, unite, comprise.
Adjective: imperial, provincial, satrapal, multinational, tributary. transnational. Achaemenid.
Adverbs: across the empire. under Persian rule, province by province.
Foreign: Hebrew: Yehuda.
Phrases: from India to Ethiopia.
Hegel definition: An empire in the modern sense, composed of dependent states that kept their own individuality, customs and laws, and in some cases their own kings, under a rule that protected their differences as light lets each object show its own colour. Within it the elements of upland, river valley and sea coast coexist, and its Syrian, Jewish and Egyptian parts set the problem that Egypt takes up.
Hegel texts:
The Philosophy of History
· The Oriental World › Persia › The Persian Empire and its Constituent Parts
Hegel citations:
The Persian Empire is an Empire in the modern sense,— like that which existed in Germany, and the great imperial realm under the sway of Napoleon; for we find it consisting of a number of states, which are indeed dependent, but which have retained their own individuality, their manners, and laws.
— The Philosophy of History, Persia › The Persian Empire and its Constituent Parts (tr. Sibree)
As Light illuminates everything—imparting to each object a peculiar vitality—so the Persian Empire extends over a multitude of nations, and leaves to each one its particular character.
— The Philosophy of History, Persia › The Persian Empire and its Constituent Parts (tr. Sibree)

Head: Syria and Phoenicia
Path: 三. Spirit › 2. Objective Spirit › iii. Ethical Life › γ. The State › c. World History › i. Oriental World › 3. Persia (Theocratic Monarchy) › c. The Persian Empire and Its Parts › i. Syria and Phoenicia
Gloss: The Syrian and Phoenician coast, its seafaring traders and the worship of Adonis.
Hegelian gloss: Syrien und das semitische Vorderasien: Phoenician industry and navigation, the cult of Adonis and its lament for the dead god, under Persian rule.
Nouns: Syria and Phoenicia. Syria, Phoenicia, the Phoenician sea-traders, Asia Minor. Tyre, Sidon, the purple trade, Carthage, Astarte, Adonis, the alphabet.
Verbs: trade, sail.
Adjective: Syrian, Phoenician.
Hegel definition: The coastal part of the empire, with rich trading cities such as Tyre and Sidon, whose Phoenician seafarers introduce a new principle: industry, in which human will, courage and intelligence work upon nature in place of dependence on its bounty. Beside the worship of Hercules stands that of Adonis, a funeral festival lamenting the departed god.
Hegel texts:
The Philosophy of History
· The Oriental World › Persia › The Persian Empire and its Constituent Parts › Syria and the Semitic Western Asia
Hegel citations:
This opens to us an entirely new principle. Inactivity ceases, as also mere rude valour; in their place appears the activity of Industry, and that considerate courage which, while it dares the perils of the deep, rationally bethinks itself of the means of safety.
— The Philosophy of History, The Persian Empire and its Constituent Parts › Syria and the Semitic Western Asia (tr. Sibree)
The feast of Adonis was very similar to the worship of Osiris—the commemoration of his death;—a funeral festival, at which the women broke out into the most extravagant lamentations over the departed god.
— The Philosophy of History, The Persian Empire and its Constituent Parts › Syria and the Semitic Western Asia (tr. Sibree)

Head: Judaea
Path: 三. Spirit › 2. Objective Spirit › iii. Ethical Life › γ. The State › c. World History › i. Oriental World › 3. Persia (Theocratic Monarchy) › c. The Persian Empire and Its Parts › ii. Judaea
Gloss: The land of the Jews, whose religion of the one God set spirit above nature.
Hegelian gloss: Judäa, where nature is reduced to the created and the One is grasped as pure spirit, though bound to one people.
Nouns: Judaea. the Hebrew religion of the One. Israel, Jerusalem, the Temple, Jehovah, the Law, Moses, the prophets.
Verbs: worship.
Adjective: Judaean, Hebrew.
Phrases: Hear, O Israel: the Lord our God is one Lord, Shema Yisrael [Heb.] [Bible].
Hegel definition: The people among whom the spiritual is purified of nature and becomes the pure product of thought: God is grasped as the one creator, and nature is reduced to a creature, external and undivine. This marks the separation of East and West. Yet the unity remains exclusive, since only the one people recognizes this God and is acknowledged by him.
Hegel texts:
The Philosophy of History
· The Oriental World › Persia › The Persian Empire and its Constituent Parts › Judæa
Hegel citations:
Nature,—which in the East is the primary and fundamental existence,— is now depressed to the condition of a mere creature; and Spirit now occupies the first place.
— The Philosophy of History, The Persian Empire and its Constituent Parts › Judæa (tr. Sibree)
This religion must necessarily possess the element of exclusiveness, which consists essentially in this,—that only the One People which adopts it, recognizes the One God, and is acknowledged by him.
— The Philosophy of History, The Persian Empire and its Constituent Parts › Judæa (tr. Sibree)

Head: Egypt
Path: 三. Spirit › 2. Objective Spirit › iii. Ethical Life › γ. The State › c. World History › i. Oriental World › 3. Persia (Theocratic Monarchy) › c. The Persian Empire and Its Parts › iii. Egypt
Gloss: The land of the Nile, of pyramids, hieroglyphs and the cult of the dead, the riddle of the ancient world.
Hegelian gloss: Ägypten, the land of the riddle, whose spirit labours toward self-knowledge and whose problem is solved only in Greece.
Nouns: Egypt. the Egyptian riddle, hieroglyphs, the Sphinx, pyramids, Isis and Osiris. the Nile, the pharaohs, the mummy, the cult of the dead, animal worship, Thebes, Memnon.
Verbs: embalm, decipher, decode.
Adjective: Egyptian, hieroglyphic.
Phrases: the riddle of the Sphinx; a riddle for themselves and for others, the solution of which is only to be found in the Greek World [Hegel, Philosophy of History, tr. Sibree].
Hegel definition: The land in which the opposed elements of the Persian world are united as a problem: spirit sunk in nature and the impulse to free it are held together in contradiction. Its symbol is the Sphinx, half animal and half human. Driven to comprehend itself, the Egyptian spirit works out its thought in stone and in enigmatic hieroglyphs without reaching a clear solution.
Hegel texts:
The Philosophy of History
· The Oriental World › Persia › Egypt
Hegel citations:
The Sphinx may be regarded as a symbol of the Egyptian Spirit. The human head looking out from the brute body, exhibits Spirit as it begins to emerge from the merely Natural—to tear itself loose therefrom and already to look more freely around it; without, however, entirely freeing itself from the fetters Nature had imposed.
— The Philosophy of History, Persia › Egypt (tr. Sibree)
It is the distinguishing feature of the Egyptian Spirit, that it stands before us as this mighty task-master. It is not splendour, amusement, pleasure, or the like that it seeks. The force which urges it is the impulse of self-comprehension; and it has no other material or ground to work on, in order to teach itself what it is—to realize itself for itself
— The Philosophy of History, Persia › Egypt (tr. Sibree)

Head: Greek World (Beautiful Ethical Life)
Path: 三. Spirit › 2. Objective Spirit › iii. Ethical Life › γ. The State › c. World History › ii. Greek World (Beautiful Ethical Life)
Gloss: The world of the Greeks, in which some are free; ethical life as beauty.
Hegelian gloss: The Greek world, where some are free: beautiful ethical life, in which the individual lives the universal as custom without reflection.
Nouns: the Greek world; beautiful ethical life, Hellas, ancient Greece, the Hellenes, the polis, classical antiquity, the youth of history, some are free. Greece, the Hellenic world, the youth of spirit, the freedom of some, the beautiful freedom, the realm of beauty. Hellenism.
Verbs: flourish, philosophize, sculpt, deliberate. bloom, beautify, shape, free.
Adjective: Greek, Hellenic, Attic, classical, beautiful, harmonious. Grecian, youthful.
Adverbs: in Greece, in the Greek manner. in the Greek world, in beauty, as youth.
Foreign: German: schöne Sittlichkeit; Greek: Hellas, Hellēnes, eleutheria [the freedom of the free man, opposed to the slave]; Sanskrit: Yavana [Greeks]; French: cité, État, société, nation.
Phrases: the Greeks knew that some are free [Hegel]; we are all Greeks [Shelley]; the glory that was Greece.
Hegel definition: The second stage of world history, comparable to youth in its concrete freshness of soul. Its centre is individuality conditioned by beauty: spirit transforms what is natural into an expression of itself, in the culture of the body, the shaping of the gods and the form of the state. The universal is willed as custom, without reflective subjectivity, and slavery is a condition of its democracy.
Hegel texts:
The Philosophy of History
· The Greek World
Hegel citations:
At an earlier stage I compared the Greek world with the period of adolescence; not, indeed, in that sense, that youth bears within it a serious, anticipative destiny, and consequently by the very conditions of its culture urges towards an ulterior aim,—presenting thus an inherently incomplete and immature form, and being then most defective when it would deem itself perfect,—but in that sense, that youth does not yet present the activity of work,—does not yet exert itself for a definite intelligent aim,—but rather exhibits a concrete freshness of the soul
— The Philosophy of History, The Greek World (tr. Sibree)
It was a necessary condition of such occupations, that the citizens should be freed from handicraft occupations; consequently, that what among us is performed by free citizens—the work of daily life—should be done by slaves.
— The Philosophy of History, The Greek World (tr. Sibree)

Head: The Elements of the Greek Spirit
Path: 三. Spirit › 2. Objective Spirit › iii. Ethical Life › γ. The State › c. World History › ii. Greek World (Beautiful Ethical Life) › 1. The Elements of the Greek Spirit
Gloss: The conditions of the Greek spirit: land, inheritance and character.
Hegelian gloss: The elements of the Greek spirit: a divided land of coast and islands, and the foreign inheritance recast as their own.
Nouns: the elements of the Greek spirit; geography of Greece, sea and mountains, colonies, borrowings from the East, freedom of the individual, the gods made human, Greek individuality. the conditions of the Greek spirit, the Greek land, the sea, the islands, the mixture of peoples, foreign origins, the natural basis, heterogeneity, the youthful spirit. archipelago.
Verbs: borrow, transform, humanize, colonize. mingle, settle, inherit, receive.
Adjective: Hellenic, maritime, mountainous, insular, humanized, cloudtopt†, cloudcapt†, cloudtouching†. elemental, geographical, heterogeneous, youthful, native.
Adverbs: among the islands. by land and sea, from foreign origins, natively.
Phrases: Hellas as the meeting of East and West; a land of islands; wine-dark sea.
Hegel definition: The conditions from which the Greek spirit forms itself: a land broken into peninsulas, islands and small districts linked by the sea, matching the versatility of independent peoples; and a mixture of native and foreign stocks, from which a unity is won through law and custom in place of natural bonds. The result is a spirit that shapes the natural, as the sculptor shapes stone, into its own expression.
Hegel texts:
The Philosophy of History
· The Greek World › The Elements of the Greek Spirit
Hegel citations:
This is the elementary character of the Spirit of the Greeks, implying the origination of their culture from independent individualities;—a condition in which individuals take their own ground, and are not, from the very beginning, patriarchally united by a bond of Nature, but realize a union through some other medium,—through Law and Custom having the sanction of Spirit.
— The Philosophy of History, The Greek World › The Elements of the Greek Spirit (tr. Sibree)
The Greek Spirit is the plastic artist, forming the stone into a work of art. In this formative process the stone does not remain mere stone,—the form being only superinduced from without; but it is made an expression of the Spiritual, even contrary to its nature, and thus transformed.
— The Philosophy of History, The Greek World › The Elements of the Greek Spirit (tr. Sibree)

Hegel definition: The three forms in which beautiful individuality realizes itself, all of them works of art: the culture of the human being, the shaping of the world of gods, and the constitution of the state. In each the natural is only the starting point and material that spirit works into its own expression, the state uniting the subjective and the objective work as a living, self-conscious universal.
Hegel texts:
The Philosophy of History

Hegel citations:
The State unites the two phases just considered, viz., the Subjective and the Objective Work of Art. In the State, Spirit is not a mere Object, like the deities, nor, on the other hand, is it merely subjectively developed to a beautiful physique.
— The Philosophy of History, The Greek World › Phases of Individuality Aesthetically Conditioned (tr. Sibree)
It is here a living, universal Spirit, but which is at the same time the self-conscious Spirit of the individuals composing the community.
— The Philosophy of History, The Greek World › Phases of Individuality Aesthetically Conditioned (tr. Sibree)

The Philosophy of History

[M]an shews his Freedom, viz. that he has transformed his body to an organ of Spirit.
— The Philosophy of History, Phases of Individuality Aesthetically Conditioned › The Subjective Work of Art (tr. Sibree)

Hegel definition: The shaping of the divine world, in which the Greek idea becomes objective as religion. — The Philosophy of History, Phases of Individuality Aesthetically Conditioned › The Objective Work of Art (tr. Sibree)

— The Philosophy of History, Phases of Individuality Aesthetically Conditioned › The Objective Work of Art (tr. Sibree)

The Substance, [the Principle] of Justice, the common weal, the general interest, is the main consideration; but it is so only as Custom, in the form of Objective Will, so that morality properly so called —subjective conviction and intention—has not yet manifested itself.
— The Philosophy of History, Phases of Individuality Aesthetically Conditioned › The Political Work of Art (tr. Sibree)

— The Philosophy of History, The Roman World (tr. Sibree)

Hegel definition: The third period, that of Spirit conscious that it is free in willing what is universal in and for itself. The Reformation establishes that human beings are by their nature destined to freedom; its consequences unfold in states; and the Enlightenment makes the verdict of Spirit itself the criterion of belief and right, until in the French Revolution thought is held to govern spiritual reality.
Hegel texts:
The Philosophy of History
· The German World › The Modern Time
Hegel citations:
This is the essence of the Reformation: Man is in his very nature destined to be free.
— The Philosophy of History, The German World › The Modern Time (tr. Sibree)
This was accordingly a glorious mental dawn. All thinking beings shared in the jubilation of this epoch.
— The Philosophy of History, The German World › The Modern Time (tr. Sibree)

Head: Absolute Spirit
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit
Gloss: The mind's knowledge of the highest truth, in the forms of art, religion and philosophy.
Hegelian gloss: Spirit knowing itself as absolute: art, religion and philosophy.
Nouns: absolute spirit; art, religion, and philosophy, the absolute knowing itself, the highest life of mind, self-knowing spirit, the divine in human knowing, culture in its highest sense, the spiritual realm, the sacred. the absolute mind, spirit knowing itself, the self-knowledge of spirit, art religion and philosophy, the highest sphere, the realm of truth, intuition representation and thought, the divine.

Foreign: Sanskrit: paramātman [supreme self], brahman; Korean: jeoldaejeok jeongsin [absolute spirit].
Phrases: spirit knowing itself as absolute [Hegel]; the true is the whole [Hegel]; the highest things.
Hegel definition: Absolute spirit is mind in which the subjective and objective are one: an identity eternally within itself and returning into itself, the single universal substance as spiritual, and a knowing for which that substance is as such. Its reality is knowledge of the absolute idea, and its sphere, generally called religion, issues from the subject and equally from absolute spirit in its community. It unfolds as art, revealed religion and philosophy.
Hegel texts:
The Philosophy of Mind
· §§553–577
Hegel citations:
The absolute mind is identity, both an identity that is eternally within itself and an identity that returns and has returned into itself: the one and universal substance as spiritual, the judgement discerning itself into itself and an awareness, an awareness for which the substance is as such.
— Encyclopedia §554 (tr. Wallace and Miller, rev. Inwood)
That this reality be knowledge of the absolute Idea and thus in identity with the concept, involves the necessary aspect that the implicitly free intelligence be in its actuality liberated to its concept, in order to be the shape worthy of the concept.
— Encyclopedia §553 (tr. Wallace and Miller, rev. Inwood)

Head: Art
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art

Hegel definition: Art is one way of bringing to mind and expressing the divine, the deepest interests of humanity and the most comprehensive truths of spirit, a task it fulfils only when free in its end and means and placed in the same sphere as religion and philosophy. It presents the absolute in sensuous form. Its beauty, born of the spirit, stands higher than that of nature, though in its highest vocation art is for us a thing of the past.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· Introduction
Hegel citations:
Now, in this its freedom alone is fine art truly art, and it only fulfils its supreme task when it has placed itself in the same sphere as religion and philosophy, and when it is simply one way of bringing to our minds and expressing the Divine, the deepest interests of mankind, and the most comprehensive truths of the spirit.
— Aesthetics, Introduction (tr. Knox)
In all these respects art, considered in its highest vocation, is and remains for us a thing of the past.
— Aesthetics, Introduction (tr. Knox)

Head: The Idea of Artistic Beauty
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › α. The Idea of Artistic Beauty
Gloss: Beauty as the subject of art: what it is, and where it is found.
Hegelian gloss: The beautiful as the idea itself, the concept united with its reality, appearing sensuously.
Nouns: the idea of artistic beauty; the ideal, the concept of beauty, aesthetic idea, the beautiful in art. the idea of the beauty of art, the nature of artistic beauty, the province of aesthetics, where beauty dwells. kalon.
Verbs: idealize, conceive beauty. conceive, determine, locate, embody.
Adjective: ideal, beautiful, aesthetic. in good taste, cute, tasteful, tasty, unaffected, pure, chaste, classical, attic, cultivated, refined, dainty, esthetic, artistic, elegant &c H1074, euphemistic, unlabored†.
Adverbs: ideally, beautifully. aesthetically, artistically, in idea.
Phrases: a thing of beauty is a joy for ever [Keats]; beauty is truth, truth beauty.
Hegel definition: The idea of artistic beauty, or the ideal, treats beauty as no abstraction of the understanding but the inherently concrete absolute concept, the absolute idea appearing in a way adequate to itself. That idea in its genuine actuality is universal, infinite and absolute spirit, which determines out of itself what is truly the true. The inquiry places art among the realms of reality and in relation to religion and philosophy.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· The Idea of Artistic Beauty, or the Ideal
Hegel citations:
For beauty, as was said already [Introduction, 8] and as is to be expounded further later [ch. I, 1(a)] is no such abstraction of the Understanding but the inherently concrete absolute Concept and, more specifically, the absolute Idea in its appearance in a way adequate to itself.
— Aesthetics, The Idea of Artistic Beauty, or the Ideal (tr. Knox)
If we wish to indicate briefly what the absolute Idea is in its genuine actuality, we must say that it is spirit, not, as may be supposed, spirit in its restrictedness and involvement with the finite, but the universal infinite and absolute spirit which out of itself determines what is genuinely the true.
— Aesthetics, The Idea of Artistic Beauty, or the Ideal (tr. Knox)

Head: The Concept of the Beautiful as Such
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › α. The Idea of Artistic Beauty › a. The Concept of the Beautiful as Such
Gloss: The beautiful considered in its general nature.
Hegelian gloss: The beautiful in its concept: the sensuous shining of the idea, free and infinite, which is not to be grasped by the understanding.

Adjective: beautiful, lovely, comely, fair, graceful, elegant, exquisite, sublime, pulchritudinous. beauteous, handsome, gorgeous, pretty, prepossessing, attractive &c H0678, delicate, dainty, refined, personable, seemly, bonny [Scot.], good-looking, well-favored, well-made, well-formed, well- proportioned, proper, shapely, symmetrical &c H0844, harmonious &c H0285, sightly. charming, delightful. rich, superb, magnificent, grand, fine, showy, specious. aesthetic, conceptual, general. bonnie.

Foreign: German: das Schöne, das sinnliche Scheinen der Idee, Schönheit, Geschmack; Latin: pulchritudo, sensus communis [the shared sense of taste] [Kant], gustus; Greek: to kalon, kallos; Sanskrit: rasa [aesthetic flavour]; Japanese: yūgen [profound grace]; French: beauté, sens commun; Italian: bellezza, gusto.
Phrases: beauty is truth, truth beauty [Keats]; the beautiful is the sensuous shining of the idea [Hegel]; beauty is in the eye of the beholder; auxilium non leve vultus habet [Lat.] [Ovid]; beauty born of murmuring sound [Wordsworth]; flowers preach to us if we will hear [C.G. Rossetti]; gratior ac pulchro veniens in corpore virtus [Lat.] [Virgil]; none but the brave deserve the fair [Dryden]; thou who hast the fatal gift of beauty [Byron].
Hegel definition: The beautiful as such is the idea in a determinate form: the unity of concept and reality as it appears to sense. The understanding cannot comprehend it, because it clings to the separation of ideal and real, sensuous and conceptual, objective and subjective, and so stays in the finite. The beautiful is infinite and free: in it the concept ensouls the existence that embodies it and is at home there.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· Concept of the Beautiful as Such
Hegel citations:
For this reason, after all, it is impossible for the Understanding to comprehend beauty, because, instead of penetrating to this unity, the Understanding clings fast to the differences exclusively in their independent separation, by regarding reality as something quite different from ideality, the sensuous as quite different from the Concept, the objective as quite different from the subjective, and thinks that such oppositions cannot be [reconciled and] unified.
— Aesthetics, Concept of the Beautiful as Such (tr. Knox)
The beautiful, on the other hand, is in itself infinite and free.
— Aesthetics, Concept of the Beautiful as Such (tr. Knox)

Head: The Idea
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › α. The Idea of Artistic Beauty › a. The Concept of the Beautiful as Such › i. The Idea
Gloss: Truth understood as the full agreement of a thing with what it ought to be.
Hegelian gloss: The concept that has given itself reality and is one with it: the true, which is the idea.
Nouns: the idea; the idea as truth, concept and reality united, the ideal content, meaning; &c H0203. truth, the concept and its reality, the unity of concept and objectivity, adequacy, correspondence, the true as such, what a thing ought to be.
Verbs: conceive, idealize, embody. agree, correspond, accord, realize, fulfil, be true.
Adjective: ideal, conceptual, true. adequate, concrete, self-accordant.
Adverbs: ideally, in idea. in truth, truly, adequately.
Foreign: German: Gehalt [import]; Latin: idea; Greek: eidos; Arabic: mithāl [ideal form].
Phrases: the idea is the true; true to the idea; as it should be.
Hegel definition: The idea is nothing but the concept, the real existence of the concept and the unity of the two. The concept alone is not yet the idea, which it is only when present in its reality and one with it. This unity is no neutralization in which each loses its qualities, as acid and alkali form a salt: the concept predominates, generating its reality out of itself, and so remains one with itself in its objectivity.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· Concept of the Beautiful as Such › The Idea
Hegel citations:
Now the Idea as such is nothing but the Concept, the real existence of the Concept, and the unity of the two.
— Aesthetics, Concept of the Beautiful as Such › The Idea (tr. Knox)
On the contrary, in this unity the Concept is predominant. For, in accordance with its own nature, it is this identity implicitly already, and therefore generates reality out of itself as its own
— Aesthetics, Concept of the Beautiful as Such › The Idea (tr. Knox)

Head: The Existence of the Idea
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › α. The Idea of Artistic Beauty › a. The Concept of the Beautiful as Such › ii. The Existence of the Idea
Gloss: Truth as it is present in the real world.
Hegelian gloss: The idea in existence, as nature and spirit, its reality in which it shows itself.
Nouns: the existence of the idea; embodiment, incarnation, realization, manifestation, appearance, sensuous existence, the idea made visible. visibility, appearance &c H0418, manifestation &c H0662. the real existence of the idea, the idea as actual, reality, actuality, objectivity, presence, the idea in the world.
Verbs: embody, manifest, realize, appear, show itself. exist, be present, actualize.
Adjective: embodied, manifest, realized, visible, sensuous. existent, actual, real, present, objective.
Adverbs: visibly, in sensuous form. actually, really, in existence, in the world.
Phrases: the idea in the flesh; made real.
Hegel definition: The idea in existence means that everything existent has truth only as an existence of the idea, which alone is genuinely actual. A thing is not true merely because it exists inwardly or outwardly, but because its reality corresponds to the concept. Truth here is not agreement between an object and my representations, but the objective realization of the concept in a self, object, action or situation; otherwise the existent is mere appearance.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· Concept of the Beautiful as Such › The Idea in Existence
Hegel citations:
Everything existent, therefore, has truth only in so far as it is an existence of the Idea. For the Idea is alone the genuinely actual.
— Aesthetics, Concept of the Beautiful as Such › The Idea in Existence (tr. Knox)
And truth not at all in the subjective sense that there is an accordance between some existent and my ideas, but in the objective meaning that the ego or an external object, an action, an event, a situation in its reality is itself a realization of the Concept.
— Aesthetics, Concept of the Beautiful as Such › The Idea in Existence (tr. Knox)

Head: The Idea of the Beautiful
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › α. The Idea of Artistic Beauty › a. The Concept of the Beautiful as Such › iii. The Idea of the Beautiful
Gloss: Truth shining through a sensuous form; beauty.
Hegelian gloss: The idea's sensuous shining: beauty, the true as it is immediately for sense and imagination.
Nouns: the idea of the beautiful; the beautiful as idea appearing, beauty as unity of content and form, the shining of truth, radiance. beauty, the beautiful, le beau ideal. pulchritude, form, elegance, grace, symmetry &c H0844, comeliness. the sensuous shining of the idea, loveliness, fairness, splendour.
Verbs: shine, radiate, appear beautifully. be beautiful, beam, bloom, become one &c H0097, set off. glow, gleam. shine through, appear, beautify.
Adjective: radiant, splendid, beautiful, luminous. brilliant, beamy†, beaming, sparkling, resplendent, dazzling, glowing, glossy, sleek. beauteous, lovely, graceful, elegant, fair, comely. shining, lucid, bright, lustrous. glorious. symmetrical, shapely, well set, finished, beautiful &c H0836, classic, chaste, severe. sensuous.

Foreign: German: Schein [appearance, shine]; Latin: splendor veritatis [the splendour of truth]; Greek: to kalon.
Phrases: beauty is the splendour of truth [attrib. Plato, scholastic]; the beautiful and the true.
Hegel definition: The idea of the beautiful is the idea so far as it is the true present immediately to consciousness in its external existence, the concept remaining in unity with its outward appearance. Beauty and truth are in one way the same, yet the true as grasped in thought is the universal idea, whereas beauty is the pure appearance of the idea to sense, in which the sensuous and objective keep no independence of their own.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· Concept of the Beautiful as Such › The Idea of the Beautiful
Hegel citations:
Now when truth in this its external existence is present to consciousness immediately, and when the Concept remains immediately in unity with its external appearance, the Idea is not only true but beautiful.
— Aesthetics, Concept of the Beautiful as Such › The Idea of the Beautiful (tr. Knox)
Now we said that beauty is Idea, so beauty and truth are in one way the same. Beauty, namely, must be true in itself. But, looked at more closely, the true is nevertheless distinct from the beautiful.
— Aesthetics, Concept of the Beautiful as Such › The Idea of the Beautiful (tr. Knox)

Head: Natural Beauty
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › α. The Idea of Artistic Beauty › b. Natural Beauty
Gloss: Beauty found in nature.
Hegelian gloss: The beauty found in nature, the idea as life, beautiful only for the beholding spirit.
Nouns: natural beauty; beauty of nature, scenery, landscape, the picturesque, the scenic, natural splendour, the beauties of nature. sight, spectacle, scene, view, prospect, vista. beauty unadorned. nature's beauty, the naturally beautiful, the first beauty, natural form, the beauty of the living. sublime.
Verbs: admire, behold, delight in, contemplate. bloom, flourish, appear, shine.
Adjective: scenic, picturesque, natural, lovely, pastoral, idyllic, unspoilt. aesthetic, pictorial. beautiful, fair. charming, delightful, exquisite, lovely &c H0836, ravishing, beatic†. unmade, living.

Hegel definition: Natural beauty is the idea as the immediate unity of the concept with its reality, so far as this unity is present immediately in sensuous, real appearance. The first existence of the idea is nature, and beauty begins as the beauty of nature. Its stages run from soulless mechanical bodies, through systems such as the solar system, to higher forms, and its deficiencies show why the ideal must take the shape of art.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· The Beauty of Nature
Hegel citations:
The beautiful is the Idea as the immediate unity of the Concept with its reality, the Idea, however, only in so far as this its unity is present immediately in sensuous and real appearance.
— Aesthetics, The Beauty of Nature (tr. Knox)
Now the first existence of the Idea is nature, and beauty begins as the beauty of nature.
— Aesthetics, The Beauty of Nature (tr. Knox)

Head: Natural Beauty as Such (the Idea as Life)
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › α. The Idea of Artistic Beauty › b. Natural Beauty › i. Natural Beauty as Such (the Idea as Life)
Gloss: Beauty in nature as the appearance of life.
Hegelian gloss: Natural beauty as the idea in its immediate existence as life, the organism whose members are animated by one soul.
Nouns: natural beauty as such; the idea as life, living beauty, organic beauty, beauty of living things, vitality as beauty, the animal form. the beauty of life, the beauty of the living, animation, vitality, ensoulment, the appearance of the soul.
Verbs: live, animate, flourish. ensoul, enliven, quicken.
Adjective: living, organic, vital, animate, lively. alive, breathing, quick, animated, lively &c H0404. ensouled.
Adverbs: in life, vitally. organically, as living.
Phrases: life as the first beauty; full of life; a living picture.
Hegel definition: Natural beauty as such is the idea in its immediate existence as life. Where the concept sinks wholly into matter, as in a metal, no ideal unity appears; in a system such as the solar system the bodies hang together yet the unity stays implicit; only in the living organism do the distinct members exist as moments of one animating subjective unity. Beauty in nature is this life as it appears to a beholder.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· The Beauty of Nature › Natural Beauty as Such
Hegel citations:
Such a body lacks the complete articulation which it would have if each of its different parts had a particular material existence of its own, nor can it have the negative ideal unity of these parts which would declare itself as their animation.
— Aesthetics, The Beauty of Nature › Natural Beauty as Such (tr. Knox)
This is the Concept's first mode of existence. Its distinctions have no independent existence, and its ideal unity does not emerge as ideal; on this account, then, such separated bodies are in themselves defective and abstract existents.
— Aesthetics, The Beauty of Nature › Natural Beauty as Such (tr. Knox)

Head: External Beauty
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › α. The Idea of Artistic Beauty › b. Natural Beauty › ii. External Beauty
Gloss: Beauty in the outward shape of a natural thing.
Hegelian gloss: The outward beauty of natural shapes, their abstract form and the unity of their sensuous material.
Nouns: external beauty; outward beauty, surface beauty, formal beauty, external form, appearance, shape, outline. figure, conformation, configuration, formation, contour &c H0230. beauty of shape, the beauty of appearance. comeliness, prettiness.
Verbs: shape, form, outline. fashion, model, mold, sculpture. appear, show.
Adjective: external, outward, formal, superficial. exterior, outside. visible, shapely.
Adverbs: outwardly, on the surface. externally, in outward shape.
Phrases: beauty is only skin deep; pretty as a picture.
Hegel definition: External beauty is the beauty of natural reality whose inner side remains indeterminate and abstract instead of attaining the concrete inwardness of soul. Its unity therefore appears as one determining the object from outside, and form and sensuous material fall apart. It is considered first as abstract form, in regularity, symmetry, conformity to law and harmony, and then as the simple unity of the sensuous material, its purity.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· The Beauty of Nature › The External Beauty of the Abstract Form
Hegel citations:
In nature there is an external reality which externally is determined, but its inner being does not get beyond indeterminacy and abstraction instead of attaining concrete inwardness as unity of soul.
— Aesthetics, The Beauty of Nature › The External Beauty of the Abstract Form (tr. Knox)
But such a concrete unity beauty has not attained at this stage, but has this unity as the Ideal still lying ahead of it.
— Aesthetics, The Beauty of Nature › The External Beauty of the Abstract Form (tr. Knox)

Head: Beauty of Abstract Form
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › α. The Idea of Artistic Beauty › b. Natural Beauty › ii. External Beauty › 1. Beauty of Abstract Form
Gloss: Beauty in the formal properties of a thing.
Hegelian gloss: Beauty as the abstract unity of external form: regularity, conformity to law, harmony.
Nouns: beauty of abstract form; formal beauty, abstract form, geometric beauty, pattern, design, order, proportion, measure; geometric pattern, arabesque. beauty of form, regularity, symmetry, conformity to law, harmony, formal unity, the abstract unity of form. formalism.
Verbs: pattern, proportion, order, design. form, regulate.
Adjective: formal, abstract, geometric, ordered, patterned. regular, symmetrical, proportionate.

Foreign: Greek: symmetria; Arabic: tanāsub [proportion]; Persian: girih [geometric ornament].
Phrases: let no one ignorant of geometry enter [attrib. Plato]; neat as a pin; in good order.
Hegel definition: Beauty of abstract form is natural form that is determinate, and so restricted, yet holds a unity and abstract relation to itself. It regulates the external manifold by that determinacy, which never becomes an immanent inwardness or soul that bears the shape, but remains an external determinacy imposed on it. Its kinds are regularity and symmetry, then conformity to law, and finally harmony.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· The Beauty of Nature › The External Beauty of the Abstract Form › Beauty of Abstract Form
Hegel citations:
The form of natural beauty, as an abstract form, is on the one hand determinate and therefore restricted; on the other hand it contains a unity and an abstract relation to itself.
— Aesthetics, The External Beauty of the Abstract Form › Beauty of Abstract Form (tr. Knox)
But, regarded more closely, it regulates the external manifold in accordance with this its determinacy and unity which, however, does not become immanent inwardness and a soul-bearing shape, but remains an external determinacy and a unity imposed on the external.
— Aesthetics, The External Beauty of the Abstract Form › Beauty of Abstract Form (tr. Knox)

Adverbs: symmetrically, regularly, evenly. uniformly.
Foreign: Latin: lucidus ordo; Greek: symmetria, eurhythmia; French: of a piece.
Phrases: Tyger Tyger, burning bright... what immortal hand or eye could frame thy fearful symmetry? [Blake]; in perfect symmetry; like for like; ab uno disce omnes [Lat.].
Hegel definition: Regularity is sameness in something external, the repetition of one and the same shape as the determining unity of objects; being abstract, its beauty is that of the abstract understanding. Symmetry adds unlikeness, connecting a form with another of its kind that differs from it, so that a new and richer unity arises. Both are chiefly determinations of quantity, external to what makes a thing what it is.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· The Beauty of Nature › The External Beauty of the Abstract Form › Beauty of Abstract Form › Regularity and Symmetry
Hegel citations:
Regularity as such is in general sameness in something external and, more precisely, the same repetition of one and the same specific shape which affords the determining unity for the form of objects.
— Aesthetics, Beauty of Abstract Form › Regularity and Symmetry (tr. Knox)
Symmetry is provided only by the uniform connection of characteristics that are unlike one another.
— Aesthetics, Beauty of Abstract Form › Regularity and Symmetry (tr. Knox)

Head: Conformity to Law
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › α. The Idea of Artistic Beauty › b. Natural Beauty › ii. External Beauty › 1. Beauty of Abstract Form › b. Conformity to Law
Gloss: The order of a thing according to a rule.
Hegelian gloss: A unity of differences that is no longer mere equality, as the curves of the egg and the ellipse.
Nouns: conformity to law; lawfulness, lawful form, regularity of a higher kind, ordered variation, the curve, the oval, the golden section, the line of beauty [Hogarth], the serpentine line. lawlikeness, regularity, rule, order, orderliness, the parabola, the undulating line.
Verbs: conform, follow a law, vary lawfully. conform to, conform to rule, accommodate oneself to, adapt oneself to, rub off corners. obey, follow a rule, regulate.
Adjective: lawful, ordered, regular, curvilinear, serpentine. conformable to rule, regular &c H0232, according to regulation. steady, constant. uniform, homogeneous, homologous, consistent, connatural†, monotonous, even, invariable, unchanged, undeviating, unvaried, unvarying. balanced. lawlike, orderly, rule-governed.
Adverbs: lawfully, according to rule. conformably, by rule, in conformity with, in accordance with, in keeping with, consistently with. regularly, in order.
Foreign: Latin: sectio aurea; French: en regle, of a piece.
Phrases: the line of beauty [Hogarth]; as regular as clockwork.
Hegel definition: Conformity to law stands above regularity and is the transition to the freedom of life, natural and spiritual, though it is not yet free subjective unity. It is a totality of essential differences that display unity and connection, admitting qualitative relations rather than mere calculable differences of size. The ellipse, and more freely the oval, show a law binding aspects that are essentially different, a secret bond the viewer only half grasps.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· The Beauty of Nature › The External Beauty of the Abstract Form › Beauty of Abstract Form › Conformity to Law
Hegel citations:
Yet, regarded by itself, conformity to law is certainly not the subjective total unity and freedom itself, though it is already a totality of essential differences
— Aesthetics, Beauty of Abstract Form › Conformity to Law (tr. Knox)
Yet once again the connection remains as a secret bond which for the spectator is partly something to which he is accustomed, partly the foreshadowing of something deeper.
— Aesthetics, Beauty of Abstract Form › Conformity to Law (tr. Knox)

Head: Harmony
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › α. The Idea of Artistic Beauty › b. Natural Beauty › ii. External Beauty › 1. Beauty of Abstract Form › c. Harmony
Gloss: The agreement of different parts in a whole.
Hegelian gloss: The unity of qualitatively different elements that belong together, as of colours and tones.
Nouns: harmony; concord, accord, consonance, euphony, attunement, agreement, unity in variety, balance, coherence, proportion. emmeleia†, unison, unisonance†, homophony, euphonism†, tonality, consent, part. concord &c H0535, concert, understanding, mutual understanding. symphony, unity. consistency, accordance, conformity &c H0073, connaturality†, connaturalness†. harmony &c H0535, accord &c H0802. concordance, agreement &c H0097. congruity, concinnity, consentaneousness†.
Verbs: harmonize, attune, accord, blend, reconcile, chime. adjust &c H0054. symphonize†, tune. agree, correspond, tally, chime in with. consort.
Adjective: harmonious, concordant, consonant, euphonious, balanced, attuned. harmonical†, in concord, unisonant†, concentual†, symphonizing†, isotonic, homophonous†, assonant, ariose†. agreeing, accordant, congruous, correspondent, coherent, consentaneous†. in accord, united. proportionate.
Adverbs: harmoniously, in harmony, in concert, in tune. in keeping.
Foreign: Latin: concordia discors [discordant concord]; Greek: harmonia; Japanese: wa [harmony]; Chinese: he er bu tong [harmony without uniformity] [Analects].
Phrases: the hidden harmony is better than the obvious [Heraclitus]; concordia discors [Lat.] [Horace]; in harmony with; all of a piece; rem acu tetigisti [Lat.]; if the shoe fits, wear it; the cap fits; auxilia humilia firma consensus facit [Lat.] [Syrus]; discers concordia [Lat.] [Ovid].
Hegel definition: Harmony stands higher than conformity to law: a relation of qualitative differences, a totality of them grounded in the nature of the thing, brought into a congruous unity in which their bare opposition is dissolved, as with the basic colours or the tonic, mediant and dominant. It is the highest stage of abstract form and approaches free subjectivity, yet is not yet soul.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· The Beauty of Nature › The External Beauty of the Abstract Form › Beauty of Abstract Form › Harmony
Hegel citations:
Therefore at this stage harmony stands higher than mere conformity to law, i.e. harmony is a relation of qualitative differences, and indeed of a totality of such differences, a totality grounded in the essence of the thing itself.
— Aesthetics, Beauty of Abstract Form › Harmony (tr. Knox)
Mere harmony does not in general manifest either subjective animation as such or spirituality, although it is the highest stage of abstract form and already approaches free subjectivity.
— Aesthetics, Beauty of Abstract Form › Harmony (tr. Knox)

Head: Beauty as Abstract Unity of Sensuous Material (Purity)
Head (German): Die Schönheit als abstrakte Einheit des sinnlichen Materials
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › α. The Idea of Artistic Beauty › b. Natural Beauty › ii. External Beauty › 2. Beauty as Abstract Unity of Sensuous Material (Purity)
Gloss: Beauty in the purity and simplicity of a material, such as a clear tone or an unmixed color.
Hegelian gloss: The beauty of a pure and simple material, a clear sky, a pure tone or colour, abstract sensuous unity.
Nouns: beauty as abstract unity of sensuous material; purity, pure colour, pure tone, clarity, limpidity, clearness, the clear sky, the pure note. transparency, lucidity, pellucidity†. pureness, simplicity, unmixedness, homogeneity, uniformity.
Verbs: purify, clarify, refine. purify &c H0759. be simple. render simple, simplify, uncomplicate.
Adjective: pure, clear, limpid, unmixed, pellucid, crystalline, immaculate. transparent, lucid, clear as crystal. clean, spotless, stainless, untainted. unadorned, bare, unornamented, undecked†, ungarnished, unarranged†, untrimmed, unvarnished. chaste, inornate†, severe. unaffected, ingenuous, sincere &c H0731, free from affectation, free from ornament. simple, plain, homely, homespun, ordinary, household, unornamental†, unbeauteous†, beautiless†. unalloyed, homogeneous. uncut.
Adverbs: purely, clearly. simply.
Foreign: German: Reinheit; Latin: simplex munditiis [Horace]; French: sans facon, en deshabille.
Phrases: clear as crystal; clear as day; veritatis simplex oratio est [Lat.].
Hegel definition: Beauty as abstract unity of the sensuous material concerns not shape but the stuff perceived, whose only unity is undifferentiated concord, purity of shape, colour or tone. Smooth surfaces, a clear sky, a mirror-like lake, a pure voice and unmixed colours please by their homogeneity. Like abstract form, this purity is lifeless and affords no truly actual unity, which requires ideal subjectivity.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· The Beauty of Nature › The External Beauty of the Abstract Form › Beauty as Abstract Unity of the Sensuous Material
Hegel citations:
In this connection the abstract purity of the stuff, in shape, colour, note, etc., is the essential thing at this stage.
— Aesthetics, The External Beauty of the Abstract Form › Beauty as Abstract Unity of the Sensuous Material (tr. Knox)
The purity of the sky, the clarity of the air, a mirror-like lake, smooth seas, delight us from this point of view.
— Aesthetics, The External Beauty of the Abstract Form › Beauty as Abstract Unity of the Sensuous Material (tr. Knox)

Head: Deficiency of Natural Beauty
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › α. The Idea of Artistic Beauty › b. Natural Beauty › iii. Deficiency of Natural Beauty
Gloss: The shortcoming of natural beauty as an expression of the mind.
Hegelian gloss: The defect of natural beauty: the living thing does not show its inner soul as free individuality; this deficiency requires art.
Nouns: deficiency of natural beauty; limitation of nature, imperfection of the natural, contingency, the dependence of natural beauty, the need for art, nature's shortfall. stain, blot, blur. blemish, disfigurement, deformity, adactylism†, flaw, defect &c H0018, injury &c H0803, spots on the sun†, eyesore, acomia†, inconcinnity†. imperfection, shortcoming, inadequacy, want, insufficiency, limitation, finitude, dependence.
Verbs: fall short, lack, fail. fall short &c H0026. disfigure &c H0803, speckle, bespeckle†. be wanting.
Adjective: deficient, imperfect, contingent, limited, wanting. incomplete, imperfect &c H0018, defective, marescent†. insufficient, inadequate, deficient &c H0130. faulty, crude &c H0206. pitted, freckled, discolored, blobber-lipped, bloodshot, injured &c H0803. foul &c H0759, dingy &c H0285, gaudy &c H0285, disfigured. frightful, hideous, odious, uncanny, forbidding, repellant, repulsive, repugnant, grotesque, bizarre, horrid, horrible, shocking &c H0672. finite. lacking, horrific, horrifying, depleted.
Adverbs: deficiently, imperfectly. inadequately.
Phrases: die Kunstschönheit ist die aus dem Geiste geborene und wiedergeborene Schönheit [Ger.] [Hegel, Aesthetics, Introduction]; nature is not enough; flawed beauty; surgit amari aliquid [Lat.].
Hegel definition: The deficiency of natural beauty explains why the ideal is necessary. The idea is not only substance but concept united with reality, and acquires actuality only through subjectivity that corresponds to the concept; only concrete individuality is true. Natural existence, even animal life, cannot show this inwardness as free, self-transparent individuality, so the imperfection of nature leads to the beauty of art as the one reality adequate to the idea.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· The Beauty of Nature › Deficiency of Natural Beauty
Hegel citations:
Our topic proper is the beauty of art as the one reality adequate to the Idea of beauty.
— Aesthetics, The Beauty of Nature › Deficiency of Natural Beauty (tr. Knox)
We must therefore pose our question thus: why is nature necessarily imperfect in its beauty, and what is the origin of this imperfection?
— Aesthetics, The Beauty of Nature › Deficiency of Natural Beauty (tr. Knox)

Head: The Beauty of Art, or the Ideal
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › α. The Idea of Artistic Beauty › c. The Beauty of Art, or the Ideal
Gloss: Beauty as made by art; the ideal: a thing shown as it ought to be, free of the flaws of nature.
Hegelian gloss: The beauty of art, the ideal: the idea brought into a shape that fits it, freed from the contingencies of nature.
Nouns: the beauty of art; the ideal, artistic beauty, the idealized, perfected form, art's beauty, the ideal type. model, pattern, archetype, exemplar, paradigm. the beautiful in art, the art-beautiful, beauty born of spirit, beauty as it ought to be, idealization.
Verbs: idealize, perfect, ennoble, transfigure. beautify, refine.
Adjective: ideal, idealized, perfected, artistic, transfigured. flawless, spirit-born.
Adverbs: ideally, in the ideal. in art, as it ought to be.
Foreign: German: das Ideal.
Phrases: the ideal is the idea as art; the ideal of beauty; perfect in every way.
Hegel definition: The beauty of art, the ideal, is beauty in which the true unfolds into external reality yet holds its separate parts in unity, so that every one of them lets the soul, the whole, appear. Art has to turn every point of its visible surface into an eye in which spirit is seen. It is considered as the ideal as such, as the ideal's determinacy in the work, and as the creative subjectivity of the artist.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· The Beauty of Art or the Ideal
Hegel citations:
Now as the pulsating heart shows itself all over the surface of the human, in contrast to the animal, body, so in the same sense it is to be asserted of art that it has to convert every shape in all points of its visible surface into an eye, which is the seat of the soul and brings the spirit into appearance.
— Aesthetics, The Beauty of Art or the Ideal (tr. Knox)
In relation to the beauty of art we have three chief aspects to consider: First, the Ideal as such Secondly, the work of art as the determinateness of the Ideal Thirdly, the creative subjectivity of the artist.
— Aesthetics, The Beauty of Art or the Ideal (tr. Knox)

Head: The Ideal as Such
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › α. The Idea of Artistic Beauty › c. The Beauty of Art, or the Ideal › i. The Ideal as Such
Gloss: Beauty perfected: a form purged of accident and flaw, in which its inner meaning shows completely; perfection, the ideal.
Hegelian gloss: Beautiful individuality, the ideal as the spirit's free, self-enclosed shape, serene in its blessedness.
Nouns: the ideal as such; ideal serenity, blissful calm, repose, tranquillity, self-sufficiency, the blessed gods, untroubled grace. pink, beau ideal, phenix, paragon, pink of perfection, acme of perfection, summit &c H0230, summity†. perfect beauty, perfection, the ideal, ideality, purification, flawlessness, the purged form, beau idéal, transfiguration.
Verbs: repose, rest serene. idealize, perfect, purify, purge, refine, transfigure.
Adjective: serene, blissful, tranquil, self-sufficient, untroubled. peaceful, halcyon. placid. calm, unruffled. ideal, flawless, pure, purified, consummate, unblemished.
Adverbs: serenely. ideally, perfectly, flawlessly, purely. cleanly.
Foreign: German: Heiterkeit [cheerfulness, serenity]; Latin: ne plus ultra.
Phrases: life is earnest, art is serene, ernst ist das Leben, heiter ist die Kunst [Ger.] [Schiller]; serene and self-contained; the picture of perfection; let us go on unto perfection [Hebrews vi, 1]; the perfection of art is to conceal art [Quintilian].
Hegel definition: The ideal as such is beautiful individuality, gathered into itself as total subjective unity and independence out of the divisions of finite life. Among its basic characteristics are serene peace and bliss, self-enjoyment in its own achievement: the ideal work confronts us like a blessed god. This serenity is no easy contentment but the triumph of concrete freedom, kept even in the seriousness of grief.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· The Beauty of Art or the Ideal › The Ideal as Such
Hegel citations:
In this respect, amongst the fundamental characteristics of the Ideal we may put at the top this serene peace and bliss, this self-enjoyment in its own achievedness and satisfaction. The ideal work of art confronts us like a blessed god.
— Aesthetics, The Beauty of Art or the Ideal › The Ideal as Such (tr. Knox)
This force of individuality, this triumph of concrete freedom concentrated in itself, is what we recognize especially in the works of art of antiquity in the cheerful and serene peace of their shapes.
— Aesthetics, The Beauty of Art or the Ideal › The Ideal as Such (tr. Knox)

Head: The Determinacy of the Ideal
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › α. The Idea of Artistic Beauty › c. The Beauty of Art, or the Ideal › ii. The Determinacy of the Ideal
Gloss: The ideal given definite content, in particular figures, characters and actions.
Hegelian gloss: The ideal drawn into particular determinacy, entering into difference, situation and action.
Nouns: the determinacy of the ideal; particularization, specification, the ideal made definite, concreteness. description, character. determinateness, definiteness, individuation, the determinate ideal, differentiation.
Verbs: specify, particularize, concretize. individualize, realize, specialize, designate, determine. define.
Adjective: determinate, particular, concrete, definite. special, individual, specific, especial. clear, unequivocal, categorical, decided. exact, precise, well-defined.
Adverbs: concretely. determinately, definitely, in particular.
Phrases: the ideal in particular form; given form.
Hegel definition: The determinacy of the ideal arises because artistic beauty, as idea, cannot stop at its universal concept but must go out into particularity, externality and finitude, and still maintain itself there. This determinacy is considered first as such; then as it develops into difference and its resolution, which is action; and finally in its external setting.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· The Beauty of Art or the Ideal › The Determinacy of the Ideal
Hegel citations:
But the beauty of art, by being Idea, cannot stop at its purely general Concept; even in virtue of this Concept it has determinacy and particularity in itself and therefore must advance out of itself into actual determinacy.
— Aesthetics, The Beauty of Art or the Ideal › The Determinacy of the Ideal (tr. Knox)
Consequently, from this point of view, the question arises in what way, despite exit into externality and finitude and therefore the non-Ideal, the Ideal can still maintain itself, and, conversely, in what way finite existence can assume the Ideality of artistic beauty.
— Aesthetics, The Beauty of Art or the Ideal › The Determinacy of the Ideal (tr. Knox)

Head: Ideal Determinacy as Such
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › α. The Idea of Artistic Beauty › c. The Beauty of Art, or the Ideal › ii. The Determinacy of the Ideal › 1. Ideal Determinacy as Such
Gloss: The ideal made definite without losing its calm, as in a serene divine figure at rest.
Hegelian gloss: The ideal in its determinacy, as the divine shown at rest, eternal power in individual shape.
Nouns: ideal determinacy as such; the divine as unity, the gods made definite, individualized divinity. ideal determinacy, the determinate ideal at rest, divine repose, the blessed calm, serenity, self-repose, the god at rest, untroubled unity.
Verbs: individualize, define. repose, rest, abide, remain calm, dwell.
Adjective: divine, individual, definite. serene, calm, reposeful, untroubled, blessed, at rest, tranquil.
Adverbs: definitely. serenely, calmly, in repose.
Phrases: the divine in definite form; calm and composed; at rest in itself.
Hegel definition: Ideal determinacy as such is the divine, which art above all must make the centre of its representations, made determinate. Pure unity can only be thought, but as determinate the divine splits into many self-reposing gods, appears as an actual human being, and lives in the senses and hearts of saints and martyrs. Thereby the whole human heart, every deep interest of the soul, becomes the living stuff of art.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· The Beauty of Art or the Ideal › The Determinacy of the Ideal › Ideal Determinacy as Such
Hegel citations:
We have seen already [in the Introduction, 8(iii)] that art has above all to make the Divine the centre of its representations.
— Aesthetics, The Determinacy of the Ideal › Ideal Determinacy as Such (tr. Knox)
For the whole human heart with everything whereby it is moved in its innermost being, everything which is powerful in it-every feeling and passion, every deeper interest in the soul-this concrete life forms the living stuff of art, and the Ideal is its representation and expression.
— Aesthetics, The Determinacy of the Ideal › Ideal Determinacy as Such (tr. Knox)

Head: Action
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › α. The Idea of Artistic Beauty › c. The Beauty of Art, or the Ideal › ii. The Determinacy of the Ideal › 2. Action
Gloss: The ideal shown as action, through conflict and its resolution.
Hegelian gloss: The ideal moving into action, through a world-situation, a situation, and the collision of powers.
Nouns: action; dramatic action, plot, story, narrative, deed, event, fable, conflict, collision. encounter. history, tale, adventures, fortunes, historiette†, ana†. proceeding, measure, step, move, stroke, coup. doing, opposition, reaction, resolution, drama. praxis.
Verbs: act, plot, unfold, develop, collide. evolve, unroll, unravel, disentangle. do, resolve, strive.
Adjective: dramatic, narrative, eventful, active. conflictual, resolved.
Adverbs: dramatically, in action. in conflict, through conflict.
Foreign: German: Kollision; Greek: mythos; French: agent, agence, agir, pratique; Italian: prassi.
Phrases: plot is the soul of tragedy [Aristotle]; actions speak louder than words; the plot thickens.
Hegel definition: Action is the ideal moved out of the inactive repose of bliss into development, which involves one-sidedness, separation and opposition, so that even the gods must struggle and submit to fate. Greatness and force are measured by the opposition out of which spirit brings itself back to unity. Action requires a general state of the world, a determinate situation that brings strain into it, and the subject's response.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· The Beauty of Art or the Ideal › The Determinacy of the Ideal › Action
Hegel citations:
For greatness and force are truly measured only by the greatness and force of the opposition out of which the spirit brings itself back to unity with itself again.
— Aesthetics, The Determinacy of the Ideal › Action (tr. Knox)
In this development alone is preserved the might of the Idea and the Ideal, for might consists only in maintaining oneself within the negative of oneself.
— Aesthetics, The Determinacy of the Ideal › Action (tr. Knox)

Head: The General World-Situation
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › α. The Idea of Artistic Beauty › c. The Beauty of Art, or the Ideal › ii. The Determinacy of the Ideal › 2. Action › a. The General World-Situation
Gloss: The general state of the world in which action takes place.
Hegelian gloss: The general state of the world, the heroic age in which the individual is the bearer of right and custom.
