Nouns: the general world-situation; the world-state, background, setting, epoch, milieu, the age of heroes, heroic age, the prosaic modern world. the state of the world, the general condition, the world-condition, individual independence, the prose of the present, the age, the times.
Verbs: set, situate, frame. condition, underlie, ground, prevail.
Adjective: heroic, prosaic, epochal, general. universal, prevailing.
Adverbs: in the age of heroes. in general, in the state of the world, at large.
Foreign: German: Heroenzeit.
Phrases: the heroic age; in those days.
Hegel definition: The general state of the world is the way in which the substantial element of spiritual reality, ethics, law and justice, holds together its manifestations and provides the ground on which individuals act. For the ideal it must take the form of independence, in which universal and individual are not yet torn apart, such as the heroic age, whose figures are themselves the bearers of right and custom.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· The Beauty of Art or the Ideal › The Determinacy of the Ideal › Action › The General State of the World
Hegel citations:
When we speak in this connection of the 'state' of something, we understand by it the general way and manner in which the substantial element is present which, as the truly essential element within spiritual actuality, holds together all its manifestations.
— Aesthetics, Action › The General State of the World (tr. Knox)
At the stage we have now reached we will bring out this characteristic as independence, and require [for artistic representation] that the general state of the world shall appear in the form of independence so as to be able to assume the shape of the Ideal.
— Aesthetics, Action › The General State of the World (tr. Knox)

Head: The Situation
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › α. The Idea of Artistic Beauty › c. The Beauty of Art, or the Ideal › ii. The Determinacy of the Ideal › 2. Action › b. The Situation
Gloss: The particular circumstances that call for action.
Hegelian gloss: The situation which, by a collision, provokes the action.
Nouns: the situation; circumstance, setting, occasion, predicament, scene, juncture, complication, collision, conflict. circumstances, state of affairs, posture of affairs, the situationless, the determinate situation.
Verbs: situate, place, complicate, complexify†. prompt, call forth, give rise to.
Adjective: situational, circumstantial, conflicted. occasional, particular, determinate.
Adverbs: circumstantially. in the circumstances, in the situation, as occasion arises.
Foreign: Latin: in situ.
Phrases: the situation calls for action; to set the scene.
Hegel definition: The situation is the particular state of affairs that opens the general condition of the world into collisions and complications, giving individuals the chance to show what they are in a determinate shape. The general state of the world is still unmoved and only the possibility of individual configuration; art must go beyond it to pictures of definite characters and actions, where the universal powers still hold sway.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· The Beauty of Art or the Ideal › The Determinacy of the Ideal › Action › The Situation
Hegel citations:
So far as individuals are concerned, the general situation is therefore indeed the stage presented to them, but it opens out into specialized situations, and, with this particularization, into collisions and complications which give the individuals opportunities to show what they are and display themselves as possessed of a determinate shape.
— Aesthetics, Action › The Situation (tr. Knox)
In this connection, art has thus not at all to sketch only a universal world situation but has to proceed out of this vague idea to pictures of definite characters and actions.
— Aesthetics, Action › The Situation (tr. Knox)

Head: Action Proper (Universal Powers, Individuals, Character)
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › α. The Idea of Artistic Beauty › c. The Beauty of Art, or the Ideal › ii. The Determinacy of the Ideal › 2. Action › c. Action Proper (Universal Powers, Individuals, Character)
Gloss: The action itself, with the moral powers at stake, the agents and their character.
Hegelian gloss: Action proper: the universal ethical powers, the individuals who act, and their character, pathos.
Nouns: action proper; universal powers, individuals, character; ethical powers, the gods as motives, character, hero, protagonist, antagonist. the deed, the acting individuals, the agent, reaction. ethos.
Verbs: act, characterize, impel, move, embody. do, will, carry out, react, resolve.
Adjective: characterful, pathetic [in the old sense], heroic, motivated. active, ethical, individual.
Adverbs: in character. in action, in deed, actively.
Foreign: German: Charakter; Latin: dramatis personae; Greek: pathos [the moving power of the soul], ēthos.
Phrases: character is destiny, ēthos anthrōpōi daimōn [Gr.] [Heraclitus]; a clash of powers; true to character.
Hegel definition: Action proper is the third stage after the state of the world and the situation, presupposing circumstances that lead to collisions, to action and reaction. Art does not begin with the external first origin of an action but takes the listener into the midst of things, since a person's proper nature, the true core of their capacity, is revealed in a single great situation and action. It treats the universal powers, the individuals and their character.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· The Beauty of Art or the Ideal › The Determinacy of the Ideal › Action › Action
Hegel citations:
We have found already that, in its external relation to the situation, the action presupposes circumstances leading to collisions, to action and reaction.
— Aesthetics, Action › Action (tr. Knox)
The totality of the circumstances of life, deeds, fates, is of course what shapes the individual, but his proper nature, the true kernel of his disposition and capacity, is revealed without all these, in one great situation and action
— Aesthetics, Action › Action (tr. Knox)

Head: External Determinacy of the Ideal
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › α. The Idea of Artistic Beauty › c. The Beauty of Art, or the Ideal › ii. The Determinacy of the Ideal › 3. External Determinacy of the Ideal
Gloss: The outward conditions of the ideal: setting, surroundings and audience.
Hegelian gloss: The ideal's external determinacy, its outer setting in nature and the human world.
Nouns: external determinacy of the ideal; setting, environment, costume, local colour, decor, the external world of the work, historical detail. pattern, diaper, powdering, paneling, graining, pargeting†, detail, repousse &c H0277, texture &c H0268, richness, tracery, molding, fillet, listel†, strapwork†, flourish, arabesque, fret, anthemion†, egg and tongue, egg and dart, astragal†, zigzag, acanthus, cartouche, pilaster &c H0277, beading, cloisonne ware, frost work, Morisco, tooling. fleuron†, flowers of rhetoric &c H1074, work of art. external surroundings, milieu, locale, backdrop, the public. modeling.
Verbs: set, costume, furnish, localize. equip, dress, array. garnish, trim, dizen†, bedizen, prink†, prank, trick out, fig out, deck, bedeck, dight†, bedight†, begawd†, titivate†, dress up, spangle, bespangle, powder, embroider, work, chase, emboss, emblazon, illuminate, illustrate, betrim†. smarten, furbish, polish, gild, varnish, whitewash, enamel, japan, lacquer, paint, grain, lacker†, parget†. ornament, embellish, enrich, decorate, adorn, bead, beautify, adonize†. surround, environ, situate, stage.
Adjective: external, local, historical, scenic. ornamental, decorative, becoming &c H0097. showy, flashy, gaudy &c H0835, garish, gairish†, gorgeous. in full dress &c H0595, dressed to kill, dressed to the nines, dressed to advantage, in Sunday best, in best bib and tucker. smart, gay, trickly†, flowery, glittering, new gilt, new spangled, fine as a Mayday queen, fine as a fivepence†, fine as a carrot fresh scraped, pranked out, well-groomed. ornamented, beautified, ornate, rich, gilt, begilt†, tesselated, festooned, cloisonne, topiary, punctated†, sesquipedal†. environmental, circumstantial.
Adverbs: in setting. outwardly, in its setting, externally.
Foreign: Latin: Moresque; French: coquillage, fleur-de-lis, champleve ware, head piece, tail piece, cul-de-lampe, en grand tenue, en grande toilette, endimanche, champleve.
Phrases: local colour; the setting of the scene; honores mutant mores [Lat.].
Hegel definition: The external determinacy of the ideal is the outer reality into which it passes through action. A human being has a surrounding world, as a god's statue has a temple: nature, with its place, time and climate; the use made of it in tools, housing and comforts; and the concrete world of family, possession, worship, war and political life. Art must configure this prose of life in a way fit for it, not cut itself off from it.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· The Beauty of Art or the Ideal › The Determinacy of the Ideal › The External Determinacy of the Ideal
Hegel citations:
To man's actual existence there belongs a surrounding world, just as the statues of a god have a temple.
— Aesthetics, The Determinacy of the Ideal › The External Determinacy of the Ideal (tr. Knox)
In all these respects, the Ideal immediately encroaches on ordinary external reality, on the daily life of the actual world, and therefore on the common prose of life.
— Aesthetics, The Determinacy of the Ideal › The External Determinacy of the Ideal (tr. Knox)

Head: The Artist
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › α. The Idea of Artistic Beauty › c. The Beauty of Art, or the Ideal › iii. The Artist
Gloss: The maker of the work of art.
Hegelian gloss: The artist, whose productive activity gives the content its shape.
Nouns: the artist; artisan, maker, creator, poet, master, virtuoso, genius, craftsman, painter, sculptor, composer. artist, limner, drawer, sketcher, designer, engraver, old master, draftsman, draughtsman, copyist, dauber, hack, enamel, enameler, enamelist, caricaturist. historical painter, landscape painter, marine painter, flower painter, portrait painter, miniature painter, miniaturist, scene painter, sign painter, coach painter, Apelles†, carver, chaser, modeler, figuriste†, statuary, Phidias, Praxiteles, Royal Academician. workman, handicraftsman. originator, inventor, author, maker &c H0768. photographer, cinematographer, lensman, cameraman, camera technician, camera buff, wildlife photographer. artificer, the creative subject.
Verbs: create, make, compose, craft, paint, sculpt. produce, fashion, originate.
Adjective: artistic, creative, masterly, virtuosic, inspired. productive, gifted.
Adverbs: artistically, masterfully. creatively, with mastery.
Foreign: Latin: artifex; Greek: poiētēs; German: Künstlerroman.
Phrases: an artist at heart; the artist's touch; photo safari; with gun and camera 1.
Hegel definition: The artist is the subjective productive activity from which the work of art springs, the work being there for the contemplation and feeling of others. This activity, the artist's imagination, permits only a few generalities, since there is no recipe for creation. It is treated as genius and inspiration, as the objectivity of creative activity, and as true originality.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· The Beauty of Art or the Ideal › The Artist
Hegel citations:
But since the work of art springs from the spirit, it needs a subjective productive activity as its cause, and as a product thereof it is there for others, i.e. for the contemplation and feeling of the public.
— Aesthetics, The Beauty of Art or the Ideal › The Artist (tr. Knox)
We might just as well ask for a recipe or prescription for managing this, or for the circumstances and situations in which a man must place himself in order to produce the like.
— Aesthetics, The Beauty of Art or the Ideal › The Artist (tr. Knox)

Head: Inspiration
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › α. The Idea of Artistic Beauty › c. The Beauty of Art, or the Ideal › iii. The Artist › 1. Inspiration
Gloss: The artist's creative power, natural gift and inspired mood.
Hegelian gloss: Imagination, the artist's power to grasp and shape; genius, the natural gift; inspiration, absorption in the subject.
Nouns: inspiration; soul. ingenuity.
Verbs: imagine, invent, create, conceive. originate, devise, coin, fabricate.
Adjective: visionary, imaginative. inventive &c H0656. original, inventive, creative, fertile. visionary &c H0656.
Foreign: German: geist, Naturell, natürlich Fähigkeit, Witz; Latin: ingenium, afflatus, furor poeticus, genus, talentum; Greek: entheos, euphyia, talanton; Arabic: ilhām [inspiration], ḥads; Sanskrit: pratibhā [genius, flash]; Spanish: duende [dark inspiration] [Lorca], ingenio, talante; French: bel esprit, génie; Italian: ingegno, talento.
Hegel definition: Imagination, genius and inspiration make up the artist's creative activity. Imagination, unlike passive fancy, is creative: it grasps reality and gives its rationality concrete shape. Genius is the general ability, and energy, to produce a true work of art, including a natural element; inspiration is that activity as the artist's state, being wholly filled with the theme and not resting until it has received artistic form.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· The Beauty of Art or the Ideal › The Artist › Imagination (Phantasie), Genius, and Inspiration
Hegel citations:
Now this productive activity of imagination whereby the artist takes what is absolutely rational in itself and works it out, as his very own creation, by giving it an external form, is what is called genius, talent, etc.
— Aesthetics, The Artist › Imagination (Phantasie), Genius, and Inspiration (tr. Knox)
For the task of imagination consists solely in giving us a consciousness of that inner rationality, not in the form of general propositions and ideas, but in concrete configuration and individual reality.
— Aesthetics, The Artist › Imagination (Phantasie), Genius, and Inspiration (tr. Knox)

Head: Fancy
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › α. The Idea of Artistic Beauty › c. The Beauty of Art, or the Ideal › iii. The Artist › 1. Inspiration › a. Fancy
Gloss: The artist's power to grasp the actual world and give an inner content an outward, concrete shape.
Hegelian gloss: Phantasie, productive imagination as opposed to passive fancy: it grasps reality and gives its rational content a consciousness of itself not in general thoughts but in concrete, individual shape.
Nouns: fancy; Phantasie, productive imagination, creative imagination, image-making, the shaping power, the inward eye. phantasy, creative power. idealist, romanticist, romancer, dreamer, rhapsodist &c H0455, fanciful projector.
Verbs: fancy, idealize, realize, dream, dream of, dream up, give to airy nothing a local habitation and a name.
Adjective: imaginary, fanciful, imagining.
Adverbs: imaginatively.
Phrases: aus der Leichtfertigkeit der Phantasie geht kein gediegenes Werk hervor [Ger.] [Hegel, Aesthetics].
Hegel definition: Fancy, in Knox's rendering of Phantasie, is the most prominent artistic ability and must not be confused with the merely passive imagination, for it is creative. It does not stop at assimilating outer and inner reality but brings to outward appearance the truth and rationality of the actual world, not in general propositions and ideas but in concrete configuration and individual reality.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· The Beauty of Art or the Ideal › The Artist › Imagination (Phantasie), Genius, and Inspiration
Hegel citations:
Yet in that case we must immediately take care not to confuse fancy with the purely passive imagination (Einbildungskraft). Fancy is creative.
— Aesthetics, The Artist › Imagination (Phantasie), Genius, and Inspiration (tr. Knox)
But secondly imagination does not stop at this mere assimilation of external and internal reality, because what the ideal work of art properly provides is not only the appearance of the inner spirit in the reality of external forms; on the contrary, it is the absolute truth and rationality of the actual world which should attain external appearance.
— Aesthetics, The Artist › Imagination (Phantasie), Genius, and Inspiration (tr. Knox)

Head: Observation
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › α. The Idea of Artistic Beauty › c. The Beauty of Art, or the Ideal › iii. The Artist › 1. Inspiration › a. Fancy › i. Observation
Gloss: The artist's gift for seeing the shapes of the world and keeping them in memory.
Hegelian gloss: The first side of Phantasie: the gift and sense for grasping actuality, which sees much, attends closely and holds the many images of the world in a retentive memory.
Nouns: observation; perception, a keen eye, an eye for detail, attentiveness, noticing, the observing eye, retentive memory, a store of images, knowledge of the world, study from life, life study, sketchbook, field notes.
Verbs: observe, notice, take in, study, watch, sketch from life, take notes.
Adjective: observant, perceptive, keen-eyed, sharp-eyed, attentive, watchful.
Adverbs: observantly, from life.
Hegel definition: Observation is the first requirement of the artist: the gift and sense for grasping actual reality and its shapes, attentively heard and seen, together with a retentive memory of them. The artist creates from the abundance of life, not of abstract generalities, and so must have seen, heard and retained much, knowing both outward forms and the passions and aims of the human soul.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· The Beauty of Art or the Ideal › The Artist › Imagination (Phantasie), Genius, and Inspiration
Hegel citations:
To embark on art and poetry with an ideal is always very suspect, for the artist has to create out of the abundance of life and not out of the abundance of abstract generalities
— Aesthetics, The Artist › Imagination (Phantasie), Genius, and Inspiration (tr. Knox)
This gift and this interest in a specific grasp of the actual world in its real shape, together with a firm retention of what has been seen, is thus the first requirement of an artist.
— Aesthetics, The Artist › Imagination (Phantasie), Genius, and Inspiration (tr. Knox)

Head: Circumspection
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › α. The Idea of Artistic Beauty › c. The Beauty of Art, or the Ideal › iii. The Artist › 1. Inspiration › a. Fancy › ii. Circumspection
Gloss: The clear-headed awareness with which the artist sorts, orders and masters the material.
Hegelian gloss: The waking Besonnenheit of the understanding: without it, without sorting and distinguishing, the artist cannot master the content, and it is foolish to think the true artist does not know what he does.
Nouns: circumspection; Besonnenheit, deliberation, presence of mind, clear-headedness, sobriety, judgment, discernment, discrimination, self-possession, control, artistic intelligence.
Verbs: deliberate, weigh, sort, discriminate, know what one is doing.
Adjective: circumspect, deliberate, clear-headed, sober, self-possessed, considered.
Adverbs: deliberately, advisedly.
Phrases: es ist thöricht zu glauben, der ächte Künstler wisse nicht was er thut [Ger.] [Hegel, Aesthetics]; Gedichte wie die homerischen seyen dem Dichter im Schlafe gekommen [Ger.] [Hegel, Aesthetics, as an absurd belief].
Hegel definition: Circumspection is the watchful discrimination of the understanding which, with depth of heart, the artist needs in order to fuse rational content with outward shape. It is absurd to suppose that poems like Homer's came to the poet in sleep: without circumspection, sorting and criticism no artist can master the material, and it is silly to believe that the genuine artist does not know what is being done.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· The Beauty of Art or the Ideal › The Artist › Imagination (Phantasie), Genius, and Inspiration
Hegel citations:
It is therefore an absurdity to suppose that poems like the Homeric came to the poet in sleep. Without circumspection, discrimination, and criticism the artist cannot master any subject-matter which he is to configurate, and it is silly to believe that the genuine artist does not know what he is doing.
— Aesthetics, The Artist › Imagination (Phantasie), Genius, and Inspiration (tr. Knox)
In order to achieve the interpenetration of the rational content and the external shape, the artist has to call in aid (i) the watchful circumspection of the intellect, and (ii) the depth of the heart and its animating feelings.
— Aesthetics, The Artist › Imagination (Phantasie), Genius, and Inspiration (tr. Knox)

Head: Experience
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › α. The Idea of Artistic Beauty › c. The Beauty of Art, or the Ideal › iii. The Artist › 1. Inspiration › a. Fancy › iii. Experience
Gloss: The depth of feeling and lived experience through which the artist makes the material their own.
Hegelian gloss: The depth of heart (Gemüt) and of animating feeling (Empfindung), which pervades and quickens the whole and holds the content in subjective unity with the artist's inmost self.
Nouns: experience; Empfindung, feeling, depth of feeling, Gemüt, heart, inwardness, lived experience, experience of life, a rich inner life, felt life, soulfulness, the animating feeling, concentration of heart.
Verbs: feel, live through, take to heart, put one's heart into.
Adjective: heartfelt, deeply felt, soulful, felt, lived, experienced.
Adverbs: feelingly, from the heart.
Hegel definition: Experience here is the concentration and depth of the artist's emotional life, through which a feeling penetrating the whole makes the material one's own inmost self. The artist must not only have looked about in the world but have drawn much that is great into their soul, been deeply gripped and lived through much; so genius may burst forth in youth, but maturity of the work comes only later.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· The Beauty of Art or the Ideal › The Artist › Imagination (Phantasie), Genius, and Inspiration
Hegel citations:
In accord with this point of view, the artist must not only have looked around at much in the world and made himself acquainted with its outer and inner manifestations, but he must have drawn much, and much that is great, into his own soul; his heart must have been deeply gripped and moved thereby; he must have done and lived through much before he can develop the true depths of life into concrete manifestations.
— Aesthetics, The Artist › Imagination (Phantasie), Genius, and Inspiration (tr. Knox)
Consequently genius does burst forth in youth, as was the case with Goethe and Schiller, but only middle or old age can bring to perfection the genuine maturity of the work of art.
— Aesthetics, The Artist › Imagination (Phantasie), Genius, and Inspiration (tr. Knox)

Head: Genius
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › α. The Idea of Artistic Beauty › c. The Beauty of Art, or the Ideal › iii. The Artist › 1. Inspiration › b. Genius
Gloss: The artist's inborn gift for true artistic production, with the energy to carry it through.
Hegelian gloss: Genie, the general capacity for true production of art together with the energy to develop and work it out; it has, unlike thought, a side of natural gift.
Nouns: genius; native genius, creative genius, the gift, the born artist. genius, flair, brilliance, fire of genius, heaven-born genius, the divine spark.
Adjective: brilliant, gifted, ingenious.
Adverbs: brilliantly, by genius.
Phrases: a stroke of genius; poeta nascitur, non fit [Lat.] [the poet is born, not made].
Hegel definition: Genius is the general ability for the true production of a work of art, with the energy to elaborate and complete it, existing only as subjective, since spiritual production is possible only to a self-conscious subject who makes such creation an aim. It requires a specific aptitude with an essential natural element, in which sense it is inborn, though it also demands long study and industry.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· The Beauty of Art or the Ideal › The Artist › Imagination (Phantasie), Genius, and Inspiration
Hegel citations:
Genius is the general ability for the true production of a work of art, as well as the energy to elaborate and complete it.
— Aesthetics, The Artist › Imagination (Phantasie), Genius, and Inspiration (tr. Knox)
With art the thing is different; it requires a specific aptitude, in which a natural element plays an essential part too.
— Aesthetics, The Artist › Imagination (Phantasie), Genius, and Inspiration (tr. Knox)

Head: Talent
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › α. The Idea of Artistic Beauty › c. The Beauty of Art, or the Ideal › iii. The Artist › 1. Inspiration › b. Genius › i. Talent
Gloss: A particular aptitude for one art or skill, as distinct from genius.
Hegelian gloss: Talent, the specific capacity for a particular art, which reaches full life only with genius; one may have talent and not genius.
Nouns: talent; aptitude, knack, bent, turn, specific gift, special ability, an ear, an eye, a feel for. talent, gift, talent &c H0474, ability, faculty, endowment, forte.
Adjective: talented, endowed.
Phrases: a good horse is hard to mount, but it carries you far, liang ma nan cheng, ran ke yi ren zhong zhi yuan [Chin.] [Mozi].
Hegel definition: Talent is the particular capacity that a particular art demands, such as for violin playing or singing. It is not immediately identical with genius, though perfect creation requires their identity: mere talent can excel only in one separate side of art and still needs the general capacity and inspiration that genius alone confers. Talent without genius gets little beyond external skill.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· The Beauty of Art or the Ideal › The Artist › Imagination (Phantasie), Genius, and Inspiration
Hegel citations:
But a mere talent can only attain to excellence in one such entirely separate side of art, and, if it is to be perfect in itself, it still requires always over again the capacity for art in general, and the inspiration, which genius alone confers.
— Aesthetics, The Artist › Imagination (Phantasie), Genius, and Inspiration (tr. Knox)
Talent without genius therefore does not get far beyond an external skill.
— Aesthetics, The Artist › Imagination (Phantasie), Genius, and Inspiration (tr. Knox)

Head: Culturation
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › α. The Idea of Artistic Beauty › c. The Beauty of Art, or the Ideal › iii. The Artist › 1. Inspiration › b. Genius › ii. Culturation
Gloss: A gift that is inborn yet belongs to a people rather than to one person, like the Italian improvisers' readiness in verse.
Hegelian gloss: Genius as Naturgabe: a natural gift which Hegel ties to the particular nationality of peoples, so that a people's art and its manner of production go together, as with the improvisers native to Italy.
Nouns: culturation; national gift, national genius, the genius of a people, Volksgeist, native gift, natural endowment, inborn talent, folk talent, inherited tradition, the spirit of a people, folk art, the vernacular, improviser, improvvisatore.
Verbs: improvise. inherit, grow up in.
Adjective: native, inborn, innate, national, vernacular, folk, indigenous.
Foreign: German: Naturgabe, Nationalität der Völker; Italian: improvvisatore.
Phrases: in dieser Weise hängt die Kunst und ihre bestimmte Productionsart mit der bestimmten Nationalität der Völker zusammen [Ger.] [Hegel, Aesthetics].
Hegel definition: Culturation names the tie between artistic gift and a people's nature: because artistic creation includes immediacy and naturalness, the arts are more or less national. Italians have song and melody almost by nature, the Greeks perfected epic and sculpture, the Romans transplanted art from Greece. Poetry spreads most widely, yet folk song is deeply national, and Italian improvisers show marvellous talent.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· The Beauty of Art or the Ideal › The Artist › Imagination (Phantasie), Genius, and Inspiration
Hegel citations:
Similarly the different arts too are more or less national, connected with the natural side of a people.
— Aesthetics, The Artist › Imagination (Phantasie), Genius, and Inspiration (tr. Knox)
In this way art and its specific mode of production hangs together with the specific nationality of peoples.
— Aesthetics, The Artist › Imagination (Phantasie), Genius, and Inspiration (tr. Knox)

Head: Sensibility (Facility)
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › α. The Idea of Artistic Beauty › c. The Beauty of Art, or the Ideal › iii. The Artist › 1. Inspiration › b. Genius › iii. Sensibility (Facility)
Gloss: The ease with which the gifted artist executes the work, so that it comes almost into their fingers.
Hegelian gloss: Leichtigkeit, the ease of inner production and of outer technical skill: what lives in the artist's Phantasie comes as it were into his fingers, as our thoughts come into our mouths.
Nouns: sensibility; facility, ease, fluency, dexterity, readiness, deftness, felicity, the knack, the touch, a sure hand, technical skill, mastery of the medium, sprezzatura, practical feeling.
Adjective: facile, fluent, deft, effortless, ready, dexterous, sure-handed.
Adverbs: effortlessly, with ease, fluently.
Foreign: Italian: sprezzatura.
Phrases: was in seiner Phantasie lebt, kommt ihm dadurch gleichsam in die Finger [Ger.] [Hegel, Aesthetics].
Hegel definition: Facility is the third mark of genius: ease in producing ideas from within and in the technical dexterity the arts require. The greater the genius, the less laborious the acquisition of skill, since the genuine artist has a natural impulse to give form at once to all that they feel and imagine, as a composer to melody or a painter to colour, though study must still perfect the gift.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· The Beauty of Art or the Ideal › The Artist › Imagination (Phantasie), Genius, and Inspiration
Hegel citations:
For the genuine artist has a natural impulse and an immediate need to give form at once to everything that he feels and imagines.
— Aesthetics, The Artist › Imagination (Phantasie), Genius, and Inspiration (tr. Knox)
What lives in his imagination comes to him, therefore, as it were to his finger-tips, just as it comes to our lips to speak out our thoughts
— Aesthetics, The Artist › Imagination (Phantasie), Genius, and Inspiration (tr. Knox)

Head: Enthusiasm
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › α. The Idea of Artistic Beauty › c. The Beauty of Art, or the Ideal › iii. The Artist › 1. Inspiration › c. Enthusiasm
Gloss: The inspired state in which imagination and execution become one.
Hegelian gloss: Begeisterung, the activity of Phantasie and of technical execution considered as a state in the artist.
Nouns: enthusiasm; Begeisterung, rapture, the creative state, possession, frenzy of creation. enthusiasm, divine afflatus, the Muse, creative fire, verve, aspiration.
Verbs: enthuse, kindle, inspire, be inspired.
Adjective: inspired, enthused, rapt.
Adverbs: inspiredly, with inspiration, in a rapture.
Phrases: sing in me, Muse [Homer]; divine inspiration.
Hegel definition: Enthusiasm, or inspiration, is the activity of imagination and technical execution taken in itself as the basic condition of the artist: the state of the artist actively forming both the inner conception and the outward execution of the work, a double activity for which it is necessary. It takes fire on a definite material that imagination seizes in order to express it artistically.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· The Beauty of Art or the Ideal › The Artist › Imagination (Phantasie), Genius, and Inspiration
Hegel citations:
Now the activity of imagination and technical execution, considered in itself as the fundamental condition of the artist, is what is generally called, in the third place, 'inspiration'.
— Aesthetics, The Artist › Imagination (Phantasie), Genius, and Inspiration (tr. Knox)
[M]oreover inspiration is the state of the artist in his active process of forming both his subjective inner conception and his objective execution of the work of art, because for this double activity inspiration is necessary.
— Aesthetics, The Artist › Imagination (Phantasie), Genius, and Inspiration (tr. Knox)

Head: Origins of Enthusiasm
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › α. The Idea of Artistic Beauty › c. The Beauty of Art, or the Ideal › iii. The Artist › 1. Inspiration › c. Enthusiasm › i. Origins of Enthusiasm
Gloss: Where inspiration comes from: not from stimulants or mere resolve, but from an occasion that brings a content.
Hegelian gloss: Hegel asks how Begeisterung arises, rejects sensuous stimulus and the bare will to produce, and finds it in an occasion, inner or outer, that hands the artist a content.
Nouns: origins of enthusiasm; the sources of inspiration, the springs of creation, the creative impulse, stimulus, spur, prompting, the spark.
Hegel definition: The origin of inspiration has prompted the most varied opinions. Since genius joins the spiritual and the natural, some suppose sensuous stimulus can produce it, others a resolve to be inspired; Hegel denies both. True inspiration kindles on a specific material that imagination seizes. That material need not come from the artist alone, for great works have often arisen from external occasions.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· The Beauty of Art or the Ideal › The Artist › Imagination (Phantasie), Genius, and Inspiration
Hegel citations:
In this matter the first question raised is about the manner of its origin, in regard to which the most varied ideas are in circulation
— Aesthetics, The Artist › Imagination (Phantasie), Genius, and Inspiration (tr. Knox)
Thus true inspiration takes fire on some specific material which the imagination seizes with a view to expressing it artistically
— Aesthetics, The Artist › Imagination (Phantasie), Genius, and Inspiration (tr. Knox)

Head: Boredom
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › α. The Idea of Artistic Beauty › c. The Beauty of Art, or the Ideal › iii. The Artist › 1. Inspiration › c. Enthusiasm › i. Origins of Enthusiasm › 1. Boredom
Gloss: Waiting for inspiration to arrive by itself, through wine or idleness; Hegel says it does not come so.
Hegelian gloss: The belief that Begeisterung comes from sensuous stimulation: but champagne yields no poetry, and the best genius may lie morning and evening in the green grass gazing at the sky and feel no breath of inspiration.
Nouns: boredom; idleness, ennui, tedium, waiting for the Muse, lying fallow, writer's block, sensuous stimulation, stimulants, intoxication, champagne, dolce far niente, daydreaming, lassitude, torpor.
Verbs: idle, laze, lie in the grass, gaze at the sky, wait for inspiration.
Adjective: idle, bored, uninspired, listless, fallow, blocked.
Foreign: Italian: dolce far niente; French: ennui.
Phrases: Champagner giebt noch keine Poesie [Ger.] [Hegel, Aesthetics]; die Wärme des Bluts macht's nicht allein [Ger.] [Hegel, Aesthetics].
Hegel definition: The belief that sensuous stimulus produces inspiration fails: heated blood achieves nothing by itself and champagne yields no poetry, as Marmontel found surrounded by six thousand bottles. Even the finest genius may lie on the grass morning and evening, enjoying the breeze and gazing at the sky, without a breath of tender inspiration reaching them.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· The Beauty of Art or the Ideal › The Artist › Imagination (Phantasie), Genius, and Inspiration
Hegel citations:
But the heat of the blood achieves nothing by itself; champagne produces no poetry, as Marmontel, e.g., tells how in a cellar in Champagne he had six thousand bottles confronting him and yet nothing poetic flowed out of them for him.
— Aesthetics, The Artist › Imagination (Phantasie), Genius, and Inspiration (tr. Knox)
So too the finest genius may often enough lie on the grass morning and evening, enjoying a fresh breeze and gazing up into the sky, but of tender inspiration not a breath reaches him.
— Aesthetics, The Artist › Imagination (Phantasie), Genius, and Inspiration (tr. Knox)

Head: Artistic Intention
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › α. The Idea of Artistic Beauty › c. The Beauty of Art, or the Ideal › iii. The Artist › 1. Inspiration › c. Enthusiasm › i. Origins of Enthusiasm › 2. Artistic Intention
Gloss: Setting out to be inspired by an act of will; Hegel says this too fails without a living content.
Hegelian gloss: Begeisterung cannot be called up by the bare spiritual intention to produce: whoever merely resolves to be inspired in order to make a poem, with no content already alive in him, will make no fine work.
Nouns: artistic intention; resolve, intention, the will to create, deliberate effort, design, ambition, forced inspiration, contrivance, laboured effort.
Verbs: set out, intend, resolve, contrive, force it, strain after effect.
Adjective: deliberate, intentional, contrived, forced, laboured.
Phrases: weder jene nur sinnliche Anregung noch der bloße Wille und Entschluß [Ger.] [Hegel, Aesthetics].
Hegel definition: Artistic intention alone cannot summon inspiration. Whoever merely resolves to be inspired in order to write a poem, paint a picture or compose a tune, without already carrying a living theme, and must hunt around for material, can on the strength of that intention neither form a beautiful conception nor produce a solid work, whatever their talent. Mere will shows the heart has not yet seized any true interest.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· The Beauty of Art or the Ideal › The Artist › Imagination (Phantasie), Genius, and Inspiration
Hegel citations:
On the other hand, neither can inspiration be summoned by a spiritual intention to produce.
— Aesthetics, The Artist › Imagination (Phantasie), Genius, and Inspiration (tr. Knox)
A man who simply resolves to be inspired in order to write a poem, paint a picture, or compose a tune, without already carrying in himself some theme as a living stimulus and must just hunt around here and there for some material, then, no matter what his talent, cannot, on the strength of this mere intention, form a beautiful conception or produce a solid work of art.
— Aesthetics, The Artist › Imagination (Phantasie), Genius, and Inspiration (tr. Knox)

Head: External Inspiration
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › α. The Idea of Artistic Beauty › c. The Beauty of Art, or the Ideal › iii. The Artist › 1. Inspiration › c. Enthusiasm › i. Origins of Enthusiasm › 3. External Inspiration
Gloss: The outside occasion that sets the artist to work: a commission, an event, a given subject.
Hegelian gloss: An external occasion, a commission or an event, which the genuine artist takes up and fills with his own life.
Nouns: external inspiration; occasion, commission, patronage, the patron, a given subject, prompt, assignment, the brief, occasional poem.
Verbs: commission, prompt, occasion.
Adjective: commissioned, occasional.
Foreign: German: Gelegenheitsgedicht.
Hegel definition: External inspiration comes from an outside occasion, such as a commission, an event, or old sagas and chronicles, to which the artist of natural talent is solicited to give form. Pindar's odes were often commissioned, and buildings and paintings frequently prescribed. All that is required is that the artist grasp an essential interest and make the subject live in itself; then inspiration arises of its own accord.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· The Beauty of Art or the Ideal › The Artist › Imagination (Phantasie), Genius, and Inspiration
Hegel citations:
Yet, on the other side, the greatest works of art have often owed their creation to some quite external stimulus.
— Aesthetics, The Artist › Imagination (Phantasie), Genius, and Inspiration (tr. Knox)
Thus the occasion for production may come entirely from without, and the one important requirement is just that the artist shall lay hold of an essential interest and make the subject-matter become alive in itself. In that event the inspiration of genius arises automatically.
— Aesthetics, The Artist › Imagination (Phantasie), Genius, and Inspiration (tr. Knox)

Head: Theme
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › α. The Idea of Artistic Beauty › c. The Beauty of Art, or the Ideal › iii. The Artist › 1. Inspiration › c. Enthusiasm › ii. Theme
Gloss: The definite content that seizes the artist and asks to be given shape.
Hegelian gloss: The determinate content, taken up by Phantasie, which is the true source of Begeisterung.
Nouns: theme; subject, subject matter, content, matter, topic, motif, argument, burden, material.
Adjective: thematic.
Hegel definition: The theme is the specific object and subject matter on which artistic interest has already concentrated before inspiration arises, and to which an artistic urge of the right kind holds firm. Where such interest is lacking, resorting to sensuous stimulus or mere will only proves that heart and imagination have fastened on nothing true. True inspiration kindles on such material and is filled by it.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· The Beauty of Art or the Ideal › The Artist › Imagination (Phantasie), Genius, and Inspiration
Hegel citations:
But if the artistic urge is of the right kind, this interest has already in advance been concentrated on a specific object and theme and kept firmly to it.
— Aesthetics, The Artist › Imagination (Phantasie), Genius, and Inspiration (tr. Knox)
[A]nd to make use of such means proves only that the heart and the imagination have not yet fastened on any true interest.
— Aesthetics, The Artist › Imagination (Phantasie), Genius, and Inspiration (tr. Knox)

Head: The Project
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › α. The Idea of Artistic Beauty › c. The Beauty of Art, or the Ideal › iii. The Artist › 1. Inspiration › c. Enthusiasm › iii. The Project
Gloss: The artist's full absorption in the work in hand, forgetting themselves in the matter.
Hegelian gloss: Begeisterung proper: the artist wholly filled by the matter and absorbed in it, letting no merely subjective particularity in, until the work is complete.
Nouns: the project; the work in hand, absorption, immersion, total engagement, devotion to the work, single-mindedness, work in progress, opus, magnum opus, labour of love.
Verbs: be absorbed, lose oneself in the work, immerse oneself, devote oneself.
Adjective: absorbed, immersed, engrossed, single-minded.
Foreign: German: Aufgehen in der Sache.
Hegel definition: Inspiration proper is nothing but being completely filled with the theme, wholly present in it, and not resting until it is stamped and polished into artistic form. Having made the matter their own, artists must forget their personality and its accidents and become only the form in which the theme takes shape; an inspiration in which the subject parades itself is a poor one.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· The Beauty of Art or the Ideal › The Artist › Imagination (Phantasie), Genius, and Inspiration
Hegel citations:
If we ask further wherein artistic inspiration consists, it is nothing but being completely filled with the theme, being entirely present in the theme, and not resting until the theme has been stamped and polished into artistic shape.
— Aesthetics, The Artist › Imagination (Phantasie), Genius, and Inspiration (tr. Knox)
But if the artist has made the subject-matter into something entirely his own, he must on the other hand be able to forget his own personality and its accidental particular characteristics and immerse himself, for his part, entirely in his material, so that, as subject, he is only as it were the form for the formation of the theme which has taken hold of him.
— Aesthetics, The Artist › Imagination (Phantasie), Genius, and Inspiration (tr. Knox)

Head: Objectivity of Representation
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › α. The Idea of Artistic Beauty › c. The Beauty of Art, or the Ideal › iii. The Artist › 2. Objectivity of Representation
Gloss: The truthfulness of the artist's presentation.
Hegelian gloss: The objectivity of representation, the artist's being entirely in the matter.
Nouns: objectivity of representation; objectivity, impersonality, fidelity, truthfulness, accuracy, realism, the work's own life. veracity, frankness, truth, sincerity, candor, honesty, plain dealing, love of truth, unreserve†. truth to the subject, self-forgetfulness, absorption in the thing, the matter itself, faithfulness. verisimilitude.
Verbs: depict faithfully, render, represent. objectify, render truly, efface oneself, lose oneself in the subject, be faithful.
Adjective: objective, impersonal, faithful, realistic, matter-of-fact. nonsubjective†. truthful, self-forgetful, disinterested.
Adverbs: objectively, faithfully. truthfully, impersonally.
Foreign: German: Sachlichkeit [matter-of-factness]; Latin: bona fides.
Phrases: the work speaks for itself; true to life; warts and all.
Hegel definition: Objectivity of representation is not the reproduction of familiar external reality, nor an inwardness too reserved to come to clear expression. True objectivity requires that nothing of the genuine matter that inspires the artist be held back: everything must be wholly unfolded so that the universal substance of the subject appears as clearly as its individual shape. The works are the artist's best part and truth.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· The Beauty of Art or the Ideal › The Artist › Objectivity of the Representation
Hegel citations:
But the aim of art is precisely to strip off the matter of everyday life and its mode of appearance, and by spiritual activity from within bring out only what is absolutely rational and give to it its true external configuration.
— Aesthetics, The Artist › Objectivity of the Representation (tr. Knox)
On the contrary, his works are the best part and the truth of the artist; what he is [in his works], that he is; but what remains buried in his heart, that is he not.
— Aesthetics, The Artist › Objectivity of the Representation (tr. Knox)

Head: Authorship
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › α. The Idea of Artistic Beauty › c. The Beauty of Art, or the Ideal › iii. The Artist › 3. Authorship
Gloss: The artist's individual manner, the general style of the art, and the originality that unites them.
Hegelian gloss: The artist's subjective manner, the objective style, and originality as their identity.
Nouns: authorship. graphoidea†, graphomania†, phrenoia†.
Foreign: Latin: stylus, sui generis uncommon, arbiter elegantiarum [judge of taste] [Tacitus on Petronius]; French: la morgue litteraire, pasticheur, baroque, manière, faire; Italian: maniera, pasticcio [pastiche], barocco, stile; Sanskrit: rīti [style]; Korean: meot [flair, style]; German: Barock; Portuguese: barroco; Dutch: manjer, handeling, wijze van doen.
Hegel definition: Authorship, in the section on manner, style and originality, concerns the identity of the artist's subjectivity with the true objectivity of the work. Having wholly identified with the topic and shaped it from inner heart and imagination, the artist unites what had been separated as genius and objectivity. This unity is the essence of genuine originality, to be reached by overcoming the one-sidedness of subjective manner and of style.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· The Beauty of Art or the Ideal › The Artist › Manner, Style, and Originality
Hegel citations:
But however far an objectivity in the sense indicated just now must be demanded of the artist, his production is nevertheless the work of his inspiration.
— Aesthetics, The Artist › Manner, Style, and Originality (tr. Knox)
This identity of the artist subjectively with the true objectivity of his production is the third chief point which we still have to consider briefly, because in this identity we see united what hitherto we have separated as genius and objectivity.
— Aesthetics, The Artist › Manner, Style, and Originality (tr. Knox)

Head: Mere Manner
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › α. The Idea of Artistic Beauty › c. The Beauty of Art, or the Ideal › iii. The Artist › 3. Authorship › a. Mere Manner
Gloss: The artist's merely personal way of doing things, which intrudes on the demands of the subject.
Hegelian gloss: Bloße Manier, the particular and contingent peculiarity of the artist, which Hegel calls the worst an artist can give himself up to.
Nouns: mere manner; manner, mannerism, the mannered, affectation, artifice, preciosity, schmaltz, kitsch. mannerism &c H0734, euphuism†, marinism†, kitsch [Broch, Greenberg].
Verbs: mannerize.
Adjective: mannered, artificial, affected, euphuistic†.
Foreign: German: Manier, Kitsch.
Phrases: die Manier das Schlechteste, dem sich der Künstler hingeben kann [Ger.] [Hegel, Aesthetics].
Hegel definition: Mere manner, or mannerism, must be essentially distinguished from originality: it concerns the particular and accidental idiosyncrasies of the artist, which come forward in place of the topic and its ideal representation. So understood it is the worst thing to which an artist can submit, since in it one indulges only personal, restricted whims, whereas art demands that such accidental peculiarity be extinguished.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· The Beauty of Art or the Ideal › The Artist › Manner, Style, and Originality
Hegel citations:
Mere manner [i.e. mannerism] must be essentially distinguished from originality.
— Aesthetics, The Artist › Manner, Style, and Originality (tr. Knox)
Looked at in this way, manner is the worst thing to which the artist can submit because in it he indulges simply in his own restricted and personal whims.
— Aesthetics, The Artist › Manner, Style, and Originality (tr. Knox)

Head: Idiosyncrasy
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › α. The Idea of Artistic Beauty › c. The Beauty of Art, or the Ideal › iii. The Artist › 3. Authorship › a. Mere Manner › i. Idiosyncrasy
Gloss: A merely accidental peculiarity of the artist, which belongs to them and not to the matter.
Hegelian gloss: Manier as the artist's contingent peculiarity (zufällige Eigentümlichkeit), concerning not the general nature of the subject but only the particular artist.
Nouns: idiosyncrasy; quirk, tic, personal trait, foible, eccentricity, habit, signature habit. idiosyncrasy, individuality, peculiarity, idiocrasy &c H0403.
Verbs: individualize.
Adjective: idiosyncratic, individual.
Adverbs: in his own manner.
Hegel definition: Idiosyncrasy is the accidental peculiarity of the individual artist that constitutes manner. It does not concern the general kinds of art, which rightly require different modes of representation, as the epic poet differs from the lyric, but only this personality and its accomplishment, and may go so far as to contradict the ideal. Art demands that the artist extinguish it.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· The Beauty of Art or the Ideal › The Artist › Manner, Style, and Originality
Hegel citations:
Manner, then, in this sense [of mannerism] does not concern the general kinds of art which in and for themselves require different modes of representation, as, e.g., the landscape painter has to view his subjects in a way different from that of the historical painter, the epic poet differently from the lyric or dramatic one; on the contrary, 'manner' is a conception appropriate only to this personality and the accidental idiosyncrasy of his accomplishment, and this may go so far as to be in direct contradiction with the true nature of the Ideal.
— Aesthetics, The Artist › Manner, Style, and Originality (tr. Knox)
But art as such cancels the mere accidentality of the topic as well as of its external appearance and therefore demands of the artist that he shall extinguish in himself the accidental particular characteristics of his own subjective idiosyncrasy.
— Aesthetics, The Artist › Manner, Style, and Originality (tr. Knox)

Head: Idiom
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › α. The Idea of Artistic Beauty › c. The Beauty of Art, or the Ideal › iii. The Artist › 3. Authorship › a. Mere Manner › ii. Idiom
Gloss: A way of working that belongs to an artist and their followers and pupils, become habit through repetition; a school's manner.
Hegelian gloss: Manier as a mode of presentation (Darstellungsweise) proper to the artist, his followers and pupils, formed into habit by frequent repetition; it finds most room in painting and music.
Nouns: idiom; school, the manner of a school, house style, workshop practice, following, imitation, pastiche, convention, formula, routine, epigone, follower, pupil, disciple. idiom.
Adjective: academical†. derivative, conventional, formulaic, imitative, epigonal, academic.
Adverbs: in the manner of the school. in the manner of.
Hegel definition: Idiom is the special mode of representation belonging to one artist, with followers and school, which repetition turns into habit, in painting and music especially, showing itself in treatment of tone, light and colour and in handling the brush. The more specialized it is, the greater the risk that it degenerates into a cold, soulless repetition in which art sinks to mere manual skill.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· The Beauty of Art or the Ideal › The Artist › Manner, Style, and Originality
Hegel citations:
A special mode of representation belonging to a particular artist and his disciples and school, and developed by frequent repetition into a habit, constitutes 'manner' here
— Aesthetics, The Artist › Manner, Style, and Originality (tr. Knox)
But since such a specific kind of treatment and representation, owing to its constantly returning anew, is generalized into a habit and becomes second nature to the artist, there is a serious risk that, the more specialized the manner is, the more easily does it degenerate into a soulless and therefore cold repetition and fabrication, in which the artist is no longer present with full sensibility and entire inspiration.
— Aesthetics, The Artist › Manner, Style, and Originality (tr. Knox)

Head: Authenticity
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › α. The Idea of Artistic Beauty › c. The Beauty of Art, or the Ideal › iii. The Artist › 3. Authorship › a. Mere Manner › iii. Authenticity
Gloss: A manner that has widened beyond private habit to keep to the nature of the matter, like Goethe's or Horace's light turn at the end of a serious poem.
Hegelian gloss: Die ächtere Manier: a manner that lifts itself out of narrow particularity and holds to the nature of the matter in a more general way, as Goethe and Horace end serious beginnings with a cheerful turn.
Nouns: authenticity; the truer manner, a personal yet general manner, the light touch, the deft turn, a cheerful ending, conversational ease. authenticity.
Adjective: authentic, genuine, natural, unforced.
Phrases: die ächtere Manier [Ger.] [Hegel, Aesthetics].
Hegel definition: Authentic or more genuine manner frees itself from restricted idiosyncrasy and broadens so that special modes of treatment cannot harden into habit, the artist holding in a general way to the nature of the things treated. Goethe's knack of ending even serious pieces with a happy turn, and Horace's way in the Epistles, are manner of this wider kind, which paves the way to style.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· The Beauty of Art or the Ideal › The Artist › Manner, Style, and Originality
Hegel citations:
Thus the more genuine manner must rid itself of this restricted idiosyncrasy, and so broaden itself within that these specialized modes of treatment cannot mortify into a pure matter of habit; for the genuine artist clings in a more general way to the nature of the things in hand and can make his own this more general mode of treatment in the way that its essence implies.
— Aesthetics, The Artist › Manner, Style, and Originality (tr. Knox)
This way of treating the thing is indeed manner too and it belongs to the subject's handling of his topic, but to a subjective procedure which is of a more general kind and so within the intended kind of representation works all the time in a necessary way.
— Aesthetics, The Artist › Manner, Style, and Originality (tr. Knox)

Head: Style
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › α. The Idea of Artistic Beauty › c. The Beauty of Art, or the Ideal › iii. The Artist › 3. Authorship › b. Style
Gloss: The way of presentation that the medium and the laws of an art demand, as distinct from an artist's manner.
Hegelian gloss: Stil, the manner of presentation that follows the conditions of the material and the demands of the art and its kinds, as in the severe, the ideal and the pleasing style.
Nouns: style; the laws of the art, the demands of the medium, the severe style, the ideal style, the pleasing style. style, diction, technique. phraseology, wording, strain, composition, mode of expression, choice of words, mode of speech, literary power, ready pen, pen of a ready writer, command of language &c H0662. turn of expression. hand, touch, the grand manner. perspicuity, perspicuousness &c H0662, plain speaking &c H0662, definiteness, definition, exactness &c H0214, explicitness, lucidness. obscurity &c H0662, involution, hard words, ambiguity &c H0662, unintelligibleness, vagueness &c H0667, inexactness &c H0214, what d'ye call 'em &c H0662 [Obs.], darkness of meaning. plainness, simplicity, severity, plain terms, plain English, Saxon English, household words.
Verbs: stylize. call a spade 'a spade', plunge in medias res, come to the point.
Adjective: stylish, stylistic. lucid &c H0662, explicit &c H0662, exact. obscure, crabbed, involved, confused. plain, simple, unornamented, unadorned, unvarnished, homely, homespun, neat, severe, chaste, pure, Saxon, commonplace, matter-of- fact, natural, prosaic, kempt†, tricksy†. dry, unvaried, monotonous &c H0662.
Adverbs: stylishly, with style. in plain terms, in plain words, in plain English, in plain common parlance, point-blank.
Foreign: German: Stil.
Phrases: le style est l'homme même [Fr.] [Buffon]; the style is the man.
Hegel definition: Style, beyond the idiosyncrasy expressed in turns of phrase, means a mode of representation that complies with the conditions of its material and with the demands and laws arising from the nature of a given kind of art, as church music differs from opera. A defect of style is either inability to make such a necessary mode one's own or caprice that puts a bad mannerism in its place.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· The Beauty of Art or the Ideal › The Artist › Manner, Style, and Originality
Hegel citations:
'Style', so interpreted, is applicable to a mode of representation which complies with the conditions of its material as well as corresponding throughout with the demands of definite species of art and the laws originating in their essence.
— Aesthetics, The Artist › Manner, Style, and Originality (tr. Knox)
In this wider meaning of the word, consequently, defectiveness of style is either the artist's inability to make his own such an inherently necessary mode of representation, or else his subjective caprice which gives free play to his own whims instead of to conformity with rules, and sets up in their place a bad mannerism of his own.
— Aesthetics, The Artist › Manner, Style, and Originality (tr. Knox)

Head: Originality
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › α. The Idea of Artistic Beauty › c. The Beauty of Art, or the Ideal › iii. The Artist › 3. Authorship › c. Originality
Gloss: The artist's own creation in which subjectivity and the matter are one.
Hegelian gloss: Originalität, the identity of the subjectivity of the artist and the true objectivity of the presentation, free of both manner and mere convention.
Nouns: originality; true originality, the original work, the new. originality, novelty, inventiveness, freshness, signature, voice. no imitation, creativeness, invention, creation. originality, invention.
Verbs: originate, innovate. strike out something new.
Adjective: original, inventive, fresh, creative, incomparable. unimitated†, uncopied†, unmatched, unparalleled, inimitable &c H0098, unique, untranslated, exceptional, rare, unexampled.
Adverbs: originally.
Foreign: German: Originalität.
Phrases: one of a kind; nothing new under the sun [Bible].
Hegel definition: Originality is not merely following rules of style but inspiration that grasps a rational material and shapes it from within, in keeping with its kind of art and the ideal. It is identical with true objectivity, at once the artist's most personal inner life and the nature of the object, and must be distinguished from caprice, witty humour and irony. Having no manner has always been the one grand manner.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· The Beauty of Art or the Ideal › The Artist › Manner, Style, and Originality
Hegel citations:
Thus originality is identical with true objectivity and links together the subjective and factual sides of the representation in such a way that the two sides are no longer opposed or strangers to one another.
— Aesthetics, The Artist › Manner, Style, and Originality (tr. Knox)
To have no manner has from time immemorial been the one grand manner, and in this sense alone are Homer, Sophocles, Raphael, Shakespeare, to be called 'original'.
— Aesthetics, The Artist › Manner, Style, and Originality (tr. Knox)

Head: The Forms of Art
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › β. The Forms of Art
Gloss: The forms in which the ideal is embodied in art.
Hegelian gloss: The forms of art: the relations of idea and shape in symbolic, classical and romantic art.
Nouns: the forms of art; art-forms, symbolic, classical, and romantic art, stages of art, artistic epochs, modes of art. the particular forms of art, the symbolic the classical and the romantic, the forms of the beautiful, the stages of the ideal, the relation of content and shape.
Verbs: develop, evolve, succeed. form, embody, particularize, differentiate, unfold.
Adjective: formal, historical, epochal. particular.
Adverbs: in succession. in its forms, form by form, successively.
Phrases: symbolic, classical, romantic; in its proper form.
Hegel definition: The forms of art are the actualizations of the idea of the beautiful, which as a totality of essential differences must issue in them: not species brought in from outside but the ideal's own more concrete determinations, spread out by its concept. Through them the idea presses on to representation, and each stage of its content has its own shape, so that defects of artistic form prove to be defects of the idea.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· Development of the Ideal into the Particular Forms of Art
Hegel citations:
Now, in more detail, the forms of art, as the actualizing and unfolding of the beautiful, find their origin in the Idea itself
— Aesthetics, Development of the Ideal into the Particular Forms of Art (tr. Knox)
The consummation of the Idea as content appears therefore simultaneously as also the consummation of form
— Aesthetics, Development of the Ideal into the Particular Forms of Art (tr. Knox)

Head: Symbolic Art
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › β. The Forms of Art › a. Symbolic Art
Gloss: Art in which meaning and shape do not yet correspond; art that hints rather than shows.
Hegelian gloss: Art in which the idea is still seeking its true expression, so that shape and meaning do not correspond; the symbol.
Nouns: symbolic art; symbolism, the symbol, the inadequacy of shape to meaning, mystery, enigma, striving, the colossal, the monstrous, Oriental art. the symbolic form of art, the pre-art, intimation, suggestion, the striving after form. hieroglyph.
Verbs: symbolize, signify, suggest, hint, strive. intimate, betoken, seek.
Adjective: symbolic, enigmatic, mysterious, colossal, monstrous, suggestive. symbolical, allusive, inadequate, ambiguous, Oriental, amphibolous†, homonymous†.
Adverbs: symbolically, enigmatically. by hint, by intimation, suggestively, ambiguously.
Foreign: German: Symbol; Greek: symbolon.
Phrases: the symbol is a riddle; the riddle of the sphinx; seeking its form.
Hegel definition: Symbolic art is the beginning of art, in nature and history, only its threshold, belonging especially to the East. Its symbol is an external existence given to contemplation which is to be understood in a wider and more universal sense, so that meaning and expression are distinct. Since the idea is still indeterminate and measureless it finds no wholly corresponding form and transcends its appearance, which gives it the character of sublimity.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· The Symbolic Form of Art
Hegel citations:
Symbol as such is an external existent given or immediately present to contemplation, which yet is to be understood not simply as it confronts us immediately on its own account, but in a wider and more universal sense.
— Aesthetics, The Symbolic Form of Art (tr. Knox)
But in this non-correspondence the Idea transcends its external existence instead of having blossomed or been perfectly enclosed in it.
— Aesthetics, The Symbolic Form of Art (tr. Knox)

Head: Unconscious Symbolism
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › β. The Forms of Art › a. Symbolic Art › i. Unconscious Symbolism
Gloss: Symbolism in which meaning and shape are joined without awareness of their difference.
Hegelian gloss: Unconscious symbolism, in which meaning and shape are joined without knowing their difference.
Nouns: unconscious symbolism; primitive symbolism, natural symbolism, unreflective symbolism, myth, mythical thinking, nature-symbol. unconscious symbolics, naive symbolism, instinctive symbol-making, the undistinguished unity, original symbolism.
Verbs: symbolize unconsciously, mythologize. symbolize unknowingly, fuse, mingle, conflate, intuit.
Adjective: unconscious, primitive, mythic, naive. unknowing, unwitting, unreflective, instinctive, original, unapprized†, unweeting†, weetless†. uninformed.
Adverbs: unconsciously, naively. unknowingly, unwittingly.
Foreign: French: bricolage [Lévi-Strauss], pensée sauvage [wild thought] [Lévi-Strauss], science du concret [science of the concrete] [Lévi-Strauss], mythème [mytheme] [Lévi-Strauss].
Phrases: the myth-making mind; without knowing it; half-known.
Hegel definition: Unconscious symbolism is the first shape of the symbolic, not yet known as mere image and simile. It rests on an immediate unification of universal spiritual meaning with a sensuous shape that is as adequate as inadequate, with no consciousness yet of their incongruity, although the link must already be formed by imagination and art. Its first presupposition is the immediate unity of the absolute with its existence in nature and human activity.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· The Symbolic Form of Art › Unconscious Symbolism
Hegel citations:
The symbol on the one hand has its basis in the immediate unification of the universal and therefore spiritual meaning with the sensuous shape which is just as adequate as inadequate; but as yet there is no consciousness of their incongruity.
— Aesthetics, The Symbolic Form of Art › Unconscious Symbolism (tr. Knox)
Thus the first presupposition of the symbolical's coming into being is precisely that immediate unity of the Absolute with its existence in the phenomenal world, a unity not produced by art but found, without art, in actual natural objects and human activities.
— Aesthetics, The Symbolic Form of Art › Unconscious Symbolism (tr. Knox)

Head: Immediate Unity of Meaning and Shape (Zoroastrian)
Head (German): Unmittelbare Einheit von Bedeutung und Gestalt
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › β. The Forms of Art › a. Symbolic Art › i. Unconscious Symbolism › 1. Immediate Unity of Meaning and Shape (Zoroastrian)
Gloss: Symbolism in which the divine is directly one with a natural thing, as light.
Hegelian gloss: The immediate unity of meaning and shape, as Zoroastrian light, which is at once the divine and natural light.
Nouns: immediate unity of meaning and shape; Zoroastrian symbolism, light as god, fire symbolism, the sun, Ahura Mazda as light, Avesta. immediate unity, immediate identity of meaning and shape, the divine as light, the Zend religion, Ormuzd, the natural as the absolute, unseparated meaning.
Verbs: shine, identify, worship. coincide, be one, unite, fuse.
Adjective: immediate, luminous, Zoroastrian, literal. unseparated, undivided, identical, one, direct.
Adverbs: immediately, literally. directly, at one, without separation.
Foreign: Avestan: ātar [fire].
Phrases: light is the good; light is the god; the sacred fire.
Hegel definition: The immediate unity of meaning and shape is the intuition in which what appears is itself taken to be the immediate presence of the absolute, with no distinction of inner and outer, soul and body, meaning and form. Its most thoroughgoing instance is the religion of Zoroaster, preserved in the Zend-Avesta, which takes the light of nature, sun, stars and fire, to be the absolute itself, without separating the divinity from the light.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· The Symbolic Form of Art › Unconscious Symbolism › Immediate Unity of Meaning and Shape
Hegel citations:
The bodily and the sensuous, the natural and the human, is not merely an expression of a meaning to be distinguished therefrom; on the contrary, what appears is itself apprehended as the immediate actuality and presence of the Absolute.
— Aesthetics, Unconscious Symbolism › Immediate Unity of Meaning and Shape (tr. Knox)
The religion of Zoroaster, namely, takes light as it exists in nature—the sun, the stars, fire in its luminosity and flames—to be the Absolute, without explicitly separating this divinity from light
— Aesthetics, Unconscious Symbolism › Immediate Unity of Meaning and Shape (tr. Knox)

Head: Fantastic Symbolism (Indian)
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › β. The Forms of Art › a. Symbolic Art › i. Unconscious Symbolism › 2. Fantastic Symbolism (Indian)
Gloss: Symbolism in which meaning and shape are joined in extravagant and fantastic forms.
Hegelian gloss: The Indian fantastic, which drives natural shapes into the measureless to reach the divine.
Nouns: fantastic symbolism; Indian symbolism, the fantastic, the grotesque, the monstrous, many-armed gods, the extravagant, exaggeration, boundlessness, Hindu iconography, avatars, mythic profusion. extravagance, monstrosity, distortion, measurelessness, the colossal, riot of imagination.
Verbs: exaggerate, multiply, fantasize, extravagate. distort, inflate, run riot, ferment.
Adjective: fantastic, grotesque, monstrous, extravagant, boundless, profuse, many-armed. unusual, uncommon, rare, curious, odd, extraordinary, strange, wonderful &c H0672, denaturalized†. whimsical, fanciful, bizarre, outlandish. distorted, out of shape, irregular, asymmetric, deformed, misshapen, androgynal†, adelomorphous†, monoclinous†, unsymmetric†, crump†, misproportioned†, simous†, taliped†, talipedic†. exuberant, inordinate, superabundant, excessive, lavish. outre, preposterous, bombastic, inflated. vast, immense, enormous, overgrown. fantastical, exaggerated, wild, measureless. increased, asymmetrical, magnified.
Adverbs: fantastically, extravagantly, a outrance†. grotesquely, without measure.
Foreign: Sanskrit: Trimūrti, avatāra, Mahābhārata.
Phrases: im rastlos raschen Überspringen von einem Extrem ins andere [Ger.] [Hegel, Aesthetics, on Indian art]; a thousand arms; out of all measure.
Hegel definition: Fantastic symbolism, characteristic of India, arises when consciousness leaves the immediate identity of the absolute with existence and meaning and shape come into conflict, which it tries to heal by joining them fancifully. A fermenting imagination leaps without rest from sensuous particulars to the most general meanings and back, taking the contradiction itself for unification, so that true beauty cannot be sought in this murky confusion.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· The Symbolic Form of Art › Unconscious Symbolism › Fantastic Symbolism
Hegel citations:
It is with this attempt alone that there arises the proper need for art.
— Aesthetics, Unconscious Symbolism › Fantastic Symbolism (tr. Knox)
True beauty, therefore, we may not seek in this field of murky confusion.
— Aesthetics, Unconscious Symbolism › Fantastic Symbolism (tr. Knox)

Head: Symbolism Proper (Egyptian)
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › β. The Forms of Art › a. Symbolic Art › i. Unconscious Symbolism › 3. Symbolism Proper (Egyptian)
Gloss: Symbolism in which meaning is hidden in shape, as in the pyramids and the sphinx.
Hegelian gloss: Symbolism proper, Egyptian, the riddle of the sphinx, where the meaning is sought in an obscure shape.
Nouns: symbolism proper; Egyptian symbolism, hieroglyph, sphinx, pyramid, mummy, the cult of the dead, Isis and Osiris, the phoenix, riddle, enigma, the symbol of symbols. puzzle, rebus. sealed book. the symbol proper, the genuine symbol, the hidden meaning, the mystery, the riddle in stone, the labyrinth, Memnon. hieroglyphics.
Verbs: encode, embalm, enshrine, riddle. symbolize, hide, conceal, veil, hint, intimate, enshroud.
Adjective: Egyptian, hieroglyphic, enigmatic, cryptic, sphinxlike. hidden, secret, recondite, mystic, cabalistic, occult, dark, acroamatical†, cryptical†. enigmatical, indecipherable. symbolic, mysterious, veiled.
Adverbs: enigmatically, in hieroglyphs. symbolically, in mystery, under a veil.
Foreign: Greek: hieroglyphika.
Phrases: sie ist das Symbol gleichsam des Symbolischen selber [Ger.] [Hegel, Aesthetics, on the Sphinx]; the riddle of the Sphinx; written in hieroglyphs.
Hegel definition: Symbolism proper, in Egypt, requires that meaning become explicitly free from the immediate sensuous shape, the natural being grasped as negative and to be superseded, and this negative accepted as a moment within the divine itself. Egypt is the country of symbols, which sets spirit the task of deciphering itself without attaining it; its works are riddles, and the sphinx is the symbol of the symbolic itself.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· The Symbolic Form of Art › Unconscious Symbolism › Symbolism Proper
Hegel citations:
This liberation can only take place in so far as the sensuous and natural is apprehended and envisaged in itself as negative, as what is to be, and has been, superseded.
— Aesthetics, Unconscious Symbolism › Symbolism Proper (tr. Knox)
The works of Egyptian art in their mysterious symbolism are therefore riddles; the objective riddle par excellence.
— Aesthetics, Unconscious Symbolism › Symbolism Proper (tr. Knox)

Head: The Symbolism of the Sublime
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › β. The Forms of Art › a. Symbolic Art › ii. The Symbolism of the Sublime
Gloss: Symbolism in which the divine exceeds every shape given to it.
Hegelian gloss: The symbolism of the sublime, in which the meaning is the one substance that exceeds every shape.
Nouns: the symbolism of the sublime; the sublime, grandeur, majesty, awe, the infinite, the overwhelming, the inexpressible. dignity, stateliness, solemnity, splendor, nobility, sublimity. the inadequacy of all shape, the beyond of form, the ineffable, the unfigurable, transcendence, excess, pantheism and the sublime.
Verbs: exalt, overwhelm, awe, tower, transcend. soar, know no bounds. exceed, surpass, overflow, outstrip, elude.
Adjective: sublime, majestic, grand, awe-inspiring, awesome, exalted, lofty, overwhelming. noble, high-minded, magnanimous. august, dignified, majestic &c H0537. high, elevated, towering, soaring, elevated &c H0238, insessorial†. imposing, solemn, transcendent, sacred. superb, magnificent. ineffable, exceeding, immeasurable. impressive.
Adverbs: sublimely, majestically. beyond all shape, beyond measure.
Foreign: German: das Erhabene, erhaben; Latin: sublimitas, sublimis; Greek: hypsos [Longinus], hypsēlos; Arabic: jalāl [majesty, sublimity]; Sanskrit: adbhuta [wonder].
Phrases: the sublime is the echo of a great soul [Longinus]; the heavens declare the glory of God.
Hegel definition: The symbolism of the sublime lifts the absolute above every immediate existent and so first purifies meaning from the sensuous present, a liberation that is abstract yet founds the life of spirit. The meaning is the one substance, grasped only by pure thought, which cannot find adequate shape in anything external. Hegel takes up Kant, for whom the sublime lies in the mind and not in any sensuous form.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· The Symbolic Form of Art › Symbolism of the Sublime
Hegel citations:
Sublimity lifts the Absolute above every immediate existent and therefore brings about the liberation which, though abstract at first, is at least the foundation of the spirit.
— Aesthetics, The Symbolic Form of Art › Symbolism of the Sublime (tr. Knox)
The sublime in general is the attempt to express the infinite, without finding in the sphere of phenomena an object which proves adequate for this representation.
— Aesthetics, The Symbolic Form of Art › Symbolism of the Sublime (tr. Knox)

Head: The Pantheism of Art
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › β. The Forms of Art › a. Symbolic Art › ii. The Symbolism of the Sublime › 1. The Pantheism of Art
Gloss: Art that sees the one divine in all things.
Hegelian gloss: The affirmative sublime, the pantheism of Indian and Persian poetry and of Christian mysticism.
Nouns: the pantheism of art; the One in all things. artistic pantheism, pantheistic poetry, the all-one, the divine in all, the immanence of the One.
Verbs: merge, dissolve, unite, love mystically. pervade, immerse, lose oneself, see God in all.
Adjective: pantheistic, mystical, devotional. immanent, all-pervading, God-intoxicated.
Adverbs: mystically, in all things. pantheistically.
Foreign: Arabic: waḥdat al-wujūd [unity of being], fanāʾ [annihilation in God], ʿishq [divine love]; Persian: Ḥāfiẓ; Sanskrit: the Bhagavad Gītā, tat tvam asi; German: Entbildung [the stripping away of images] [Eckhart], Gelassenheit [releasement] [Eckhart, Heidegger].
Phrases: God in all things; a world in a grain of sand.
Hegel definition: The pantheism of art is not the crude belief that every single thing is God, which no religion or philosophy holds, but the intuition of the all as one substance immanent in individuals, which vanish before it. Belonging primarily to the East, it sees the divine in the most excellent of things while passing beyond each, so that the substance rises sublime above them. Only poetry can express it, not visual art.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· The Symbolic Form of Art › Symbolism of the Sublime › The Pantheism of Art
Hegel citations:
The 'everything' in what has been called 'Pantheism' is therefore not this or that individual thing, but rather is 'everything' in the sense of the All, i.e. of the one substance which indeed is immanent in individuals
— Aesthetics, Symbolism of the Sublime › The Pantheism of Art (tr. Knox)
Such a way of looking at things can, on this account, be expressed artistically only in poetry, not in the visual arts
— Aesthetics, Symbolism of the Sublime › The Pantheism of Art (tr. Knox)

Head: Indian Poetry
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › β. The Forms of Art › a. Symbolic Art › ii. The Symbolism of the Sublime › 1. The Pantheism of Art › a. Indian Poetry
Gloss: The pantheism of Indian poetry, which finds the One in the best of every kind of thing.
Hegelian gloss: Die indische Poesie: Krishna declaring himself the brightest of lights and the best of each kind, the one essence in all its many shapes.
Nouns: Indian poetry. Indian pantheism. the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna, the Vedas, the Upanishads, Brahman, the One in all, the best of each kind.
Phrases: aham ātmā guḍākeśa sarvabhūtāśayasthitaḥ [Skt.] [Bhagavad Gita 10.20]; I am the Spirit seated deep in every creature's heart [Bhagavad Gita 10.20, tr. Arnold].
Hegel definition: Indian poetry offers the first example of pantheistic poetry.
