Its supreme divinity is the most abstract unity, specified in particular gods who revert into Brahma, the one permanent foundation of everything. In the Bhagavad Gita Krishna declares himself the origin and destruction of the whole world, the taste in water and the splendour of sun and moon, immanent in all things and yet transcending each.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· The Symbolic Form of Art › Symbolism of the Sublime › The Pantheism of Art › Indian Poetry
Hegel citations:
Thus it is already clear that this universal constitutes the one permanent and self-identical foundation of everything.
— Aesthetics, The Pantheism of Art › Indian Poetry (tr. Knox)
Here such a substantial unity is expressed in the most striking way, in respect both of immanence in what is present and also transcendence over everything individual.
— Aesthetics, The Pantheism of Art › Indian Poetry (tr. Knox)

Head: Persian Poetry
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › β. The Forms of Art › a. Symbolic Art › ii. The Symbolism of the Sublime › 1. The Pantheism of Art › b. Persian Poetry
Gloss: The Persian mystical poetry of Rumi and Hafez, in which the self gives itself up to the divine beloved in joy.
Hegelian gloss: Die mohammedanische Poesie: in Jalāl al-Dīn Rūmī and Hafez the subject gives itself to the One in blissful, intoxicated love, the rose and the nightingale.
Nouns: Persian poetry. Sufi poetry, Rumi, Jalāl al-Dīn Rūmī, Hafez, the beloved, the rose and the nightingale, Persian pantheism, Mohammedan mysticism, Rūmī, Hafiz, Jāmī. Sufism.
Verbs: intoxicate.
Adjective: Sufi, Sufic, ecstatic.
Hegel definition: Mohammedan poetry, above all Persian, develops oriental pantheism more freely and subjectively. The poet who longs to see the divine in everything sacrifices personality, and in the enlarged inner life grows serene, free and blissful, intimate with natural things, the beloved and the tavern. Jalal-ed-Din Rumi is praised above all, and this happy depth of feeling contrasts with the wistful inwardness of the northern romantic.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· The Symbolic Form of Art › Symbolism of the Sublime › The Pantheism of Art › Mohammedan Poetry
Hegel citations:
Since the poet longs to descry the Divine in everything and does actually descry it, in face of it he now sacrifices his own personality, but he all the same apprehends the immanence of the Divine in his inner being thus enlarged and freed; and therefore there grows in him that serene inwardness, that free good fortune, that riotous bliss characteristic of the Oriental who, in renouncing his own particularity, immerses himself entirely in the Eternal and the Absolute
— Aesthetics, The Pantheism of Art › Mohammedan Poetry (tr. Knox)
On the other hand, a free, happy, depth of feeling is characteristic of Orientals, especially the Mohammedan Persians, who openly and cheerfully sacrifice their entire selves to God and to everything praiseworthy
— Aesthetics, The Pantheism of Art › Mohammedan Poetry (tr. Knox)

Head: Christian Mysticism
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › β. The Forms of Art › a. Symbolic Art › ii. The Symbolism of the Sublime › 1. The Pantheism of Art › c. Christian Mysticism
Gloss: The mysticism of Eckhart and Angelus Silesius, in which God and soul are found in one another.
Hegelian gloss: Die christliche Mystik: in Angelus Silesius and Eckhart the identity of God and the soul is expressed with boldness and depth of intuition.
Nouns: Christian mysticism. Angelus Silesius, Meister Eckhart, mystical union. the Cherubinic Wanderer, Jakob Böhme, the birth of God in the soul, the ground of the soul.
Phrases: the rose is without why [Angelus Silesius]; die Ros' ist ohn warum [Ger.] [Angelus Silesius]; ich weiß, daß ohne mich Gott nicht ein Nu kann leben [Ger.] [Angelus Silesius].
Hegel definition: Christian mysticism affords pantheistic unity as felt by the subject, who senses God present in consciousness and its unity with God; it developed this more subjective way within Christianity. Hegel cites Angelus Silesius, who expressed with the greatest audacity and depth of intuition the substantial existence of God in things and the union of self and God. Eastern pantheism stresses instead contemplating the one substance in all phenomena.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· The Symbolic Form of Art › Symbolism of the Sublime › The Pantheism of Art › Christian Mysticism
Hegel citations:
Now the pantheistic unity, emphasized in relation to the subject who feels himself in this unity with God and senses God as this presence in subjective consciousness, is afforded in general by mysticism, developed as it has been in this more subjective way within Christianity too.
— Aesthetics, The Pantheism of Art › Christian Mysticism (tr. Knox)
As an example I will only cite Angelus Silesius, who, with the greatest audacity and depth of intuition and feeling, has expressed in a wonderfully mystical power of representation the substantial existence of God in things and the unification of the self with God and of God with human subjectivity.
— Aesthetics, The Pantheism of Art › Christian Mysticism (tr. Knox)

Head: The Art of the Sublime (Hebrew Poetry)
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › β. The Forms of Art › a. Symbolic Art › ii. The Symbolism of the Sublime › 2. The Art of the Sublime (Hebrew Poetry)
Gloss: Art that exalts the one God above all creation.
Hegelian gloss: The negative sublime of Hebrew poetry, where God's power is praised and the creature is nothing before him.
Nouns: the art of the sublime; Hebrew poetry, the Psalms, the prophets, Job, the creator God, praise, nothingness of creatures, divine majesty. sublime art, sacred poetry, the nullity of the creature, the glory of God, the praise of the Lord, creation as accident, the one Lord. psalmody.
Verbs: praise, exalt, glorify, magnify, humble. give thanks, bless, sing praises. laud, eulogize, extol, belaud†. honor, dignify, sing praises to &c H0535, aggrandize. abase.
Adjective: sublime, psalmic, prophetic, exalted, majestic. transcendent, sacred. august, grand, majestic &c H0537. lofty, Hebraic, hymnic.
Adverbs: sublimely, in praise. exaltedly, to the glory of God.
Foreign: Hebrew: Tehillim [Psalms], kavod [glory].
Phrases: let there be light: and there was light [Bible]; what is man, that thou art mindful of him? [Bible]; vanity of vanities.
Hegel definition: The art of the sublime in the strict sense, Hebrew poetry, grasps the one substance as pure inwardness and might, independent of finitude: God is imageless, and the world, however splendid, is posited as negative, created, subject to his power and serving him. External existence is degraded before the substance, and this is the only way the shapeless God can be illustrated. In the ideal, by contrast, inner and outer pervade each other.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· The Symbolic Form of Art › Symbolism of the Sublime › The Art of the Sublime
Hegel citations:
Only through this intuition of the being of God as the purely spiritual and imageless, contrasted with the mundane and the natural, is spirit completely wrested from nature and sense and released from existence in the finite.
— Aesthetics, Symbolism of the Sublime › The Art of the Sublime (tr. Knox)
In sublimity, on the contrary, external existence, in which the substance is brought before contemplation, is degraded in comparison with the substance, since this degradation and servitude is the one and only way whereby the one God can be illustrated in art
— Aesthetics, Symbolism of the Sublime › The Art of the Sublime (tr. Knox)

Head: Conscious Symbolism of the Comparative Art-Form
Head (German): Die bewusste Symbolik der vergleichenden Kunstform
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › β. The Forms of Art › a. Symbolic Art › iii. Conscious Symbolism of the Comparative Art-Form
Gloss: Symbolism in which meaning and shape are knowingly compared.
Hegelian gloss: The conscious symbolism of comparison, in which the separation of meaning and shape is known and their joining is the poet's act.
Nouns: conscious symbolism of the comparative art-form; comparison, simile, likeness, conscious analogy, figurative art, deliberate symbolism. conscious symbolism, comparative art, the comparative form, deliberate comparison, the known separation of meaning and shape, wit, ingenuity, the subordinate symbolic forms. figuration.
Verbs: compare, liken, figure. relate, juxtapose, set side by side.
Adjective: comparative, figurative, analogical, deliberate. conscious, knowing, intentional, witty.
Adverbs: comparatively, by comparison. consciously, knowingly, deliberately.
Foreign: French: comparaison; Greek: synkrisis, antithesis, parathesis; Italian: paragone; Latin: comparatio, contrapositum, adpositum.
Phrases: as it were; compare and contrast.
Hegel definition: Conscious symbolism, the comparative form of art, is that in which the meaning is not only explicitly known but expressly posited as different from the external way of representing it. Their relation no longer rests in the meaning itself but is a more or less accidental connection produced by the poet's subjective activity, wit and invention, which may start either from something perceived or from an inner idea.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· The Symbolic Form of Art › Conscious Symbolism of the Comparative Art-Form
Hegel citations:
By conscious symbolism, I mean, we are to understand that the meaning is not only explicitly known but is expressly posited as different from the external way in which it is represented.
— Aesthetics, The Symbolic Form of Art › Conscious Symbolism of the Comparative Art-Form (tr. Knox)
[O]n the contrary, it becomes a more or less accidental concatenation produced by the subjective activity of the poet, by the immersion of his spirit in an external existent, by his wit and his invention in general.
— Aesthetics, The Symbolic Form of Art › Conscious Symbolism of the Comparative Art-Form (tr. Knox)

Head: Comparisons Starting from the External Object
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › β. The Forms of Art › a. Symbolic Art › iii. Conscious Symbolism of the Comparative Art-Form › 1. Comparisons Starting from the External Object
Gloss: Comparison that begins from an outward object and draws a meaning from it.
Hegelian gloss: Comparisons that begin from an outer object and draw a meaning from it.
Nouns: comparisons starting from the external object; fable, parable, proverb, apologue, metamorphosis; external likeness. figure, trope, metaphor, figurativeness, image, imagery. comparison from the object, the outward object as starting point, the given case, the natural occurrence, the lesson drawn, fable parable and proverb, application, moral. exemplum.
Verbs: compare, illustrate, moralize. draw a meaning, interpret, apply, read into, extract.
Adjective: illustrative, exemplary, moralizing. interpretive, applied, object-based.
Adverbs: by example. from the object, by application, from without inward.
Phrases: by way of illustration; to draw a lesson from; there's a moral in it.
Hegel definition: Comparisons originating from the external object begin with something perceived and draw a meaning from it. They comprise fable, then parable, apologue and proverb, and finally metamorphoses, subordinate and hybrid kinds that are hard to arrange into definite species. Generally imperfect, a mere search for true art, they are treated only in relation to the general forms of art and not as kinds of poetry.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· The Symbolic Form of Art › Conscious Symbolism of the Comparative Art-Form › Comparisons Originating from the External Object
Hegel citations:
But the kinds indicated belong to the praeambula or the symbolic form of art because they are generally imperfect and therefore a mere search for true art
— Aesthetics, Conscious Symbolism of the Comparative Art-Form › Comparisons Originating from the External Object (tr. Knox)
We will articulate these kinds of art with more precision by dealing first with fable, then with parable, apologue, and proverb, and finally by considering metamorphoses.
— Aesthetics, Conscious Symbolism of the Comparative Art-Form › Comparisons Originating from the External Object (tr. Knox)

Head: Fable
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › β. The Forms of Art › a. Symbolic Art › iii. Conscious Symbolism of the Comparative Art-Form › 1. Comparisons Starting from the External Object › a. Fable
Gloss: A short story that teaches a moral, often using animals.
Hegelian gloss: The fable, a natural event used to illustrate a universal moral truth.
Nouns: fable; beast fable, Aesop's fables, apologue, moral tale, parable; Aesop, La Fontaine, Panchatantra. fairy tale, nursery tale. animal tale, Phaedrus, Reynard the Fox, the fabulist.
Verbs: fable, moralize, tell a tale. point a moral, teach, relate.
Adjective: fabulous [in the old sense], allegorical, moral, didactic, Aesopian. Aesopic, apologal.
Adverbs: in fable. by fable, with a moral.
Foreign: Latin: fabula, fabula docet; Greek: mythos, ainos; Arabic: Kalīla wa-Dimna; Sanskrit: Pañcatantra, Hitopadeśa; Pali: Jātaka.
Phrases: the moral of the story; de te fabula narratur [Lat.] [the tale is told of you] [Horace]; sour grapes.
Hegel definition: A fable, in Aesop's original form, represents a relation or occurrence in nature, especially among animals, taken as it truly is and not invented at whim, so told that a general lesson for human life, chiefly its practical side, can be drawn from it. It is no longer a religious reading of nature as revealing the divine will but an everyday event yielding a maxim, warning or prudential rule.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· The Symbolic Form of Art › Conscious Symbolism of the Comparative Art-Form › Comparisons Originating from the External Object › Fable
Hegel citations:
In keeping with this definition, the genuine fable of Aesop is the representation of some situation or other in animate and inanimate nature, or of an event in the animal world not devised capriciously, as may be supposed, but taken as it actually is in the world and truly observed
— Aesthetics, Comparisons Originating from the External Object › Fable (tr. Knox)
Instead there is an entirely commonplace course of natural occurrences; from its detailed representation there can be abstracted, in a way we can understand, an ethical maxim, a warning, a doctrine, a prudential rule, and it is presented for the sake of this reflection and displayed to contemplation.
— Aesthetics, Comparisons Originating from the External Object › Fable (tr. Knox)

Head: Parable, Proverb, Apologue
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › β. The Forms of Art › a. Symbolic Art › iii. Conscious Symbolism of the Comparative Art-Form › 1. Comparisons Starting from the External Object › b. Parable, Proverb, Apologue
Gloss: A short story or saying that conveys a general truth.
Hegelian gloss: The parable, proverb and apologue, a common occurrence given a higher meaning.
Nouns: parable, proverb, apologue. trope, metaphor, simile, personification. reflection &c H0651, conclusion &c H0669, golden rule &c H0775, principle, profession of faith &c H0667, settled principle, accepted principle, formula. first principles, a priori fact, assumption &c H0667. axiom, theorem, scholium†, truism, postulate.
Adjective: phylacteric†, axiomatic.
Foreign: Latin: ipse dixit, principia, locus communis, indignatio; Greek: parabolē, topos, topēgoria, deinōsis; French: mot, lieu commun; Hebrew: mashal; Sanskrit: subhāṣita [well-said verse]; Chinese: chengyu [set idiom]; Korean: sokdam [proverb].
Hegel definition: Parable, proverb and apologue take up events from ordinary life and give them a deeper, more general meaning. Unlike the fable they look not to nature and animals but to familiar human doings. The parable enlarges a seemingly trivial case to suggest a deeper meaning; the proverb states the universal immediately in a particular case; the apologue brings out in the example itself the maxim it contains.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· The Symbolic Form of Art › Conscious Symbolism of the Comparative Art-Form › Comparisons Originating from the External Object › Parable, Proverb, Apologue
Hegel citations:
But at the same time parable is distinct from fable by reason of the fact that it looks for such occurrences not in nature and the animal world, but in human action and doings as everyone has them familiarly before his eyes
— Aesthetics, Comparisons Originating from the External Object › Parable, Proverb, Apologue (tr. Knox)
These are not comparisons where the universal meaning and the concrete phenomenon appear outside one another and contrasted with one another. The former is immediately expressed with the latter.
— Aesthetics, Comparisons Originating from the External Object › Parable, Proverb, Apologue (tr. Knox)

Head: Parable
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › β. The Forms of Art › a. Symbolic Art › iii. Conscious Symbolism of the Comparative Art-Form › 1. Comparisons Starting from the External Object › b. Parable, Proverb, Apologue › i. Parable
Gloss: A story of everyday life that points to a higher, general meaning.
Hegelian gloss: Die Parabel: an occurrence from ordinary life given a higher significance, so that the meaning is grasped through the familiar happening, as in the Gospel parables.
Nouns: parable. similitude, exemplum, moral tale. the prodigal son, the good Samaritan, story with a moral.
Verbs: exemplify, teach, point a moral.
Adjective: parabolic.
Adverbs: in a parable, in parables.
Phrases: the parable of the sower [Bible].
Hegel definition: A parable takes events from everyday human life and gives them a deeper and more general meaning, so as to make that meaning intelligible and perceptible through the occurrence. Unlike the fable it draws on human action, enlarging a case that seems trivial into something of general interest. Cyrus' two days of labour and feasting and the Gospel parable of the sower are examples.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· The Symbolic Form of Art › Conscious Symbolism of the Comparative Art-Form › Comparisons Originating from the External Object › Parable, Proverb, Apologue › Parable
Hegel citations:
Parable has with fable the general affinity that it takes up events drawn from the sphere of ordinary life but attributes to them a deeper and more general meaning with the aim of making this meaning intelligible and perceptible through this occurrence
— Aesthetics, Parable, Proverb, Apologue › Parable (tr. Knox)
The parable of the sower [in all the Synoptics], for example, is a story in itself trivial in content, and it is important only because of the comparison with the doctrine of the Kingdom of Heaven.
— Aesthetics, Parable, Proverb, Apologue › Parable (tr. Knox)

Head: Proverb
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › β. The Forms of Art › a. Symbolic Art › iii. Conscious Symbolism of the Comparative Art-Form › 1. Comparisons Starting from the External Object › b. Parable, Proverb, Apologue › ii. Proverb
Gloss: A short common saying, drawn from a single case, that holds good generally.
Hegelian gloss: Das Sprichwort: a single case taken from ordinary life and so stated that it carries a general meaning.
Nouns: proverb. adage, saw, maxim, aphorism, gnome, apophthegm, saying, dictum, byword. apothegm, sentence, motto, word, moral, phylactery, protasis†, periapt†, telesm†. received truth, wise maxim, sage maxim, received maxim, admitted maxim, recognized maxim, true saying, common saying, hackneyed saying, trite saying, commonplace saying.
Verbs: proverbialize, coin.
Adjective: proverbial, gnomic, aphoristic, sententious, apophthegmatic.
Adverbs: proverbially, as the saying goes, as the saying is, as they say, sententiously.
Phrases: a word to the wise.
Hegel definition: A proverb is a middle form that can be expanded into fable or apologue. It presents a single case, mostly from daily human life, which is to be taken in a universal meaning, as that one hand washes the other. Here universal and concrete appearance do not stand apart as in comparison, the one being immediately expressed with the other. Goethe composed many such aphorisms.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· The Symbolic Form of Art › Conscious Symbolism of the Comparative Art-Form › Comparisons Originating from the External Object › Parable, Proverb, Apologue › Proverbs
Hegel citations:
A middle stage within this sphere is formed by the proverb.
— Aesthetics, Parable, Proverb, Apologue › Proverbs (tr. Knox)
They adduce an individual case which is drawn for the most part from day-to-day human life, but which is then to be taken in a universal meaning.
— Aesthetics, Parable, Proverb, Apologue › Proverbs (tr. Knox)

Head: Apologue
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › β. The Forms of Art › a. Symbolic Art › iii. Conscious Symbolism of the Comparative Art-Form › 1. Comparisons Starting from the External Object › b. Parable, Proverb, Apologue › iii. Apologue
Gloss: A short tale used as an example to teach a moral, where the meaning is told openly.
Hegelian gloss: Der Apolog: a parable in which a single case is presented as an example of a general meaning that it does not merely signify but contains.
Nouns: apologue. deev†, lamia†. fairy tale, fable. lesson. beast fable, moral fable, didactic tale, example story.
Verbs: moralize, preach.
Adjective: didactic, moral.
Adverbs: by way of a moral.
Hegel definition: An apologue, or moral fable, may be seen as a parable that does not use the individual case merely as a simile to illustrate a universal meaning but expresses the maxim within that cloak, the maxim being contained in the case told as an example. Goethe's God and the Bayadere is one, and the narrative may end by giving its lesson without comparison.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· The Symbolic Form of Art › Conscious Symbolism of the Comparative Art-Form › Comparisons Originating from the External Object › Parable, Proverb, Apologue › Apologue
Hegel citations:
The apologue, thirdly, may be regarded as a parable which does not use the individual case merely as a simile to illustrate a universal meaning but in this cloak itself brings out and expresses the universal maxim—since the maxim is actually contained in the individual case which yet is recounted as only an individual example.
— Aesthetics, Parable, Proverb, Apologue › Apologue (tr. Knox)
In the apologue the narrative may be so conducted that its conclusion provides the lesson itself without any mere comparison
— Aesthetics, Parable, Proverb, Apologue › Apologue (tr. Knox)

Head: Metamorphoses
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › β. The Forms of Art › a. Symbolic Art › iii. Conscious Symbolism of the Comparative Art-Form › 1. Comparisons Starting from the External Object › c. Metamorphoses
Gloss: Stories of transformation from one shape into another.
Hegelian gloss: The metamorphoses, transformations of human beings into natural things.
Nouns: metamorphoses; transformation, metamorphosis, shape-shifting, transfiguration, Ovid's Metamorphoses, changes, transmutation, Daphne into laurel, Narcissus into flower. transmigration. shape-changing, change of form, Ovid, Daphne, Arachne, Niobe, the degradation into nature.
Verbs: metamorphose, transform, change shape, transmute, turn into. transfigure, transmogrify, transume†. change, shape-shift.
Adjective: metamorphic, transformative, shape-shifting, protean, Ovidian. transformed, transmuted.
Adverbs: in transformation. by transformation, in changed shape.
Foreign: Arabic: maskh [transformation]; Chinese: wuhua [the transformation of things; the butterfly dream] [Zhuangzi].
Phrases: in nova fert animus mutatas dicere formas corpora [Lat.] [Ovid]; changed into a tree; to change one's shape.
Hegel definition: Metamorphoses are symbolic and mythological tales that oppose natural to spiritual, giving a rock, animal, flower or spring the meaning of a degradation and punishment of a spiritual being who falls into guilt or endless grief, as Niobe weeps as stone. By distinguishing natural and spiritual they form the transition from symbolic mythology to mythology proper, in which natural content becomes gods of human shape.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· The Symbolic Form of Art › Conscious Symbolism of the Comparative Art-Form › Comparisons Originating from the External Object › Metamorphoses
Hegel citations:
The rock is not just stone but Niobe who weeps for her children.
— Aesthetics, Comparisons Originating from the External Object › Metamorphoses (tr. Knox)
The metamorphoses, on the contrary, make the essential distinction between the natural and the spiritual, and they form in this respect the transition from symbolic mythology to mythology strictly so-called
— Aesthetics, Comparisons Originating from the External Object › Metamorphoses (tr. Knox)

Head: Comparisons Starting from the Meaning
Head (German): Vergleichungen, die von der Bedeutung anfangen
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › β. The Forms of Art › a. Symbolic Art › iii. Conscious Symbolism of the Comparative Art-Form › 2. Comparisons Starting from the Meaning
Gloss: Comparison that begins from a meaning and finds an image for it.
Hegelian gloss: Comparisons that begin from a meaning and find an image to clothe it.
Nouns: comparisons starting from the meaning; riddle, allegory, metaphor, image, simile; meaning seeking an image. trope, metonymy [Gramm.], synecdoche [Sem.], figurativeness, imagery. similitude, allegory &c H0906. parallel, type &c H0906, image &c H0834. comparison from the meaning, the meaning as starting point, image-finding, illustration, figuration.
Verbs: figure, image, allegorize. illustrate, clothe, embody, exemplify.
Adjective: figurative, allegorical, metaphoric. metaphorical, typical, parabolic, allusive. illustrative, comparative, image-seeking.
Adverbs: figuratively. by illustration, from the meaning outward.
Phrases: the meaning comes first; to put it figuratively; in a manner of speaking.
Hegel definition: Comparisons that start from the meaning take general ideas, reflections, feelings or maxims and find in the concrete world a picture that makes the abstract content perceptible. Because the two sides are indifferent to each other, their link is subjectively made and shows itself as such, so that the art of the poet as maker stands out; in genuine works such images should be only accessories.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· The Symbolic Form of Art › Conscious Symbolism of the Comparative Art-Form › Comparisons which Start from the Meaning
Hegel citations:
Now if the meaning is in this way the starting-point, then the expression, the reality, appears as the means, drawn from the concrete world for the sake of making the meaning, as the abstract content, definitely picturable, visible, and perceptible.
— Aesthetics, Conscious Symbolism of the Comparative Art-Form › Comparisons which Start from the Meaning (tr. Knox)
Therefore their bearing on one another, not lying objectively in the nature of the case, is something manufactured subjectively which no longer conceals this subjective character but makes it recognizable through the manner of the representation.
— Aesthetics, Conscious Symbolism of the Comparative Art-Form › Comparisons which Start from the Meaning (tr. Knox)

Head: Riddle
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › β. The Forms of Art › a. Symbolic Art › iii. Conscious Symbolism of the Comparative Art-Form › 2. Comparisons Starting from the Meaning › a. Riddle
Gloss: A question or statement that hides its meaning.
Hegelian gloss: The riddle, a meaning concealed in features whose solution is outside them.
Nouns: riddle; enigma, puzzle, conundrum, rebus, charade, brain-teaser, mystery. nut to crack, logogriph†, Sphinx. paradox, puzzle &c H0662, sealed book. poser, dark saying.
Verbs: riddle, puzzle, perplex, mystify, pose, solve, guess. confound, bewilder. puzzle &c H0667. propound, unriddle.
Adjective: enigmatic, riddling, puzzling, cryptic, mysterious, sphinxlike. enigmatical, dark.
Adverbs: enigmatically, in riddles. darkly.
Foreign: Latin: aenigma; Greek: ainigma, griphos; Korean: susukkekki [riddle].
Phrases: the riddle of the Sphinx; a riddle wrapped in a mystery inside an enigma [Churchill]; to speak in riddles.
Hegel definition: A riddle belongs to conscious symbolism: its inventor knows the meaning completely and deliberately chooses a veiling shape through which it is to be guessed. Unlike the symbol proper, which stays an unsolved problem, it is wholly soluble. It joins scattered traits in a striking and apparently senseless way that points to a unity, the solving word, putting ingenuity to the test, and belongs especially to the art of speech.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· The Symbolic Form of Art › Conscious Symbolism of the Comparative Art-Form › Comparisons which Start from the Meaning › Riddle
Hegel citations:
But the riddle belongs to conscious symbolism and it is distinguished at once from the symbol, strictly so-called, by reason of the fact that the meaning is clearly and completely known to the inventor of the riddle; and the shape that veils it, through which the meaning is to be guessed, is therefore chosen deliberately for this semiveiling.
— Aesthetics, Comparisons which Start from the Meaning › Riddle (tr. Knox)
Symbols in the strict sense are, both before and after, unsolved problems, while the riddle is absolutely solved
— Aesthetics, Comparisons which Start from the Meaning › Riddle (tr. Knox)

Head: Allegory
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › β. The Forms of Art › a. Symbolic Art › iii. Conscious Symbolism of the Comparative Art-Form › 2. Comparisons Starting from the Meaning › b. Allegory
Gloss: The presentation of an abstract meaning through a personified figure.
Hegelian gloss: Allegory, an abstract meaning personified, the cold allegorical figure.
Nouns: allegory; extended metaphor, personification, figure, emblem, moral allegory, Pilgrim's Progress, Everyman, the Roman de la Rose. trope, metaphor, image, imagery. type, representation &c H0834. prosopopoeia, abstraction personified, allegorical figure, Justice with her scales, the frosty allegory.
Verbs: allegorize, personify, figure, emblematize. employ a metaphor, adumbrate, shadow forth, apply, allude to. embody.
Adjective: allegorical, emblematic, figurative, personified, moral. metaphorical, typical, parabolic, allusive. allegoric, abstract, cold.
Adverbs: allegorically. emblematically, in personified form.
Foreign: Greek: allegoria, psychomachia; Arabic: majāz [figurative speech]; Sanskrit: anyokti [allegorical speech]; Korean: pungyu [allegory].
Phrases: Justice is blind; to read between the lines; in the guise of.
Hegel definition: Allegory is the opposite of the riddle: it brings the qualities of a universal idea before our view through sensuous likenesses, aiming at complete clarity. It personifies abstractions such as justice, war or spring, but the subject remains an abstract idea with the empty form of subjectivity, without the individuality of a Greek god or a saint, so that it is rightly called frosty and cold.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· The Symbolic Form of Art › Conscious Symbolism of the Comparative Art-Form › Comparisons which Start from the Meaning › Allegory
Hegel citations:
The first concern of allegory therefore consists in personifying, and therefore conceiving as a subject, general abstract situations or qualities belonging to both the human and the natural world, e.g. religion, love, justice, discord, glory, war, peace, spring, summer, autumn, winter, death, fame.
— Aesthetics, Comparisons which Start from the Meaning › Allegory (tr. Knox)
It is therefore rightly said of allegory that it is frosty and cold and that, owing to the intellectual abstractness of its meanings, it is even in its invention rather an affair of the intellect than of concrete intuition and the heartfelt depth of imagination.
— Aesthetics, Comparisons which Start from the Meaning › Allegory (tr. Knox)

Head: Metaphor, Image, Simile
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › β. The Forms of Art › a. Symbolic Art › iii. Conscious Symbolism of the Comparative Art-Form › 2. Comparisons Starting from the Meaning › c. Metaphor, Image, Simile
Gloss: The expression of one thing in terms of another.
Hegelian gloss: The metaphor, image and simile, in which a meaning and its image are joined by the poet.
Nouns: metaphor, image, simile.
Verbs: employ a metaphor, personify, allegorize, adumbrate, shadow forth, apply, allude to.
Adjective: antithetical.
Foreign: Latin: translatio, conceptus; Greek: metaphora; French: facon de parler, subtilité ingénieuse, concept, idée, pensée, représentation; Arabic: istiʿāra [metaphor]; Sanskrit: rūpaka [metaphor]; Italian: concetto [conceit], argutezza [the wit of conceits] [Tesauro]; Spanish: agudeza [Gracián]; German: Begriff.
Phrases: mutato nomine de te fabula narratur [Lat.] [Horace].
Hegel definition: Metaphor, image and simile make up the figurative sphere, uniting the clarity of allegory with the pleasure of the riddle. A meaning clearly before the mind is illustrated through a cognate external expression, without any riddle to be solved first, so that it shines through perfectly. In these forms the poet joins meaning and image, with the two sides separated to different degrees.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· The Symbolic Form of Art › Conscious Symbolism of the Comparative Art-Form › Comparisons which Start from the Meaning › Metaphor, Image, Simile
Hegel citations:
Now the figurative unites the clarity of the allegorical with the pleasantry of the riddle.
— Aesthetics, Comparisons which Start from the Meaning › Metaphor, Image, Simile (tr. Knox)
The meaning clearly confronting our minds is illustrated in the shape of some cognate external expression, yet so that thereby no problems arise which have first to be deciphered; what does arise is a figurative expression through which the envisaged meaning shines in perfect clarity and at once makes plain what it is.
— Aesthetics, Comparisons which Start from the Meaning › Metaphor, Image, Simile (tr. Knox)

Head: Metaphor
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › β. The Forms of Art › a. Symbolic Art › iii. Conscious Symbolism of the Comparative Art-Form › 2. Comparisons Starting from the Meaning › c. Metaphor, Image, Simile › i. Metaphor
Gloss: A comparison compressed into a single word or phrase, the image put in place of the thing itself.
Hegelian gloss: Die Metapher: an abbreviated comparison, in which image and meaning are not set apart but only the image is given and the meaning is read from it.
Nouns: metaphor. trope, figure, kenning, conceit, transference. phrase &c H0662, enallage†, catachresis†, metonymy [Gramm.], synecdoche [Sem.], autonomasia†, irony, figurativeness, metalepsis†, anagoge†, personification, prosopopoeia†, allegory, apologue†, parable, fable, allusion, adumbration, application. figure of speech, way of speaking, colloquialism. exaggeration, hyperbole &c H0662.
Verbs: metaphorize, figure. transfer.
Adjective: metaphorical, figurative, tropical [in the rhetorical sense]. catachrestical†, typical, tralatitious†, parabolic, allegorical, allusive, anagogical†, ironical, colloquial.
Adverbs: metaphorically, figuratively, so to speak. so to say, so to express oneself, as it were.
Phrases: all the world's a stage [As You Like It]; a figure of speech.
Hegel definition: Metaphor is implicitly already a simile, an entirely compressed and abbreviated comparison that does not set image and meaning against each other but presents the image alone, extinguishing its literal sense and letting the intended meaning be recognized at once from the context, as in a sea of tears. Its meaning thus has only incidental artistic standing, as an adornment.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· The Symbolic Form of Art › Conscious Symbolism of the Comparative Art-Form › Comparisons which Start from the Meaning › Metaphor, Image, Simile › Metaphor
Hegel citations:
The metaphorical expression, that is, names only one side, the image; but in the connection in which the image is used, the meaning proper which is intended is so near the surface that it is immediately given at the same time, as it were without direct separation from the image.
— Aesthetics, Metaphor, Image, Simile › Metaphor (tr. Knox)
It is an entirely compressed and abbreviated comparison, in that it does not oppose image and meaning to one another but presents the image alone
— Aesthetics, Metaphor, Image, Simile › Metaphor (tr. Knox)

Head: Image
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › β. The Forms of Art › a. Symbolic Art › iii. Conscious Symbolism of the Comparative Art-Form › 2. Comparisons Starting from the Meaning › c. Metaphor, Image, Simile › ii. Image
Gloss: A fuller picture drawn from another sphere and set out for itself to show the meaning.
Hegelian gloss: Das Bild: a developed metaphor, in which a whole situation from another sphere is portrayed to express a meaning that is not itself named.
Nouns: image. imagery. parallel, type, image &c H0834. picture, emblem, poetic image, word-picture, extended metaphor.
Verbs: image.
Adjective: imagistic.
Hegel definition: An image stands between metaphor and simile, a metaphor extended in which the meaning is not separately set against the object compared. It joins two independent situations so that one supplies the meaning made intelligible by the picture of the other, as Goethe's poem on Mahomet portrays the prophet's rise through a spring swelling into a mighty river, only the title showing the meaning.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· The Symbolic Form of Art › Conscious Symbolism of the Comparative Art-Form › Comparisons which Start from the Meaning › Metaphor, Image, Simile › Image
Hegel citations:
For it has such a close affinity with metaphor that it is strictly only a metaphor in extenso which therefore now acquires in turn a great resemblance to simile, but with this difference, namely that, in the image as such, the meaning is not explicitly separated out and contrasted with the concrete external object expressly compared with it.
— Aesthetics, Metaphor, Image, Simile › Image (tr. Knox)
An image occurs especially when two phenomena or situations (more or less independent when taken by themselves) are unified, so that one situation affords the meaning which is to be made intelligible by the image of the other.
— Aesthetics, Metaphor, Image, Simile › Image (tr. Knox)

Head: Simile
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › β. The Forms of Art › a. Symbolic Art › iii. Conscious Symbolism of the Comparative Art-Form › 2. Comparisons Starting from the Meaning › c. Metaphor, Image, Simile › iii. Simile
Gloss: A comparison stated openly with "like" or "as", setting the image beside the meaning.
Hegelian gloss: Das Gleichnis: image and meaning both expressly set out side by side, the poet lingering on the likeness, as in Homer's similes.
Nouns: simile. comparison, likeness, similitude, analogy. the epic simile, Homeric simile.
Verbs: liken, compare.
Adjective: analogical, similitive.
Adverbs: by way of likeness.
Phrases: my love is like a red, red rose [Burns].
Hegel definition: Simile sets image and meaning entirely apart, each presented by itself and then related through the likeness of their content. It may seem idle repetition and wearisome superfluity, since the meaning is already explicit. Its proper purpose lies in the poet's imagination, which, however clear about the subject, is driven to give it a concrete shape and so displays its own boldness.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· The Symbolic Form of Art › Conscious Symbolism of the Comparative Art-Form › Comparisons which Start from the Meaning › Metaphor, Image, Simile › Simile
Hegel citations:
In simile, on the contrary, both sides, image and meaning, are completely severed
— Aesthetics, Metaphor, Image, Simile › Simile (tr. Knox)
However clearly he makes himself aware of the subject-matter which he intends to express, however far he has brought this subject home to his mind in its more abstract universality and has expressed it [to himself] in this universality, still he finds himself equally driven to seek a concrete shape for the subject and to make perceptible to himself in a sensuous appearance the meaning already before his mind.
— Aesthetics, Metaphor, Image, Simile › Simile (tr. Knox)

Head: Disappearance of the Symbolic Art-Form
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › β. The Forms of Art › a. Symbolic Art › iii. Conscious Symbolism of the Comparative Art-Form › 3. Disappearance of the Symbolic Art-Form
Gloss: The passing away of symbolic form.
Hegelian gloss: The disappearance of the symbolic form, when meaning and shape fall apart.
Nouns: disappearance of the symbolic art-form; the end of symbolism, the prosaic turn, didactic and descriptive poetry, the epigram. the end of the symbolic, the vanishing of the symbolic form, dissolution, decay, the falling apart of meaning and shape, the transition to classical art.
Verbs: dissolve, fade, prosify. disappear, vanish, pass away, fall apart, give way.
Adjective: prosaic, waning, transitional. vanishing, dissolving, disappearing.
Adverbs: prosaically. in dissolution, at the end, in passing.
Phrases: the symbol fades into prose; the meaning slips away; the end of the symbol.
Hegel definition: The disappearance of the symbolic form comes when meaning and shape are posited as wholly external to each other. In symbolic art they never fully interpenetrated, though some kinship held them; since in comparison only caprice joins them, the link becomes mere adornment, leaving on one side a ready-made meaning and on the other bare externality, in subordinate forms that show the symbolic destroying itself.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· The Symbolic Form of Art › Conscious Symbolism of the Comparative Art-Form › Disappearance of the Symbolic Form of Art
Hegel citations:
Yet if it is not the Concept of the thing itself but only caprice which brings together the meaning and the artistic shape, then both are to be posited as wholly external to one another, so that their association is an unrelated attachment to one another and a mere adornment of one side by the other.
— Aesthetics, Conscious Symbolism of the Comparative Art-Form › Disappearance of the Symbolic Form of Art (tr. Knox)
Therefore, as an appendix, we have here to treat of those subordinate forms of art which proceed from such a complete diremption of the factors belonging to genuine art and, in this absence of relation, expose the self-destruction of the symbolic.
— Aesthetics, Conscious Symbolism of the Comparative Art-Form › Disappearance of the Symbolic Form of Art (tr. Knox)

Head: Didactic Poetry
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › β. The Forms of Art › a. Symbolic Art › iii. Conscious Symbolism of the Comparative Art-Form › 3. Disappearance of the Symbolic Art-Form › a. Didactic Poetry
Gloss: Poetry that teaches.
Hegelian gloss: Didactic poetry, in which the meaning is given in prose and the art is only external ornament.
Nouns: didactic poetry; didactic verse, instructive poetry, Hesiod's Works and Days, Lucretius' De rerum natura, Virgil's Georgics, Pope's Essay on Man, moral verse. didactics, the didactic poem, instructive verse, teaching poem, gnomic poetry, the Georgics, De Rerum Natura, Works and Days, lesson, precept, instruction.
Verbs: instruct, teach, versify, moralize. educate, edify, enlighten &c H0662. inculcate, preach.
Adjective: didactic, instructive, moralizing, pedagogical, georgic. educational, doctrinal, instructional. preceptive, gnomic, sententious, edifying.
Adverbs: didactically. instructively, sententiously.
Foreign: Arabic: urjūza [didactic verse].
Phrases: utile dulci [Lat.] [the useful with the sweet] [Horace]; to point a moral; teaching in verse.
Hegel definition: Didactic poetry arises when a meaning is grasped on its own account, already fully formed in prose, and merely embellished externally with artistic ornament for instruction. It is not among the proper forms of art, since art can concern only externals such as metre, diction and episodes that stand beside the content and do not penetrate it. Early Greek philosophy, Hesiod, Lucretius and Virgil offer examples.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· The Symbolic Form of Art › Conscious Symbolism of the Comparative Art-Form › Disappearance of the Symbolic Form of Art › Didactic Poetry
Hegel citations:
Didactic poetry is not to be numbered amongst the proper forms of art.
— Aesthetics, Disappearance of the Symbolic Form of Art › Didactic Poetry (tr. Knox)
What has become prosaic in itself is not to be reshaped poetically; it can only be dressed up
— Aesthetics, Disappearance of the Symbolic Form of Art › Didactic Poetry (tr. Knox)

Head: Descriptive Poetry
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › β. The Forms of Art › a. Symbolic Art › iii. Conscious Symbolism of the Comparative Art-Form › 3. Disappearance of the Symbolic Art-Form › b. Descriptive Poetry
Gloss: Poetry that describes.
Hegelian gloss: Descriptive poetry, which describes external things without a meaning.
Nouns: descriptive poetry; descriptive verse, landscape poetry, nature poetry, topographical poetry, Thomson's Seasons. description, word-painting, depiction, portrayal, the descriptive poem, the seasons, the times of day.
Verbs: describe, depict, paint in words. represent, delineate, portray, figure, shadow forth. picture.
Adjective: descriptive, pictorial, topographical, scenic, pastoral, ekphrastic. depictive, picturesque, graphic.
Adverbs: descriptively, picturesquely. graphically, pictorially.
Foreign: Greek: ekphrasis; Chinese: shanshui shi [mountain-and-water poetry], tianyuan shi [fields-and-gardens poetry]; French: représentation; Latin: descriptio.
Phrases: ut pictura poesis [Lat.] [as painting, so poetry] [Horace]; to paint a picture.
Hegel definition: Descriptive poetry is the opposite of didactic: it starts from external things, natural surroundings, buildings, seasons and times of day, and sketches them in their ordinary appearance without penetrating them with spiritual meaning. Such sensuous content belongs only to the external side of art, which has a right to appear only as the reality of spirit, individuality and action, not as externality cut off from spirit.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· The Symbolic Form of Art › Conscious Symbolism of the Comparative Art-Form › Disappearance of the Symbolic Form of Art › Descriptive Poetry
Hegel citations:
[H]ere conversely the external material confronts us on its own account in its individuality and external appearance, not penetrated by spiritual meanings
— Aesthetics, Disappearance of the Symbolic Form of Art › Descriptive Poetry (tr. Knox)
Such a sensuous content belongs entirely to only one side of true art, namely to the external existence which in art has the right of appearing solely as the reality of spirit, of individuality and its actions and events on the stage of a surrounding world, but not of appearing on its own account as mere externality cut adrift from spirit.
— Aesthetics, Disappearance of the Symbolic Form of Art › Descriptive Poetry (tr. Knox)

Head: The Ancient Epigram
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › β. The Forms of Art › a. Symbolic Art › iii. Conscious Symbolism of the Comparative Art-Form › 3. Disappearance of the Symbolic Art-Form › c. The Ancient Epigram
Gloss: A short poem of inscription.
Hegelian gloss: The old epigram, an inscription on a thing, its explanation.
Nouns: the ancient epigram; epigram, inscription, epitaph, dedication, Greek Anthology, Martial, terse verse. epigraph, votive inscription, distich, Simonides, superscription.
Verbs: epigrammatize, inscribe, quip. dedicate, engrave, entitle.
Adjective: epigrammatic, terse, pithy, laconic, lapidary, significative†, significatory†. concise, brief, compressed, condensed, pointed, trenchant. inscriptional, epigraphic.
Adverbs: epigrammatically, pithily. tersely, in a distich.
Foreign: Greek: epigramma; Sanskrit: muktaka [single-stanza poem]; Chinese: jueju [quatrain]; Japanese: haiku.
Phrases: brevity is the soul of wit [Hamlet]; go tell the Spartans, stranger passing by [Simonides]; short and sweet.
Hegel definition: The ancient epigram follows from the one-sidedness of didactic and descriptive poetry, which art cannot retain without cancelling itself, so that external reality is again brought into relation with inwardly grasped meaning. It is an inscription on a thing that states what the object is, in a sentence about its meaning, joining abstract universal and concrete appearance more deeply than their mere juxtaposition.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· The Symbolic Form of Art › Conscious Symbolism of the Comparative Art-Form › Disappearance of the Symbolic Form of Art › The Ancient Epigram
Hegel citations:
Consequently, as it turns out, the didactic and the descriptive cannot be retained in this one-sidedness whereby art would be entirely cancelled, and once more we see external reality brought into relation with what is grasped inwardly as meaning, and the abstract universal with its concrete appearance.
— Aesthetics, Disappearance of the Symbolic Form of Art › The Ancient Epigram (tr. Knox)

Head: Classical Art
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › β. The Forms of Art › b. Classical Art
Gloss: Art in which meaning and shape are in perfect correspondence; the art of the human form.
Hegelian gloss: Art in which meaning and shape are adequate, the free spiritual individuality in human form: classical art.
Nouns: classical art; classicism, the classical ideal, Greek art, perfect unity of form and content, harmony, idealized human form, antiquity, the Antique, Hellenism. the classical form of art, the art of the ideal, the adequacy of form and content, the perfect correspondence, the human figure, plastic art, the beautiful.
Verbs: idealize, perfect, harmonize, classicize. correspond, embody, fit, humanize.
Adjective: classical, classic, Hellenic, ideal, harmonious, perfect, serene. adequate, plastic, anthropomorphic, Greek.
Adverbs: classically, in the classical manner. ideally, adequately, in perfect correspondence.
Foreign: French: classique, classicisme, néoclassique, néoclassicisme; German: klassik, Klassizismus; Italian: classicismo, neoclassico, neoclassicismo; Latin: classicus.
Phrases: Schöneres kann nicht sein und werden [Ger.] [Hegel, Aesthetics, on classical art]; noble simplicity and quiet grandeur [Winckelmann]; a classic; timeless beauty.
Hegel definition: Classical art is the centre of art: a self-enclosed, free totality uniting content with its wholly adequate shape, the reality coinciding with the concept of beauty that symbolic art strove for in vain. Its inner being is free, independent meaning that signifies itself, that is, spirit, which makes itself its own object and takes an external form identical with its inwardness, in the human shape.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· The Classical Form of Art
Hegel citations:
The centre of art is a unification, self-enclosed so as to be a free totality, a unification of the content with its entirely adequate shape.
— Aesthetics, The Classical Form of Art (tr. Knox)
For classical beauty has for its inner being the free independent meaning, i.e. not a meaning of this or that but what means [Bedeutende] itself
— Aesthetics, The Classical Form of Art (tr. Knox)

Head: The Process of Formation of Classical Art
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › β. The Forms of Art › b. Classical Art › i. The Process of Formation of Classical Art
Gloss: The development by which classical art arises.
Hegelian gloss: The process by which classical art arises, from the degradation of animal forms to the victory of the new gods.
Nouns: the process of formation of classical art; the emergence of classical art, the overcoming of the animal, theogony, the war of gods. the genesis of classical art, the coming-to-be, emergence, formation, development, shaping, the purification of the natural, the self-production of the classical.
Verbs: form, emerge, overcome. shape, arise, develop, purify, come to be.
Adjective: formative, emergent. genetic, developmental, nascent.
Adverbs: in formation. by degrees, in the making.
Phrases: from beast to god; the old order passes.
Hegel definition: The shaping of classical art is the process by which spirit withdraws into itself from nature, lifts itself above it and overcomes it, so that it can make nature a positive existence of its freedom. What it transcends is not bare nature but the symbolic form, with its gods seen in animals; invalidating and transforming this false link produces the ideal. Greek formation of foreign material is essentially negative transformation.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· The Classical Form of Art › The Process of Shaping the Classical Art-Form
Hegel citations:
The spirit must first withdraw into itself from nature, lift itself above it, and overcome it, before it can prevail in it without hindrance as in an element which cannot withstand it, and transform it into a positive existence of its own freedom.
— Aesthetics, The Classical Form of Art › The Process of Shaping the Classical Art-Form (tr. Knox)
It is by invalidating and transforming this false linkage that the Ideal first produces itself as the Ideal, and therefore has to develop within itself, as a factor belonging to itself, what is to be overcome.
— Aesthetics, The Classical Form of Art › The Process of Shaping the Classical Art-Form (tr. Knox)

Head: Degradation of the Animal
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › β. The Forms of Art › b. Classical Art › i. The Process of Formation of Classical Art › 1. Degradation of the Animal
Gloss: The lowering of the animal from divine status.
Hegelian gloss: The animal degraded from the divine: animal sacrifice, hunts, metamorphoses.
Nouns: degradation of the animal; demotion of the animal, the end of animal gods, animal sacrifice, metamorphosis as punishment, the beast subordinated. debasement of the animal, abasement, demotion, the animal as attribute, the hunt, the animal as degraded.
Verbs: degrade, demote, sacrifice, subordinate. debase, abase, lower, humble, embase†.
Adjective: degraded, demoted, subordinate. debased, abased, lowered, bestial, subhuman.
Adverbs: below the human. degradingly, as punishment, beneath the human.
Phrases: the beast made servant; dethroned; cast down.
Hegel definition: The degradation of the animal marks the passage to classical art: whereas Indians and Egyptians revered animals as visible presences of the divine, spirit's self-consciousness dispels respect for the dull inwardness of animal life, and this lowering of the animal world itself becomes the content of religious ideas and art, in animal sacrifice, hunts and metamorphoses.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· The Classical Form of Art › The Process of Shaping the Classical Art-Form › The Degradation of the Animal
Hegel citations:
The self-consciousness of spirit is what alone makes respect for the dark and dull inwardness of animal life disappear.
— Aesthetics, The Process of Shaping the Classical Art-Form › The Degradation of the Animal (tr. Knox)
Now the next step that we have to mention in connection with the transition to classical art consists in debasing the high dignity and position of the animal world and making this degradation itself into the content of religious ideas and artistic productions.
— Aesthetics, The Process of Shaping the Classical Art-Form › The Degradation of the Animal (tr. Knox)

Head: The Battle of the Old and New Gods
Head (German): Der Kampf der alten und neuen Götter
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › β. The Forms of Art › b. Classical Art › i. The Process of Formation of Classical Art › 2. The Battle of the Old and New Gods
Gloss: The struggle between the old nature-gods and the new gods of mind.
Hegelian gloss: The struggle of the old nature gods and the new spiritual gods, the Titans and the Olympians.
Nouns: the battle of the old and new gods; Titanomachy, Gigantomachy, the Titans, Cronus and Zeus, the Olympians victorious, theogony, Hesiod's Theogony, the overthrow of the elder gods. Tartarus, the pit beneath Hades, the prison of the Titans. the war of the gods, the Giants, Cronus, Uranus, Prometheus, the overthrow of the Titans, the victory of Zeus, nature-powers and spiritual gods.
Verbs: overthrow, war, supplant, succeed, depose, uncrown†. battle, dethrone, vanquish, subdue, hurl down, unthrone†, disenthrone†, disbench†.
Adjective: titanic, Olympian, theogonic, primeval, chthonic. warring, victorious, vanquished, dethroned.
Adverbs: in the war of the gods. in battle, in strife, victoriously.
Foreign: German: Götterdämmerung [twilight of the gods].
Phrases: Zeus overthrows Cronus; the war in heaven; Titans and Olympians.
Hegel definition: The battle of the old and new gods is the higher stage of the debasement of the natural: the genuine gods of classical art have free self-consciousness as individual spiritual powers, with knowledge and will, so that the human shape belongs to their very meaning. Mere personification of natural powers such as sun, sea and earth is insufficient, and the old nature gods must be overcome by the new spiritual ones.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· The Classical Form of Art › The Process of Shaping the Classical Art-Form › The Battle between the Old Gods and the New
Hegel citations:
[S]ince the genuine gods of classical art have for their inner character free self-consciousness as the self-reposing power of the individual spirit, they can also come into our view only as possessed of knowledge and will, i.e. as spiritual powers.
— Aesthetics, The Process of Shaping the Classical Art-Form › The Battle between the Old Gods and the New (tr. Knox)
In this way the human shape in which they are represented is not, as might be supposed, a mere form which is tacked on to their content purely externally by imagination, but is implied in the meaning, the content, the inner itself.
— Aesthetics, The Process of Shaping the Classical Art-Form › The Battle between the Old Gods and the New (tr. Knox)

Head: Positive Retention of Negated Features
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › β. The Forms of Art › b. Classical Art › i. The Process of Formation of Classical Art › 3. Positive Retention of Negated Features
Gloss: The keeping of features of the old gods in the new.
Hegelian gloss: The positive retention of the negated features, the mysteries, the old gods' place in the new.
Nouns: positive retention of negated features; survivals, vestiges, the old gods honoured, the Furies made Eumenides, the Erinyes become kindly ones, mysteries, assimilation, syncretism, misjoining†, misjoinder†. preservation of the old, retention, survival, vestige, residue, remnant, the old in the new, the natural basis preserved, the animal attribute. leftover.
Verbs: retain, honour, preserve, assimilate. keep, conserve, carry over, incorporate, sublate.
Adjective: residual, vestigial, preserved, assimilated. retained, surviving, sublated.
Adverbs: still honoured. in preserved form, as a vestige, positively.
Phrases: the Furies become the Kindly Ones [Aeschylus]; what survives.
Hegel definition: Positive retention of negated features means that despite the victory of the new gods the old ones remain in classical art, partly as before and partly transformed and still venerated. Unlike the jealous national God of the Jews, the Greek gods are particular divinities amid a group of others. The Mysteries were the first form in which the Greeks preserved the old gods, though no deep wisdom seems hidden in them.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· The Classical Form of Art › The Process of Shaping the Classical Art-Form › Affirmative Retention of the Negatived Features
Hegel citations:
Despite the victory of the new gods, however, the old ones now still remain in the classical art-form partly in their original form as considered up to this point, partly retained and venerated in a transformed shape.
— Aesthetics, The Process of Shaping the Classical Art-Form › Affirmative Retention of the Negatived Features (tr. Knox)
Now the first form in which we find the Greeks preserving the old gods is the Mysteries.
— Aesthetics, The Process of Shaping the Classical Art-Form › Affirmative Retention of the Negatived Features (tr. Knox)

Head: The Ideal of Classical Art
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › β. The Forms of Art › b. Classical Art › ii. The Ideal of Classical Art
Gloss: The perfect union of mind and human form.
Hegelian gloss: The ideal of classical art: spirit and human body in perfect union.
Nouns: the ideal of classical art; the classical ideal, Olympian serenity, the perfect human form of the divine, idealized beauty, the statue of the god. the ideal of beauty, the union of spirit and human form, the anthropomorphic ideal, the beautiful individuality, the Greek gods, perfect embodiment, adequacy of form and content.
Verbs: idealize, perfect. unite, embody, humanize.
Adjective: ideal, Olympian, serene, perfect. anthropomorphic, embodied, adequate, classical.
Adverbs: ideally. perfectly, in human form.
Phrases: the gods in human form; noble simplicity and quiet grandeur; serene beauty.
Hegel definition: The ideal of classical art is attained where classical art actually achieves its innermost concept: it grasps the spiritual, drawing nature and its powers into its sphere, and gives it the human shape, deed and action, through which spirit shines clearly in complete freedom, the sensuous being no mere symbol but spirit's adequate existence. It is considered in its universality, its particular gods and their individuality.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· The Classical Form of Art › The Ideal of the Classical Form of Art
Hegel citations:
For the classical Ideal, our subject now, consists only in the fact that classical art actually attains and sets forth what constitutes its innermost Concept and essence.
— Aesthetics, The Classical Form of Art › The Ideal of the Classical Form of Art (tr. Knox)
[B]ut for its form it adopts the human shape, deed, and action, through which the spiritual shines clearly in complete freedom, making the sensuous shape its own, not at all as an external thing merely symbolically significant but as a reality which is the adequate existence of spirit.
— Aesthetics, The Classical Form of Art › The Ideal of the Classical Form of Art (tr. Knox)

Head: The Classical Ideal in General
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › β. The Forms of Art › b. Classical Art › ii. The Ideal of Classical Art › 1. The Classical Ideal in General
Gloss: The classical ideal in its general nature: serene, self-contained, perfect.
Hegelian gloss: The classical ideal in general: serene, blessed and yet with a breath of mourning.
Nouns: the classical ideal in general; ideal beauty, classical beauty, repose, serenity, blessed self-containment, a breath of mournfulness, idealized humanity. the nature of the classical ideal, self-containedness, blessedness, cheerfulness, perfection, completeness, calm grandeur, noble simplicity [Winckelmann]. Heiterkeit.
Verbs: idealize, repose. rest, perfect, complete, harmonize.
Adjective: ideal, serene, self-contained, tranquil, melancholy. reposeful, calm, blessed, harmonious.
Adverbs: serenely. perfectly, in repose, in general.
Foreign: French: calme, serein, silencieux, immobilité, sérénité, silence.
Phrases: in dieser Schmerzlichkeit des göttlichen Friedens [Ger.] [Hegel, Aesthetics, on the classical ideal]; die seligen Götter trauern gleichsam über ihre Seligkeit oder Leiblichkeit [Ger.] [Hegel, Aesthetics, on the classical ideal]; blessed and serene.
Hegel definition: The classical ideal in general arises through the free transformation of earlier material: it is generated by spirit in the inward being of poets and artists, who took tradition as ingredients and drew the proper content and form from their own spirit. Its gods are serene and blessed, yet the depth of that serenity holds the negative, and they seem to mourn over their blessedness and bodily form, where their coming fate can be read.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· The Classical Form of Art › The Ideal of the Classical Form of Art › The Ideal of Classical Art in General
Hegel citations:
[T]his Ideal is generated by the spirit and therefore has originated in the most inward and personal being of poets and artists who have created it with clear and free deliberateness
— Aesthetics, The Ideal of the Classical Form of Art › The Ideal of Classical Art in General (tr. Knox)
The blessed gods mourn as it were over their blessedness or their bodily form.
— Aesthetics, The Ideal of the Classical Form of Art › The Ideal of Classical Art in General (tr. Knox)

Head: The Circle of Particular Gods
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › β. The Forms of Art › b. Classical Art › ii. The Ideal of Classical Art › 2. The Circle of Particular Gods
Gloss: The gods as a family of distinct divine powers.
Hegelian gloss: The circle of particular gods, a plurality of spiritual powers.
Nouns: the circle of particular gods; the pantheon, the Olympians, Zeus, Hera, Athena, Apollo, Artemis, Aphrodite, Ares, Hermes, Hephaestus, Poseidon, Demeter, Dionysus, the twelve gods, arpents†. the Olympian circle, the family of gods, the divine household, polytheism, plurality of gods, the divine powers, Olympus.
Verbs: preside, rule, patronize. encircle, range, divide, assign, distribute, people.
Adjective: Olympian, polytheistic, divine, pantheonic. plural, manifold, familial, particular.
Adverbs: in the pantheon. in a circle, as a family, severally.
Foreign: Greek: dodekatheon.
Phrases: the twelve Olympians; a pantheon.
Hegel definition: The circle of particular gods follows because divinity made visible in immediate existence necessarily becomes many shapes: polytheism is essential to classical art. Each god is an independent individual, no mere allegory of a universal quality but a comprehensive totality bearing attributes of others, so that their blessedness is universal self-repose with power to act in many ways. They form no systematic whole.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· The Classical Form of Art › The Ideal of the Classical Form of Art › The Group of Particular Gods
Hegel citations:
Polytheism is absolutely essential to the principle of classical art
— Aesthetics, The Ideal of the Classical Form of Art › The Group of Particular Gods (tr. Knox)
The group of Greek gods is a plurality of individuals in which each single god, even if endowed with the specific character of a particular person, is still a comprehensive totality, containing also in itself the attribute of another god.
— Aesthetics, The Ideal of the Classical Form of Art › The Group of Particular Gods (tr. Knox)

Head: The Individuality of the Particular Gods
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › β. The Forms of Art › b. Classical Art › ii. The Ideal of Classical Art › 3. The Individuality of the Particular Gods
Gloss: The character of each god as an individual.
Hegelian gloss: The individuality of the particular gods, each with its own character and attributes.
Nouns: the individuality of the particular gods; divine personality, attributes, epithets, myths, local cults, the characters of the gods. divine individuality, the character of each god, personality, the particular god, distinctive character, determinate individuality, attribute, sphere, province. theomorphism.
Verbs: characterize, individualize, personify. distinguish, particularize.
Adjective: individual, characteristic, mythic. particular, distinctive, personal, determinate.
Adverbs: individually. each in his sphere, distinctively.
Phrases: grey-eyed Athena; rosy-fingered dawn [Homer]; each god in his sphere; the attributes of the gods.
Hegel definition: The individuality of the particular gods goes beyond abstract particularity of character, since the classical ideal must set individuality in motion, relating it to an opposite, so that each god enters further particular traits. These bring contingency, as traits no longer led back to the substantial meaning surround the gods as arbitrary external accessories, and so raise the question where the material of their individuality comes from.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· The Classical Form of Art › The Ideal of the Classical Form of Art › The Individuality of the Gods
Hegel citations:
Now since the classical Ideal does not abide by the individuality that reposes in itself but has to set it in motion, bring it into relation with an opposite and show itself effective thereon, the character of the gods too does not stop at inherently substantial determinacy but enters into further particularizations.
— Aesthetics, The Ideal of the Classical Form of Art › The Individuality of the Gods (tr. Knox)
But with this sort of individuality there is bound up at the same time the contingency of the particular traits which are no longer brought back to the universal element in the substantial meaning
— Aesthetics, The Ideal of the Classical Form of Art › The Individuality of the Gods (tr. Knox)

Head: The Dissolution of Classical Art
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › β. The Forms of Art › b. Classical Art › iii. The Dissolution of Classical Art
Gloss: The passing away of classical art.
Hegelian gloss: The dissolution of classical art.
Nouns: the dissolution of classical art; decline of classical art, Hellenistic decadence, the end of the gods, fate, satire, prose. the end of classical art, downfall, disintegration, the unhappy consciousness of antiquity, the passing of the ideal, the transition to romantic art.
Verbs: dissolve, decline, decay. perish, pass away, wane.
Adjective: declining, decadent, Hellenistic, late. dissolving, waning, moribund.
Adverbs: in decline. in dissolution, at the end.
Phrases: the twilight of the gods; the gods are dead.
Hegel definition: The dissolution of classical art springs from the germ of decline the classical gods carry within them. Spiritual individuality, adequate to immediate bodily existence, broke up into a group of gods whose particular character is not absolutely necessary and so is surrendered to contingency, where the gods find the source of their dissolution, in fate, in anthropomorphism and at last in satire.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· The Classical Form of Art › The Dissolution of the Classical Form of Art
Hegel citations:
The germ of their decline the classical gods have in themselves, and when the deficiency implicit in them is revealed to our minds through the development of art itself they therefore bring in their train the dissolution of the classical Ideal.
— Aesthetics, The Classical Form of Art › The Dissolution of the Classical Form of Art (tr. Knox)
But this individuality broke up into a group of divine individuals whose determinate character is not absolutely necessary and therefore from the start is surrendered to the contingency in which the eternally powerful gods acquire alike for the Greek mind and for artistic representation the source of their dissolution.
— Aesthetics, The Classical Form of Art › The Dissolution of the Classical Form of Art (tr. Knox)

Head: Fate
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › β. The Forms of Art › b. Classical Art › iii. The Dissolution of Classical Art › 1. Fate
Gloss: The necessity that stands over gods and men.
Hegelian gloss: Fate, the necessity above the gods, the cold unity they cannot reach.
Nouns: fate; necessity, the Fates, destiny, doom, lot, Nemesis; kismet. destination, fatality, election, foreordination, fatalism, inevitableness. necessitation, obligation, compulsion &c H0712, subjection &c H0527, stern necessity, hard necessity, dire necessity, imperious necessity, inexorable necessity, iron necessity, adverse necessity, what must be. fate &c H0144. predestination, preordination, predetermination. destiny &c H0144. ananke, heimarmene, the Norns, blind necessity, weird†.
Verbs: fate, destine, doom, foreordain, decree. impend, hang over, await, preordain, have in store for. foredoom, devote, predestine, cast a spell &c H1164, necessitate, compel &c H0712. be doomed, be destined, have no choice, have no alternative, befated†. ordain, overrule.
Adjective: fated, fateful, destined, doomed, inexorable, ineluctable. elect, uncontrollable, irresistible, irrevocable, resistless. impending, in store. inevitable, unavoidable, avoidless†. inescapable, blind.
Adverbs: fatefully, inexorably, as fate would have it. by fate, ineluctably, inevitably.
Foreign: Latin: fatum, Parcae, providentia [providence, as against fatum] [Boethius]; Greek: anankē, moira, Moirai, heimarmenē, kēr [the death-fate allotted to each]; Arabic: qadar; Turkish: qismet; Sanskrit: niyati; Korean: unmyeong [fate], palja [one's lot, destiny]; German: Geschick [the sending of being] [Heidegger]; French: destin, fatalité, sort, nécessité, fortune; Italian: fortuna, fato, destino; Dutch: schicksel.
Phrases: even the gods do not fight against necessity [Simonides]; fata viam invenient [Lat.] [the fates will find a way] [Virgil]; it is written; the threads of fate.
Hegel definition: Fate is the abstract and shapeless necessity that stands higher than the plural gods, overpowering gods and men while remaining incomprehensible. Thought dissolves the gods' plurality into one divinity under whose might they strive. The tranquil mourning that marks the sculpted god in blessed repose already constitutes its fate, showing that something higher stands above and that a passage to universal unity is needed.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· The Classical Form of Art › The Dissolution of the Classical Form of Art › Fate
Hegel citations:
It is this mourning which already constitutes their fate because it shows that something higher stands above them, and that a transition is necessary from their existence as particulars to their universal unity.
— Aesthetics, The Dissolution of the Classical Form of Art › Fate (tr. Knox)
But, looking around for the manner and shape of this higher unity, we find it, contrasted with the individuality and relative determinacy of the gods, in what is inherently abstract and shapeless, namely necessity, the fate which, in this abstraction, is just the higher in general that overpowers gods and men but remains in itself incomprehensible and inconceivable.
— Aesthetics, The Dissolution of the Classical Form of Art › Fate (tr. Knox)

Head: Dissolution of the Gods through Anthropomorphism
Head (German): Auflösung der Götter durch ihren Anthropomorphismus
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › β. The Forms of Art › b. Classical Art › iii. The Dissolution of Classical Art › 2. Dissolution of the Gods through Anthropomorphism
Gloss: The decay of the gods through their being made too human.
Hegelian gloss: The decay of the gods through anthropomorphism, their becoming merely human.
Nouns: dissolution of the gods through anthropomorphism; humanization of the gods, all-too-human gods, Xenophanes' critique, demythologization, divine scandal, the gods ridiculed. the decay of the gods, the twilight of the gods, the fall of the gods, finitude of the gods, contingency, particularity, the loss of the divine.
Verbs: humanize, debunk, demythologize, ridicule. anthropomorphize, degrade, decay, fall, dissolve.
Adjective: anthropomorphic, all-too-human, demythologized. humanized, finite, decadent, fallen.
Adverbs: humanly. in human fashion, all too humanly, in decay.
Phrases: if oxen and horses or lions had hands, and could paint with their hands … horses would paint the forms of the gods like horses, and oxen like oxen [Xenophanes, fr. 15, tr. Burnet]; the gods made human; all too human.
Hegel definition: The dissolution of the gods through anthropomorphism follows because absolute necessity is no attribute of theirs: their particular side is given free play and runs into the externalities and finitude of human life, which pervert them into the reverse of the divine. The mind can no longer rest in them, since they lack infinite subjectivity, inwardness that knows itself, which true totality requires.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· The Classical Form of Art › The Dissolution of the Classical Form of Art › Dissolution of the Gods through their Anthropomorphism
Hegel citations:
The downfall of these beautiful gods of art is therefore necessitated purely by their own nature, since in the end the mind cannot any longer find rest in them and therefore turns back from them into itself.
— Aesthetics, The Dissolution of the Classical Form of Art › Dissolution of the Gods through their Anthropomorphism (tr. Knox)
Therefore the plastic Ideal lacks the aspect of being represented as inwardness knowing itself as infinite.
— Aesthetics, The Dissolution of the Classical Form of Art › Dissolution of the Gods through their Anthropomorphism (tr. Knox)

Head: Satire
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › β. The Forms of Art › b. Classical Art › iii. The Dissolution of Classical Art › 3. Satire
Gloss: Poetry that mocks the decline of a world.
Hegelian gloss: Satire, the prose of the disappointed spirit at odds with a corrupt world, the Roman form.
Nouns: satire; lampoon, burlesque, invective, pasquinade, diatribe, mockery, ridicule, Juvenal, Horace, Persius, Lucian, Menippean satire, Roman satire. derision, irony, persiflage, raillery. libel, skit. the satirist, Tacitus, the prose of a declining world.
Verbs: satirize, lampoon, mock, ridicule, deride, pillory, skewer. caricature. scoff at, twit, taunt &c H0535, sneer at &c H0230. scoff, sneer, gibe, jeer. parody, travesty. lash, scourge, castigate.
Adjective: satirical, satiric, mocking, sardonic, caustic, biting, Juvenalian, Horatian. sarcastic, cynical, cutting, withering, censorious. derisory, derisive, ironic, ironical, Hudibrastic†, scurrilous &c H0535. trenchant, acrimonious. mordant, scathing.
Adverbs: satirically, mockingly. mordantly, caustically, bitingly.
Foreign: Latin: satura; Arabic: hijāʾ [satirical verse]; Korean: pungja [satire]; Spanish: esperpento [grotesque deformation] [Valle-Inclán].
Phrases: difficile est saturam non scribere [Lat.] [it is hard not to write satire] [Juvenal]; castigat ridendo mores [Lat.]; to hold up to ridicule; biting satire.
Hegel definition: Satire is the form in the transition out of classical art, where the opposition between spirit and the corrupt world persists, giving a prosaic relation in place of poetic reconciliation. Unlike symbolic forms, whose shape and meaning were strangers yet friendly, here sides once perfectly interfused separate because they can no longer agree, turning from peaceful reconciliation to enmity. It flourished on Roman soil.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· The Classical Form of Art › The Dissolution of the Classical Form of Art › Satire
Hegel citations:
[T]he result is that the classical art-form appears as superseded, since this relation leads to the downfall of the plastic gods and the beautiful world of men.
— Aesthetics, The Dissolution of the Classical Form of Art › Satire (tr. Knox)
[A]nd if therefore the sides joined together in such a perfect unity are detached from one another, this only happens because they can no longer agree with one another and must desert their peaceful reconciliation for incompatibility and enmity.
— Aesthetics, The Dissolution of the Classical Form of Art › Satire (tr. Knox)

Head: Romantic Art
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › β. The Forms of Art › c. Romantic Art
Gloss: Art in which the mind withdraws into its own inwardness, beyond what any outward form can hold.
Hegelian gloss: Art in which spirit withdraws into its own inwardness and the outward shape becomes inadequate: romantic art.
