Nouns: romantic art; romanticism, Christian art, inwardness, subjectivity, spiritual depth, the infinite within, longing, the medieval and modern, the soul's inner life. aspiration. the romantic form of art, the art of inwardness, subjective inwardness, absolute inwardness, the infinite subjectivity, spiritual beauty, the beauty of soul, the art of the heart.
Verbs: interiorize, spiritualize, yearn, transcend. turn inward, withdraw, internalize, overflow.
Adjective: romantic, inward, spiritual, Christian, yearning, subjective, soulful. intrinsic, inherent. mental. infinite, medieval.
Adverbs: romantically, inwardly. spiritually, beyond form.
Foreign: German: Romantik, Innerlichkeit, Sehnsucht, romantisch; French: romantique.
Phrases: [der Geist geht] zur Versöhnung seiner in sich selber zurück [Ger.] [Hegel, Aesthetics, on romantic art]; the inward life; heart's longing.
Hegel definition: Romantic art arises because there is something higher than the beautiful appearance of spirit in sensuous shape: spirit is pushed back from reconciliation in the body to reconciliation within itself. The ideal's solid totality falls apart into subjective being and external appearance, so that spirit may reach deeper reconciliation in its own inwardness, where outward shape is no longer adequate, though classical art attained the height of beauty.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· The Romantic Form of Art
Hegel citations:
Therefore classical art became a conceptually adequate representation of the Ideal, the consummation of the realm of beauty. Nothing can be or become more beautiful.
— Aesthetics, The Romantic Form of Art (tr. Knox)
Yet there is something higher than the beautiful appearance of spirit in its immediate sensuous shape, even if this shape be created by spirit as adequate to itself. For this unification, which is achieved in the medium of externality and therefore makes sensuous reality into an appropriate existence [of spirit], nevertheless is once more opposed to the true essence of spirit, with the result that spirit is pushed back into itself out of its reconciliation in the corporeal into a reconciliation of itself within itself.
— Aesthetics, The Romantic Form of Art (tr. Knox)

Head: The Religious Domain of Romantic Art
Head (German): Der religiöse Kreis der romantischen Kunst
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › β. The Forms of Art › c. Romantic Art › i. The Religious Domain of Romantic Art
Gloss: The sphere of religion in romantic art.
Hegelian gloss: The religious domain of romantic art: the infinite subject reconciled with God.
Nouns: the religious domain of romantic art; Christian art, sacred art, religious painting, devotional art, iconography, altarpiece, Madonna, Pietà, Passion, the Nativity. the religious sphere, the religious circle, the sacred subjects, the divine history, religious inwardness, the heart reconciled with God.
Verbs: depict, venerate, illuminate. sanctify, hallow, devote, reconcile.
Adjective: sacred, devotional, religious, iconographic. Christian, holy, spiritual.
Adverbs: devotionally. religiously, in the sphere of religion.
Phrases: ad maiorem Dei gloriam [Lat.]; the life of the spirit.
Hegel definition: The religious domain of romantic art has for its substantial content the reconciliation of God with the world and so with himself, spirit's union with its essence and the satisfaction of the heart, so that the ideal seems at home again, though in a form quite unlike the classical, which could not admit self-division, grief, sacrifice and renunciation, nor a world of evil to be reconciled.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· The Romantic Form of Art › The Religious Domain of Romantic Art
Hegel citations:
In its representation of absolute subjectivity as the whole of truth, romantic art has for its substantial content the reconciliation of God with the world and therefore with himself, the unification of the spirit with its essence, the satisfaction of the heart, and therefore at this stage the Ideal seems at last to be completely at home.
— Aesthetics, The Romantic Form of Art › The Religious Domain of Romantic Art (tr. Knox)
[A]nd, thirdly, since the underlying principle is the unseparated unity of the individual in himself and in his external world, there cannot appear as an essential factor the negativity of diremption within the self, of bodily and spiritual grief, of sacrifice and renunciation.
— Aesthetics, The Romantic Form of Art › The Religious Domain of Romantic Art (tr. Knox)

Head: The Redemptive History of Christ
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › β. The Forms of Art › c. Romantic Art › i. The Religious Domain of Romantic Art › 1. The Redemptive History of Christ
Gloss: The story of Christ's life, death and resurrection.
Hegelian gloss: The history of redemption, Christ's life, passion, death and resurrection, the human appearance of the absolute.
Nouns: the redemptive history of Christ; the Passion, the life of Christ, the Nativity, the Crucifixion, the Resurrection, the Stations of the Cross, redemption, salvation. the story of Christ, the Entombment, the Ascension, the sacred history, the gospel story, the suffering God.
Verbs: suffer, redeem, save, crucify, resurrect. die, rise, ascend, atone.
Adjective: redemptive, salvific, passional, Christological. sacred, evangelical, suffering.
Adverbs: redemptively. for our salvation, on the Cross.
Foreign: Latin: Ecce Homo, via dolorosa; Italian: Pietà.
Phrases: ecce homo [Lat.] [Bible]; consummatum est [Lat.] [it is finished] [Bible]; the passion of Christ.
Hegel definition: The redemptive history of Christ presents spirit's reconciliation with itself as God's appearance in the world: an individual man is God and God an individual man, so that in Christ every individual beholds their own reconciliation with God as actual. Since this unity is no immediate coalescence, the process of spirit must appear as this man's history: suffering, death, resurrection through death's grief, and presence as spirit in the church.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· The Romantic Form of Art › The Religious Domain of Romantic Art › The Redemptive History of Christ
Hegel citations:
The simple heart of this reconciliation is the coalescence of absolute essentiality with the individual human subject; an individual man is God, and God an individual man.
— Aesthetics, The Religious Domain of Romantic Art › The Redemptive History of Christ (tr. Knox)
This history of the spirit, consummated in one individual, contains nothing except what we have already touched on above, namely that the individual man casts aside his individuality of body and spirit, i.e. that he suffers and dies, but conversely through the grief of death rises out of death, and ascends as God in his glory, as the actual spirit which now has indeed entered existence as an individual, as this subject, yet even so is essentially truly God only as Spirit in his Church.
— Aesthetics, The Religious Domain of Romantic Art › The Redemptive History of Christ (tr. Knox)

Head: Religious Love
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › β. The Forms of Art › c. Romantic Art › i. The Religious Domain of Romantic Art › 2. Religious Love
Gloss: The love of the soul for God.
Hegelian gloss: Religious love, the spirit's reconciliation felt in the heart, as in the Madonna.
Nouns: religious love; divine love, devotion, adoration, the love of Mary, the Madonna, maternal love, mystical love. aspiration, homage. yearning, passion, fervor, rapture. love of God, holy love, spiritual love, the love of Christ, Mary's love, mother-love, charity, agape, blessedness, bliss, self-surrender, Candlemas†.
Verbs: love, adore, worship, cherish. lift up the heart, aspire, revere &c H0535. surrender, give oneself, bless.
Adjective: loving, devotional, adoring, tender, merciful. affectionate, ardent, rapturous, devoted. holy, blessed, blissful, self-surrendering, maternal, seraphic.
Adverbs: lovingly, devotedly. in love, blissfully.
Foreign: Latin: caritas, amor Dei; Greek: agapē; Arabic: ʿishq ilāhī [divine love]; Sanskrit: bhakti [devotion].
Phrases: God is love, Deus caritas est [Lat.] [Bible]; ubi caritas et amor, Deus ibi est [Lat.]; the love of God; mother and child.
Hegel definition: Religious love is the one form that meets the demand that absolute spirit, reconciled with itself, be felt and contemplated in art: the depth of feeling of a spirit free and satisfied in itself. Its content is the return out of another into self; its essence is to give up self-consciousness, forget oneself in another self, and in that surrender possess oneself.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· The Romantic Form of Art › The Religious Domain of Romantic Art › Religious Love
Hegel citations:
This depth of feeling, which alone corresponds to the essential nature of the spirit which is free and satisfied in itself, is love.
— Aesthetics, The Religious Domain of Romantic Art › Religious Love (tr. Knox)
The true essence of love consists in giving up the consciousness of oneself, forgetting oneself in another self, yet in this surrender and oblivion having and possessing oneself alone.
— Aesthetics, The Religious Domain of Romantic Art › Religious Love (tr. Knox)

Head: The Spirit of the Community
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › β. The Forms of Art › c. Romantic Art › i. The Religious Domain of Romantic Art › 3. The Spirit of the Community
Gloss: The life of the believing community, with its martyrs, penitents, miracles and legends.
Hegelian gloss: The spirit of the community, its martyrs, repentance and conversion, miracles and legends.
Nouns: the spirit of the community. the life of the congregation.
Foreign: Latin: Legenda Aurea; Greek: martyrion, metanoia; Arabic: shahāda [martyrdom, witness], karāmāt [saints' miracles]; Sanskrit: prāyaścitta [penance].
Hegel definition: The spirit of the community broadens the reconciliation made visible in Christ to the plurality of human beings, since God's true reality is not immediate existence but spirit, existing in knowing and inner life. The individual rises to freedom only by converting natural, finite personality, in three ways: martyrdom repeating the passion bodily, repentance and conversion inwardly, and miracles superseding the course of nature.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· The Romantic Form of Art › The Religious Domain of Romantic Art › The Spirit of the Community
Hegel citations:
This absolute existence of God as pure universality, alike ideal and subjective, is therefore not restricted to this individual [Jesus] who in his history has made visible the reconciliation of human and divine personality, but is broadened into the human consciousness which is reconciled with God, in short into mankind which exists as a plurality of individuals.
— Aesthetics, The Religious Domain of Romantic Art › The Spirit of the Community (tr. Knox)
This transcendence of finitude enters here in a threefold way: First, as the external repetition of the Passion story; this becomes actual physical suffering-martyrdom.
— Aesthetics, The Religious Domain of Romantic Art › The Spirit of the Community (tr. Knox)

Head: Martyrdom
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › β. The Forms of Art › c. Romantic Art › i. The Religious Domain of Romantic Art › 3. The Spirit of the Community › a. Martyrdom
Gloss: Suffering endured for the faith, in which the body is given up to prove the spirit.
Hegelian gloss: Die Martyrien: the endurance of pain and torment for faith, the negation of the natural self carried out in the flesh, which in art can turn to the cruel and merely horrible.
Nouns: martyrdom. passion, witness, the martyrs. mortification, maceration, flagellation, penance &c H0714, lustration†.
Verbs: martyr, suffer, testify.
Adjective: martyred.
Adverbs: in martyrdom.
Phrases: the blood of the martyrs is the seed of the Church [proverbial]; semen est sanguis Christianorum [Lat.] [Tertullian, Apologeticus 50]; the noble army of martyrs.
Hegel definition: Martyrdom is the endurance of cruelty and freely willed renunciation, sacrifice and privation, through which spirit is to be transfigured, grief being an end in itself and the glory measured by the horror suffered. Physical torture inflicted by persecutors or self-imposed provides its chief topic, so that beauty is easily damaged, such repugnant externals being too far from it for healthy art to choose them.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· The Romantic Form of Art › The Religious Domain of Romantic Art › The Spirit of the Community › Martyrs
Hegel citations:
In martyrdom this negative—grief—is an end in itself, and the magnitude of the transfiguration is measured by the awfulness of what the man has suffered and the frightfulness to which he has submitted.
— Aesthetics, The Spirit of the Community › Martyrs (tr. Knox)
But since in such situations the conversion of the inner life can only be portrayed in dreadfulness and in the brutality of the tortures, the sense of beauty is easily damaged and the topics in this sphere constitute a very hazardous material for art.
— Aesthetics, The Spirit of the Community › Martyrs (tr. Knox)

Head: Repentance and Conversion
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › β. The Forms of Art › c. Romantic Art › i. The Religious Domain of Romantic Art › 3. The Spirit of the Community › b. Repentance and Conversion
Gloss: The inward turning of the soul from sin to God, without outward torment.
Hegelian gloss: Die Buße und Bekehrung: the inward conversion of the heart, which achieves in the spirit what martyrdom sought through the body.
Nouns: repentance and conversion. repentance, penance, contrition, conversion, Damascus road. penitence, compunction, remorse, regret &c H0672. Magdalen, prodigal son. acknowledgment, confession &c H0662, apology &c H0714, recantation &c H0679, resipiscence†. sackcloth and ashes, shrift, purgation. recantation, palinode, renunciation, abjuration†, palinody†, revokement†. proselyte.
Verbs: repent, convert. be sorry for, be penitent, rue, recant &c H0679, cry peccavi.
Adjective: penitent, converted, penitential. repenting, repentant, contrite, conscience-stricken, self-accusing, self-convicted.
Adverbs: penitently, in penance.
Hegel definition: Repentance and conversion transfer the negation of the sinful self into the inner life, expressed only in spiritual grief and change of heart, and so give ground more fit for ideal art than bodily torture. Faith can make a crime alien to its doer and wash it away. Painting does best to concentrate the conversion in a single picture, as with Mary Magdalene.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· The Romantic Form of Art › The Religious Domain of Romantic Art › The Spirit of the Community › Repentance and Conversion
Hegel citations:
This ground is the conversion of the inner life which expresses itself solely in its spiritual grief, in its change of heart.
— Aesthetics, The Spirit of the Community › Repentance and Conversion (tr. Knox)
Therefore things go most favourably for painting when it concentrates the conversion into one picture alone, without further detailing the crime.
— Aesthetics, The Spirit of the Community › Repentance and Conversion (tr. Knox)

Head: Miracles and Legends
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › β. The Forms of Art › c. Romantic Art › i. The Religious Domain of Romantic Art › 3. The Spirit of the Community › c. Miracles and Legends
Gloss: The miracles and legends of the saints, where the divine breaks into the course of nature.
Hegelian gloss: Die Wunder und Legenden: the divine shown as breaking the natural connection of things, which for art easily becomes the merely fanciful and adventurous.
Nouns: miracles and legends. miracles, legends, hagiography, miracle, legend, the lives of the saints, the saints.
Verbs: work miracles, canonize.
Adjective: miraculous, legendary, hagiographic, saintly.
Adverbs: miraculously, by miracle.
Phrases: saints and miracles.
Hegel definition: Miracles and legends represent the divine breaking into common contingent reality, inverting and interrupting the natural course of things so as to move hearts. Hegel objects that the divine rules nature only as reason, through the unchangeable laws it has implanted, so that legends easily pass into the abstruse, tasteless, senseless and laughable when faith is to be stirred by what is irrational.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· The Romantic Form of Art › The Religious Domain of Romantic Art › The Spirit of the Community › Miracles and Legends
Hegel citations:
In fact, however, the Divine can touch and rule nature only as reason, i.e. as the unchangeable laws of nature itself which God has implanted in it
— Aesthetics, The Spirit of the Community › Miracles and Legends (tr. Knox)
This is why the legends often pass over without difficulty into what is abstruse, tasteless, senseless, and laughable, because spirit and heart are supposed to be moved towards faith in the presence and activity of God precisely by what is absolutely irrational, false, and non-divine.
— Aesthetics, The Spirit of the Community › Miracles and Legends (tr. Knox)

Head: Chivalry
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › β. The Forms of Art › c. Romantic Art › ii. Chivalry
Gloss: The secular world of the knight.
Hegelian gloss: The chivalry of the secular world, the subject's own infinity as honour, love and fidelity.
Nouns: chivalry; knighthood, chivalric code, courtliness, knight-errantry, gallantry, courtesy, the Round Table, the Grail quest. baron, thane, banneret†, atheling†, marquisate†, baronetcy†. good manners, good breeding, politeness, urbanity, gentility, breeding. the knightly world, the code of chivalry, prowess, valour, the tournament, the joust, the paladin.
Verbs: knight, dub, champion, quest, defend, serve one's lady. joust, tilt, ride forth, serve.
Adjective: chivalrous, chivalric, knightly, gallant, courtly, valiant. courageous, brave, valorous, intrepid, high-spirited, mettlesome. courteous.
Adverbs: chivalrously, gallantly.
Foreign: French: chevalerie, preux chevalier; Italian: cavalleria; Spanish: caballería; Arabic: furūsiyya [chivalry], futuwwa; Chinese: wuxia [martial chivalry], jianghu [rivers and lakes, the world of wandering knights]; Japanese: bushidō.
Phrases: sans peur et sans reproche [Fr.] [without fear and without reproach]; knight in shining armour; chivalry is not dead.
Hegel definition: Chivalry is the secular sphere of romantic art. The heart, perfected in simple religious bliss, must leave the heavenly kingdom, look into itself and win a worldly content proper to the individual subject, so that religious inwardness becomes worldly. The infinitude of the person then fills mundane life in honour, love and fidelity, feelings in which one sees oneself affirmed directly in others and not only through a third thing.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· The Romantic Form of Art › Chivalry
Hegel citations:
The heart which is only now perfected in its simple bliss has therefore to leave the heavenly kingdom of its substantive sphere, to look into itself, and attain a mundane content appropriate to the individual subject as such.
— Aesthetics, The Romantic Form of Art › Chivalry (tr. Knox)
Therefore the earlier religious inwardness now becomes one of a worldly kind.
— Aesthetics, The Romantic Form of Art › Chivalry (tr. Knox)

Head: Honor
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › β. The Forms of Art › c. Romantic Art › ii. Chivalry › 1. Honor
Gloss: The knight's sense of personal worth.
Hegelian gloss: Honour, the infinite worth of the person in their own eyes.
Nouns: honour; personal honour, point of honour, dignity, repute, reputation, good name, face, prestige, esteem, the code duello, vindication, affront, insult, vilipendency†. distinction, name, good repute, high repute, fame. glory, honor, luster &c H0251, respectability &c H0731, good report, fair name. deference. estimation, good opinion, golden opinions, approvement†. indignity. stateliness, solemnity, grandeur, splendor, nobility, majesty, sublimity, optimacy†. trophy, medal, prize, award, laurels, crown, chaplet, civic crown, insignia &c H0661, feather in one's cap &c H0537, decoration &c H0537, triumphal arch, Victoria Cross, Iron Cross. triumph &c H1161, flying colors &c H0478. monumentum aere perennius [Horace]. title, knighthood &c H0764. highness, excellency, grace, lordship, worship, reverence, reverend, esquire, sir, master, Mr, signor, senor, mynheer†, your honor, his honor, serene highness, handle to one's name. decoration, laurel, palm, wreath, garland, bays, ribbon, riband, blue ribbon, cordon, cross, coronet, star, garter, feather, feather in one's cap, epaulet, epaulette, colors, cockade, livery, order, arms, shield, scutcheon, reward &c H0703, cestus†, hatchment†, calisthenics†. self-respect, pride, personal worth, inviolability, satisfaction, the duel. accolade. punctilio, amour propre.
Verbs: honour, respect, vindicate, defend one's honour, avenge an insult, demand satisfaction. regard, revere, esteem &c H0535, look up to. dishonor. avenge, challenge, uphold one's honour. diss.
Adjective: honourable, honoured, dignified, reputable, touchy, punctilious. high-principled, high-minded, scrupulous, respectable. in good odor in, favor, in high favor, creditable. great, proud, noble, honorable, worshipful, lordly, grand, stately, august, princely. inviolable, irrevealable†, unbribed†.
Adverbs: honourably, on one's honour, upon my honour. with honour.
Foreign: German: Mein Herr; French: point d'honneur, vergogne, honte, fierté; Italian: punto d'onore, bella figura, brutta figura [good and bad showing], omertà [the code of silence], vergogna; Spanish: pundonor, vergüenza [shame as honour]; Arabic: sharaf [honour], ʿirḍ [personal honour]; Chinese: mianzi [face]; Japanese: giri; Korean: chemyeon [face, honour]; Greek: aidōs; Latin: verecundia.
Phrases: death before dishonour; tout est perdu fors l'honneur [Fr.] [all is lost save honour] [Francis I, attrib.]; on my honour; a point of honour; for valor.
Hegel definition: Honour, unknown to classical art, is the romantic value an individual ascribes to themselves on their own account, as infinite as they are in their own eyes. Its injury touches not property or position but the personality and its idea of itself, which is placed wholly in some particular possession. Its measure depends not on what a person actually is but on that idea; in it one first has affirmative consciousness of infinite subjectivity.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· The Romantic Form of Art › Chivalry › Honour
Hegel citations:
In honour, therefore, the man has the first affirmative consciousness of his infinite subjectivity, no matter what the circumstances.
— Aesthetics, Chivalry › Honour (tr. Knox)
The measure of honour thus does not depend on what the man actually is but on what this idea of himself is.
— Aesthetics, Chivalry › Honour (tr. Knox)

Head: Chivalric Love
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › β. The Forms of Art › c. Romantic Art › ii. Chivalry › 2. Chivalric Love
Gloss: The knight's devotion to a lady.
Hegelian gloss: Love, the self's surrender to another self, the beauty of feeling.
Nouns: chivalric love; courtly love, the troubadours, minnesang, adoration of the lady, the lady fair, romance, love-service; Majnūn and Laylā. knightly love, romantic love, gallantry, the lady, the mistress, the beloved, devotion, adoration, the troubadour.
Verbs: woo, court, serve, adore, pine, serenade. dally, philander, make love, pay one's court to, pay one's addresses to. idolize, become enamored, fall in love with, lose one's heart. love, sigh.
Adjective: courtly, romantic, chivalrous, ardent, unrequited, chaste. tender, amorous, amatory, passionate, devoted. gallant, adoring, enamoured, lovelorn.
Adverbs: courteously, devotedly. gallantly, for love, in love's service. politely.
Foreign: German: Minne; French: amour courtois; Occitan: fin'amor; Arabic: ʿudhrī love [chaste, unrequited love], ghazal [love lyric]; Italian: cicisbeo [a married woman's escort]; Spanish: donjuanismo.
Phrases: love conquers all, omnia vincit amor [Lat.] [Virgil]; a damsel in distress; faint heart neer won fair lady; kisses honeyed by oblivion [G. Eliot].
Hegel definition: Chivalric love is the surrender of the person to another, the sacrifice of independent consciousness so as to have knowledge of oneself only in the other, whereas honour keeps personality in absolute independence. Yet love also realizes honour's need for recognition. It arises in feeling, with a basis in spiritualized nature, and its infinity lies in losing self-consciousness in another and there finding and enjoying oneself.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· The Romantic Form of Art › Chivalry › Love
Hegel citations:
While in honour the fundamental characteristic is personal subjectivity envisaged in its absolute independence, in love the supreme thing is rather the surrender of the person to an individual of the opposite sex, the sacrifice of one's independent consciousness
— Aesthetics, Chivalry › Love (tr. Knox)
What constitutes the infinity of love is this losing, in the other, one's consciousness of self, this splendour of disinterestedness and selflessness through which alone the person finds himself again and becomes a self, this self-forgetfulness in which the lover does not exist, live, and care for himself, but finds the roots of his being in another, and yet in this other does entirely enjoy precisely himself
— Aesthetics, Chivalry › Love (tr. Knox)

Head: Fidelity
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › β. The Forms of Art › c. Romantic Art › ii. Chivalry › 3. Fidelity
Gloss: The knight's loyalty to a lord.
Hegelian gloss: Fidelity to a lord, personal loyalty.
Nouns: fidelity; faithfulness, loyalty, fealty, allegiance, devotion, constancy, steadfastness, trustiness, troth, vassal loyalty, staunchness. homage, deference. incorruption, incorruptibility. self-denial, self-sacrifice. honesty. faith, vassalage, liege service, the vassal, the liegeman.
Verbs: be faithful, keep faith, stand by, abide, cleave. serve, follow, swear fealty, pledge faith.
Adjective: faithful, loyal, constant, steadfast, staunch, true, trusty, devoted. true blue, true to the core. as good as one's word. unwavering, unswerving. leal†, liege.
Adverbs: faithfully, loyally, steadfastly. truly, in fealty.
Foreign: Latin: fides; Sanskrit: niṣṭhā [devotion]; Chinese: zhong [loyalty]; Korean: chung [loyalty].
Phrases: semper fidelis [Lat.]; Treue um Treue [Ger.]; loyal to the last; to keep faith.
Hegel definition: Fidelity, in romantic subjectivity's worldly sphere, is not constancy in love or the friendship of equals, such as youth forms, but loyalty toward a superior, someone of higher rank or a master. The Greeks knew it in servants such as the swineherd of Odysseus, and Shakespeare shows it as a matter wholly of the mind in Kent's wish to serve Lear.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· The Romantic Form of Art › Chivalry › Fidelity
Hegel citations:
While fidelity in friendship and love subsists only between equals, fidelity as we have to consider it now affects a superior, someone higher in rank, or a master.
— Aesthetics, Chivalry › Fidelity (tr. Knox)
It is inherent essentially in the principle of our deeper life that, on the whole, every man fends for himself, i.e. is himself competent to take his place in the world.
— Aesthetics, Chivalry › Fidelity (tr. Knox)

Head: The Formal Independence of Individual Characteristics
Head (German): Die formelle Selbständigkeit der individuellen Besonderheiten
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › β. The Forms of Art › c. Romantic Art › iii. The Formal Independence of Individual Characteristics
Gloss: The freedom of individual character in romantic art.
Hegelian gloss: The formal independence of individual character, cut loose from substantial ends.
Nouns: the formal independence of individual characteristics; independent characters, self-contained individuals, secular heroes, the adventurer, modern character. formal independence, formal firmness of character, particular character, individual peculiarity, self-will, the subjective character, formal freedom, the contingency of character. individualism.
Verbs: stand alone, act independently. assert oneself, particularize, individualize.
Adjective: independent, self-reliant, secular, individualistic. formal, individual, particular, self-willed, subjective, peculiar.
Adverbs: independently. formally, individually, on its own account.
Phrases: the individual on his own; a law unto oneself; a character of one's own.
Hegel definition: The formal independence of individual character is the third sphere of romantic art, in which religious material and chivalry with its lofty aims have vanished, and the particular, existent world stands on its own feet. What gives satisfaction is thirst for present reality, delight in the finite, so that people wish to see the present as it is, recreated by art, even at the cost of beauty and ideality.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· The Romantic Form of Art › The Formal Independence of Individual Characters
Hegel citations:
In this third sphere of the romantic form of art, therefore, the religious materials have vanished together with chivalry and the lofty views and aims which it generated out of its inner being and to which nothing in the present and in reality directly corresponds.
— Aesthetics, The Romantic Form of Art › The Formal Independence of Individual Characters (tr. Knox)
In his present world man wants to see the present itself as it is-even at the cost of sacrificing beauty and ideality of content and appearance-as a live presence recreated by art, as his own human and spiritual work.
— Aesthetics, The Romantic Form of Art › The Formal Independence of Individual Characters (tr. Knox)

Head: Independence of Individual Character
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › β. The Forms of Art › c. Romantic Art › iii. The Formal Independence of Individual Characteristics › 1. Independence of Individual Character
Gloss: The firmness of an individual character.
Hegelian gloss: The independence of individual character, formally firm, as in Shakespeare's figures.
Nouns: independence of individual character; strong character, firmness, steadfastness, Shakespearean characters, Macbeth, Richard III, Juliet, formal greatness, inflexibility, monomania. firmness of character, self-reliance, resoluteness, strength of will, consistency, obduracy, the self-reliant character, Othello.
Verbs: persist, hold fast, will absolutely. stand firm, will, resolve, stand on oneself.
Adjective: strong-willed, firm, inflexible, self-consistent, tragic, monomaniacal. resolved, determined, strong-minded, resolute &c H0801, self-possessed, decided, unhesitating, unflinching. unbending, unyielding. steadfast, self-reliant, self-subsistent.
Adverbs: resolutely, single-mindedly. firmly, steadfastly, unbendingly.
Phrases: I am in blood stepp'd in so far [Macbeth]; to stand on one's own two feet; firm of purpose.
Hegel definition: The independence of individual character is the particular subject, a whole and individual person, whose world is restricted and accidental and who rests not on a substantial, justified pathos but formally on mere subjectivity. It appears in two forms: energetic firmness that puts the whole power of a one-sided individuality into specific ends, and an inward totality that cannot unfold and express itself.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· The Romantic Form of Art › The Formal Independence of Individual Characters › The Independence of the Individual Character
Hegel citations:
What the individual is, is not carried and sustained by the substantial inherently justified element in his make-up, but by his character's mere subjectivity, which therefore instead of resting on something substantial and on an explicitly firm 'pathos' rests only formally on its own individual independence.
— Aesthetics, The Formal Independence of Individual Characters › The Independence of the Individual Character (tr. Knox)
On the one side there is the energetically self-sustaining firmness of character which limits itself to specific ends and puts the whole power of its one-sided individuality into the realization of these ends
— Aesthetics, The Formal Independence of Individual Characters › The Independence of the Individual Character (tr. Knox)

Head: Adventures
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › β. The Forms of Art › c. Romantic Art › iii. The Formal Independence of Individual Characteristics › 2. Adventures
Gloss: The chance events that befall the knight-errant.
Hegelian gloss: Adventures, the contingency of the external world, which the knight-errant meets.
Nouns: adventures; adventure, venture, exploit, escapade, quest, romance, knight-errantry, the picaresque, Don Quixote, Ariosto, Orlando Furioso, the contingent. pursuit, enterprise &c H0676, adventure &c H0676, quest &c H0667. enterprise, emprise†, pilgrimage. essay, trial, attempt. errantry, derring-do, accident, chance encounter, wandering, aventure. pastime. quixotry.
Verbs: adventure, venture, quest, wander, rove, roam. tempt fortune, try one's fortune. hazard, run the gauntlet &c H0801. range, traverse, scour the country. fare forth.
Adjective: adventurous, venturesome, picaresque, errant, quixotic. venturous, cavalier. enterprising, dashing, chivalrous, heroic. roving, chance, accidental.
Adverbs: adventurously. at a venture, at hazard, by chance, on the quest.
Foreign: Arabic: riḥla [journey]; German: Bildungsroman, Entwicklungsroman, Erziehungsroman, Zeitroman, Schlüsselroman [roman à clef], Fernweh [longing for far places]; Spanish: quijotismo, picarismo, picaresca; French: roman-fleuve.
Phrases: the knight of the woeful countenance [Cervantes]; to seek one's fortune; tilting at windmills.
Hegel definition: Adventures are the fundamental form of romantic events and actions: spirit withdrawn into itself treats the external world as a place released from it, a scene of complications and endless contingency, and goes into it with contingent ends it does not weave into a consistent whole. Its collisions are determined from outside and by accident, so that what matters is asserting oneself more than accomplishing a lasting work.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· The Romantic Form of Art › The Formal Independence of Individual Characters › Adventures
Hegel citations:
For the fixedly enclosed mind, it is just as much a matter of indifference to which circumstances it turns as it is a matter of accident which circumstances confront it.
— Aesthetics, The Formal Independence of Individual Characters › Adventures (tr. Knox)
Adventure, which provides for the form of events and actions the fundamental type of the romantic, is constituted by this relativity of ends in a relative environment, the specific character and complication of which do not lie in the individual person but are determined from without and accidentally
— Aesthetics, The Formal Independence of Individual Characters › Adventures (tr. Knox)

Head: The Dissolution of Romantic Art
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › β. The Forms of Art › c. Romantic Art › iii. The Formal Independence of Individual Characteristics › 3. The Dissolution of Romantic Art
Gloss: The passing away of romantic art into imitation of nature and into humour.
Hegelian gloss: The dissolution of romantic art into the imitation of nature and humour, subjective and objective.
Nouns: the dissolution of romantic art; the end of art, the pastness of art; the free artist. the end of romantic art, decay, decline, disintegration. fax.
Verbs: dissolve. disintegrate, fall apart.
Adjective: post-romantic. dissolving, decadent, late.
Adverbs: in dissolution, at the end, in decline.
Foreign: German: Humor, Nachahmung, nachmachen, kopieren, nachbilden; Latin: facetiae, canorae nugae, imitatio, similitude; French: plaisanterie, mot, mot pour rire, jeu d'esprit, représentation; Italian: ben trovato, imitazione, rassimiglianze, rittrare; Korean: haehak [folk humour].
Phrases: art, considered in its highest vocation, is and remains for us a thing of the past [Hegel].
Hegel definition: The dissolution of romantic art makes plain what romanticism already implied: the material art grasps becomes wholly contingent and external, since inwardness withdrawn into itself leaves the outer world free to go its own way. Any matter may then embody the heart, and everything, supreme or trivial, finds a place, until art splits into imitation of prosaic reality on one side and subjective humour on the other.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· The Romantic Form of Art › The Formal Independence of Individual Characters › Dissolution of the Romantic Form of Art
Hegel citations:
Now here above all there at once comes into consideration the complete contingency and externality of the material which artistic activity grasps and shapes.
— Aesthetics, The Formal Independence of Individual Characters › Dissolution of the Romantic Form of Art (tr. Knox)
In the presentations of romantic art, therefore, everything has a place, every sphere of life, all phenomena, the greatest and the least, the supreme and the trivial, the moral, immoral, and evil
— Aesthetics, The Formal Independence of Individual Characters › Dissolution of the Romantic Form of Art (tr. Knox)

Head: Imitation of Nature
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › β. The Forms of Art › c. Romantic Art › iii. The Formal Independence of Individual Characteristics › 3. The Dissolution of Romantic Art › a. Imitation of Nature
Gloss: Art that copies the ordinary world as it is, in genre scenes and still lifes.
Hegelian gloss: Die subjektive Kunstnachahmung des Vorhandenen: faithful portrayal of everyday reality, as in Dutch painting, whose interest lies in the artist's skill and the life of the passing moment.
Nouns: imitation of nature. realism, naturalism, genre painting, Dutch painting, still life, imitation of the given, prosaic naturalness, the novel. facsimile, counterpart, likeness. mimicry, simulation, impersonation, representation &c H0834, semblance.
Verbs: imitate, copy. mirror, reflect, reproduce.
Adjective: realistic, naturalistic, imitative, prosaic.
Adverbs: realistically.
Hegel definition: The imitation of nature takes contingent daily reality, domestic and civil life, as subject, and art dissolves into portraiture, painting and poetry especially. Measured by the ideal such products fall short, yet they are works of art through the artist's conception and execution, fidelity and marvellous skill, which make significant what has no significance in itself, and the vivacity with which life is breathed into it.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· The Romantic Form of Art › The Formal Independence of Individual Characters › Dissolution of the Romantic Form of Art › The Subjective Artistic Imitation of the Existent Present
Hegel citations:
Therefore the question soon arises whether such productions in general are still to be called works of art.
— Aesthetics, Dissolution of the Romantic Form of Art › The Subjective Artistic Imitation of the Existent Present (tr. Knox)
On the other hand, art has still another feature which is here essentially of special importance: the artist's subjective conception and execution of the work of art, the aspect of the individual talent which can remain faithful both to the manifestations of spirit and also to the inherently substantial life of nature, even in the extreme limits of the contingency which that life reaches, and can make significant even what is in itself without significance, and this it does through this fidelity and through the most marvellous skill of the portrayal.
— Aesthetics, Dissolution of the Romantic Form of Art › The Subjective Artistic Imitation of the Existent Present (tr. Knox)

Head: Subjective Humour
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › β. The Forms of Art › c. Romantic Art › iii. The Formal Independence of Individual Characteristics › 3. The Dissolution of Romantic Art › b. Subjective Humour
Gloss: Humour in which the artist's own wit and whims dissolve every fixed content.
Hegelian gloss: Der subjektive Humor: the artist's subjectivity making itself the content, breaking up every objective shape by wit and the play of fancies, as in Jean Paul; Sterne and Hippel show its truer form.
Nouns: subjective humour. Jean Paul, Laurence Sterne, humour, whimsy, irony. ridicule, sardonic smile, sardonic grin, irrision†, scoffing &c H0535, quiz†, banter, persiflage, raillery, quizzing, asteism†. jest, jape, jibe, levity, quips and cranks, capital joke, standing jest, standing joke, private joke, conceit, quip, quirk, crank, quiddity, concetto†, brilliant idea, merry thought, bright thought, happy thought, sally, flash of wit, flash of merriment, scintillation, witticism, smart saying, bon-mot, epigram, jest book, dry joke, quodlibet, cream of the jest. derision, mockery. Witz.
Verbs: joke, play. deride, taunt, snigger, laugh in one's sleeve, tease, badinage, rally, chaff, twit, roast, haze [U.S.], tehee†, fleer†, show up. crack a joke, make a joke, cut jokes, perpetrate a joke, pun, perpetrate a pun, make fun of, make merry with, kid, kid around, fool around, set the table in a roar &c H0672.
Adjective: humorous, whimsical, playful, ironic. witty, attic, quick-witted, nimble-witted, smart, jocular, jocose, facetious, waggish, kidding, joking, puckish, playful &c H0672, merry and wise, pleasant, sprightly, light, spirituel†, sparkling, epigrammatic, full of point, comic &c H1149, playsome†. derisory, derisive, mock, mocking, sarcastic, ironical, quizzical, burlesque, Hudibrastic†, scurrilous &c H0535. ridiculous, ludicrous, comical, droll, funny, laughable, pour rire, grotesque, farcical, odd, whimsical as a dancing bear, fanciful, fantastic, queer, rum, quaint, bizarre, screaming, eccentric &c H0073, strange, outlandish, out of the way, baroque, weird, awkward &c H0848.
Adverbs: humorously. jokingly, in joke, in jest, in sport, in play.
Phrases: tongue in cheek; adhibenda est in jocando moderatio [Lat.]; gentle dullness ever loves a joke [Pope]; leave this keen encounter of our wits [Richard III]; just joking, just kidding; surely you jest!
Hegel definition: Subjective humour brings the artist's own person onto the stage: instead of shaping a topic objectively, the humourist enters the material and by flashes of wit and striking turns dissolves whatever would make itself objective or hold firm shape. It is only play with topics, a rambling of subjective views, easily growing flat; Jean Paul is the favourite example, astonishing in jumbling the remotest things.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· The Romantic Form of Art › The Formal Independence of Individual Characters › Dissolution of the Romantic Form of Art › Subjective Humour
Hegel citations:
Now humour is not set the task of developing and shaping a topic objectively and in a way appropriate to the essential nature of the topic, and, in this development, using its own means to articulate the topic and round it off artistically; on the contrary, it is the artist himself who enters the material
— Aesthetics, Dissolution of the Romantic Form of Art › Subjective Humour (tr. Knox)
The main thing remains the hither and thither course of the humour which uses every topic only to emphasize the subjective wit of the author.
— Aesthetics, Dissolution of the Romantic Form of Art › Subjective Humour (tr. Knox)

Head: Objective Humour
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › β. The Forms of Art › c. Romantic Art › iii. The Formal Independence of Individual Characteristics › 3. The Dissolution of Romantic Art › c. Objective Humour
Gloss: Humour that stays with its object, joining the artist's feeling to the thing with warmth and depth.
Hegelian gloss: Der objektive Humor: an inward humour of feeling that does not destroy the object but dwells in it intimately, as in Goethe's West-Eastern Divan, the close of romantic art.
Nouns: objective humour. Goethe's West-Eastern Divan, humour of the heart, the deep wit of feeling, intimate humour.
Adjective: genial, heartfelt, warm-hearted.
Adverbs: with heartfelt humour.
Hegel definition: Objective humour arises when satisfaction in externality or in subjective portrayal deepens into the heart's immersion in the object, so that the artist grows intimate with it, in a sensitive abandonment that remains an inner movement of imagination devoted to the object, expressible only briefly. Goethe's West-Eastern Divan is among its brilliant modern instances, at the close of romantic art.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· The Romantic Form of Art › The Formal Independence of Individual Characters › Dissolution of the Romantic Form of Art › The End of the Romantic Form of Art
Hegel citations:
But if this satisfaction in externality or in the subjective portrayal is intensified, according to the principle of romantic art, into the heart's deeper immersion in the object, and if, on the other hand, what matters to humour is the object and its configuration within its subjective reflex, then we acquire thereby a growing intimacy with the object, a sort of objective humour.
— Aesthetics, Dissolution of the Romantic Form of Art › The End of the Romantic Form of Art (tr. Knox)
But what we may regard as necessary here is rather a sensitive abandonment of the heart in the object, which is indeed unfolded but remains a subjective spirited movement of imagination and the heart
— Aesthetics, Dissolution of the Romantic Form of Art › The End of the Romantic Form of Art (tr. Knox)

Head: The System of the Individual Arts
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › γ. The System of the Individual Arts
Gloss: The particular arts in their system.
Hegelian gloss: The system of the particular arts, from architecture through sculpture to painting, music and poetry.
Nouns: the system of the individual arts; the arts, the fine arts, classification of the arts, architecture, sculpture, painting, music, poetry, the hierarchy of the arts, the sister arts, the Muses. art, fine arts, painting &c H1030, sculpture &c H0987, engraving &c H1030. drawing. carving, statuary, insculpture†. the system of the arts, the individual arts, the particular arts, the division of the arts, architecture sculpture painting music and poetry. beaux-arts.
Verbs: classify, rank, order. systematize, divide, articulate.
Adjective: artistic, systematic, hierarchical. individual, particular, several.
Adverbs: by art form. systematically, severally, art by art.
Foreign: Sanskrit: catuḥṣaṣṭi kalāḥ [the sixty-four arts]; Chinese: liuyi [the six arts]; Japanese: geidō [the way of art].
Phrases: the nine Muses.
Hegel definition: The system of the individual arts is the third part of aesthetics, treating the work of art actualized in the sensuous element, since only as an object presented to sense does beauty explicitly become the ideal. The totality of artistic beauty here falls apart into independent members, each an individual art able to present all the art forms, developing as the forms do from symbolic to romantic and each flowering and decaying.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· The System of the Individual Arts
Hegel citations:
But it is implicit in the very conception of beauty that it shall make itself objective externally as a work of art presented to immediate vision, to sense and sensuous imagination.
— Aesthetics, The System of the Individual Arts (tr. Knox)
This real world of art is the system of the individual arts.
— Aesthetics, The System of the Individual Arts (tr. Knox)

Head: Architecture
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › γ. The System of the Individual Arts › a. Architecture
Gloss: The art of building.
Hegelian gloss: Architecture, the art of the external, which shapes inorganic nature to an enclosure for spirit.
Nouns: architecture; architectonics, building, construction, design, edifice, structure, frozen music. fabrication, erection, edification, diaster†. fabric, pile. formation. the builder's art, tectonics, masonry.
Verbs: build, construct, design, erect, raise, edify, frame. fabricate. set up, rear. plan, contrive, project, devise.
Adjective: architectural, architectonic, structural, monumental, constructional. tectonic, constructive, built.
Adverbs: architecturally, structurally. in stone.
Foreign: German: Baukunst; Latin: architectura; Greek: architektonikē; Sanskrit: vāstu-śāstra [science of building].
Phrases: architecture is frozen music [Schelling, attrib.]; firmitas, utilitas, venustas [Lat.] [firmness, commodity, delight] [Vitruvius]; built to last.
Hegel definition: Architecture is treated first among the particular arts, as art's beginning in concept and in existence. That beginning is not to be found in historical conjectures or charming tales about a cavern or a tree trunk, which make origins seem intelligible without deriving them from the concept. It must be established by deriving it from the very concept of art, whose content now emerges into real, external existence.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· Architecture
Hegel citations:
By making its content emerge into a determinate existence in the real world, art becomes a particular art and therefore we can now speak for the first time of art realized and so of the actual beginning of art.
— Aesthetics, Architecture (tr. Knox)
Yet in answering the question of where art has begun alike in conception and in reality, we must throughout exclude both the empirical facts of history and also the external reflections, conjectures and natural ideas that are so easily and variously propounded about it.
— Aesthetics, Architecture (tr. Knox)

Head: Symbolic Architecture
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › γ. The System of the Individual Arts › a. Architecture › i. Symbolic Architecture
Gloss: Architecture that is a symbol in itself.
Hegelian gloss: Symbolic architecture, building that is meaningful in itself without a further purpose.
Nouns: symbolic architecture; independent architecture, monument, megalith, menhir, the tower of Babel, ziggurat, totem, the colossal. self-sufficient architecture, building as symbol, symbolic building, the architecture of the East, meaning in mass.
Verbs: raise, erect, pile up. set up, rear. symbolize, signify, mean, betoken, embody.
Adjective: symbolic, monumental, megalithic, colossal. huge, immense, enormous, mighty, vast, stupendous, mammoth, gigantic. symbolical, independent, self-sufficient, significant.
Adverbs: monumentally. symbolically, in itself.
Phrases: let us build us a city and a tower, whose top may reach unto heaven [Bible]; a monument to.
Hegel definition: Independent or symbolic architecture builds works that express a universal idea for no other purpose. Art's primary need is to present a thought produced by spirit as a human work; unable at first to give abstract, indefinite national insights a spiritual shape, it seizes matter with mass and weight, so that meaning and sensuous reality relate only symbolically. The building is a wordless language present for its own sake, meant to stimulate thought.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· Architecture › Symbolic Architecture
Hegel citations:
On this account the relation between the meaning and the sensuous reality whereby the meaning is to issue from [the artist’s] conception into the spectator’s can be only of a purely symbolical kind.
— Aesthetics, Architecture › Symbolic Architecture (tr. Knox)
But at the same time a building which is to reveal a universal idea to spectators is constructed for no other purpose than to express this lofty idea in itself, and therefore it is an independent symbol of an absolutely essential and universally valid thought, or a language, present for its own sake, even if it be wordless, for apprehension by spiritual beings.
— Aesthetics, Architecture › Symbolic Architecture (tr. Knox)

Head: National Architecture
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › γ. The System of the Individual Arts › a. Architecture › i. Symbolic Architecture › 1. National Architecture
Gloss: Building that expresses the unity of a people, as a tower or monument.
Hegelian gloss: Building that unites a people, the tower of Babel and the Bel temple.
Nouns: national architecture; buildings uniting peoples, the Tower of Babel, Babylonian ziggurat, the Temple of Bel, collective monument, communal building. national monument, the tower of Belus, the unifying work, the common work, the bond of a people, rallying point, the work of nations.
Verbs: unite, gather, build together. bind, rally, build in common, raise.
Adjective: national, communal, Babylonian, collective. unifying, monumental, towering.
Adverbs: in common. as one people, together.
Foreign: Arabic: Bābil [Babel].
Phrases: the Tower of Babel; to make a name for ourselves.
Hegel definition: National architecture is building whose content is the holy understood, with Goethe, as what links many souls together. In the story of the tower in the plains of the Euphrates, all the peoples laboured in common, and the aim of the work was the community of its builders, a new and wider union beyond family ties. Herodotus' account of the tower of Bel at Babylon, rising in eight stages, gives a historically surer instance.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· Architecture › Symbolic Architecture › Architectural Works Built for National Unification
Hegel citations:
‘What is holy?’ Goethe asks once in a distich, and answers: ‘What links many souls together.’
— Aesthetics, Symbolic Architecture › Architectural Works Built for National Unification (tr. Knox)
The ensemble of all the peoples at that period worked at this task and since they all came together to complete an immense work like this, the product of their labour was to be a bond which was to link them together
— Aesthetics, Symbolic Architecture › Architectural Works Built for National Unification (tr. Knox)

Head: Sculptural Architecture
Head (German): Bauwerke schwankend zwischen Architektur und Skulptur
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › γ. The System of the Individual Arts › a. Architecture › i. Symbolic Architecture › 2. Sculptural Architecture
Gloss: Building that takes the form of free-standing sculpture.
Hegelian gloss: Building passing over into sculpture, as columns and obelisks.
Nouns: sculptural architecture; buildings between architecture and sculpture, columns, obelisks, colossi, Memnons, sphinxes, stupas, lingams. inorganic sculpture, architectural sculpture, the colossus, the sphinx, the Memnon, building as figure, free-standing monument, symbolic figure. menhir, stele, monolith.
Verbs: carve, erect, shape. sculpt, raise, mass, set up.
Adjective: sculptural, columnar, colossal. sculpturesque, monumental, free-standing, inorganic.
Adverbs: half building, half statue. sculpturally, monumentally, in the mass.
Phrases: the colossi of Memnon; standing stones; set in stone.
Hegel definition: Architecture wavering between building and sculpture adopts more concrete meanings and for their symbolic expression uses more concrete forms, alone or assembled into great buildings, yet handles them architecturally rather than sculpturally. As art enters actual historical views and religious ideas, it loses itself in the contingent, so that architecture and sculpture are confused, though architecture remains decisive.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· Architecture › Symbolic Architecture › Architectural Works wavering between Architecture and Sculpture
Hegel citations:
The next advance which we must proceed to consider is this, that architecture adopts more concrete meanings as its content
— Aesthetics, Symbolic Architecture › Architectural Works wavering between Architecture and Sculpture (tr. Knox)
The fundamental character here is that architecture and sculpture are confused, even if architecture remains the decisive element.
— Aesthetics, Symbolic Architecture › Architectural Works wavering between Architecture and Sculpture (tr. Knox)

They served as places of assembly, as subterranean cathedrals, and are constructions built for religious wonder and spiritual assembly

Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › γ. The System of the Individual Arts › a. Architecture › i. Symbolic Architecture › 3. Transition to Classical Architecture › c. Architecture of Purpose
Gloss: Building that serves an end outside itself.

Head: Classical Architecture
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › γ. The System of the Individual Arts › a. Architecture › ii. Classical Architecture
Gloss: Architecture that serves a purpose and is beautiful in doing so.
Hegelian gloss: Building that serves a purpose and is beautiful in serving it, the house of the god, with function and form in harmony.
Nouns: classical architecture; Greek architecture, Roman architecture, the orders, classicism, the temple, the colonnade, Palladianism, neoclassicism. architecture proper, the classical style, the columnar style, beauty in service, purposive beauty, the house of the god. peristyle, entablature, pediment.

Hegel definition: Classical architecture is subservient to an end and meaning not immanent in itself: an inorganic surrounding structure ordered by gravity and severe regular forms. Its beauty lies in appropriateness to purpose, freed from confusion with the organic and symbolic, a totality that lets its single purpose shine through all its forms and in the music of its proportions reshapes the useful into beauty.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· Architecture › Classical Architecture
Hegel citations:
The beauty of classical architecture consists precisely in this appropriateness to purpose which is freed from immediate confusion with the organic, the spiritual, and the symbolic; although it subserves a purpose, it comprises a perfect totality in itself which makes its one purpose shine clearly through all its forms, and in the music of its proportions reshapes the purely useful into beauty.
— Aesthetics, Architecture › Classical Architecture (tr. Knox)
Architecture at this stage, however, does correspond with its real essential nature because it cannot entirely endow the spiritual with an adequate existence and therefore can only frame the external and spiritless into a reflection of the spiritual.

Hegel definition: The general character of classical architecture is that spiritual meaning does not reside in the building itself but has attained free existence outside it, in sculpture or in living human activity, which architecture serves. Phrases: column, beam, and roof; the grammar of building; stone by stone.
Hegel definition: The particular determinants of architectural forms are the material, wood or stone, the specific forms of the temple, and the temple as a whole. Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· Architecture › Classical Architecture › The Particular Determinants of the Architectural Forms
Hegel citations:
Apart from all this the chief point in the temple, god’s house, on which everything turns is not the enclosure but the carrying beams and what they carry.
— Aesthetics, Classical Architecture › The Particular Determinants of the Architectural Forms (tr. Knox)
For this mechanical matter building in wood proves to be the first and the most appropriate to nature.
— Aesthetics, Classical Architecture › The Particular Determinants of the Architectural Forms (tr. Knox)

Head: Form: Wood and Stone Buildings
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › γ. The System of the Individual Arts › a. Architecture › ii. Classical Architecture › 2. Particular Formations of Classical Architecture › a. Form: Wood and Stone Buildings
Gloss: Building in timber and in stone, and the shapes each gives.
Hegelian gloss: Building in wood and in stone, the stone column keeping the memory of the tree trunk and timber beam.
Nouns: form: wood and stone buildings; post and lintel, trabeation. material, raw material, bricks and mortar. tower, steeple, spire, turret, dome, cupola.
Verbs: build. shape.
Adjective: trabeated.
Hegel definition: The question whether wooden or stone building was original turns on purpose: the tree supplies posts and beams ready formed, rectilinear pieces suited to the severe purposiveness of classical architecture, while stone is a shapeless mass that must be split and worked and invites excavation. Yet classical architecture, developing into beauty, builds in stone while keeping recognizable the principle of timber.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· Architecture › Classical Architecture › The Particular Determinants of the Architectural Forms › Building in Wood and Stone
Hegel citations:
[W]hereas wood owing to its natural form with rectilinear stems is directly more serviceable for the severer purposiveness and mathematical proportions that are the basis of classical architecture.
— Aesthetics, The Particular Determinants of the Architectural Forms › Building in Wood and Stone (tr. Knox)
But, conversely, classical architecture does not stop at all at building in wood but proceeds on the contrary, where it develops into beauty, to build in stone, with the result that while in its architectural forms the original principle of building in wood is still always recognizable, specific characteristics nevertheless enter which are not inherent in building in wood as such.
— Aesthetics, The Particular Determinants of the Architectural Forms › Building in Wood and Stone (tr. Knox)

Head: Wood Building
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › γ. The System of the Individual Arts › a. Architecture › ii. Classical Architecture › 2. Particular Formations of Classical Architecture › a. Form: Wood and Stone Buildings › i. Wood Building
Gloss: Building in timber, whose posts and beams are the first shapes of architecture.
Hegelian gloss: Der Holzbau: building in wood, the hut, whose posts and beams supply the original forms that stone architecture keeps.
Nouns: wood building. timber construction, beam, timber building, woodwork, carpentry, the hut. framework, rafter, girder, lintel, joist, corner stone, transom, travis†, trave†, modillion†.
Verbs: frame, mortise.
Adjective: wooden, timber, timbered, framed, ligneous.
Adverbs: in timber, in wood.
Phrases: the column remembers the tree.
Hegel definition: Building in wood is the first and most natural way to meet the temple's mechanical problem, since its basic determinants are the post that bears and the cross-beams that bind posts together. The tree affords both without extensive workmanship, wood already having a definite linear form whose pieces can be joined at right or other angles into corner posts, supports, beams and roof.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· Architecture › Classical Architecture › The Particular Determinants of the Architectural Forms › Building in Wood and Stone
Hegel citations:
For here the basic determinants are (i) the stanchion as load-bearing, and (ii) the cross-beams which provide the simultaneously necessary binding of stanchions together.
— Aesthetics, The Particular Determinants of the Architectural Forms › Building in Wood and Stone (tr. Knox)
Without any need for extensive and difficult workmanship, the tree affords both stanchions and beams, because wood has already in itself a definite formation; it consists of separate linear pieces, more or less rectangular, which can be directly put together at right, acute, or obtuse angles, and so provide corner-columns, supports, cross-beams, and a roof.
— Aesthetics, The Particular Determinants of the Architectural Forms › Building in Wood and Stone (tr. Knox)

Hegelian gloss: Der Steinbau: building in stone, the temple column recalling the tree trunk, freed from wood into the solidity of stone.

Adjective: stone, lithic, hewn.
Adverbs: in stone.
Phrases: the stone remembers the wood; timber turned to stone.
Hegel definition: Building in stone starts from a shapeless mass that must be split and worked before pieces can be piled and joined, and huge blocks invite excavation, serving symbolic and romantic architecture. Classical architecture nonetheless builds in stone when it becomes beautiful, preserving the original principle of timber in its forms while introducing characteristics that wood does not contain.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· Architecture › Classical Architecture › The Particular Determinants of the Architectural Forms › Building in Wood and Stone
Hegel citations:
On the other hand, stone does not have from the start such a firmly specific shape, but, compared with a tree, is a formless mass which, for some purpose, must be split and worked on before the separate stones can be brought together and piled on one another, and before they can be built together into a unity again.
— Aesthetics, The Particular Determinants of the Architectural Forms › Building in Wood and Stone (tr. Knox)
From this point of view, building in stone is especially predominant in independent architecture
— Aesthetics, The Particular Determinants of the Architectural Forms › Building in Wood and Stone (tr. Knox)

Hegel definition: The specific forms of the temple develop the house as its model, with load-bearing masses, what they carry, and the enclosure in three dimensions, whose differences must appear and fit together on mathematical principles. The Greek peculiarity is to shape supporting as such, making the column fundamental: unlike a wall it does not enclose but stands free, and unlike a mere post has proportion of its own.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· Architecture › Classical Architecture › The Particular Determinants of the Architectural Forms › The Specific Forms of the Temple
Hegel citations:
The peculiarity of Greek architecture is at once seen to consist in the fact that it gives shape to this supporting as such and therefore employs the column as the fundamental element in the purposiveness of architecture and its beauty.
— Aesthetics, The Particular Determinants of the Architectural Forms › The Specific Forms of the Temple (tr. Knox)
The column has no other purpose, but to be a support
— Aesthetics, The Particular Determinants of the Architectural Forms › The Specific Forms of the Temple (tr. Knox)

Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › γ. The System of the Individual Arts › a. Architecture › ii. Classical Architecture › 2. Particular Formations of Classical Architecture › c. Classical Temple as a Whole
Gloss: The temple as a complete whole.
Hegelian gloss: The classical temple as a whole, open, low and spread out, serene and cheerful, the house of a god who dwells among men.
Nouns: classical temple as a whole; the Parthenon, the Erechtheum, the Pantheon, the temple as unity, cella, stylobate, pediment. the temple, the whole temple, the fane, the shrine, the peristyle, the entablature, the totality, harmony of parts, completeness. temenos.
Verbs: crown, complete, harmonize. unite, enclose.
Adjective: complete, harmonious, unified, monumental. whole, entire, total, peripteral.
Adverbs: as a whole. in its entirety, wholly, completely.
Foreign: Greek: naos, pronaos, opisthodomos, acroterion.
Phrases: the Parthenon on the Acropolis; open to the light; serene and spread out.
Hegel definition: The classical temple as a whole unites its parts by juxtaposition and thorough eurhythmy, and is more than satisfying to behold. It does not strive upward but spreads in breadth, so that the eye is drawn across it, unlike Gothic building that struggles toward the sky; its ornament never impairs simplicity, and the Greeks kept a beautiful mean with well-proportioned variety.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· Architecture › Classical Architecture › The Particular Determinants of the Architectural Forms › The Classical Temple as a Whole
Hegel citations:
In general the Greek temples present us with an aspect which is satisfying, and, so to say, more than satisfying.
— Aesthetics, The Particular Determinants of the Architectural Forms › The Classical Temple as a Whole (tr. Knox)
Confronted by it the eye scarcely needs to direct its glance upwards; on the contrary it is allured by the breadth, while the medieval German [i.e. Gothic] architecture almost struggles upwards immeasurably and lifts itself to the sky.
— Aesthetics, The Particular Determinants of the Architectural Forms › The Classical Temple as a Whole (tr. Knox)

Hegelian gloss: The orders and manners of classical building, Greek and Roman.

Hegel definition: The styles of classical architecture differ most strikingly in their columns: the Greek Doric, Ionic and Corinthian orders, than which nothing more beautiful or fitting was found, the Tuscan belonging to simple timber work and the so-called Roman being only richer Corinthian. Rome added the arch and vault and a general character of its own.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· Architecture › Classical Architecture › The Different Styles in Classical Architecture
Hegel citations:
Primarily noticeable in this connection are those architectural styles whose difference comes out in the most striking way in the columns.
— Aesthetics, Classical Architecture › The Different Styles in Classical Architecture (tr. Knox)
The most familiar Orders are the Doric, Ionian, and Corinthian. Neither earlier nor later was anything discovered more architecturally beautiful or appropriate to its purpose.
— Aesthetics, Classical Architecture › The Different Styles in Classical Architecture (tr. Knox)

Head: Greek
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › γ. The System of the Individual Arts › a. Architecture › ii. Classical Architecture › 3. Styles of Classical Architecture › a. Greek
Gloss: The building of the Greeks.
Hegelian gloss: The Greek orders, each a different measure of the relation of bearing and borne.
Nouns: Greek architecture; Hellenic architecture, the Greek orders, Athens, the Acropolis, the stoa, the propylaea. Grecian building, the Greek temple, the orders, the column, the colonnade, the Parthenon.

Adverbs: in the Greek manner. in the Grecian style.
Foreign: Greek: entasis [swelling of the column].
Phrases: the Acropolis; the three Greek orders; the measure of bearing.
Hegel definition: The Greek orders are distinguished chiefly by the ratio of height to thickness of columns, the kinds of base and capital, and the spacing between columns, each choice altering the column's whole character. The shaft must stay plain, tapering with an almost imperceptible swelling, decorated only by fluting, since the column has nothing to do but support and rise firm, straight and independent.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· Architecture › Classical Architecture › The Different Styles in Classical Architecture › Doric, Ionic, and Corinthian Orders
Hegel citations:
The chief points of importance are the relation between the height and the diameter of the columns, the different sorts of pedestal and capital, and the greater or lesser distances between the columns.
— Aesthetics, The Different Styles in Classical Architecture › Doric, Ionic, and Corinthian Orders (tr. Knox)
[B]ecause the column has nothing to do but fulfil the task of supporting, and in fulfilling it to rise firm, straight, and independent
— Aesthetics, The Different Styles in Classical Architecture › Doric, Ionic, and Corinthian Orders (tr. Knox)

Head: Doric
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › γ. The System of the Individual Arts › a. Architecture › ii. Classical Architecture › 3. Styles of Classical Architecture › a. Greek › i. Doric
Gloss: The oldest and plainest Greek order, with a sturdy fluted column and a plain capital.
Hegelian gloss: The Doric, the oldest and most serious order, closest to wooden construction, sturdy and plain.
Nouns: Doric; the Doric order, Doric column, fluting, echinus, abacus, triglyph, metope, masculine simplicity, the Parthenon, Paestum. the Doric capital, entasis, sturdiness, plainness, severity.
Verbs: build in the Doric manner. flute, bear, support, simplify.
Adjective: Doric, sturdy, austere, masculine, simple, unadorned. Dorian, plain, severe, massive, baseless, fluted.
Adverbs: austerely. plainly, sturdily, severely, simply. badly.
Phrases: Doric severity; the manly order; plain and stern.
Hegel definition: Doric belongs to the stage where security of the building is the chief concern, with heavy forms in which load-bearing material and gravity dominate. Its columns are the broadest and lowest, giving an impression of simple, serious, unadorned masculinity; standing mostly without bases, with the simplest capitals, it remains nearest to timber building, as triglyphs and metopes show.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· Architecture › Classical Architecture › The Different Styles in Classical Architecture › Doric, Ionic, and Corinthian Orders
Hegel citations:
In the earliest buildings the fundamental consideration is the security of the building, and architecture does not go beyond this.
— Aesthetics, The Different Styles in Classical Architecture › Doric, Ionic, and Corinthian Orders (tr. Knox)
In general, however, the distinctive character of the Doric style is that it is still nearer the original simplicity of building in wood, although it is more susceptible of decorations and adornments than the Tuscan is.
— Aesthetics, The Different Styles in Classical Architecture › Doric, Ionic, and Corinthian Orders (tr. Knox)

Head: Ionic
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › γ. The System of the Individual Arts › a. Architecture › ii. Classical Architecture › 3. Styles of Classical Architecture › a. Greek › ii. Ionic
Gloss: The Greek order with a slender column and a capital of scroll-shaped volutes.
Hegelian gloss: The Ionic, more slender and graceful, with its spiral volutes.
Nouns: Ionic; the Ionic order, volute, scroll capital, slender column, base, feminine grace, the Erechtheum. the Ionic column, the Ionic capital, scroll, spiral, slenderness, grace, elegance. dentil, fillet.
Verbs: build in the Ionic manner. curl, slim.
Adjective: Ionic, slender, graceful, voluted, elegant. Ionian, scrolled, feminine.
Adverbs: gracefully. slenderly, elegantly.
Phrases: Ionic grace; the matronly order.
Hegel definition: Ionic architecture, still simple, rises from Doric's solidity to the slender, graceful and elegant: columns seven to ten diameters high, set on moulded bases, tapering to a slender top with deep flutes, and capitals enriched with shell-like curls. It requires a lighter architrave and no longer points to an origin in building with wood.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· Architecture › Classical Architecture › The Different Styles in Classical Architecture › Doric, Ionic, and Corinthian Orders
Hegel citations:
While the Doric style already develops into a character of pleasing solidity, Ionic architecture, though still simple, rises to what is typically slender, graceful, and elegant.
— Aesthetics, The Different Styles in Classical Architecture › Doric, Ionic, and Corinthian Orders (tr. Knox)
Granted this attractive slenderness and decoration of the columns, Ionic architecture now demands a bearing architrave which is less heavy and therefore is applied to making the building more graceful.
— Aesthetics, The Different Styles in Classical Architecture › Doric, Ionic, and Corinthian Orders (tr. Knox)

Nouns: Corinthian; the Corinthian order, acanthus capital, foliage, ornate column, Callimachus, luxury, opulence. the Corinthian column, the Corinthian capital, acanthus, acanthus leaf, the bell, helix, caulicolus, richness, ornateness. abacus, fleuron.

Adverbs: ornately. richly, luxuriantly.
Phrases: the acanthus capital; the maidenly order; leaves of acanthus.
Hegel definition: The Corinthian style keeps basically to the Ionic and its slenderness but develops it into tasteful brilliance with the final wealth of ornament, no longer letting the origin in wood glint through. Its column is no loftier but appears more slender and richer through a higher capital adorned with acanthus leaves, of which the Greeks told a charming story of a girl's grave.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· Architecture › Classical Architecture › The Different Styles in Classical Architecture › Doric, Ionic, and Corinthian Orders
Hegel citations:
Finally, the Corinthian style abides fundamentally by the Ionian but, keeping the same slenderness, it develops it into a tasteful brilliance and reveals the final wealth of decoration and ornament.
— Aesthetics, The Different Styles in Classical Architecture › Doric, Ionic, and Corinthian Orders (tr. Knox)
The Corinthian column is not loftier than the Ionic, because usually, with similar fluting, its height is only eight or eight-and-a-half times the diameter of its lower part, yet owing to a higher capital it appears more slender and, above all, richer.
— Aesthetics, The Different Styles in Classical Architecture › Doric, Ionic, and Corinthian Orders (tr. Knox)

Adjective: arched, vaulted, domed, arcuated, cupolated, aduncated†, arclike†, alveolate†, calathiform†, favaginous†, faveolate†, favose†, scyphiform†, scyphose†, infundibul†, infundibular†, infundibuliform†, campaniform†. curved, curvilinear, bowed, semicircular, curviform†, curvilineal†, devex†, recurvous†, crump†, falciform†, falcated†, luniform†, lunular†, conchoidal†, cordiform†, cordated†, lentiform†, bicorn†, bicornuous†, bicornute†, clypeate†, clypeiform†, cymbiform†, embowed†, galeiform†, hamate†, hamiform†, hamous†, linguiform†, lingulate†, lobiform†, navicular†, peltate†, remiform†, rhamphoid†, rostrate†, rostriferous†, rostroid†, scutate†, scaphoid†, uncate†, unguiform†, clavated†, hummocky†, moutonne†, mammiliform†, papulous†, papilose†. concave, hollow. round-headed. curving.

Hegel definition: The Roman construction of arch and vault makes Roman architecture a middle form between Greek and Christian. The Greeks developed column and horizontal beam, but an arch joining two supports is related to a centre that has nothing to do with the column, its parts carrying and continuing one another, so that the column begins to lose its purpose as mere support. The Pantheon is an outstanding example.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· Architecture › Classical Architecture › The Different Styles in Classical Architecture › The Roman Construction of Arch and Vault
Hegel citations:
Secondly, Roman architecture can be regarded as a middle form between Greek and Christian because what especially begins in it is the use of the arch and vaultings.
— Aesthetics, The Different Styles in Classical Architecture › The Roman Construction of Arch and Vault (tr. Knox)
For the arch in its rise, its curve, and its fall is related to a central point which has nothing to do with a column and its support. The different parts of the arch mutually carry, support, and continue one another, so that they are exempt from the aid of a column to a far greater extent than a superimposed beam is.
— Aesthetics, The Different Styles in Classical Architecture › The Roman Construction of Arch and Vault (tr. Knox)

Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › γ. The System of the Individual Arts › a. Architecture › ii. Classical Architecture › 3. Styles of Classical Architecture › c. General Character of Roman Architecture
Gloss: The general nature of Roman building: grand, practical and civic.
Hegelian gloss: Roman building, grand, practical and magnificent, serving the purposes of the state and of luxury.
Nouns: general character of Roman architecture; Roman engineering, grandeur, utility, magnificence, amphitheatre, Colosseum, basilica, baths, forum, aqueducts, roads. Roman building, Roman grandeur, practicality, engineering, the aqueduct, the triumphal arch, the villa, the road, the Pantheon.
