Hegel definition: Roman architecture generally differs wholly in range and character from the Greek: the Romans were skilful in the mechanics of building and made richer, more magnificent works with less nobility and grace. New purposes arose, theatres, amphitheatres and the luxurious villas and baths of private life, whereas the Greeks lavished beauty only on public buildings. It later served Italians and French as a model.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· Architecture › Classical Architecture › The Different Styles in Classical Architecture › General Character of Roman Architecture
Hegel citations:
Whereas the Romans are skilful in the mechanics of building, and although their buildings are richer and more magnificent, they have less nobility and grace.
— Aesthetics, The Different Styles in Classical Architecture › General Character of Roman Architecture (tr. Knox)

— Aesthetics, Architecture › Romantic Architecture (tr. Knox)

Hegel definition: The general character of romantic building is that enclosure is fundamental while mere utility is transcended: houses of God, entirely suited to worship, rise freely to a pinnacle so that purpose vanishes in the look of independent existence. — Aesthetics, Romantic Architecture › General Character of Romantic Architecture (tr. Knox)

Thus, while the buildings of classical architecture in the main lie on the ground horizontally, the opposite romantic character of Christian churches

Hegel definition: The form of exterior and interior in romantic building gives the inside new importance, since the whole is meant as enclosure, and the interior shows through the outer shape and determines it. Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· Architecture › Romantic Architecture › Particular Architectural Formations › The Form of the Exterior and the Interior

Therefore while in the temples of classical architecture the external form is the chief thing and, owing to the colonnades, remains independent of the construction of the interior, in romantic architecture the interior of the building not only acquires a more essential importance because the whole thing is meant to be an enclosure only, but the interior glints also through the shape of the exterior and determines its form and arrangement in detail.
— Aesthetics, Particular Architectural Formations › The Form of the Exterior and the Interior (tr. Knox)
Enter the interior of a medieval cathedral, and you are reminded less of the firmness and mechanical appropriateness of load-carrying pillars and a vault resting on them than of the vaultings of a forest where in lines of trees the branches incline to one another and quickly meet.

· Sculpture
Hegel citations:
It is along this road of spirit’s return into itself out of matter and mass that we encounter sculpture.
— Aesthetics, Sculpture (tr. Knox)

— Aesthetics, Sculpture (tr. Knox)

Head: Principle of Sculpture
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › γ. The System of the Individual Arts › b. Sculpture › i. Principle of Sculpture
Gloss: The fundamental nature of sculpture.
Hegelian gloss: The principle of sculpture: spirit wholly present in a bodily shape, at rest in itself.
Nouns: principle of sculpture; spirit in bodily form, the ideal human figure, three-dimensionality, plasticity, the body as expression of spirit. the nature of sculpture, the plastic principle, corporeality, the heavy mass, spatial totality, the bodily shape of spirit, objective individuality. embodiment.

Hegel definition: The principle of sculpture proper is the miracle of spirit giving itself an image of itself in something purely material, so forming the external thing that it is present in it and recognizes there the fit shape of its inner life. It asks what kind of spiritual life can appear in visible spatial form, how forms must be shaped to show it beautifully, and why this unity is the classical ideal.

Aesthetics
· Sculpture › The Principle of Sculpture Proper

Sculpture in general comprises the miracle of spirit’s giving itself an image of itself in something purely material. Spirit so forms this external thing that it is present to itself in it and recognizes in it the appropriate shape of its own inner life.
— Aesthetics, Sculpture › The Principle of Sculpture Proper (tr. Knox)
Thirdly, this unification corresponds with what we have already come to know as the ideal of the classical art-form, so that the plasticity of sculpture turns out to be the real and proper art of the classical ideal.
— Aesthetics, Sculpture › The Principle of Sculpture Proper (tr. Knox)

Hegel definition: The essential content of sculpture is the objectivity of spirit in self-repose, the stage at which spirit has not distinguished itself from its universal substance or from its bodily existence and so has not withdrawn into subjective self-awareness. It excludes the self that holds to its own particular, accidental character, as in self-satisfaction, in favour of the universal and eternal content of spirit.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· Sculpture › The Principle of Sculpture Proper › The Essential Content of Sculpture
Hegel citations:
To this more abstract aspect of the visible material there peculiarly corresponds, as content, the objectivity of spirit in its self-repose, i.e. the stage at which spirit has not distinguished itself either from its universal substance or its existence in body and therefore has not withdrawn into the self-awareness of its own subjectivity.
— Aesthetics, The Principle of Sculpture Proper › The Essential Content of Sculpture (tr. Knox)
But this self can detach itself from what in knowing, willing, imagining, feeling, acting, and accomplishing constitutes the universal and eternal content of the spirit, and retain a hold on its own particular and fortuitous character.
— Aesthetics, The Principle of Sculpture Proper › The Essential Content of Sculpture (tr. Knox)

Hegel definition: The beautiful sculptural form takes the human figure as its given fundamental type, a product of nature and not devised by art, much as architecture takes the house. Aesthetics
· Sculpture › The Principle of Sculpture Proper › The Beautiful Sculptural Form
Hegel citations:
The fundamental type is therefore given to sculpture, not devised by it.

Spirit and soul must be essentially distinguished from one another. For soul is only this ideal simple self-awareness of the body as body, while spirit is the self-awareness of conscious and self-conscious life with all the feelings, ideas, and aims of this conscious existent.

Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· Sculpture › The Principle of Sculpture Proper › The Beautiful Sculptural Form › Exclusion of Particulars

Verbs: compose, still, blank. exclude, omit, leave out, forgo, banish, suppress, abstract from.
Adjective: impassive, expressionless, calm, composed, eyeless. quiescent, motionless, fixed. unruffled, quiet, tranquil. sightless, blank-eyed, unmoved, unexpressive.
Adverbs: impassively. without expression, without glance.
Phrases: the blind eyes of the gods; the blind gaze of statues; eyes without pupils.
Hegel definition: Exclusion of mien keeps sculpture free of the accidents of personality: the artist may not present facial expression that shows the subject's own inner life and momentary feeling, such as pride, envy or scorn, nor the fleeting smile or flash of an eye. Those changes suit painting; sculpture must reproduce the permanent features of spiritual expression in face and posture.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· Sculpture › The Principle of Sculpture Proper › The Beautiful Sculptural Form › Exclusion of Mien
Hegel citations:
Consequently the artist is forbidden, so far as the face is concerned, to propose to go as far as presenting the mien [or a facial expression].
— Aesthetics, The Beautiful Sculptural Form › Exclusion of Mien (tr. Knox)
Changes of this character, which are a suitable subject for painting, sculpture has to waive.
— Aesthetics, The Beautiful Sculptural Form › Exclusion of Mien (tr. Knox)

Head: Substantive Individuality
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › γ. The System of the Individual Arts › b. Sculpture › i. Principle of Sculpture › 2. Beautiful Sculptural Form › c. Substantive Individuality
Gloss: Individual character as the embodiment of what is enduring.
Hegelian gloss: Individuality embodying the substantial, the god or hero as the universal in an individual shape.
Nouns: substantive individuality; self-contained individuality, essential character, enduring type. substantial individuality, the substantial character, the enduring, the abiding, the permanent, the universal in the individual, ethos, the god as substantial individual, fixity, constancy. haecceity, individuation.
Verbs: individuate, persist. endure, abide, embody, stand fast.
Adjective: substantive, essential, self-contained. substantial, enduring, abiding, permanent, lasting, constant, universal, objective.
Adverbs: substantively. substantially, enduringly, abidingly, permanently.
Phrases: individual yet universal; the universal in one figure; a god among gods.
Hegel definition: Substantive individuality is sculpture's essential task: to implant in the human figure spiritual substance in an individuality not yet subjectively particularized, bringing figure and substance into harmony so that only the universal and permanent in the bodily forms is emphasized and the fortuitous and transient stripped away, while the figure still does not lack individuality.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· Sculpture › The Principle of Sculpture Proper › The Beautiful Sculptural Form › Substantive Individuality
Hegel citations:
Thus it turns out that the task of sculpture essentially consists in implanting in a human figure the spiritual substance in its not yet subjectively particularized individuality
— Aesthetics, The Beautiful Sculptural Form › Substantive Individuality (tr. Knox)
[W]hile the fortuitous and the transient is stripped away, although at the same time the figure must not lack individuality.
— Aesthetics, The Beautiful Sculptural Form › Substantive Individuality (tr. Knox)

Head: Sculpture as the Art of the Classical Ideal
Head (German): Die Skulptur als Kunst des klassischen Ideals
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › γ. The System of the Individual Arts › b. Sculpture › i. Principle of Sculpture › 3. Sculpture as the Art of the Classical Ideal
Gloss: Sculpture as the art best suited to the perfect union of mind and body.
Hegelian gloss: Sculpture as the art which reaches the classical ideal, the adequate unity of spirit and body.
Nouns: sculpture as the art of the classical ideal; Greek sculpture, the classical ideal, perfection of form. the plastic art, the art of the ideal, the centre of classical art, the interpenetration of spirit and body, the adequate embodiment, the perfect fit of mind and body. classicism, ideality.
Verbs: perfect, idealize. embody, unite, interpenetrate, suit, fit, correspond.
Adjective: classical, ideal, perfect. plastic, adequate, fitting, suited, consummate.
Adverbs: classically. ideally, adequately, pre-eminently, par excellence.
Phrases: the classical art par excellence; noble simplicity and quiet grandeur; the ideal made flesh.
Hegel definition: Sculpture is more than any other art the art of the ideal, forming the centre of classical art: beyond the symbolic in the clarity of its spiritual content and its adequacy to it, yet still ignoring the inner subjectivity indifferent to outward shape. Its figures come from an imagination that sets aside all accidents, creating as the gods do by eternal ideas, a sense preeminently at home in Greece.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· Sculpture › The Principle of Sculpture Proper › Sculpture as the Art of the Classical Ideal
Hegel citations:
The first inference from the foregoing considerations is that sculpture more than any other art always points particularly to the Ideal.
— Aesthetics, The Principle of Sculpture Proper › Sculpture as the Art of the Classical Ideal (tr. Knox)
Sculpture must configurate in the way that within their own sphere the gods create according to eternal Ideas, while abandoning everything else in the rest of reality to the freedom and self-will of the creature.
— Aesthetics, The Principle of Sculpture Proper › Sculpture as the Art of the Classical Ideal (tr. Knox)

Head: The Ideal of Sculpture
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › γ. The System of the Individual Arts › b. Sculpture › ii. The Ideal of Sculpture
Gloss: The perfected human figure as sculpture presents it.
Hegelian gloss: The ideal human figure as sculpture shapes it.
Nouns: the ideal of sculpture; ideal sculpture, perfected human form, the canon, Polyclitus' canon. the sculptural ideal, the ideal figure, the ideal body, the divine in human shape, plastic beauty, perfection of form, the gods of Greece. kouros.
Verbs: idealize, perfect, measure. embody, beautify, ennoble.
Adjective: ideal, canonical, perfected. plastic, godlike, statuesque, flawless. Polyclitan.
Adverbs: ideally, by the canon. perfectly, in perfect form.
Foreign: Greek: kanōn.
Phrases: the Canon of Polyclitus; the measure of man; the perfect body.
Hegel definition: The ideal of sculpture presupposes, as all perfect art does, an imperfect stage, a sculpture still symbolic in character, such as the Egyptian. There art is hieroglyphic, a rough sketch that merely recalls its object, as a child's figure or a crude devotional image does, arousing a general idea. The ideal instead requires the living expression of the object's presence in a form fully shaped.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· Sculpture › The Ideal of Sculpture
Hegel citations:
In proceeding to consider the ideal style of sculpture we must once again recall that perfect art is necessarily preceded by imperfect, not merely in technique, which is not our prime concern here, but in the conception of the universal Idea and the manner of portraying it ideally.
— Aesthetics, Sculpture › The Ideal of Sculpture (tr. Knox)
So art at first is hieroglyphic, not an arbitrary and capricious sign but a rough sketch of the object for our apprehension.
— Aesthetics, Sculpture › The Ideal of Sculpture (tr. Knox)

Head: General Character of the Ideal Sculptural Form
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › γ. The System of the Individual Arts › b. Sculpture › ii. The Ideal of Sculpture › 1. General Character of the Ideal Sculptural Form
Gloss: The general nature of the ideal sculptural figure.
Hegelian gloss: The ideal sculptural form in general, the human figure purified to the expression of the divine.
Nouns: general character of the ideal sculptural form; serenity, repose, balance, proportion, harmony of parts. the nature of the ideal figure, the plastic ideal, self-containedness, universality, the human form, objectivity, the free beautiful body. sublimation.
Verbs: balance, compose. idealize, embody, universalize, generalize.
Adjective: serene, balanced, harmonious, proportioned. ideal, plastic, self-contained, reposeful, universal, general.
Adverbs: serenely. ideally, in general, in repose.
Phrases: calm and noble; calm and self-contained; beyond time and change.
Hegel definition: The general character of the ideal sculptural form is the way the classical ideal is realized in the human figure. The difference between human expression of spirit and animal life gives only a vague criterion, since the human form is not ideal from the start; a closer one comes from Greek masterpieces, whose understanding Winckelmann above all advanced by precisely characterizing the forms.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· Sculpture › The Ideal of Sculpture › General Character of the Ideal Sculptural Form
Hegel citations:
But this criterion still remains vague, because the human form as such is not from the start already completely of an ideal kind either as body or as an expression of the spirit.
— Aesthetics, The Ideal of Sculpture › General Character of the Ideal Sculptural Form (tr. Knox)
[I]t is Winckelmann above all who with the enthusiasm of his reproductive insight no less than with intelligence and sound judgement put an end to vague chatter about the ideal of Greek beauty
— Aesthetics, The Ideal of Sculpture › General Character of the Ideal Sculptural Form (tr. Knox)

Head: Particular Aspects of the Ideal Form
Head (German): Die besonderen Seiten der idealen Gestalt
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › γ. The System of the Individual Arts › b. Sculpture › ii. The Ideal of Sculpture › 2. Particular Aspects of the Ideal Form
Gloss: The particular features of the ideal sculptural figure.
Hegelian gloss: The particular features of the ideal form: profile, posture, drapery.
Nouns: particular aspects of the ideal form; profile, posture, drapery. particular features, particulars, details, specific aspects, the eye, the mouth, the chin, the hair. silhouette, contour.
Verbs: shape, pose, drape. particularize, detail, specify, distinguish, enumerate.
Adjective: particular, formal. special, specific, detailed, several.
Adverbs: in detail. in particular, specifically, severally.
Phrases: profile, pose, and drapery; the line of the brow; stance and drapery.
Hegel definition: The particular aspects of the ideal form, treated chiefly after Winckelmann, concern how Greek artists made the human form express spirit. That expression must spread over the whole body but is concentrated in the face, the other members reflecting spirit only in their position. So Hegel considers the head, then the position and movement of the body, and then the principle of drapery.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· Sculpture › The Ideal of Sculpture › Particular Aspects of the Ideal Form in Sculpture
Hegel citations:
Although the expression of spirit must be diffused over the appearance of the entire body, it is most concentrated in the face, whereas the other members can reflect the spirit only in their position, provided that that has been the work of the inherently free spirit.
— Aesthetics, The Ideal of Sculpture › Particular Aspects of the Ideal Form in Sculpture (tr. Knox)
Our consideration of the ideal forms will begin with the head; then, secondly, we will go on to discuss the position of the body, and then we end with the principle for the drapery.
— Aesthetics, The Ideal of Sculpture › Particular Aspects of the Ideal Form in Sculpture (tr. Knox)

Head: Greek Profile
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › γ. The System of the Individual Arts › b. Sculpture › ii. The Ideal of Sculpture › 2. Particular Aspects of the Ideal Form › a. Greek Profile
Gloss: The face in profile, with brow and nose in a single line.
Hegelian gloss: The Greek profile, brow and nose in one line, the spiritual brow dominating the animal mouth.
Nouns: Greek profile; the Grecian nose, straight profile, unbroken line of brow and nose, the classical profile. Grecian profile, the straight line of brow and nose, the facial angle, Camper's angle, the brow, the forehead, the nose, the ideal head, physiognomy.
Verbs: profile, line. align, outline, straighten.
Adjective: Grecian, classical, straight, noble. straight-nosed, rectilinear, ideal, facial. orthognathous.
Adverbs: in profile. in a straight line, sidewise. sideways.
Phrases: the Grecian nose.
Hegel definition: The Greek profile joins forehead and nose in an almost straight or gently curved unbroken line, at a right angle to a line from the nose's root to the ear. In animals the mouth dominates as the organ of need; in the human face a second centre in brow and eye expresses spirit's theoretical relation to things, and the nose mediates between that and the organs of nourishment.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· Sculpture › The Ideal of Sculpture › Particular Aspects of the Ideal Form in Sculpture › The Greek Profile
Hegel citations:
This profile depends on a specific connection between forehead and nose: in other words on the almost straight or only gently curved line on which the forehead is continued to the nose without interruption
— Aesthetics, Particular Aspects of the Ideal Form in Sculpture › The Greek Profile (tr. Knox)
Therefore the human face has a second centre in which the soulful and spiritual relation to things is manifested.
— Aesthetics, Particular Aspects of the Ideal Form in Sculpture › The Greek Profile (tr. Knox)

Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › γ. The System of the Individual Arts › b. Sculpture › ii. The Ideal of Sculpture › 2. Particular Aspects of the Ideal Form › b. Position and Movement of the Body
Gloss: The stance and motion of the sculpted body.
Hegelian gloss: The stance and movement of the body, the upright free posture, at rest yet animated.
Nouns: position and movement of the body; posture, pose, stance, attitude, gesture, movement, balance. position, footing, standing. bearing, carriage, gait, repose, rest, sitting, reclining, striding. ponderation.
Verbs: pose, stand, lean, gesture, shift weight. sit, recline, stride, poise, move.

Foreign: Italian: contrapposto.
Phrases: the weight on one leg; at rest yet alive.
Hegel definition: Position and movement of the body make trunk and limbs, beautiful sensuously but not directly expressive like the face, give a glimpse of spirit, so that spirit appears poured over the whole figure. It appears through position freely determined from within, movement or repose, and the situation shown. Upright posture, an act of will by which a person tears loose from the ground, already expresses spirit.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· Sculpture › The Ideal of Sculpture › Particular Aspects of the Ideal Form in Sculpture › Position and Movement of the Body
Hegel citations:
For otherwise the expression of the inner life would be concentrated solely in the face, while in the plasticity of sculpture the spirit should appear precisely as effused over the whole figure and not independently isolated and contrasted with the body.
— Aesthetics, Particular Aspects of the Ideal Form in Sculpture › Position and Movement of the Body (tr. Knox)
This standing is an act of will, for, if we give up willing to stand, our body collapses and falls to the ground.
— Aesthetics, Particular Aspects of the Ideal Form in Sculpture › Position and Movement of the Body (tr. Knox)

Head: Individuality of the Ideal Sculptured Figure
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › γ. The System of the Individual Arts › b. Sculpture › ii. The Ideal of Sculpture › 3. Individuality of the Ideal Sculptured Figure
Gloss: The individual character of the ideal sculpted figure.
Hegelian gloss: The individuality of the ideal figure, its particular character among the gods and heroes.
Nouns: individuality of the ideal sculptured figure; distinguishing features, attributes, character types, individual gods. individual character, individuation, particularity, the particular god, the determinate figure, distinguishing marks, type, personality within the ideal. iconography, xoanon.
Verbs: distinguish, characterize. individualize, individuate, particularize, differentiate.
Adjective: distinctive, individual, characteristic. distinguishing. representative, typical, symbolic. special, particular, specific, proper, personal, original. individualized, determinate.
Adverbs: distinctively. individually, characteristically.
Phrases: known by their attributes; each god his own; the character of a deity.
Hegel definition: Individuality of the ideal figures means that sculptures must show substantial individuals who are also particular persons, the group of Greek gods. A single supreme beauty in one statue is foolish, since the ideal's beauty lies in individuality and character, broadening abstract beauty into an ensemble of figures, though Christian virtues resting on the breach of body and spirit have no place among them.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· Sculpture › The Ideal of Sculpture › Individuality of the Ideal Sculptured Figures
Hegel citations:
For the beauty of the ideal consists precisely in its not being a purely universal norm but in essentially having individuality and therefore particularity and character.
— Aesthetics, The Ideal of Sculpture › Individuality of the Ideal Sculptured Figures (tr. Knox)
In this way alone are sculptures vitalized, and the one abstract beauty is broadened into an ensemble of inherently specific shapes.
— Aesthetics, The Ideal of Sculpture › Individuality of the Ideal Sculptured Figures (tr. Knox)

Head: Attributes, Weapons, Adornments
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › γ. The System of the Individual Arts › b. Sculpture › ii. The Ideal of Sculpture › 3. Individuality of the Ideal Sculptured Figure › a. Attributes, Weapons, Adornments
Gloss: The emblems and ornaments by which a sculpted figure is identified.
Hegelian gloss: The attributes, weapons and adornments by which the individual gods are known.
Foreign: French: bijouterie.
Hegel definition: Attributes, weapons and adornment are external accessories that great sculpture keeps simple, moderate and limited, so that nothing is there beyond what lets the work be understood, since the figure and its expression provide the spiritual meaning. Such marks are nonetheless needed to recognize gods, whose common divinity makes them closely akin.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· Sculpture › The Ideal of Sculpture › Individuality of the Ideal Sculptured Figures › Attributes, Weapons, Adornment
Hegel citations:
[T]hese externals are, in the great works of sculpture, kept simple, moderate, and limited, so that there is nothing of that kind except what is required to let us understand the work and identify its subject
— Aesthetics, Individuality of the Ideal Sculptured Figures › Attributes, Weapons, Adornment (tr. Knox)
Even so, however, such indications are necessary to enable us to recognize the individual gods.
— Aesthetics, Individuality of the Ideal Sculptured Figures › Attributes, Weapons, Adornment (tr. Knox)

Head: Attributes
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › γ. The System of the Individual Arts › b. Sculpture › ii. The Ideal of Sculpture › 3. Individuality of the Ideal Sculptured Figure › a. Attributes, Weapons, Adornments › i. Attributes
Gloss: The emblems by which each god is known: Zeus's eagle, Athena's owl, Hermes' staff.
Hegelian gloss: Die Attribute: the signs, eagle, owl, trident or thyrsus, by which the individual gods are told apart, marks whose meaning is often only conventional.
Nouns: attributes. attribute, emblem, symbol, insignia, thunderbolt, trident, caduceus, aegis, lyre, owl, eagle. badge, token, insigne, trapping, the thyrsus, brocatelle†.
Verbs: identify. betoken, mark.
Adjective: emblematic, symbolic, attributive, identifying. representative, typical.
Adverbs: by emblem, emblematically, by attribute.
Phrases: Zeus with his thunderbolt; the thunderbolt of Zeus; known by their tokens.
Hegel definition: Attributes proper in sculpture lose their independent and symbolic character and appear only beside the figure as external signs related to some aspect of a particular god, often animals, as Zeus's eagle or Juno's peacock, or tools such as the thyrsus of Bacchus. Antiquaries have pursued them pedantically, and since several gods share some, they do not always identify one alone.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· Sculpture › The Ideal of Sculpture › Individuality of the Ideal Sculptured Figures › Attributes, Weapons, Adornment
Hegel citations:
In sculpture these lose their independent and symbolic character still more, and they only retain the right of appearing on or beside the figure, which represents itself alone, as an external indication closely related to one or other aspect of the specific gods.
— Aesthetics, Individuality of the Ideal Sculptured Figures › Attributes, Weapons, Adornment (tr. Knox)
Yet even so here again the difficulty arises that the attributes, like the figure, do not every time serve to identify one god only, because they are common to several.
— Aesthetics, Individuality of the Ideal Sculptured Figures › Attributes, Weapons, Adornment (tr. Knox)

Head: Weapons
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › γ. The System of the Individual Arts › b. Sculpture › ii. The Ideal of Sculpture › 3. Individuality of the Ideal Sculptured Figure › a. Attributes, Weapons, Adornments › ii. Weapons

Hegel definition: Differences of age and sex, and of gods, heroes, humans and animals, must mark living individuality through the figure's own free and beautiful form and expression, not merely by accessories. The Greeks harmonized the smallest traits with the whole; youthful forms flow delicately into one another and are the harder to make, while mature figures show their distinctions more definitely.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· Sculpture › The Ideal of Sculpture › Individuality of the Ideal Sculptured Figures › Differences of Age and Sex, and of Gods, Heroes, Men, and Animals

Head: Portrayal of Individual Gods
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › γ. The System of the Individual Arts › b. Sculpture › ii. The Ideal of Sculpture › 3. Individuality of the Ideal Sculptured Figure › c. Portrayal of Individual Gods
Gloss: The representation of each god in sculpture.
Hegelian gloss: The portrayal of the individual gods, each with its own character.
Nouns: portrayal of individual gods; Zeus of Olympia, Athena Parthenos, Apollo Belvedere, Venus de Milo, Hermes of Praxiteles, Aphrodite of Knidos. the gods in sculpture, divine image, cult statue, the type of each god, Zeus, Hera, Apollo, Athena, Aphrodite, Hermes, Dionysus, the Jupiter of Phidias, characteristic type. dodecatheon, pantheon.
Verbs: portray, sculpt, represent. depict, embody, individualize, typify, characterize.

Adverbs: in marble, in ivory and gold. individually, each in his kind, characteristically.
Phrases: the Zeus of Phidias; the Olympians; the twelve gods.
Hegel definition: Portrayal of the individual gods shows how the Greeks, despite their gods' universality and ideality, kept them individual and distinct without fixed portrait types, invention being subtlest where the substantial type remained its basis. Phidias gave Zeus supremacy, cheerful and benign; Neptune is wilder, Pluto darker; Juno has the greatest majesty among the goddesses.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· Sculpture › The Ideal of Sculpture › Individuality of the Ideal Sculptured Figures › Portrayal of the Individual Gods
Hegel citations:
[B]ut in this matter the amazing way in which the Greeks have solved this problem in sculpture consisted precisely in their having, despite the universality and ideality of their gods, still preserved their individuality and distinction from one another

Amongst the female figures Juno has the greatest majesty in form and expression, just as Zeus has amongst the male figures.
— Aesthetics, Individuality of the Ideal Sculptured Figures › Portrayal of the Individual Gods (tr. Knox)

Head: Different Kinds of Sculpture
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › γ. The System of the Individual Arts › b. Sculpture › iii. Different Kinds of Sculpture

Hegelian gloss: The kinds of sculpture, by mode of portrayal, by material and by historical stage.

Adverbs: by kind. variously, severally, in kind.
Phrases: in the round and in relief; statue and group.
Hegel definition: The different kinds of sculpture arise because the ideal, being individuality, broadens into a group of gods and its outward execution divides into sorts. These are considered by mode of portrayal, as single statues, groups and reliefs, the last passing toward painting; by the external material in which they are realized; and by the stages of sculpture's historical development.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· Sculpture › The Different Kinds of Portrayal and Material
Hegel citations:
Since the ideal is to be understood essentially as individuality, not only does the inner artistic vision broaden out into a group of ideal and separate gods, but the external mode of portrayal and its execution in existing works of art fell apart into the different sorts of sculpture.
— Aesthetics, Sculpture › The Different Kinds of Portrayal and Material (tr. Knox)
[F]irst, the mode of portrayal which, in actual execution, forms either single statues or groups until finally, in reliefs, it makes the transition to the principle of painting
— Aesthetics, Sculpture › The Different Kinds of Portrayal and Material (tr. Knox)

Head: Modes of Portrayal

Nouns: modes of portrayal; single figure, group, relief, freestanding sculpture, sculpture in the round. high relief, low relief, bassorilievo†, altorilievo†, mezzorilievo†, intaglio, anaglyph†, medal, medallion, cameo. manner of presentation, mode of representation, mode of treatment, rendering, depiction, statue group and relief, form of display. alto-rilievo, basso-rilievo.

Foreign: French: bas relief.

Hegel definition: Modes of portrayal distinguish sculptures independent of anything else, for which surroundings are merely a prepared place, from those that decorate spaces in or on buildings, whose relation to the building determines their form and largely their content. In the main single statues exist on their own account, while groups and above all reliefs give up independence to serve architecture.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· Sculpture › The Different Kinds of Portrayal and Material › Modes of Portrayal
Hegel citations:
For the former the surroundings are no more than a place prepared already by art, while in the case of the latter the essential thing is always their relation to the building that they decorate, and this determines not only the form of the sculpture but also, for the most part, its content too.
— Aesthetics, The Different Kinds of Portrayal and Material › Modes of Portrayal (tr. Knox)
In this connection we may say, on the whole and in the main, that single statues exist on their own account, whereas groups, and a fortiori reliefs, begin to give up this independence and are employed by architecture for its own artistic ends.
— Aesthetics, The Different Kinds of Portrayal and Material › Modes of Portrayal (tr. Knox)

Head: Single Statue
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › γ. The System of the Individual Arts › b. Sculpture › iii. Different Kinds of Sculpture › 1. Modes of Portrayal › a. Single Statue

Foreign: Greek: kouros, korē.
Phrases: the Discobolus; a figure alone.
Hegel definition: The single statue has the proper function of sculpture itself, to provide images in temples, where its surroundings bear upon it. Here sculpture keeps its most perfect purity, setting the gods in beautiful, simple, inactive repose without a definite situation, or in free, naive ones. It departs from this when the position hints at an action's beginning or end.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· Sculpture › The Different Kinds of Portrayal and Material › Modes of Portrayal › The Single Statue
Hegel citations:
The original function of single statues is the real function of sculpture as such, i.e. to furnish images in temples
— Aesthetics, Modes of Portrayal › The Single Statue (tr. Knox)
Here sculpture retains its most perfect purity because in executing the figure of the gods it sets them in beautiful, simple, inactive repose in no specific situation
— Aesthetics, Modes of Portrayal › The Single Statue (tr. Knox)

Head: Groups
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › γ. The System of the Individual Arts › b. Sculpture › iii. Different Kinds of Sculpture › 1. Modes of Portrayal › b. Groups
Gloss: Several figures composed together.
Hegelian gloss: The group, figures brought together in an action and a situation.
Nouns: groups; sculptural group, ensemble, composition, Laocoön, pediment groups, the Niobids, the Tyrannicides. statuary group, grouping, pediment group, the Laocoön group, the Niobe group, the Dioscuri, figures in relation. tableau.

Adverbs: together, in a group. in combination, in concert.
Phrases: Laocoön and his sons; figures in action.
Hegel definition: Groups arise as sculpture proceeds to situations in movement, conflict and action, expanding a more concrete liveliness into opposition and reaction among several figures. Peaceful juxtapositions come first, then groups displaying discord and grief, which the Greeks bound to architecture, as in pediments. The Laocoon keeps nobility and beauty amid profound grief, yet belongs to a later age.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· Sculpture › The Different Kinds of Portrayal and Material › Modes of Portrayal › Groups
Hegel citations:
For what comes into appearance with a more defined action is a more concrete liveliness which is expanded into oppositions and reactions and therefore into essential relations between several figures and their interlacing.
— Aesthetics, Modes of Portrayal › Groups (tr. Knox)
The most essential thing to consider in the case of this group is that despite the profound grief and profound truth it conveys, despite the convulsive contraction of the body and the tension of all the muscles, still nobility and beauty are preserved, and not in the remotest degree is there any approach to grimaces, distortion, or dislocation.
— Aesthetics, Modes of Portrayal › Groups (tr. Knox)

Hegel definition: Reliefs are the mode in which sculpture takes a long step toward painting: figures stand on one surface and sculpture's third dimension begins to vanish, though ancient relief keeps to the plane without perspective, favouring figures in profile and actions that proceed along a single line, such as processions. Reliefs adorn walls and vessels in the greatest variety.

The last mode of presentation whereby sculpture takes an important step towards the principle of painting is the relief, first the high relief and later the bas-relief.

But the ancient relief does not yet come so near to painting as to proceed to perspective differences between foreground and background

Nouns: materials for sculpture; medium, stone, marble, bronze, wood, ivory, gold, clay, terracotta, plaster, gems, glass. raw material, stuff, metal. papier-mache, ceramic ware, porcelain, earthenware, enamel, faience. granite, adamant, iron, steel. substance, wax, limestone, porphyry, basalt, alabaster, albata†, eburin†, ceruse†.

Hegel definition: The materials of sculpture must be examined because individuality particularizes not only subjects and modes but matter, different kinds of subject and treatment having a secret sympathy with kinds of material. The Greeks amaze by technical skill as much as invention, since complete mastery of the material belongs to the ideal, which wholly enters the sensuous and fuses inner with outer.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· Sculpture › The Different Kinds of Portrayal and Material › Materials for Sculpture
Hegel citations:
For different kinds of subject-matter and mode of treatment are closely connected with different kinds of physical material and have a secret sympathy and harmony with them.
— Aesthetics, The Different Kinds of Portrayal and Material › Materials for Sculpture (tr. Knox)
Yet this developed skill in the completely perfect handling of the material is inherent in the very nature of the ideal itself, because the ideal has, as its principle, entire entry into the sensuous field and the fusion of the inner life with its external existence.

Hegelian gloss: Ivory, gold, bronze and marble, the materials of the classical ideal.

Hegel definition: Ivory, gold, bronze and marble are the materials of first importance. Phidias used ivory and gold for his Zeus and Athene; bronze was the most widespread material of antiquity, cast by the Greeks with supreme mastery; and stone, above all marble, with its permanence, purity, soft sheen and absence of colour, harmonizes most directly with sculpture's aim.

Head: Bronze
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › γ. The System of the Individual Arts › b. Sculpture › iii. Different Kinds of Sculpture › 2. Materials for Sculpture › b. Ivory, Gold, Bronze, Marble › iii. Bronze

Hegel definition: Bronze was antiquity's most widespread and favoured material, cast by the Greeks with supreme mastery for gods and other works. Adverbs: in miniature.
Hegel definition: Precious stones and glass complete the materials. Greek gems, cameos and pastes are beyond price, repeating in the smallest compass the whole range of sculpture in supreme perfection. Their topics were drawn not from the artists' own invention but, apart from Bacchic scenes and dances, from myths and traditions; allegory belongs only to later art.

For productions in these varied kinds of material the Greek artists did not take as a basis situations fabricated by themselves but drew their topics every time, except for Bacchanalia and dances, from myths about the gods and traditions

Hegel texts:

Hegel texts:

To these most important sorts of material we have to add, in conclusion, precious stones and glass.

[B]ecause, although in the smallest compass, they repeat in supreme perfection the whole range of sculpture from the simple figure of a god, through the most varied kinds of grouping, to all possible conceits

Head: Historical Stages in the Development of Sculpture
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › γ. The System of the Individual Arts › b. Sculpture › iii. Different Kinds of Sculpture › 3. Historical Stages in the Development of Sculpture
Gloss: The historical course of sculpture.
Hegelian gloss: The historical course of sculpture, from Egypt through Greece and Rome to Christian art.
Nouns: historical stages in the development of sculpture; Egyptian, archaic Greek, classical, Hellenistic, Roman, Christian sculpture. the history of sculpture, the stages of sculpture, the course of sculpture, epochs, periods, Egyptian Greek and Christian sculpture, the severe style, the ideal style, the pleasing style. archaism, megatherium†.
Verbs: develop, evolve. unfold, progress, advance, mature, decline.
Adjective: historical, archaic, classical, Hellenistic. developmental, successive, progressive.
Adverbs: historically. by stages, successively, in the course of time.
Phrases: from the archaic smile to Laocoön; from Egypt to Rome; the rise and fall of the ideal.
Hegel definition: Historical stages of sculpture arise because the ideal has behind it the symbolic mode it must surmount and ahead the romantic that supersedes it, and both use the human form. So the history includes Egyptian sculpture as preamble, Greek sculpture with the Roman as its proper development, and Christian sculpture with its own principle.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· Sculpture › Historical Stages in the Development of Sculpture
Hegel citations:
Both the symbolic and the romantic forms of art likewise take the human form as the medium of their portrayals; they cling to its spatial outline and therefore display it visibly in the manner of sculpture.
— Aesthetics, Sculpture › Historical Stages in the Development of Sculpture (tr. Knox)
Consequently when our business is with the historical development of sculpture we have to discuss not merely Greek and Roman sculpture, but oriental and Christian sculpture as well.
— Aesthetics, Sculpture › Historical Stages in the Development of Sculpture (tr. Knox)

Head: Egyptian Sculpture
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › γ. The System of the Individual Arts › b. Sculpture › iii. Different Kinds of Sculpture › 3. Historical Stages in the Development of Sculpture › a. Egyptian Sculpture
Gloss: The sculpture of Egypt.
Hegelian gloss: Egyptian sculpture, rigid, symmetrical and without the freedom of individual life.
Nouns: Egyptian sculpture; Egyptian statuary, rigid frontality, stiff posture, symmetry, colossi, the seated pharaoh, animal-headed gods. the Memnon statues, the sphinx, the fixed type, canon of proportion, stiffness, rigidity, immobility, frontality, lifelessness, granite, basalt. colossus.
Verbs: carve, stylize. hew, stiffen, fix, typify, repeat.
Adjective: Egyptian, frontal, rigid, hieratic, stylized. Pharaonic, colossal, stiff, immobile, typical, lifeless.
Adverbs: rigidly, frontally. stiffly, by rule.
Phrases: the arms at the sides; arms at their sides; fixed by convention.
Hegel definition: Egyptian sculpture is a starting point and source for Greek forms, an imperfect art that classical art had to negate. Its content begins to meet the ideal but cannot be ideally treated because it still belongs to a symbolic outlook that cannot fuse universal meaning with individual visible shape; despite technical perfection it lacks inner creative freedom.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· Sculpture › Historical Stages in the Development of Sculpture › Egyptian Sculpture
Hegel citations:
Now this [pre-classical] process of becoming classical consists in the fact that the content of the presentation begins to meet the ideal, yet remains incapable of an ideal treatment because it still belongs to the symbolic outlook which cannot form into one the universality of the meaning and the individual visible shape.
— Aesthetics, Historical Stages in the Development of Sculpture › Egyptian Sculpture (tr. Knox)
The first thing to mention is the lack of inner and creative freedom, despite all perfection of technique.
— Aesthetics, Historical Stages in the Development of Sculpture › Egyptian Sculpture (tr. Knox)

Head: Greek and Roman Sculpture
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › γ. The System of the Individual Arts › b. Sculpture › iii. Different Kinds of Sculpture › 3. Historical Stages in the Development of Sculpture › b. Greek and Roman Sculpture
Gloss: The sculpture of Greece and Rome.
Hegelian gloss: Greek and Roman sculpture, the realized ideal and its decline.
Nouns: Greek and Roman sculpture. antique statuary, the antique.
Verbs: sculpt, chisel, model.
Adjective: classical. antique, plastic.
Adverbs: classically.
Hegel definition: Greek and Roman sculpture shows sense of self fully alive, removing the Egyptian defects, though without violent leap: Aeginetan and Etruscan works are preliminaries, the ideal arrives when artistic freedom replaces the typical and traditional, and in Roman art classical sculpture begins to dissolve as spiritual animation yields to portraiture.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· Sculpture › Historical Stages in the Development of Sculpture › Greek and Roman Sculpture
Hegel citations:
This sense of self we see completely made alive for the first time, so far as sculpture is concerned, in the Greeks, and therefore we find all the deficiencies of this Egyptian preamble expunged.
— Aesthetics, Historical Stages in the Development of Sculpture › Greek and Roman Sculpture (tr. Knox)
Thirdly, in Roman art we see the dissolution of classical sculpture beginning.
— Aesthetics, Historical Stages in the Development of Sculpture › Greek and Roman Sculpture (tr. Knox)

Head: Greek Sculpture
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › γ. The System of the Individual Arts › b. Sculpture › iii. Different Kinds of Sculpture › 3. Historical Stages in the Development of Sculpture › b. Greek and Roman Sculpture › i. Greek Sculpture
Gloss: The sculpture of Greece, the realization of the ideal in the human form.
Hegelian gloss: Die Skulptur der Griechen, in which the classical ideal is perfectly achieved, from the Aeginetan marbles to Phidias.
Nouns: Greek sculpture. classical sculpture, Phidias, Polyclitus, Praxiteles, Lysippus, Myron, the archaic smile, Hellenistic sculpture, Attic sculpture, Scopas, the Elgin marbles, the Aeginetan marbles, the Apollo Belvedere, the Laocoön, the canon.
Verbs: idealize, perfect.
Adjective: Greek, Phidian, idealized, Attic, Praxitelean, ideal.
Adverbs: in the antique manner, ideally.
Phrases: the glory of the Parthenon marbles; the glory that was Greece; Phidias and Praxiteles.
Hegel definition: Greek sculpture brings the sense of self fully to life, though even within it the ideal must strip off early defects. Its beginnings, as in Aeginetan works, remain tied to the typical and to merely natural life; the summit comes when artistic freedom works universal meaning wholly into individual shape, giving a spiritually animated beauty.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· Sculpture › Historical Stages in the Development of Sculpture › Greek and Roman Sculpture
Hegel citations:
[I]n this development we have not to make any violent leap from the imperfections of a still symbolic sculpture to the perfection of the classical ideal
— Aesthetics, Historical Stages in the Development of Sculpture › Greek and Roman Sculpture (tr. Knox)
[N]ot the life of that spiritually animated beauty which displays the life of the spirit unseparated from the life of its natural shape
— Aesthetics, Historical Stages in the Development of Sculpture › Greek and Roman Sculpture (tr. Knox)

Head: Roman Sculpture
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › γ. The System of the Individual Arts › b. Sculpture › iii. Different Kinds of Sculpture › 3. Historical Stages in the Development of Sculpture › b. Greek and Roman Sculpture › ii. Roman Sculpture
Gloss: The sculpture of Rome, given to portraits and the record of public life.
Hegelian gloss: Die Skulptur der Römer, which keeps the Greek forms but turns to portrait and likeness, where the ideal begins to dissolve.
Nouns: Roman sculpture. Roman portraiture, the bust, Roman portrait bust. portrait statue, imperial portraiture, the Ara Pacis, Trajan's Column, historical relief.
Verbs: portray.
Adjective: Roman, veristic.
Hegel definition: Roman sculpture begins the dissolution of classical sculpture: conception and execution no longer rest on the ideal proper, and the poetry of spiritual animation and inner nobility peculiar to Greek art gives way to a preference for portraiture and truth to nature. Even so it stands high, inferior to Greek essentially in lacking that poetry.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· Sculpture › Historical Stages in the Development of Sculpture › Greek and Roman Sculpture
Hegel citations:
The poetry of spiritual animation, the inner breath and nobility of a representation perfect in itself, these excellences peculiar to Greek plastic art, disappear and give place on the whole to a preference for something more like a portrait.
— Aesthetics, Historical Stages in the Development of Sculpture › Greek and Roman Sculpture (tr. Knox)
Nevertheless in this its own sphere, it is always at such a high stage that essentially it is only inferior to Greek because it lacks what is really perfect in a work of art, the poetry of the ideal in the strict sense of the word.
— Aesthetics, Historical Stages in the Development of Sculpture › Greek and Roman Sculpture (tr. Knox)

Head: Christian Sculpture
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › γ. The System of the Individual Arts › b. Sculpture › iii. Different Kinds of Sculpture › 3. Historical Stages in the Development of Sculpture › c. Christian Sculpture
Gloss: Sculpture in the service of Christianity.
Hegelian gloss: Christian sculpture, which cannot fully express the inwardness of the romantic content.
Nouns: Christian sculpture; medieval sculpture, Gothic statuary, portal figures, crucifix, Pietà, Michelangelo's David, Donatello, Bernini. church sculpture, cathedral sculpture, the Madonna, saints' figures, tomb effigy, altarpiece carving, Michelangelo, the Nuremberg masters, Peter Vischer. reliquary, patera†, eileton†, Sangraal†, urceus†.
Verbs: carve, sculpt, devote. adorn, serve, ornament.
Adjective: Christian, Gothic, devotional, Renaissance, Baroque. ecclesiastical, medieval, subservient, ornamental, expressive.
Adverbs: devotionally. in the service of the church.
Phrases: the Pietà; stone cannot weep enough.
Hegel definition: Christian sculpture has from the start a principle that does not cohere directly with sculpture's material: romantic art concerns inward life withdrawn from the external, and grief, torture, death, resurrection and love find no adequate form in three-dimensional shape. So it yields to painting and music and serves chiefly as architecture's adornment, acquiring a pictorial principle.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· Sculpture › Historical Stages in the Development of Sculpture › Christian Sculpture
Hegel citations:
Therefore in the romantic field sculpture does not afford, as it does in Greece, the distinctive characteristic of the other arts and indeed of the whole of existence.
— Aesthetics, Historical Stages in the Development of Sculpture › Christian Sculpture (tr. Knox)
On the contrary the religious sculpture of romantic art remains, to a greater extent than Greek, an adornment of architecture.
— Aesthetics, Historical Stages in the Development of Sculpture › Christian Sculpture (tr. Knox)

Head: Romantic Arts
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › γ. The System of the Individual Arts › c. Romantic Arts
Gloss: The arts that express the inner life rather than the body.
Hegelian gloss: The romantic arts, painting, music and poetry, in which the inner life of the subject is expressed.
Nouns: romantic arts; painting, music, and poetry, the arts of inwardness, the subjective arts. the arts of subjectivity, painting music and poetry, the art of the soul, inner life, interiority, feeling, the heart.

Adjective: romantic, inward, expressive, subjective. soulful, spiritual, non-plastic.
Adverbs: inwardly. subjectively, from within, in feeling.
Phrases: the arts of the soul; the art of the inner life.
Hegel definition: The romantic arts, painting, music and poetry, arise from the principle of subjectivity, spirit withdrawing out of the external world into an inner existence, so that it no longer coincides indissolubly with its body. The unity achieved by sculpture dissolves, its factors becoming independent: the divine grasped as subject and personality, and the human subject unfolding the whole heart, reunited through the common principle of subjectivity.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· The Romantic Arts
Hegel citations:
Subjectivity is the essential nature of the spirit which is explicitly ideal in its own eyes and withdraws out of the external world into an existence within; and consequently it no longer coincides in indissoluble unity with its body.
— Aesthetics, The Romantic Arts (tr. Knox)
But both sides here have their point of reunification in the principle of subjectivity which is common to both.
— Aesthetics, The Romantic Arts (tr. Knox)

In sculpture the god confronts our vision as a mere object; but in painting, on the other hand, God appears in himself as a spiritual and living person who enters the Church and gives to every individual the possibility of placing himself in spiritual community and reconciliation with him.
— Aesthetics, Painting (tr. Knox)

Head: General Character of Painting
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › γ. The System of the Individual Arts › c. Romantic Arts › i. Painting › 1. General Character of Painting
Gloss: The general nature of painting.
Hegelian gloss: The general character of painting, the reduction of three dimensions to the surface, the inner made visible.
Nouns: general character of painting; the plane surface, two dimensions, illusion of depth, inner life made visible, the reflected world. the nature of painting, the painterly, pictorial character, semblance, appearance, visibility, inwardness, subjectivity, reduction to the plane, the art of seeming. planarity.
Verbs: flatten, project, illude. appear, seem, show, picture, depict.
Adjective: planar, two-dimensional, illusionistic. painterly, pictorial, visible, apparent, inward, subjective.
Adverbs: on the flat. pictorially, in appearance, to the eye, in general.
Phrases: a window onto the world [Alberti]; depth on a flat surface; the window on the world.
Hegel definition: The general character of painting rests on its essential principle, the subjectivity of mind that embraces heaven and earth in feeling, idea and action, which places its centre in romantic and Christian art. The question is which content by its nature matches painting's means. Antiquity painted well but could not bring painting to the development it reached in the Christian Middle Ages and after.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· Painting › General Character of Painting
Hegel citations:
I have specified as the essential principle of painting the subjectivity of mind which in the life of its feelings, ideas, and actions embraces the whole of heaven and earth and is present in a variety of situations and external modes of appearance in the body
— Aesthetics, Painting › General Character of Painting (tr. Knox)
If, this granted, we ask for a reason why painting has been brought to its own proper height through the content of romantic art alone, the answer is that the spiritual depth of feeling, the bliss and grief of the heart is precisely this deeper content which demands spiritual animation and which has paved the way to the higher artistic perfection of painting and made that necessary.
— Aesthetics, Painting › General Character of Painting (tr. Knox)

Head: Chief Determinant of Subject-Matter
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › γ. The System of the Individual Arts › c. Romantic Arts › i. Painting › 1. General Character of Painting › a. Chief Determinant of Subject-Matter
Gloss: What chiefly determines the content of painting.
Hegelian gloss: The content of painting: the inner life of the subject, feeling, love, piety.
Nouns: chief determinant of subject-matter; subjective inwardness, the feeling soul, the human heart, emotional content, the subject of the picture. determining factor, governing content, subject, theme, inner life, subjectivity, feeling, the heart, inwardness, particularity. interiority.
Verbs: express, depict feeling. determine, govern, condition, dictate, select.
Adjective: inward, emotional, heartfelt. determining, decisive, governing, chief, principal.
Adverbs: inwardly. chiefly, principally, above all, decisively.
Phrases: the soul's depths in colour; the heart's own story; love and piety.
Hegel definition: The chief determinant of painting's subject matter is subjectivity aware of itself. The individual shows an inner life of its own rather than passing wholly into the universal, and lets the external go its own way; painting can therefore take in nature, religion and human life down to fleeting moments, and makes the heart its content, bringing before us the individual's feeling.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· Painting › General Character of Painting › The Chief Determinant of the Subject-matter
Hegel citations:
The chief determinant of the subject-matter of painting is, as we saw, subjectivity aware of itself.
— Aesthetics, General Character of Painting › The Chief Determinant of the Subject-matter (tr. Knox)
Thus painting does of course bring to our vision the inner life in the form of an external object, but the real content which it expresses is the feeling of the individual subject
— Aesthetics, General Character of Painting › The Chief Determinant of the Subject-matter (tr. Knox)

Head: Sensuous Material of Painting
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › γ. The System of the Individual Arts › c. Romantic Arts › i. Painting › 1. General Character of Painting › b. Sensuous Material of Painting
Gloss: The material of painting: surface, light and color.
Hegelian gloss: The material of painting: the surface, and light and colour as its element.
Nouns: sensuous material of painting; colour, paint, pigment, surface, light and shade, the visible as such, clairobscur†. plane, flat, canvas, panel, ground, chiaroscuro, hue, tint, visibility, semblance, two dimensions. sfumato, tonality.
Verbs: colour, pigment, shade. flatten, illumine, show.
Adjective: chromatic, coloured, visual. planar, two-dimensional, luminous, visible.
Adverbs: in colour. on the flat, on canvas, to the eye.
Foreign: Italian: morbidezza [softness of flesh tones].
Phrases: the visible made spiritual; the magic of colour.
Hegel definition: The sensuous material of painting is the surface, with light and colour. Painting contracts three dimensions to two, a reduction implicit in the principle of inwardness and no defect or caprice but the necessary advance beyond sculpture: the object does not remain a real spatial existent but becomes a reflection of spirit, a pure appearance in the domain of spirit presented to spirit.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· Painting › General Character of Painting › The Sensuous Material of Painting
Hegel citations:
Painting, however, does allow space to persist and extinguishes only one of the three dimensions, so that a surface becomes the medium of its representations.
— Aesthetics, General Character of Painting › The Sensuous Material of Painting (tr. Knox)
So painting does indeed work for our vision, but in such a way that the object which it presents does not remain an actual total spatial natural existent but becomes a reflection of the spirit in which the spirit only reveals its spiritual quality by cancelling the real existent and transforming it into a pure appearance in the domain of spirit for apprehension by spirit.
— Aesthetics, General Character of Painting › The Sensuous Material of Painting (tr. Knox)

Head: Principle of Artistic Treatment
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › γ. The System of the Individual Arts › c. Romantic Arts › i. Painting › 1. General Character of Painting › c. Principle of Artistic Treatment
Gloss: The governing principle of painting's treatment of its subject.
Hegelian gloss: The principle of treatment in painting: the subjective appearance, given back to the viewer.
Nouns: principle of artistic treatment; technique, handling, treatment, execution, facture, brushwork, painterly approach. governing principle, guiding rule, manner of treatment, conception, subjectivity of treatment, inwardness, particularization. illusionism, trompe-l'œil.

Adjective: technical, painterly, skilful, daedalian†. governing, guiding, principial, artistic, subjective, inward.
Adverbs: skilfully. in principle, artistically, in treatment.
Phrases: the hand of the master; appearance for its own sake; the reflection of reflection.
Hegel definition: The principle of artistic treatment in painting admits two extremes: depth of subject, religious and moral seriousness in ideal form, and, with insignificant subjects, their detail as they are and the painter's skill. Standing between the plastic ideal and immediate actual detail, painting has both an ideal kind, with the universal as its essence, and a kind presenting the individual closely.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· Painting › General Character of Painting › Principle of the Artistic Treatment
Hegel citations:
More than architecture and sculpture, painting admits of two extremes: what is made the chief thing is (a) the depth of the subject-matter, i.e. religious and moral seriousness in the treatment and presentation of the ideal beauty of form, and (ft), in the case of insignificant subjects chosen by the artist, the details of them as they actually are and the subjective skill of the artist in his work.
— Aesthetics, General Character of Painting › Principle of the Artistic Treatment (tr. Knox)
For this reason two kinds of painting come before us: (i) the ideal kind with the universal as its essence, and (ii) the other which presents what is individual in its closeness of particular detail.
— Aesthetics, General Character of Painting › Principle of the Artistic Treatment (tr. Knox)

Adverbs: in particular. specifically, in detail, severally.
Phrases: subject, colour, and craft; the painter's eye; brush and palette.
Hegel definition: The particular characteristics of painting concern its subject matter, its sensuous material and the artistic treatment of both. Its content corresponds to that of romantic art, but one must ask which spheres of it best suit painting; its material, colour on a plane surface, must be specified in the forms it can express; and differences of treatment answering to content and material yield particular genres.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· Painting › Particular Characteristics of Painting
Hegel citations:
(i) The subject-matter, as we have seen, corresponds with the content of the romantic form of art; but we must raise the further question of what specific spheres of the wealth of this art-form are pre-eminently fitted and appropriate to portrayal in painting.
— Aesthetics, Painting › Particular Characteristics of Painting (tr. Knox)
(iii) Similarly, there is a question about the specific nature of the artistic treatment and portrayal which corresponds in different ways with the differing character of the subject-matter and therefore introduces particular genres of painting.
— Aesthetics, Painting › Particular Characteristics of Painting (tr. Knox)

Hegel definition: The romantic subject matter of painting is the concentration of spirit in itself, the full range of deep feeling expressed in the external, which sculpture must renounce and music cannot show. Its centre is religious love without desire, reconciled and blessed, above all the Madonna's love for her child, and it reaches to deep oneness with everyday surroundings and the joy of independent existence.
Hegel texts:

Whereas painting can link both sides together; in the external itself it can express the full range of deep feeling

Head: Conception
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › γ. The System of the Individual Arts › c. Romantic Arts › i. Painting › 2. Particular Characteristics of Painting › c. The Painter's Craft › i. Conception
Gloss: The painter's grasp of the subject.
Hegelian gloss: The painter's grasp of the subject as one situation, a single moment that holds the whole.
Nouns: conception; conception, idea, design, invention, the first idea, sketch, vision. apprehension, grasp, view, treatment, the way of seeing, the painter's vision, imagination, motif, the cartoon, the draft, the study. inventio.
Verbs: conceive, design, envisage, sketch. apprehend, imagine, invent, envision, picture, project, draft, outline.
Adjective: conceptual, inventive, original. imaginative, visionary, envisaged, designed, ideal.
Adverbs: in conception. in idea, in design, imaginatively, originally, in the mind's eye.
Foreign: Italian: concetto, disegno; French: dessein, dessin [design as intention and as drawing]; German: Zeichnung; Latin: designo.
Phrases: disegno interno [It.] [inner design]; the pregnant moment; one situation that holds the whole.
Hegel definition: Conception, the painter's grasp of a subject, starts close to sculpture and architecture in isolated figures at rest and advances to specific situations. Since painting cannot show a succession of changes and can seize only one moment, that moment must show the whole situation in its bloom, concentrating what preceded and what follows, as in the moment of victory in a battle.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· Painting › Particular Characteristics of Painting › Conception, Composition, and Characterization
Hegel citations:
From this there follows the quite simple reflection that in this one moment the whole of the situation or action must be portrayed in its bloom, and that therefore painting must look for the instant in which what preceded and what followed is concentrated in one point.
— Aesthetics, Particular Characteristics of Painting › Conception, Composition, and Characterization (tr. Knox)
For example, in the case of a battle this would be the moment of victory: the fighting is still visible, but at the same time the outcome is already certain.
— Aesthetics, Particular Characteristics of Painting › Conception, Composition, and Characterization (tr. Knox)

Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › γ. The System of the Individual Arts › c. Romantic Arts › i. Painting › 2. Particular Characteristics of Painting › c. The Painter's Craft › ii. Composition

Aesthetics
· Painting › Particular Characteristics of Painting › Conception, Composition, and Characterization

Head: Characterization
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › γ. The System of the Individual Arts › c. Romantic Arts › i. Painting › 2. Particular Characteristics of Painting › c. The Painter's Craft › iii. Characterization

Hegel definition: Characterization distinguishes painting from sculpture's ideal plasticity: the mental and physical particularity of personality has free scope and need not be raised to ideal beauty. Painting develops the whole variety of accidental particulars, so that we see not plastic ideals of gods and men but particular persons, since what is central is the soul's deep feeling and living subjective character.
Hegel texts:

· Painting › Particular Characteristics of Painting › Conception, Composition, and Characterization
Hegel citations:
Painting, on the other hand, does not confine particularity of character to that ideal but develops precisely the whole variety of even accidental particulars, so that now we see confronting us not those plastic ideals of gods and men but particular persons in all the accidents of their particular character.
— Aesthetics, Particular Characteristics of Painting › Conception, Composition, and Characterization (tr. Knox)
[B]ecause what is central now is the deep feeling of the soul and its living subjective character.
— Aesthetics, Particular Characteristics of Painting › Conception, Composition, and Characterization (tr. Knox)

But what above all it introduces for the treatment and artistic elaboration of the religious sphere is the living actuality of the spiritual and corporeal existence into which now all the figures are materialized and animated.

Now if there is added to this natural endowment the elevation and adornment of the inner life by the deep feeling of religion, by that spiritual trait of a more profound piety which soulfully animates the originally more decided assurance and complete acceptance of existence in this sphere of salvation, then we have before us an original harmony between a figure and its expression which, when it reaches perfection, gives us a vivid reminder, in this sphere of romantic and Christian art, of the pure ideal of art.

Head: Flemish and German Painting

Hegel definition: Flemish and German painting neither could nor wished to attain the free ideal forms of the Italians; it expressed depth of feeling and self-sufficient mind, joined to individual characters troubled by worldly cares who thereby won civil virtues. — Aesthetics, Historical Development of Painting › Flemish and German Painting (tr. Knox)
The final achievement of German and Flemish art is its utterly living absorption in the world and its daily life, and consequently the differentiation of painting into the most varied kinds of portrayal which are distinguished from one another, and one-sidedly developed, in respect of both subject-matter and treatment.

Head: German Painting
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › γ. The System of the Individual Arts › c. Romantic Arts › i. Painting › 3. Historical Development of Painting › c. Flemish and German Painting › ii. German Painting
