Hegelian gloss: Die oberdeutsche Malerei: the old painting of upper Germany, close to the Netherlandish school, intense in piety and expression.
Nouns: German painting. Dürer, Holbein, Cranach, the old German masters, Schongauer, Grünewald. the Isenheim altarpiece, woodcut, the Danube school.
Adjective: German, Düreresque.
Hegel definition: German painting, which Hegel joins to that of the Low Countries, expresses depth of feeling in faith together with the stubborn individuality of characters. North German masters excelled in torments and ugliness, showing in the Passion the crudity and hatred of soldiers, with confused crowds and little harmony, though painters such as Dürer kept inner nobility and rose above mere barbarity.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· Painting › Historical Development of Painting › Flemish and German Painting
Hegel citations:
As for German painting we may affiliate what is strictly German to that of the Low Countries.
— Aesthetics, Historical Development of Painting › Flemish and German Painting (tr. Knox)
This is the sphere in which especially the masters of North Germany excel when, in scenes from the Passion story, it is the crudity of the soldiers, the malignity of the mockery, the barbarity of their hatred of Christ in his suffering and death, that they reveal with great energy in characterizing the greatest uglinesses and deformities which are external forms corresponding to an inner corruption of heart.
— Aesthetics, Historical Development of Painting › Flemish and German Painting (tr. Knox)

Head: Music
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › γ. The System of the Individual Arts › c. Romantic Arts › ii. Music
Gloss: The art of expressing the inner life through sound in time.
Hegelian gloss: Music, the art of inner feeling, whose material is tone, sound vibrating in time, which seizes the inmost self.
Nouns: music; tone, sound, harmony, melody, composition, tonal art, the art of the inner life. concert, strain, tune, air, melody &c H1053, aria, arietta†, work, number, opus, sonata, rondo, pastorale, cavatina†, roulade†, fantasia, concerto, overture, symphony, variations, cadenza, fugue, canon, quodlibet, serenade, dithyramb, operetta, oratorio, movement, stave, toccata. rhythm, measure, timbre, intonation. opera. cadence, resonance &c H0274. the art of sound, the art of tones, minstrelsy, musicianship, song, Euterpe, Polyhymnia, Orpheus, the music of the spheres. tonality, euphony, sonority.
Verbs: compose, play, sing, perform, harmonize, orchestrate. execute, accompany, sing a second, play a second, set to music, arrange. chant, hum, warble, carol. make music, intone, pipe, fiddle, strum.
Adjective: musical, melodic, harmonic, tonal, sonorous, symphonic. instrumental, vocal, choral, lyric, operatic, harmonious &c H1053, Wagnerian. resonant. tuneful, melodious, euphonious, dulcet, Orphic, philharmonic.
Adverbs: musically, melodiously. tunefully, harmoniously, in tones, in sound. andantino†, maestoso†, spiritoso†, vivace†, veloce†, prestissimo†, capriccioso†, scherzando†, rallentando†, affettuoso†, desto†.
Foreign: German: Tonkunst, Vorspiel; Latin: musica; Greek: mousikē; French: piece of music, rondeau; Italian: notturno, passamezzo; Arabic: ṭarab [musical ecstasy], maqām [melodic mode]; Sanskrit: rāga.
Phrases: die letzte subjektive Innerlichkeit als solche [Ger.] [Hegel, Aesthetics, on music]; all art constantly aspires towards the condition of music [Walter Pater]; music hath charms; the food of love; in notes by distance made more sweet [Collins]; like the faint exquisite music of a dream [Moore]; music arose with its voluptuous swell [Byron]; music is the universal language of mankind [Longfellow]; music's golden tongue [Keats]; the speech of angels [Carlyle]; will sing the savageness out of a bear [Othello]; music hath charms to soothe the savage beast.
Hegel definition: Music is the romantic art that carries painting's inwardness further, taking subjective inner life as such for its content and cancelling spatial appearance for sound moving in time. Like architecture it rests on quantitative proportion, but its material is tone freed from heavy matter, so that it joins soul and deepest feeling with the most rigorous mathematical law.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· Music
Hegel citations:
Consequently what dominates in music is at once the soul and profoundest feeling and the most rigorous mathematical laws
— Aesthetics, Music (tr. Knox)
Architecture takes heavy visible masses in their peaceful juxtaposition and external spatial shape, whereas music takes the soul of tone, working itself free from spatial matter, in the qualitative differences of sound and in the movement of the ever-rolling stream of time.
— Aesthetics, Music (tr. Knox)

Head: General Character of Music
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › γ. The System of the Individual Arts › c. Romantic Arts › ii. Music › 1. General Character of Music
Gloss: The general nature of music.
Hegelian gloss: Music as the art of the inward, which cancels spatial objectivity and has its element in the vibrating, vanishing tone.
Nouns: general character of music; inwardness, temporality, sound, the abolition of space, pure feeling. the nature of music, subjective inwardness, interiority, the inner life, feeling, tone, the note, vibration, the vanishing of the tone, transience, evanescence, objectless inwardness.
Verbs: sound, resonate. vibrate, ring, die away, fade, vanish, express, echo, move.
Adjective: temporal, inward, sonorous. inner, subjective, tonal, evanescent, transient, fleeting, objectless, non-spatial, audible. ineffable.
Adverbs: in time. inwardly, in sound, in tones, fleetingly, successively.
Phrases: sound vanishes as it arises; sound that vanishes as it sounds.
Hegel definition: The general character of music is set out by comparing it with the visual arts and poetry, then showing how it grasps and portrays content, and finally explaining its special effect on the mind. As a romantic art it dissolves the classical identity of inner life and external existence, being able to express only feeling and accompanying articulated ideas with its sounds.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· Music › General Character of Music
Hegel citations:
(c) In the light of this manner of treatment we can explain more specifically the special effect which music, in distinction from the other arts, produces on our minds.
— Aesthetics, Music › General Character of Music (tr. Knox)
[B]ut music remains capable rather of expressing only the element of feeling
— Aesthetics, Music › General Character of Music (tr. Knox)

Head: Comparison with Visual Arts and Poetry
Head (German): Vergleich mit den bildenden Künsten und der Poesie
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › γ. The System of the Individual Arts › c. Romantic Arts › ii. Music › 1. General Character of Music › a. Comparison with Visual Arts and Poetry
Gloss: How music differs from the visual arts and from poetry.
Hegelian gloss: Music compared with the visual arts and poetry.
Nouns: comparison with visual arts and poetry; music and architecture, music and poetry, the sister arts. music and painting, music and sculpture, the arts compared, parallel, analogy, contrast, difference, affinity.
Verbs: compare. liken, distinguish, differentiate, set beside.
Adjective: comparative. contrastive, analogous, distinct, akin.
Adverbs: by comparison. comparatively, in comparison, by contrast, side by side.
Foreign: Latin: ut pictura poesis; Italian: paragone.
Phrases: architecture is frozen music; painting is silent poetry.
Hegel definition: Comparing music with the other arts shows an affinity with architecture, since both follow laws of quantitative proportion drawn from the spirit's invention and not from existing things. Yet they stand in opposite realms: architecture raises enduring heavy masses to be seen from outside, whereas the swiftly vanishing world of sound passes through the ear into the heart.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· Music › General Character of Music › Comparison with the Visual Arts and Poetry
Hegel citations:
In this respect too music may be compared more closely with architecture which derives its forms, not from what exists, but from the spirit’s invention in order to mould them according to the laws of gravity and the rules of symmetry and eurhythmy.
— Aesthetics, General Character of Music › Comparison with the Visual Arts and Poetry (tr. Knox)
[F]or architecture erects its colossal buildings to endure in symbolic forms to be looked at from outside; but the world of sounds, quickly rustling away, is directly drawn by the ear into the inner life of the heart and harmonizes the soul with emotions in sympathy with it.
— Aesthetics, General Character of Music › Comparison with the Visual Arts and Poetry (tr. Knox)

Head: Musical Treatment of Subject-Matter
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › γ. The System of the Individual Arts › c. Romantic Arts › ii. Music › 1. General Character of Music › b. Musical Treatment of Subject-Matter
Gloss: The manner in which music treats its content.
Hegelian gloss: The musical treatment of content, which takes it in the form of feeling.
Nouns: musical treatment of subject-matter; expression, word-painting, programme music, affect. musical conception, musical expression, the setting, tone-painting, characterization, the expression of feeling, sentiment, mood, the passions, imitation. Stimmung.
Verbs: express, set, paint in sound. treat, render, convey, voice, depict, characterize, evoke, interpret.
Adjective: expressive, programmatic, affective. characteristic, descriptive, pictorial, evocative, emotive, lyrical.
Adverbs: expressively. musically, in tones, in sound, evocatively.
Foreign: German: Affektenlehre [doctrine of affections].
Phrases: music as the language of feeling; the feeling without the object; a mood in sound.
Hegel definition: Music's treatment of its subject matter can free itself from any text, but then remains empty and is not yet art; only as the adequate expression of a spiritual content is it genuine art. Its task is to make the veiled inner life resound, so that inwardness is the form in which it grasps everything, above all as feeling, from cheerfulness to grief, awe and love.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· Music › General Character of Music › Musical Treatment of the Subject-matter
Hegel citations:
Only if music becomes a spiritually adequate expression in the sensuous medium of sounds and their varied counterpoint does music rise to being a genuine art
— Aesthetics, General Character of Music › Musical Treatment of the Subject-matter (tr. Knox)
Inwardness as such is therefore the form in which music can conceive its subject-matter
— Aesthetics, General Character of Music › Musical Treatment of the Subject-matter (tr. Knox)

Head: Effect of Music
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › γ. The System of the Individual Arts › c. Romantic Arts › ii. Music › 1. General Character of Music › c. Effect of Music
Gloss: The power of music over the soul.
Hegelian gloss: The power of music, which seizes the self in its simple inwardness.
Nouns: effect of music; emotional power, catharsis, enchantment, transport, rapture, ecstasy, the spell of music, Orpheus. happiness, felicity, bliss, beatitude, ravishment. transport of love, gyneolatry†. the power of music, the sway of music, emotional effect, the stirring of the soul, emotion, exaltation, elevation, consolation, solace, magic, fascination, Amphion, the Sirens, David's harp. entrancement.
Verbs: move, transport, enchant, enrapture, soothe. please, charm, delight, captivate, fascinate, entrance, bewitch, enravish†. affect, stir, touch, thrill, melt, rouse, calm, console, uplift, carry away, ravish, spellbind, sway, adeem†, reave†.
Adjective: moving, enchanting, rapturous, soothing, stirring. affecting, touching, thrilling, ravishing, entrancing, bewitching, spellbinding, uplifting, consoling, Orphic. stimulating, reassuring, captivating.
Adverbs: movingly. stirringly, touchingly, enchantingly, powerfully, to tears.
Foreign: Arabic: ṭarab; Korean: heung [exuberant joy].
Phrases: music has charms to soothe a savage breast [Congreve]; music soothes the savage breast; to be carried away.
Hegel definition: The effect of music springs from its working directly on the heart, the simple concentrated centre of human life, without intellectual considerations. Unlike a statue or picture, which remain outside as objects we can view freely, a piece of music vanishes as it sounds, penetrates the secret of all movements of the soul and captivates a consciousness no longer facing an object.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· Music › General Character of Music › Effect of Music
Hegel citations:
For it is precisely this sphere of inner sensibility, abstract self-comprehension, which music takes for its own and therefore brings movement into the seat of inner changes, into the heart and mind as this simple concentrated centre of the whole of human life.
— Aesthetics, General Character of Music › Effect of Music (tr. Knox)
[T]he result is that music with its movements penetrates the arcanum of all the movements of the soul.
— Aesthetics, General Character of Music › Effect of Music (tr. Knox)

Phrases: rhythm, harmony, melody; time, harmony and melody; the hidden soul of harmony [Milton].
Hegel definition: The particular characteristics of music concern the means by which notes become not a natural shriek of feeling but its developed artistic expression. A single note is independent and complete, gaining its own definiteness only through relation to others, a relation external to it, made by a composer for a hearer. These means are the measure of time, harmony and melody.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· Music › Particular Characteristics of Music's Means of Expression
Hegel citations:
[T]he next question is about the means that make it possible and necessary for the notes not to be a purely natural shriek of feeling
— Aesthetics, Music › Particular Characteristics of Music's Means of Expression (tr. Knox)
Bringing different notes together in specific relations is therefore something, if not contradicting the essence of the note, still only artificial and not otherwise already present naturally.
— Aesthetics, Music › Particular Characteristics of Music's Means of Expression (tr. Knox)

Head: Time, Bar, Rhythm
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › γ. The System of the Individual Arts › c. Romantic Arts › ii. Music › 2. Particular Characteristics of Music › a. Time, Bar, Rhythm
Gloss: The measuring of music in time: beat, measure and rhythm.
Hegelian gloss: The measurement of tone in time: beat, bar, rhythm.
Nouns: intonation, tone. rest.
Foreign: Greek: rhythmos; Italian: a tempo; Sanskrit: tāla [rhythmic cycle]; Japanese: ma [interval]; Korean: jangdan [rhythmic cycle].
Hegel definition: Time, bar and rhythm treat the purely temporal side of musical sound. Music sets bodies vibrating and takes up only the duration of that movement, so that time dominates it; the bar is the mathematically regulated measure of time; and rhythm animates this abstract rule by stressing some beats and subordinating others. The self finds itself again in the ordered flow.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· Music › Particular Characteristics of Music's Means of Expression › Time, Bar, Rhythm
Hegel citations:
If we take in the first place the purely temporal aspect of musical sound, we have to discuss (a) the necessity of time's being in general the dominant thing in music; (6) the bar as the purely mathematically regulated measure of time; (c) rhythm which begins to animate this abstract rule by emphasizing some specific beats and subordinating others.
— Aesthetics, Particular Characteristics of Music's Means of Expression › Time, Bar, Rhythm (tr. Knox)
[M]usic however does not adopt movement as it occurs in space, and therefore there is left for its configuration only the time in which the vibration of the body occurs.
— Aesthetics, Particular Characteristics of Music's Means of Expression › Time, Bar, Rhythm (tr. Knox)

Head: Time-Measure
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › γ. The System of the Individual Arts › c. Romantic Arts › ii. Music › 2. Particular Characteristics of Music › a. Time, Bar, Rhythm › i. Time-Measure
Gloss: The regular division of time into equal units that music lays over the flow of sound.
Hegelian gloss: Das Zeitmaß: the uniform measure of time, which the self lays on the indeterminate flow of time to find itself again in it.
Nouns: time-measure. tempo, time signature, movement, pace, speed, metronome, rubato. pacing.
Verbs: keep time, measure. count, mark time, tap, drum, throb.
Adjective: timed, regular, isochronous.
Adverbs: in tempo, in time.
Hegel definition: Time-measure is the rule music must give to time, which of itself is a uniform stream and undifferentiated duration. Because time shares the principle active in the self, whose inner life music objectifies, the self needs time determined: by gathering its experiences it interrupts the empty succession, and the beginning and ending of notes gives that flow definite divisions.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· Music › Particular Characteristics of Music's Means of Expression › Time, Bar, Rhythm
Hegel citations:
Yet music cannot leave time in this indeterminacy; it must on the contrary determine it more closely, give it a measure, and order its flow by the rule of such a measure.
— Aesthetics, Particular Characteristics of Music's Means of Expression › Time, Bar, Rhythm (tr. Knox)
Contrasted with this empty progress, the self is what persists in and by itself, and its self-concentration interrupts the indefinite series of points of time and makes gaps in their abstract continuity
— Aesthetics, Particular Characteristics of Music's Means of Expression › Time, Bar, Rhythm (tr. Knox)

Head: Bar
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › γ. The System of the Individual Arts › c. Romantic Arts › ii. Music › 2. Particular Characteristics of Music › a. Time, Bar, Rhythm › ii. Bar
Gloss: The bar, a fixed group of beats with its own stress, repeated through the music.
Hegelian gloss: Der Takt: the regular repetition of equal units of time, given a definite unity by stress, which orders the uniformity of time-measure into a rule.
Nouns: bar. measure, metre, beat, pulse, the downbeat, the upbeat, accent, stress, arsis, thesis, duple time, triple time, common time. meter, foot, numbers, accentuation &c H0662, dactyl, spondee, trochee, anapest.
Verbs: beat. recur in regular order.
Adjective: metrical, measured, accented, duple, triple.
Adverbs: in measure, to the beat, regularly.
Phrases: in three-four time.
Hegel definition: The bar establishes a definite unit of time as the measure and rule of the succession and of the notes' arbitrary durations, and renews it in uniform repetition, as regular columns do in architecture. In this uniformity self-consciousness finds itself again, the more fully since the unity belongs neither to time nor to the notes but is put into time by the self.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· Music › Particular Characteristics of Music's Means of Expression › Time, Bar, Rhythm
Hegel citations:
Accordingly the simple purpose of the bar is (a) to establish a specific temporal unit as the measure and rule both for the marked interruption of the previously undifferentiated temporal succession and also for the equally arbitrary duration of single notes which now are brought together into a definite unity
— Aesthetics, Particular Characteristics of Music's Means of Expression › Time, Bar, Rhythm (tr. Knox)
But the satisfaction which the self acquires, owing to the bar, in this rediscovery of itself is all the more complete because the unity and uniformity does not pertain either to time or the notes in themselves; it is something which belongs solely to the self and is inserted into time by the self for its own self-satisfaction.
— Aesthetics, Particular Characteristics of Music's Means of Expression › Time, Bar, Rhythm (tr. Knox)

Head: Rhythm
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › γ. The System of the Individual Arts › c. Romantic Arts › ii. Music › 2. Particular Characteristics of Music › a. Time, Bar, Rhythm › iii. Rhythm
Gloss: Rhythm, the living play of stresses and durations within and against the bar.
Hegelian gloss: Der Rhythmus: the animation of the bar by accents, the free movement that enlivens the abstract rule of the measure.
Nouns: rhythm. cadence, syncopation. periodicity, alternation, alternity†. syncope. oscillation, vibration, pulsation.
Verbs: pulse, syncopate. pulsate.
Adjective: rhythmic, rhythmical, cadenced, syncopated, pulsing. periodic, recurrent.
Adverbs: rhythmically.
Phrases: in the beginning was rhythm [attrib. Hans von Bülow].
Hegel definition: Rhythm alone properly animates time and bar, asserting the essential divisions within abundant variation. Accent laid on certain parts of the bar gives each kind its own rhythm; in accompaniment it must not clash with poetic metre; and the melody's animated rhythm is free from the bar's strict return, its sharpest counter-thrust in syncopation, so that it avoids pedantry and monotony.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· Music › Particular Characteristics of Music's Means of Expression › Time, Bar, Rhythm
Hegel citations:
This is brought about by means of rhythm which alone brings proper animation to the time and the bar.
— Aesthetics, Particular Characteristics of Music's Means of Expression › Time, Bar, Rhythm (tr. Knox)
What may be demanded in this connection is, in brief, freedom from the pedantry of metre and the barbarism of a uniform rhythm.
— Aesthetics, Particular Characteristics of Music's Means of Expression › Time, Bar, Rhythm (tr. Knox)

It treats the difference of instruments and the voice, the quantitatively determined system of notes, scales and keys, and the concrete opposition and modulation of notes, whose forward movement rests not on caprice but on laws in which everything musical has its necessary foundation.
Hegel texts:

· Music › Particular Characteristics of Music's Means of Expression › Harmony
Hegel citations:
This more essential province of music comprises the laws of harmony.
— Aesthetics, Particular Characteristics of Music's Means of Expression › Harmony (tr. Knox)
This juxtaposition and change does not rest on pure accident and caprice, but is subject to specific laws in which everything genuinely musical has its necessary foundation.
— Aesthetics, Particular Characteristics of Music's Means of Expression › Harmony (tr. Knox)

Head: Melody
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › γ. The System of the Individual Arts › c. Romantic Arts › ii. Music › 2. Particular Characteristics of Music › c. Melody
Gloss: A succession of tones forming a whole; tune.
Hegelian gloss: Melody, the free soul of music, which moves within harmony.
Nouns: melody; tune, air, strain, aria, song, theme, motif, line. melody &c H1053, arietta†. chant, song &c H1067, canzonet†, lay, ballad, ditty. intonation, tone. descant, songfulness, tunefulness, phrase, subject, leitmotif. melisma. appoggiato†, appoggiatura†, acciaccatura†.
Verbs: sing, hum, carol, warble, intone. trill. harmonize. lilt, croon, pipe, whistle, sol-fa†.
Adjective: melodic, melodious, tuneful, lyrical, songful. musical, melic†, tunable, sweet, dulcet, canorous†, mellow, mellifluous, soft, clear, clear as a bell, silvery, euphonious, euphonic, euphonical†, symphonious, enchanting &c H0672, fine-toned, full-toned, silver-toned. lilting, flowing, singable, singing, arioso.
Adverbs: melodiously, tunefully. in tune, sweetly, songfully.
Foreign: Greek: melos; Italian: cantilena, cantabile; Sanskrit: rāga; Korean: garak [tune].
Phrases: heard melodies are sweet, but those unheard are sweeter [Keats]; the soul of music; a tune you can hum.
Hegel definition: Melody is the poetic element of music, the soul's language, pouring inner joy and sorrow into notes while raising itself above the force of feeling into a free abiding with itself. Time, rhythm and harmony are only its lawful ground. It floats independently above them yet exists only through them, finding true freedom not against necessity but in freeing itself from arbitrary caprice.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· Music › Particular Characteristics of Music's Means of Expression › Melody
Hegel citations:
The poetic element in music, the language of the soul, which pours out into the notes the inner joy and sorrow of the heart, and in this outpouring mitigates and rises above the natural force of feeling by turning the inner life’s present transports into an apprehension of itself, into a free tarrying with itself, and by liberating the heart in this way from the pressure of joys and sorrows—this free sounding of the soul in the field of music—this is alone melody.
— Aesthetics, Particular Characteristics of Music's Means of Expression › Melody (tr. Knox)
But in this close link with harmony; the melody does not forgo its freedom at all; it only liberates itself from the subjectivity of arbitrary caprice in fanciful developments and bizarre changes and only acquires its true independence precisely in this way.
— Aesthetics, Particular Characteristics of Music's Means of Expression › Melody (tr. Knox)

Hegel definition: The relation of music's means of expression to content arises with melody, the sphere of free invention. Head: Epic
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › γ. The System of the Individual Arts › c. Romantic Arts › ii. Music › 3. Relation Between Expression and Content › c. The Execution of Musical Works of Art › i. Epic
Gloss: Performance that gives the work faithfully, the performer receding behind it as an epic rhapsode does.
Hegelian gloss: The first kind of execution, which gives itself wholly to the work and reproduces only what is there, like the epic reciter who disappears behind his matter.
Nouns: epic; faithful performance, objective rendering, self-effacing performance, fidelity to the score, straight reading, Werktreue. reproduction, delivery.
Verbs: reproduce, deliver.
Foreign: German: Werktreue.
Phrases: faithful to the score.
Hegel definition: The epic manner of execution gives itself wholly to the work, as the rhapsodist lets personality retire behind the events reported, the more effaced the better. Where a composition has objective solidity, the performer must add nothing and be an obedient instrument, though not a mechanical barrel-organ player: life and soul must be given in the composer's sense, with technical freedom.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· Music › Relation between Music's Means of Expression and their Content › The Execution of Musical Works of Art
Hegel citations:
Epic, in which the poet intends to unfold for us an objective world of events and ways of action, leaves no alternative for the rhapsodist in his recital but to make his individual personality retire in favour of the deeds and events which he is reporting.
— Aesthetics, Relation between Music's Means of Expression and their Content › The Execution of Musical Works of Art (tr. Knox)
The executant artist not only need not, but must not, add anything of his own, or otherwise he will spoil the effect.

Head: The Virtuosic
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › γ. The System of the Individual Arts › c. Romantic Arts › ii. Music › 3. Relation Between Expression and Content › c. The Execution of Musical Works of Art › ii. The Virtuosic
Gloss: Performance in which the player's own brilliance becomes the matter: virtuosity, improvisation, display.

Phrases: the virtuoso; the performer as co-creator.
Hegel definition: The virtuosic manner of execution belongs to works in which the composer's freedom and caprice predominate: the performer is not restricted to rendering what is given but composes in interpreting, fills gaps, deepens the superficial and ensouls the soulless, appearing independent and productive, as Italian singers do in cadenzas, so that we witness the very production of a work of art.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· Music › Relation between Music's Means of Expression and their Content › The Execution of Musical Works of Art
Hegel citations:
Here the bravura of the virtuoso is in its right place, while genius is not restricted to the mere execution of what is given but has a wider scope so that the executant artist himself composes in his interpretation, fills in gaps, deepens what is superficial, ensouls what is soulless and in this way appears as downright independent and productive.
— Aesthetics, Relation between Music's Means of Expression and their Content › The Execution of Musical Works of Art (tr. Knox)
