Foreign: Latin: copia verborum, usus loquendi; French: gens de lettres, homme de lettres, littérateur, belles-lettres, feuilleton, bas-bleu [bluestocking].
Phrases: history and oratory as prose arts; a whole and its parts.
Hegel definition: The poetic work of art, unlike prose works of history and oratory, must be formed into an organic whole. Its dominant subject, an action or a feeling, must have unity, with everything related to it concretely and freely; the universal and the individuals in whom it appears must stay vitally interwoven, as the Iliad is sustained by the wrath of Achilles.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· Poetry › The Poetic Work of Art as Distinguished from a Prose Work of Art › The Poetic and the Prose Work of Art
Hegel citations:
In connection with the poetic work of art in general, we need only repeat the demand that, like any other product of free imagination, it must be formed and rounded into an organic whole.
— Aesthetics, The Poetic Work of Art as Distinguished from a Prose Work of Art › The Poetic and the Prose Work of Art (tr. Knox)
The universal, which is to be represented, and the individuals, in whose character, histories, and actions, it appears poetically, may therefore not fall apart from one another or be so related that the individuals become servants of purely abstract universals
— Aesthetics, The Poetic Work of Art as Distinguished from a Prose Work of Art › The Poetic and the Prose Work of Art (tr. Knox)

Head: The Poet's Creative Activity
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › γ. The System of the Individual Arts › c. Romantic Arts › iii. Poetry › 1. Poetry as Distinct from Prose › c. The Poet's Creative Activity
Gloss: The creative activity of the poet.
Hegelian gloss: The poet's activity, which must have both inspiration and the clarity of the shaping understanding.
Nouns: the poet's creative activity; poetic creation, inspiration, the poet's labour, the Muse, invention. poetizing subjectivity, the poet, the maker, the bard, genius, talent, imagination, fancy, enthusiasm, afflatus, the divine frenzy, composition, making. author, writer, poet, novelist. cummings, playwright, compiler, bard, screenwriter, biographer, lyricist, dramatist, essayist, polemic, fabulist†. joint author, space writer, folk writer, literary hack, hack writer, word-painter, e. e. cummings, de Sade, film writer, folk poet, de la Mare, poet laureate.
Verbs: create, invent, sing, compose. make, poetize, imagine, conceive, fashion, shape, bring forth.
Adjective: creative, inspired, inventive. poetizing, imaginative, originative, productive, poietic.
Adverbs: creatively. inventively, imaginatively, with inspiration, by genius.
Foreign: Latin: furor poeticus; Greek: poiēsis, enthousiasmos.
Phrases: the poet's eye, in a fine frenzy rolling [A Midsummer Night's Dream]; the poet's eye in a fine frenzy rolling; poeta nascitur.
Hegel definition: The poet's creative activity is less tied than that of other artists to a perceptible material, so that poetic talent is more general and independent, needing only a gift for rich imaginative formulation. The task is both easier, with fewer technical hurdles, and harder, since depth of imagination must replace visible form while the poet reaches all depths of spirit through words.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· Poetry › The Poetic Work of Art as Distinguished from a Prose Work of Art › The Poet's Creative Activity
Hegel citations:
Poetry is exempt from the complete embodiment of its productions in a particular material, and therefore a talent for it is less subject to such specific conditions and so is more general and independent
— Aesthetics, The Poetic Work of Art as Distinguished from a Prose Work of Art › The Poet's Creative Activity (tr. Knox)
[B]ecause the less poetry has to create an external embodiment [that can be seen or heard], the more it has to seek a substitute for this lack of perceptibility in the inner proper kernel of art, i.e. in the depth of imagination and genuinely artistic treatment.
— Aesthetics, The Poetic Work of Art as Distinguished from a Prose Work of Art › The Poet's Creative Activity (tr. Knox)

Head: Poetic Expression
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › γ. The System of the Individual Arts › c. Romantic Arts › iii. Poetry › 2. Poetic Expression
Gloss: The language of poetry.
Hegelian gloss: The language of poetry, which is image and representation rather than the prose of the understanding.
Nouns: poetic expression; poetic language, diction, imagery, versification. poetic speech, the poetic word, verbal art, wording, utterance, phrasing, figures of speech, verse, metre, rhyme. figuration, tropology.
Verbs: express, image. utter, voice, word, phrase, versify, clothe in words.
Adjective: expressive, poetic. verbal, linguistic, figurative, metrical, eloquent.
Adverbs: poetically. in words, in verse, expressively, figuratively.
Phrases: winged words; the language of the gods; image rather than prose.
Hegel definition: Poetic expression covers the poetic way of imagining, diction and the music of words. Words are neither symbols nor spatial embodiments but signs, which in poetry must be made an end for contemplation. The origin of poetic speech lies not in the choice of words or in sound but in the kind of imagining, though it exists only in words that are spoken.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· Poetry › Poetic Expression
Hegel citations:
But as communications of poetic conceptions, these signs too must, in distinction from the prosaic mode of expression [where they are mere means], be made an end for contemplation and appear shaped accordingly.
— Aesthetics, Poetry › Poetic Expression (tr. Knox)
[B]ut the words are only signs of ideas and therefore the real origin of poetic speech lies neither in the choice of single words and the manner of their collocation into sentences and elaborate paragraphs, nor in euphony, rhythm, rhyme, etc., but in the sort and kind of ideas [or of the way of imagining things].
— Aesthetics, Poetry › Poetic Expression (tr. Knox)

Head: Poetic Imagination
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › γ. The System of the Individual Arts › c. Romantic Arts › iii. Poetry › 2. Poetic Expression › a. Poetic Imagination
Gloss: The poet's inventive power of imagination.
Hegelian gloss: The poetic imagination, which makes the inner vivid as image, original rather than abstract.
Nouns: poetic imagination; poetic vision, imagery, figuration, the inner image, poetic idea. fancy, phantasy, the poetic image, poetic representation, picturing, concreteness, vividness, the pictorial, metaphor, simile, personification, the mind's eye. ingenium.
Verbs: imagine, envision, figure. picture, image, visualize, body forth, conjure up, depict.
Adjective: imaginative, visionary, imagistic. pictorial, figurative, vivid, graphic, concrete, fanciful, picturesque.
Adverbs: imaginatively. vividly, graphically, pictorially, in images.
Foreign: Italian: meraviglia [wonder, the poet's aim] [Marino].
Phrases: to see a world in a grain of sand [Blake]; bodying forth the forms of things unknown.
Hegel definition: The poetic way of imagining shapes its subject inwardly, with the imaginative idea itself serving as what stone, colour or tone are to other arts. It holds together the extremes that ordinary consciousness separates, accidental particulars and abstract universals, and is figurative: it brings concrete reality before us so that essence is recognized in and inseparably from outer individuality.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· Poetry › Poetic Expression › The Poetic Way of Imagining Things
Hegel citations:
The power of poetry’s way of putting things consists therefore in the fact that poetry gives shape to a subject-matter within, without proceeding to express it in actual visible shapes or in series of melodies
— Aesthetics, Poetic Expression › The Poetic Way of Imagining Things (tr. Knox)
On the contrary, a way of putting things is poetic only when these extremes are kept undivided and mediated with one another
— Aesthetics, Poetic Expression › The Poetic Way of Imagining Things (tr. Knox)

Head: Poetic Diction
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › γ. The System of the Individual Arts › c. Romantic Arts › iii. Poetry › 2. Poetic Expression › b. Poetic Diction
Gloss: The choice and arrangement of words in poetry.
Hegelian gloss: Poetic diction, the choice and order of words, elevated beyond ordinary speech.
Nouns: poetic diction; diction, phrasing, wording, style, poetic vocabulary, archaism, kenning. phraseology, manner, strain, composition, mode of expression, choice of words, mode of speech, literary power, ready pen, pen of a ready writer, command of language &c H0662, authorship. expression, set phrase, sentence, paragraph, figure of speech &c H0906, idiom, idiotism†, turn of expression. term, vocable. phrase &c H0662, figure, trope, metaphor, enallage†, catachresis†, metonymy [Gramm.], synecdoche [Sem.], autonomasia†, irony, figurativeness, image, imagery, metalepsis†, type, anagoge†, simile, personification, prosopopoeia†, allegory, apologue†, parable, fable, allusion, adumbration, application. flourish, flowers of speech, flowers of rhetoric, frills of style, euphuism†, euphemism. well rounded periods, well turned periods, flowing periods, the right word in the right place, antithesis. poeticism, epithet, periphrasis, circumlocution, inversion, word-order, period, verbal expression, periphrase†. euphuist†.
Verbs: phrase, word, express. word it, give words to, give expression to, voice, arrange in words, clothe in words, put into words, express by words, couch in terms, find words to express, speak by the card, call, denominate, designate, dub. formulate, turn a phrase, coin.
Adjective: poetic, elevated, archaic, figurative. lofty, sublime, eloquent, vehement, impassioned. antithetical, alliterative, figurative &c H0906, artificial &c H0662. neologic†, neological†, obsolete &c H0235, colloquial, Anglice†. metaphorical, catachrestical†, typical, tralatitious†, parabolic, allegorical, allusive, anagogical†, ironical, tropical. verbal, lexical, stylistic, periphrastic, ornate, choice.
Adverbs: in poetic diction. in words, verbally, stylistically, figuratively.
Foreign: Latin: elocutio; Greek: lexis; French: la morgue litteraire, précieuse, mot juste; Spanish: conceptismo, culteranismo.
Phrases: what oft was thought, but ne'er so well expressed [Pope]; the best words in the best order; elevated speech.
Hegel definition: Poetic diction follows from poetry's need to embody its conceptions in language. Art ought to place us on ground different from everyday life, religion and philosophy, so poetry must avoid prosaic triviality and the tone of edification or speculation, above all the categories of the understanding, using special words, old or boldly new, and fitting sentence construction without sinking into rhetoric.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· Poetry › Poetic Expression › Poetic Diction
Hegel citations:
In general, a poetic conception only becomes poetry in the narrower sense when it is actually embodied and cast in words.
— Aesthetics, Poetic Expression › Poetic Diction (tr. Knox)
Poetry can do this, so far as its diction is concerned, only if it uses a language different from the one we are already accustomed to in these other spheres.
— Aesthetics, Poetic Expression › Poetic Diction (tr. Knox)

Head: Versification
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › γ. The System of the Individual Arts › c. Romantic Arts › iii. Poetry › 2. Poetic Expression › c. Versification
Gloss: The making of verse.
Hegelian gloss: Versification, the musical element of poetry, which raises language above prose.
Nouns: versification; prosody, metre, metrics, scansion, verse, measure, foot, line, stanza, strophe. canto, couplet, antistrophe†. rhyme, assonance, meter, numbers, rhythm, accentuation &c H0662, dactyl, spondee, trochee, anapest, hexameter, pentameter. rhyming, making verses, orthometry†, altimetry†. verse-making, versifying, verse-craft, poetic form, rhythmics, caesura, enjambment, tercet.
Verbs: versify, scan, measure, metrify. poetize, make verses. compose, turn a verse, rhythmize, indite.
Adjective: metrical, prosodic, versified, scanned. rhythmic, rhythmical, measured, stanzaic, strophic, rhymed.
Adverbs: metrically, in verse. in metre, in measure, rhythmically, in numbers.
Foreign: Arabic: ʿarūḍ [prosody]; Sanskrit: chandas [metre].
Phrases: verse is a measured speech; the music of verse; scan a line.
Hegel definition: Versification arises because a poetic idea is not only clothed in words but uttered, passing into the sound of words and syllables. Versified prose makes no poetry, yet metre or rhyme is absolutely necessary to it, as its one sensuous fragrance. It opens a new ground beyond ordinary speech, so that to ban verse as unnatural is superficial.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· Poetry › Poetic Expression › Versification
Hegel citations:
[N]evertheless, metre or rhyme is absolutely necessary for poetry, as its one and only sensuous fragrance, and indeed it is even more necessary than the rich imagery of a so-called ‘beautiful’ diction.
— Aesthetics, Poetic Expression › Versification (tr. Knox)
For this reason it is only a superficial theory which proposes to ban versification on the ground that it is unnatural.
— Aesthetics, Poetic Expression › Versification (tr. Knox)

Head: Rhythmic Verse
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › γ. The System of the Individual Arts › c. Romantic Arts › iii. Poetry › 2. Poetic Expression › c. Versification › i. Rhythmic Verse
Gloss: Verse measured by the length or stress of syllables.
Hegelian gloss: The measure of syllables by quantity, the rhythm of ancient verse.
Nouns: rhythmic verse; quantitative verse, classical metre. foot. prosody, scansion, cadence.
Verbs: scan, measure. metrify, quantify.
Adjective: quantitative. rhythmic, rhythmical, measured.
Adverbs: metrically, rhythmically, by quantity, in measure.
Hegel definition: Rhythmic versification is the system without rhyme, whose chief thing is not isolated sound but temporal duration and movement. It rests on the fixed measure of long and short syllables fitted into relations and metres, the enlivening of rhythm by accent and caesura against word accent, and the euphony of sounds, which classical languages possess in full.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· Poetry › Poetic Expression › Versification › Rhythmic Versification
Hegel citations:
The chief thing in rhythm is not sound picked out and isolated as such but temporal duration and movement.
— Aesthetics, Versification › Rhythmic Versification (tr. Knox)
Secondly, the enlivenment of rhythm by accent, caesura, and the opposition between verbal and verse-accentuation.
— Aesthetics, Versification › Rhythmic Versification (tr. Knox)

Head: Tempo
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › γ. The System of the Individual Arts › c. Romantic Arts › iii. Poetry › 2. Poetic Expression › c. Versification › i. Rhythmic Verse › 1. Tempo
Gloss: The time-measure of verse: the length of syllables, their grouping into feet, and the beat that orders them.
Hegelian gloss: Das Zeitmaß, the first element of rhythmic verse: the fixed measure of long and short syllables in time.
Nouns: tempo; time-measure, quantity, duration, length, pace, movement. quantity.
Hegel definition: Tempo is the fixed time of syllables in their difference of long and short. Since words of many syllables and monosyllables yield an accidental mixture without measure, poetry, as music fixes the duration of notes by tempo, lays down particular combinations of longs and shorts as the law governing the temporal duration of the succession of syllables.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· Poetry › Poetic Expression › Versification › Rhythmic Versification
Hegel citations:
First, the fixed tempo of the syllables in their simple difference between long and short and the numerous ways of fitting them together in specific relations and metres.
— Aesthetics, Versification › Rhythmic Versification (tr. Knox)
To regulate this accidental character is just as much the duty of poetry as it was the task of music to determine with precision, by means of the unity of tempo, the unordered duration of single notes.
— Aesthetics, Versification › Rhythmic Versification (tr. Knox)

Head: Natural Syllables
Head (German): Natürliche Länge und Kürze der Silben
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › γ. The System of the Individual Arts › c. Romantic Arts › iii. Poetry › 2. Poetic Expression › c. Versification › i. Rhythmic Verse › 1. Tempo › a. Natural Syllables
Gloss: The natural length and shortness of syllables, by vowel or by position.
Hegelian gloss: The natural length and brevity of syllables, given by the sounds themselves or by position, on which ancient rhythm rests.
Nouns: natural syllables; long syllable, short syllable, natural length, vowel length, length by position, quantity by nature, quantity by position, breve, macron. syllable-length, longs and shorts, mora.
Verbs: lengthen, shorten.
Adjective: syllabic.
Phrases: long and short.
Hegel definition: Natural syllables have their length and shortness grounded in the speech sounds themselves, vowels and consonants. Diphthongs and long vowels are long by nature, and in ancient languages position, two or more consonants between vowels, lengthens a short syllable through the longer time needed to articulate it; modern languages use other criteria.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· Poetry › Poetic Expression › Versification › Rhythmic Versification
Hegel citations:
The basis of their simple difference is provided by the speech-sounds themselves, by the letters to be pronounced, i.e. by consonants and vowels.
— Aesthetics, Versification › Rhythmic Versification (tr. Knox)
[I]n order to get over the consonants the tongue requires a longer time for articulation, and a delay is produced which, despite the shortness of the vowel preceding the consonants, makes the syllable rhythmically long even if it is not naturally so.
— Aesthetics, Versification › Rhythmic Versification (tr. Knox)

Head: Syllabic Temporal Relations (Feet)
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › γ. The System of the Individual Arts › c. Romantic Arts › iii. Poetry › 2. Poetic Expression › c. Versification › i. Rhythmic Verse › 1. Tempo › b. Syllabic Temporal Relations (Feet)
Gloss: The feet that combine long and short syllables into units of time.
Hegelian gloss: The syllabic time-relations, the feet, which bind long and short syllables into definite proportions.
Nouns: syllabic temporal relations; feet, foot, amphibrach, bacchius, cretic, molossus, paeon, ionic, iambus. dactyl, spondee, iamb, trochee, anapaest, pyrrhic, choriamb, tribrach, anapest.
Adjective: dactylic, iambic, trochaic, spondaic, anapaestic, anapestic†.
Hegel definition: Feet are the time relations of syllables into which poetry binds long and short. The simplest are relations of equals, such as the dactyl and anapaest, where two shorts may be gathered into a long as a spondee; a long beside a short makes a more marked difference, as in iambus and trochee; more complex are the cretic and bacchius.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· Poetry › Poetic Expression › Versification › Rhythmic Versification
Hegel citations:
The simplest of these is the relation of equals to one another, e.g. the dactyl and the anapaest, in which the short syllables may be brought together again, on specific rules, into a long one, so as to produce a spondee.
— Aesthetics, Versification › Rhythmic Versification (tr. Knox)
Secondly, a long syllable may be placed beside a short one, so that a more profound difference in duration is produced, even if in the simplest form, as in an iambus or a trochee.
— Aesthetics, Versification › Rhythmic Versification (tr. Knox)

Head: Beat and Metre
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › γ. The System of the Individual Arts › c. Romantic Arts › iii. Poetry › 2. Poetic Expression › c. Versification › i. Rhythmic Verse › 1. Tempo › c. Beat and Metre
Gloss: The regular beat and the metres built from feet: hexameter, trimeter and the stanzas of the ode.
Hegelian gloss: Takt and Versmaß: the regular return of the same time-measure, built from feet into lines and metres.
Nouns: beat and metre; beat, bar, time, metrical pattern, dimeter, trimeter, tetrameter. hexameter, elegiac couplet, Sapphic stanza, Alcaic, iambic trimeter, pentameter, meter, metre, numbers.
Verbs: beat time, mete.
Adjective: hexametric, Sapphic, metrical.
Adverbs: in hexameters.
Phrases: arma virumque cano [Lat.] [dactylic hexameter]; the dactylic hexameter.
Hegel definition: Beat and metre concern how single time relations are ranged into lines governed by rules for number and kind of feet and for beginning, middle and end, and then into stanzas. The great difference from music is the beat: poetry, which has its stability in the ideas it expresses, keeps a time measure but need not submit to a fixed beat.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· Poetry › Poetic Expression › Versification › Rhythmic Versification
Hegel citations:
This is the reason why, in the third place, poetry ranges the single timerelations into lines governed by a rule in relation to the sort and number of feet and to their beginning, middle, and end.
— Aesthetics, Versification › Rhythmic Versification (tr. Knox)
This may be given as a reason for the demand that while in poetry a time-measure, but not a beat, must remain the rule, this aspect shall be dominated to a relatively stronger extent by the sense and meaning of the words.
— Aesthetics, Versification › Rhythmic Versification (tr. Knox)

Head: Accent
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › γ. The System of the Individual Arts › c. Romantic Arts › iii. Poetry › 2. Poetic Expression › c. Versification › i. Rhythmic Verse › 2. Accent
Gloss: The life that stress and pause give to the bare measure.
Hegelian gloss: Der Rhythmus proper, the animation of the time-measure by accent and caesura.
Nouns: accent; stress, emphasis, rhythmic animation. rhythm, accentuation &c H0662.
Hegel definition: Accent, with caesura, is what really animates rhythmic time measure, corresponding to the rhythmical beat in music. Each time relation has its own accent, certain positions emphasized by law and attracting the rest into a rounded whole, and this opens great variety in the value of syllables as accent falls on long or short ones.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· Poetry › Poetic Expression › Versification › Rhythmic Versification
Hegel citations:
But the really animating thing in rhythmical time-measure is introduced only by accent and caesura
— Aesthetics, Versification › Rhythmic Versification (tr. Knox)
In poetry too each specific time relation has in the first place its particular accent, i.e. specific positions are emphasized in accordance with a law, and these then attract the others and thus alone form with them a rounded whole.
— Aesthetics, Versification › Rhythmic Versification (tr. Knox)

Head: Metrical Accent and Caesura
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › γ. The System of the Individual Arts › c. Romantic Arts › iii. Poetry › 2. Poetic Expression › c. Versification › i. Rhythmic Verse › 2. Accent › a. Metrical Accent and Caesura
Gloss: The stress that the metre itself places, and the pause that divides the line.
Hegelian gloss: The verse-accent on particular syllables of the foot, and the caesura, which cuts across the feet and keeps the line from falling apart into its units.
Nouns: metrical accent and caesura; verse accent, metrical stress, diaeresis, pause, break, masculine caesura, feminine caesura. caesura, ictus, arsis, thesis.
Hegel definition: Metrical accent and caesura enliven verse where feet must not coincide with words: a word running past the end of a foot links rhythms, and the pause at its end with the verse accent becomes a deliberate interval. The caesura, required in every line, breaks the cold monotony and brings connection and life into the flow.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· Poetry › Poetic Expression › Versification › Rhythmic Versification
Hegel citations:
Above all, however, as I have mentioned before, the start and finish of the single feet must not rigidly correspond with the beginning and end of single words
— Aesthetics, Versification › Rhythmic Versification (tr. Knox)
The caesura breaks this cold monotony and introduces a connection and more of a life into the flow of the verse, a flow that a line’s undifferentiated regularity would make spiritless.
— Aesthetics, Versification › Rhythmic Versification (tr. Knox)

Head: Sense-Accent
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › γ. The System of the Individual Arts › c. Romantic Arts › iii. Poetry › 2. Poetic Expression › c. Versification › i. Rhythmic Verse › 2. Accent › b. Sense-Accent
Gloss: The stress that falls by meaning on the important word, which may cross the metrical accent.
Hegelian gloss: The sense-accent, which the meaning lays on the significant word and which may agree or contend with the metrical accent.
Nouns: sense-accent; logical stress, rhetorical accent, sense stress, meaning-stress, word accent.
Adjective: emphatic.
Hegel definition: Sense accent is the emphasis syllables and words receive from the poetic idea they signify, which hovers over their metrical value, stressing some and setting back others as insignificant, so that spiritual life is breathed into the verse. Poetry must not yield to it so far as directly to oppose the rules of metre.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· Poetry › Poetic Expression › Versification › Rhythmic Versification
Hegel citations:
Besides, however, in the second place, there hovers over all the validity that syllables and words have in their metrical position, the value that they have of signifying a poetical idea.
— Aesthetics, Versification › Rhythmic Versification (tr. Knox)
Owing to this immanent sense of theirs they likewise become relatively emphasized or must be put in the background as insignificant, and in this way alone is the ultimate extreme of spiritual life breathed into the verse. But poetry must not yield to this to the extent of directly opposing the rhythmic rules of metre.
— Aesthetics, Versification › Rhythmic Versification (tr. Knox)

Head: Expressive Fit
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › γ. The System of the Individual Arts › c. Romantic Arts › iii. Poetry › 2. Poetic Expression › c. Versification › i. Rhythmic Verse › 2. Accent › c. Expressive Fit
Gloss: The fit between the movement of the verse and what it says.
Hegelian gloss: The correspondence of the rhythmic movement with the content and its feeling, in which the verse's tempo and accent express the matter.
Nouns: expressive fit; the fit of movement to content, sound echoing sense, expressive rhythm, mimetic rhythm, onomatopoeia.
Phrases: the sound must seem an echo to the sense [Pope].
Hegel definition: Expressive fit is the correspondence that versification, especially rhythmic movement, must have with its subject matter and above all with a particular movement of feeling. The calmly rolling hexameter suits epic narrative, and with the pentameter the elegy; the rushing iambus fits dramatic dialogue; the anapaest suggests something spirited and joyful.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· Poetry › Poetic Expression › Versification › Rhythmic Versification
Hegel citations:
The whole character of versification must have corresponding to it, especially in connection with rhythmical movement, a specific sort of subject-matter, above all a specific sort of movement in our feelings.
— Aesthetics, Versification › Rhythmic Versification (tr. Knox)
The iambic, again, rushes forward and is especially appropriate to dialogue in drama
— Aesthetics, Versification › Rhythmic Versification (tr. Knox)

Head: Sound of Syllables
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › γ. The System of the Individual Arts › c. Romantic Arts › iii. Poetry › 2. Poetic Expression › c. Versification › i. Rhythmic Verse › 3. Sound of Syllables
Gloss: The sound of syllables and words in themselves, which comes forward as rhythm recedes.
Hegelian gloss: The sound of the syllables, which gains weight as the rhythmic element recedes.
Nouns: sound of syllables; sound, euphony, tone, verbal music, vowel music, word music. cadence.
Hegel definition: The sound of syllables is the third element of rhythmic verse, which is not exhausted by the shaping of time but extends to the sound of words. Here there is an essential difference between classical languages, which keep rhythm as the chief thing, and modern ones, which are chiefly suited to rhyme.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· Poetry › Poetic Expression › Versification › Rhythmic Versification
Hegel citations:
But thirdly this first sphere of rhythmical versification is not exhausted by the mere figuration and enlivenment of temporal duration but is extended to the actual sound of syllables and words.
— Aesthetics, Versification › Rhythmic Versification (tr. Knox)
But in this matter of sound there is clearly an essential difference between the classical languages, where rhythm is firmly retained as the chief thing, in the way described, and the modem languages which are chiefly apt for rhyme.
— Aesthetics, Versification › Rhythmic Versification (tr. Knox)

Head: Inflected Languages
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › γ. The System of the Individual Arts › c. Romantic Arts › iii. Poetry › 2. Poetic Expression › c. Versification › i. Rhythmic Verse › 3. Sound of Syllables › a. Inflected Languages
Gloss: Languages like Greek and Latin whose endings and long syllables carry the rhythm.
Hegelian gloss: The ancient languages, in which inflectional endings and natural length give the syllables a quantity independent of meaning.
Nouns: inflected languages; inflection, endings, terminations, case endings, quantitative languages, the classical languages, Greek and Latin.
Hegel definition: Inflected languages such as Greek and Latin develop the root by declension and conjugation into many sounding syllables, which only modify it, so that the chief meaning and the sounding accent separate, as in amaverunt. The ear is then free to follow the sounds and shape their natural longs and shorts rhythmically.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· Poetry › Poetic Expression › Versification › Rhythmic Versification
Hegel citations:
For example, in Greek and Latin, owing to the declensions and conjugations, the root syllable is developed into a wealth of variously sounding syllables which do have a meaning in themselves, but only as modifications of the root
— Aesthetics, Versification › Rhythmic Versification (tr. Knox)
[W]ith the result that the chief meaning and the sounding accent are separated.
— Aesthetics, Versification › Rhythmic Versification (tr. Knox)

Head: Root-Accented Languages
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › γ. The System of the Individual Arts › c. Romantic Arts › iii. Poetry › 2. Poetic Expression › c. Versification › i. Rhythmic Verse › 3. Sound of Syllables › b. Root-Accented Languages
Gloss: Languages like German in which stress falls on the root syllable that carries the meaning.
Hegelian gloss: The modern languages, in which the accent falls on the root syllable of meaning, so that sense rather than natural length governs the stress.
Nouns: root-accented languages; root accent, root syllable, stem stress, accentual languages, stress-timed languages, the modern languages, the Germanic languages.
Hegel definition: Root-accented languages such as modern German split what the ancients inflected into separate words, leaving the root a simple whole whose weighty meaning draws the accent to itself. Since stress then marks sense, it drowns the natural length of other syllables, and a rhythm independent of the root and its meaning can no longer exist.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· Poetry › Poetic Expression › Versification › Rhythmic Versification
Hegel citations:
If now, as is the case in full measure with our modem mother-tongue for example, these roots lay claim to the accent almost exclusively for themselves, this is throughout a preponderating accent on the meaning or sense
— Aesthetics, Versification › Rhythmic Versification (tr. Knox)
[A]nd since the emphasis and the chief meaning are linked together, this coincidence of the two does not make conspicuous but drowns the natural length or shortness of the other syllables.
— Aesthetics, Versification › Rhythmic Versification (tr. Knox)

Head: Eclipse of Rhythm
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › γ. The System of the Individual Arts › c. Romantic Arts › iii. Poetry › 2. Poetic Expression › c. Versification › i. Rhythmic Verse › 3. Sound of Syllables › c. Eclipse of Rhythm
Gloss: The fading of quantitative rhythm in the modern languages, whose place rhyme takes.
Hegelian gloss: Das Zurücktreten des Rhythmus: where the accent of meaning overrides quantity, rhythm recedes and the sound of the syllables, in rhyme, takes its place.
Nouns: eclipse of rhythm; the receding of rhythm, the loss of quantity, the passing of metre, the turn to sound, accentual verse.
Hegel definition: The eclipse of rhythm follows in modern languages, where time and the sound of syllables are surpassed by something more ideal, the sense of words, so that independent rhythmic shaping is damped. If the sensuous element is still to counterbalance intellect, nothing remains but the express and isolated sound of syllables as such, which leads to rhyme.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· Poetry › Poetic Expression › Versification › Rhythmic Versification
Hegel citations:
In such [modern] languages there is little room for rhythm, or the soul has little freedom any longer to spread itself in it
— Aesthetics, Versification › Rhythmic Versification (tr. Knox)
[N]o other material can be adopted except the express, firmly isolated, figured sound of the linguistic] syllables as such.
— Aesthetics, Versification › Rhythmic Versification (tr. Knox)

Head: Rhyme
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › γ. The System of the Individual Arts › c. Romantic Arts › iii. Poetry › 2. Poetic Expression › c. Versification › ii. Rhyme
Gloss: The likeness of sound at the ends of lines.
Hegelian gloss: Rhyme, the echo of like sounds at the ends of lines, the inward self hearing itself in modern verse.
Nouns: rhyme; rhyme, rime, accentual verse. verse, crambo†. unison, homophony, euphony. jingle, tag, echo, return of sound.
Verbs: rhyme, chime. pair, answer, clink.
Adjective: rhymed, rhyming, accentual. rimed, chiming, jingling, echoing, consonant, homophonous.
Adverbs: in rhyme. in couplets, rhymingly.
Foreign: German: Stabreim; Italian: terza rima; Arabic: sajʿ [rhymed prose].
Phrases: neither rhyme nor reason; the echo at the line's end.
Hegel definition: Rhyme belongs to romantic poetry, which, growing more inward, withdraws from the natural length of syllables and plays with the sounds of words for their own sake. It is no accidental invention but necessary: the soul's need to apprehend itself is satisfied by returning like sounds, indifferent to regulated time, which bring us back to ourselves and bring verse near to music.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· Poetry › Poetic Expression › Versification › Rhyme
Hegel citations:
Thus viewed, rhyme is not something accidentally elaborated in romantic poetry alone, but has become necessary in it.
— Aesthetics, Versification › Rhyme (tr. Knox)
The need of the soul to apprehend itself is emphasized more fully, and it is satisfied by the assonance of rhyme which is indifferent to the firmly regulated time-measure and has the sole function of bringing us back to ourselves through the return of the same sounds.
— Aesthetics, Versification › Rhyme (tr. Knox)

Head: Alliteration
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › γ. The System of the Individual Arts › c. Romantic Arts › iii. Poetry › 2. Poetic Expression › c. Versification › ii. Rhyme › 1. Alliteration
Gloss: The rhyme of initial sounds, as in Germanic verse.
Hegelian gloss: Alliteration (Stabreim), the earliest and most abstract echo, the binding of words by their initial sounds.
Nouns: alliteration; head rhyme, initial rhyme, staves, alliterative verse. alliteration.
Verbs: alliterate.
Adjective: alliterative.
Hegel definition: Alliteration, developed most thoroughly in old Scandinavian poetry, repeats a single letter, the initial one, without requiring whole syllables to recur. It is the most imperfect kind of rhyme, so weak that the words must already carry accent on their first syllable and stand close together, and meaningful words are chiefly chosen for it.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· Poetry › Poetic Expression › Versification › Rhyme
Hegel citations:
The principle of alliteration, or one-letter rhymes, is the most imperfect kind of rhyme because it does not demand the recurrence of whole syllables but only insists on the repetition of one and the same letter, and the initial letter at that.
— Aesthetics, Versification › Rhyme (tr. Knox)
Alliteration we find developed in the greatest thoroughness in the older Scandinavian poetry
— Aesthetics, Versification › Rhyme (tr. Knox)

Head: Assonance
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › γ. The System of the Individual Arts › c. Romantic Arts › iii. Poetry › 2. Poetic Expression › c. Versification › ii. Rhyme › 2. Assonance
Gloss: The rhyme of vowels alone, as in Spanish romances.
Hegelian gloss: Assonance, the echo of vowels, especially in Spanish verse, between alliteration and full rhyme.
Nouns: assonance; vowel rhyme, near rhyme. assonance, consonance, half-rhyme.
Verbs: assonate.
Adjective: assonant.
Hegel definition: Assonance stands between alliteration and full rhyme: it repeats the same letters, chiefly vowels, in the middle or at the end of different words, not initial letters. It need not close a line, though final syllables especially enter into it, and it flourishes richest among Latin peoples, above all the Spaniards with their sonorous language.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· Poetry › Poetic Expression › Versification › Rhyme
Hegel citations:
Assonance does not affect the initial letters but already approaches rhyme, because it is an identically sounding repetition of the same letters in the middle or at the end of different words.
— Aesthetics, Versification › Rhyme (tr. Knox)
In its richest development this assonance appears amongst the Latin nations, especially the Spaniards whose sonorous language is especially fitted for the recurrence of the same vowels.
— Aesthetics, Versification › Rhyme (tr. Knox)

Head: Rhyme Proper
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › γ. The System of the Individual Arts › c. Romantic Arts › iii. Poetry › 2. Poetic Expression › c. Versification › ii. Rhyme › 3. Rhyme Proper
Gloss: Full end-rhyme, and the stanza forms built on it.
Hegelian gloss: Rhyme proper, the full echo of like sounds at the line's end, in which the modern inward self hears itself; with it the rhymed stanza forms.
Nouns: rhyme proper; full rhyme, perfect rhyme, stanza forms, rhyme royal, Spenserian stanza, ballad stanza. end-rhyme, rhyme scheme, couplet, sonnet, internal rhyme, masculine rhyme, feminine rhyme, eye rhyme, tercet, rime riche, like ending, end-sound. quatrain, sestet, octave, refrain, envoi, triplet, distich. ottava rima, terza rima.
Hegel definition: Rhyme proper brings to maturity what alliteration and assonance achieve imperfectly: a complete accord between whole stems apart from initial letters, with one, two or three syllables. Its place is the line's end, in simple return or artful interlacings that satisfy, tease and content the ear, and lyric, loving it for its subjectivity, develops it into stanza systems.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· Poetry › Poetic Expression › Versification › Rhyme
Hegel citations:
What in this way alliteration and assonance are qualified to achieve only imperfectly, rhyme finally brings to life in full maturity.
— Aesthetics, Versification › Rhyme (tr. Knox)
Amongst the particular sorts of poetry it is especially lyric which is fondest of using rhymes owing to its subjective character, i.e. its inner feeling and its mode of expressing it.
— Aesthetics, Versification › Rhyme (tr. Knox)

Head: Unification of Verse and Rhyme
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › γ. The System of the Individual Arts › c. Romantic Arts › iii. Poetry › 2. Poetic Expression › c. Versification › iii. Unification of Verse and Rhyme
Gloss: The joining of rhythmic measure and rhyme.
Hegelian gloss: The union of accentual rhythm and rhyme in modern verse.
Nouns: unification of verse and rhyme; rhymed metrical verse, modern prosody. the union of metre and rhyme, combination, blending, fusion. iamb, trochee.
Verbs: combine, unite. unify, join, blend, fuse, marry, wed, reconcile.
Adjective: rhymed and metred. combined, united, blended, rhymed, metrical.
Adverbs: in rhymed verse. jointly, together.
Phrases: the marriage of metre and rhyme; accent and rhyme; the stressed syllable.
Hegel definition: The union of rhythmic versification and rhyme is considered chiefly in modern languages, which have partly restored rhythm or joined it with rhyme. Lacking the plasticity of ancient quantity, they compensate with metrical accent and caesura, which now coincide with word accent; and the combination is allowed only within limits, since the two systems rest on opposed principles.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· Poetry › Poetic Expression › Versification › Unification of Rhythmical Versification and Rhyme
Hegel citations:
But while in the way indicated we have distinguished and contrasted rhythmic versification and rhyme, the question arises whether a unification of the two is not conceivable and has not actually occurred.
— Aesthetics, Versification › Unification of Rhythmical Versification and Rhyme (tr. Knox)
This element is the metrical accent and the caesura, which now instead of proceeding independently of the word-accent coincide with it.
— Aesthetics, Versification › Unification of Rhythmical Versification and Rhyme (tr. Knox)

Head: Classical Metres in Modern Languages
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › γ. The System of the Individual Arts › c. Romantic Arts › iii. Poetry › 2. Poetic Expression › c. Versification › iii. Unification of Verse and Rhyme › 1. Classical Metres in Modern Languages
Gloss: The imitation of ancient metres in modern languages, such as the German hexameter.
Hegelian gloss: The attempt to carry the classical metres into the modern languages, as in Klopstock's odes and Voss's Homer, where the accent of meaning resists quantity.
Nouns: classical metres in modern languages; accentual hexameter, German hexameter, English hexameter, English Sapphics, imitation of classical metres, Klopstock's odes, Voss's Homer.
Hegel definition: Classical metres in modern languages were attempted by Klopstock, who largely forsook rhyme to imitate the ancients, and by Voss, while Goethe doubted whether their wide folds suit us. Modern languages lack natural quantity, since verbal accent given by meaning makes lengths uncertain, so that ancient plasticity cannot be achieved and imitation succeeds only in the more strongly marked rhythms.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· Poetry › Poetic Expression › Versification › Unification of Rhythmical Versification and Rhyme
Hegel citations:
If we keep to German, for example, I need only refer, in connection with the first of these, to Klopstock who wanted little to do with rhyme and instead imitated the classics in both epic and lyric with deep seriousness and untiring industry.
— Aesthetics, Versification › Unification of Rhythmical Versification and Rhyme (tr. Knox)
Modern languages, on the other hand, lack a natural measure like this because in them the verbal accent, given by the meaning, may itself make a syllable long in contrast to others which are without this significance.
— Aesthetics, Versification › Unification of Rhythmical Versification and Rhyme (tr. Knox)

Head: Rhymed Accentual Verse
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › γ. The System of the Individual Arts › c. Romantic Arts › iii. Poetry › 2. Poetic Expression › c. Versification › iii. Unification of Verse and Rhyme › 2. Rhymed Accentual Verse
Gloss: Modern verse that unites accentual rhythm with rhyme.
Hegelian gloss: The rhymed accentual verse of the modern languages, which joins the rhythm of stressed syllables with the echo of rhyme.
Nouns: rhymed accentual verse; iambic pentameter, heroic couplet, tetrameter couplet. rhymed iambics, the alexandrine, the stanza, rhymed verse.
Adjective: accentual-syllabic.
Hegel definition: Rhymed accentual verse combines rhythm and rhyme to a restricted extent. Word accent alone does not occupy the ear enough, so that sounding syllables are needed as supplement, and against rhyme's strength the metre must offer a counterweight, making the beat prominent, as in German rhymed iambics and trochees; rhyme suits only simple metres, not imitated classical stanzas.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· Poetry › Poetic Expression › Versification › Unification of Rhythmical Versification and Rhyme
Hegel citations:
For the dominant distinction between longs and shorts by the word-accent is not throughout a sufficient material principle; and on the sensuous side it does not occupy the ear to an extent that would make it unnecessary for poetry, where the spiritual side predominates, to have recourse to a supplement in the sounding and resounding of syllables and words.
— Aesthetics, Versification › Unification of Rhythmical Versification and Rhyme (tr. Knox)
But rhyme in general has to be combined only with such metres as, taken in themselves in rhythmically treated modem languages, cannot shape the sensuous element strongly enough, because of their simple alternation of longs and shorts and the firm repetition of similar feet.
— Aesthetics, Versification › Unification of Rhythmical Versification and Rhyme (tr. Knox)

Head: Different Genres
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › γ. The System of the Individual Arts › c. Romantic Arts › iii. Poetry › 3. Different Genres
Gloss: The kinds of poetry.
Hegelian gloss: The kinds of poetry: epic, the objective; lyric, the subjective; drama, their unity.
Nouns: different genres; poetic genres, epic, lyric, dramatic, literary kinds, genre. poem, epic poem, ode, idyl, eclogue, pastoral, sonnet. dramatic poetry, lyric poetry, ballad, lay. kinds of poetry, species of poetry, the poetic kinds, the three genres, the division of poetry, classification, kind, sort, species, type, class, category, taxonomy.
Verbs: classify. divide, distinguish, differentiate, categorize, group, specify.
Adjective: generic. poetic, poetical, lyrical, dithyrambic, elegiac. specific, classificatory, typological.
Adverbs: by genre. generically, by kind, by species, severally.
Foreign: German: Gattung.
Phrases: epic, lyric, drama; epic, lyric and drama; the three kinds.
Hegel definition: The different genres of poetry arise within an art that takes spiritual life as its matter and keeps the middle way between the perceptible and pure inwardness, in imagination, giving a complete world through language. Its works exist only as spoken by living persons, and it divides into epic, which sets out the matter objectively, lyric, which expresses the subject, and drama, which unites them.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· Poetry › The Different Genres of Poetry
Hegel citations:
On the contrary it has to keep to the middle way between the extremes of what is directly visible or perceptible by the senses and the subjectivity of feeling and thinking.
— Aesthetics, Poetry › The Different Genres of Poetry (tr. Knox)
For poetry too has to give us a complete world, the substantive essence of which is spread out before us artistically with the greatest richness precisely in its external reality, i.e. in human actions, events, and outbursts of feeling.
— Aesthetics, Poetry › The Different Genres of Poetry (tr. Knox)

Head: Epic Poetry
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › γ. The System of the Individual Arts › c. Romantic Arts › iii. Poetry › 3. Different Genres › a. Epic Poetry
Gloss: Narrative poetry recounting the deeds of a people or a hero.
Hegelian gloss: Epic, which presents an action as a world, in the totality of a people's life and ethos; the poetry of an objective whole.
Nouns: epic poetry; epic, heroic poem, saga, romance, lay, narrative poetry. tradition, legend, story, tale. fable. epopee, epopoeia, heroic verse, heroic poetry, heroic song, the bible of a people, national epic, folk epic, rhapsody, rhapsode, bard, the Iliad, the Odyssey.
Verbs: narrate, sing, recount. relate, recite. tell, chant, rhapsodize, chronicle, celebrate, immortalize.
Adjective: epic, heroic, narrative, Homeric. historic, traditional, legendary. epical, bardic, rhapsodic, national, storied, anecdotic†.
Adverbs: epically. in epic form, in heroic verse, at length.
Foreign: Greek: epos; French: chanson de geste, récit [Genette, Ricoeur], raconter, décrire; Sanskrit: mahākāvya [great poem].
Phrases: die vielen epischen Bibeln [Ger.] [Hegel, Aesthetics, on the epic]; arms and the man; sing, goddess.
Hegel definition: Epic, whose name means word or saga, tells what a matter is that has been turned into word: an inherently independent content, brought before the mind in all its relations and events, in the whole sweep of circumstances and development, the topic in the entirety of its existence. It is considered in its general character, its principal particulars and its historical development.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· Poetry › Epic Poetry
Hegel citations:
What is to be brought before our minds is the topic as such in all its relations and events, in the sweep of all the circumstances and their development, the topic in the entirety of its existence.
— Aesthetics, Poetry › Epic Poetry (tr. Knox)
This premissed, we will first describe the general character of epic; secondly, cite the particular points of principal importance in epic proper; thirdly, mention certain particular modes of treatment which have actually occurred in individual epics within the historical development of this kind of poetry.
— Aesthetics, Poetry › Epic Poetry (tr. Knox)

Head: General Character of Epic
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › γ. The System of the Individual Arts › c. Romantic Arts › iii. Poetry › 3. Different Genres › a. Epic Poetry › i. General Character of Epic
Gloss: The general nature of epic.
Hegelian gloss: The general character of the epic: the national bible, the objective world of a people.
Nouns: general character of epic; objectivity, breadth, totality of a world, narrative distance, the bard behind the tale. the epic manner, epic breadth, epic calm, epic objectivity, externality, the event, the occurrence, the objective world, fullness, circumstantiality, detachment, impersonality, the self-effacing poet. epopee.
Verbs: narrate, encompass. tell, relate, recount, unfold, depict, embrace.
Adjective: objective, broad, comprehensive. epic, impersonal, detached, calm, leisurely, circumstantial, expansive, external.
Adverbs: objectively, at length. broadly, calmly, impersonally, in detail, in full.
Phrases: the whole world of a people; the bible of a people; a whole world in one poem.
Hegel definition: The general character of epic shows first in its simplest, imperfect forms, epigraph, maxim and gnomic collections, where the necessary and self-grounded is expressed without personal feeling, then is rounded into a totality whose centre is a specific sphere of life. Perfect epic presents a whole world of a people through a concrete event, so that epic works become a nation's bibles.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· Poetry › Epic Poetry › General Character of Epic
Hegel citations:
The epic character in this mode of treatment consists in this, that maxims like these are not expressions of personal feeling or purely individual reflection
— Aesthetics, Epic Poetry › General Character of Epic (tr. Knox)
Thirdly, as I have already indicated, such apophthegms may be lifted from their fragmentary character and independent separation, ranged together into a greater whole, and rounded off into a totality which is entirely of an epic sort.
— Aesthetics, Epic Poetry › General Character of Epic (tr. Knox)

Head: Particular Characteristics of Epic
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › γ. The System of the Individual Arts › c. Romantic Arts › iii. Poetry › 3. Different Genres › a. Epic Poetry › ii. Particular Characteristics of Epic
Gloss: The particular features of epic.
Hegelian gloss: The particular characteristics of the epic.
Nouns: particular characteristics of epic; world-situation, action, unity. specific features, particulars, special determinations, details, the epic world, the epic action, the epic whole, the hero, episodes. diegesis, narration.
Verbs: specify. particularize, detail, distinguish, enumerate, determine.
Adjective: particular. special, specific, several, distinct, respective.
Adverbs: in particular. specifically, in detail, severally.
Phrases: world, deed, and whole; tell it from the beginning; in medias res.
Hegel definition: The particular characteristics of epic proper are drawn above all from the Homeric poems, since little can be said generally apart from history. They concern the general state of the world needed as ground for an epic event, the nature of that individual event, and the form in which the two are woven into a work of art, an action ramified into its whole age and nation.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· Poetry › Epic Poetry › Particular Characteristics of Epic Proper
Hegel citations:
Yet this difficulty can be removed if we pick out from the many epic bibles one in which we acquire a proof of what can be established as the true fundamental character of epic proper. This one consists of the Homeric poems.
— Aesthetics, Epic Poetry › Particular Characteristics of Epic Proper (tr. Knox)
We saw right at the beginning that what is accomplished in the genuinely epical event is not a single casual deed, and that consequently it is not a purely accidental happening which is related, but an action ramified into the whole of its age and national circumstances
— Aesthetics, Epic Poetry › Particular Characteristics of Epic Proper (tr. Knox)

Head: The Epic World-Situation
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › γ. The System of the Individual Arts › c. Romantic Arts › iii. Poetry › 3. Different Genres › a. Epic Poetry › ii. Particular Characteristics of Epic › x. The Epic World-Situation
Gloss: The state of the world in which epic action takes place.
Hegelian gloss: The epic world-situation, the heroic age in which the individual and the community are one.
Nouns: the epic world-situation; the heroic age, the national world, background, setting, the age of heroes. the heroic world, the heroic condition, the general world-condition, the world of the epic, the national spirit, customs, manners, mores, the patriarchal state, the scene, the mythic age, the youth of a people.
Verbs: set, situate. ground, frame, presuppose, locate, depict, lay the scene.
Adjective: heroic, national, primeval. epic, patriarchal, pre-political, mythic, legendary, ancestral, archaic. chivalric.
Adverbs: in heroic times. in the age of heroes, of old, in olden times.
Phrases: once upon a time; when gods walked among men.
Hegel definition: The epic world-situation is a state of life already present to individuals yet closely bound to them by primitive common life: the relations of family and people developed, but not yet fixed in institutions and laws valid apart from living individuals, resting on custom, justice and character. So heroes share an objective community while their action appears to spring freely from their own will.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· Poetry › Epic Poetry › Particular Characteristics of Epic Proper › The General World-Situation of Epic
Hegel citations:
The state of human life most suitable as the background of an epic is that in which it exists for individuals already as a present reality but which remains most closely connected with them by the tie of a common primitive life.
— Aesthetics, Particular Characteristics of Epic Proper › The General World-Situation of Epic (tr. Knox)
Thus in epic we find an underlying community of objective life and action, but nevertheless a freedom in this action and life which appear to proceed entirely from the subjective will of individuals.
— Aesthetics, Particular Characteristics of Epic Proper › The General World-Situation of Epic (tr. Knox)

Head: Individual Epic Action
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › γ. The System of the Individual Arts › c. Romantic Arts › iii. Poetry › 3. Different Genres › a. Epic Poetry › ii. Particular Characteristics of Epic › xx. Individual Epic Action
Gloss: The deed of the epic hero.
Hegelian gloss: The individual epic action, an event in which the whole of a people's life is engaged.
Nouns: individual epic action; the hero's deed, quest, war, wandering, the wrath of Achilles, the return of Odysseus. exploit, feat, enterprise, adventure, undertaking, expedition, campaign, voyage, journey, homecoming, combat, battle, the epic event, the hero. emprise.
Verbs: quest, fight, wander, return. undertake, achieve, rove, strive, overcome.
Adjective: heroic, adventurous, martial. individual, valiant, valorous, warlike, questing.
Adverbs: heroically. valiantly, bravely, in battle, on the quest.
Foreign: Greek: nostos [homecoming].
Phrases: tell me, O Muse, of that ingenious hero [Homer]; one deed that moves a world.
Hegel definition: The individual epic action proceeds on the ground of a world open to conflicts between whole nations: from a national undertaking a particular aim arises, interwoven with the life of the whole people and revealing every side of its character, faith and action. Individually definite, it takes the form of an event, in which outer reality has as full a right as inner will.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· Poetry › Epic Poetry › Particular Characteristics of Epic Proper › The Individual Epic Action
Hegel citations:
However firmly the aim of an epic action rests on a universal foundation, it must still be individually alive and definite.
— Aesthetics, Particular Characteristics of Epic Proper › The Individual Epic Action (tr. Knox)
But on this foundation a particular aim must arise, the realization of which, being most intimately interwoven with the life of the whole nation, brings into view every aspect of the national character, faith, and action.
— Aesthetics, Particular Characteristics of Epic Proper › The Individual Epic Action (tr. Knox)

Head: Epic as a Fully Unified Whole
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › γ. The System of the Individual Arts › c. Romantic Arts › iii. Poetry › 3. Different Genres › a. Epic Poetry › ii. Particular Characteristics of Epic › xxx. Epic as a Fully Unified Whole
Gloss: The epic as a complete whole.
Hegelian gloss: The epic as a whole, unified yet broad, episodic, governed by circumstance.
Nouns: epic as a fully unified whole; epic unity, totality, organic whole, episodes. wholeness, completeness, integrity, roundedness, unity of action, the self-contained whole, the rounded whole, digression, retardation, breadth. epic simile.
Verbs: unify, encompass. unite, integrate, round off, complete, embrace, comprise, hold together.

Hegel definition: The epic as a fully unified whole must gather everything connected with the action and its ground, differ from lyric and drama in development, and round a widely dispersed content into concrete unity. Its content is the entirety of a world in which an individual action happens, with both inner life and outer reality, the whole poetry of human existence.

The contents of the epic, as we saw, are the entirety of a world in which an individual action happens.

But in epic, over and above the encompassing national life on which the action is based, both inner life and outer reality have their place, and thus here there is spread out before us all the detail of what can be regarded as the poetry of human existence.
— Aesthetics, Particular Characteristics of Epic Proper › The Epic as a Fully Unified Whole (tr. Knox)

Head: Historical Development of Epic
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › γ. The System of the Individual Arts › c. Romantic Arts › iii. Poetry › 3. Different Genres › a. Epic Poetry › iii. Historical Development of Epic
Gloss: The historical course of epic.
Hegelian gloss: The historical course of the epic from the East through Greece to the romantic world.
Nouns: historical development of epic; Oriental, classical, romantic epic. the history of epic, the course of epic, the stages of epic, the epic tradition, the rise of the novel, the modern bourgeois epic.
Verbs: develop. evolve, unfold, progress, arise, pass over, decline.
Adjective: historical. developmental, successive, progressive, chronological.
Adverbs: historically. by stages, successively, through the ages.
Phrases: from Gilgamesh to Milton; from Valmiki to Milton; the course of the epic.
Hegel definition: The historical development of epic matters more than that of sculpture, since epic displays the substantial kernel of a nation's life and belongs to every people, though epic proper reached perfection in Greece beside sculpture. Hegel distinguishes the oriental epic centred in the symbolic, the classical epic of the Greeks and its Roman imitation, and the romantic epics of Christian peoples.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics

Consequently we should not regard it as a matter of accident that epic poetry and sculpture both appeared in Greece in this original and unsurpassed perfection.

(c) the rich and many-sided development of romantically-epic poetry amongst the Christian peoples who yet first came on the scene in their Germanic heathenism.
— Aesthetics, Epic Poetry › The Historical Development of Epic Poetry (tr. Knox)

Nouns: Oriental epic; Mahābhārata, Gilgamesh, the Book of Job. the Indian epic, the Persian epic, Shāhnāmeh, Firdausi, Vālmīki, Vyāsa, Antar, the Moallakat, the Purāṇas. sloka.

Hegel definition: Oriental epic stays close to the substantial whole in which individual consciousness is absorbed, so that characters never reach the independence drama demands. Epics proper occur only in India and Persia, in colossal proportions; China, prosaic in outlook, has none; and the Indian Ramayana and Mahabharata show splendour and fantastic confusion, loosely unified and measurelessly enlarged.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics

Nevertheless epics proper are to be found only in India and Persia, but then in colossal proportions.

— Aesthetics, The Historical Development of Epic Poetry › The Oriental Epic (tr. Knox)

Head: Classical Epic of Greece and Rome
Head (German): Das klassische Epos der Griechen und Römer
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › γ. The System of the Individual Arts › c. Romantic Arts › iii. Poetry › 3. Different Genres › a. Epic Poetry › iii. Historical Development of Epic › xx. Classical Epic of Greece and Rome
Gloss: The epic poetry of Greece and Rome.
Hegelian gloss: The classical epic of Homer, and its imitations in Virgil.
Nouns: classical epic of Greece and Rome; Iliad, Odyssey, Aeneid, Homer, Virgil, Hesiod, Apollonius, Lucan. the Homeric poems, the Argonautica, the Theogony, Works and Days, the Pharsalia, the epic cycle, the rhapsodes, the Homeridae, the heroic hexameter. epithet.
