Adverbs: in hexameters. in the classical manner, in heroic verse.
Phrases: arma virumque cano [Lat.] [Virgil]; Homer sometimes nods; the wine-dark sea.
Hegel definition: Classical epic takes us first into the truly epic world of art, above all in Homer, whose poems hover beautifully between the universal ethical order and individual character, spirit and nature, intention and outcome. Later Greek epic lost its naive freshness, and Rome, lacking an epic bible, produced the artistic epic, finest in the Aeneid, with historical and didactic poetry.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· Poetry › Epic Poetry › The Historical Development of Epic Poetry › The Classical Epic of Greece and Rome
Hegel citations:
[W]e find in the Homeric poems for the first time a world hovering beautifully between the universal foundations of life in the ethical order of family, state, and religious belief, and the individual personal character
— Aesthetics, The Historical Development of Epic Poetry › The Classical Epic of Greece and Rome (tr. Knox)
On the contrary, alongside the artistic epic proper, of which the Aeneid remains the finest example, the historical epic and the didactic poem were there from early times
— Aesthetics, The Historical Development of Epic Poetry › The Classical Epic of Greece and Rome (tr. Knox)

Head: Romantic Epic
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › γ. The System of the Individual Arts › c. Romantic Arts › iii. Poetry › 3. Different Genres › a. Epic Poetry › iii. Historical Development of Epic › xxx. Romantic Epic
Gloss: The epic poetry of the Christian Middle Ages and after.
Hegelian gloss: The romantic epic of the Middle Ages, the Nibelungen, Dante, the epics of chivalry.
Nouns: romantic epic. the Lusiads, Ossian, the Edda, Camões.
Verbs: sing. romance, narrate.
Adjective: medieval, romantic. Germanic.
Adverbs: in the romantic manner. in romance, in the Middle Ages.
Foreign: German: Nibelungenlied; French: Chanson de Roland; Italian: Divina Commedia, Gerusalemme Liberata; Portuguese: Os Lusíadas.
Hegel definition: Romantic epic enters through the faith, deeds and fates of new peoples, Germanic and Latin: the remains of their pagan days, such as the Ossian poems and the Edda, and the medieval epics of national heroes, like the Cid and the Nibelungenlied, of religion, and of chivalry, until the renaissance turned to new matter and forms.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· Poetry › Epic Poetry › The Historical Development of Epic Poetry › The Romantic Epic
Hegel citations:
Consequently a new breath and spirit could enter epic poetry only through the outlook, religious faith, deeds, and fates of neo peoples.
— Aesthetics, The Historical Development of Epic Poetry › The Romantic Epic (tr. Knox)
It is a string of pearls, each single picture is a rounded whole in itself, and yet each is so fitted in to the other that they are ranged together into a single whole
— Aesthetics, The Historical Development of Epic Poetry › The Romantic Epic (tr. Knox)

Head: Christian Epic
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › γ. The System of the Individual Arts › c. Romantic Arts › iii. Poetry › 3. Different Genres › a. Epic Poetry › iii. Historical Development of Epic › xxx. Romantic Epic › a. Christian Epic
Gloss: The epic of Christian faith, above all Dante's Divine Comedy.
Hegelian gloss: The Christian epic, whose world is the eternal action of divine justice and love, its great example Dante's Divine Comedy.
Nouns: Christian epic; sacred epic, the Messiah, the Messiade, Klopstock. Inferno, Purgatorio, Paradiso, the Commedia; hell, purgatory, paradise &c H1184. Divine Comedy, Paradise Lost, the Christian epic, Dante, Milton, Jerusalem Delivered, Tasso.
Adjective: Dantean, Miltonic, Christian.
Phrases: nel mezzo del cammin di nostra vita [It.] [Dante].
Hegel definition: Christian epic has its richest work, the greatest of the Catholic Middle Ages, in Dante's Divine Comedy. Instead of a particular event its subject is the eternal action, the love of God, set in Hell, Purgatory and Paradise, into whose changeless existence the living world of human deeds and fates is plunged and judged, individuals standing solidified for ever like images of bronze.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· Poetry › Epic Poetry › The Historical Development of Epic Poetry › The Romantic Epic
Hegel citations:
Instead of a particular event it has for its subject-matter the eternal action, the absolute end and aim, the love of God in its imperishable activity and unalterable sphere, and for its locality Hell, Purgatory, and Paradise; into this changeless existent it plunges the living world of human action and suffering and, more particularly, the deeds and fates of individuals.
— Aesthetics, The Historical Development of Epic Poetry › The Romantic Epic (tr. Knox)
For as individuals mere in their passions and sufferings, in their intentions and their accomplishments, so now here they are presented for ever, solidified into images of bronze.
— Aesthetics, The Historical Development of Epic Poetry › The Romantic Epic (tr. Knox)

Head: Chivalric Epic
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › γ. The System of the Individual Arts › c. Romantic Arts › iii. Poetry › 3. Different Genres › a. Epic Poetry › iii. Historical Development of Epic › xxx. Romantic Epic › b. Chivalric Epic
Gloss: The epic and romance of knights, their honour, love and adventure.
Hegelian gloss: The chivalric epic, whose matter is the knight's honour, love and loyalty, and its adventures, down to Ariosto's comic play with them.
Nouns: chivalric epic; knight-errantry, romance of adventure, the quest. El Cid, Orlando Furioso, the chivalric epic, the medieval epic, chanson de geste, the Song of Roland, the Arthurian romances, Parzival, Tristan, romance of chivalry, Ariosto, romaunt.
Verbs: quest, rove, adventure, crusade.
Adjective: chivalric, knightly, Arthurian, Carolingian, Ariostan.
Adverbs: chivalrously.
Phrases: knights and ladies; the matter of Britain.
Hegel definition: Chivalric epic concerns love, honour and, with religious aims, mystic knighthood: individual actions touching no national interest, by heroes free yet lacking the realism of the Greek ones, tending to ballad or romance-like adventure around great sagas, of Charlemagne, Arthur and Amadis. Later Ariosto brought chivalry into comic light, letting its fantasy merrily destroy itself.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· Poetry › Epic Poetry › The Historical Development of Epic Poetry › The Romantic Epic
Hegel citations:
The actions achieved here, and the events, do not affect any national interests; on the contrary, they are the actions of individuals with the individual himself as such as their substance
— Aesthetics, The Historical Development of Epic Poetry › The Romantic Epic (tr. Knox)
Here therefore I will only draw attention to the brilliant adroitness, the attraction and wit, the charm and racy naivete with which Ariosto (whose poem still moves within the poetic aims of the Middle Ages) in a purely hidden way makes the fantastic merrily destroy itself within by incredible buffooneries.
— Aesthetics, The Historical Development of Epic Poetry › The Romantic Epic (tr. Knox)

Head: The Novel
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › γ. The System of the Individual Arts › c. Romantic Arts › iii. Poetry › 3. Different Genres › a. Epic Poetry › iii. Historical Development of Epic › xxx. Romantic Epic › c. The Novel
Gloss: The modern middle-class epic in prose.
Hegelian gloss: The novel, the modern bourgeois epic, whose usual conflict is between the poetry of the heart and the prose of circumstances that opposes it.
Nouns: the novel; the modern bourgeois epic, prose fiction, the novelist, novel of education, Bildungsroman, picaresque novel, Don Quixote, Wilhelm Meister.
Verbs: novelize.
Adjective: novelistic.
Foreign: German: Roman, Bildungsroman.
Phrases: die moderne bürgerliche Epopöe [Ger.] [Hegel, Aesthetics].
Hegel definition: The novel, which Knox calls romance, is the modern popular epic: it has again the wealth of interests, characters and events and the broad background of a world, but lacks the primitive poetic situation of epic proper, presupposing a prosaically ordered world in which it wins back poetry's right. Its typical collision is between the poetry of the heart and the opposing prose of circumstances.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· Poetry › Epic Poetry › Particular Characteristics of Epic Proper › The Epic as a Fully Unified Whole
Hegel citations:
But it is quite different with romance, the modern popular epic.
— Aesthetics, Particular Characteristics of Epic Proper › The Epic as a Fully Unified Whole (tr. Knox)
Consequently one of the commonest, and, for romance, most appropriate, collisions is the conflict between the poetry of the heart and the opposing prose of circumstances and the accidents of external situations
— Aesthetics, Particular Characteristics of Epic Proper › The Epic as a Fully Unified Whole (tr. Knox)

Head: Lyric Poetry
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › γ. The System of the Individual Arts › c. Romantic Arts › iii. Poetry › 3. Different Genres › b. Lyric Poetry
Gloss: Poetry expressing the inner life of the poet.
Hegelian gloss: Lyric, which expresses the poet's inwardness, the self's own feeling and reflection.
Nouns: lyric poetry; lyric, lyrics, song, ode, ballad, sonnet, elegy, hymn, the lyrical I, melic poetry. poem, epode†, idyl, eclogue, pastoral, bucolic, dithyramb, anacreontic†, roundelay, madrigal. anthology, lay, love song, drinking song, war song, lullaby. song &c H1067, canzonet†, ditty. lyricism, song-poetry, melos, the poetry of feeling, the poetry of subjectivity, verse, canzone, lied, chanson, threnody, psalm, lyricist. songcraft.
Verbs: sing, express, effuse. pour forth, lyricize, carol, chant, voice, utter.
Adjective: lyric, lyrical, songlike, melic, effusive. poetic, poetical, tuneful, dithyrambic, elegiac. subjective, inward, heartfelt, emotional, odic, hymnic.
Adverbs: lyrically. in song, tunefully, from the heart, subjectively.
Foreign: French: rondeau; Arabic: ghazal, qaṣīda; Chinese: ci [lyric song]; Japanese: tanka, haiku.
Phrases: the spontaneous overflow of powerful feelings [Wordsworth]; the poet's own heart.
Hegel definition: Lyric poetry gives not the external thing but the poet's inner vision and feeling of it, the subjective side of creation predominating. Spirit turns from the objectivity of the matter into its own consciousness to display its presence in the heart's experience and imagination, in genuine feelings of universal validity, liberating the spirit not from feeling but in it.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· Poetry › Lyric Poetry
Hegel citations:
Out of the objectivity of the subject-matter the spirit descends into itself, looks into its own consciousness, and satisfies the need to display, not the external reality of the matter, but its presence and actuality in the spirit’s own subjective disposition, in the experience of the heart and the reflections of imagination, and at the same time to display the contents and activity of the inner life itself.
— Aesthetics, Poetry › Lyric Poetry (tr. Knox)
Indeed it has on the contrary a higher vocation: its task, namely, is to liberate the spirit not from but in feeling.
— Aesthetics, Poetry › Lyric Poetry (tr. Knox)

Head: General Character of Lyric
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › γ. The System of the Individual Arts › c. Romantic Arts › iii. Poetry › 3. Different Genres › b. Lyric Poetry › i. General Character of Lyric
Gloss: The general nature of lyric.
Hegelian gloss: Lyric as the self-expression of the subject, which gives voice to the self in a particular situation.
Nouns: general character of lyric; subjectivity, self-expression, the inner world, mood, the moment of feeling. inwardness, interiority, feeling, sentiment, emotion, the heart, self-utterance, reflection, the individual voice, particularity, the occasion. effusion.
Verbs: express, confess. feel, utter, voice, pour out, reveal, give vent.
Adjective: subjective, expressive, personal. inward, inner, emotional, heartfelt, confessional, intimate, individual.
Adverbs: subjectively. inwardly, personally, from within, from the heart.
Phrases: the heart's own speech; I sing myself; the heart laid bare.
Hegel definition: The general character of lyric answers the need for self-expression and the mind's apprehension of itself in it, opposite to the epic need to hear an objective whole. Its content is the individual with the details of situation and concern, and the way judgement, joy, admiration and grief come to self-consciousness; it may touch all national life, though one poem only one side.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· Poetry › Lyric Poetry › General Character of Lyric
Hegel citations:
What leads to epic poetry is the need to listen to something which is unfolded as an independent and self-complete totality, objective over against the subject; whereas in lyric what is satisfied is the opposite need, namely that for self-expression and for the apprehension of the mind in its own self-expression.
— Aesthetics, Lyric Poetry › General Character of Lyric (tr. Knox)
The content of a lyric work of art cannot be the development of an objective action extending through all its connections into the whole wealth of a world; on the contrary, it must be the individual person and therefore with all the details of his situation and concerns, as well as the way in which his mind with its subjective judgement, its joy, admiration, grief, and, in short, its feeling comes to consciousness of itself in and through such experiences.
— Aesthetics, Lyric Poetry › General Character of Lyric (tr. Knox)

Head: Particular Aspects of Lyric
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › γ. The System of the Individual Arts › c. Romantic Arts › iii. Poetry › 3. Different Genres › b. Lyric Poetry › ii. Particular Aspects of Lyric
Gloss: The particular features of lyric.
Hegelian gloss: The particular aspects of the lyric: the poet, the poem, its kinds.
Nouns: particular aspects of lyric; poet, poem, kinds of lyric. specific features, special sides, particulars, details, the poet's subjectivity, the lyric work, lyric species, mood, occasion. lyricality.
Verbs: specify. particularize, detail, distinguish, enumerate, differentiate.
Adjective: particular. special, specific, several, respective, distinct.
Adverbs: in particular. specifically, in detail, severally.
Phrases: singer, song, and kind; poet, poem, kind; the lyric moment.
Hegel definition: The particular aspects of lyric are the personality of the poet and the ramification of kinds, which matter here as they did not in the study of primitive epic, because lyric's principle is the individualizing and particularizing of subject matter and forms. They are treated as the lyric poet, the lyric work as product of subjective imagination, and the kinds.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· Poetry › Lyric Poetry › Particular Aspects of Lyric Poetry
Hegel citations:
On the contrary the most important topics for discussion here are the personality of the poet and the ramification of the different kinds into which lyric can expand, since it has as its principle the individualizing and particularizing of its subject-matter and its forms.
— Aesthetics, Lyric Poetry › Particular Aspects of Lyric Poetry (tr. Knox)
(a) We have to direct our attention to the lyric poet; (b) then we must consider the lyric work of art as a product of his subjective imagination; (c) and finally mention the kinds of lyrical portrayal which emanate from its essential nature.
— Aesthetics, Lyric Poetry › Particular Aspects of Lyric Poetry (tr. Knox)

Head: The Lyric Poet
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › γ. The System of the Individual Arts › c. Romantic Arts › iii. Poetry › 3. Different Genres › b. Lyric Poetry › ii. Particular Aspects of Lyric › x. The Lyric Poet
Gloss: The poet as the speaking subject of the lyric.
Hegelian gloss: The lyric poet, the subject in whom the world is concentrated.
Nouns: the lyric poet; lyricist, songster, bard, singer, troubadour, minnesinger, Sappho, Pindar, Hafez, Li Bai, Petrarch, Goethe. poet, lyrist†, scald, skald†, minstrel, versifier. vocalist, melodist, songstress, chaunter†, chauntress†, cantatrice†. rhapsode, songwriter, sonneteer, odist, hymnist, elegist, the singing subject, the lyrical I, Anacreon, Horace, Klopstock, Schiller, Walther von der Vogelweide.
Verbs: sing, compose, express. pour forth, give voice, utter, voice, confess, lament, rhapsodize.
Adjective: lyrical, songful, Sapphic, Pindaric. poetic, poetical, lyric. bardic, Anacreontic, Horatian, Petrarchan, self-expressive.
Adverbs: in song. lyrically, from the heart, in his own voice.
Foreign: German: meistersinger; French: trouvere, poète maudit.
Phrases: Sappho, the tenth Muse; the world in one heart; the sweet singer.
Hegel definition: The lyric poet, a poetic concrete person, is the centre and proper content of lyric, the inner link joining universal reflections and particular feelings into living individuality. The poet does not act or enter dramatic conflict but lends words to inner life so as to awaken the same spirit in hearers, and even a commissioned bard such as Pindar chiefly portrays himself.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· Poetry › Lyric Poetry › Particular Aspects of Lyric Poetry › The Lyric Poet
Hegel citations:
Thus as the centre and proper content of lyric poetry there must be placed the poetic concrete person, the poet, but he must not proceed to actual deeds and actions or become involved in the movement of dramatic conflicts.
— Aesthetics, Particular Aspects of Lyric Poetry › The Lyric Poet (tr. Knox)
Consequently in his poems he is not so much concerned to honour the hero whose fame he spreads in this way as to make himself, the poet, heard.
— Aesthetics, Particular Aspects of Lyric Poetry › The Lyric Poet (tr. Knox)

Head: Lyric Work of Art
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › γ. The System of the Individual Arts › c. Romantic Arts › iii. Poetry › 3. Different Genres › b. Lyric Poetry › ii. Particular Aspects of Lyric › xx. Lyric Work of Art
Gloss: The lyric poem as a work of art.
Hegelian gloss: The lyric poem as a unity of feeling, its occasion and its musical form.
Nouns: lyric work of art; poem, song, lyric piece, the lyric's unity of mood. lyric poem, the lyric, verse, piece, stanzaic form, unity of feeling, concentration, brevity, inner unity. stanza.
Verbs: compose. versify, shape, round off, concentrate, sing.
Adjective: lyrical, unified. lyric, brief, concentrated, compact, rounded, stanzaic.
Adverbs: lyrically. in a single mood, briefly, in stanzas.
Phrases: a short poem of feeling; the occasion of the poem.
Hegel definition: The lyric work of art allows boundless variety of turns and tones, so that only its difference from epic can be considered, in unity, development and outer metre and delivery. Its centre of unity is the poet's inner life, which, to hold the poem together, must enter a definite mood or situation and identify with it; most lyrical is a mood of heart gathered on a concrete situation.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· Poetry › Lyric Poetry › Particular Aspects of Lyric Poetry › The Lyrical Work of Art
Hegel citations:
The central point of unity in a lyric must therefore be regarded as the inner life of the poet.
— Aesthetics, Particular Aspects of Lyric Poetry › The Lyrical Work of Art (tr. Knox)
What is most completely lyrical from this point of view is a mood-of-the heart-concentrated on a concrete situation, because the sensitive heart is what is inmost in the subjective life, and most that life’s own
— Aesthetics, Particular Aspects of Lyric Poetry › The Lyrical Work of Art (tr. Knox)

Head: Kinds of Lyric Proper
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › γ. The System of the Individual Arts › c. Romantic Arts › iii. Poetry › 3. Different Genres › b. Lyric Poetry › ii. Particular Aspects of Lyric › xxx. Kinds of Lyric Proper
Gloss: The kinds of lyric, such as hymn, ode and song.
Hegelian gloss: The kinds of lyric: hymn and dithyramb, the ode, the song, each a different relation of self and object.
Nouns: kinds of lyric proper. lyric.
Verbs: serenade, celebrate.
Adverbs: in song. by kind, severally.
Foreign: German: Lied; French: rondeau; Arabic: ghazal; Japanese: haiku; Korean: sijo [Korean three-line verse], hyangga [Silla songs]; Italian: stornello [Tuscan folk song]; Spanish: cante jondo, quejío [the flamenco lament], saeta.
Phrases: hymn, ode, and song.
Hegel definition: The kinds of lyric proper differ by the attitude the poet consciously takes to the subject. In one the poet's individuality vanishes into contemplation of God or the gods, as in hymns, dithyrambs and psalms; in odes the poet's own subjective personality is foremost; and in song the endless variety of lyric moods and reflections is spread out.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· Poetry › Lyric Poetry › Particular Aspects of Lyric Poetry › The Kinds of Lyric Proper
Hegel citations:
The difference between them has its basis in the attitude which the poet consciously adopts to his subject-matter.
— Aesthetics, Particular Aspects of Lyric Poetry › The Kinds of Lyric Proper (tr. Knox)
Lastly, the whole endless variety of lyric moods and reflections is spread out at the stage of the song.
— Aesthetics, Particular Aspects of Lyric Poetry › The Kinds of Lyric Proper (tr. Knox)

Head: Religious Lyric
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › γ. The System of the Individual Arts › c. Romantic Arts › iii. Poetry › 3. Different Genres › b. Lyric Poetry › ii. Particular Aspects of Lyric › xxx. Kinds of Lyric Proper › a. Religious Lyric
Gloss: The lyric that lifts the soul to God.
Hegelian gloss: The religious lyric, in which the self raises itself to the divine and loses itself in it.
Nouns: religious lyric; sacred poetry, devotional verse, religious poetry.
Hegel definition: Religious lyric is the aspect in which the poet rises above the private character of personal ideas and feelings and sinks into universal contemplation of God or the gods, whose greatness and power pervade the whole inner life and make individuality disappear. Hymns, dithyrambs, paeans and psalms belong to it, developed differently by different peoples.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· Poetry › Lyric Poetry › Particular Aspects of Lyric Poetry › The Kinds of Lyric Proper
Hegel citations:
In one aspect of lyric, the poet transcends the particular and private character of his ideas and feelings and immerses himself in the universal contemplation of God or the gods whose greatness and power pervades the entire inner life and makes the individuality of the poet disappear.
— Aesthetics, Particular Aspects of Lyric Poetry › The Kinds of Lyric Proper (tr. Knox)
Hymns, dithyrambs, paeans, psalms belong to this class which again is developed in different ways by different peoples.
— Aesthetics, Particular Aspects of Lyric Poetry › The Kinds of Lyric Proper (tr. Knox)

Head: Hymn
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › γ. The System of the Individual Arts › c. Romantic Arts › iii. Poetry › 3. Different Genres › b. Lyric Poetry › ii. Particular Aspects of Lyric › xxx. Kinds of Lyric Proper › a. Religious Lyric › i. Hymn
Gloss: The song of praise to God or the gods.
Hegelian gloss: The hymn, in which the self, raised to the divine, sings its praise with self-forgetting objectivity.
Nouns: hymn; hymnody, song of praise, the Homeric hymns. hymn, paean, anthem, canticle.
Verbs: hymn, praise.
Adjective: hymnic, hymnal, paeanic.
Hegel definition: The hymn is the religious lyric in which the poet concentrates the sphere of the divine into one objective picture and, having completed it in inner contemplation, sets it before others to praise the power and glory of the god celebrated. The Homeric Hymns give situations and stories of the god, mostly mythological and illustrated solidly as in epic.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· Poetry › Lyric Poetry › Particular Aspects of Lyric Poetry › The Kinds of Lyric Proper
Hegel citations:
The poet who rises above the restrictedness of his own inner and outer circumstances and situations and the ideas connected with these, and takes as his subject-matter what appears to him and his nation to be absolute and divine, may (i) concentrate the sphere of the divine into one objective picture, and then this picture, sketched and completed for his inner contemplation, he may place before others to the praise of the power and glory of the god so celebrated.
— Aesthetics, Particular Aspects of Lyric Poetry › The Kinds of Lyric Proper (tr. Knox)
These stories are principally mythological, not treated merely symbolically at all, but given solid illustration, as in epic.
— Aesthetics, Particular Aspects of Lyric Poetry › The Kinds of Lyric Proper (tr. Knox)

Head: Dithyramb and Psalm
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › γ. The System of the Individual Arts › c. Romantic Arts › iii. Poetry › 3. Different Genres › b. Lyric Poetry › ii. Particular Aspects of Lyric › xxx. Kinds of Lyric Proper › a. Religious Lyric › ii. Dithyramb and Psalm
Gloss: The ecstatic song of Dionysus, and the Hebrew psalm.
Hegelian gloss: The dithyramb and the psalm, in which the soul is carried away beyond itself toward the god in ecstasy or longing.
Nouns: dithyramb and psalm.
Hegel definition: Dithyramb and psalm are the more lyrical form of religious elevation, a soaring of the soul in worship in which the poet, shaken by the might of the object, cannot shape any single objective picture and gets no further than exultation. The Old Testament Psalms are the impressive instance of this flight of praise toward the one God.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· Poetry › Lyric Poetry › Particular Aspects of Lyric Poetry › The Kinds of Lyric Proper
Hegel citations:
A converse (ii) and more lyrical type is a dithyrambic soaring, a subjective elevation in worship.
— Aesthetics, Particular Aspects of Lyric Poetry › The Kinds of Lyric Proper (tr. Knox)
More impressive, on the other hand, we find in many of the sublime Psalms in the Old Testament this soaring flight of praise, this jubilation of the soul as it lifts its eye to heaven and cries out to the one God in whom the Psalmist finds the end and aim of his consciousness, the proper source of all might and truth, the proper object of all glory and praise.
— Aesthetics, Particular Aspects of Lyric Poetry › The Kinds of Lyric Proper (tr. Knox)

Head: Dithyramb
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › γ. The System of the Individual Arts › c. Romantic Arts › iii. Poetry › 3. Different Genres › b. Lyric Poetry › ii. Particular Aspects of Lyric › xxx. Kinds of Lyric Proper › a. Religious Lyric › ii. Dithyramb and Psalm › 1. Dithyramb
Gloss: The ecstatic choral song of Dionysus, in which the singer is carried out of himself.
Hegelian gloss: Die Dithyrambe: subjective elevation in worship, the poet shaken by the power of the god and borne beyond himself in rapture.
Nouns: dithyramb. Bacchic song. Dionysian hymn, Bacchic frenzy, ecstatic song.
Verbs: rhapsodize.
Adjective: dithyrambic.
Phrases: the dithyramb.
Hegel definition: The dithyramb is subjective elevation in worship: the poet, enraptured and stunned in the inmost heart, in a mood wholly without definition, is absorbed directly into the absolute and sings in jubilation the infinity and its splendid manifestations. The Greeks soon interrupted such outbursts with mythical narratives, which grew into drama with the chorus.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· Poetry › Lyric Poetry › Particular Aspects of Lyric Poetry › The Kinds of Lyric Proper
Hegel citations:
The poet, enraptured by the power of his object, shaken as it were and stunned in his inmost heart, and in a mood wholly without definition, is incapable of producing any single objective picture or shape and cannot get beyond an exultation of soul.
— Aesthetics, Particular Aspects of Lyric Poetry › The Kinds of Lyric Proper (tr. Knox)
These descriptions, intercalated between the lyrical outbursts, then gradually became the chief thing, and, by presenting a living and complete action explicitly in the form of an action, developed into drama
— Aesthetics, Particular Aspects of Lyric Poetry › The Kinds of Lyric Proper (tr. Knox)

Head: Psalm
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › γ. The System of the Individual Arts › c. Romantic Arts › iii. Poetry › 3. Different Genres › b. Lyric Poetry › ii. Particular Aspects of Lyric › xxx. Kinds of Lyric Proper › a. Religious Lyric › ii. Dithyramb and Psalm › 2. Psalm
Gloss: The Hebrew song of praise and lament before the one God.
Hegelian gloss: Der Psalm: the Hebrew lyric that exalts the Lord's power and glory and cries out of the depths, the soul raised in longing toward God.
Nouns: psalm. the Psalms, psalter, psalmist, psalmody, chant, antiphon†. the Psalms of David, songs of praise, the penitential psalms.
Verbs: chant, praise, lament.
Adjective: psalmic, psalmodic.
Phrases: out of the depths have I cried unto thee, O Lord [Bible]; the Lord is my shepherd [Bible].
Hegel definition: The psalm, in the sublime Old Testament Psalms, is the soul's jubilant flight of praise as it lifts its eyes to heaven and cries to the one God in whom it finds its end and the source of all might and truth. Its ecstasy swells into a vague enthusiasm that cannot put into words what it feels, juxtaposing images in disorder with irregular rhythm.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· Poetry › Lyric Poetry › Particular Aspects of Lyric Poetry › The Kinds of Lyric Proper
Hegel citations:
Such an elevation and lyrical sublimity contains ecstasy and therefore there is no such absorption in a concrete subject-matter as enables the imagination, satisfied and at peace, to let things be
— Aesthetics, Particular Aspects of Lyric Poetry › The Kinds of Lyric Proper (tr. Knox)
Instead of a peaceful picture, imagination seizes on external phenomena and juxtaposes them fragmentarily and in disorder, and since in its inner life it does not achieve any firm articulation of its particular ideas, it avails itself in its external expression of only an arbitrary and irregular rhythm.
— Aesthetics, Particular Aspects of Lyric Poetry › The Kinds of Lyric Proper (tr. Knox)

Head: Prophetic Lyric
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › γ. The System of the Individual Arts › c. Romantic Arts › iii. Poetry › 3. Different Genres › b. Lyric Poetry › ii. Particular Aspects of Lyric › xxx. Kinds of Lyric Proper › a. Religious Lyric › iii. Prophetic Lyric
Gloss: The lyric of the prophets, which speaks to the people in God's name.
Hegelian gloss: The prophetic lyric of the Hebrew prophets, which laments and warns the people from its relation to God.
Nouns: prophetic lyric; the prophets, prophecy, oracle, the Hebrew prophets, vatic poetry, vates, jeremiad.
Adjective: prophetic, vatic.
Hegel definition: Prophetic lyric belongs to the Hebrew prophets, who, opposed to the multitude, usually strike a fundamental tone of grief and lament over their people's condition, sensing its estrangement and falling away from God, and are fired by sublime zeal and political wrath, which carries them toward a lyric of exhortation.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· Poetry › Lyric Poetry › Particular Aspects of Lyric Poetry › The Kinds of Lyric Proper
Hegel citations:
The Prophets, in their opposition to the multitude, usually have a fundamental tone of grief and lamentation for the situation of their people; they have a sense of their people’s alienation and falling away from God, and at the same time they are animated by a sublime glow of zeal and political wrath. All this then leads them further in the direction of hortatory lyric.
— Aesthetics, Particular Aspects of Lyric Poetry › The Kinds of Lyric Proper (tr. Knox)

Head: Ode
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › γ. The System of the Individual Arts › c. Romantic Arts › iii. Poetry › 3. Different Genres › b. Lyric Poetry › ii. Particular Aspects of Lyric › xxx. Kinds of Lyric Proper › b. Ode
Gloss: The ode, in which the poet's self rises to a great subject.
Hegelian gloss: The ode, in which the poet's inwardness takes up a lofty object and both struggle for mastery.
Nouns: ode; the lofty ode. ode, epode†.
Adjective: odic.
Hegel definition: Odes are lyric in which the poet's own subjective personality is most important. The poet may choose a weighty topic, gods, heroes, love or friendship, and seem wholly mastered by it, yet masters it in turn, interrupting its course with personal reflections, or may confer dignity on trifles; the captivating topic and free subject stand in tension.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· Poetry › Lyric Poetry › Particular Aspects of Lyric Poetry › The Kinds of Lyric Proper
Hegel citations:
There is a second aspect of lyric, namely those kinds of lyric poetry that may be called by the general name of ‘Odes’ in the newer sense of that word. Here, in contrast to the preceding stage, it is at once the independently emphasized subjective personality of the poet which is the most important thing of all
— Aesthetics, Particular Aspects of Lyric Poetry › The Kinds of Lyric Proper (tr. Knox)
The result is that mastery belongs not to the topic but to his subjective enthusiasm, engrossed by the topic.
— Aesthetics, Particular Aspects of Lyric Poetry › The Kinds of Lyric Proper (tr. Knox)

Head: Odes of Mastery
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › γ. The System of the Individual Arts › c. Romantic Arts › iii. Poetry › 3. Different Genres › b. Lyric Poetry › ii. Particular Aspects of Lyric › xxx. Kinds of Lyric Proper › b. Ode › i. Odes of Mastery
Gloss: The Pindaric ode, in which the poet masters his great subject.
Hegelian gloss: The Pindaric ode, where the poet's inspiration masters the subject, celebrating victors while ranging freely through myth.
Nouns: odes of mastery; Pindaric ode, Pindar, victory ode, epinician ode, triad, strophe and antistrophe. epinicion.
Adjective: Pindaric.
Hegel definition: Odes of mastery, such as many of Pindar's, arise from the opposition between the topic's captivating might and the poet's freedom flashing out against it. This drives the swing and boldness of language and images, apparent lawlessness, digressions and sudden transitions, while the poet's genius resolves the discord into a unified whole that raises the poet above the subject.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· Poetry › Lyric Poetry › Particular Aspects of Lyric Poetry › The Kinds of Lyric Proper
Hegel citations:
It is mainly the pressure of this opposition which necessitates the swing and boldness of language and images, the apparent absence of rule in the structure and course of the poem, the digressions, gaps, sudden transitions, etc.
— Aesthetics, Particular Aspects of Lyric Poetry › The Kinds of Lyric Proper (tr. Knox)
This sort of lyrical enthusiasm is the origin of many of Pindar’s Odes, but all the same their victorious inner magnificence is disclosed by their rhythm which moves variously and yet is given a measure fixed by rule.
— Aesthetics, Particular Aspects of Lyric Poetry › The Kinds of Lyric Proper (tr. Knox)

Head: Expressionist Odes
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › γ. The System of the Individual Arts › c. Romantic Arts › iii. Poetry › 3. Different Genres › b. Lyric Poetry › ii. Particular Aspects of Lyric › xxx. Kinds of Lyric Proper › b. Ode › ii. Expressionist Odes
Gloss: The Horatian ode, which gives the poet's own reflective mood.
Hegelian gloss: The Horatian ode, where the subject is mastered less than the poet's own mood and reflection is expressed.
Nouns: expressionist odes; Horatian ode, Horace, the ode of reflection, carmen, Klopstock's odes.
Adjective: Horatian.
Hegel definition: In odes of this second kind the subject need not be weighty: the poet becomes so important to himself that, taking even slight things, trifling occasions and accidents, as matter, he confers on them dignity and nobility or higher interest, with no struggle against the topic's importance. Much in Horace's odes is of this sort, as in Klopstock.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· Poetry › Lyric Poetry › Particular Aspects of Lyric Poetry › The Kinds of Lyric Proper
Hegel citations:
But, secondly, the subject-matter need not be really important or of intrinsic value; on the contrary, the poet becomes of such importance to himself in his individuality that now, because he takes even rather insignificant things as his subject, he confers on them dignity and nobility, or, at the very least, a higher interest.
— Aesthetics, Particular Aspects of Lyric Poetry › The Kinds of Lyric Proper (tr. Knox)
In this case the poet has no struggle with the importance of his topic; on the contrary he elevates what is inherently unimportant in external occasions, trifling accidents, etc., to the height on which he senses and visualizes himself.
— Aesthetics, Particular Aspects of Lyric Poetry › The Kinds of Lyric Proper (tr. Knox)

Head: Song
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › γ. The System of the Individual Arts › c. Romantic Arts › iii. Poetry › 3. Different Genres › b. Lyric Poetry › ii. Particular Aspects of Lyric › xxx. Kinds of Lyric Proper › c. Song
Gloss: The song, the lyric that is sung.
Hegelian gloss: The song, in which the self expresses its mood most simply and is apt to be sung.
Nouns: song; lied, lyric song. song, song &c H1067, lay, ditty, canzone, chanson.
Verbs: sing.
Adjective: songlike.
Hegel definition: Song spreads out the endless variety of lyric moods and reflections, where national differences and the traits of individual poets show most fully. Simple in material, movement, metre and language, it begins in the heart, holds tranquilly to one situation or feeling and rounds it into a whole, and every people is most at home in its songs.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· Poetry › Lyric Poetry › Particular Aspects of Lyric Poetry › The Kinds of Lyric Proper
Hegel citations:
Consequently it is in song that particular national differences and the special characteristics of individual poets are most completely in evidence.
— Aesthetics, Particular Aspects of Lyric Poetry › The Kinds of Lyric Proper (tr. Knox)
Therefore every people is most at home and comfortable in its songs.
— Aesthetics, Particular Aspects of Lyric Poetry › The Kinds of Lyric Proper (tr. Knox)

Head: Song Proper
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › γ. The System of the Individual Arts › c. Romantic Arts › iii. Poetry › 3. Different Genres › b. Lyric Poetry › ii. Particular Aspects of Lyric › xxx. Kinds of Lyric Proper › c. Song › i. Song Proper
Gloss: The simple song proper, of the people, of company and of the church.
Hegelian gloss: The song proper, in its simplest forms, rooted in a people, a company or a congregation.
Nouns: song proper; art song, simple song.
Hegel definition: The song proper, meant for singing to oneself or in company, needs little substance or lofty grandeur, which would hinder direct self-expression; whatever joy or grief is deeply felt finds its place there. Fleeting and ever renewed, it must still have universal validity, arousing the same feeling so that it passes from mouth to mouth.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· Poetry › Lyric Poetry › Particular Aspects of Lyric Poetry › The Kinds of Lyric Proper
Hegel citations:
First, the song proper, meant for warbling in private or for singing in company.
— Aesthetics, Particular Aspects of Lyric Poetry › The Kinds of Lyric Proper (tr. Knox)
But all the same every song must not so much be a presentation of the personality of the poet himself as have a universal validity which makes it impress and please everyone and arouse the same feeling so that now it goes from mouth to mouth.
— Aesthetics, Particular Aspects of Lyric Poetry › The Kinds of Lyric Proper (tr. Knox)

Head: Folk Song
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › γ. The System of the Individual Arts › c. Romantic Arts › iii. Poetry › 3. Different Genres › b. Lyric Poetry › ii. Particular Aspects of Lyric › xxx. Kinds of Lyric Proper › c. Song › i. Song Proper › 1. Folk Song
Gloss: The songs of a people.
Hegelian gloss: The folk song, in which a people's feeling finds its voice anonymously.
Nouns: folk song; Volkslied, folk ballad, the song of the people, work song. folk song, ballad, lullaby, roundelay.
Adjective: balladic.
Hegel definition: Folk songs, because of their immediacy, generally remain at the level of song and usually demand a tune. Their subject is national deeds and events in which a nation feels its very life and which live in its memory, or else the feelings and situations of the classes, sympathy with nature and intimate human relations, in every note of joy and grief.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· Poetry › Lyric Poetry › Particular Aspects of Lyric Poetry › The Kinds of Lyric Proper
Hegel citations:
Their subject-matter consists of national deeds and events in which the nation has a sense of its very own life and which are alive in its memory.
— Aesthetics, Particular Aspects of Lyric Poetry › The Kinds of Lyric Proper (tr. Knox)
Alternatively they directly express the feelings and situations of the different classes, sympathy with nature, and the most intimate human relationships, and they strike most various notes of joy or of grief and melancholy.
— Aesthetics, Particular Aspects of Lyric Poetry › The Kinds of Lyric Proper (tr. Knox)

Head: Convivial Song
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › γ. The System of the Individual Arts › c. Romantic Arts › iii. Poetry › 3. Different Genres › b. Lyric Poetry › ii. Particular Aspects of Lyric › xxx. Kinds of Lyric Proper › c. Song › i. Song Proper › 2. Convivial Song
Gloss: Songs for company: drinking songs, table songs, rounds.
Hegelian gloss: The convivial song, which expresses the shared pleasure of company.
Nouns: convivial song; drinking song, table song, glee, catch, round, skolion, carousal song.
Hegel definition: Convivial songs belong to an enriched culture that delights in cheerful society, full of wit, graceful turns and gallantry, or else turns sentimentally to nature and narrow situations. Mere description soon becomes trivial; the poet must rise above immediate desire through free contemplation, as in many songs of Anacreon, Hafiz and Goethe's Divan.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· Poetry › Lyric Poetry › Particular Aspects of Lyric Poetry › The Kinds of Lyric Proper
Hegel citations:
In contrast to these there are, secondly, songs of a culture which has already been enriched in many ways and which delights in cheerful conviviality, so that the songs are full of the greatest variety of wit, graceful turns of phrase, little incidents, and other expressions of gallantry.
— Aesthetics, Particular Aspects of Lyric Poetry › The Kinds of Lyric Proper (tr. Knox)
This carefree freedom, this expansion of the heart and satisfaction of mind gives the loveliest charm of spiritual freedom and poetry to many of Anacreon’s songs, for example, as well as to the poems of Hafiz and Goethe’s West-östliche Divan.
— Aesthetics, Particular Aspects of Lyric Poetry › The Kinds of Lyric Proper (tr. Knox)

Head: Church Song
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › γ. The System of the Individual Arts › c. Romantic Arts › iii. Poetry › 3. Different Genres › b. Lyric Poetry › ii. Particular Aspects of Lyric › xxx. Kinds of Lyric Proper › c. Song › i. Song Proper › 3. Church Song
Gloss: The hymns of the congregation.
Hegelian gloss: The church song, the congregation's common voice before God.
Nouns: church song; chorale, church hymn, Lutheran chorale, hymn tune, Kirchenlied. carol, motet.
Hegel definition: Church song shows that a higher, universal content is not excluded from song: most Protestant hymns for the edification of the faithful express longing for God, prayer for mercy, repentance, hope, confidence and doubt. They arise as the concern of an individual heart but are expressed universally, so that everyone may or should share them.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· Poetry › Lyric Poetry › Particular Aspects of Lyric Poetry › The Kinds of Lyric Proper
Hegel citations:
They express the longing for God, a prayer for his mercy, the repentance, hope, confidence, doubt, faith, etc., of the Protestant heart
— Aesthetics, Particular Aspects of Lyric Poetry › The Kinds of Lyric Proper (tr. Knox)
[B]ut they are expressed in a universal way so that these feelings and situations may or should be at the same time the concern of more or less everyone.
— Aesthetics, Particular Aspects of Lyric Poetry › The Kinds of Lyric Proper (tr. Knox)

Head: Sonnet, Sestina, Elegy, Epistle
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › γ. The System of the Individual Arts › c. Romantic Arts › iii. Poetry › 3. Different Genres › b. Lyric Poetry › ii. Particular Aspects of Lyric › xxx. Kinds of Lyric Proper › c. Song › ii. Sonnet, Sestina, Elegy, Epistle
Gloss: The reflective song forms: sonnet, sestina, elegy, epistle.
Hegelian gloss: Forms in which reflection enters the song: the sonnet, sestina, elegy and verse epistle.
Nouns: sonnet, sestina, elegy, epistle, villanelle, epigram, epithalamium, madrigal, idyl, eclogue, pastoral, romance, occasional poem.
Adjective: epigrammatic.
Hegel definition: Sonnets, sestinas, elegies and epistles form a group that already rises above song: immediacy of feeling is raised to the communication of reflection and meditation that looks about in every direction and gathers particular insights under general categories. Knowledge and culture prevail, and although the individual still joins universal and particular, a wider view is taken.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· Poetry › Lyric Poetry › Particular Aspects of Lyric Poetry › The Kinds of Lyric Proper
Hegel citations:
These kinds are already rising beyond the previously considered sphere of song.
— Aesthetics, Particular Aspects of Lyric Poetry › The Kinds of Lyric Proper (tr. Knox)
The immediacy of feeling and expression is raised here to a communication of reflection and of a meditation that looks around in every direction and brings together under more general categories individual insights and emotional experiences: knowledge, scholarship, culture in general should prevail.
— Aesthetics, Particular Aspects of Lyric Poetry › The Kinds of Lyric Proper (tr. Knox)

Head: Sonnet
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › γ. The System of the Individual Arts › c. Romantic Arts › iii. Poetry › 3. Different Genres › b. Lyric Poetry › ii. Particular Aspects of Lyric › xxx. Kinds of Lyric Proper › c. Song › ii. Sonnet, Sestina, Elegy, Epistle › 1. Sonnet
Gloss: The fourteen-line poem, in which a feeling is turned over in reflection within a strict form.
Hegelian gloss: Das Sonett: a form in which reflection enters the song, the feeling worked out with art and turned toward a thought, as in Petrarch.
Nouns: sonnet. Petrarchan sonnet, Shakespearean sonnet, octave and sestet, quatorzain, sonnet sequence, Petrarch.
Verbs: sonnetize.
Foreign: Italian: sonetto.
Phrases: scorn not the sonnet [Wordsworth].
Hegel definition: The sonnet, of which the Italians gave brilliant examples, shows an exquisitely reflective sensibility that does not express its mood or perception directly and in deeply felt concentration, but takes many detours, looks widely into mythology, history, past and present, and yet returns into itself and remains coherent and self-restrained.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· Poetry › Lyric Poetry › Particular Aspects of Lyric Poetry › The Kinds of Lyric Proper
Hegel citations:
For example, the Italians especially have given us in their sonnets and sestinas a brilliant example of an exquisitely reflective sensibility which in any given situation does not directly express with deeply felt concentration the mere moods of longing, grief, desire, etc., or perceptions of external objects, but allows itself many detours, looks far afield and circumspectly into mythology, history, the past and the present, and yet always returns into itself and remains coherent and self-restricted.
— Aesthetics, Particular Aspects of Lyric Poetry › The Kinds of Lyric Proper (tr. Knox)

Head: Sestina
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › γ. The System of the Individual Arts › c. Romantic Arts › iii. Poetry › 3. Different Genres › b. Lyric Poetry › ii. Particular Aspects of Lyric › xxx. Kinds of Lyric Proper › c. Song › ii. Sonnet, Sestina, Elegy, Epistle › 2. Sestina
Gloss: The poem of six stanzas whose six end-words return in shifting order.
Hegelian gloss: Die Sestine: an artful form of the troubadours and Petrarch, in which the same end-words come back in changing order.
Nouns: sestina. end-word repetition, six stanzas, envoi, tornada, Arnaut Daniel.
Foreign: Italian: sestina.
Hegel definition: The sestina belongs with the sonnet to cultivated reflective poetry, brilliantly practised by the Italians. Since neither song's simplicity nor the ode's elevation is permitted in it, singability disappears, and in compensation the language itself, in its sounds and ingenious rhymes, becomes the notes of a spoken melody.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· Poetry › Lyric Poetry › Particular Aspects of Lyric Poetry › The Kinds of Lyric Proper
Hegel citations:
Since neither the simplicity of the song nor the elevation of the ode is permissible in this kind of cultured poetry, singability disappears but, in compensation, as the opposite of a musical accompaniment, the language itself in its sounds and ingenious rhymes becomes the notes of a spoken melody.
— Aesthetics, Particular Aspects of Lyric Poetry › The Kinds of Lyric Proper (tr. Knox)

Head: Elegy
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › i. Art › γ. The System of the Individual Arts › c. Romantic Arts › iii. Poetry › 3. Different Genres › b. Lyric Poetry › ii. Particular Aspects of Lyric › xxx. Kinds of Lyric Proper › c. Song › ii. Sonnet, Sestina, Elegy, Epistle › 3. Elegy
Gloss: The poem of lament and reflection, mourning a loss or a vanished time.
Hegelian gloss: Die Elegie: the reflective lyric of mourning and longing, in which feeling is mixed with general reflection.
Nouns: elegy. dirge, threnody. lament, elegiac couplet, mourning poem, Tibullus, Propertius.
Verbs: elegize, lament.
Adjective: elegiac.
Phrases: the curfew tolls the knell of parting day [Gray].
Hegel definition: Elegy is grouped with sonnet, sestina and epistle as a form in which reflection enters lyric and rises beyond song. Unlike sonnet and sestina, whose singability gives way to verbal music, it may keep a more epic character in its measure of syllables, in reflections and apophthegms, and in a descriptive portrayal of feelings.
Hegel texts:
Aesthetics
· Poetry › Lyric Poetry › Particular Aspects of Lyric Poetry › The Kinds of Lyric Proper
Hegel citations:
Elegy, on the other hand, may keep a more epic character in the measure of syllables, in reflections, apophthegms, and a descriptive portrayal of feelings.
— Aesthetics, Particular Aspects of Lyric Poetry › The Kinds of Lyric Proper (tr. Knox)
Within this comprehensive stage, a second group consisting of sonnets, sestinas, elegies, epistles, etc., may be included.
— Aesthetics, Particular Aspects of Lyric Poetry › The Kinds of Lyric Proper (tr. Knox)

Head: Epistle

Hegel definition: The laughable is any contrast between the substantial and its appearance, between an end and its means, in which the appearance cancels itself, so that realizing the end is the end's own undoing. Comedy makes this its principle. It makes the subject master of everything that counts as essential in what it wills, and lets its aims, being without substance, perish through its own willing and through outward chance alike. The subject does not perish with them: in their dissolution it enjoys itself, untroubled, as the infinite power over every finite content. In tragedy substantial ends destroy one another; in comedy what is null destroys itself, and the self survives it, cheerful, as the absolute. With this, art dissolves itself.

Every contrast between something substantive and its appearance, between an end and the means, may be laughable; this is a contradiction in which the appearance cancels itself and the realization of an end is at the same time the end’s own destruction.

A world in which man as subject or person has made himself completely master of everything that counts to him otherwise as the essence of what he wills and accomplishes, a world whose aims are therefore self-destructive because they are unsubstantial.
— Aesthetics, Dramatic Poetry: the principle of comedy (tr. Knox)
[The principle for comedy is when] the mastery of all relations and ends is given as much to the individual in his willing and action, as to external contingency.
— Aesthetics, Dramatic Poetry (tr. Knox)
As regards the mental side of these phenomena, we know with regard to laughter that it is generated by an immediately obvious contradiction, by something turning at once into its opposite, hence by something immediately self-annihilating, -assuming that we are not involved in this null content, do not regard it as our own; for if we felt ourselves injured by the destruction of this content, then we should weep. If, for example, someone proudly striding along falls over, this can give rise to laughter over it, because he experiences in his person the simple dialectic that what happens to him is the opposite of what he intended. Hence what provokes laughter in genuine comedies also essentially lies in the immediate veering round of a purpose in itself null into its opposite; whereas in tragedy it is substantial purposes which destroy themselves in their mutual opposition. With the dialectic befalling the object of comedy, the subjectivity of the spectator or listener attains to a serene and untroubled enjoyment of itself, since it is the absolute ideality, the infinite power over every limited content, consequently the pure dialectic by which, in fact, the comic object is annihilated. Herein lies the ground of the gaiety into which we are transported by the comic. But the physiological appearance of this gaiety, which particularly interests us here, is in harmony with this ground. For in laughter, the subjectivity attaining to untroubled enjoyment of itself, this pure self, this spiritual light, embodies itself as a glow spreading over the countenance, and at the same time the spiritual act by which the soul repels the ridiculous from itself finds a bodily expression in the forcibly interrupted expulsion of the breath.
— Encyclopedia, Philosophy of Spirit §401, Addition (tr. Wallace and Miller)

Hegel definition: In its act of differentiating, the idea releases the other to exist as free and independent, and this other is the world. Hegel definition: Human beings must come to realize within themselves the infinite antithesis of good and evil, and know that as natural beings they are evil.
