— Lectures on the History of Philosophy 1825–6, Greek Philosophy › The Seven Sages and the Milesians (tr. Brown)

Head: Anaximander
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › iii. Philosophy › β. History of Philosophy › b. Greek Philosophy › i. From Thales to Aristotle › 1. Presocratics › b. Anaximander
Gloss: The Milesian who made the boundless the source from which all things arise and to which they return.
Hegelian gloss: Anaximander, whose principle is the infinite (to apeiron), an indeterminate matter from which the opposites separate out.
Nouns: Anaximander. the boundless, the unlimited. Anaximander of Miletus, the indefinite, the separating out of opposites, the gnomon, the first map.
Foreign: Greek: to apeiron [the boundless].
Phrases: they pay penalty to one another for their injustice [Anaximander].
Hegel definition: For Anaximander, the pupil of Thales, the principle is the infinite, what is undefined or lacks determination, matter as such. Like the other early principles it takes a natural form. He is also reported to have had the infinite plurality of worlds come forth from the One, a procession that Hegel counts a sensuous representation without necessity or concept.
Hegel texts:
Lectures on the History of Philosophy
· Greek Philosophy › The Seven Sages and the Milesians
Hegel citations:
[W]hat is undefined or lacks determination, matter as such.
— Lectures on the History of Philosophy 1825–6, Greek Philosophy › The Seven Sages and the Milesians (tr. Brown)
This procession is indeed a succession; it is no concept but a sensuous representation
— Lectures on the History of Philosophy 1825–6, Greek Philosophy › The Seven Sages and the Milesians (tr. Brown)

Head: Anaximenes
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › iii. Philosophy › β. History of Philosophy › b. Greek Philosophy › i. From Thales to Aristotle › 1. Presocratics › c. Anaximenes
Gloss: The Milesian who held that all things come from air, thinned into fire or thickened into water and earth.
Hegelian gloss: Anaximenes, for whom the principle is air, the infinite in sensuous form and soul-like, from which things arise by rarefaction and condensation.
Nouns: Anaximenes. air. Anaximenes of Miletus, rarefaction and condensation, the breath of the world.
Foreign: Greek: pneuma, aēr.
Hegel definition: Anaximenes, a pupil of Anaximander, makes air the principle. With the early Ionians the principle always takes a natural form, water, air, and the like, so that the universal has a physical shape. Hegel holds the material element nonetheless to have philosophical significance, though each such principle is something particular and therefore defective.
Hegel texts:
Lectures on the History of Philosophy
· Greek Philosophy › The Seven Sages and the Milesians
Hegel citations:
Anaximenes, who was a pupil of Anaximander, makes air into the principle
— Lectures on the History of Philosophy 1825–6, Greek Philosophy › The Seven Sages and the Milesians (tr. Brown)
The principle always takes a natural form: air, water, and so forth. The universal principle has a physical shape.
— Lectures on the History of Philosophy 1825–6, Greek Philosophy › The Seven Sages and the Milesians (tr. Brown)

Head: Pythagoras
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › iii. Philosophy › β. History of Philosophy › b. Greek Philosophy › i. From Thales to Aristotle › 1. Presocratics › d. Pythagoras
Gloss: The philosopher of Samos and Croton for whom number is the essence of things, founder of a religious brotherhood.
Hegelian gloss: Pythagoras, who makes number the principle, midway between the sensuous and the concept, the first thought-determinations.
Nouns: Pythagoras. number, the Pythagoreans, Philolaus, the Italian school. Pythagoras of Samos, the tetractys, the harmony of the spheres, transmigration of souls, metempsychosis, the Pythagorean brotherhood, the limit and the unlimited, the monad and the dyad, Croton.
Adjective: Pythagorean.
Phrases: all things are numbers [the Pythagoreans].
Hegel definition: The main thesis of the Pythagorean philosophy is that number is the being of things, the organization of the universe being a system of numbers and numerical relationships. It is a bold step beyond sensible principles. The mathematical domain serves Pythagoras in education because it stands midway between the sensible and supersensible worlds, a preliminary exercise leading to what is in and for itself.
Hegel texts:
Lectures on the History of Philosophy
· Greek Philosophy › Pythagoras and the Pythagoreans
Hegel citations:
The main thesis of Pythagorean philosophy is simply that number is the being of things, and the organization of the universe is a system of numbers and numerical relationships—in short, that number as such is the being of all things.
— Lectures on the History of Philosophy 1825–6, Greek Philosophy › Pythagoras and the Pythagoreans (tr. Brown)
Pythagoras makes use of the mathematical domain, because it stands midway between the sensible and supersensible worlds, as a preliminary exercise for the purpose of leading up to what is in and for itself.
— Lectures on the History of Philosophy 1825–6, Greek Philosophy › Pythagoras and the Pythagoreans (tr. Brown)

Head: Xenophanes
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › iii. Philosophy › β. History of Philosophy › b. Greek Philosophy › i. From Thales to Aristotle › 1. Presocratics › e. Xenophanes
Gloss: The poet-philosopher of Colophon who mocked the gods of Homer and taught one unmoved god.
Hegelian gloss: Xenophanes, the beginner of the Eleatic school, who denies coming-to-be and makes the One the principle, against the gods made in man's image.
Nouns: Xenophanes. Xenophanes of Colophon, the critique of anthropomorphism, the one god, the rhapsode.
Phrases: if oxen and horses had hands, they would draw the gods like oxen and horses [Xenophanes].
Hegel definition: Xenophanes belongs with the Eleatics, who find no satisfaction in the sensible and mythical world and so arrive at the pure, abstract thought that being belongs only to the One. To him is ascribed the argument that nothing can come to be. In his fragments he speaks strongly against the Greek representation of the gods in human shape and with human vices.
Hegel texts:
Lectures on the History of Philosophy
· Greek Philosophy › The Eleatics
Hegel citations:
[B]y so doing arrive at this pure, abstract thought that being belongs only to the One.
— Lectures on the History of Philosophy 1825–6, Greek Philosophy › The Eleatics (tr. Brown)
Xenophanes expresses himself very strongly in opposition to the Greeks' representation of the gods.
— Lectures on the History of Philosophy 1825–6, Greek Philosophy › The Eleatics (tr. Brown)
He inveighs in similar fashion, as Plato did later on in opposition to Homer and Hesiod, against their ascription to the gods of all that they find shameful in the human race—murder, theft, and adultery.
— Lectures on the History of Philosophy 1825–6, Greek Philosophy › The Eleatics (tr. Brown)

Head: Parmenides
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › iii. Philosophy › β. History of Philosophy › b. Greek Philosophy › i. From Thales to Aristotle › 1. Presocratics › f. Parmenides
Gloss: The philosopher of Elea who taught that being is and non-being is not, so that change and plurality are illusion.
Hegelian gloss: Parmenides, with whom philosophy proper begins: pure being, the One, thought for which non-being simply is not.
Nouns: Parmenides. being, the One, the Eleatics, the Eleatic school, Melissus. Parmenides of Elea, the way of truth, the way of opinion, the well-rounded sphere.
Adjective: Eleatic, Parmenidean.
Foreign: Greek: to eon.
Phrases: being is, non-being is not [Parmenides]; to gar auto noein estin te kai einai [Gr.] [Parmenides].
Hegel definition: For Parmenides the One, grasped in its immediacy, is being. Only being is, and what is nothing is not at all; non-being cannot be known or expressed, and so change has no truth. With this, consciousness raised itself into the domain of free thought, and pure thought made itself its own object.
Hegel texts:
Lectures on the History of Philosophy
· Greek Philosophy › The Eleatics
Hegel citations:
Only being is, and what is nothing is not at all. With this, consciousness raised itself up into the domain of free thought, and pure thought made itself the object and maintained itself therein.
— Lectures on the History of Philosophy 1825–6, Greek Philosophy › The Eleatics (tr. Brown)
For one path, only being is, and non-being is not. This is the path of conviction, of truth.
— Lectures on the History of Philosophy 1825–6, Greek Philosophy › The Eleatics (tr. Brown)

Head: Zeno of Elea
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › iii. Philosophy › β. History of Philosophy › b. Greek Philosophy › i. From Thales to Aristotle › 1. Presocratics › g. Zeno of Elea
Gloss: The Eleatic who defended Parmenides by paradoxes showing that motion and plurality contradict themselves.
Hegelian gloss: Zeno, the originator of dialectic, who shows the contradiction in motion, Achilles and the tortoise, the arrow, by thinking it through.
Nouns: Zeno of Elea. Zeno's paradoxes, Achilles and the tortoise, the flying arrow, the dichotomy, the stadium, dialectic, reductio ad absurdum.
Verbs: reduce to absurdity.
Adjective: Zenonian.
Phrases: the flying arrow is at rest [Zeno].
Hegel definition: Zeno says the same as Parmenides but proceeds more dialectically: he confronts the many and shows that the manifold is not, that it annihilates itself, since whatever involves change is self-contradictory. It was primarily he who elaborated the dialectic, as in the arguments against motion, among them the Achilles, in which the faster body cannot overtake the slower.
Hegel texts:
Lectures on the History of Philosophy
· Greek Philosophy › The Eleatics
Hegel citations:
Plato says that Parmenides established being, whereas Zeno proceeded more dialectically yet said the same thing, except that he confronted the 'many' and showed that this 'many', this manifold, this limited domain, is not, that instead it annihilates itself.
— Lectures on the History of Philosophy 1825–6, Greek Philosophy › The Eleatics (tr. Brown)
Thus it was primarily Zeno who elaborated the dialectic.
— Lectures on the History of Philosophy 1825–6, Greek Philosophy › The Eleatics (tr. Brown)
Zeno says the contrary, that the second cannot overtake the first
— Lectures on the History of Philosophy 1825–6, Greek Philosophy › The Eleatics (tr. Brown)

Head: Heraclitus
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › iii. Philosophy › β. History of Philosophy › b. Greek Philosophy › i. From Thales to Aristotle › 1. Presocratics › h. Heraclitus
Gloss: The philosopher of Ephesus for whom all things flow and the unity of opposites is the law of the world.
Hegelian gloss: Heraclitus, the first concrete thinker: becoming as principle, the unity of being and nothing, the idea in its speculative form.
Nouns: Heraclitus. becoming, flux, the logos, fire. Heraclitus of Ephesus, the Obscure, the unity of opposites, strife the father of all, the ever-living fire.
Adjective: Heraclitean.
Phrases: panta rhei [Gr.] [all flows] [attrib. Heraclitus]; you cannot step twice into the same river; es ist kein Satz des Heraklit, den ich nicht in meine Logik aufgenommen [Ger.] [Hegel, Lectures on the History of Philosophy].
Hegel definition: Where the Eleatics said that only being is, Heraclitus says that everything flows and nothing is fixed: becoming is the principle. Being no more is than non-being, and becoming contains the identity of the two. By becoming is understood arising and perishing, neither of which is on its own account.
Hegel texts:
Lectures on the History of Philosophy
· Greek Philosophy › Heraclitus
Hegel citations:
The Eleatics said that only being is, that it is what is true. Heraclitus says that everything is becoming, that becoming is the principle.
— Lectures on the History of Philosophy 1825–6, Greek Philosophy › Heraclitus (tr. Brown)
[F]or becoming contains the identity of the two, of being and non-being.
— Lectures on the History of Philosophy 1825–6, Greek Philosophy › Heraclitus (tr. Brown)

Head: Empedocles
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › iii. Philosophy › β. History of Philosophy › b. Greek Philosophy › i. From Thales to Aristotle › 1. Presocratics › i. Empedocles
Gloss: The Sicilian who explained the world by four roots, earth, water, air and fire, joined by love and parted by strife.
Hegelian gloss: Empedocles, who joins the elements by love and parts them by strife, a synthesis still without the concept.
Nouns: Empedocles. the four elements, love and strife, the roots. Empedocles of Acragas, the four roots, Etna, mixture and separation.
Adjective: Empedoclean.
Hegel definition: Empedocles holds to four elements that neither come to be nor pass away, everything arising through their union and separation, and adds friendship and enmity as further principles. In these, Aristotle reports, good and evil emerge for the first time as principles. Purpose as the self-determining concept is what Aristotle misses in earlier philosophy and believes he can find in friendship.
Hegel texts:
Lectures on the History of Philosophy
· Greek Philosophy › Empedocles
Hegel citations:
[E]verything has come about only through the specific union and separation of these four.
— Lectures on the History of Philosophy 1825–6, Greek Philosophy › Empedocles (tr. Brown)
Empedocles employed friendship and enmity as principles too, and so he has six principles.
— Lectures on the History of Philosophy 1825–6, Greek Philosophy › Empedocles (tr. Brown)

Head: Leucippus
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › iii. Philosophy › β. History of Philosophy › b. Greek Philosophy › i. From Thales to Aristotle › 1. Presocratics › j. Leucippus
Gloss: The founder of atomism, who taught that the world is made of indivisible atoms moving in the void.
Hegelian gloss: Leucippus, with whom the One becomes principle as the atom, being-for-self, and the void as the negative.
Nouns: Leucippus. the Atomists, atoms and void. the founder of atomism, the full and the empty, the indivisibles.
Adjective: atomist.
Hegel definition: With Leucippus and Democritus the principles become more ideal: the atom and the nothing, or void. The one is what has being for itself, simple relation to self through negation of other-being, and so an essential thought-determination that must play its part in every logical philosophy, though not as what is ultimate. The void is the negative of the one.
Hegel texts:
Lectures on the History of Philosophy
· Greek Philosophy › Leucippus and Democritus
Hegel citations:
In Leucippus and Democritus, in contrast, we see principles that are more ideal, the atom and the nothing.
— Lectures on the History of Philosophy 1825–6, Greek Philosophy › Leucippus and Democritus (tr. Brown)
The more concrete definition of the one, of unity, or of being, is that the one is being-for-self, namely, being, or simple relation to self.
— Lectures on the History of Philosophy 1825–6, Greek Philosophy › Leucippus and Democritus (tr. Brown)
This thought-determination must play a part in every logical philosophy, as an essential moment though not as what is ultimate.
— Lectures on the History of Philosophy 1825–6, Greek Philosophy › Leucippus and Democritus (tr. Brown)

Head: Democritus
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › iii. Philosophy › β. History of Philosophy › b. Greek Philosophy › i. From Thales to Aristotle › 1. Presocratics › k. Democritus
Gloss: The philosopher of Abdera who carried atomism into an account of the senses and of the cheerful life.
Hegelian gloss: Democritus, who carries on the atomism of Leucippus, telling what is by convention, sweet and bitter, from what truly is, atoms and void.
Nouns: Democritus. the atom. Democritus of Abdera, the laughing philosopher, cheerfulness, convention and reality.
Adjective: Democritean.
Phrases: by convention sweet, by convention bitter, in reality atoms and void [Democritus].
Hegel definition: Democritus, the friend and pupil of Leucippus, is said to have elaborated his teacher's doctrine, though what belongs historically to him cannot be decided. Atomism takes the full and the empty, atom and void, as the principles of all things, what is true and has being in and for itself. As a whole the doctrine remains quite undeveloped.
Hegel texts:
Lectures on the History of Philosophy
· Greek Philosophy › Leucippus and Democritus
Hegel citations:
Democritus is said to have elaborated the teaching of Leucippus further, although it is not possible to decide what historically belongs to him in particular.
— Lectures on the History of Philosophy 1825–6, Greek Philosophy › Leucippus and Democritus (tr. Brown)
The principle is therefore that the atom and the void are what is true
— Lectures on the History of Philosophy 1825–6, Greek Philosophy › Leucippus and Democritus (tr. Brown)

Head: Anaxagoras
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › iii. Philosophy › β. History of Philosophy › b. Greek Philosophy › i. From Thales to Aristotle › 1. Presocratics › l. Anaxagoras
Gloss: The philosopher who brought philosophy to Athens and made mind the cause that orders all things.
Hegelian gloss: Anaxagoras, with whom the understanding, Nous, is first recognized as the principle, the self-determining universal.
Nouns: Anaxagoras. the seeds, homoeomeries, mind. Anaxagoras of Clazomenae, Nous, mind as the principle, the sun a fiery stone.
Adjective: Anaxagorean.
Phrases: nous orders all things [Anaxagoras]; like a sober man among random talkers [Aristotle, on Anaxagoras].
Hegel definition: With Anaxagoras the universal, objective element is for the first time said to be thought in and for itself: understanding, or Nous, is the orderer and cause of the world. Being, becoming, and the one are thoughts, nothing sensuous. The universal is defined as self-determining activity, which still has to develop itself purely on its own account.
Hegel texts:
Lectures on the History of Philosophy
· Greek Philosophy › Anaxagoras
Hegel citations:
He says that what is universal in and for itself, what is objective, is thought in and for itself.
— Lectures on the History of Philosophy 1825–6, Greek Philosophy › Anaxagoras (tr. Brown)
In Anaxagoras the universal is defined as the self-determining activity.
— Lectures on the History of Philosophy 1825–6, Greek Philosophy › Anaxagoras (tr. Brown)

Head: Socratism
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › iii. Philosophy › β. History of Philosophy › b. Greek Philosophy › i. From Thales to Aristotle › 2. Socratism
Gloss: The turn of philosophy from nature to the human being and its inner judgment.
Hegelian gloss: The turn to subjectivity: the Sophists and Socrates.
Nouns: Socratism; the turn to the subject, ethical reflection, the examined life, dialectic of question and answer, the Socratic method. the Socratic turn, the Socratic principle, the anthropological turn, the turn to man, the turn inward, the principle of subjectivity, inwardness, subjective reflection, moral consciousness, self-knowledge, self-examination, conscience, the inner oracle, the inner judge, moral philosophy, ethics, the search for definitions, the universal, the concept, conviction, insight, humanism, morality over custom, the Good as end, philosophy brought down from heaven [Cicero]. subjectivism.
Verbs: question, examine, refute. turn inward, reflect, know oneself, examine oneself, define, seek the universal, moralize, humanize, judge for oneself, call to account, interrogate, deliberate.
Adjective: Socratic, elenctic, dialectical, ethical. anthropological, humanistic, moral, reflective, inward, subjective, self-examining, introspective, conscientious, questioning, maieutic, ironic.
Adverbs: Socratically. inwardly, reflectively, ethically, morally, from within, from conviction, by self-examination, by question and answer.
Foreign: Greek: elenchos.
Phrases: the unexamined life is not worth living [Plato, Apology]; man the measure.
Hegel definition: In the second division come the Sophists, Socrates, and the Socratics, with the principle of subjectivity. Beyond the object that thought has before it there is now the thinking subject that has these thoughts. This subjectivity of thinking is an essential feature, the self-relating, determining form, and the question becomes what content the universal receives through it.
Hegel texts:
Lectures on the History of Philosophy
· Greek Philosophy › The Sophists, Socrates, and the Socratic Schools
Hegel citations:
Previously one had before oneself only objects, a content—the absolute, God. But this is not the whole of what is present here, and the second factor is the thinking subject that has these thoughts.
— Lectures on the History of Philosophy 1825–6, Greek Philosophy › The Sophists, Socrates, and the Socratic Schools (tr. Brown)

Head: Sophists
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › iii. Philosophy › β. History of Philosophy › b. Greek Philosophy › i. From Thales to Aristotle › 2. Socratism › a. Sophists
Gloss: Teachers who made thought a tool of argument and persuasion, treating the individual as the measure of all things and dissolving inherited certainties.
Hegelian gloss: The Sophists, who made thought a power of argument, dissolving everything fixed.
Nouns: Sophists; Protagoras, Gorgias, Prodicus, Hippias, Thrasymachus, rhetoric, relativism, man the measure, sophistry, paid teachers, eristic, cleverness, education in virtue. sophist, the Sophistic movement, sophistic, the Greek Enlightenment, Antiphon, Critias, Callicles, Euthydemus, Polus, rhetorician, rhetor, orator, professor of wisdom, teacher of virtue, itinerant teachers, fee-taking, oratrix†, oratress†. the art of persuasion, the art of words, eloquence, oratory, disputation, antilogic, the double arguments, argument on both sides, reasons and counter-reasons, culture, cultivation. subjectivism, scepticism, conventionalism, nature and convention, might is right, the advantage of the stronger. quibbling, speciousness, casuistry, captiousness, sophism, paralogism, fallacy, chicanery, special pleading, equivocation, moodishness†.
Verbs: argue, persuade, teach rhetoric, make the weaker argument the stronger. sophisticate, dispute, debate, wrangle, declaim, orate, harangue, convince, argue both sides, argue for and against, reason away, explain away, refine, quibble, cavil, equivocate, relativize, unsettle, dissolve, call in question, teach for pay, profess wisdom, cultivate, educate.
Adjective: sophistical, rhetorical, relativist, eristic, clever, eristical†. Protagorean, Gorgianic, specious, plausible, captious, casuistical, disputatious, argumentative, eloquent, persuasive, glib, subtle, ingenious, over-subtle, subjectivist, sceptical, conventionalist, mercenary, enlightened, cultivated.
Adverbs: sophistically. speciously, plausibly, rhetorically, persuasively, cleverly, captiously, eloquently, relatively, by convention, for a fee, on both sides.
Foreign: German: Räsonnement, Bildung; Greek: sophistēs, dissoi logoi, nomos, physis, antilogia, eristikē, aretē, paideia, deinotēs, pantōn chrēmatōn metron anthrōpos.
Phrases: man is the measure of all things [Protagoras]; making the worse appear the better cause.
Hegel definition: The Sophists were the teachers of Greece, through whom general culture came into existence. Calling themselves teachers of wisdom, they traveled from city to city, and their art was to make someone a powerful speaker, turning things around and viewing them from many sides. The bad sense of the name, as refuting or proving anything on false grounds, must be set aside.
Hegel texts:
Lectures on the History of Philosophy
· Greek Philosophy › The Sophists
Hegel citations:
The Sophists are the teachers of Greece, for through them what we call 'general culture' came into existence in Greece.
— Lectures on the History of Philosophy 1825–6, Greek Philosophy › The Sophists (tr. Brown)
He says that the art of the Sophist is that of making someone a powerful speaker
— Lectures on the History of Philosophy 1825–6, Greek Philosophy › The Sophists (tr. Brown)
We have to set this bad sense of the term aside and put it out of our minds; we must treat the position of the Sophists in Greece more precisely than that.
— Lectures on the History of Philosophy 1825–6, Greek Philosophy › The Sophists (tr. Brown)

Head: Socrates
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › iii. Philosophy › β. History of Philosophy › b. Greek Philosophy › i. From Thales to Aristotle › 2. Socratism › b. Socrates
Gloss: The thinker who made inner reflection the judge of truth and goodness, seeking through questioning the general definitions behind moral words; the turn from received custom to examined conviction.
Hegelian gloss: Socrates, whose principle is that the self must find truth by its own thinking; the good as the end.
Nouns: Socrates; the gadfly, the midwife of ideas, maieutics, Socratic irony, the hemlock, the trial, the turn to conscience and the concept. the son of Sophroniscus, the Athenian gadfly, the wisest of men, the torpedo-fish, the stingray, the martyr of philosophy, Xanthippe, the Apology, the agora, the Delphic oracle. the elenchus, cross-examination, the Socratic method, Socratic ignorance, the examined life, self-knowledge, the definition, induction, the universal, virtue as knowledge, the daemon, the inner voice, the divine sign, subjective freedom, moral reflection, inwardness, the principle of subjectivity.
Verbs: question, examine, refute, deliver ideas, drink the hemlock. interrogate, cross-examine, cross-question, catechize, elicit, draw out, define, induce, profess ignorance, dissemble ignorance, confute, convict of ignorance, sting, awaken, know oneself, obey the inner voice.
Adjective: Socratic, ironic, maieutic, elenctic. questioning, interrogative, catechetical, dialectical, self-examining, self-knowing, inductive, definitional, daemonic, dissembling, gadfly-like.
Adverbs: Socratically. ironically, maieutically, elenctically, dialectically, interrogatively, by question and answer, by cross-examination.
Foreign: Latin: nosce te ipsum; Greek: maieutikē, eirōneia, the daimonion [inner voice], elenchos, gnōthi seauton, aretē, ti esti, epagōgē; Arabic: Suqrāṭ; Korean: sanpasul [maieutic method].
Phrases: I know that I know nothing; know thyself [Delphic, taken up by Socrates]; the unexamined life is not worth living.
Hegel definition: The principle of Socrates is that human beings have to discover and learn from themselves what their vocation and final goal are, and what is true in and for itself; they must attain truth by and through themselves. It is the return of consciousness into itself, away from merely particular subjectivity. By irony and questioning he elicited consciousness of the universal, the good, the true, and the beautiful.
Hegel texts:
Lectures on the History of Philosophy
· Greek Philosophy › Socrates
Hegel citations:
The principle of Socrates is that human beings have to discover and learn [erkennen] from themselves what their vocation and final goal are, and also what the world's purpose is, what is true in and for itself; they must attain truth by and through themselves.
— Lectures on the History of Philosophy 1825–6, Greek Philosophy › Socrates (tr. Brown)
[H]e elicited from them consciousness of the universal, of what is valid in and for itself, of the good, the true, and the beautiful.
— Lectures on the History of Philosophy 1825–6, Greek Philosophy › Socrates (tr. Brown)

Head: The Socratic Schools
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › iii. Philosophy › β. History of Philosophy › b. Greek Philosophy › i. From Thales to Aristotle › 2. Socratism › c. The Socratic Schools
Gloss: The schools that each took up one side of Socrates' teaching.
Hegelian gloss: The Socratic schools, each taking up one side of Socrates.
Nouns: the Socratic schools; Megarians, Cyrenaics, Cynics, the minor Socratics. the Socratics, the lesser Socratics, the imperfect Socratics, the one-sided Socratics, the Megaric school, the Cyrenaic school, the Cynic school, the Elian-Eretrian school, Phaedo of Elis, Menedemus, disciples of Socrates, followers of Socrates, the Socratic circle, the Socratic succession, sect, school, offshoot, one-sidedness, partial Socratism.
Verbs: follow, diverge. take up, develop one-sidedly, branch off, split, part ways, found a school, inherit, appropriate, adhere.
Adjective: Socratic, sectarian. post-Socratic, one-sided, partial, minor, lesser, derivative, epigonal, divergent, schismatic.
Adverbs: after Socrates. one-sidedly, partially, severally, divergently, in the wake of Socrates, each in its own way. unilaterally.
Phrases: the children of Socrates.
Hegel definition: The Socratics are those disciples who remained relatively close to Socrates in their way of philosophizing. Leaving Plato aside, they offer only a more abstract grasp of the Socratic mode, more definite and therefore more one-sided, in a diversity of types. That conflicting philosophies issued from his teaching follows from the abstractness and indefiniteness of his principle.
Hegel texts:
Lectures on the History of Philosophy
· Greek Philosophy › The Socratic Schools
Hegel citations:
[W]e find in them only a more abstract grasp of the Socratic mode, one more definite but therefore more one-sided, and appearing in a diversity of types.
— Lectures on the History of Philosophy 1825–6, Greek Philosophy › The Socratic Schools (tr. Brown)
[I]t is inherent in the abstractness and indefiniteness of his principle itself.

Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › iii. Philosophy › β. History of Philosophy › b. Greek Philosophy › ii. Dogmatism and Skepticism › 2. Skepticism
Gloss: The philosophy that finds an equal argument against every claim and so suspends judgment, seeking peace in holding no opinion.

Skepticism is the dialectic of everything determinate, and the universal, the indeterminate, or the infinite is not exalted above the dialectic, since the universal, the indeterminate, the infinite—which stand over against the particular, the determinate, and the finite respectively—are themselves only something determinate too

— Lectures on the History of Philosophy 1825–6, Greek Philosophy › Skepticism and the New Academy (tr. Brown)

Foreign: Latin: Cartesius, res cogitans and res extensa, intuitus, deductio, naturae simplices, admiratio, leges naturae; French: tourbillon (vortex), matière subtile (subtle matter), morale par provision (provisional morality), générosité (generosity), esprits animaux (animal spirits), bête-machine (beast-machine), arbre de la philosophie (tree of philosophy).
Phrases: cogito, ergo sum [Lat.]; je pense, donc je suis [Fr.]; inutile et incertain [Pascal, Fr.]; the tree of philosophy — metaphysics the roots, physics the trunk, ethics the branches [Descartes, Fr. arbre de la philosophie]; methodical doubt.
Hegel definition: Descartes starts from the I think, which is utterly certain. Everything may be doubted, God, corporeal things, the world, except that we are; being is immediately bound up with the I. In the famous cogito ergo sum thinking and being are inseparably bound together, though they remain distinct.
Hegel texts:
Lectures on the History of Philosophy
· Modern Philosophy › René Descartes
Hegel citations:
This 'I think' is then the starting point; it is what is utterly certain
— Lectures on the History of Philosophy 1825–6, Modern Philosophy › René Descartes (tr. Brown)
This is the famous cogito ergo sum; in it thinking and being are thus inseparably bound together.
— Lectures on the History of Philosophy 1825–6, Modern Philosophy › René Descartes (tr. Brown)

Head: Spinoza
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › iii. Philosophy › β. History of Philosophy › d. Modern Philosophy › i. Rationalism › 2. Spinoza
Gloss: The thinker who overcame the split between mind and matter by making both aspects of a single infinite substance, God or nature, of which all things are passing modes.
Hegelian gloss: Spinoza, the one substance, the necessary beginning of all philosophy.
Nouns: Spinoza; the one substance, God or nature, mode, affect, affection, attribute, adequate ideas, monism, pantheism, parallelism, ratio, conatus, determinism, the Ethics, tractatus, blessedness; Spinozism, acosmism.
Verbs: unify, determine, see under the aspect of eternity.
Adjective: Spinozist, monist, pantheist, determinist.
Adverbs: under the aspect of eternity, necessarily.
Foreign: Latin: affectus, scientia intuitiva, natura naturans, natura naturata, beatitudo, imaginatio.
Phrases: Deus sive Natura, sub specie aeternitatis, amor dei intellectualis, determinatio negatio est, conatus sese conservandi [Lat]. Worship likeness and images, that is paper and ink [Spinoza], entweder Spinozismus oder keine Philosophie [Ger.] [Hegel, Lectures on the History of Philosophy]; omnis determinatio est negatio [Hegel, Lat.], der gottbetrunkene Mensch [Novalis, Ger.], le prince des philosophes [Deleuze, Fr.].
Hegel definition: For Spinoza only absolute substance truly is, the unity of thinking and being, and the particular is something altogether limited. The great merit of this way of thinking, which must be the foundation of every authentic view, is its renunciation of everything determinate for the One; what is unsatisfying is that the One is fixed and immobile, and the free subject a mere transient modification.
Hegel texts:
Lectures on the History of Philosophy
· Modern Philosophy › Benedict Spinoza
Hegel citations:
Spinoza's simple reality [das Einfache] is absolute substance; only absolute substance truly is
— Lectures on the History of Philosophy 1825–6, Modern Philosophy › Benedict Spinoza (tr. Brown)
The great merit of the Spinozist way of thinking in philosophy is its renunciation of everything determinate and particular, and its orientation solely to the One—heeding and honoring only the One, acknowledging it alone.
— Lectures on the History of Philosophy 1825–6, Modern Philosophy › Benedict Spinoza (tr. Brown)
This view [Ansicht] must be the foundation of every authentic view.
— Lectures on the History of Philosophy 1825–6, Modern Philosophy › Benedict Spinoza (tr. Brown)

Head: Leibniz
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › iii. Philosophy › β. History of Philosophy › d. Modern Philosophy › i. Rationalism › 3. Leibniz
Gloss: The thinker who answered the single substance with infinitely many self-contained centres of activity, each mirroring the whole universe and kept in step by a harmony set in advance.
Hegelian gloss: Leibniz, the monads, individuality against Spinoza's substance.
Nouns: Leibniz; monads, pre-established harmony, the best of all possible worlds, principle of sufficient reason, principle of contradiction, identity of indiscernibles, theodicy, calculus, apperception, unconscious perception. monadology.
Verbs: harmonize, justify, calculate.
Adjective: Leibnizian, monadic, optimistic.
Adverbs: harmoniously.
Foreign: German: Monadologie; French: petites perceptions [unconscious perception], monade, harmonie préétablie, meilleur des mondes possibles; Korean: danja [monad].
Phrases: the best of all possible worlds [Leibniz, mocked by Voltaire]; monads have no windows [Leibniz]; two great principles [Leibniz].
Hegel definition: Leibniz stands in glaring contradiction to Spinoza's substantial unity, in which everything determinate is transitory. Against absolute unity he makes the absolute multiplicity of individual substances his principle, though it is unified in God, the monad of monads. Monads, distinct from atoms, are utterly singular, indivisible, simply one.
Hegel texts:
Lectures on the History of Philosophy
· Modern Philosophy › Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz
Hegel citations:
Over against this principle of absolute unity Leibniz made the absolute multiplicity of individual substances his principle—although this multiplicity is unified in God, the monad of monads.
— Lectures on the History of Philosophy 1825–6, Modern Philosophy › Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz (tr. Brown)
Monads are what is utterly singular, indivisible, simply one.
— Lectures on the History of Philosophy 1825–6, Modern Philosophy › Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz (tr. Brown)

Head: Empiricism
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › iii. Philosophy › β. History of Philosophy › d. Modern Philosophy › ii. Empiricism
Gloss: Philosophy that takes experience through the senses as the source of knowledge.
Hegelian gloss: Empiricism, which takes experience as the source of knowledge.
Nouns: empiricism; British empiricism, experience as source of knowledge, ideas of sensation and reflection, induction, a posteriori knowledge, sensationalism, primary qualities, secondary qualities.
Verbs: observe, induce, derive from experience.
Adjective: empiricist, empirical, inductive, a posteriori.
Adverbs: empirically.
Foreign: Latin: tabula rasa, a posteriori.
Phrases: nihil est in intellectu quod non prius fuerit in sensu [Lat.]; nothing in the intellect that was not first in the senses; experience is the teacher.
Hegel definition: The philosophy that rests knowledge on experience, still that of the English and the French, holds that what is true, what we know, rests upon observation and its analysis according to general characteristics drawn from it. This is a metaphysical empiricism, the procedure of the ordinary sciences, opposed in method to Spinoza, who begins from definitions.
Hegel texts:
Lectures on the History of Philosophy
· Modern Philosophy › Critique and Second Period of Metaphysics: Locke, Leibniz, and Others
Hegel citations:
This is a metaphysical sort of empiricism, and it is the procedure in the ordinary sciences.
— Lectures on the History of Philosophy 1825–6, Modern Philosophy › Critique and Second Period of Metaphysics: Locke, Leibniz, and Others (tr. Brown)

Head: Locke
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › iii. Philosophy › β. History of Philosophy › d. Modern Philosophy › ii. Empiricism › 1. Locke
Gloss: The thinker who traced all ideas back to sensation and reflection and denied innate ideas; knowledge as built up from experience on a blank slate.
Hegelian gloss: Locke, who derived ideas from sensation and reflection.
Nouns: Locke; the mind as blank slate, ideas from experience, primary and secondary qualities, the Essay Concerning Human Understanding, natural rights, liberalism, the social contract.
Verbs: derive, inform, consent.
Adjective: Lockean, empiricist, liberal.
Adverbs: in the Lockean manner.
Phrases: tabula rasa [Lat.]; white paper, void of all characters [Locke], lives, liberties and estates [Locke]; the mind a blank slate; ideas of sensation and reflection.
Hegel definition: Locke's thought is that our general ideas rest upon experience. Against Spinoza, who begins from definitions, he shows how ideas such as substance, cause, and effect stem from experience; this concerns their empirical origin in consciousness. General ideas are creations of the understanding, which makes them from representations obtained from sensation and reflection by a combining activity.
Hegel texts:
Lectures on the History of Philosophy
· Modern Philosophy › John Locke
Hegel citations:
In brief, Locke's philosophical thought is that our general ideas rest upon experience
— Lectures on the History of Philosophy 1825–6, Modern Philosophy › John Locke (tr. Brown)
On the contrary, they are the creatures, the creations or inventions, of the understanding. The understanding makes them through representations that it has obtained from sensation and reflection.
— Lectures on the History of Philosophy 1825–6, Modern Philosophy › John Locke (tr. Brown)

Head: Berkeley
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › iii. Philosophy › β. History of Philosophy › d. Modern Philosophy › ii. Empiricism › 2. Berkeley
Gloss: The thinker who drew from experience the conclusion that nothing material exists apart from perception: to be is to be perceived.
Hegelian gloss: Berkeley, who held that to be is to be perceived.
Nouns: Berkeley; immaterialism, subjective idealism, to be is to be perceived, denial of matter, God as perceiver, notion, spirit.
Verbs: perceive, deny matter, idealize.
Adjective: Berkeleyan, immaterialist, idealist.
Adverbs: immaterially.
Foreign: Latin: esse est percipi.
Phrases: esse est percipi [Lat.]; language of nature [Berkeley], I refute it thus [Johnson, kicking a stone].
Hegel definition: Berkeley, who held that to be is to be perceived.
Hegel texts:
Vorlesungen über die Geschichte der Philosophie III
· Idealismus und Skeptizismus › Berkeley

Head: Hume
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › iii. Philosophy › β. History of Philosophy › d. Modern Philosophy › ii. Empiricism › 3. Hume
Gloss: The thinker who showed that experience cannot justify necessary connection, reducing cause and effect to habit and so undermining the claims of both reason and experience to certainty.
Hegelian gloss: Hume, whose skepticism showed that experience cannot ground universality and necessity.
Nouns: Hume; scepticism about causation, custom and habit, the bundle self, the is-ought gap, the problem of induction, impressions and ideas, mitigated scepticism, association of ideas, sympathy.
Verbs: doubt, attribute to custom, question.
Adjective: Humean, sceptical, naturalist.
Adverbs: Humeanly.
Phrases: reason is, and ought only to be, the slave of the passions [Hume]; commit it then to the flames [Hume], relations of ideas and matters of fact [Hume]; custom is the great guide of human life; a bundle of perceptions.
Hegel definition: Examining what is subsumed under experience, Hume found there the determination of the universal and of necessity, and drew attention consistently to the fact that if we keep to the empirical standpoint, experience is indeed the foundation of what we know but contains neither universality nor necessity. Perception gives one thing following another, not the connection of cause and effect.
Hegel texts:
Lectures on the History of Philosophy
· Modern Philosophy › David Hume
Hegel citations:
Hume consistently drew attention to the fact that when we keep to this [empirical] standpoint, then experience, outer and inner, is indeed the foundation of what we know, but the characteristics of universality and necessity are not contained or given within experience.
— Lectures on the History of Philosophy 1825–6, Modern Philosophy › David Hume (tr. Brown)
[B]ut what we perceive is only the fact that now something occurs and then something else follows upon it.
— Lectures on the History of Philosophy 1825–6, Modern Philosophy › David Hume (tr. Brown)

Head: Critical Philosophy (German Idealism)
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › iii. Philosophy › β. History of Philosophy › d. Modern Philosophy › iii. Critical Philosophy (German Idealism)
Gloss: Philosophy that begins by examining the powers and limits of reason itself, and finds in the self the source of the order of experience.
Hegelian gloss: Critical philosophy, which examines the faculty of knowledge itself, and German idealism.
Nouns: critical philosophy; German idealism, transcendental philosophy, Kant, Fichte, Schelling, the critique of reason, the Copernican revolution. criticism [Kantian], critical idealism, transcendental idealism, the critical turn, the tribunal of reason, the critique of knowledge, epistemology, post-Kantian idealism, classical German philosophy, the transcendental method, the limits of reason. transcendentalism.
Verbs: critique, ground, deduce, posit, construct. criticize, examine, delimit, legitimate, justify, synthesize.
Adjective: critical, transcendental, idealist, Kantian. criticist, post-Kantian, epistemological, reflective, subjective-idealist, a priori.
Adverbs: transcendentally. critically, reflectively.
Foreign: German: Deutscher Idealismus, Naturphilosophie, Kritizismus, Kritik, Transzendentalphilosophie.
Phrases: es ist hiemit eben so, als mit den ersten Gedanken des Copernicus bewandt [Ger.] [Kant, Critique of Pure Reason Bxvi]; the Copernican turn.
Hegel definition: The recent philosophy begins from the thesis that universality and necessity have a source other than perception, the I in its self-consciousness. Kant's philosophy is called critical because its first aim is a critique of knowing: before getting at the truth, we are to examine the instrument, to see whether it can accomplish what is required of it. Fichte, Jacobi, and Schelling follow.
Hegel texts:
Lectures on the History of Philosophy
· Modern Philosophy › Recent Philosophy: Kant, Fichte, Jacobi, Schelling
Hegel citations:
This is the principal thesis of the Kantian philosophy, which is also called critical philosophy because its first aim is to be a critique of knowing.
— Lectures on the History of Philosophy 1825–6, Modern Philosophy › Recent Philosophy: Kant, Fichte, Jacobi, Schelling (tr. Brown)
[W]e must first investigate the nature or type of the instrument in order to see whether it is capable of accomplishing what is required of it.
— Lectures on the History of Philosophy 1825–6, Modern Philosophy › Recent Philosophy: Kant, Fichte, Jacobi, Schelling (tr. Brown)

Head: Kant
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › iii. Philosophy › β. History of Philosophy › d. Modern Philosophy › iii. Critical Philosophy (German Idealism) › 1. Kant
Gloss: The thinker who turned philosophy into a critique of reason, showing that the mind supplies the forms and categories of experience, so that we know things only as they appear, never as they are in themselves.
Hegelian gloss: Kant, who found the categories in the self and declared the thing in itself unknowable.
Nouns: Kant; the critical turn that asks how knowledge is possible, the critique of pure reason, transcendental idealism, the thing in itself, phenomena and noumena, the categories, the synthetic a priori, the categorical imperative, autonomy, the sublime, transcendental aesthetic, transcendental analytic, Determining judgment, Reflective judgment, faculties, sensibility. noumenon.
Verbs: critique, limit, legislate, deduce.
Adjective: Kantian, critical, transcendental, deontological.
Adverbs: transcendentally, critically.
Foreign: German: Ding an sich [thing-in-itself], Anschauung [Intuition]; Korean: muljache [thing in itself].
Phrases: thoughts without content are empty, intuitions without concepts are blind [Kant]; sapere aude [Lat.]; the starry heavens above and the moral law within; dare to know.
Hegel definition: Kant holds that cause and effect and the other categories are intrinsically modes of conjunction, belonging to the subject, and asks how synthetic judgments a priori are possible. We do not know the thing in itself: we have determinations of feeling and categories of thought, modes of the activity of the I, so that what we know are only phenomena.
Hegel texts:
Lectures on the History of Philosophy
· Modern Philosophy › Immanuel Kant
Hegel citations:
Kant poses the philosophical question therefore in this way: How are synthetic judgments a priori possible?
— Lectures on the History of Philosophy 1825–6, Modern Philosophy › Immanuel Kant (tr. Brown)
So we do not in this way know the thing in itself; instead we have on the one hand only determinations of feeling that are connected with our organs, and on the other hand categories of thought, that is, determinate modes of the activity that I am. Thus what we know and define are only phenomena.
— Lectures on the History of Philosophy 1825–6, Modern Philosophy › Immanuel Kant (tr. Brown)

Head: Fichte
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › iii. Philosophy › β. History of Philosophy › d. Modern Philosophy › iii. Critical Philosophy (German Idealism) › 2. Fichte
Gloss: The thinker who removed the unknowable thing-in-itself and derived the whole world of experience from the activity of the self, which sets itself up and marks out its own limits.
Hegelian gloss: Fichte, who made the I the principle and removed the thing in itself.
Nouns: Fichte; the self-positing I, the I and the not-I, subjective idealism, striving, the vocation of man, intellectual intuition, productive imagination.
Verbs: posit, strive, act.
Adjective: Fichtean, subjective, activist.
Adverbs: by self-positing.
Foreign: German: das Ich, Wissenschaftslehre [science of knowledge], Tathandlung [deed-act], Anstoß [check], intellektuelle Anschauung [intellectual intuition], Produktive Einbildungskraft [productive imagination].
Phrases: the I posits itself [Fichte]; what sort of philosophy one chooses depends on what sort of person one is [Fichte]; I = I.
Hegel definition: Fichte's philosophy is a more consistent development of Kant's. It begins with the I, the transcendental unity of self-consciousness, which is what is certain. Where Kant took the categories empirically from logic, Fichte's great merit is to have called for and attempted their derivation from the I. The I is active and produces its determinations, yet remains burdened with the antithesis of the not-I.
Hegel texts:
Lectures on the History of Philosophy
· Modern Philosophy › Johann Gottlieb Fichte
Hegel citations:
[I]t should be regarded as a more consistent presentation and development of Kant's philosophy.
— Lectures on the History of Philosophy 1825–6, Modern Philosophy › Johann Gottlieb Fichte (tr. Brown)
Fichte went beyond this, and that is his great merit. He called for, and sought to complete, the derivation or construction of the categories of thought from the I
— Lectures on the History of Philosophy 1825–6, Modern Philosophy › Johann Gottlieb Fichte (tr. Brown)

Head: Schelling
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › iii. Philosophy › β. History of Philosophy › d. Modern Philosophy › iii. Critical Philosophy (German Idealism) › 3. Schelling
Gloss: The thinker who treated nature and mind as two expressions of a single underlying identity, so that nature is visible mind and mind is invisible nature.
Hegelian gloss: Schelling, the philosophy of identity, nature and spirit as one absolute.
Nouns: Schelling; philosophy of nature, the absolute as indifference of subject and object, identity philosophy, intellectual intuition, art as organ of philosophy, the late philosophy of revelation, potencies, powers.
Verbs: intuit, identify, unite.
Adjective: Schellingian, romantic, organic, intuitive.
Adverbs: intuitively.
Foreign: German: Naturphilosophie, Identitätsphilosophie, Indifferenz [nondifference], Potenzen [potencies].
Phrases: nature is visible spirit, spirit invisible nature [Schelling]; the night in which all cows are black [Hegel].
Hegel definition: Schelling begins from immediate knowing, intellectual intuition, but its content is no longer indeterminate: it is the absolute as concrete, internally self-mediating, the absolute unity or indifference of the subjective and the objective. Presupposing such an intuition makes philosophy look like an artistic talent, though by nature it can become universal, its soil being thinking.
Hegel texts:
Lectures on the History of Philosophy
· Modern Philosophy › Friedrich Wilhelm Joseph Schelling
Hegel citations:
[A]s the absolute unity of the subjective and the objective—in other words, as the absolute indifference of the subjective and the objective.
— Lectures on the History of Philosophy 1825–6, Modern Philosophy › Friedrich Wilhelm Joseph Schelling (tr. Brown)
By its very nature, however, philosophy can become universal, for its soil is thinking, the universal, and that is the very thing that makes us all human.
— Lectures on the History of Philosophy 1825–6, Modern Philosophy › Friedrich Wilhelm Joseph Schelling (tr. Brown)

Head: The Hegelian System
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › iii. Philosophy › γ. The Hegelian System
Gloss: The philosophical system that grasps the whole of reality as the self-development of reason.
Hegelian gloss: The system that grasps the absolute as spirit, in which the history of philosophy is completed.
Nouns: the Hegelian system; Hegelianism, Hegel's philosophy, absolute idealism, dialectic, speculative philosophy, the encyclopaedia, Right Hegelians, Left Hegelians, Young Hegelians, neo-Hegelianism. Hegelism, the System, panlogism, speculative idealism, objective idealism, philosophy of the absolute, the absolute system, Old Hegelians, British idealism, dialectics, triad. sublation.
Verbs: systematize, sublate, mediate, reconcile. comprehend, speculate, totalize, dialecticize, overcome, unify.
Adjective: Hegelian, dialectical, speculative, systematic, absolute. panlogical, idealist, triadic, totalizing, all-comprehending, encyclopaedic, Hegelianizing.
Adverbs: dialectically, systematically. speculatively, absolutely, triadically, in and for itself.
Phrases: what is rational is actual, and what is actual is rational [Hegel]; the true is the whole [Hegel]; the rational is actual.
Hegel definition: Hegel's system is the science of the Idea or the Absolute. Since what is concretely true is so only in unfolding itself and holding itself together in unity, that science must be a system. A system in this sense is not a philosophy resting on a restricted principle that shuts out others: it contains all particular principles within itself. Each part of philosophy is a circle closing upon itself, and the whole is a circle of circles.
Hegel texts:
The Encyclopaedia Logic
· §§14–18
Hegel citations:
Free and genuine thought is inwardly concrete; hence it is Idea, and in all its universality it is the Idea or the Absolute. The science of it is essentially a system, since what is concretely true is so only in its inward self-unfolding and in taking and holding itself together in unity, i.e., as totality.
— Encyclopedia §14 (tr. Geraets, Suchting and Harris)
It is erroneous to understand by "system" a philosophy whose principle is restricted and [kept] distinct from other principles; on the contrary, it is the principle of genuine philosophy to contain all particular principles within itself.
— Encyclopedia §14 (tr. Geraets, Suchting and Harris)

Head: Phenomenology of Spirit (1807)
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › iii. Philosophy › γ. The Hegelian System › a. Phenomenology of Spirit (1807)
Gloss: The account of the mind's journey through its forms of awareness, from bare sense-certainty to complete self-knowledge; the introduction to the system.
Hegelian gloss: The Phenomenology of Spirit, the science of the experience of consciousness, the ladder to the standpoint of science.
Nouns: Phenomenology of Spirit; the voyage of discovery, the ladder to science, the science of the experience of consciousness, the Bildungsroman of spirit, the Preface, the Jena book written as Napoleon passed, the world-soul on horseback. the Phenomenology, the way of despair, the pathway of doubt, the path of natural consciousness, the shapes of consciousness, gallery of images, the Calvary of absolute spirit, the coming-to-be of science, the first part of the system, the introduction to the system.
Verbs: ascend, educate, experience. journey, traverse, pass through, undergo, progress, climb, learn, recollect.
Adjective: phenomenological, educative, propaedeutic. introductory, preparatory, experiential, formative, developmental, initiatory, pedagogic.
Adverbs: step by step. by stages, stage by stage, shape by shape, by degrees, experientially, progressively.
Foreign: German: Vorrede; Korean: Jeongsinhyeonsanghak [Phenomenology of Spirit].
Phrases: the world-soul on horseback [Hegel on Napoleon]; the true is the bacchanalian revel [Hegel]; the highway of despair; the substance as subject.
Hegel definition: The Phenomenology of Spirit of 1807, announced as the first part of the system of science, presents the coming-to-be of science, or of knowing. It leads consciousness from immediate, sensuous certainty along a long path to the element of science, supplying the individual with the ladder to that standpoint. The dialectical movement consciousness practises on itself, out of which each new object arises, is experience, so that the work is a science of the experience of consciousness.
Hegel texts:
The Phenomenology of Spirit
· ¶¶1–808
Hegel citations:
This coming-to-be of science itself, or, of knowing, is what is presented in this phenomenology of spirit as the first part of the system of science.
— The Phenomenology of Spirit ¶27 (tr. Pinkard)
Conversely, the individual has the right to demand that science provide him at least with the ladder to reach this standpoint.
— The Phenomenology of Spirit ¶26 (tr. Pinkard)
This dialectical movement which consciousness practices in its own self (as well as in its knowing and in its object), insofar as, for consciousness, the new, true object arises out of this movement, is properly what is called experience.
— The Phenomenology of Spirit ¶86 (tr. Pinkard)

Head: Science of Logic
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › iii. Philosophy › γ. The Hegelian System › b. Science of Logic
Gloss: The study of the basic concepts of thought in their necessary development.
Hegelian gloss: The Science of Logic, the pure thought determinations, the idea in the element of thinking.
Nouns: Science of Logic; the Greater Logic, logic as metaphysics, the exposition of God before the creation, the realm of shadows, Being, Essence, Concept, objective and subjective logic. the Logic, the Nuremberg Logic, the Doctrine of Being, the Doctrine of Essence, the Doctrine of the Concept, system of pure reason, science of pure thought, pure science, kingdom of pure thought, the truth without veil. thought-determinations.
Verbs: unfold, develop, determine. deduce, derive, think through, categorize, mediate.
Adjective: logical, ontological, categorial, systematic. speculative, dialectical, presuppositionless, immanent, pure.
Adverbs: logically. dialectically, speculatively, immanently, categorially, in pure thought.
Foreign: German: Reich der Schatten.
Phrases: the presentation of God as he is in his eternal essence before the creation of nature and a finite spirit [Hegel].
Hegel definition: The Science of Logic is Hegel's exposition of pure thought, whose introduction declares that no science needs more to begin with the matter itself, without preliminary reflections. Its subject matter and method are not given in advance but generated in the course of the work, and what precedes it can only make its standpoint more intuitable. To study it, to dwell and labour in this realm of shadows, the world of simple essentialities freed from all sensuous concretion, is the absolute discipline of consciousness.
Hegel texts:
The Science of Logic
· Introduction
Hegel citations:
In no science is the need to begin with the fact [Sache] itself, without preliminary reflections, felt more strongly than in the science of logic.
— The Science of Logic, Introduction (tr. di Giovanni)
To study this science, to dwell and to labor in this realm of shadows, is the absolute culture and discipline of consciousness.
— The Science of Logic, Introduction (tr. di Giovanni)

Head: Encyclopaedia of the Philosophical Sciences
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › iii. Philosophy › γ. The Hegelian System › c. Encyclopaedia of the Philosophical Sciences
Gloss: The outline of the whole system in its three parts.
Hegelian gloss: The Encyclopaedia, the whole system as a circle of circles: logic, nature and spirit.
Nouns: Encyclopaedia of the Philosophical Sciences; the Encyclopaedia, the system in outline, the circle of sciences, compendium, the lectures. epitome, conspectus, synopsis, digest, abstract, précis, abridgment, handbook, manual, textbook, syllabus, summa, the Heidelberg Encyclopaedia, the Berlin Encyclopaedia, the system as a whole. encyclopaedism, systematicity.
Verbs: outline, summarize, encompass. epitomize, abridge, condense, compass, embrace, comprise, survey.
Adjective: encyclopaedic, systematic, comprehensive. synoptic, compendious, summary, all-embracing, all-inclusive, cyclopaedic, circular.
Adverbs: in outline, encyclopaedically. synoptically, compendiously, summarily, in compendium, in brief, as a whole.
Foreign: German: the Zusätze [additions].
Phrases: a circle of circles [Hegel]; the whole of the system.
Hegel definition: The Encyclopaedia presents philosophy in outline, restricted to the beginnings and fundamental concepts of the particular sciences. Unlike an ordinary encyclopaedia, which is an aggregate of sciences taken up contingently and brought into an external order, it treats the whole of philosophy as one science that may also be considered as made up of several. Each part is a whole that leads beyond itself, so that the whole is a circle of circles.
Hegel texts:
The Encyclopaedia Logic
· §§1–18
Hegel citations:
Each of the parts of philosophy is a philosophical whole, a circle that closes upon itself; but in each of them the philosophical Idea is in a particular determinacy or element. Every single circle also breaks through the restriction of its element as well, precisely because it is inwardly [the] totality, and it grounds a further sphere.
— Encyclopedia §15 (tr. Geraets, Suchting and Harris)
The whole presents itself therefore as a circle of circles, each of which is a necessary moment, so that the system of its peculiar elements constitutes the whole Idea—which equally appears in each single one of them.
— Encyclopedia §15 (tr. Geraets, Suchting and Harris)
As an Encyclopaedia, science is not presented in the detailed development of its particularisation; instead, it has to be restricted to the beginnings and the fundamental concepts of the particular sciences.
— Encyclopedia §16 (tr. Geraets, Suchting and Harris)

Head: Logic (一)
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › iii. Philosophy › γ. The Hegelian System › c. Encyclopaedia of the Philosophical Sciences › i. Logic (一)
Gloss: The first part of the system: pure thought, studied in itself.
Hegelian gloss: The logical idea, the science of the idea in and for itself.
Nouns: logic; the first part, the science of the pure idea, Lesser Logic, the idea in and for itself. the Encyclopaedia Logic, the Shorter Logic, science of thought, pure thought, realm of pure thought, the categories, system of thought-determinations, doctrine of being, doctrine of essence, doctrine of the concept. logicality.
Verbs: think, determine, unfold. reason, conceive, categorize, develop, derive.
Adjective: logical, ideal, pure. categorial, abstract, speculative, dialectical, noetic.
Adverbs: in pure thought. logically, abstractly, in the abstract, in the element of thought.
Foreign: German: kleine Logik.
Phrases: the science of the idea in and for itself [Hegel].
Hegel definition: Logic, the first part of the Encyclopaedia, is the science of the pure Idea, the Idea in the abstract element of thinking. Its thinking is not merely formal: it is the self-developing totality of determinations and laws that thought gives to itself. Logic is the hardest science, since it deals with pure abstractions and demands practice in moving within pure thought, and could also be called the easiest, since its content is our own thinking and its most familiar determinations.
Hegel texts:
The Encyclopaedia Logic
· §§19–244
Hegel citations:
The Logic is the science of the pure Idea, that is, of the Idea in the abstract element of thinking.
— Encyclopedia §19 (tr. Geraets, Suchting and Harris)
The Logic is the most difficult science, inasmuch as it has to do, not with [sensible] intuitions nor even, like geometry, with abstract sense-representations, but with pure abstractions, and inasmuch as it requires a trained ability at withdrawing into pure thought, holding onto it and moving within it.
— Encyclopedia §19 (tr. Geraets, Suchting and Harris)

Head: Nature (二)
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › iii. Philosophy › γ. The Hegelian System › c. Encyclopaedia of the Philosophical Sciences › ii. Nature (二)
Gloss: The second part of the system: thought in the form of outward, material existence.
Hegelian gloss: The philosophy of nature, the science of the idea in its otherness.
Nouns: nature; the second part, philosophy of nature, the idea in its otherness. realm of nature, externality, self-externality, the idea outside itself, the material world, the physical world, creation, mechanics, physics, organics, petrified intelligence [Schelling].
Verbs: externalize, appear, manifest. go outside itself, alienate itself, materialize, embody, fall away from itself.
Adjective: natural, external. material, physical, corporeal, outward, self-external, spatiotemporal.
Adverbs: in nature. outwardly, externally, materially, in space and time.
Foreign: German: Naturphilosophie, Außersichsein.
Phrases: the idea in the form of otherness [Hegel].
Hegel definition: The philosophy of nature is a thinking consideration of nature, the idea in the form of otherness, which seeks the universal in forces, laws and genera and grasps it in its own immanent necessity, presupposing empirical physics. Since externality is nature's specific character, nature shows necessity and contingency rather than freedom. It proceeds through mechanics, physics and organics.
Hegel texts:
The Philosophy of Nature
· §§245–376
Hegel citations:
Not only must philosophy be in agreement with our empirical knowledge of Nature, but the origin and formation of the Philosophy of Nature presupposes and is conditioned by empirical physics.
— Encyclopedia §246, Remark (tr. Miller)
Consequently, Nature exhibits no freedom in its existence, but only necessity and contingency.
— Encyclopedia §248 (tr. Miller)

Head: Spirit (三)
Path: 三. Spirit › 3. Absolute Spirit › iii. Philosophy › γ. The Hegelian System › c. Encyclopaedia of the Philosophical Sciences › iii. Spirit (三)
Gloss: The third part of the system: mind, in which thought returns to itself and closes the circle that leads back to the beginning.
Hegelian gloss: The philosophy of spirit, the science of the idea that returns into itself from its otherness.
Nouns: spirit; the third part, philosophy of spirit, the idea returned to itself, mind, soul, culture. philosophy of mind, realm of spirit, self-knowing reason, the idea in and for itself, subjective spirit, objective spirit, absolute spirit, self-consciousness, freedom, return into self, the closing of the circle. pneumatology.
Verbs: return, know, free oneself. come to itself, return into itself, comprehend itself, recollect, close the circle.
Adjective: spiritual, mental, free. self-conscious, self-knowing, self-returning, intellectual, noetic, pneumatic.
Adverbs: spiritually, in and for itself. mentally, self-consciously, for itself, freely.
Foreign: German: Philosophie des Geistes.
Phrases: the idea that has returned to itself out of its otherness [Hegel]; spirit knows itself.
Hegel definition: The philosophy of spirit is the third part of the Encyclopaedia, the science of the idea that returns into itself from its otherness in nature. It treats spirit as subjective, objective and absolute. Its knowledge is the most concrete and therefore the highest and most difficult, answering the command to know oneself, understood as knowledge of what is genuinely human, since all activity of spirit is an apprehension of itself.
Hegel texts:
The Philosophy of Mind
· §§377–577
Hegel citations:
The knowledge of mind is the most concrete knowledge, and thus the highest and most difficult.
— Encyclopedia §377 (tr. Wallace and Miller, rev. Inwood)
All activity of the mind is, therefore, only an apprehension of itself, and the aim of all genuine science is just this, that mind shall recognize itself in everything in heaven and on earth.
— Encyclopedia §377, Addition (tr. Wallace and Miller, rev. Inwood)
